I... I just can't. This is the epitome of stealth games. Any other game, whether a different franchise, or even sequels with better graphics, can't hold a candle to Chaos Theory. It has the most realistic feel of any action/thriller game I've ever played. You are given minimal help throughout the mission. There are certain moments in games when you get lost, have no idea what you're doing, etc. Splinter Cell: Chaos Theory is the embodiment of that feeling. This game is legendary. Also, the graphics are not half bad. I can run maximum settings with my Inspiron 660 with an AMD Radeon 7770.
The AI's are pretty phenomenal. It's hard not to get immersed in the world of Chaos Theory right off the bat. I once chose to spare a guard because he was talking about what a pathetic paycheck he gets, and how he'll never be able to afford motion sensor lights. It's very impressive how well this game can both absorb you and excite you--all with minimal blood and gore.
This is a game about making decisions, critical thinking, and strategy. Approaching a guard silently from behind, hoping he won't turn around, moments like that make your heart explode. It's amazing how well the game makes you absorb that true stealth badass identity. You can feel yourself in Fisher's every movement. The way he draws his knife as approaching an enemy, his clever interrogation dialogue; all of these contribute to his hard-core character.
SC:CT will not dissapoint. Some might take one glance at it and say, "Oh, 2005. Not for me." This is one of my favorite games, and just keeps climbing up the list. Dry, self-aware wit, stellar lighting, and interesting plot make Chaos Theory what it is today. $10 for a legend.

It’s interesting playing Hard Reset Redux after playing Shadow Warrior (2013). I can clearly see the beginnings of SE’s combat system and the enhancements to it in the Redux edition only highlight what they had started. It’s not the most polished FPS system I’ve ever experienced and the newly added Katana is situational at best. But you can see how they started with Hard Reset, created Shadow Warrior based on what they started and then took what they learned from SE and made HRR an even better game. HRR isn’t a perfect game because of it, but it’s so cool to see a developer learning and improving over time and watch it reflected in their continuing releases. It’s not even like the Cyber Katana even feels out of place! Though a lot of the enemies have a tendency to explode so getting close is a risky venture at best. It’s a visually unique FPS even if the fidelity is a bit lacking. Enemies are colorful and distinctive enough so as to avoid melting into each other. The city is a constantly dreary cyberpunk city that doesn’t forget that it can use color and vistas to make some impressive visuals.
Cutscenes in this game use a stylized graphic novel look with voice over to piece together the various different events happening in the game. I’m never certain if I like this look but I’ll admit that I’ll take it over a badly CGI-ed scene or in-game cutscene that doesn’t look good. The acting is b-grade sci-fi quality. It’s good enough to be believable but some performances weren’t the best, mostly in the side-characters. As for the combat itself, it isn’t too bad. It gets a bit repetitive and I maybe would have liked to see more variety in enemy types towards the end of the game. They tended to just add more in crazier combinations which is fine, it just wasn’t as interesting to fight. I know there was some complaints about the game being too short but I frankly found the length to be just fine all things considered. There’s even some pretty interesting boss fights that don’t outstay their welcome.
As for my thoughts on the game as a whole. I think it’s a very solid shooter. The two weapon platform system where each uses different ammo while being able to transform into four weapons is…odd. I can’t say I like or dislike it though. It’s a style choice clearly aimed at making the game more cyberpunk, but some annoyances crop up when you want a specific weapon from each platform and you’re unable to get to them in one click. The ability to upgrade them into four different modes with their own significant upgrades helps keep the combat interesting as well. There’s a few unique gun ideas that work. I think the game is pretty reasonably paced and has a decent amount of content for its asking price.
Hard Reset Redux is a first person linear shooter that has arena/corridor combat with quite a few enemies. Most enemies just require you to hit any part of them while others have armor that has to be shot off before they can be downed. HRR’s combat is based on two gun platforms: the CLN Modular Assault Rifle and the EEF-21 Plasma Rifle. The assault rifle dishes out ranged damage with bullets and can be modified to do more damage, faster. It can be upgraded to a shotgun, RPG and sniper rifle variant on the platform. The plasma rifle unleashes electric based shots that at first operates like an assault rifle but can be upgrades for close range electrical attacks, slowing fields and shoot-through-wall shots. Upgrades are acquired by collecting enough credits by defeating enemies or collecting caches throughout the level. Exploring the levels and finding secrets will give you access to bonus credits though running the game straightforward will give you access to many of the upgrades normally. I actually like this system because most upgrades substantially improve and/or change the guns in a meaningful way. Both weapons look rather cool in the Cyberpunkness. The assault rifle even glows bright red after a barrage of shots are fired. It’s the little details that can make the difference. In HRR, there’s no regenerating health so you’re going to have to rely on health and shield pickups that fall off enemies or can be found all over the levels. However, avoiding enemy attacks are easier to deal with thanks to the newly added dash. The third weapon, the Cyber Katana, can’t be upgraded and doesn’t have any special powers attached to it. Though the dashing ability at least allows you to use it effectively.
The combat is about doing a lot of dashing, keeping an eye on what attack larger robots are about to execute and keeping your distance from enemies that want to give you a (charging/explosive) hug. Littered throughout the levels are environmental hazards that the player can use to take out a swarm of robots. Including but not limited to exploding electrical traps, oil barrels, A/C units and more. The environments aren’t destructible though so don’t expect to blow up a bunch of gas cans and create a new path. The environmental hazards at least help to change up the combat and require you to keep an eye on your surroundings because those hazards can hurt you as well. Outside of some fatigue with it towards the end of the game and the Katana’s questionable usefulness, HRR’s combat system is quite good.
Hard Reset Redux is an overall fun game and competently crafted FPS. The story isn’t really that memorable though I believe they really tried to make it so. The combat is pretty good overall and certainly Redux has improved it to be a lot more enjoyable. The dashing, the optional Katana and better enemy placement doubtless made this a more painless experience than the original doubtless was. The amount of content is very reasonable and there’s a pretty good amount of exploration on these linear levels to keep things interesting. I think it’s worth getting. Even if there isn’t one specific reason as to why I like it. If you need a cyberpunk shooter, I think Hard Reset Redux is worth getting. If you don’t like the changes from the Redux edition, they give you the original Hard Reset at no extra cost. I always like it when developers do that.

Great game and charming. Ive been playing since it was on nexon and was heartbroken when it closed down. However now that it is back and no longer held back by the fat greedy hands of nexon it is better than before. Things to note about this game is that some form of grind still exists like in any other F2P MMO.
However it is one of the most fair MMOS for free players there are out there. Id compare it to warframe in terms of fairness since you can acquire cash items with in game currency. Ive only spent about 10 dollars since the release of this game a year ago and do plan to spend more later on to support this wonderful game.
It constantly updates every 2 weeks and there is ALWAYS an event going on! Things id warn new players is that the game does limit how much you can play a day with FP (Fatigue Points) but there ways to regain them with buyable pots to refill the bar or making a new character since they dont share FP. Another thing is the grind since you will be grinding mostly for endgame gear rather than leveling up. The current level cap is 86 but the challenge comes from acquiring gear for endgame content. Another thing is the RNG this game can have with certain things, from epics ( the best gear in the game), cash items, sometimes events.
Regardless of these negative points the game more than makes up for it with the loyal community and incredible developers. Neople are the parent company of the game and they host a stream every 2 weeks as well and are in contact with the DFOG community often. They tend to listen to feedback and answers questions.
Overall id rate this game in comparison to other MMO's a 8/10
and would totally recommend to new and old players alike.
An important part of an MMO is how fair it can be and much you can access as a free player and this one is one of the most fair ones ive played.

Not technically a god game, more zen-like puzzle involving planets and 'terraforming' at a low poly level.
Start off by naming a solar system, each has 5 moons circling a sun. Objective is to fill worlds by placing coloured tiles containing different biomes. New tiles are discovered by highlighting in the correct order and completion of each level comes from maxing out specific groups. Progress further and planets change from rounded objects to more complex shapes and order of tiles becomes much more difficult as well. Colours flash rather then stay lit so it turns into a game of  concentration/memory.
Runs on unity, screen resolutions of 4k+ are supported and controls were all mouse driven. Not sure how many planets Awe contains but for some casual puzzling with a relaxing soundtrack it's hard to go wrong for the price. Cheers.

Hard Reset Redux review:
Played the original Hard Reset. It was fun but I got a lot of fps drops and after a long time playing I got motion sickness.
Hard Reset Redux doesn't have any fps drops and I didn't get motion sickness. The dash move is an excellent addition. In the original the player took a lot of damage from attacks that couldn't be dodged. Now every attack is dodgeable. If you enjoyed the original Hard Reset I would recommend this. At 85% discount it's definitely worth it.
Original Hard Reset Review:
Hard Reset is a FPS game set in a cyberpunk world. The story is pathetic and I skipped the cut scenes. Thats ok, because this is a great (Mostly old school) FPS. The movement is fast and the enemies agressive. Unfortuneatly the dev's stumbled a bit in that department. The fell for the old trap of thinking more enemies = old school. The enemies also have a lot of unavoidable attacks. The level design is average, but it has a few cool moments and lots of secrets. When this first came out, I really wanted to like it.  Heck, when it first came out, I DID like it.  I'm going to go straight to my pros and cons.
PROS:
1) Classic Puzzle Quest gameplay - If you have enjoyed any of the other PQ games, the gameplay is back.  You get 3 characters on your team, who provide 1-3 abilities each.  It's still fun and addicting.  This is not my problem with the game at all.
2) Big cast - There are 33 characters and counting in this game.  Each brings something new to the table.  Sure, several of the characters are different versions of the another character (there are 3 different Wolverines), but they usually play differently enough that you won't mind.
CONS:
1) Poorly timed updates - In a game like this, nerfs are a fact of life.  But nerfing a character in the middle of an event that focuses on that character is a jerk move.  Especially now that they are introducing...
2) Tournaments with entrance fees - This might not be so bad if it had been there from the start, but as a new feature, it feels like the wrong direction for the game.  To make matters worse, you can't find out the available characters for use in the  tournament until AFTER paying the costs.
3) Rising costs - There are several neat features that were introduced as crutches to help players with weaker rosters, like Shields to protect against attacks in PVP and Boosts (extra starting energy or damage) to give yourself an extra edge.  These started off being available at a decent price, but then skyrocketed without warning after everyone came to depend on them.
4) Speed-run - I don't know about you, but I like to play games at my own pace, and you can in this game... for the Prologue.  After that, each chapter is available for a limited time and disappears at the end of that time.  I completely missed Chapter 1 because of this and if you are starting now, it might be too late for you to see Chapter 2 as well.  This is made worse by the fact that some of the fights in these chapters have opponents with levels over 200 (your characters are capped at 141 until you manage to level the very rarest characters) and the fact that some levels are UNPLAYABLE unless you have a specific character in your roster!  Missing part of the story because you couldn't get a 4* Invisible Woman (the rarest character) is unacceptable.
5) Slow leveling - When I started playing, this was my biggest complaint, but I adapted to it.  I would have still recommended this if it were the only problem.  However, it is still a problem you should be aware of.  Characters require THREE forms of leveling.  First, you need covers acquire or level up your skills.  Second, there is a very rare form of currency called Hero Points that can replace the need for covers, but you will likely need it for other purposes, because it is very rare unless you pay to buy more of it with real currency.  Third, you need ISO, which is the experience of the game.  At first, you'll think you are getting a ton of it, because low level characters can get a level after a fight or two.  Once your characters start to get mid-level, you will need to win ~20 fights to level a single character by one level.  With 30+ characters that have a max level anywhere from 50 to 230, you will need a LOT of ISO and even buying it with cash won't help because it is crazy expensive.
SUMMARY
I love the gameplay and being able to play with Marvel superheroes.  I was willing to cope with the slow leveling until the developers started making a ton of poor decisions that favored those who are insanely high-leveled or spending cash.  I want to love this game, and if it had been released as a Single-Player game like all of the others, I probably would.  But the way it is, I just can't.
This is a fun little MtG game, but the main thing it needs is a 'concede' button.  It would eliminate rage-quitting and mean you don't need to grind through unwinnable games in the story matches.

This game is fun, and is likely the best Duels of the Plansewalkers game I've played, BUT:
As other reviewers have mentioned there is a still lot of work to be done. Some core MTG mechanics are different than the physical game, and there are a lot of bugs. I'm not going to reiterate these, just scroll through the reviews.
The thing that is truely bothersome is the lack of draft play. The way the game is set up now makes it hard for new players to play online without hours and hours of grinding for cards (or paying lots of money for 6-card booster packs) to catch up with people who have been playing for  a year or more. The game could clearly become a REMARKABLE Magic Draft game though.
I go into my thoughts on how a draft feature should be implemented below, while still giving the devs a solid cash flow.
_______________________________________________________
Keeping in mind a retail booster pack costs ~$4, the draft could be set up such that:
A player pays $8 to participate in a draft. Drafts would only be available bi-weekly. The draft would have 8 players, and would first prioritize connecting with invited friends, then fill in any remaining slots with Random Online Players or AI.
Once the lobby has been set up, the draft is setup just like in real life - each player gets 3 booster packs of 15 cards, players pick one card and pass the rest of the booster around the table, etc. As Duels games have been incredibly lame for making non-randomized boosters in the past, these boosters would need to be randomized - eg, any card in the set should be a possibilty! It should be just like opening real life boosters in a draft!
Once the draft is done, the lobby is disconnected and players can create their draft deck. The player would be able to use this draft deck for 2 weeks, in a mode called Draft VS.  However, if a player wants to keep the cards he drafted and add them to his collection for use in constructed games, the player could pay another $4 to add the cards to his collection. Once the cards are added to his collection, they can be used in constructed modes forever. However, after the two week period, or whenever the next bi-weekly draft cycle starts, (regardless of whether the player is going to participate in a draft or not) the cards obtained in the prior draft would not be usable in Draft VS anymore.
Draft VS is a mode where players can play against Friends or Online Players Draft Decks. - Only Draft Decks would be usauble here - It should include 1v1 and 2-Headed Giant.
If the devs fixed the issues other reviewers have mentioned, and added the draft feature, it would be an INCREDIBLY good title - and a moneymaker.

Luckily got the game for free but it was honestly the most painful, broken, unoptimized game I've ever played in my life.
Campaign:
*Flawed with Bugs and glitches that will make the game unable to progress (E.G, Connor or Rhinna getting stuck and leaving the player unable to progress).
*Some parts of the campaign are borderline impossible on Guerella difficulty (E.G. The run from the Church to the Helicopter on mission 5).
*Enemies will pull completely unfair and unexpected kills against you by spawning behind you, shooting you through solid cover or even spamming grenades.
*Bullet spread on some weapons are ridiculous in both Campaign and Multiplayer (Seriously, use a SCAR-H LMG for a 2 second burst)
*Sound design is borderline non-existant (Character's speech not in sync with model or sometimes not even what the subtitles portray them to be saying)
Multiplayer:
*The most lag free servers in EU are 100 Ping at least which causes absurd gameplay.
*Server list is somehow laggier than the game itself, which is saying alot.
*Half the servers are fake.
*Most Admin owned servers have rules that are ridiculous (Pistol/Knife only, No Vehicles, Grenades = Ban, what is this? Battlefield 4?).
*The amount of servers availble at any time are extremely limited.
*Map Exploits plentiful and abused on almost every match.
*Hackers common and unstopable.
*Hit Registration worse than Ubisoft's.
Optimization/Quality:
*Even for a game of it's time, the game's quality will leave you wondering if your graphics card died.
*Frames per Second Drops (Screen Freezes) are frequent and annoying.
*Crashes even occur on the most optimized of PCs.
*Running in Fullscreen mode will cause the fullscreen to be displayed at the size of a standard windowed mode on next startup.
*Airborne controls for aircraft sometimes not responding to commands to raise or lower altitude at all.
Overall, the game feels like it simply tried to copy all the mechanics of a Call of Duty game and failed to even do that. The storyline had potential but in all honesty, I cannot reccomend this game unless you're an achievement hunter looking to boost your achievement counter or you got this game for free like I did on Humbe Bundle.
Sorry Kaos Studios, I would give this game a rating but in all honesty, to even give a Participation Sticker reading "You tried" is stretching the credit I can give for this game.
And to all of you who actually spent money on this game and gone through the experiences I did? You have my condolences.

So after around 4 years returning to this game , back from the PS3 version I will say
that the PC version thrives , I picked it up on the Free Humble Bundle after forgetting about this great game
but seeing the sequel on offer that I have been meaning to get, and at a great price may I add, I oculdn't resist it felt like i was getting The sequel and all the dlc for free because for £13 I really wouldn't mind paying that price for this game,
-Lets get into it shall we.
Right so I like the story, but it's too much in the sense of typicall patriotism , and what I mean by that is , one single man has the rest of the divided scattered resistance on his shoulders , the game portrays it that way to give you a major feel in your role to give you the sense of importance, but it's a heavy take on the Call of Duty way of things. Regardless still fun to play the campaign and feel some emotion through parts of the game I.e the Napalm incident.
The Multiplayer, while the console servers were shut down a long time ago , thankfuly the PC servers are still up, and progressing again feels like a breath of fresh air, It has that great mix of Call of Duty and Battlefield Multiplayer to it that , needs ot be experienced , Homefront was one of the first games to bring it a scorestreak CoD like system that's called Battlepoints, cap objectives, get kills, assists , count towards two support options that can be called in or equipped.
The Guns feel Balenced and good and unique for every situation , The ACR feels nice with a good DPS  but with a trade off for higher recoil, whereas the M4 has a high rate of fire with a less damage output, the SMG sometimes can feel underpowered with the close to Mid ranges , the M249 feels sluggish but can be worked with if you put on a scope, where as the SCAR LMG feels just right , like a LMG / Assault Rifle hybrid which in a sense that's what it is. I've always been dissapointed with the lasck of a few secondary firearms always using the good ol' M9 spam trigger finger gets a little dull , I would rather had liked to have seen a TT Tokarev like repoduction for the KPA and a P250 for the US. but non the less the Guns feel okay if you can get past a few minor hiccups.

My advise:  Buy it on sale.  $15 or under would be OK.
To the devs:  Game is good but too expensive for what it is - I wish the missions were more varied.  I wish you could really ramp up the difficulty and the AI was an actual competitior. Alright, lets get down to it.
As a die hard Civ fan, I was anxiously waiting up until release; where I started getting some mixed feelings. (Note that I have nearly 200 hours played, all of which are offline.)
So, whats good about this game?
- A fresh, but familiar feel.
- A large graphic overhaul from the previous, Civ.
- A very impressive Tech. Tree.
- The true introduction of a "Third Party". Aliens>Barbarians.
- The initial depth of the game is very impressive. Where as Civ. V didn't really pick up until the release of Brave New World.
- A much more relevant, and sophisticated espionage system.
- Finally, it runs near the effeciency of Civ. V. Key word here is, "near".
The not so good:
- Religion is now a thing of the past. This has basically removed a fairly large layer of the game.
- Technology at and around the early phase is dreadfully slow.
- The story is relatively boring. There's no real immersion, I don't lose track of time, and suddenly find myself playing 3 hours later.
- The maps. This is a doozy. It feels like they just took the Civ V design, and then took a colour pallet and just re-painted it. There are no real texture changes. Just colours. It just looks, boring?
All in all, the game meets my expectations. It's hard to come up with another Civ. game after the arguably best Civ game from the franchise. However, I believe Fraxis has the potential to make this game better. Which alone, is enough for me to recommend it to any strategy game player out there.

I would usually recommend this game, but due to borderline game breaking bugs I think it may be best to hold off buying entirely (unless the devs fix the bugs) unless you're really into the experience. I bought it on sale, so I got out my money's worth even with the bugs.
Good:
* very atmospheric game: the good strories, music and art style play into this
* the game play (assuming it would be bug free) is generally decent
* runs pretty well on my machine
Bad:
* once you've figured out the game mechanics, it becomes more boring farily quickly. I think it could benefit from heavier randomization, in particular the zones themselves and where to find loot in them. Some zones have two variants, but it still feels very moot
* the controls are clunky at times (i.e. in combat when multiple targets at the same point it becomes hard to target someone, and generally unresponsive, in the base you sometimes select characters you don't really want to)
* and the bugs...
Bugs (spoilers):
* It appears characters can just die by freezing just a day before you win, the bug has been acknowledged by the devs afaik
* sometimes characters will just disappear permanently (not talking about suicide or sending them away, they just disappear without any kind of notifcation or anything. Apprently related to accepting missions)
* people get upset over "stealing" items that don't belong to anyone anymore (i.e. killed people) or containainers turn into "steal" from "take" for no reason (not very immersive either)
* enemy AI is exploitable (I've had them in places climb a ladder, get shot upstairs, fall down and repeat the entire process; or just shooting them from above with similar results, ai just sitting there waiting to get shot)
Considering the goal is to keep your survivor group together and alive, loosing someone over a bug is a no go. In particular if you consider this has rouge-like savegames, loosing someone 8-10 hours into a savegame that doesn't have any restore point because of a bug I consider game-breaking. Adding in the wonky controls it can make for a rather frustrating experience.
If you still want it for the style and experience, I'd at the very least recommend getting it on a sale. I don't really think the full price (about 20€ at the time of writing) is justified for the current quality and content.

I am a veteran player and I have logged thousands of hours before DFO Global was released on Steam.
As a big fan of fighting games, hack and slash, and brawlers, DFO manages to scratch an itch that no other game can reach.
This game combines extremely tight fighting game mechanics with MMO ideas, and lots of pop culture references to achieve a new kind of depth that no other game can truly replicate. There has been many attempts, but those "clones" fell quickly under their own lack of polish, updates, or from the weak foundation supporting their mechanics. DFO's mechanics work because they are being re-examined and re-adjusted since its Korean release in 2004.
DFO has also remained near the top of the list of Korea's most popular online games
(
, and still floats amongst juggernauts such as Overwatch and League of Legends.
I've written
that attempts to cover the mechanics of the game as well as providing resources for new players, and it also explains the history of DFO (along with the "dark ages" from when the game was mismanaged by Nexon America).
For those who experienced the horrors of Nexon America, consider giving this game another chance. Neople is a separate entity to Nexon America, and they have literally changed the game's storyline to depict two separate universes where you visit the old one to find that it's being consumed by a mysterious cancer.
Neople has shouldered the heavy burden of cleaning up the mess left behind by Nexon America, and have proven to us that they truly care about their game and their fans (they also stream and interact with the community, directly implementing our feedback into the game and addressing our concerns).
And for those who enjoy beat-em-ups/brawlers, this is a new type of brawler with a diverse pool of classes such that everyone will find a character whose playstyle they will truly enjoy.
Just don't pick blind because it's a 2.4% chance of finding your ideal class.

This is a nice game of resource management and taking chances. Although it is mostly skill that gets you through combative encounters, enough can go wrong with little mistake on your part to cause severe problems for you (such as a good character who is severely injured or killed).
There's enough meat to this game for you to want to read about the other characters and try to figure out which ones make for the best teams.
The save system is a bit brutal as it auto saves. So it's hard to run through the game correcting small mistakes with reloading. Instead, your small mistakes become game-long woes that you have to add to your list of problems you have to overcome.
There's also some strategy in the way you trade resources. For example, there's a vendor that sometimes shows up at your house and he is excellent to buy bulky but inexpensive construction materials from so you can save your scavenging inventory space for better things.
There is some variation in the levels you get and how they are initially set up. Some areas have guards placed in slightly different arrangements so that in one playthrough getting all the loot at some outpost is much easier than in another playthrough, but it is slight and not all zones have it (and typically they just have an either or setup and it isn't elabourate). It's a shame they didn't make more use of that mechanic.
One big con I had was, SPOILER ALERT, no bad guys ever came to your door. You would think since you're in the middle of a war that the invading army might show up at your place and like extort food or something from you or you'd have to fight in your own home to defend it or whatever. Kind of a shame since it would be cool to have the ability to plan out and build your defenses.
The game isn't very long and there's not a whole heck of a lot of replay to this game even though that seems odd considering it's a rogue like. But there's just a lot of boilerplate crap you need to get through in the beginning of a new game and things don't really heat up until quite a bit later...and then it's just one little mistake and you screw up your entire game and it autosaves and you throw your hands up and quit.
That's actually a pretty bad thing about the game. I mean, the sound and artwork is great for its theme. I'm so happy that this isn't about zombies even though it literally perfectly fits for that theme. I would love to see more skills and mechanics put into the game  and more interesting levels with more complicated puzzles or plots or character interactions bartering etc.
The somewhat variable time limit of the game is nice to keep things balanced, but it would be nice if I could just continue playing in a sandboxy mode or something. I don't know. I guess what I'm saying is I wish there was more...which usually means the game is worth a thumbs up, despite it's problems.

Chaos Theory is the 3rd in the critically acclaimed Splinter Cell series which is based on Tom Clancy's series of novels with the similar name. This is an 8 year old game that actually aged quite well: some of the levels look quite good and the game utilises the lighting and shadow effects superbly.
You play as Sam Fisher, member of a secret US black ops team, and are dispatched to various locations in order to find evidence, defuse a bomb, eliminate a terrorist, capture someone alive, etc. Although the game is linear, throughout the missions you are given secondary and opportunity objectives, therefore, the game tries to lengthen the singleplayer experience as much as possible. At the end of each level you are given a rating in accordance with the number of objectives you completed. In addition to this, the game counts whether or not you killed someone - this, in fact, lowers your score so it's best to focus on the stealth approach, otherwise achieving 100% is impossible. While making sure you are not seen by anybody or any cameras you can also knock your enemies out and hide the bodies.
I like how varied the environment is: Sam can use a lot of objects, can climb a lot of things and can hang from a lot of places. There are also minigames in each level: you can do a lot of lockpicking, hacking and before knocking out or killing someone it's worth interrogating them to get some more intel for your objective. These interrogations can be funny due to the well-written script.
It is unfortunate that coop and multiplayer are not played anymore, so, if this is on sale, make sure you grab it but only for the singleplayer experience.

After having been patched, Hard Reset Redux looks as good or even better than the original game, but most importantly it runs at higher FPS and it plays better! I was skeptical at first to the addition of a dash move and laser sword. Well, the sword is pretty much useless since you already have two awesome guns by the time you get it. They added some cannon fodder zombie enemies to the game, useful if you want to try the sword, but they don't appear that often. The dash move however, is great. The original game had pretty sluggish player movement and a lot of situations where it was hard to dodge charging enemies or projectiles, but now with the dash move this is much easier and it feels more fun to be so mobile. It works the same as in Shadow Warrior, if you've played that. Thanks to the dash move the game is much easier than the original, but there's always Insane or Heroic mode if you feel it's not challenging enough.
If you haven't play the game before, get this version. If own the original and wouldn't mind replaying what is largely the same game, get this version, it's worth it with the 85% off discount!

In retrospect, my favorite part of Far Cry 2 was rattling through the countryside, riding POV in the driver's seat of a decaying European-built 2-door saloon. Handling maps with my in-game hands and exploring sans HUD added a great level of immersion, and when the engine began to wear down, I'd pop the hood and make repairs.
Jalopy is the next step forward along that road. When you'd rather not get shot at by African mercenaries, you can instead take a leisurely drive across the last gasps of the Soviet Union, buying and selling wine and cigarettes to finance your road trip. Manipulating the controls in first person is fiddly but immersive, and I really felt the sense of making a long journey. When the weather is nice, you can reach across the Laika's dingy cabin, wind down the manual windows, and switch on some soothing late-eighties europop as you and your faithful car enjoy the day.
Jalopy is in early access and is a little buggy, but the creator is responsive and helpful, and appreciates receiving bug reports.
This is the road trip simulator I never knew I wanted, and I look forward to seeing how it develops.
PS: Always have a jerry can in your trunk. I ran out of petrol in the parking lot of a gas station and couldn't fill up my Laika from the pump five yards away.

Hard Reset Redux is a remake that somehow is perfect for anyone who hated the original.
Hard Reset should have been a sure fire success. Beautiful neon blue cyberpunktropolis world design, hordes of robots to blast, designed at a "below-AAA" level so it might just be fun...
But it really wasn't. Tanky enemies, unsatisfying shooting, boring levels, a goofy upgrade system... it ran through the Painkiller/Serious Sam motions without the joy of those games.
Then the devs went on to make the new Shadow Warrior, beautiful sakura pink Nihonland world design, hordes of demons to blast, below AAA level... Fun, right?
Again, no. It added a cool sword and a great dodge but kept literally every problem from Hard Reset, only with less interesting weapons and even TANKIER enemies.
So having made the same game twice, the devs go back and make the first one again. Only now, it's fun.
To be honest, they only needed to do one thing to make the game fun: make the enemies less tanky. And they did. And it's a fun ride now. Also added, supposedly fancier graphics (The original was no slouch in the graphics department, and the changes, if any, are difficult to notice. I have not done side-by-side comparisons*.), SW's dodge move, a cyber katana, also from SW, and load times that don't make you want to kill yourself.
And yet all these simple changes make HR Redux a far superior game, not quite Doom level, but certainly worth your time. Sure, it's easier, but HR was not hard in a clever way. It's easy to make a game harder than Doom. It's hard as nails to make a game as good as Doom.
Also the story does an EXCELLENT job of convincing gamers why they should skip cutscenes in shooting games. Who the hell writes all this stupid, lifeless, pretentious crap that relates nothing to the gameplay?
It's got a campaign of decent length, survival modes, and it comes with the original version if you wanted to try it as a period piece. Give it a shot.
* EDIT: Commenter Decline has, reporting the following:
"After playing the redux more and going back to the original I have to say that the lighting is far better [in the Redux], the AA is terrible (only fxaa) and the textures are nowhere near as sharp. If I could have the sharpness of the original with the lighting of the redux, I would be happy."

The game had some serious issues at the launch, but now all of these issues were fixed and just some minor issues remain, which will hopefully patched in the future.
I can recommend this game to anyone who wants to play a complex, and high demanding card game without such crap as random effects. In this regard Magic is still the king of all card games which exists out there. Magic duels adapts the basic rules perfectly 1:1.
If you are Magic player by yourself and you want every single card in this game plus all game formats, then you will be probably dissappointed, still, there are over 600 cards in this game which is pretty much in my opinion, and the quantity is still growing from time to time. Every new Magic Set is getting it's own expansion in Magic Duels.
The best thing about this game is that it's totally free. The microtransactions are one of the fairest I've ever seen in a videogame. There are no limited cards for which you have to pay. One packs costs either real- or ingame money (gold).
You get for every daily Quests between 40 to 120 Gold. One pack with 6 cards costs 150 gold. Plus you become 30 Gold for every win against another player. If you win your first match on a new day you become 15 Gold extra, this is a huge amount plus there are community quests every week. Not to mention that there are a singeplayer campaign and tutorials quests which give ALSO gold. All in all that makes a huge sum.
Basically if you enjoy playing this game, you can open on average 2 packs with 6 cards every day.
If you have the maximum amount of one card. It gets out of the pool of cards which you can pull, instead you get a card which you can use. That's a clever system, so you get always something useful out of your boosters.
In comparison games like Hearthstone let you open on average 1 pack all 3 days with only 5 cards where you get often always the same crap. And that for quests which forces you to win up to 5 times. (by magic the maximum is 2 times)
I really like how fair the game treats me as a player, even  if don't buy any cards. I have always a good feel of progession and even some of the default cards are really powerful. I really like this game so much that I spent a bit real game money, just to show my appreciation to this underrated game here on steam. Something I've never done before on games like Hearthstone or something else.
In comparison free2play games like hearthstone aren't nearly as generous with their reward system, although they have a much greater player base.
I hope that Review gave you a good overview, this game don't deserve such low ranking here on steam.

Right so I've played this game for quite some time and it's a faily enjoyable timesink. I've been told it's like puzzle quest, only you have multiple people on your team so you can choose who to take hits from and there are more tactics to it.
There is a pay-to-win strategy in that you can spend all your money to get tokens to buy powerful heroes (or villains) and have them on your team. The most powerful ones are the most expensive ones, obviously, with the biggest level cap. You can sell old cards you don't want as you have a limited roster of heroes to have and a limit of 3 in each battle.
Beyond that, if you've played puzzle quest or any matching game you've got the idea of the game play to get at least 3 in a row, but here different characters deal different damage. For example, my group has Storm, Hawkeye and Iron Man. Iron Man deals the most damage with red so when they're matched he attacks and is open to attacks. Black ones Storm is most powerful at so she ends up in the firing line. they all have abilities based on colours you collect so there's also the tactic of wanting a really powerful ability to activate, but you can't use it unless you have X amount of this coloured jewel. For example, Iron Man's best power is Ultra Feron Beam which, at the moment, requires 19 Blue. 19 is a huge number, but with it he deals a huge amount of damage (which one-shots most villains by the time I get the amount) and even if it doesn't defeat them, it stuns them for 1 turn. Some abilities are direct attacks, stuns, destroys tiles, transforms tiles so depending on who's in your group, you can string together a large amount of abilities and combos to win the game.
I only play this at a time sink for when I want to hear background commentary on a game or movie and it works well for that. Also every day if you win a combat you get given a special daily reward which can be anything from hero points (also attained in game) to hero cards. You also  will want to re-play many battles as there are alternate rewards where you can have the chance to win 1 out of 4 choices, but only a chance which forces a grind, but a enjoyable grind.

Grid 2 truly is an excellent racing game. Firstly, it is very well optimised, running smoothly whilst still looking pretty good even on my crappy laptop. Handling strikes a nice balance between sim and arcade. It's easy enough to get the hang of but rewards those who are more skillful particularly on braking and turn in. The different handling models feel distinct and from my multiplayer experience there isn't one with a severe advantage over the other.  I also think the seperation of single and multiplayer works in the game's favour since moving from one to the other feels fresher than in other games (though some shared progress would have been appreciated). The multiplayer is the stronger of the two but the single player  does have some very good qualities. The game does a great job at creating a convincing scenario for the campaign to take place in and the first half in particular is a lot of fun. However, I found the last season of WSR to drag on a bit due to some tracks being used considerably more than others (if you prefer street circuits you won't have as big an issue with this) though event variety helped aleviate this. Also the car balancing within the classes was questionable at times and in Tier 3 I experienced one event where I felt I could only win in the Caterham/Ariel Atom group though keep in mind  this may have been down to me prefering a grip based driving style. Multiplayer is where you should spent most of your time as the playlist setup for online events is simple and easy to get addicted to. The learning curve was not as steep as I expected thanks to a decent starting car selection which I see being used by more experienced players quite regularly.
As for the lack of cockpit view. Its not a sim game. There's a hood cam. It does the job. Use that and have some fun.

This game is a unique blend of big-picture simulation and puzzle like supply chain management that I think anyone who likes sim or puzzle games should look into. I definitely recommend it on sale to a fan of either genre.  Otherwise, it is more of a niche game than I thought it would be, which makes it tough for me to recommend to the average gamer.  I followed this game since the first dev vlogs came out, then bought it in the beta phase, and for me there was just enough that the game did well that made it worth me supporting it before release.
:
+ Supply Chain Management Tycoon: This is something unique that it does very well regarding drug creation/production. If you're not into Sim and Puzzle type games, then think twice before buying the game.
+ Scenario Variety and Customization: Dozens of scenarios of varying difficulties with the ability to create your own.
+ AI / Competition: I didn't find competing companies to be unrealistically hard or easy. With 3+ competitors, innovation to different drug types are imperative.
+ Macro management (other than supply chain): Dev explicitly stated that the game wasn't designed for micro managing a pharmacy company. Big picture management is done well though with plenty of Research & Development opportunities, and it doesn't bog you down with price management or small stuff.
+ Subtle ethical decisions: Some people wanted to be hit over the head with this, but again, it seemed secondary in the eyes of the dev. The decisions currently come in the form of...Do I leave this side effect or weak cure as is because my profit will be higher? Do I stop production on a drug that is still in demand just to move on to higher level cures with larger profits? Do I "research" corporate espionage in order to see my competitors' profit margins, etc?
:
-Incentiveize the game play loop: There's 3 completion levels for each scenario indicating how well the player did, but that, scenario uniqueness, or making a specific type of drug (e.g. hair growing male enhancement drug) seems about it for replay motivation.
-Starting drug RNG (may be fixed): I've read about a number of players restarting scenarios until their initial unlocked drug combo was ideal. This may be more of a player min/maxing issue, and I think a patch meant to address this, but I don't know how well this helped.
-Micro management (by design): As mentioned above, the game wasn't designed for that, and this may bug some people. Just supply chain and big picture stuff is what is mostly in this game.

GRID Autosport has been one of my favorite racing games for a pretty long while now. That being said, I don't recommend this faulty software for anything over $15.
There are countless instances of saved games being corrupted irrecoverably. My first save profile was suddenly corrupted, making it useless. All of my time spent on my profile, all of the cars that I've worked months and months to buy, since you can only get a new garage slot after leveling up. This gets to be a MAJOR grind, especially when you've done it before.
After I started the game up, I found my latest profile, which was even more accomplished than my previous corrupted one to be corrupted.
I shouldn't need to back up the very hard to locate save file every time I start the game. This has made be very disappointed, because GRID Autosport's gameplay (multiplayer in particular) is rather fun and has kept me interested for many many many hours. Hours that gone now for good.
Codemasters, the publisher of the game did promise a fix for the save corruption back in November 2014. It doesn't work.
Here's my bottom line advice: If you want the game, don't buy it on steam. You might want a refund at some point. Steam doesn't even answer help tickets anymore, and would never give a refund for what I perceive to be a DEAL-BREAKING defective product. I definitely wish I could get a refund, as I play games expecting them to not remove 900 hours of playing put in.
If I was to play GRID Autosport again, I have no cars, no money to buy cars, not enough garage slots for even 5 cars. It would take me a long time of playing to get back to where I was, and here is what it comes down to: it's not worth the time. The game isn't good enough to be allowed to steal my time.
I don't recommend this game due to a major defect that has persisted for years now. Fixes were promised, never delivered.
On the other hand, if you find the game on sale, and you're not too serious about racing, it's a fun game that is twice as expensive at it should be allowed to be.

I like the more diverse technology web. You get to chose what ability many buildings will have the first time you build them creating many more possibilities for how you develope. The aliens (native species) seem to like you when you're not attacking them but they will still occasionally attack even when they do. They go blue, yellow, then red when they get angree which is quite different than the Civ V barbarian tribes that just plain hate you.
The spy network is another interesting game development. Being able to steal reasources from oponents without them knowing is helpful. The trade network is also a good addition to the game. With each trade route you can see the potential exchange of goods you will receive, and if you check not to renew the route, you can see what new offers are on the table when the route is complete.
I think the city view should have a toggle for showing the man power placement. Those people icons make it difficult to see the resources that each tile produces. Perhaps making the people icons small like the resource icons would help. Knowing what resources are made on each tile is useful for placing satelites. In orbital view, the tiles should also be lit up with their resource production icons. This might be an option I haven't looked for during the one day trial though.
All in all, those reviews that say Civ V is better probably come from people who aren't willing to accept technologies and concepts beyond what has actually happened here on earth. They want to live in the past. I like the creativity that went into this version of the game.

I have a love/hate relationship with Codemasters. The DIRT series has been fantastic, but it was hijacked by DLC and Ken Block. GRID was...well, lets not even begin to discuss why GRID 2 was pathetic. GRID (1) was an amazing game, and if you loved that, then i'm certain that when you play this, you will get a nice fuzzy feeling, reminding you of the joy that you had playing the original grid. As you can see, i have not played Autosport for very long, but i already feel like i can tell you that Codemasters have done well to go back to what made GRID so special.
If you're looking for a new TOCA, then this game won't deliver for you - i think that those days are gone for codemasters. With their DLC policy, and their habit of spewing out new F1 games all the time, it's clear that the financial team have had a bit of a deathgrip on the devs who just want to make amazing games with endless content.
I know this isn't shaping up to be much of a 'review' of the game, but i hope that this helps to give you an idea of what to expect when buying Autosport. The gameplay is very nice - I use a G27, and the game has plenty of support for wheels. One thing i would suggest is, before you play, get all of your settings in order. For some reason, when i started, there was a 20% deadzone on my steering, clutch, accelerator and brakes which is pretty stupid. Physics are, (so far) perfectly fine, and the AI is much better than i expected it to be. All of my experiences with Codemasters games have had great AI, so it was surprising to me that so many people said how it was 'too aggressive' or 'blind' - In my personal (brief) experience, i have found the AI to be challenging, and rough, but that's how you're supposed to drive! I had a lot of fun battling for positions in an experience very much unlike iracing, gran turismo, forza and raceroom. It's a breath of fresh air playing a game that lets you be a bit crazy at the wheel!
The career mode is good, but not as fun as the original GRID. There is a similar leveling up system, but it is a little bit impersonal when compared with the experience that you had in GRID 1. There is no garage on the main menu, and most of the game is very 'clinical', getting you straight into the racing.
I have only had  a short time with this game, and i'm excited to play more. I feel that, if codemasters decides to make a new GRID, without terrible, terrible DLC, it will be at the level that the sequel to GRID1 should've been

I would usually recommend this game, but due to borderline game breaking bugs I think it may be best to hold off buying entirely (unless the devs fix the bugs) unless you're really into the experience. I bought it on sale, so I got out my money's worth even with the bugs.
Good:
* very atmospheric game: the good strories, music and art style play into this
* the game play (assuming it would be bug free) is generally decent
* runs pretty well on my machine
Bad:
* once you've figured out the game mechanics, it becomes more boring farily quickly. I think it could benefit from heavier randomization, in particular the zones themselves and where to find loot in them. Some zones have two variants, but it still feels very moot
* the controls are clunky at times (i.e. in combat when multiple targets at the same point it becomes hard to target someone, and generally unresponsive, in the base you sometimes select characters you don't really want to)
* and the bugs...
Bugs (spoilers):
* It appears characters can just die by freezing just a day before you win, the bug has been acknowledged by the devs afaik
* sometimes characters will just disappear permanently (not talking about suicide or sending them away, they just disappear without any kind of notifcation or anything. Apprently related to accepting missions)
* people get upset over "stealing" items that don't belong to anyone anymore (i.e. killed people) or containainers turn into "steal" from "take" for no reason (not very immersive either)
* enemy AI is exploitable (I've had them in places climb a ladder, get shot upstairs, fall down and repeat the entire process; or just shooting them from above with similar results, ai just sitting there waiting to get shot)
Considering the goal is to keep your survivor group together and alive, loosing someone over a bug is a no go. In particular if you consider this has rouge-like savegames, loosing someone 8-10 hours into a savegame that doesn't have any restore point because of a bug I consider game-breaking. Adding in the wonky controls it can make for a rather frustrating experience.
If you still want it for the style and experience, I'd at the very least recommend getting it on a sale. I don't really think the full price (about 20€ at the time of writing) is justified for the current quality and content.

this is a great puzzle game, very simple concept really well excecuted with plenty of content: 127 levels on 7 different boards, plus 4 boards generated every day once you unlock daily levels. it can take a while, but thankfully you don't need to complete every level on a board to unlock the next, and once you gain access to one, you can play all the levels there in any order. otherwise most players (including me) would be stuck on the circle board or level 1 (ONE!) of the double diamond board for a long time. the latter looks pretty easy until you realize it's the trickiest one of them all, at least on that board (nothing beats circle 14).
the presentation is also worth mentioning. it's colorful and has plenty of settings, unlike most minimalistic puzzle games that tend to take minimalism really seriously and offer no customization whatsoever. there are volume sliders, resolution options, windowed mode, various music tracks, background options, statistics (moves, levels completed, dailies completed, game time), and my favorite: speed settings, plural, because you can customize separately how fast you want pegs to move and the level complete animation to play. really nice. displaying level numbers would be something to consider adding, but there's a level select screen and you can move between levels while playing, so it's not a huge deal, though exactly because of the latter it'd be useful to know where you are on the board.
levels start out easy, then get a lot more challenging, as I mentioned, but it's a really fun game and should be in every puzzle gamer's library. at the price of a single euro/dollar I'd recommend it even if it had half as many levels and no dailies, but as it is, it's an even better value for money, and I'd also like to mention 'customer support' as a positive, very helpful developer, worth supporting what he does.

I love this game.
Currently, this is a very simple early alpha game. There is very little gameplay depth, a lack of finish on just about everything, and FPS issues regardless of hardware. There are also countless bugs or unexplained shenanigans. But I've loved every moment of the over 10,000 kilometres I've driven my Laika.
This game's store page does not reveal the full story. It's a trading economy game in which you utterly rely on your car, the Laika. Basically you buy and sell goods: You can earn money in a few different ways.
The first way to earn money is fraud - at the local motel in each town, knock on the doors and (sometimes) collect the nightly fees of other occupants.
The second way to earn money is theft - finding crates of goods while you drive from town to town. A percentage of these crates are locked, and you must have a crowbar to pry them open.
The final way to earn money is to buy goods at local stores that you hope to sell later for a profit in towns which demand these goods more.
The spending goal of earning this money? Upgrading your Laika, of course!
I would bet you didn't expect this to be an economics game. Don't worry, the driving itself is well thought out too. There is just enough variance in scenery and paths that you are kept on your toes, and the car is not easy to drive when run-down. Searching for crates while trying to drive a car with 3 flat tires is a real challenge, especially in Bulgaria.
I don't want to spoil any details of locations for you, as the exploration is enjoyable too. I've found what differs between locations to be cuturally and geographically accurate, at least in a simplistic way.
The car's radio can play maybe 4 songs on repeat, which are all thematically perfect and relaxing to listen to. Hoping for more, similar songs on this radio in the future!
I feel the lack of a sprint function in this game is very suitable for this relaxed theme, and makes utter reliance on your Laika essential - as it should be.
Finally, I'd like to share my most recent experience with the game as a sample of the mid/endgame. I was driving the return route from Bulgaria to Yugoslavia, gradually ascending the mountains then rocketing down the other side. As it was the return route, The border checkpoint would be at the end. My goal was to transport at least 1 of each local brand of coffee back with me, until I found a place to sell it for great profit. I had stopped a few times to replace puntured tyres and pick up good from crates, so as the sun set I was still about 160km out from my goal. The going can be especially tough in Bulgaria, so careening downhill in the wet with a heavy-loaded car and minimal visibility became a real challenge. The thrill I didn't expect from this game kicked in.
When I finally reached the border checkpoint, I was told that coffee was a banned import in Yugoslavia. Since I was transporting 52 bags of coffee, the fine would be $520. That was far more than I could afford, and far more than the worth of the coffee. It was also an issue I wouldn't have had if the border had been right next to the town, as it is in normal-direction travel.
The guards told me to return to the town, since I couldn't afford the fine. However, I will simply save and quit, and attempt the run again from the Bulgarian town (the good prohibited is selected randomly).
I hope you find such a great experience from Jalopy as I have! Of course, it will continue to update - but I trust this developer to continue to know what a fun game is.

A neat "puzzle" and problem-solving game.   Sure, you could cure a big disease and get paid handsomely for it too... the problem is that you'll cure your customer base.  Wouldn't it be better to have return customers by alleviating their condition without curing it?  You'll make a bit less per pill, but since it won't cure them, they'll have to purchase it every month.
Now that you've seen the light, how do you produce this pill with your current factory?  Oh, that machine costs too much to run - let's make a slightly weaker version of the pill by using a different machine. Sure, the pill isn't as effective as before, but you make $20 more ...
See how this goes?
I'd recommend this game for anyone who enjoys a good business sim.  The financial decisions are tougher than the "puzzle" decisions, so though I'd still recommend the game for problem-solver types, I think they'd have to enjoy business games too, whereas business game fans don't necessarily need to enjoy puzzles.

Out of all of these characters, the only ones I liked where Boone (dont get attached to him, just saying) and Reina, Connor is your basic badass ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ soldier and Hopper is the doubtful mechanic of the bunch.
The gameplay, while solid, has flaws in itself, especially during one mission that lets you pick out guns from a storage locker, which includes Silencers <-- *pay attention* but the objective that comes next not only involves you going loud (defeating the purpose), you also *THROW AWAY YOUR GUN IN A DUMPSTER*. it's just poor execution and makes me wonder: "why did you even give me the option for silenced weapons in the first place?"
There are also 61 collectibles. 61, there's only 7 missions, try to figure that out.
And about the multiplayer: its basically Modern Warfare 2 but in the worst way people imagined: Killstreaks arent worth anything because of the amount of BP you start with ALLOWS you to use them anyway, which includes vehicles. but hey, atleast you dont have to worry about grenade launchers, because who needs that when you can have a Apache shoved down your throat when you start the game? :D
Overall opinion: get this game on a heavy sale or free even, but dont put a 20 down on this one.

This is incredibly compulsive for all the apparent simplicity of its appearance.  The creator of the very good puzzler Knights has managed again to take a simple board concept and create puzzling of the highest calibre.  The difficulty does not seem too great for the first 50 levels but it is pleasing in how it shapes your perspective of the game.  Then it does start to get really hard in places to the point where you laugh at your own naivety in thinking the whole game was going to be that easy.  By that point it is too late - you are hooked.
I prefer to write reviews once I have virtually completed a game but this is far from the case here - I just wanted to express my appreciation for the job the creator has done and I am really looking to whatever he makes next, if Knights and this game are anything to go by.
Highly recommended.

Splinter Cell Chaos Theory is a stealth-action game taking place after the previous game, Splinter Cell Pandora Tomorrow (which is not on Steam, sadly). This is the best game in the Splinter Cell franchise, and the best stealth game in general, in my opinion. One of my favorite things about this game is the fact that there are multiple ways to go about getting past a certain obstacle. Plenty of gadgets, the ability to whistle at enemies, tampering with the lights, sneaking up behind enemies and forcing information out of them--all of this is the definition of an amazingly crafted stealth game. Also, being able to go through the game not killing anyone is an option. The story on the other hand is not amazing, but still enough to keep you interested in what's goin on. This game is fantastic, and anyone looking for a stealth focused experience should definitely buy this game.

This War of Mine...a game that will change your aspects about war.
This game is not your ordinary "war game" that's about shooting and awesome battles...no...it is about the POV of the "affected ones" or the civilian.
Have you ever thought of being in a war? Have you ever thought of surviving through a war? This is a question that the game answers.
This game is a game that will place yourself in a situation that everybody does not want in. That feeling of being in a war is quite horrific and terrifying in a sense that you wont know when you'll get shot by a sniper or a soldier or even by your fellow countrymen.
This game is basically about a group of survivors that is trying to survive in a war. You will make decisions that will either be good or bad for your group. Survival is the key in this game.
Barter and trade with the populace in some areas in the city. Steal and be sneaky to get the things that your group needs. Kill or be killed. Sometimes the game will place you in situations where you kill a person and reflect on what you did. Is it good or bad? Well...these decisions are yours to answer of course.
Through my first few hours, I already felt those emotions raining down on me. There were times where I almost lost one member in the group, but good thing that member survived.
I truly give this game my seal of approval and a score of 10/10. It has good gameplay and truly...it is a masterpiece. This War of Mine...I game that will go in my memories until the day I die.

A lot of people have some strange kinks when it comes to games. Maybe you like immersive inspect animations, Maybe you like when a SPAS-12 is portrayed with it's stock unfolded. Maybe you like the sight of old school guns in a modern setting (Like an Springfield rifle or a Luger.)
My thing personally is, for all intents and purposes, MMOs that have the one class who's traits begin and end with "I have a gun". Not even some fancy♥♥♥♥♥ancient weapon that channels magic or anything, but who just a f*cking glock or beretta.
There's something hilarious about having a bunch of classes that are all "I have this ancient weapon that channels the blood of my enemies into attack power!" or "I wield a mighty staff using an elite set of masterful skills!"... And there is one class who boils down to "Hi. I have a gun. It shoots bullets. Now♥♥♥♥♥♥off"
Dungeon Fighter Online has the best damn implementation of a "Guns" class I've ever seen in a MMORPG.
The Gunner in this game is the most amazing♥♥♥♥♥♥I've played with in a long time. For one, you actually have a multitude of primary weapons to unlock, from pistols to revolvers to crossbows to experimental handcannons, the works.
Next are the skills and abilities. Now, something to know is that most MMORPGs with a "gun" class don't really take the opportunity to go nuts with the whole "You can shoot guns" thing. You either have a rifle, a pistol, or dual pistols.
DFO, on other hand, says "♥♥♥♥ it who wants to blow♥♥♥♥♥♥up"
An entire catagory of skills is dedicated to allowing you to use bigger and better guns, from miniguns to flamethrowers to laser cannons,  etc.
Hell, one of the skills is a melee attack in which you knee someone with the force to send them flying into the air, at which point you pull out another minigun and light them up before they fall down. That♥♥♥♥♥♥never gets old.
And once you get to choose your extra sub-class (or whatever it's called), pick Destroyer. Holy hell, that is like the gates of ♥♥♥♥ing heaven opening up to give your sorry♥♥♥♥♥some weapons capable of nuclear warfare.
Launcher (and subsequently, the Destroyer) allows you to use heat-seeking rocket launchers, satallite lasers, black hole launchers, and a grand finishing move involving you going nuts with a death ray and deep frying the entire room.
Are massive ♥♥♥♥ing guns not part of your Gun class ideals? Well fear not, cause there are 3 other sub-classes to pick, and they are fun in their own rights as well.
The Ranger allows you to pull off amazing and fancy kick and somersault moves, alongside pistol tricks and augments. You basically become a magical John Woo with the amount of Gun-fu♥♥♥♥♥♥you can pull off.
Mechanic can build all sorts of robots, sentry guns, walking explosives, and other such allies to help with combat. Some of the end game abilities include a giant robot god tearing a hole in the fabric of space time and punching into the room. Yes, you read that right.

The game is far from being perfect by any means. There's plently of bugs scattered about, 2 headed giant connectivty probelsm or so I'm told, some issues with hackers/griefers online, and a few odd crashes. However if you look past all that and give it a chance you'll find a pretty solid free to play Magic the Gathering game.
It does a very good job of explaining the basics of the game that any new player to Magic should have no trouble figruing out what they're doing. It contains a nice amount of tutorials that range from basic how to play to giving a quick look as to how the new mechanics work. And the best part of these tutorials? You actually get in game currency for playing through them, giving even more encouragement for newer players to go through them.
At time of writing the game just recieved an update that brought two new sets to the game bringing the total number of card sets to 4 and a starter box. It should be noted the 4 sets are not full complete sets but rather 75% or so of the set they are based off of. Supposed they had to keep you playing MTGO or paper somehow. But despite the sets not being the complete sets and limit of how many of each card you can have by rarity,there are still dozens of potenetial decks that can be built and in the very least perform decently aganist the AI.
In regards to obatining cards and where the free to play aspect comes in is that cards must be gotten via packs from the in game store. Each pack cost 150 coins the in game currency. Now this is where I feel the f2p aspect was done very well. Of course you can just buy coins for money and unlock every card in the game instantly if you so chose, but if you don't take that path or are unable well don't worry. This game is easily the most generous I've seen a f2p game be with in game currency. Every week see a community goal for roughly 60 coins, and everyday you receive a fairly easy to complete quest that rewards 60-100 coins. You can hold up to three quest at a time and you're allowed to reroll a quest once day making it fairly easy to have 300 coins worth of quests at a given time. AI matches reward 5-15 coin dependant on difficulty, online play gives 20 coins a win and a 30 coin bonus for first win of the day. There is also story mode and the forementioned tutorials that reward coins for first time completion. A dedicated player can easy get 3-4 packs a day if they grind out the daily coin cap and do the daily quest, and even more casual players are likely to find it easy to get at least 1 pack a day.
The only other thing of note is the story mdoe mentioned above. Magic's story has been fairly stechy and not on the forefront and used to be primarly told from novels found in fat packs once upon a time ago. The story mode here isn't much to write home about. The story is mostly told in a paragraph or so before and after any battle in story mode and everynow and again a very questionable cutscene. The story is mostly just a summary to begin with those inertested int he story however will find much more at the actual Magic the Gathering website. The story it's self is rather simple and gives you a preconstructed deck that changes as you progress much like the old duels of the planeswalkers games. The main appeal to the story each chapter rewards enough coin to buy 1 pack from the shop, with the very first story rewards 7 packs worth of coins for those just starting the game.
So in closing it stands as a pretty fair f2p game that doesn't make you feel forced to dump money to do anything. The game certainly has flaws without doubt but still stands as a solid and much cheaper alternative to MTGO or paper, not to mention the interface is far more appealing than MTGO's. So don't let the negativity around the game scare you away, it's not as bad as many people claim it to be. Besides it's a free download that's around a gig and a half so worst case scenrio you don't like it and uninstall it.

If I had more than 2 hours to try it out, I would have given it more time. However, a game SHOULD be able to grab you within the first 2 hours and I have to say that this one leaves a TERRIBLE first impression.
This is coming from someone who only had time to mess around in single player (since multiplayer was buggy and lagged)
First, as it is with a lot of open world games these days, the world it painfully empty. Right out of the gate, you're thrown into the world with nothing but your clothes and hands. That's not a bad thing, but there is literally nothing to do besides collect any plant you find for the first 10-20 minutes and pray you don't get yourself lodged between a rock and a tree (like I did multiple times), which will make single player literally unplayable since you can't get free and logging out then back in doesnt work either.
There's no immediate sense of a goal or challenge to overcome, unless you count the confusion and boredom of picking up plants and finds random things to craft or level as an obstacle to overcome. In the distance I could see mountains with a large temple-like statue, but to my dismay it looked to be part of the skybox. I don't know that for sure, but other than those mountains and two other notable landmarks, there's not much else to look forward to.
The combat is promising, but nowhere near functionable. If you don't out-level the enemy, good luck trying to kill it. Every enemy I came across was strong, but not in the good way. They are faster than you and hit harder than you, so the only way to really get them off your butt is to leap into the water. I would normally try to fight and dodge them, but -- while YOU have attack animations and cooldowns -- THEY do not have much that stops them from just wailing on you over and over. All the ai has to do is get near you and they instantly do damage, whether you attempt to dodge or not.
Close combat is out of the question unless you, I guess, grind out some heavy gear or are twice their level. Don't get me wrong, I enjoy grinding, but there HAS to be some substance or else it gets dull and painful very fast.
I value the appearence of my character more than anything in an rpg, so as you can imagine, the character creation♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off. Seriously... FOUR hairstyles??? I'm the kind of person that will play through missions and quests and progress because I'm excited to see what kind of armor or clothes I'll find or make next! But here, there's none of that. "Oh yay... another basic cloak. Oh but it's BLUE this time... I guess."
Not every wizard has to wear a long bland dress and wear a funny hat, you know. Ditch the "realism" when it comes to outfits please. It's boring and not very creative.
I couldn't get to the flying parts, which is what I came here for, because I was hitting the two hour limit and unfortunately, MOST of those two hours was navigating the graphics menu and loading screens!!
Even with the graphics all the way down (making the game look like a Unity asset flip btw), it STILL stuttered and froze and dropped frames on my computer that can stream games like Dead By Daylight, Archeage, Black Desert, and ARK just fine. As it is now, this game is NOT streamer friendly unless you have an absolute BEAST. And if you're like me, who can't STAND poorly optimized games, this game will make you DREAD having to return to it's menus for anything because every option takes forever to load and puts it at risk of crashing.
I'm refunding the game for now. But I'll continue to follow up on  the updates from time to time and hopefully it will be at a spot where I can stream it and enjoy the full thing. But, like I said, it needs WAY more time in development.

I was careening through the mud-roads of Turkey, and my Trabant 601 had just about had it. I hadn't been to a repair shop since Yugoslavia, and all of my engine parts were in need of desperate repair. I couldn't stop at this point for fear of my engine not re-starting. Visibility is low. My journey has dragged late into the night, mud is everywhere, and my wipers are useless. Most of my navigation is done through my rolled down passenger side window.
Then, I see it, the beautiful bridge that leads to the city of Istanbul. After lots of long dirt roads and poorer Communist countries, the sheer wealth of the bridge and ensuing city was overwhelming.
Of course, at this moment, one of my tires blows. Earlier in my journey I had accidentally pushed my car while changing a tire, causing me to lose my jack. This meant that I would have to make it to the gas station to get a new jack, so I could change my tire.
Another tire blew out before I finished the bridge. This left my car in all-out scramble mode. The handling was so shaky and the visibility so bad that it was at times better to drive in reverse. I had to avoid collisions at all costs, my car on its' last legs.
Eventually, I find the gas station, just to have my Trabi stop about 10 feet short. Out of all things, I had ran out of gas. Somehow, I was prepared for this one with a full refill tank in the trunk. Soon, I had reached the gas station.
But one final suspense remained: My funds. I was running low, and the only supplies I had managed to find were three bottles of wine. With the price fluctuating greatly, I could be walking out of the store with any amount of money, from a few measly mark all the way up to a few hundred mark.
Luck was on my side as my wine sold for a couple hundred. I was able to make necessary repairs to my car, pay for the motel, and continue my journey.
---
