"Ceville" is a classic Point & Click adventure, a comedy that follows the adventures of Ceville, former tyrant of a fantasy kingdom, now dethroned and searching for revenge, and a way to recover his throne. The main appeal of the story is the main character: this time, you control the villain, and it's a blast: Ceville is a really fun character, in his comical way. Forget about complex antagonists, with vague moral compasses and troubled backgrounds, because Ceville is just the epitome of the classic "Bad Guy". He twirls his mustache, hates good actions, is always rubbing his hands together and machinations perfidious plans, and he's deeply amused by other people's misfortune.
If you're used to the good ol' adventure games, you'll feel right at home in this game. Lots of witty lines of dialog, funny characters and tons of puzzles, around a game that doesn't feel too long or too short. The game isn't very hard, most of the puzzles can be solved through logic, and you can press "SPACE" to see every interactive element in the screen, so "pixel hunting" isn't even a factor.
Now, for the cons, the biggest one: Game crashes a lot. At least, it did for me. During the second Act, when you get access to the Map, every time I pulled it out, there was a chance the game would crash to desktop, or just freeze, which made that part very annoying. There's no way to fix or avoid it, so if you're unlucky, all you can do is to be patient and load the game again every time it happens. It's quite telling that in a game where you can't die, the game auto-saves every 5 minutes, rotating through 10 different files.
Other than that, while the writing is good, sometimes the humor relies on references too much. And the ending is really abrupt.
But other than that, I recommend it to any fans of the adventure genre, just be warned about the technical issues.

OK, so let me tell you about the one aspect of GRID 2 that was irritating enough for me to stop playing it for a few weeks, and then when I came back to it, irritating enough, again, to uninstall it for good.
I am well aware that pretty much every racing game uses "tournament" modes to prolong gameplay hours.
That's fine with me.
But GRID 2 takes that concept to a ridiculous level.
You have the Touge and Faceoff "tournaments".
Here's how they work:
You need to win a 1-on-1 race. Three times in a row. On the SAME EXACT TRACK.
I will not really even try to explain here why this is NOT a tournament mode, but merely a "hey, you know what's fun? beating the same race, three times in a row" brainfart of an idea someone came up with at a design meeting and walked away really proud of themselves.
So yes, I'm thumbing this game down in my review because of this very idea, which in my personal opinion, completely broke the otherwise nearly-perfect arcade racer for me.

Played about 60 hours worth of the game so far, and have enjoyed it.  I have compeleted most of the missions offered in the game and have dabbled in the free-play/custom game mode.
Big Pharma is essentially a one part puzzle - one part economic/business simulator, as most of my fellow recommenders have already mentioned.
As it is a two part game, both aspects of it become important at different times.
Early game, the business aspect I feel is the more forefront of the two. Money is tight, and the AI at times can be brutal competitors either flooding the market for a product or squeezing you out of one. Not to say the game is too difficult, but for those who love business simulations, the early game is your niche.  Late game however, the game gives way to its puzzle aspect as the more pressing of the two. You both lose opportunities to flex your capital might as well as simply run out of space to place your production lines, usually resulting in having to forgo certain markets alltogether just to produce a high tier product. And one that is impossible to optimize at that. Some of the late game markets are quirky too  I feel - The Male Contraception treatments are apparently permanent (in any form, but pill form specifically just boggles my mind).
For those who love business simulations though, I'd recommend giving the game a go.  Its drawbacks to me are more quirky than actual problems with the game itself and you can get decent value from the game at its listed price.
In addition, I tink Mark Allsworth did a decent job with the games soundtrack.

It's easy to see that the developers have tried hard to make a good game based on a new idea. And they have gone 95% of the way, but the games still feels like a beta version of the real game. The controls are clumsy: you move around with the same right button as you sell; switching between tabs takes so much time, although you do it all the time; I still try to push escape to get to the main view (because it's natural!), but only get to the menu; the default building hotekys are on the numeric keyboard (do you think everyone has it?) and I still haven't found a hotkey for belts.
At the same time, the gameprocess is overloaded by messages and different areas in which your attention is required, which doesn't let you focus on something in particular, but always distracts you. The analysis of market is not well presented, so it's hard to understand what is the best course of action at the moment. Finally, fitting your equipment in the factory is interesting the first two minutes, but then you are kind of tired playing tetris and are more interested in concentrating on more important stuff, but nope, you cannot. And if you want to double your production you cannot copy a segment of your conveyor, but have to rebuild it againg with all the connections, which feels like a complete loss of time.
This game is a good try and may become something good in the end, but for the moment it is largely overpriced (I wouldn't pay more than 5$ for it) and in my opinion needs large sales and an army of beta-testers to make it playable for more than two hours. So be aware: for the moment this game is not what you expect. But it still has a change to become a good one.

A surprisingly deep experience in the strategy genre. The game hits you over the head with the options for the custom game. Granted, it'll take a bit of time to understand all the elements the game, and the tutorial could be better at teaching you the game's elements. But once you get an understanding of everything the game has to offer, you'll find surprising depth. The game's strategy design is where it shines: what elements are adjustable and ones that are not are done with purpose and reason in my opinion. Dealing with competitors that actually can affect your gameplay in slight and even more direct ways was fun, and it made me a bit sad that there's no MP element of the game, as I really felt like the game could have truly shined there. When it comes down to it: I felt this game did something that I feel a lot of developers could learn from: start with a great base design, add the options later on, and designed it from the player's angle: and what they'd want. Rather impressed in the long run, and can recommend to strategy gamers out there.

Got it for free from Humblebundle and am glad I didn't spend a cent on this game. Here's why:
- 3 hour campaign
- AI that flips between brain dead and aimbot that ONLY TARGETS THE PLAYER
- Infinitely respawning enemies (thought I was playing a war game, not a horde mode)
- Friendly NPCs will magically push you out of the way to get to their waypoint or they will get confused and start walking side to side to get around you
- Low quality assets (It's a linear game; you control EVERYTHING the players sees)
- Repeated assets. One ladder company got real rich after the North Koreans decided they were going to buy the same exact length, color and type of ladders in bulk
- A CoD style campaign with all the "flashiness" (lens flare and bloom ahoy) but somehow even less substance than a CoD campaign
- Lots of small cutscenes breaking up the gameplay FREQUENTLY (Press E to jump, Press E to climb ladder, Press E to Press E)
- No FOV changer in menus or campaign; default FOV is 70
- FOVs above 90 (I played most of this at 120) break some single player assets and animations
- Has Denuvo DRM which actually forced me to reinstall the game as the Denuvo keys stopped working and it thought I was playing a pirated copy. This was whilst online on Steam launching from the Steam Library
- Graphical errors/issues. Could be due to me being on Windows 10 and/or having a 10-series NVidia card, but the issue remains that things like
can happen (look closely at the wall near the gun model)
But, I'll give it credit where it's due:
+ Headshots will always instant-kill enemies
+ Campaign
to have a deeper meaning and show the atrocities of war (the result is debatable)
+ Sometimes the physics can give you a chuckle when your grenades explode with the force of a Fat Man.
Overall, difficult to impossible to recommend. And I hear that the sequel is worse. Can't wait to play that.

Overiew: Most of my almost 100 hours put into this game was building my main castle.  To me, that's the main focus of this game; building your own epic castle.  It's great that the only limit to how big or small you can build your castle is your imagination.  Combat is getting better, AI still needs some work but shows potential.  Community is really small, hopefully it grows.  I spent most of my time on a PvP server by myself; most amout of players on at one time was 11.
Things i liked:
- Building castles and towers was really fun.  Details on the Ornate were very nice, looking forward to marble (might spend more time just to build another castle).
- Farming wasn't that bad, generally the supplies you need are just on the ground or in mob camps which made it easy to get supplies.
- Flying was fun
- Very large, open world to explore.  I found several spots that I said "that would be a good spot to build a castle".
Things that i didn't like:
- Not enough people on to PvP
- Raiding while people are offline was WAY to easy and anonymous so it's hard to get revenge.
- AI still a bit weak on a lot of monsters.
- Staff weapons were dominant; could AFK farm almost everything.  Fireball has infinite range.
- End game was lacking.  After building my castle exactly how i wanted it, I found myself saying "now what?"
Recommend: Yes I'd still recommend it, even though it needs a lot of work.  It is still an early release game, but dev's have been working to make it better consistently.  I really enjoyed my time; spread out over a month, it kept me entertained and I don't feel like I wasted my money on it.

I'm not someone who typically games. I was an original PS fan and then I moved on to the Elder Scrolls: Morrowind.
That was the last game I really put a lot of hours into and I've been more of a casual gamer since (match 3 and puzzle games mostly, if I'm to be honest). My husband is a huge gamer (408 games on steam alone) and he has always wanted me to get into a game I can play with him.
After buyuing me quite a few against my wishes, he bought me Citadel. Well, 2 weeks and 39 hours later I have out leveled him and matched him (only 1 shy) in hours.
I love the magickal element to it but actually spend most of my time building up my base and collecting materials for potions and item crafting. I enjoy the world and the fact that the people who play on pvp aren't total douches that kill you for no reason. lol. (one of my biggest qualms with most pvp games.)
The music adds a nice ambiance to the game and while I think the character customization can definitely be fleshed out, it IS an early access game. On that subject-- the developers release patches ALL the time trying to improve spell balances and it really seems like the NPC's are getting fleshed out with their evasive tactics.
I am very happy with the controls and the leveling seems to be paced very well. It isn't too difficult but isn't so easy it makes the game almost pointless.
The final thing I'll say was that it was very good foresight on the developers part(s) that there are pve serves as well as pvp. I was incredibly leery about starting out a total newb on a pvp server so to start learning the game without fearing other players would attack me and take all my progress was a wonderful way to really get into the gameplay.
I can not wait for the storyline and quests to be added-- I am a definite fan of this game and look to be playing many more hours of it!

So, this is a '90s-styled shooter in most of the good ways, and a few of the bad ways. You'll be marching from battlescene to battlescene where the path back is conveniently locked off and robots come marching in to be shot.
The guns and enemies, then, make up most of the action here. The guns are satisfying to fire, satisfying and with multiple fire options, though unlocking the different ones goes a little too slowly for my taste, and depending on what upgrade paths you take you may not see some at all until a second playthrough. Guns never need to reload but they can run out of ammo, which feels more like a way to force you to switch between the weapon trees occasionally than a need to conserve resources. However, the game doesn't particularly guide you on what you need - get at least a rocket launcher or other direct-fire heavy weapon before the first big boss, as a hint. Levels are laden with destructible traps to unleash on enemies, which at least gives a bit of strategy to setting up certain fights, but as my arsenal increased I found myself more relying on that than the environment.
Enemies are nicely varied, with some gimmicks that at least keep them above the standard dull sorts you see in most shooters (guy what shoots at you and guy that charges at you). They do tend towards being terrible bullet sponges at times (at least on Hard, which is what I played) and battles can be a bit wearying when they stretch on too long. The final boss, however, was rather clever and hopefully is a sign of what we might see in their future games. Overall, though, the pace is solid, and never keeps you idling for long.
In general the gloomy cyberpunk world is intriguing and I wish we got to see more of it, but mostly we just get tiny glimpses. In Exile - the last section of the game that was originally DLC - it switches that out for a massive brown-and-garbage factory. And though they do manage some interesting bits with the environment, particuarly in areas with garbage compressors or gigantic presses, it's still one big mass of brown and pipes. The story, similarly, seems to be going somewhere but never really finds an ending. The developers liked Ashley Wood's motion comic-styled cinematics from Metal Gear Solid: Peace Walker so much they copied them wholesale, but the result fits well with the theme. Hopefully there will be a Hard Reset 2 to finish the tale, but the story's not the main feature here.
It may sound like I'm a bit harsh, but for the most part I enjoyed Hard Reset. Though it really starts to repeat itself even within its ten hour length, in general it does its shooting aptly and the devs show off their experience with People Can Fly rather well. Just bear in mind it's not sophisticated- you're there to shoot robots and barrels (in that order), and if you want to see that rather well done, that's what you'll find.
I would like to see THG played as a single player and against my own decks, other than that nothings wrong with this game, it's one that I'll keep

how wrong am I ..
Graphics: the latest patch, they added back the 'baked AO' and that's it. My recollection of Hard Reset in 2011 was difficulty, it was balls hard. So hard in fact I never finished the game and I am one who almost finishes every game I start. My problem was your character felt too slow compared to the enemies who all were much faster. That put you at an extreme disadvantage and ultimately a lot of deaths and frustration. Fast forward 5 years and out of nowhere, though very trendy, here comes Hard Reset Redux. A little polish, a few key additions and though debatable looking at recent reviews a much better game and experience to ME than the original.
Lets first address the biggest failure to Hard Reset and what no remaster, redux or any other remagic can fix and that is story. There is a story present, character introduction and such but being told through comic strips and bad voice acting does not help. Its disappointing seeing as you are the ONE to save humanity a much simpler story line would sufficed instead of constant corporation gibberish. It actually starts out simple to comprehend but goes off the rails quickly where I was Vinny Barbarino asking who? What? Where? Hard Reset has all the ingredients to be a Blade Runner or Dredd, but we ended up with Judge Dredd or Battlefield Earth, well not THAT bad.
As much as the story disappoints it does not take away what is essentially Doom with robots and that's gameplay. Hard Resets gameplay is old school it's a fast first-person circle strafe arena shooter with the basic of basic mission design. This design entails you to enter an area, find switch to unlock door and kill all enemies you encounter with no mercy. You do not crouch, you do not jump, recharge health, or have unlimited ammo as all of these are scattered across the maps as pick ups. This part of the game is awesome and makes up for 98% of the game time. I have to mention level design here as it is exceptional. Especially if you think about this is a 5 year old game how you can look across a linear city skyline game map and see where you have been or that's where you will go is quite impressive.
If you are one of those into leaderboards or challenges there is a scoring system in place after each chapter based on your time, destruction, deaths  and other factors. Also, new to the redux version is the added dash mechanic that completely makes the above problems I mentioned from the original obsolete. Instead of being overwhelmed you can now dodge and dash away from enemies(no cooldown).Some are arguing in reviews this makes the game easier, I agree, but it increases the fun factor exponentially and that's what really matters.
There is not a whole lot of variety to the enemies you will encounter but their attacks and depending on the amount thrown at you at specific times will keep you constantly moving and dodging while cycling through what weapons to utilize. There are hulking mechs that try to run you over(dash), fire a barrage of rockets(dash) , little suicide bombing bowling balls, and an old favorite from half-life 2 the manhack. I mean they are not called the manhack but they are flying blades, what else would you call them. There are a few others but I would guess before the start of chapter 3 you have seen almost all of your opponents and it never bothered me because I was using different strategies, weapon modes, and the environments were constantly changing.  The bosses in Hard Reset are also a lot of fun and unique as most are set up with multiple stages and thankfully not too difficult but can extend into a long fight depending on your upgrades(10-20 minutes). Again the fights are not too difficult on hard, but still very tense.
In order to tackle the enemies you are given only 2 of the most unique common weapons I have used in a video game. One weapon is your traditional hybrid of every gun you have used in every game ala shotgun, machine gun, grenade launcher, etc. While your energy gun uses electricity as its base component. Instead of bullets it basically replaces all forms of the common guns abilities  with electricity which makes sense as your enemies are machines. While you receive upgrades for the guns, you don't actually switch weapons, but they transform. Think transformers in the form of a gun or if you ever played Vanquish but more mechanical. Its is a really cool effect and both weapons and upgrades are useful to the fact you will be chaining together combos for maximum damage. Easily one of the reasons I like the game a lot are these two weapons BUT also the fact their is a ton of environmental destruction which using your guns can make for some massive explosions. Also, in this new version the Katana sword has been added but I found getting in close with enemies you will lose a lot of health so I rarely used it and in all actuality its not needed.
As with all remasters Hard Reset comes with some graphical upgrades and while I thought the original, from what I saw, looked amazing the new lighting and textures in the redux are noticeable.Hard Reset is a beautiful game and the cyber punk world that was created is impressive. I have to admit the first 2 levels are really dark and dreary and actually don't impress that much  but the further you go its easily evident a lot of work went into the upgrade and it looks like a game for 2016.
Hard Resets sound is excellent as all of it comes with thundering bass of explosions, bullet hell, metal crunching but is also noticeable to the small details such as the echoes of you walking the empty streets to the drip of rain into a puddle . The regular machine gun is a little too high pitched but the impact of metal on metal is impactful. The soundtrack for Hard Reset is also excellent with reminders of Mass Effect with more use of  techno synthesizers and if someone told me Trent Reznor(Nine Inch Nails) was the artist I wouldn't be surprised. Note, he isn't. If you want to check it out its all located
I love games that have robots/aliens as the main enemy such as Vanquish, Binary Domain, Crysis 3, Mass Effect  to name just a few and Hard Reset just does that in a fantastic looking world with some of the most unique weapons I have ever used in a game. Its attention to details in the world to fast old school gameplay, level and  sound design make me hope this isn't just a revisit for the developer but more of a welcome back because I am ready for a Harder Reset. First off: I own this game from their website before the steam release, so my playtime is higher than the 0.4 hours it claims right now.
TLDR: Even though I like many aspects of the game, I can not recommend it at its price as it will not keep you entertained for very long.
Do I somewhat like the game? Yes.
Would I recommend it? Not really, especially not for 23 Euros.
I love the setting, I feel there should be way more disease/medical-related games and I do enjoy the graphics, by which I mean I don't mind the simplicity. I like the making of new drugs, the setting up of belts/arrangements, the tight budget, the slight humour, the ideas like exploration and the reasearch tree.
So why wouldn't I recommend it? Because it gets boring, and it does so rather quick. The reason for this is, that its repetetive. Gamesessions usually are done in 1-3 Hours depending on difficulty and consist of you researching new techs and producing new medications with increased difficulty in the setup of your conveyer-belts.
The Problem is that its the same each mission. And the Drugs/Ingredients are completly interchangeable. Unless youre a "Letsplayer" you wont care for the name of the made-up Drugs/Ingredients within seconds but they will just be stats like "increase/decrease concentration by 3" so thats all you do.
You find the easiest way to reach that wanted concentration. And theres only (when fully researched) like 3 ways of increasing decreasing, meaning +/- 1 ; +/-3 ; half/double. So thats not hard! In fact nothing is really "hard" in this game. Theres no need to make difficult choices, as you will most likely produce every medice you can as far as research and exploration go, since every "tick" gives money, theres also no need to think about if you should keep the medicine going - if it ticks in money, keep it, if it loses money, replace it.
The result is a very easy game and the "challange" comes from increasingly hard scenarios. But this doesn't mean anything interesting like "do this-and-that with 3 rooms" or so, no, while there are ~5 different types on missions they all play the same, as you just need to make more of the best kind of medicine, cure a number of people, make some money or something along those lines, so they all mean you build up your, lets say "empire" and then at some point you win. And weather your task is to make 5-super-medicines or to make X Million $ doesnt matter as you do the very same thing. The Difficulty of the Game (which does go quite high in the late game) only comes from increasingly narrow timelimits, so the medium and hard difficulty is identical, except in one you need to make (lets say, not sure about the real number right now as it doesnt matter) 5 Milion in 10 years and on hard its 10 Million in 5 Years.
So after 10 hours lets say you will start more than your 10th game (the easy games go by rather fast) and you will do the very same thing the 10th time in a row, still not caring. And since setting up the conveyer belt-systems is the only real aspect, and you do that about once every 5 minutes, you will have done that about 120 times. And then its just routine, theres no fun to be had (there hasn't been in quite a while) and all you do is click your new belt, wait for money to pour in, click your new belt a.s.o.

I didn't want to do a review of this so soon, but I had the torrent of this and logged a good 20 or so hours into it before it went on sale on Steam, so I think that is enough to have a good enough idea and experience to do one.
First off the presentation of GAS is very well done. The introduction, the personalization and the way everything flows is very refreshing. The racing scene is pretty deep with various disciplines to choose from, though you will eventually have to do every one of them to get into the GRID series.
The visuals are absolutely spectacular, especially for a game that only came out for PC and last gen consoles. GAS really shows off the best the EGO 3 engine has to offer and what's is capable of, even if it was built and made for 360/PS3.
The AI is much improved over GRID 2 and the "hard" difficulties are actually a challenge for once. Codemasters said this was wheel to wheel racing and that it is.
Before I dwell deeper into the review, here is a breakdown of the pros and cons IMO;
+Graphics/Visuals
+Sound
+Presentation
+Multiple Disciplines
+Teammate
-Forced Drifting
-Upgrade System
-Teammate (yes both a pro and a con)
-Lack of detailed in-car cockpit view
-Forced to play all disciplines
-Some disciplines not as well done as others
-Lacking car selection
-Team Offers
One of the stand out negatives you will be faced with, is the fact you are forced to play all disciplines and some of those disciplines are clearly inferior to others. Open Wheel, Street and Touring are very well done and thought out. However Tuner and Endurance is a joke. Tuner would of been great, if it wasn't the one buzz kill and sole aspect that completely ruins the discipline and that is drifting. Drifting in this game, as most other games that incorporate it are utter trash and more work than it needs to be. Codemasters stated that GAS was "bringing racing and the series back to its roots". However, drifting is not grass roots racing, nor is it really racing at all. It is an extreme niche and is more of an art form then racing, and should of either been taken out completely or been an optional DLC add-on like Drag Racing is. I liked Drifting, 10 years ago when it was a fad....
Some other notable negatives to touch on is the team mate mechanic. Though the presentation and potential is there, the execution is not. Not sure what the point of them really are, as more often than not, they suck and almost always bring your team rating down. They give you the option to assign various driving mechanics to them while racing like HOLD, PUSH and ATTACK, but I’ve found that none of the settings really matter and even on PUSH and ATTACK setting they still more often than not, drop back in the pack. I hope they expand more on this in later titles and have more customization for the player to fine tune teammate(s).
The last thing I want to mention are the team offers and upgrades. Team offers are somewhat pointless as the only differences between them are the level of tuning you can do, XP you can earn and simple pre-installed upgrades already applied to the team cars. Why offer any type of "upgrade" mechanic if the player has no control over them, other than to take them off? Better teams have more upgrades pre-installed, but it's a roll of the dice on which ones you get and it seems to be based on what difficulty you had set the previous championship. i.e. you have better team offers and pre-installed upgrades the higher you set the difficulty,  which this alone is counter-productive. I always tend to set my racing games to the hardest they can be, but I am not everyone.
All in all though this is a great game. By no means is this a racing simulator, but I would rank it up with Shift and Shift 2 as not a full on sim, but not a full on arcade racer either. Though at least with Shift 2 you have an upgrade system lol.
Stunning visuals and sound will leave you wanting more. Plenty of real world tracks and rendered cities to race in with a mediocre amount of cars, but good enough selection, though some choice as to what cars we race in would been better.
In the end I give this a 7 /10

Homefront: A game that I once remember being one of the most advertised games around 2010 and '11 that would be released with so much disinterest (at least with me) and sold pretty badly that it could be one of the reasons why THQ went the way of the dodo. But is it good and worth playing? Not really at least with the singleplayer campaign. Multiplayer is the sole reason why people are still playing this as well as the postive reviews. This review will be focued on the Single-player side becuase I not much of a fan of multiplayer games in general and there are reviews that does fouced on that well.
Story: The game story is an alternate future which North Korea somehow untified with the south and took over Asia and conviently with the Saudi-Iranian war that ruined the oil industry that caused a huge effect with the US econamy with the nation divided that gives the Koreans a chance to take over the country that also didn't cause a confilct with US ailies in a span of less than twenty years. It's a stupid, unrealistic concept but since it is written by the same writter of the original Red Dawn. so expect a war between the all-good americans that are in the army (becuase it seem any other american that isn't a victimise civilian, is a tratior or post-apocolyptic dwellers and raiders) against the one-dementional korean baddies. But it isn't as bad writing as the awful as those campaigns in CoD or Battlefield. The main plot is about a pilot (the player) being rescued by the the Colorado Resistance to pull off a plan to steal fuel tanks to be delivered to the US army (who are still being active after the Korean invasion?) to be able to take back San Francisco. With such a simple plot why does the story seem so unfocused and boring in all its 4 hour run? All characters are so flat and under-developed that no matter what struggle or tragedy there in I couldn't be able to care. The one character i seem to have a real reaction for is Connor, for not the good reason. At Best he's a typical miltary leader who barks orders at people. But at worse, he's a murderous  psychopath who revels at killing any korean soilder and he doesn't mind using chemical warface in battle and even enjoys watching them suffer in agony. He treats his comardes like garbage at times and it makes me hope there's an option to kill him in gameplay so I can never listen to his voice again. But another problem with the story is that there certain scenes that are clearly made for shock valve given this is a game based on war and while these sinarios are shocking on its own, it undercut the emtions out of it becuase it is focued from the viewpoint of paper-thin characters i don't care about stops me from even being shocked in the first place. And thanks to it four hour length the plot became nothing but a sight-seeing shooting tour. going one place to the next.
Gameplay:  Homefront is a relic of it's time. While the game is only 6 years old, Gaming treads were so different back then. Every shooter that was popular at the time was a present day miltiary shooter, the most popular being COD and Battlefield. It's no suprise that THQ wanted Homefront to be like CoD to replicate it's success. So yes, the game is a heavly scripted corridor shooter with regenated health that heals you faster than Deadpool's healing factor. let me tell you Homefront is one of the most frustrating game i have played recently. Why? Because while the enemy AI is really stupid often standing out in the open or even walking towards towards even though you can easily shoot them. But of course instead of fixing the AI, the Devs instead gave them insanely good aiming even hiting you in impossible angles. And with your suprisingly your health is low even with the fast regen, you can easily die so quickly unless you dive for the nearest cover to heal. But if you don't keep moving, the enemies will respawn so it add more to the fustration. It's not unplayable or anything but so generic and boring. The guns have no recoil nor a sataifying kick to them so it feel like im just firing a  pee-shooter most of the time. There's no challenge: just point and shoot. There's some vehical sections but it pretty short except for the helicopter section which i pretty typical of FPS. There's many time who can control a giant fast tank called the golioth but you don't hop in to control it but just look at a binonculars to point and left-click on locked on enimies to kill so just more point and shoot.
Presentation: While the PC port of the game done by Digital Extreme who also did the multiplayer is pretty good with decent option at a time where PC ports were often terrible. The game textures and enviroments are pretty dated with textures that are muddy and simple even back in 2011. The animations are still and limited with lip-synicng also limited as well, But of course it was a game with less of a AAA budget not counting the marketing so it expected and i seen games came out later look worse than this. At least the lighting it not bad.
Conculsion: Homefront is not the worst game in the world, it's a below-average military shooter at least with the single-player campaign. What really disapoints me is the amount of wasted potienal with this game as the idea of North-Korea taking over the US is a unqiue idea still to this day. If the campiagn was more longer and have much better written characters with actual level design not this corridor nonsense. It could've been a classic. What a shame.

Please note: I'm recommending this game to Civ Fanatics (like myself and those likely to read this review), but not necessarily to the overall Steam population.
I know many who play Civ games and try to explain why they love them and sit hours playing them to non-Civ players. It was hard to put your finger on when Civ II and Civ III reigned supreme, and has just gotten easier since. The series has gotten more interesting, more beautiful, and overall more user friendly, while still maintaining the basic "this is Civilization!" aura and mentality of the original. Civ V is appealing enough to bring more people into the world of Civilization, so the next game in the franchise should continue where it left off right?
Beyond Earth feels very Civ - in gameplay, most mechanics etc. There are a few tweaks that I really liked - more Europa Universalis-esque questing system (and bonuses), and a thoroughly aggravating yet more realistic AI system. The problem lies in the visuals and overall feeling of the game. Does anyone remember SimCity Societies? Not a terrible overall game, but most SimCity fanatics that bought it because it was "next" were thoroughly disappointed. It didn't feel right. Beyond Earth suffers from a similar problem; it is Civ, but it doesn't look as appealing, draw you in quite as much, nor does it give you the sense of accomplishment of destroying France.
So, I recommend it to other Civ'ers to try, but be prepared - it feels like a very unfamiliar step in the wrong direction.

You want the truth, so here it is: I wish Steam had a stars rating system... I'd give it 3 out of 5.  This game is very good, and really is worth the purchase.  (At least until something better comes along.)
Some will criticize it as being "simcade", harping on "mediocre physics", etc., and they're right that it's a simcade but not right about the physics at all.  So here's how it really is.  The physics are top notch, simulation grade.  However, great physics don't make a simulator.  True, great physics are a requirement of being a simulator, but a simulator is more than just a set of well implemented physics rules.  That is where such critics get confused: they tend to view physics and simulation as one and the same, but that's just not reality.  The handling and physics models really are quite good.  (The only aspect of physical simulation I think they could improve greatly on is the force feedback - it's good, but not great.)
However, this game is a GAME, first and foremost.  What separates it from the likes of iRacing is not "bad physics" (again, they're quite good) but the approach to development, which is very game oriented.  For instance, many of the cars DON'T actually handle like their real world counterparts (for instance the GT-R is far more "understeery" than it is in real life)... however, they DO handle very much like *A* real car... just not necessarily the car being represented.  I believe the reason it is that way is because of lack of research - research I'd guess the developer didn't feel was necessary since the goal was balanced gameplay, and as long as they acheived balanced trade-offs within a given class of car, and it was approximately true to life, that was "good enough".  (However, in my opinion, it's NOT good enough, but I digress.)
Another aspect that is very game-ish rather than simulation-ish, is the A.I. (computer driven) cars/players are extremely and frustratingly aggressive.  I read in the developer's blog how proud they were of their aggressive A.I., but I feel they missed the mark.  In real life racing, there is aggression, no doubt, but there is also a sense of caution... no pro race car driver will intentionally derail another driver into a potentially fatal crash - unless they want to be arrested for manslaughter.  Gently tapping/touching/etc. to throw another driver off their game, sure, that happens in real life (and is very controversial)... but repeated hammering until you spin out of control or completely T-boning your car is absolutely NOT realistic.  At times, Grid Autosport reminds me of the old game "frogger", where it feels like the point is to dodge speeding cars as you cross the road, cars that are actually trying to hit you (or at least don't care at all if they do.)  To make this worse, if you return the aggression, the A.I. cars are very difficult to disorient or make slide/spin, whereas they can feel free to derail you at will.  This is the most frustrating aspect of Grid Autosport.  To introduce this kind of A.I. logic is to add a layer of "random chance"... a layer that is very inappropriate in a purely skill oriented venue.
Frankly, I don't think that Codemasters (the developer) really understands their audience - we want the wonderful online gameplay and comradery (which is excellent by the way), great cars to drive (and they are) in an immersive and realistic environment (also quite good), but we don't want to waste our time on "games of chance".  Racing is a purely skill oriented discipline... there's no element of random chance whatsoever (not counting weather, which Grid Autosport doesn't have anyhow.)  We want the good aspects of "gameplay" with the best of simulation... because we want to believe that we're real live race car drivers... that's the illusion we want to buy when we give them our money.  This is where Codemasters really misses the mark - they don't seem to get that at all - they seem only to understand the "rules of game design" without considering what we the audience really, truly want: A racing simulation that keeps us immersed and believing that it’s real but gives us a sense of PROGRESSION and ACHEIVEMENT found primarily in games.  Ruining the illusion with random chance and puerile A.I. ruins the experience, and wastes our time and money.
The bottom line is that the physics are excellent (if you can forgive inaccurate representations of specific cars), the graphics are excellent, online racing is outstanding, but the A.I. is horrible, frustrating, and hardly fun at all.  If it weren't for the great online gameplay, I'd say avoid this title, but on the whole, it's worth getting.

One of my first Steam buys, and money well-spent-- of course, I got it on sale.  ;-)
I don't think it's going to replace some of the great point-and-click classics, but it's a nice little game in its own right and is worth a look.
It features nice 3D graphics (especially for its time), very good voice acting (eveything is voiced), quite humorous, and a good story.  There are three playable characters: Ceville (the sniveling deposed ruler), Ambrosious the (hilariously) pompous knight, and Lilly (a cute little girl who has great banter with Ceville).  Sometimes you play multiple characters simultaneously, and there are points where you have to do one thing as one character, switch to another, and complete a task.
Note that there are a few clearly-identifiable timed elements (a clock will tick) where you have to do something within, say, 10 seconds.  There are no failures that require a re-load, and you can save any time.  You can double-click to skip run animations, and you can hold the spacebar to reveal hidden objects.
Most of the puzzles are quite fair and reasonable-- there were a few I had to get help with...which IMO is a good thing.  Many of the puzzles are combining inventory items in a (usually) intuitive way...and using dialog trees to open up new paths.
Anyway, give it a try next time it's on sale!

Summary: Ceville is a very nice adventure game with a good sense of humor, but is also one of the buggiest games I've played on Steam.
OK, so Ceville is a very typical adventure game, inspired by Monkey Island and various other classic series. It is funny, traditional, and quite challenging in some parts.
You play mainly as a deposed king trying to regain his throne and his little assistant Lilly. The two travel through a very typical fantasy world and solve puzzles to advance the story. It's all quite charming.
Some of the puzzles are very obtuse and while many of the solutions are satisfying, some left me saying, "Oh...that was....the solution?"
This game froze up constantly on Windows 7. It usually freezes up when traveling between map locations during the lengthy second chapter. Fortunately, the game autosaves every five minutes and F5 quicksaves. I got used to saving before traveling.
If you like typical adventure games, this one is a good one and should be played by anyone. Just get used to saving often. :)

A solid entry for the franchise. As a fan of Blood Money, a new entry for the Hitman franchise made me very excited, but skeptical. I played half of it on the 360, finished it all on PC.  And it's very....different. The levels feels more linear and the story involved is very personal for Agent 47. Every "contract" is directly connected and are not a contract at all. Just targets for 47 so he can carry on with the story.
PROS:
-Replayability, many routes to take and many goofy ways to kill your target
-Top notch voice acting
-Visuals are impressive to this day
-Gameplay is more modernized, cover system, improved shooting mechanics, and a better detection system
-Nicely designed levels
-Instinct is a nice way to observe surroundings, enemy patrols, and ways to kill your target
CONS:
-Terrible storyline, starts out interesting, then just goes to rediculous. Antagonists are just generic disney bad dudes, characters aren't developed enough for me to care, it becomes a mess.
-People can see through your disguise. I understand what they were going for, but my god this gets annoying real fast. It's as if each person knows each other by heart.
-Checkpoint system is something I don't prefer. I understand they tried to challenge the player from save scumming, but this, in my opinion, makes replayability less enaging

BadShock 2 does it again: poor shooting part, terrible sound and mediocre gameplay.
Game is more balanced than the first BadShock - you will always have money for ammo; drill is useful as well. Most of fighting plasmids are useless compared to winter blast which allows you to kill any enemy in a couple of magazines. Hacking minigame became better, no more insane clicking. Game literally showers you with Adam so magic is more useful.
Weapons are weird again. Rivet gun is just a bad sniper rifle since it can oneshot a low-tier enemy across the room. Hacking tool should've been moved to another button, not third slot. Why would they put a TOOL among WEAPONS is beyond my understanding (same applies to camera). Minigun is terrible and needs upgrades to shoot straight. Double-barrel is the best gun in the game (shock upgrade is useless). Spear gun is a joke since it requires aiming and projectiles travel slowly. Enemies strafe a lot so headshots with spears are almost impossible unless you lock them with electricity or ice, but then why bother with spears? Launcher is launcher, nothing unusual.
And all of these guns sound horrible even with sound fix (maybe except upgraded shotgun).
Enemies can be researched AGAIN, which means that you need to pull out that useless camera and start recording BEFORE actually doing something = wasted time and probably lost health. At least camera autoswitches to the last weapon after start of the recording unlike camera from BadShock 1. Blinking enemies are back as well for reasons unknown - probably that one guy in charge of them wasn't fired after the release of first game.
Story is meh - go through the corridors to save the princess from her mother. Sound is broken even after fixes. Game has a nice chance to crash after playing an audiolog, so I gave up on listening to those after 4th level.
Game is worth a single playthrough, there is no point in replaying it. 6/10 would not play again.

Dont let my hours fool you, ive been playing this game almost everyday since its neople re-release (it was previously run by nexon) and its the only MMO ive been able to stick with. I was bored one day and was trying to find an old school beat'em up game and i wondered if they had any MMO games like that, then i found this and haven't stopped playing it since. The game may seem really easy when you first start playing but thats because its all about the endgame content and they want you to get there as fast as you can, with all the leveling events and things that can boost exp gain. Once you get there though the real grind begins, as there is like 2-3 different sort of tiers for endgame gear and each of them takes awhile to get, but you'll need it for the endgame dungeons.
One thing that might turn people off of the game is the fatigue point system, you have around 150~ fatigue points (unless you buy neo premium contract) and each time to enter a dungeon it requires 1 (special dungeons take 8 and no more) and then each room after you enter that dungeon takes another FP so you'll run out fairly quickly at lower levels, although that doesnt really matter because there is something like 40+ different classes/sub classes and i can garuntee most people have atleast 5 different characters they play. The game doesnt really have a pay2win aspect because almost everything you buy with money is comestic, and other players are willing to buy it and sell it for the in game currency anyway so you'll never have to spend real money on the game if you play enough.
Overall i really enjoy the game, i mean hell i wouldnt be playing it if i didnt since its impossible for me to find an MMO and stick with it

Recently purchased this again. Was one of my favourite games when it came out, not just in the stealth genre, but in general, it made the idea of sneaking around, and also not killing, fun.
I cannot speak for multiplayer or coop, so please think of this as only a single player review.
Story isn't the strongest point, but is still pretty good, nothing fancy. The gameplay is where the game shines. Intuitive controls and a good hud system to allow players to exploit their environment to the fullest, with a good balance of choices which allow the player to feel in control of Sam, despite linear and clear missions. You decide if you want to sneak, when to distract, what tools to use, from which direction to leap upon guards etc. I feel it's hard to put into words how the game manages to pull off beautifully many things, aiming for Sam to be a stealthy ninja, a predator, a covert operative with many tricks, moves and gadgets up his sleeve, which add up to a fun balance of power, not making the player feel too powerful (the difficulty isn't hard for this game, which isn't too offputting) but not too weak. AI has a variety of tricks, though it isn't anything mindblowing, it is still enough to remind the player that you better anticipate some pushback from the npcs.
I think the campaign was short, I haven't played it through yet (again), but the length and replayability is still decent.
Graphics are still highly enjoyable for an older game and has solid frames per second with highest settings. A proper mix of dynamic shadows, decent shaders and textures, solid animations and physics, allowed me to still immerse myself into the game without being distracted by too much unrealism. Doesn't mean you should expect the quality of modern games, but this game does enough, in my opinion, to still be eyecandy, the basic solid kind of candy, like milk chocolate.
Happily reinstalling this game on my mediocre laptop, I didn't find many problems, which I were slightly expecting, due to so many, not merely old games, but newer ones also having so many problems (which can nevertheless be fixed in many cases). The major problem is that shader model 3 doesn't work for me, the screen goes white, but upon investigation I think it has more to do with the intel HD graphics card than the game, or my drivers anyway (SM2 is still good and looks good). My laptop is a win7, intel dual core 2gHz, 4gRAM with shared graphics card memory, dedicated only 64mb. So it might just work for the majority. I should add that I always add the admin rights and compatibility mode XPSP3 by habit, so that might also have had something to do with it.
People who are not even fans of stealth games might find SCCT a luring gateway drug into the world of patient stalking and picking your own time when to pick npcs off one by one with satisfaction.

Ever had a hankering for swords, sorcery, and castles? The world of Ignus in Citadel: Forged with Fire is like the awkward love child of Dungeons and Dragons mixed with Ark: Survival Evolved. A massive online sandbox RPG, Citadel is one of the newest games released on Steam’s Early Access platform. Developed by Virtual Basement (ARK: Survival Evolved) and Blue Isle Entertainment (Valley), Citadel: Forged with Fire has the potential to be one of the best build-em-up sandbox RPG’s on the market.
One of the largest and best features of this game is its world. My brother and I have been exploring since the beginning of early access and both of us agree that these two independent studios have taken the Unreal Engine 4 to some pretty impressive heights. The environments are lush and beautiful with resources aplenty. The forests feel alive with animals, fairies, orcs and dragons, while the deserts and frosty regions are tempered with enormous fire giants, undead, and… well… more orcs.
The second best feature is the incredibly simple, yet robust crafting system. Mostly involving drag and drop, you pick what type of construction you want to do, then place it where you need. Want to create a small village like in Kokiri Forest from the Zelda series? Go for it. Feel a bit more ambitious? Then maybe rebuilding Winterfell from A Song of Ice and Fire is more your thing, like my brother and I did. Perhaps you’re more into the impregnable fortress type castle-builder. Well, there’s no shortage to what you can come up with and create. At the end of the day, the sky’s the limit and while I can’t speak for everyone, I certainly found this aspect of the game to be almost therapeutic.
Overall gameplay, like the crafting system, is fairly simple in its execution. You have a limited health and mana pool as well as carrying capacity, though you can improve these as you level up. There’s no stamina bar so no worries about tripping over yourself trying to escape that dragon who’s trying to turn you into lunch. You’ll wield a few different weapon types from axes to staves and gauntlets, with more powerful versions unlocked as you level and invest Knowledge points into their respective skill trees. The same goes for your armor.
This brings us to one of the most important aspects of the game; your Knowledge pool. As you level, you will receive a limited amount of “points” to invest in crafting, whether its arms, armor, potions, structures, spells, etc. As you get further down the tiers of each knowledge set, the amount of points required increase exponentially, so it’s wise to plan out what you intend to use and build so you don’t end up wasting Knowledge. Fortunately, if you do screw up, you can learn to craft a potion that wipes your Knowledge and allows you to reallocate your points at level 40.
Leveling up, like most RPG’s, takes longer the higher you are and allows you to also invest “upgrades” to your health, mana, attack, and carrying capacity in addition to gaining Knowledge points. Also, certain tiers of crafting only unlock after reaching certain levels. Depending on whether you choose to play on a PvP or PvE server, you’ll find spending your points to be a very tactical experience.
Other prominent features include animal taming, guilds/houses, PvP, character creation and mass exploration. If you can see it, you can most likely reach it either by walking or flying. Animal taming can be useful if you want an ally in combat or a pack horse to carry all that stone you’re lugging around to build your castle. All in all the system is a bit too simplistic for my tastes. Guilds/Houses are a bit of a limited functionality in the current build of the game, but do allow you to pair up with your friends and build/own structures together. Since it’s so early in the game, I don’t expect much from this mechanic yet, but it has great potential and is great for building community towns/cities and such.
My experience with the PvP has been limited so far as I’ve mostly been exploring the PvE servers, but the system has a lot to work on before it becomes viable. Much of the time you’ll end up either dying a lot to other players or watching your time invested into building a base go to waste as players mercilessly destroy them. I’d feel a lot better about it if they included a PvP flag system like other MMO’s, but again these are features that may be included in future updates or in the final build of the game.
The developers are very active, which is a huge plus point. From communicating often with the player-base through Reddit, their site, or the consistent updates, they are committed to not only improving the game, but adding content that the players are interested in.
Being only in Steam Early Access, there are plenty of issues with the game. The worst that I’ve encountered so far is the terrible optimization of the game and engine. My brother and I have tested the game on two good rigs (one running on a GTX 1070 and the other on a GTX 780) with only a 5-10 FPS improvement between them. Depending on where you are in the game or what’s going on, you can experience some awful stuttering and frame drops. The developers are aware of these issues and are steadily improving them through patches, but as of the latest build, they are still present for even really good PC’s.
Other issues include a notable lack of craftable furniture, a very limited character creation system, too simple enemy AI, and a limited set of armor and weapons. As with the optimization issues, the developers are working on improvements and additions as the game continues in development. As a side note, once purchased, all of these updates are free and no paid DLC or content has been announced so far.
All in all, for an Early Access game, Citadel: Forged with Fire is an incredibly enjoyable experience for anyone who enjoys survival RPG’s and world building. While some of the issues concerning optimization, customization and enemy AI can bring down the experience, I strongly feel that the potential of the game as well as its current features outweigh these temporary issues. So get out there and create your perfect world in the land of Ignus!

Essentially "MOBA Team Fight: The Game", this is a great experience with friends or on solo queue. Very team-oriented action, you can play for 5-10 minutes at a time, easy to learn and fun to master.
Unlike actual Mobas, you don't have to wait 30-45 minutes killing little ai-controlled bots before you and your team are max level, have purchased all of your items, and can now confidently engage the other team at your best. In Battlerite there are no hero levels, there is no gold to collect or items to buy, just the other team to fight to the death and it is intense!
In Battlerite you start off with all of your abilties, and each of them is a skill shot. Even your basic attack is a unique ability that can miss if you are not careful. Landing a hit on your opponent gives you energy that can be used for special abilities, including your ultimate. This game rewards you for aiming your attacks and dodging your opponents, which means that you can make some awesome comebacks in this game. Gone are the days of watching an auto-attack arrow defy logic and curve mid-air to hit you.
While there are no items to buy during a match, you do get to choose 5 "Battlerites" before the match begins. These are basically minor buffs to individual abilities that your character has, such as adding a slowing affect to an ability or reducing its cooldown. Nothing game-breaking, but it does allow you to customize to your playstyle. All Battlerites are available for free, so there is no "pay to win" trickery here. Your character is just as good as your opponent's.
The game is free to play, so give it a try and see if you enjoy it. It is a breath of fresh air for fans of Mobas that want to have fun without having to farm first.

In my mind, this new version of "Hard Reset" is an either-or sort of proposition. The revisions made to the game are welcome, but really quite minor. Certain enemies make their debuts at different times, a quicksave feature is added (hooray!), and you get a melee weapon...
...but I can't say that I found the sword to be all that helpful.
And its the same game. It looks almost exactly the same, the geometric level flow is the same, and the encounters are only rarely different. It's cool of Flying Wild Hog to release this iteration at all, but I also have to say that this really feels like it ought to have been a patch on the original product.
Plus, for some reason, they just had to create cyborg zombies for this version. Zombies - seriously, can we get over this phenomenon already? Everyone's done it at least twice. It's unnecessary, especially when you already have a good stable of aggressive opponents for the player to duke it out with. (Mercifully, there aren't that many zombie encounters, and they seem to go away entirely in the late game.)
If you don't have the original, get this version, because this "Hard Reset" is clearly the "real" one. If you've already played through "V1.0," though, you may as well skip "Redux." The developer's efforts are to be appreciated, but this just isn't enough of a revamp for it to actually be a separate product.

I am a big fan of logistic-puzzle games and thought that this might take the gameplay of Spacechem or Factorio in exciting new directions. Unfortunately, the logistics puzzles and business simulation don't really play off of each other well, and the game quickly becomes tedious.
The two halves of the game don't play well together. The logistics lines are a little bland and mostly come down to twiddling the concentration of a drug up, then down, then up again to evolve its attributes and get them to the right concentration. This might be more fun if you could go whole-hog laying out a complicated production line, but the business side of things ensure that's generally unprofitable. Everything operates at just a 1:1 or 1:2 ratio, so there's no thrill of big, powerful throughput like you get with a massive Factorio setup or a speedy Spacechem reaction.
The business level isn't that interesting, either. Your profit is dependent on the efficiency and margin of your manufacturing lines. Sometimes competitors will interfere by saturating your drug's market, which reduces your profits. Often, a competitor will beeline patent technology just to force you to replace your best drug every other year. That's just annoying. The business layer is also your chief source of waiting, as you twiddle your thumbs waiting for the next ingredient or technology to unlock.
The GUI is also a bit of a chore. You'll frequently be flipping back and forth between the "Ingredients" and "Cures" tabs to try to figure out what steps you need to evolve your drugs, which ingredients provide the desired attributes, and finally what concentration you'll sell it at, and whether competitors are saturating the market.
There are some clever things. Sometimes you will sell a drug with a bad side-effect profile just because it's not profitable to sell a more refined form of the drug. Or maybe your drug will be too effective and demand will go down, or maybe your one drug's side effects will drive sales for another drug. These are all twiddly little fringe cases, and they're not cause enough to keep me playing.

Wow, this game --- is actually kinda good.
First off: I am normally not a fan of straight up racing games like this, usually I need some free roaming and tuning and cop-destroying in my racing games, a la some of the Need for Speeds. And I like racing games where I feel good without being actually that good at the game. The more arcady the feel, the better.
But this game is kinda inbetween those Arcade-Racers I love and those Hard-Core-Racing games I kinda hate and it is fun that way.
The driving is more challenging than in a Most Wanted, but you can get the hang of it, even without a real steering wheel, gas pedals and a nice racing seat. And that is good. Because I've only got a keyboard and a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ office chair. This way you can actually get BETTER at this game with time instead of acing through every race until the end credits roll.
The cars are not moddable in the same way they are in some of those "Underground"-racers: No fancy new spoilers can be attachede to your hot ride, neither can you replace your seatbelts with some pythons. Without the upgrading (and probably the hoody), you actually have to learn your cars, not upgrade them until they are as indestructible as a concrete wall and can turn on a dime. The race variety is good, it kind of reminds me of Underground 1 which I played to death back then when I actually bought racing games regularly. A standard race here, a 1-vs-1 there, some ♥♥♥♥♥♥ "drive-by-all-those-♥♥♥♥ING-cars"-thing next to the garbage bin, a time trial with a new car here... Bleed clearly takes inspiration from Mega Man and other classic 2D games, which is both a strength and a weakness. Running through levels blasting baddies with various weapons is certainly a tried and true formula, and the use of bullet time, quadruple jumps, and varying enemy types do shake the formula up a bit. However, it never transcends those old classics or subverts the formula, and the game never stops feeling safe. That being said, you won't be bored. Good level design, a quick pace that allows you to get right back into the action as soon as you die, and solid art direction certainly make for an enjoyable experience. The only real stumbling block is some unintuitive controls that make you jump forward when you'd rather jump up, but it isn't a deal-breaker and eventually you can adjust to it.
So if you aren't looking for anything revolutionary and instead just want a safe but fun game, consider this a soft recommendation for Bleed.

Let me specify something- for 8 years, this has been my favorite game of all time. I played the absolute♥♥♥♥♥♥out of the xbox version of it- and while it may feel more suited to a controller, it can be handled just as well on a mouse and keyboard (though you may want to bind the keys to your liking). Since there's less of them- we'll start with the bad things, shall we?
Stealth games NEED good, balanced cpu opponents. While the game gets the awareness of guards correct on a standard basis- the dudes you're sneaking past can be remarkably stupid, and occasionally even the converse of that, as it has its faults sometimes with twitchy/schizophrenic AI.
The character models' faces can be REALLY ugly. Mainly, that comes from stretching in an exaggerated expression, as grabbing someone and holding a knife to their neck raises their eyebrows roughly 3 feet above their face, and their mouths even wider than the area aforementioned. Their eyelids are also triangles.
Another fault for the PC version is that it doesn't quite have the sound design that the xbox version did- sound effects don't fade and echo like they should. Which is kind of bizarre! It's not often that the console counterpart ends up sounding better than PC master race's version.
There are a few issues in the multiplayer modes:
Co-op
-Game can desync and completely ♥♥♥♥ up a mission that you and your partner had spent an hour on
-Framerate is LOCKED TO 30 FRAMES FOR SYNCHRONIZATION PURPOSES
-This game absolutely hates when you Alt+Tab and will kick you off the server for doing it too much
Versus
-Opens separate program
-Completely different (and less visually appealing) engine
-Resolutions only offered in 4:3 format (but can be easily fixed by editing default.ini)
-Some of the maps are so huge it boggles your ♥♥♥♥ing mind that ubi thought only 4 players could support it
Now then- I've told you what isn't so hot about the game, and if all of that turns you off, that's okay.
So what makes Chaos Theory so great?
Make no mistake, gameplay is the breading AND the frosting on this delicious cake. The engine is completely revamped from its' predecessors, which is a magical thing that they were able to tear down what they had before that was already superb, and make something that is nearly perfect. There's a new sound meter, that lets you take a look at just how noisy you are in a situation, which makes for a better sense of immersion- rather than LOUD/NOT LOUD. The new engine the game runs on feels substantially smoother than SC or Pandora Tomorrow (which is still yet to see a steam release); All of your actions, as well as the AI's, both look and feel realistic. There's no half-hearted spring step like the original, nor do guards have to hug walls to get past eachother. All you have to worry about is coming up with the method to either stun your foe, eliminate him, or how to slip past him unnoticed. I often prefer the latter, but when in co-op, you can't really trust your partner, nor yourself to be this stealthy. You're better off quick-saving frequently or just knocking out whomever you encounter (or both!).
Sound-wise, the game sounds awesome. Stellar voice acting, great sound effects, and some of the greatest music in a game ever. In fact, Ubisoft was so pleased by composer Amon Tobin's work, they released the soundtrack a MONTH before the game was due. Tobin was able to create the tense atmosphere of the game, all while retaining the feel that you're a ghost's shadow. You ARE what goes bump in the night. Needless to say, the game's OST has wound up on every different generation of an MP3 player I've had.
Seriously. Just listen to it.
The voices in the game sound smooth and believable at every time. There's no forced lines like there were in Pandora Tomorrow, where there was that occasional young voice in the ambient audio tracks that absolutely did not fit the bill for the lines or the character he was given.
"DON'T SHOOT, I'M AMERICAN"
That line is going to haunt me til the day I die.
Like I've explained before, the game still looks nice, visually. The environments look polished, with the lights shining in just the right spots that make the game still a pleasure to look at, nearly a decade after release. The character models are very nicely detailed in terms of both texture, and shape. With bumps and edges on not just their faces, but clothing as well. In a game about stealth, you could imagine how important shadows and lighting are- and the balancing of the light-index along with the visuals work great (although this excludes a few particular downloadable co-op levels). The Co-op looks just like the Singleplayer, and doesn't sacrifice the engine for the sake of performance. But the extra levels included in the v1.05 patch leave a LOT to be desired. It feels like there was a completely different designer who had absolutely no spatial awareness, and didn't even understand how lighting works- and that large, stretched blood textures serve no purpose when there is no body they are connected to. Stay away from those maps if you wish not for your partner and yourself to succumb to occular leprosy.
How do I love thee, Versus? Let me count the ways.
1. When I grabbed parker and threw him off a ledge, breaking his neck.
2. Charging into and scaring the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of Binary_2 right after the elevator doors opened on 'Club House'.
3. Both Parker and I getting killed after bd648 fired a grenade into the rafters, taking the ceiling along with it.
4. wwchicken running headlong into yet another proximity mine next to the VIDEO GAMES terminal in 'River Mall'.
Versus makes its' return from Pandora Tomorrow, and with a vengeance. Gameplay is considerably more balanced, providing an easier challenge for the mercs. Mercs can now hit spies in the FACE, and knock them down- which levels the playing field, since spies have a tendency to sneak up and break your neck. You can also customize your loadouts for both classes, which is nice when you're trying to balance the game to fit your playstyle. Spies are still stuck with their shocker rifle, but mercs have the option to take either their default assault rifle, an SMG, or a shotgun. There's various things you can use on both sides as well, including spy traps, tracking bullets, and even stealth camouflage. It's all there, and it's a blast to play. I have no idea why there's so few people playing such a fantastic game. I mean, Counterstrike came out 13 years ago, and it's still one of the most played games on Steam.

Great game, often considered the highlight of the Splinter Cell series. Chaos Theory has 3 complete modes in single-player, co-op, and versus, at the time of its release very unique. Steam downloads a basic user interface, which then downloads the main game client alongside XIGNCODE3. However, you are never informed of this. In fact, there is no uninstall option inside of Windows itself to not only remove this game, but XIGNCODE3 as well.
Steam is only responsible for the initial user interface download, if you try to uninstall it like any other Steam game you only remove that portion, not the game itself. To actually delete the game I had no other option other than to find the folder and drag it into the trash. Deleting XIGNCODE3 is another story. You have to go into your Windows registry and manually delete "xhunter", find and remove another "xhunter1.sys" file from your Windows directory.
The game itself wasn't for me, but having programs installed to my computer without my knowledge raises a red flag.

Hard Reset Redux is a special kind of shooter that takes the simplicity of the genre and blends it with a cyberpunk setting.
The game takes players to a cyberpunk world that is inspired by the works of great writers like Philip K.♥♥♥♥♥♥and Neal Stephenson. The story is told through a series of comic panels while the game is loading, these give players the details they need of whats going on.
When it comes to the gameplay, if one has played a title like Serious Sam then they will feel right at home with Hard Reset Redux. You're armed with two weapons and the objective is to battle through the levels while completing an objective. Both weapons can be upgraded with new features (like a built in shotgun) using points earned through combat and finding hidden secrets.
The combat requires players to just shoot the wave of enemies while using the environment to their advantage. The levels have a plethora of explosive barrels waiting to be used, while electrical generators offer a tactical advantage of crippling the enemy.
Overall; this is a simple shooter and a second chance to experience a cult classic that old school gamers will appreciate.

Let me start by saying I personally love the game and can't wait to see what they add next, along with that they really listen to the community when it comes to content. For example a few weeks ago everyone was blowing the message boards up with how it would be cool if they made a Phoenix and boom like two weeks later it's in the game. The game has fun magical mechanics and you can tame everything in the game and have it fight for you and even ride some of them, or just fly around on a broom whatever floats your boat. The world is large, not Skyrim large but still a good size, and it has a lot of great places with epic views begging you to build your base there. With all that said it is still in early access and I think a lot of people that have done a review on this game forget that. I thoroughly enjoyed Hard Reset Redux, but I get that it probably isn't for everyone. It's a bare-bones, single-player, swarm-based first person shooter, set in an absolutely beautiful cyberpunk world.
Being a big fan of the genre, I was mesmerized at the environments the art directors came up with, and found myself F12'ing frequently due to the games sheer beauty.
The game play itself is reminiscent of 90s FPS', which by todays standards can be repetitive. Despite the fact that I grew up playing Wolf3d, Doom & ROTT, I still found myself playing Hard Reset in short intervals of between 30mins~1hr. Due to its simplicity, nothing felt lost playing like this.
The levels are linear and secrets are scattered throughout.
The game does tend to feel somewhat arcade-like, which is a positive for me. Weapon selection & constant movement is very important; if you don't keep moving, dashing & changing between weapon modes, you will die a lot.
There is a fairly decent amount of enemy variety in the game, and the boss fights are at times challenging, yet refreshing.
The only things I can possibly fault the game on is that I did find the story somewhat incoherent & lacking a proper conclusion. It's as if the developers had hoped to produce a sequel. The voice acting also made me cringe at times.
Conclusion: Frantic & at times challenging gameplay; Awesome weapons & character leveling system; truly beautiful environments and a fantastic soundtrack. I definitely recommend Hard Reset Redux for anyone who is a fan of mindless old-school first person shooters & cyberpunk fiction.
