DFO is an MMO that uses a combat system inspired by 2d fighting games (and such things like streets of rage). It’s nearly a decade old and has a crazy following in Korea, and it’s one of the top grossing f2p games worldwide (One year it was above league of legends, not sure about other years. 2016 according to google, it’s 3rd place in the world, beating out Dota 2). Mostly because this game is big in China too…
Now, I’m a longtime player of this game (this game has existed in NA outside of steam for a year now), I know the game inside and out, and I’ll be real about what’s fun about this game, and what isn’t.
DFO’s greatest strength is its 2d-fighting-game-inspired combat. You can hit enemies to knock them out of their attacks, knock them into the air, and keep juggling them with various attacks, just like a fighting game. There’s super armor (on certain frames of attacks, for both players and monsters), which prevents you from stunning/launching foes, grabs that let you ignore that super armor and throw an enemy (and which give you some invincibility frames, so you can escape crowds), some classes can block and counter…
But DFO is just “inspired by” fighting games, it still takes a note from MMO design. The combos are nowhere near as tight (most of the time…), and instead of having lots of different attacks based on your inputs, you have lots of skills that you can put on a dozen hotkeys (although, you can still “manually input” them, so you can still have your down forward skill key inputs. You can even customize what input you want each skill to be. You even get a small cooldown and mp reduction for inputting this way, and there’s some weapons that give you bonus damage for not using hotkeys). Also, most of them have cooldowns, so you have to manage both the hitbox/launch properties of the attack and the cooldown.
It’s fun and satisfying, and it keeps me coming back. It’s hard to really describe why, but I guess it’s the fact that it’s simple enough that it’s not exhausting to keep up, but also has enough going on and enough chances for you to display some skill that there’s still fun in just fighting regular stuff (like using a super armor move to block a knock-back or counter an attack, at just the right time). It's also easy to learn, as you gain skills every few levels, giving you time to get used to a few skills at a time.
There are a lot of classes, which have themes and playstyles that are pretty unique. For example, the blade master class isn't just a swordsman, he's a master of every blade. So you switch weapons in the middle of combat to gain bonuses, and your skills will function differently depending on which weapon type is equipped.
Leveling is really easy. A bit too easy, actually, the dungeons you do may not challange you until like level 65+. Great for new players, but you may find yourself wishing you could practice longer combos...there's a scenario hard mode, but unlocking it is kind of dumb (clear a certain dungeon in a certain time under x hits. Doesn't tell you which one except in loading screen tips sometimes).
Also, game runs really well on anything. Trust me, we've had some terrible laptops do okay. Connection is peer 2 peer, so if you solo, you shouldn't lag much. If you party with people nearby, you'll be fine. Even a distance like New York to Louisiana is okay.
Dunno much about PvP. Rare hackers, less rare laggers, slightly unbalanced classes. PvE gear matters, but not to an unwinnable extent (you can only do so much damage in one combo before gravity increases on a juggled player).
Graphics are decent. Game has it's own style, and there's an option in the setting for a texture upscape if you don't like clean, sharp pixels like I do. Music is amazing, there's actually a crazy amount of tracks. some of which I wish wasn't hidden away.
3 things I bet you wanna know. P2W? Grindy? FP system?
FP: I know you'll hate this sytem at first, but there's a lot of ways to increase how long you can play (especially with these events, neo premium gives you a lot of FP). It's barely a bother once you're done leveling, trust me. This system discourages gold botters, it really works.
P2W?: Not everything is cosmetic. There are ways to get ahead with cash, but there's nothing locked off for a free player, and even paying players still need to work hard to get ahead. From my point of view, other people being able to pay to gain something a bit faster then they usually would doesn't really make me have less fun, but I can understand if you think otherwise.
The main thing to note is there is no content (as in, actual dungeons/raids) that is locked off or made extremely unreasonable because you didn't pay. People will try to tell you that epics are "needed" for anton raid, but that's only true for 3 or so really poorly balanced classes (out of 40+). Almost every class can get in with gear that is reasonable to obtain.
The really two things you’ll narrow your eyes at are the clone avatars and the demon invites. First, just think of the clone avatars as a pretty small stat boost, which opens up some room for emblems (which are easily obtainable ingame) with provide a moderate stat boost. Unlike the other things, it’s not quite so reasonable to obtain a set of clone avatars ingame, you’d need to buy a package off auction house (which can be moderately expensive) to get them. People often sell these for money.
The demon invites are something you get as a side bonus when you spend real money. You get them all the time ingame, but they’re the keys to hell mode, where the best items await (behind a crazy rng wall. You don’t need this level of gear on most classes to see all the content. I’m serious). You get a decent amount just for doing daily challenges, spending mileage on them, and finding them in dungeons, and you can buy more (for a pretty high price) off auction house. But because crazy rng, it’s never enough, and this is where the people who spend thousands really see their advantage (well, that and gold from selling packages to buy even more demon invites).
Grindy?: If you’re wondering how bad the grinding is, leveling is easy, getting acceptable gear for pvp doesn’t take too long. Getting good PvE gear though…there’s 2 ways it works. The kind of gear that will let you do all the content on most classes is farmed by doing daily things that don’t take too long, but you have to do it over many days to finish. There are events and other activities you can do to speed it up, if you desire. The other is hell mode, which is pure rng and is for true Korean-MMO fans, and costs demon invites as stated before. Well, there’s also stuff you buy directly with gold, getting them otherwise is impractical.
Speaking of events, Neople (the company) is extremely generous with events. I’d be a lot more suspicious of those contracts I spoke of earlier if I didn’t have 100+ days of every contract just from events literally handing them out for free. There’s always like 4 events going on, it’s kind of crazy.
The community, as of the time I write it, is always willing to help with questions and information, and sometimes lower level quest materials. But finding parties for lower level content isn’t easy, because soloing is just so fast and easy now. As far as I see, higher level content has enough random groups forming at peak times, and there’s lots of great guilds willing to help for that (including mine. NewWorld is always recruiting, by the way!)

TL:DR Version: Static graphics are worse, dynamic graphics are improved... plus a katana.
I read into a lot a of the reviews about the graphic updates and some of the other more technical stuff that a lot of people here think are actually a downgrade, and certainly a lot can be said about the original. However, with a little more research I found that the reason for this is not the fact that the developer wanted to throttle gameplay or make make the game "easier to run" but because they were switching focus from eye catching static objects, to eye catching dynamic objects.
A quote from the developer themselves puts this in better perspective saying something along the lines of "Where as certain static aspects of the game seem to look worse, the changes are geared towards the moving objects that the player will be interacting with most. Things like barrels, enemies, and the environment look better when moving." They go on to say that the Redux uses a Dynamic SSAO instead of the baked ambient occlusion system and that they converted to the newer Roadhog V2 engine.
Though I can't say that I notice a huge difference, and many fans of the original may disagree with me here, at least the concerns were addressed and explained. I would say that your best bet is to purchase Shadow Warrior, and pick this up with the discount (it comes with both the Redux and the original). It's a great shooter and a very nice transition to the constant barrage of mainsteam shooters.

This game is amazing! It has a really good concept and idea. Basically in this game it takes place during 1990 and you start out with a car called the Laika 601 Deluxe (based off a real German car called the Trabant 601 Deluxe) given to you by your uncle. You drive all across Eastern Europe and so far the countries you can drive through are Germany, CSFR (Czech and Slovak Federative Republic), Hungary, Yugoslavia, Bulgaria, and Turkey. Each country presents it's own challenges whether it's off road, rainy, or bumpy, etc. You have the ability to completely customize your car to your own style, you can upgrade your car with useful parts like the roof rack, tool rack, bull bar, and more. You can also change the engine which consists of the engine block, carburettor, air filter, ignition coil, fuel tank, battery and the water tank. For example you could make it be fast, fuel efficient, durable, etc. As well you can paint the car and put decals on it, you can even mix colors! Every time you travel to a country or from a country you are given three routes you can take, it shows you how long the route is, the weather, and what you may encounter on the route, like a gas station or pot holes for an example. While driving through routes you can find boxes or crates, when you open these you can find goods which you can keep or sell. You also can find broken down cars and you can steal parts from them. In addition AI driven cars are on the road, be careful not to hit them or you can get a ticket. You always need to be prepared for what happens, you can bring extra gas, oil, tires, water, etc. When you finish a route you arive at a town or city (depending what country your in) and you can find a gas station, motel, Laika shop, and a border to the next country. This game is fairly simple to pick up once you play for a bit and it has a well built tutorial in the beginning. The game does have some bugs right now but they aren't game breaking. This game has a very promising future, and the developers are always active. At times this game can get a little bit repetitive but all in all it's really fun! I would rate this game a 9/10 and if you are thinking about getting this game I promise you it's worth it! Oh, I forgot to say this but in my opinion I just love the realism of the interior of the car! I mean, it has the egnition, handbrake, radio, window wipers and so much more! This game just makes me feel like i'm actually in the car which I absolutely adore! Sorry the review is so long, it's just there's so much to say about the game!

Never owned any previous version of Hard Reset, I wasn't impressed by the demo a few years ago, but having Shadow Warrior on my account gave me a nice deal here, so an initial 10 hours for €3 ain't too shabby, not one bit broseph.
First off, I don't like shooting robots and with the risk of sounding like an insane person, I prefer flesh over metal. But it's not a kid's game, it's pretty challenging in fact, even on Normal and not necessarily for the right reasons. Hard, Insane and Hero mode await those who are hungry for more. If it weren't for the quicksave option, I wouldn't have even considered it. An old school shooter with autosave only is a very bad mix, unless there's one around every corner, so avoid the Extended Edition. Speaking of "old school", Hard Reset doesn't have crouch and for a game that has plenty of secrets, that seems like a gross oversight. Dash mode helps with getting to tougher spots, but it's hit or miss.
Story has never mattered in games like these and at one point those comic book slideshows with voice overs will eventually run out and then you'll just see loading screens between levels until the end of the game, when it's time for a final cutscene. Someone did something they shouldn't have and you're there to clean up their mess. Kill everyone in sight, end of story. I also shot the cleaning robots. They moved.
There are technically two weapons (with upgrades), three if you count the Katana, which isn't very practical here, but it's there if you need it. Weapon modes are nice, making up for the lack of guns that look different on your HUD but serve the exact same purpose. It takes a while to upgrade them, for the game to actually start getting fun and it wouldn't surprise me one bit if you don't get past the first 2 or 4 hours. There's nothing special about this game but I finished it, so there must've been something that tickled me. RPG and Railgun were my two preferred weapon modes, while environmental damage did the rest.
Hard Reset Redux is a serviceable FPS with 115 achievements, annoying enemies and tight spots full of explosives. Why is it that small non-human enemy types are usually goofy, clumsy and make silly noises? What's the psychology behind that design? Is it scary when you're swarmed by hordes of critters with sawblades, propellers and bombs? I suppose, but why do they remind me of children or circus folk? Quick disclaimer: I did not play the original, this is my first contact with HR. So I don't know how it compares with the original, whether this is better or worse.
Pretty good shooter! Fast action and good challenge. Level design is good; levels are linear and very creative, making you revisit parts of the same level to do different things and throwing different enemies to force you to use the space differently. It may not sound like much but you see the same room in quite different perspectives when fighting against short, fast land bots when compared to flying, slow bots that force you to study the room vertically. There is plenty of environment hazards and you are encouraged to use them, and it's pretty fun to do so.
I'm not a huge fan of the weapon system though. It works like this: you have two main weapons (3, counting the added sword in this version, but I'll get to that later) a plasma type and normal fire weapon. Each type has subtypes like machine gun, grenade etc. You change the type with q and the subtype with numbers or mouse wheel. Honestly I just don't see the advantage. Some of these seem redundant, with their differences maybe being invisible stats, but are applied in the same way. But in the heat of battle it's very inefficient to switch between weapons. Sometimes I press 4 quickly to use the RPG, but I'm on plasma so I have to press Q to move to fire weapon, which in this version means it will go to the sword before, then I have to press Q again, now I can press 4 to get the rpg. In this case I believe less would be more. And the sword isn't helping much here. I mean, it is a decent melee weapon! I loved using it against the human tests (zombie like enemies) but the added type further emphasizes the awkwardness of the system.
And last, the game tries to tell a story. I assume it does, at least, because it has cutscenes between levels. With dialogue. It's mostly cringy writing with an abuse of stuff like "what a..." "what in the name..." fuuuuck" "what the fuuuuck" "seriously, what the fuuuck" "♥♥♥♥!". While the plot itself is interesting, it's also hard to follow. I'm not sure what happened at the—rather abrupt—end, and a few moments don't seem to make a world of sense to me. The whole thing adds nothing significant to the game. One could think that adding nothing means no harm done but that's not entirely true (the argument doesn't belong in this review though). Point is, if all they wanted was some context they could do that with a lot less cut scenes and dialogues. It would do the same work with less cringe and plot holes.
Pretty fun game nonetheless.
EDIT: Oh, and for $3 on sale? this is quite possibly one of the highest quality/price ratio ever. I would recommend this game even at full price, with that discount it is absolutely worth it!

The game has been rebalanced significantly making it a lot easier that the original. In fact, Hard difficulty is easier than Normal in the OG Hard Reset. However, HR was hard for all the wrong reasons:
- bullet spongy enemies? - check
- enemies dealing unreasonable amounts of damage? - check
- having only a sprint function limited by stamina which was woefully inadequate in dealing with mentioned enemies? - check
To put it in perspective; imagine DooM (2016) having player movement at around half speed, no double jump, enemies having twice the HP and dealing twice as much damage. Challenging as hell? Yes. Fun? Not really.
In Redux all of this has been remedied:
- bullet spongy enemies? - a thing of the past
- amounts of damage? - toned down
- sprint function limited by stamina? - you now have infinite stamina and a dodge move from Shadow Warrior (2013)
While it is more accessible, it's also lots more fun! No longer do you feel ill equipped in dealing with your foes. Gone are moments of having to awkwardly attempt (and fail) to dodge enemies charging at you. No longer are you forced to spam crowd control abilities just to have a chance at winning a fight (though they are still very effective). No longer is your character infinitely less mobile than in the cutscenes.
In my mind there is no reason to take the OG HR over Redux, unless you enjoy the artificial difficulty.

Well, Steam asked me to write a review so here it is. I've played Maplestory almost since its inception with many leaves of absences throughout. Although I only have a few hours of Maple on Steam, I played it through the launcher offered by Nexon.
When Maplestory first came out with the first four and original Explorers (I can't believe they added a ton more classes under the original Explorer umbrella...), those were truly the golden days. Each class was very balanced, and the variety was just right. There was enough so that you weren't stuck seeing the same class over and over again, but not so many so that you'd end up seeing only part of the classes. It was a lot simpler back then with a very linear "correct" way to level. I still remember the "standard" way to getting to lvl 70. Oh, and leveling was a lot harder back then. Nowadays, you can easily get to lvl 70 and beyond in a whole day if you truly wanted to, almost killing the sense of achievement and pride in getting to your 3rd job. Even getting to your 2nd job proved fun.
Nowadays and recently, Nexon inundated the game with so many classes, and each newer class proves markedly and noticeably stronger than the last. When Pirates first came out, they were so much more overpowered than any other of the four classes. After that, more and more classes came out, and there seemed to a very one-sided shift to the newer classes. Nowadays, it's extremely rare to find a cleric or a regular assassin anymore. Also, nowadays it's extremely hard to make money as a new player without forking over a ton of cash or otherwise getting lucky with Gachapon.
tl;dr Maplestory was once a great game and arguably one of the first pioneers of the MMORPG. It had a great storyline and a great community up until around 5 years ago. Then, they started releasing a ton of updates and changing everything. Nowadays, there's a much steeper learning curve with so much stuff to learn. The community has degenerated tremendously with no real substance in it anymore. Nexon now just seems bent on suckering money out of everyone, and resembles a pay-to-win game, which one will notice after leveling up to a certain point.
- This is really a wall of tributes from veteran players. A lot of their stories really do reflect how great the game once was.

I used to really love this game about 7 years ago. It was pretty exciting as far as MMOs went because you actually had to work for levels, but even then the grind felt so tedious. Maplestory has definitely done a huge improvement in terms of grinding and leveling but that's about as far as they go for good things.
Overall, this game is NOT the game you want to play if you're just joining now. The game still holds some nostalgia for long time veterans looking to relive old memories or haunts but the goggles get taken off soon when you realize how badly the game has changed. There is no making money in this game, only spending real life money to make maplestory money (mesos). The leveling system is absolute crap and will have you spending days in one map pressing at most three keys to kill monsters. The bridge between p2w and f2p is massive and the only way to bridge it is by throwing more money at Nexon. The class system is utter crap because the new jobs will always be better than the older ones. Nexon forgets about their older classes so that they can make the new ones flashier and more exciting so it gets you to spend more money on them. The storyline to Maplestory sounds like it was written by a five year old, and in game quests do little to elaborate that storyline nor do they reward you enough for the grind. All the quests can be summarized by "kill x amount of mobs, collect x amount of drops and come back, or talk to x, collect y for x, and kill 100 of z for x and come back". The community is garbage since they're all circlejerking each other on how good their equips are because they spent thousands of dollars making them godly, and party questers only care about who does the most damage and will kick you if they see you do subpar damage.
This game is a waste of your time and money. Don't even bother with it.
Maplestory went p2w ages ago when potentials first came out. At first, nx was just used to look nice or have a pet that marginally helped with gameplay. Then this obvious money ploy came out and the gap between p2w and f2p became massive and there is no middle ground. Want to make good in game money? Too bad, the only way to do that is bossing to sell the drops. "Ok, my range is good enough for bossing now". Alright, spend 3k(3$, the nx is 1:1 to irl money) nx buying Scissors of Karma in the cashop so you can actually sell it to people and buy a shop from the cashop as well to sell it on the free market. While it may seem easy to get a decent bossing range for the profitable drops, it's really not. Nexon obviously only cares about the people who spend money on their game because pretty much all of the end game bosses except maybe Zakum require you to have godly potentials on all your equipment and weapons and a 200k+ ranges to even fathom killing them.
The quests in this game are so tedious it's not even worth doing 99% of them. The only ones people ever bother with are the prequests for bosses and even then they're huge time wasters. Maplestory brings nothing new to the MMO table as far as quests go. The only three quest archetypes they have are the "gather x, kill x, or talk to x who is continents away from you and takes hours to get there". Many of the collect and kill quests also have quest specific items that have insanely low drop rates that will have you grinding at the same monster for hours hoping that your etc tab doesn't fill up with useless crap. Even when you DO finish the quests the rewards are utter crap. Like I said before, people only do the prequests that let you go to the boss room because they're the only ones worth doing. The rest of the quests scattered around Maplestory will give you meager amounts of xp that you could've gotten thrice over by grinding in half the time and money that will barely be enough to pay for travel fees, much less potions to grind more. TL;DR, quests are a waste of your time.
The class system of Maplestory is...meh at best. Even though Maplestory boasts a large array of classes, the older ones will always get the short end of the stick. Since it seems that Nexon's only goal in life is to make money and♥♥♥♥♥♥on their players in the meantime, this means that the new shiny class that just came out will be infinitely better than the older classes. If you want to play the class that will do the most damage, has the coolest looks, or just kills things the fastest, it will NOT be from the older classes. The class system in this game is very much an "anything you can do, I can do better" style. Let's take a look at Luminous, one of the newer mage classes of the game, and Ice/Lightning mages that have been around since the game launched in 2006. Ice/Lightning mages have a skill called Chain Lightning. It bounces between 6 enemies and even hit enemies on lower platforms because of its large range but it can only travel in one direction. Luminous also have a skill similiar to Chain Lightning but it's called Reflections. Reflections hits 8 enemies (already better than Chain Lightning), but it can also loop back on itself and curve much more than Chain Lighting could ever do.
The grinding system of this game is terrible. Although it wasn't as bad as pre Big Bang patch, the leveling is system is still tedious and grind heavy. There are limited areas to grind since there are only ~24 channels for each world which means that finding a map to grind on can get tedious when all the channels are full. There are plenty of alternatives to the monsters you can kill, but the xp you get from them is negligible at best or the map is so huge that killing them takes more effort than it's worth. Even if you can get past how grindy the game is, leveling is still an absolute monster. Even before the level cap was raised to 250, getting to 200 (the previous max) is unfathomable. Around level 160 the exp gained from mobs stagnates to about 0.001% per mob and you have to get a full 100% to level. Oftentimes on my lvl 150 chars I find myself dozing off while grinding because grinding is so repetitive and boring. Although killing monsters isn't as bad as "mash 1 button and win", Maplestory steps it up by being "press 3 buttons and win". All the classes have such a myriad of buffs to reapply on horrendously short durations so you can look forward to having to recast those every 2 minutes if you want to level.

I only recently got round to playing this. I enjoyed it slightly more than Bioshock, and it was infinitely better than Bioshock Infinite. It was still a disappointment in some ways, especially for someone who loved Deus Ex, System Shock, Vampire TM Bloodlines and so on, but at least I knew what to expect after Bioshock.
The inventory system was incredibly dumbed down. I mentioned this in my reviews for the other Bioshock games, I won't repeat that here. Likewise the problems with the whole Plasmid/Adam/Eve system.
Again, the teaser trailer made the game look a lot more exciting and impressive than it really is, so was misleading.
Bioshock 2 had a few extra issues of its own.
Sound effects often cut out for me, leaving me unable to hear much until the action calmed down.
Bioshock 2 is set years after the events of Bioshock, yet every room is packed with Eve hypos and first aid kits and food – why haven't they all been used up? Who is still making the donuts?
Finally, you can get Little Sisters to harvest Adam – but only from particular corpses, old ones, even though you just killed a heavily-spliced enemy that is all fresh – no, that Adam is lost. And you can’t drag the corpse to a better place, one that is safer for harvesting - it is always in the middle of the room so you and the Little Sister will get attacked from multiple angles. It's silly. Gaminess over-riding believability.
I still maintain that the true Bioshock game has yet to be made.

Marvel Puzzle Quest is meant to be a puzzle game with RPG-ish elements where you can level up your character and increase the damage of their attacks by spending points on them. The thing is that you rarely get these points (coins in-game). You can tell that this game is the typical free-to-play game when they hit you with the fact that you either have to waste health packs on your heroes to recharge their health or wait 10 minutes to heal your heroes. Marvel Puzzle Quest is really designed as the average mobile game where you come back after your characters are able to be used (i.e. Injustice Mobile). So this is a Marvel version of puzzle quest, which is basically bejeweled except your actions control characters' attacks. There is a cool factor to this where you can increase the powers of your heroes by using resources you collect (Iso-8 Crystals) BUT you can't even purchase these upgrades until you purchase another "layer" of your character... AND THE THING IS that you can't do that without COINS, YES RARE♥♥♥♥♥COINS!!! Level 1 upgrades are 125 coins and I just want to point out that 200 coins costs 2 DOLLARS!!! Why do the creators try to screw us like this? But besides this In-Game-Purchase BS, the story really isn't even interesting, and the dialogue is quite boring. If only the heroes and villains had voices behind them it would be more interesting. This game does have some pros to it buy mostly cons. Not recommended...maybe to puzzle quest fans and very patient people but it doesn't change the fact that this game has tedious recharge times, boring dialogue and an uninteresting story.

I heard about this game and saw a couple of lets plays on it, then bought it.  It is a very simple game, but it is not easy.  You start with a production floor, which can be increased.  The production floor is randomly generated, so it is different on every game.  The ingredients are also randomly generated with both positive and negative affects.  There are 20+ challenges with 3 different levels of completion each.  Not to mention the equipment and upgrades.
Is it repetitious at times, yes, but so are every other game in a similar genre.  The randomized aspects of the game keeps you from doing the same exact thing from challenge to challenge.  And the game does not take itself too seriously.  Yes, you can make a migraine medication that has headaches as a side affect.  And lets not forget the names of the medications you create.  You can name them yourself, or have the computer do it for you.  With a female contraception called (by the computer) Jeff's Preg Be-Gone, how could you name anything better than that.
Overall, it is a good game, and I paid full price for it, $25.  I do not normally pay full price on games, but wanted to support the developer.

Definitely enjoyed the game.  My thoughts after playing through Single Player CAMPAIGN (vanilla) only:
Pros:
-Loved the similarity to Warcraft and references to pop culture (Mil'Kuniss, GoT references, etc.)
-Features Kevan Brighting (The Stanley Parable) narrating your actions similar to Bastion.
-The game itself was a success, but I felt like a few of the key mechanics were slightly lacking (listed below) so I didn't list them up here.
Cons:
-Unit management could use some work (picking and dropping, selecting, the whole shebang)
-Paid DLC for extra campaign missions/whatever
-My narrator/dialogue kept getting interrupted by different things in the game (new dialoge, level ending).  Dunno what was causing it (couldn't find an answer online), but it saddened me because I loved the narrator and I also felt like I was missing information.
-Short campaign
Overall, I enjoyed the game.  It definitely had a Warcraft feeling to it which made me nostalgic.  Kevan Brighting narrating, along with the nods to pop culture, had me hooked.  I can't wait for Dungeons 3 to come out; I feel like with a little polish on the game overall (script, story/length, mechanics), 3 could be amazing.
Note: I frown on paid DLC, and the price-tag on these for the content advertised seems steep.  If they were on sale right now though, I probably would have picked them up on the spot, just so I could get me some more of this game.

+ In contrast to the previous entries in the series,
instead opts to go the more realistic route in terms of handling and gameplay. There is a definite increase in the learning curve when it comes to the handling; if you play the game similarly to how you played the first two games, you will notice that both understeering and oversteering will happen more often and you will need to use your brakes on tight corners much sooner than you’d expect. However, none of this is a negative point to the game. While it does end up making the gameplay more challenging, it only adds to the immersion that the game tries to create by taking a more faithful approach to real motorsports
+ As expected, the graphics--while not a huge leap in graphical prowess compared to the jump from the first to the second game--doesn’t fail to impress (for the most part). The lighting especially is probably some of the best I’ve seen in a videogame period. Though there may be some disappointing downgrades in some areas (such as the crowds and damage indications are noticeably worse, or barely any different than
), overall, they’re still at the high standard that the series has set out to achieve from the beginning
+ There is also a noticeable jump in difficulty compared to the previous games. I could relatively easily complete the earlier games on Hard difficulty, but in
on Medium difficulty, some races it can be a struggle to even get a podium finish (most notably on the Touring and Endurance disciplines). For me, I saw this as a positive, as I was challenged to perform to my best in order to succeed.
- Spending around 28 ½ hours in order to complete the career mode (essentially complete the GRID Legends Series) was somewhat of a struggle I must admit. I didn’t mind the long length. But it was the simple fact that you will be essentially be repeating the same events over and over (but in progressively better vehicles), which is very tedious to say the least. Granted some events requiring you to do two races on the same track back-to-back is how it is portrayed in motor sporting, but to the average gamer, it will only come off as the developers being lazy and just padding out the game by making you do the same races again and again. Being forced to play events you may not enjoy very much (such as drifting) in order to complete the career also only makes the whole experience more tiring than it should be
- Adding on to the previous point, the majority of the tracks this time are essentially cut from the previous games and added here again, to an even bigger extent than before, with very few new tracks being added at all. Some championships even make you do the same track again (but possibly in reverse, or the longer/shorter version of the track), which becomes extremely repetitive. A bigger variety in the amount of tracks available would have been such a good way to diminish the tedious nature the game ends up putting on display
- The same problem that existed in the first game has resurfaced here in terms of teammates being useless. You can direct them to play aggressively or defensively, but it ultimately has zero impact on how they perform in a race. It seems like they only put in teams to make it emulate motor sporting in general better, but it really just seems pointless to do so when they rarely perform higher than even 8th position
- Lastly, the dialogue again this time is probably the worst it has been in the series so far, with barely more than a few lines that just get repeated continuously, it’s as if they’re not trying anymore.
• While Codemasters did listen to fans and decided to re-implement the in-car view to the series here, people have complained (and it is definitely noticeable) that the view itself is blurry and poorly done. As I’ve stated before I don’t play using this view, but if this is the sort of thing that you dislike, then take this into consideration before deciding to purchase the game.

Not that great a selection of MP maps, but this means that you can learn the available maps much faster and know where to approach from or hide.  The game makes use of Battle Points that you earn as you capture objectives or kill players.  These BP's can then be used to buy equipment.  The equipment you want to buy you have to setup before each map starts.  This is a nice feature, but flawed.  There are different soldier classes, but every class can select any equipment that they may need.  This means that if you want to drive in an APC or Tank you may find yourself coming up against a sniper with a rocket launcher all of a sudden.  There is also a couple of drones that you can buy with the BP's, and they can be as annoying as *****!!!!  Couple of the maps that I have played has degenerated into a sniper shootout or a drone war.  This to an extent makes things a bit annoying.  Your uniform is also very bright that there is no chance of hidding in a bush.
Some of the cover that you can crouch behind, has an ability of clipping your bullets, although you have a clear line of sight past the cover.
Will I recommend the game, mmmm...  well maybe.  I got this game for free on the Humble Bundle store.  Will I buy it... Definately NOT!!!   So if you can get the game for free, give it a try, but if you come from the Battlefield franchise, rather give this one a pass.

Preface: I "recommend" this game, but only because there's no in-between choice.
The big additions in Hard Reset Redux from the initial 2011 release are readjusted enemy spawns and damage, infinite sprinting, quick dashes, and a katana.
The new enemy spawns and stats are much easier than before. Enemies as a whole hit softer and have less health, and many of the encounters have less going on (though there are a lot more flying enemies). "Insane" mode in Redux (the hardest difficulty before the beat-it-in-one-go Heroic mode) is probably the same difficulty as Hard in the original, or maybe even easier than that if you're judicious with the sprinting and dashes.
Much of the difficulty in the original game was through how limited the player's movement is, making it easy to get boxed in by swarms of enemies or constantly pegged by projectiles. It was a more methodical shooter than many gave it credit for, and it rewarded planning over raw reflexes. Redux's infinite sprint and new dashes a la Shadow Warrior makes that almost completely moot. It's now possible to dash circles around enemies and dodge just about everything, making combat feel much faster and reflexive (especially with the katana), but also undeniably easier.
The katana is introduced about three or four levels in, and it's pretty much a simplified version of Shadow Warrior's - left click to swing, right click to hold for a harder swing. Redux's dismemberment system is less visceral than SW's, and the fact that the sword is so basic and has no upgrades like the guns means that there's no need to ever use it, so it's really just a novelty. I enjoyed softening up crowds of enemies and then jumping in to slice them to pieces, but it's still probably more efficient to just gun them down. There's a new "zombie" enemy essentially designed for the sword, but they're extremely weak and barely even attempt to attack, which is perhaps telling of the sword's usefulness otherwise.
Someone described Redux as "Hard Reset with a Shadow Warrior mod," and that's a pretty good summary. I would probably recommend Redux only to people who really liked Shadow Warrior or couldn't get into the original Hard Reset. I enjoyed it a lot, but I also loved SW and considered HR to be just good. If you are someone who sincerely thinks HR was a great game, Redux will probably be a letdown.
If this would be your first go-around with Hard Reset, however, I'd recommend you give the original version a shot first. If you end up getting too frustrated with it, then give Redux a go - it might be right up your alley. On the other hand, if the original HR clicks with you, then only look at Redux if you're interested to see what a faster, easier version feels like.
(A side note: After beating Redux, I went back to the original and played it on "Insane", and l ended up enjoying it much more than I did before, and maybe even more than Redux itself. Of course, that's just me.)

Got this game for free from HumbleBundle. For a free game, it's not terrible. At it's best, it's a pretty average military FPS. But I find it a hard game to recommend for any price more than a few bucks.
First off, this campaign is
It only took me about three and a half hours to complete on the normal difficulty without rushing anything. Not only that, the game ends on what feels like a cliffhanger for a sequel that'll never get made (Homefront: The Revolution is apparently not related to this game's story). You can replay it if you really want the collectables and achievements, but there's not much else.
Other than the length, the campaign is your typical, linear, heavily-scritped, military FPS campaign. The actual shooting mechanics are pretty good and a few of the combat sequences can be fun to fight through. Unfortunately, most of the time the game wants to hold your hand through the story by having you follow slow NPCs or wait for them to tell you to do something. Not only that, but the campaign can get buggy at times with NPCs getting you stuck in a doorway or friendly characters ignoring enemies right in front of them.
The story itself is also pretty diappointing. It's starts off strong with a good intro to the game's world, but then fizzles out in the end. I personally didn't care for any of the characters and the dialogue is mostly pretty cliché. The game tries to show some "shocking" moments that instantly lose thier effectiveness once the shooting starts back up.
The multiplayer portion of the game fares a little better that the single player mainly because it has some neat ideas that were new at the time of the game's release. The gameplay is what you get when you mix Battlefield's large maps and vehicles with Call of Duty's perks and shooting mechanics. During a match, you'll earn BattlePoints for objectives and kills which you can use to buy equipment on the fly (like armor, RPGs, and airstrikes) or spawn in a vehicle. Players who are on a killstreak have their area marked on the enemy team's map making it more risky for them to stay in one place.
Matches can be fun and intense about half of the time and frustrating for the other half. Maps can get too chatoic very quickly when there's constant helicopters, tanks, drones, and airstrikes littering the map. Unless you're camping with a sniper rifle or good with an RPG, don't expect to last long as a normal infantry soldier. Bad spawn points and lag can also detract from the experience. There were times where I spawned in the vicinity of an enemy or got immediately blasted by an airstrike. The player count is currently on the low side, so don't expect too many populated servers.
My overall score: 2.5/5. It has it's moments, especially in the multiplayer, but is mostly underwhelming.

I've been playing for a while now, and I played many hours of the previous Duels of the Planeswalkers games, at the game's urging I am finally writing a review.
Pros:
If you are a fan of MtG, and want to play an online version, this is the best-looking interface out there by far.
It is free-to-play, and daily quests and rewards for multiplayer victories allow you to buy boosters at a pretty steady pace, even if you spend no money. You could even grind against the AI if you wish to do so.
They are releasing content that is contained in the current paper magic sets, which is pretty cool. They slipped up with Oath of the Gatewatch, choosing not to release it at all until the release of Shadows over Innistrad, but perhaps going into the future they'll consistently release content contemporaneous with the paper sets.
Cons:
The game is pretty buggy.  Multiplayer can lock up quite a bit when it looks for a new player. Most frustratingly, there are points when you cannot exit matchmaking if its taking way longer than is acceptable, forcing you to close the program entirely. I was unable to even play single player matches after the latest update until I learned that in order to make it work properly I had to delete all my decks and make them over again. It wasn't the end of the world, but it was extremely dumb.
Whenever you go into your collection, a pop-up appears inviting you to the Magic Duels store. There is no way to make that go away that I can find in the game. Additionally, whenever you win your first online match of the day, another pop up appears inviting you to write a review about the game. In fact, the reason I am writing this now is in the hopes that I can make one of the pop ups dissapear forever, because they become extremely annoying after a while.
There is a cool feature introduced in multiplayer that when a player quits the match it gives you the option to keep playing or to exit the match, with the assurance that your rewards will stay the same regardless. The problem is that it only happens some of the time, and the rest of the time you have to finish the match against the computer (or let's just say I finish it out just to be sure I get my rewards.) Why does this happen?
While the GUI is the best that an online Magic game has ever had, it is nowhere near as good as the one for Hearthstone. The difference in animation, sound, and overall presentation is pretty sizeable. Not that it's bad necessarily, but it could be better.
The game gives out daily quests, which is good, but some types of quests can only be completed with decks made using the Deck Wizard (a guided process that does not allow you full customization options for your deck). While it's true you can cycle those quests away, IMO there should not be such a restriction on those types of quests that they don't even explain is there. I only found about it through the forums. Regardless, progress achieved in a quest should count regardless of the process used in creating the deck that fulfilled the requirement. The fact that it doesn't happen is pretty ridiculous.
Conclusion:
While I enjoy the game, I was torn on what review to give it. IMO it still doesn't compete with its largest competitor, Hearthstone, but if you're a fan of MtG, this is the most fun way to play it outside of paper. Ultimately I would only recommend playing it if you're already a fan or want to try the game out for free. In either case, though, I would not recommend spending money on it. I have not spent a penny on it and do not plan to in the near future. So I guess I can't really recommend it if in doing so, people would then start paying into it. It is not really there as a game that deserves that at this point in time. However, if you establish that you will just enjoy the game for what it is, like I do, and don't feel the pull to spend money on it, you can have some fun.
*Update*
Once again, persistent pop-ups asking me to leave a review (though I already left one) pull me back here to update my old review in the vain hope that the developers will actually read it and make them go away in the future. This aspect of the game has not been improved unfortunately, but other really annoying issues about the game have been fixed, such as the ability for players to pause the game and leave, forcing you to either remain in the game forever, or quit the game and take a loss. Also, obviously, there is more new content with the new set. I don't want to go too in depth about the good or bad aspects (as I aleady have), but suffice to say you may only find yourself getting really into this game if you are particularly interested in playing Magic (which I am), but due to the game's shortcomings and issues still unfixed after several months it is hard for me to recommend the game to general players, and certainly not to spend money in.

I've been thinking about how to review this game, ever since I heard of the steam release. I've played this game for a very long time, dating back to when Nexon was publishing the game, and ran it into the ground. I'm a bit of a fanatic, you see.
I think it's only fair that I criticize the game as harshly as I can muster, to present a realistic representation of it. You should know in advance that in spite of its many shortcomings, I still recommend it, because there's nothing else quite like it on the market. The only games that have come close shut down long before an english translation was even in the realm of possibility, because Neople pretty much has a monopoly on this specific subset of online brawlers. Anyway, on to the meaty stuff.
The interface is terrible. It's not uncommon for games of Korean origin to have confusing interfaces that simultaneously overload you with information, while simultaneously failing to deliver critical information when you need it. To be fair to Neople, they've done a lot to clean it up since its initial launch. But i've recommended this game to a few of my friends, and an increasingly common complaint is the interface. The moment you login, you're bombarded with notifications about events that you have no appreciation or understanding of, before you even know how to move your character, manage your inventory, attack the monsters, and use your skills. I personally don't have a problem parsing the visual overload, but i've been playing this game whenever it's available in English since the original Nexon release several years ago.
Controller support is rubbish. It technically works, it automatically detects dpads and analog sticks so you can move around right away. But no other button is bound, meaning you have to go through and manually bind jump, attack, two skill activator buttons, 12 skill hotkeys, 6 item slots, and several other buttons, possibly before you even know that you'll be expected to use them. No effort has been made on Neople's part to adapt the interface to better suit controllers or even provide default bindings for common controllers like Xinput devices, which adds a lot of setup time to your first launch. To really play the game with as little keyboard and mouse interaction as possible, most players rely on external programs like Xpadder, since it allows you to macro things up in a way that the game itself does not support. Again, not a problem for a diehard fan like me that already knows how to play the game, but it presents a significant barrier to someone new to this game that claims partial controller support on the store page.
The bulk of your leveling experience will be spent snoring your way through dungeons that are too easy. It's not until much later that you'll unlock access to higher difficulties for scenario dungeons, which could lead to many players getting bored of the game before they get to see what it really has to offer.
A big point in Neoples' favor is that, once you acclimate to the game, there's a ton of content on offer - nearly limitless dungeons to explore, dozens of completely different playable characters to explore them with, and multiple systems in place that encourage you to play more than one character, too. The in-game shop is generous with its pricing on non-cosmetic items, letting you buy valuable perks that affect long-term gameplay like stash space for pennies on the dollar. Many events that they run shower you with premium items and avatars, which means many people who treat this game as truly free to play can still play it without ever feeling the need to drop a dime. If you really want to differentiate yourself, you will need to drop some real money on Avatars (or fork over in-game gold to other players that have done so already), and there are ways for you to support the continued development of the game in the form of monthly subscription packs, cosmetic perks, and items that can slightly alleviate certain end-game specific grinds.
I don't know if Neople putting this game on Steam will get them the revenue they're expecting. But i'll certainly be doing my part to spread the word, and continue to support this one of a kind game.

After I finished the original Bioshock 1 I immediately wanted the sequel to see how it would continue and what happened after the first game. I wanted a game that would show me just what happened after Jack left Rapture and the city was left to rot for 10 years at the bottom of the ocean. I guess I got just what I want, which is probably my main complaint about this game. It feels like afterwash from the original in a way that it feels like I'm playing a DLC for the original or maybe even reading a fan continuation. The environments you got to explore, while still pretty cool, weren't usually as big or as major to Rapture as the ones and Bioshock 1. I feel like they should have added the older locations into this game on top of the fresh environments to make it feel like you're going through the same city. Also, to make sure that people don't get confused about the lore, no more bathyspheres.
The story isn't anything to write home about, either. You control a special Big Daddy named Subject Delta who, can you guess what the main conflict is going to be? Yeah, he's looking for his Little Sister who was kidnapped. I mean, she was already kidnapped, but she was... Kidnapped... Back... It's a bit predictable, unlike the Bioshock 1, but the story still held suprises for me, even without a major twist in the middle. The characters have to be either the best or the worst thing in this game when it comes down to it. I really liked the characters like Sinclair, who reminded me of Atlas from the first game and Eleanor, your little/big sister. The antagonist was... Okay to say the least. Like the first game it had a pretty powerful message with it but I felt she talked a little too much. I know. It's a pretty stupid thing to complain about, but when she radios you every 5 MINUTES SAYING THE EXACT SAME f*$#ING THING OVER AND OVER AGAIN YOU GET A BIT TIRED, OKAY? As for the other characters, they were kind-of forgettable. Each section has a different character belonging to it, and at the end you get to either kill or spare them. Now, the endings system is alot bigger than Bioshock 1's was as in there are 6 endings instead of just 2. It has the same Harvest or Rescue Little Sisters system (with a fun Little Sisters protect minigame thing!) But, like I said, it also has different characters to kill or to claim mercy on. First is Grace, who I could understand sparing. The second guy I could also understand sparing and still being labeled as good. But the third guy, oh my gosh why are you even supposed to spare him and still be labeled as good? He begs you to kill him in audio recordings because he's insane and he is a giant mutant blob who can't move for Gods sake! How are you helping ANYONE by not killing him? I actually didn't know what to do when I got to this point because they both seemed bad thing to do. If you do kill him, you get labeled as a murderer in the ending, though! But what about those hundreds of splicers and big daddies you mowed through like overgrown weeds! They're insane too, but don't they deserve a chance at life if a giant mutant blob who can't move does?
All in all, I liked the new gameplay and plasmid system. The weapons for your Big Daddy self were also really cool. I especially liked the one where you could hack from a distance or place mini turrets. Anyway, that's just my two cents on this game. If you enjoyed the first I would recommend it for everything it has to offer.

Is this game worth it? I can't say from a Free-to-Play perspective as I bought the game when it was in Early Access.
Is the All-Champions Pack worth 30 USD? I would say yes.
Because it is FTP I would recommend you try it out for yourself. If you like MOBA-style combat, but dislike the laning and gold grinding for items, I'd say this game may be what you're looking for. If it does have a beta mode called "Battlegrounds" that does have MOBA elements like lanes and creeps with an objective that you must destroy to win.
This is basically an Area-Based, top-down fighting game where almost all skills are skill-shots. Even the healing. Like any MOBA, positioning plays a major role in how well you do in fights. Fights are either 2v2 or 3v3. Team choices also play a major role in how well you do. There is a practice mode against AIs and a playground where you can try out all champs and Battlerites.
What are Battlerites? Battlerites are modifiers for your skills that add certain effects like increased duration or decreased cooldowns. Some also add healing and increased dmg, but some can change how you use them by giving them the ability to add debuffs that can factor into how you use your other skills. As of Nov. 22, 2017, you can pick a set of 5 Battlerites and save them into a "build" that you then choose at the start of a match. All 5 are applied at the beginning and cannot be changed or switched out for that match.
There is a pretty diverse set of champions to play. The devs did a good job on making each champion have a unique style of fighting. They recently added (Nov. 22, 2017) a ranged champion that takes many elements from Samus Aran from the Metroid games. They all are voice acted and have a range of customization options from weapon skins to victory poses to outfits. There are mounts, but mounts only serve to get you into the battle faster, as none have any benefits.
There are 3(!) different currencies in the game. The first Gems (a dark blue icon) is the premium currency used to buy gold and event chests. Gems are bought with your real money. The second is Tokens ( the light green icon) are used to buy all the skins. Tokens can be earned from leveling up heroes, found in chests, and recieved when you get a duplicate item in chests. The third currency, Battle Coins (gold icon), are used to purchase Silver Chests and Champions if you are a Free-To-Play player. Also, if you ever aquire a legendary outfit for a champ, you can purchase a different color.

Nice RTS-like game that got me into this dungeonkeeper genre. I got it for free at bundlestars or something, but after playing through the campaign, which took me like 17 hours (with some idle), I am tempted to buy the dlc to also give it a go as an undead.
In this game you build a dungeon as an evil overlord. You can send your units to the overworld once you have enough of them to defeat the "alliance". The campaign introduces all units gradually throughout the missions and incorporates some very obvious (and a little obnoxious) GoT, Warcraft and LoTR references and more. I did eventually have to shut up the narrator in the settings, he just got way to talkative.
The graphics remind me a lot of Warcraft 3, and this is probably what Warcraft 4 would've looked like if it was released by the same blizzard that made the third one.
It surely has some flaws though, like creatures running around while not proriotizing tasks that might seem more important. But it could also just be up to the player to balance out his dungeon. It seems to try and find a balance between fighting with your creatures and using traps, but the traps feel like a huge resource drain, rather than functional things. I also would've liked to play a little longer as the chaotic evil in the campaign, those two missions felt quite rushed, especially the second one where you just get to upgrade to the max.
Other than it having some flaws, and not being too challenging (but maybe you're not looking for one) it's an excellent game to sit back, play and have some fun with.

According to description, Big Pharma is a game about creating medicine recipes and selling them for profit. But it focuses more on production process then profit. It is safe to say Big Pharma is a game about creating an efficient production line to achieve your (scenario) goal.
The game has a tutorial, but instead of (usual) series of interactions, tutorial itself is actually a guide-like-text in “tutorial scenarios”. If player can follow the text, it is quite helping and explains the details to a certain degree. Still, for the first few games, it is highly expected that the player will revisit these tutorials. It is also worth noting that the game expects the player to have “planning skills” because it never mentions how a good/efficient layout should be.
In this game, player is given a set of machines, and a number of ingredients. Every ingredient has one curing effect and one to three bad side effects (There are 4 effect slots on each ingredient). Each effect on an ingredient is active on certain “concentration range” and is most effective at a certain concentration. This concentration and activation of effects are the elements that create the base of the game. The player is expected to create a production line using the given machines, to activate the positive effect on an ingredient and create a medicine. Of course, bad side effects are present and are to be avoided. Curing effects on the final medicine increase the value and side effects causes it to lose rating resulting in losing value.
Illnesses and cure recipes are known, and when you produce a medicine, more advance version is unlocked, up to level 5 medicines. Although illnesses and cure recipes are known, ingredients are not. For each game, ingredients are randomly generated. Only things consistent among games are that each ingredient having only one curing effect and activation range of effects. From effect combinations to how much those effects change final medicine’s value is random. This increases replayability value. But it is also random for scenarios; therefore it affects the actual difficulty of the scenarios. One time the game may be too challenging and other time, it may be too easy.
Another randomly generated content is layout for production buildings. In each map, there are several (depending on the size of the map) partitioned buildings. The player is randomly given a partition at the beginning and buys the rest. The buildings and sockets are premade but layout of the buildings is random. Depending on the layout and starting position, the game may be annoying. Annoyance comes from shape of the buildings or the socket positions/count in a partition. Sockets are the points of entry/exit for the ingredients and medicines, on the walls of the buildings. Although there are at least 2 sockets in almost every partition, it can be more. Starting a partition with 4 sockets enables the player to have two production lines, without the need to but new partitions. Also a bad shaped building may prevent you to complete an advance production line required for the higher level medicines.
There are also exploration, research, patenting and “company management”. Research is the common knowledge. Player hires scientists to do research. Research unlocks new machines and some infrastructure projects such as cheaper machine prices or ability of exploring different types of lands. Exploration is the same thing as research but unlocks new ingredients instead. On a normal game, only the most basic machines and only 2 ingredients are available at the start. Rest is unlocked through researching and exploration. That said, researching and exploration are just a tab in the game and not the main focus. Same thing applies for the “company management”. Other than patenting process, company management is just an info tab showing player’s medicines, yearly revenue and profit. Also rivals’ basic info can be seen in company management. There is a research that enables to see detailed info about your rivals but it is pretty much useless. Patenting is what the name suggests. Patenting a medicine prevents the others from selling the same medicine for a limited time. The length of time depends on how much player chooses to spend on the patent.
Rivals in the game serve two purposes. One of them is to cause saturation because they use the same ingredient as the player and produce (mostly) the same medicine. This saturation increases the cost of ingredients and lowers the demand for a specific cure effectively lowering value of medicines. The other purpose is to patent medicine preventing the player to sell the same medicine. Of course the player has access to patenting after researching it too. This creates a nice “patent war” situation in the game, but patenting is pretty expensive and mostly not worth it until late game.
As with all of the production themed games, most of the time in the game will be spend in paused mode. The player will try to make a good choice of ingredient-medicine pair to avoid side effects. After that, he/she will spend an equal time to position each machine in a way that they will occupy the least space. Since it is the nature of the game it is not a bad thing. Still, it is worth noting that machines can only be rotated in 4 directions and belts (connections between the machines) can’t be multi-layered (although they can be crossed and it mostly works well). These limitations may annoy some people, but also some “puzzle people” may welcome them because it gives the production a puzzle feel.
The interface is very well designed and the player is never lost in it. It has a futuristic design and goes well with the game. The sound effects of the game are nice and do not bother the player. But the game is a bit quiet. It needs a few more soundtracks.
Finally, a personal note: Everything in the game is sold back at half the original price. Especially at the beginning, you  may struggle with the design and make lots of mistakes. Buying and selling the belts will cause you to lose lots of money. To prevent this, plan and imagine the whole process in your mind, put all the machines first and then put the belts. It is also possible to get the “free belts” mod from the official site.
All menus and tabs are cleverly put together in a clear and simple manner.
Game elements go well together.
There is nothing to get in the way during interaction with objects and interface.
It does not support workshop but has a separate mod support.
This results in the campaigns becoming too easy or too hard.
Sometimes building designs are too narrow or weirdly shaped and they do not allow a good production line.
Although some of the content is randomized, after a while, the game feels repetitive due to its focus on production. This may be a deal breaker for some people.
If you think this game as a production tycoon game -as I did- it is well made (considering this is developed by a one-man-company). Overcoming the challenge to get rid of the bad side effects and creating a high rating medicine gave me enough satisfaction, so I recommend it. But because it focuses on production, it may be insufficient for some people.

Those of us who hate Drifting get nickel and dimed by DLC that should have been included in the game itself.
I like the difficulty of this game. I like that it's hard, that it makes me think about what I'm doing, that it's closer to a simulator than most games are these days. That's all great. I really wish I could give this game the thumbs up.
But I can't.
This game has decided that "drifting," a showboating activity, should be an integral part of racing. The Majority of cars you have access to in this game are "Drift Cars."
Or to put it another way, this game features cars with looser back ends than a trucker with irritable bowel syndrome in a budget diner. You can't slide around a corner in any of these cars without the back end kicking out, because the game wants you to take your car sideways.
I really enjoyed the "grip" style cars, where when one slid around a corner, the back end stayed right where it should, instead of trying to rub itself on a guardrail.
But Codemasters decided to make grip cars DLC. In the beginning of Season 4, instead of offering me a Drift Car, a Balanced Car, and a Grip car, it offered me two drift cars, and the chance to unlock more cars. Great, I said, and went through the painful process of unlocking each secret car one by one, only to discover that they are all bleeding drift cars. Every single one of them.
I can get my hands on a grip car if I purchase some DLC.
Which I'm not doing.
Instead, I'm telling you not to spend money on this game, and uninstalling it immediately.
Codemasters, I'm never buying a racing game from you again.
Cutting grip cars from the game and then trying to sell them back to me as DLC was a terrible idea, and one that's lost codemasters a customer.

"Oh God, not another race!" is the phrase I use the most when playing this game. The reason being that when I bought a racing game, I was hoping I'd be racing.

Let's get the obvious out the way, yes it's another Dungeon Keeper wannabe. If the screenshots haven't given you that impression already then gameplay-wise yes, it's very similar to the inspiration but that's only half of the game. Not only you build an undergound lair with traps and treasuries, you are also in command of your evil forces on the surface. Yes, this game is also a real time strategy game where you can strike back at the invading heros by sending them to the surface and destroying their encampments.
The plot is straightforward with you being an evil entity banished into a spirit form and is out to exact revenge by taking over the kingdom with an army of doom, the Horde.
The game is very reference heavy, if you like that sort of thing. Referencing all kinds of fantasy themed books, movies, tv-shows and other video games and is all presented to you by Kevan Brighting, the same who narrated the life of a man named Stanley. Who isn't afraid to break the fourth wall too while he tells the story of the rise of your evil empire.
I recommend this game if you enjoy base management and real time strategy games.

Every year or so I reinstall the best game ever made, period: Freelancer. Never has a game been so far ahead of its time. Combat is complex enough to be exciting, simple enough to make it easy to pick up and play. Story is a bit cheesy but it's lots of fun. And Edison Trent is one of the coolest characters in all of video games. He doesn't brood about his past, he doesn't think he is the best pilot in the galaxy. He is plesant but not uptight. It's refreshing to have an 'everyman' who actually acts like a normal human being.
Anyway, this game fails all of those things. No main character, really, story isn't cinematic. Combat is definitely more like a sea ship experience which is fine. It packs in a lot of depth and thought in theory, but most of the time it's just 'line something up in your general sights and let autotarget do the rest'. Freelancer is far more exciting and rewarding with dogfights and systems that trade complexity for less hand holding.
What works better than Freelancer is all of the other little things that slowly became gripes for me in Freelancer. Scanning, missions (it's still go here, shoot things, but hacking bounty boards, answering distress calls, unidentified signals, mining, etc really fills it out), flight rules based upon location, a much larger breadth of equippable systems from shields to scanners and beyond, the mere fact that you don't have to use trade lanes to travel fast (as far as I've seen so far), on top of all the little things that made mechanics in Freelancer great (trade, factions, patrols, etc), it makes for a better world mechanic.
tldr: Freelancer is better at core mechanics and polish, Rebel Galaxy improved all the side stuff. It scratches the itch, but Freelancer is still the best space arcade sim out there. Definitely play this if you love Freelancer, you'll have a good, but not great, time.

The gameplay itself has its ups and downs. One thing that really annoys me is the constant lag spikes at points where I assume the game is loading in new elements. Granted, my rig is not the greatest, but the game would suffer in FPS when a new area needs to be loaded, sometimes during a fight. The AI of this game is truly one of its biggest failings, from simple things like obstructing doorways and excessive scripted events blocking off new areas, to walking past enemies completely, throwing grenades at your position, or just standing idle. The enemies are not much better, either somehow killing you incredibly quickly, or just not being able to hit you at all.

After Grid 2, I felt there was a lot of good things to be made in the next instalment in the GRID series and I was happy to find out that many were improved. I have invested easily twice the time when comparing to GRID 2 and there was a reason for this. The multi-disciplined Events offer you a lot more variety and it's great for those who are a fan of mixing different race styles. From Endurance races to Tuner and Street you also have Touring Events and Open Wheel as well giving you different tastes of what's available in the racing words. For me all were great aside of any Drift events. It's nothing personal but I love to race in all sorts of classes but when it comes to win by points in a corner by making good use of your handbrake the racer fan in me feels a bit bored.
As you advance in all events you will get a chance of having better sponsors interested in you with more difficulty and challenging objectives to complete such beating a rival time, finish above 5th place, then 3rd place and so on.
There is a clear effort in making this game a pleasant experience for the racing fans but even after so many efforts there is still much to be done. Endurance races are great but it lacks some proper tuning and the duration of most of them are not really what I would call endurance since the bigger ones are around 12 minutes long. Qualifications are back and it's a great opportunity to set a time to start on a better position.
The audio is the best effort I've seen in the grid series. You really do not need any soundtrack or any other sound effect. You just need to remove all the hud in the game, increase the volume and you will have such a good time driving while pushing to the max to the next gear. There are also little things that did not go unnoticed. For instance, you can ask (with the D-pad) what is the current state of your car (gearbox, engine damage, etc) as well the position of your rival, team-mate and so on. If you are entering a tunnel and you ask for this info you can see there's a difference in the sound from the speaker since the signal may be weaker. These little things are always appreciated. One last thing regarding the sound: I loved GRID 2 main theme and it's a such a shame that I felt a downgrade regarding the tunes/themes in the menus (not to mention these menus are quite... bland).
Then there are the community feedback that Codemasters did or tried to achieve with things like the Cockpit view. For many racing fans this view not only is a must but it's also the only view they play their racing games. So, in order to keep fans happy Codemasters implemented this view but to be honest this was the most poor effort I've seen in adding something that is a big request in these games. First I thought that my eyes were deceiving me because I've played and seen many recent games with great looking cockpit views like Driveclub and Project Cars so it crossed my mind I was not being fair to GRID Autosport since this game was released some time ago. Then I just remembered. Games like Dirt 2 or Dirt 3 do have a cockpit view and they are quite nicely done, if you ask me. So what happened here? Was no time to develop a better view and they just tried a quick solution? For those who haven't seen it, go check it out. It's a dark, blurry mess with no details at all. Seriously. This was such a wasted opportunity and I can see why so many fans were upset with all this.
One thing I also liked was the Cups between the major events. This would be races without a team member and they had a great selection of either prototypes or older gems, something I'm fond of. But still, I wish I could have seen more of them.
In the end, I had great fun with Autosport. I played more than 50 hours, I did more than 400 races, leveled up every single category to level 10 or above and finished all the major events, all cups with many qualifications as well.
Side Curiosity: It is thanks to Ben Gouldstone, the Senior Game Designer of Driveclub that the racetrack from Algarve, in Portugal is a reality after he gave this feedback to the Codemasters team. It's great to see when companies are open to all sorts of feedback in order to bring more variety and content to their games.
