Small summary at bottom.
Do not compare this to HoN, Dota, Dota 2 or LoL. It's nothing like those games, if that's what you're looking for, go play them. It's an arena fighter that's intended to be played 3v3. It has low cooldowns and reaction skills rather than big aoe nukes/targeted abilities.
The visual style would have to be described as "tribal". It's not technically impressive but there's good design here and everything in the game is clear when you know the effects, similar to most "moba"'s in that way. Bloodline (character) design is focused more on reflecting the role of the character rather than looking cool (like some other games), so you get a feel for the mobility of a bloodline without knowing it for example.
Balance is pretty good. It's hard to tell at my level of play, I was Grade 9 for a while but after a long break I was grade three. But it doesn't seem very relevant because I've had a team of grade 3&4 go up against a team of grade 9-7 and win. I feel the teams are usually quite balanced however, you trade rounds and you don't get a lot of stomps (when you know your character and the opponents, otherwise the game is going to be very hard). I think that people complain about balance or blame the game because they expect their dota/lol/hon/whatever skills to carry over. This game isn't on nearly the same phase. You never cast all your long cool down abilities at once, you save some of them for a rainy day and react to your enemies.
Playing around ultimate abilities is vital for example, there's some that are completely unstoppable except for moving out of the way then there are some that are easily countered with trances/stuns. But even on the level I played on people didn't do this very much. You could easily get full ultimates off without any real problems.
There's profile-stat gains (traits), these are extremly insignificant. They affect your health/attackspeed/swiftness/cooldowns/energygain and cap etc by about 9% (tops, one of those). Which rarely comes into play. There's situational traits you can spec into, things like recieving 15% more healing when below 20% (generally 15% more healing for your next heal). Which can be really useful sometimes but it generally doesn't affect the outcome of a game. Also you're usually not great at the game at level 1. So you won't face people who have played the game for a long time usually.
Then there's medallions, these are bought for bloodcoins, you do not have access to a stock of these form the start. Which may seem stupid and unbalanced but they're very situational and I rarely use them. They're things like 1.5 seconds of slow for 30% of your energy, shield for 2.5 seconds that shield up to 300 damage (think 1700 is a pretty average health pool). Generally not worth it but will save you in certain situations. These are unlocked for 650-2000 bloodcoin. And imo the cheapest one is the most useful because mobility is very important in this gamre and it increases your MS for 3 seconds by 40% for only 25% energy.
Payment model:
The prices have been re-scaled since I last checked. Every bloodline was about 18k then and some slightly more expensive, currently they're all 10k. Using daily bloodcoin bonus (about 15 games a day) you earn you earn 75% of your base coin gain using the daily bonus. I've played 10 matches and depleted 570 coins from the daily bonus, I've been playing for about 30minutes. I've gotten 132 coins per game on average.  According to random sources online (and self-estimate) game lenght is about 5 mintues on average. Meaning you get about 1500 coins per hour. 6.6 hours for a champion/hero may seem like a long time for some. But this game isn't like the others, each character can easily be played for a very long time. They have more depth to them. Compared to a game like dota which unlocks all heroes from the start, it's obviously quite bad. But compared to League of legends it's nothing really. You also get one free bloodline (out of 7 you can pick from) after completing a few quests, extremely easy to do, I recommend holding off choosing until you've found one you like though.
Each one of them have 7 skills and two "ex"-abilities, ex abilities are powered up versions of an ability which costs power (gained by pickup or dealing damage/healing). They all have some special twist to them also, for example Harbinger heals himself via lifesteal on almost every attack, which changes how he's played drasticly. Inhibitor can boost damage via applying 3 stacks of his primary attack and can heal himself (when attacking) using his secondary attack. If he attacks a target with stacks of the other type they're popped for either extra heling to Inhibitor or extra damage to his enemies.
They all have twists like this in some way, some push away enemies, some root them, some spells synergizes with others some attacks just combo very nicely. It's a very special game and a competent player can solo 1v3 inferior players, you never feel that the game has ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥tted you in some way because you either wasted your spells inappropriately or your enemies played competently. There's no farm in the game and you're always on even ground. Most of the time it's hard to complain at the team because they usually pick a role different from you and they don't get focused the same way you do. Only exception is the tank+healer combo, generally the tank is supposed to make sure the enemies are either focusing him or that he's defending the healer in some way. Running around alone as a tank is generally stupid.
Matchmaking:
People complain that the game is dead, it's not on EU servers for me anyway. I get games rather quickly, not as quickly as you would hope considering the short game time. Compared to dota/lol the ratio of amount of time spent waiting divided by the time spent playing is higher, I estimate about 2x. But it's not an unbearable time. It's about 45seconds-1minute avg it seems.
I used to have problems with unbalanced bloodlines (there was this new one that was just way OP) but it has been fixed i think. And this is a problem with every moba. The only game that escapes slightly is Dota 2 because they release it on the test client/old WC3 Dota first so people play there and have opinions.
The game has an automated tournamnet system where you can sign up to, there's both open (any rank) and rank limited tournaments. When you win tournaments you earn tournament tickets you can spend on cosmetics like avatars/skins etc.
Also the supreme pack is a nice buy because that pretty much unlocks all of them, 25 out of 27 (assuming you spend your bloodcoins from the pack on a bloodline) (25€). I wouldn't bother with bloodcoin boosts, maybe if you get satisfaction from feeling you've earned them or the grinding is a thing for you but you consider it a bit harsh. I think they should look them over and make them more like Dota 2 boosts where you feel the amount of money spent is insignificant.
Summary:
-Way way faster phased than LoL/Dota 2 (doesn't necessarily mean it's better obviously but if you like fast games this is good)
-Each character has more depth to it and are generally very interesting roles, healers don't just cast heals all game, it's your primary "attack" but you do other things too
-Bloodline rotation every day (good/bad? dunno, lets you find what you like quickly)
-Game-deadness is overstated you do get games, I can imagine being a completely new player is tough though. You will learn quickly if you read up on the most popular characters (read them as you see)
-VERY short games, 5 minutes per game. Quick to get into a game and just play compared to other mobas.
-Skillful, no hero targeted spells. You shoot your own projectiles and you can hit or miss every spell or attack.
-Balanced lineups (but with focus on roles). It's hard to win without a healer, luckily people know this and pick accordingly
-Very Unique

I have mixed feelings about the campaign, but ultimately it left me unsatisfied. The gunplay is fun, but that's about the best I can say. Instead there's a big focus on set pieces, which is nice spectacle, but left me feeling like I was halfway watching a movie. The campaign is also really short (I beat it in <4 hours, and I am not great at video games) and feels rushed. It tries to tell a dark story about the horrors of war, but in the end it felt more like it was trying to be edgy. It needs you to care about the characters, but it's hard when the game gives zero time for character development.

Very great for a free to play game. Keep up with events, you wouldn't have to spend much on it save for looks. There is a service but it's almost given to you through events if you're dedicated enough to play.
You can customize your own button inputs for skills so you don't have to stick with the hotkeys. Makes playing with a controller great (Using a Steam Controller too).
Course this game was released way back then, but it's still holding up pretty well.
Now you may hear about how its repeatative, with fighting the same dungeons and enemies over again, especially if you make alts (which you'd most likely do and want to do), but each time is different based on who you're playing as. Pretty much whacking a punching bag but chaning how you fight every once in a while.
When it comes to PvP, however, I have no clue because I don't so there's that.
Cash shop isn't as expensive as it was when NA Nexon had it, and there's also a Mileage system that is a Cash Shop with its own in-game currency based on how much you play. Mileage shop doesn't have as much as the Cash Shop, but hey, it's a free to play.
Now there's the fatigue point system. Pretty much a limit on how long you can play on a certain character for a day. There are ways to fill it back up (once a day with certain items), and the weekend has it increased. It's a good way to not have you binge on the entire game, and keeps rare loot drops a bit more possible than having people endlessly grind them forever in a day.
In the end, it's free. Try it if you're just curious. I like it, I'll say I like it, I hope you like it, but I won't kill you for not liking it (someone might though!).

Hard Reset: Redux is an improved edition of Hard Reset that was released in 2012. A cyberpunk first person shooter.  Flying Wild Hog studio is well known for another other game, Shadow Warrior. The original game was not released on the consoles, so it is nice to see them get some love in this improved release of the title.
The game play does not differ from the original. You play through a grim world set in the future where the landscape is completely overrun by robots. These robots are the reason for the human race becoming near extinct. Your job, playing as Major Fletcher, is to face these dangerous enemies and fight for your races’ future.
Combat is very fast paced and hectic, leaving the player often facing hordes of enemies at once and some pretty powerful bosses too. You have access to multiple different types of weapons, a multi-function rifle, which can be improved to include attachments such as RPGs, grenade launchers, shotguns or mines, or a futuristic canon which has similar attachments, and this version of the game also comes with a new weapon, a cyber-katana sword. I can only assume this comes from the Shadow Warrior game as it plays very similar to how the melee combat works in that game. The other new feature to the game play, is the ability to perform quick dodges, this allows the player to easily manoeuvre out of the way of the enemies attacks and melee swings with a little finesse, rather than bunny hopping around the map. This quick dodge can also be used to zip across the map at speed.  The boss fights are challenging, as they incorporate waves of enemies as well different mechanics in order to defeat them. The level design is pretty well set out too; there was only a handful of times where I was completely lost and couldn’t work out where to go, each mission’s path is fairly linear, but it does allow for moments of exploration into side rooms and secret areas for extra loot and experience.
Graphically, Hard Reset Redux has been improved significantly, utilizing the latest version of the Road Hog engine. The upgrade features better lighting and special effects, on top of a generally snappier game in terms of performance too. The voice acting is few and far between, but sound effects were all on point.
If you played the original game, you may notice that some of the levels were shortened, or as the developers put it, “re-balanced” to allow for a better pace of game play. That being said, I managed to get just over seven hours of game play out of a single play through this game. The option for a New Game+ mode is also present upon finishing which is something I will definitely be giving ago.  The lack of a multiplayer mode may prove to be a slight error on the dev’s part, as the longevity of the game will not last more than two play throughs at the very least.
I really enjoyed my time playing through the improved version of Hard Reset – it had been a few years since I played the original so it was nice to revisit this game – it is definitely improved in both gameplay and the technical side of the game. Owners of the original game on Steam will be happy to hear they will get a heavy discount on Redux (85% off) which is well worth it! Personally I am not sure it is worth the full price of $19.99 – if you don’t have the original, you may want to wait for the sale season.

So, first game review ever. I also own the first Bioshock, but can't review it because I didn't get it from Steam. But I digress. This game is the perfect followup to the first Bioshock. My first playthrough was on hard, and it makes the struggle through Rapture a constant war and bloodbath that is intense and challenging, even as a powerful Big Daddy. The new weapons really changed things up, while keeping and improving the original plasmids. Combat flows more naturally, since you don't have to switch betweens weapons and plasmids but can use them simultaneously.
Now, the setting. Instead of an objectivistic society, now it is collectivist, striving for a disolving of the individual into "the family." I can't say too much about the plot without spoilers, but Big Daddies always have a Little Sister, and you are no exception. The story is strong, I think stronger than most give it credit for. It is good in its own right, but everyone (naturally) compares it to the first game, which has an exceptionally good story.
Crashing? I play on Mac (yes, it actually runs on Mac). And actually, it crashes only rarely, and no problem with my save files. Mostly, it has crashed in the Protector Trials, but even then, only occasionally.
With lots to explore, easter eggs that can almost make ya weep, combat that can feel totally awesome (turning yourself into a flamethrower is a real joy), and deep philosophical and moral questions at its heart, this game is excellent and I highly recommend it, even if you don't have the first game. That being said, get the first game. It's a masterpiece.

Have you ever played an RTS where you get really immersed in building the perfect base, but every new level throws away your hard work and forces you to start again from scratch? Big Pharma is like a distilled version of that.
It has 35 levels, all of which start you near the bottom of the tech tree. Pretty much every level will start the same - 10-20 minutes of building low-level supply chains, trying to get a profit while you wait for research to unlock. To make matters worse, building the supply chains is actually really tedious as you have to jump through the menus to research each stage of the process before you build it. You're constantly fighting to make a profit, and many of the levels have time limits.
Don't let my high playtime fool you - I was afk for a lot of that. Big Pharma is only good for about 3 hours. After that, there's just too much tedium and not enough fun.

For the first couple of days I played this game I was a little frustrated.  It seemed that the items were very overpriced (and they are), and that I couldn't get anything I wanted.  However, If you are smart at how you spend your money, use your items, and which characters you play, you can do very well in this game with little or no cash.  The real game is in the PvP, which isn't PvP at all really.  The Prologue, is just that, a starting to the real game.  Once you get 3 characters around 25-30 you can actually start playing the game which is all in building various teams who's abilities compliment each other.  I started out with Iron Man Model 35, Storm Modern, and Black Widow Modern.  This team will take you very far.  Now the anchor of my team is Black Widow Original.  She can heal and steal AP so I almost always end a fight with full health.  She does very well with Wolverine or Thor.  As you can see I've spent many hours playing this game on my PC (although half or more was probably AFK time.)  I've spent $10 on this game and I've felt it was a good choice.  My husband also plays and he spent $5.  We both spent the money to buy hero coins which we used to open slots for more characters. You will need at least 12 to get started and I currently have 18. 18 slots is enough to keep my favorites.  I never felt the need or pressure to buy for anything else.
A note on the PvP, you get to choose who you play.  If you don't like the team, press skip, and you will be presented with another choice.  You can find teams you can beat at any level and since the very dumb AI is controlling the opposing team you can generally beat teams much higher level with smart play.  You get either 70 or 140 ISO-8 for every match you win, and you should be winning nearly all of them since you get to choose who you fight.  With an average of 105 ISO-8  per match and matches lasting about 3 minutes  you can level up characters very quickly in RPG terms.  However it probably seems slow for a casual mobile app.  You get points in tournaments based on the ranking of the team you fight, not their level, so with smart picks and persistence you can rank well and get good rewards early on, but if you have to come in first, you're going to have to work hard and wait a long time.  In addition to the end of tournament rewards, there are frequently progression rewards which you get regardless of your final ranking.  As there are frequently multiple tournaments hapening simultaneously and shield trainer always available, even after you've exhauseted the story line rewards there is always plenty to do and more characters to collect.
I find Marvel Puzzle Quest fun and surprisingly addictive, yet not at all pay to win.  In fact, the items are so expensive that several hundred dollars wouldn't get you very far. So those who do spend mony don't have any real advantage beyond saving a few minutes.  In summary, if you can get over the slow grind to level 30, this game really takes off and becomes much more fun.  Don't spend hero coins or money on anything other than opening up more roster slots until you fully understand what you are getting in return (i.e. hardly anthing). Participate in the tournaments early and often as this is where the ISO-8 you need to level your characters comes from even if you don't place well.  I'm not surprised that the people who only played an hour don't like it, though.  It's not really a play for a few minutes kinda game.  It's much better suited to long sessions on the PC.  It's the most fun I've had for $10 in a while.

I played through single player with my Logitech G27 Racing Wheel. I didn't try playing it with a controller, but I do know that this game is designed to be controller friendly.
I found this game to give a really fun racing experience without being punishingly difficult or realistic. Unlike games that are designed to be simulations first, it really feels like GRID 2 is designed to be a fun game first.
The fun comes from a few things.
First of all, the racing does really feel "intense" - this comes through thanks to all the great visuals and sounds. It's not easy to describe, but there's just loads of polish on the overall aesthetic. The wide variety of levels and locations really helps here as well.
Second of all, they have lots of little ways to prevent you from getting frustrated. My favorite mechanic is the flashback mechanic - it basically lets you rewind time to undo a mistake you made. This is really great because not only does it prevent you from going "oh no, I need to restart the whole race...", it also gives you the opportunity to learn much more quickly. There's a limit to how many times you can do this so it doesn't make the game too easy. Furthermore, they have a wide range of difficulty settings for all levels of experience. I have only played a few racing games and found the Easy difficulty to be decently challenging without being frustrating. Finally, they have this guy who is talking to you all the time who will ocassionally offer useful suggestions and keep you focused on what to do during a race (and it doesn't get annoying, in my opinion).
Third, the overarching story of trying to get fame for the WSR feels like a pretty significant goal. There's lots of different ways you can advance the story (for example, if you don't like a particular type of event you can focus on other types of events).
My major issue with the game is that, towards the fourth WSR series, I felt like the content was becoming a bit same-y and it started to feel like a bit of a grind.
Overall, if you are interested in having a fun racing experience as a change from a hardcore, realistic racing sim, this game is pretty fun. I haven't played many other PC games in the genre, though, so take this recommendation with a grain of salt.

I had a lot of fun playing this game.  It has a lot of interesting features, but also some major drawbacks.
First, lets go over the pros.  There are 14 characters to choose from and although the control scheme for all of them is mostly the same, they all play and feel very different.   Each character is unique enough to drive you to try them all.  All of them have obvious strengths and weaknesses.  I didn't really feel like there were any characters that were blatantly OP or broken.  Some people are claiming that this game is Pay2Win, but that is mostly innacurate.  Aside from additional costumes ect. there are weapons and armor you can buy with either points earned in game, or with "gems" you get from paying real currency.  These items will increase your characters stats depending on which ones you buy.  However, ALL of these armor and weapons require you to rank up in order to buy them (including the real currency only ones).  So by the time you are ranked up enough to actually buy these items, you will probably be playing against players who are more experienced with the game and will still be able to outplay you no matter how much money you spend.
The one negative thing I could say about this game is the way you get into games.  It is a server list system.  There is no quick match or anything like that.  You have to go into the server list, filter out all the full lobbies and find one that people are actually playing on.  This can become pretty tedious.  You will end up spending more time finding a server and waiting for people to join than you will actually playing the game.  There is also no system in place to punish abandoners.  I've had plenty of games where 1 or 2 guys just quit if they start losing.  Getting completely stomped or completely stomping the other team isnt really fun.
Overrall I would say this is a fun game and you should give it a shot.  Its free and its not as Pay2Win as other people are describing because they didn't see the part about how you have to rank up in order to buy things.

Four years beyond its relase, I'm finally getting around to Hitman Absolution. This is a fantastic game.
While the game is far from open-world, you will be presented with a wide variation of options in order to complete each objective. Each decision, every hallway, each vent you climb into, do you take this guards life or spare it....the decisions and implications weigh on you instantly and the replay value becomes self-evident. Often I was considering how I could approach a particular mission on my next playthrough. The graphics are good though and hold up well. This is coupled with a performance that should allow you to remain well over 60fps, resulting in a really clear display that is very immersive.
I just completed the campaign and I'm already strategizing how I can tackle each mission differently then I did on my first run through.
The story is just good enough to keep things moving a long but it does border on cheesy. The villains unfortunately fall into B-Movie corniness, and not even in the Jean-Claude Van Damm/Steven Segal fashion of the 90s...but the game play mechanics make up for this in spades.
Go in blasting away, set up an explosion, assassinate from afar, or creep through undetected and make your kill look like an accident. I love how this game gives you the option to carry out each level on your own terms.
The AI is some of the best I've seen in games, creating a solid challenge while punishing impatience and reckless actions. The result is a game that offers a great balance of challenge and enjoyability.
Hitman Absolution gets an 8 out of 10. With a more solid story this game would've been an all-time great. But as it stands this is a fantastic game and if you can get it on sale, I promise you will not be dissapointed at all.
I'm looking forward to the next game in this series...I added it to my wishlist after the second mission.

A survival game, where you need to plan ahead of time what you will need to be getting during the exploration phase. Your resources are limited, time is precious, and you will be constantly be making decisions on what you will bring back to the shelter with your limited inventory space.
Wood ? Sure I'll take that we need a lot of it, wow heck it takes a lot of space.
Components ? Yes, I have to build a lot of stuff.
Meds ? Oh yes, these fetch for a great reward when exchanged for basic components, and a cold comes faster than you might think.
Food ? I don't have enough space now, we are a bit hungry, but I can come back tomorrow night for that, and starve myself a bit more.
Weapon parts ? We were raided last night, we managed to fend those thieves off, but we will need at least a knife to keep them in their place the next day...
Electric part ? I don't have enough space in my inventory right now, but we need to build that upgraded stove at all cost before winter freezes us to death...
Books, cofee, cigarettes ? I don't have enough space in my inventory right now, but with the hunger, the sickness, we could all use some more comfort in those little things.
Our cook got wounded last night when some pillagers tried to force their way in our shelter. The war front is blocking access to the hospital. He can hold himself alive by staying in bed, but we will need to find bandages fast, or learn cooking...
Water ? I wish I had brought back every single drop of water when I could. All we can do now, in the middle of winter, is burn every last bit of wood and books we have to try and melt snow to get the water we need to cook some food.
A complete run lasts for about 8h, and the game cen be replayed with different set up in a really enticing way.

One may be tempted to write this one off as just an 'anti-war message' by War Child; but this is one of the smartest, most immersive war-based gaming experiences you can hope for.
There is no 'restart' option, and no 'load saved game' button; nothing to remind you that you're playing a game. The gloomy menu just says 'survive' (a small quit button's tucked away in a corner), which allows you to select a file of richly drawn characters, with back stories inspired from real life.
In the game itself, there is sometimes nothing to hold you back from "winning" (per se) except for an unethical decision, say, to rob a passive elderly couple that begs you not to steal their food. The theme makes it weirdly difficult to remember that you're dealing with 1s and 0s. Even at the best of time, there's little sense of triumph.
This is an extraordinary rouge-like game with excellent replay-value, which creatively delivers its message about the devestation of war.

I'd say the game is so-so overall. I disliked the original when it came out but I loved Shadow Warrior, so I decided to give this a chance.
For me the game plays much better than the original. I love the new dash mechanic (when my head doesn't bounce off the ceiling causing a fall damaged death, it's not well implemented) and the enemy encounters feel more balanced and less frustrating. More flying enemies makes fights more interesting. I definately recommend cranking the difficulty as Normal makes the enemies dish out little damage. Though considering the frustrating level design in the late game, I was perfectly fine playing on Normal difficulty.
As far as the graphics go, whether they look better or not is subjective. My issue with the original was that the effects and bloom and what-not obstructed my view and made enemies hard to see. I do not have this problem with the Redux, so they are improved as far as I'm concerned.
Unfortunately many of my issues with the original are present, as well as issues I had with Shadow Warrior. The weapons lack punch and aren't exciting to use, but that's not my biggest issue with the weapons. So many weapons are redundant. For example the Blaster has better range and spread over the shotgun, and seems to do more damage up close. I feel like the NRG and bullet gun could have been combined and overlapping weapons could have been cut. As far as the sword goes, it's fun in a silly way, but after the second half of the game the enemies deal too much melee damage for it to be effective. Oddly enough the bulkier enemies can be shredded with the sword if you time your dashes, but only if you have a lot of room to move.
In the last game I found the levels lacking. They can be hit or miss. For the most part I find them too flat with less height variation than Doom, just like in Shadow Warrior. Unlike Shadow Warrior, I found the levels way to samey and I was occasionally lost dispite the smaller and more linear levels. Many levels have sections and rooms that repeat. There's few markers to indicate progress and variation. Even dead bodies blend in with the junk. Level flow isn't great either. The open arena like sections can be interesting with all the envirormental hazards, especially with the enemies more fragile this time around. It's just ashame that the weapons couldn't be more exciting.
It's old school, but the game is more than generous with health and ammo packs. So no starvation AND no health regen is a huge relief. There's a regenating shield a la Halo, but whatever. I would have liked more old school features like automap, but I only got lost a few times.
I changed my review to Not Recommended because the third act is just awful in level design. I found myself constantly in claustrophobic stretches where I might get pinned against a well. It's frustratating and not well laid out. Everything up to the first boss battle is great, but man did it tank after that. This is kind of typical of shooter games as the end game content is usually the least polished.
The new version also has some signs of consolitis. Whenever the slo-mo upgrade is activated, my mouse speed doubles. Coupled with the adrenaline of having low health, I can't aim worth at damn when I need precision the most. The zoom function also changes sensitivity. This is a massive oversight and signs of an outsourced port. Hopefully this gets corrected.
I'm still slugging my way through the game to beat it. It's not very good, but as I said in my previous review most games are worse. If you play every shooter out there, then give this a go. If you're selective, don't bother.

Big Pharma...
I need to say two things about the game at the start:
1. The game is REALLY good, if you like repetitive puzzles with some niche changes over the cause of alot of different challenges pre-set by the game. It also has some sort of custom games mode - I have not touched on it so there might even be infinite amount of games you can play.
2. The game itself doesn't try to make you interested in playing more of it. It is a game that you pick up and play and then put down again - it doesn't have a character to it that makes every drug/medicine you make unique in its own flavour. You basically just try to figure out how many positive things you can put on a single thing and sell it.
Do I recommend the game? No. The game has an artificial longevity that is repeated in the same pattern over and over and over again. There simply is nothing 'unique' about each challenge you do since you will still build the same machines in every playthru' even if in different ways and shapes - they are still the same.
Same thing with the drugs... you need to compete against a competitor's painkillers? Then here's your one ingredience with a side effect - now make it good. Rince and repeat.
The game has replayability in the fact that all of the side effects and beneficial effects are random to some degree but like I said before, you are still building the same machines over and over again. Nothing happens except your own ♥♥♥♥-ups which some people find intriguing and I do too... in competitive games, not in games that makes me want to think and figure out what to do next.
And this game doesn't really do anything to try and challenge you - there are some mechanics like patents which can make you lock out your competitor's drugs for some time and they can do the same to you but, mechanics like those are just infurating when dealing with an AI where as these mechanics have a place in games when you are able to screw over one of your friends; you are able to get a reaction from them.
Overall the game is brilliantly made but doesn't do a whole lot with it. I bought it for 18,39€ where as I think the game's value would be around 9,99€ to 12,99€ - consider it when its on a sale but AVOID IT AT FULL OR NEAR FULL PRICE!

The game focuses on setting up the production lines - it really isn't a business sim, but I don't think the game suffers because of it. Combining ingredients to get the desired effects, working within the confinements of your factory - there is plenty to think about. It can be very satisfying to tweak a production line to operate more efficiently, or to engineer out one of the pesky side effects. Probably do to my inability to think ahead, I'd have to re engineer my plans to overcome an obstacle I didn't anticipate. Researching better equipment opens up more options to formulate your products.
On the first advanced scenario, money was much tighter and the game provided a tense challenge. Sometimes competing against the AI feels arbitrary, maybe because they're mostly just messages that pop up. I don't feel like they're going through the same process as me. They are effective though - I would curse them when they patented a cure that was on my production line and they provide for some interesting moments.
My two main wishes are more fast forward levels and an online leaderboards so I can chase my friends' scores. Another nice touch would be to have a 'random' setting for each parameter when setting up a custom game. Many times games are more enjoyable if the player doesn't know quite what to expect and have to adjust their play once they discover what's going on.
I've read some people's complaints about the amount of content included in Big Parma and I don't get where they're coming from. There are many scenarios, taking hours to complete. Setting up a custom game offers more play for those who want it too.

Despite some of the design choices that changed the game radically from what I played months ago, this is still the purest arena PvP game I've ever played. If you ever enjoyed WoW arena or Guildwars style PvP, play this game. It's a balanced, polished, entertaining package. The main game mode is a fast-paced, two-minute best of five arena slugfest between two teams of three. It plays more like Counter-Strike than DotA or LoL, so don't think there will be any items or creeps or towers in here. All you will find is pure combat. It's a MOBA in all sense of the word - an online battle arena, more like an Isometic Street Fighter than anything else. This game is unique, its own genre - give it a chance and you won't be disappointed.

GRID Autosport is a very good game yet there's something missing from it. It could be because we've seen it all before, as there's nothing majorly brand new to the series in this game, however it does feel more like the original GRID than GRID 2. Which is a good thing for the original GRID's fans. A lot of tracks are repeated from GRID 1 & 2, but that's not a bad thing as most of these are the 'good' tracks including the made up San Francisco and Chicago one's.
There's a nice selection of cars in game which beats its predecessors, I think, by quite a bit. A nice bit of variety, but no way near the amount of vehicles that you'd get in Forza or Gran Turismo. Then again there isn't really any need for that many. The handling of the cars is more similar to the original GRID with that essence of both arcade and simulation (GRID 2's was arcade) however it does lean more on the simulation side a bit more this time. This game was made in about a year as it came out due to complaints from the original GRID's fans. Oh it also has in- car cam in it now, more about that below in the Pro's & Con's bit:
Pro's:
Nice variety of cars/ disciplines- Touring Cars- Street Racers- Open Wheel & more.
Graphics- As always, great graphics from Codemasters. Sharp and shiny.
Lot's of tracks- Whether they be made up or real life, you will find a track that you like.
Online- Is (I think) better than the Career mode. You can look up or set up custom sessions. But if you can't be bothered looking through things let it plough you face first in to a mixture of races! You can also be in clubs and change car skins/ livery's whatever you want to call it.
Menu- I like the menu's
Handling- I think it's pretty damn good, no more drifting in every single car like in GRID 2.
Con's:
Music- Lack's music. GRID 1 & 2 had more variety and had a big part in the games.
In- car cam- It's there, it's just blurry. There's also a dashboard cam. I'm not too bothered about it, I just don't get why they would have a good one in GRID 1 and not its sequels.
Repeat tracks- Only bad for people who have played the other GRID's and want something new.
AI- This one was difficult, they're nice and aggressive, but you can't help but feel they have the upper- hand some of the time. It's difficult to spin them out, but it's easy for them to do it to you.
Career- A bit bland the further you go in to it, plus having a teamate makes you not want to have one. Also you can't make your own livery's.

> There's an option to adjust the music volume, and even *turn it off*.

If you buy it, and you SHOULD, don't approach it too seriously. Lots of fun, and in the sale there really isn't an excuse to *not* own this.
If you've read this far, then you're already half-interested in it. You *won't* be disappointed if you buy it.

An atmospheric title that achieves what it sets out to do, despite hitting a few gameplay bumps along the way.
The title conveys a brutal and unforgiving world embedded in a seemingly endless war.  Dark, dismal art and a mournful soundtrack drive this point home.  Roguelike progression mechanics and meaningful decision making reinforce that sense of dread and dismay.
Some hitches in the gameplay might sour your experience.  Movement animations add substancial delays between issuing a command and seeing it carried out, and must be accounted for in dicey situations such as while sneaking around.  Characters have skills and status effects, but it's not always clear what impact those will have outside of thematics.
If you're interested in games that explore dark concepts (such as Papers Please or Spec Ops, The Line), this game will likely interest you.  I would also recommend this game to anyone interested in an atmospheric budget indie title.  You could certainly do worse for the money, and if nothing else, the game explores a familiar conecpt from a less familiar perspective and is worth a play for that.

Hard Reset Redux is an improved version of the fast-paced old-style FPS game Hard Reset. The game is set in a dark cyberpunk world where you play as Major Fletcher to fight against the machines to protect the last of humanity. The story was told through comic strip style images, and voice dialog. The graphics in the Redux version are improved from the original, but it wasn’t such a significant upgrade that I was blown away by them. Much like the original, the music and sound effects were done well, and the voice acting wasn’t amazing, but it was decent. The story is the same as in the original; it was decently written, but as my second time playing the game, I was more focused on just killing stuff.
I played the game on normal mode since I remembered the original being very difficult in some parts, but the Redux version was a lot easier than the original was. The new quick dash move makes life so much easier to dodge enemies, and just create a little breathing room. For me, the next best thing was the new cyber-katana that was added. At first I thought it was terrible weapon, since I thought being in melee range would just get me killed, but against certain types of enemies, this sword is fantastic! I used it a lot more than I thought I would, and it was really fun to use.
There were two other weapon types, but each type you can upgrade into completely different gun modes. Most of the weapon types were very useful in different circumstances, but there were a few that I felt were mediocre at best, so I didn’t really use them.
If you’re expecting DOOM, Hard Reset Redux is not up to par, but it’s still a similar style of combat, and fun to play. The game took me about 5 hours to complete, and this was the second time I played through the campaign. The dash ability and katana was great additions to the game, and I enjoyed the Redux playthrough much more than the original. It was almost four years ago that I played the original Hard Reset, and I had gotten it for dirt cheap in a bundle. I liked the original back then, and wanted to play it again, so I had no problem spending three bucks on the Redux version; it was worth it to me.

EDIT: Initially, I recommended this game, but the more I play the more all these bugs are killing the joy...
The engine seems to be the same as Civilization V and the game is very similar. Hapiness has been replaced by health and gold has been replaced by energy so low hapiness (health) does no longer descrease gold (energy) income which is a nice change. Technology tree is in the form of a net, where nodes have 1-2 leaf technologies (technologies that do no lead to any other technologies). There are multiple paths to upgrade units and already built units auto-upgrade when you select an upgrade. The rest is like in Civilization 5 - trading, spying, diplomacy, zone of control, fighting, building cities. A limit of 3 air units per city is a nice change. And finally, the biggest feature is deploying satellites. These can give bonuses to production/energy/culture/food yield, bonuses to units strength, spread/clean miasma (aka radioactive fog),shoot or even spawn basic/strategic resources.
There are quite a lot of bugs
- once any specialist is assigned manually, specialists are no longer assigned automatically
- in unit upgrade panel sometimes multiple unit models are displayed together (overlapping)
- sometimes air unit attack graphics get screwed up and the unit keeps circling and attacking 5-10 times... it is necessary to play with auto combat enabled
- game crashes in later stages where majority of the map is revealed (and that was on a small map...)
- sometimes it is not possible to build a building which requires certain resource to be within city borders and upgraded even if it is
- often when starting a new game "next turn" button doesn't work and I have to exit to main menu and start a new game... of course all the setup gets cleared

Don't be fooled by the simple, clean UI---Big Pharma is a surprisingly deep simulator where the logistical puzzle of placing machinery to assemble your drugs is the least of your worries.  For me, the real difficulty of the game was interacting with the drug market, where you must balance drug prices, market saturation & also keep an eye on what your competitors are doing (if they're importing the same ingredient as you, for example, that ingredient may become oversaturated & its price will rise, hurting your bottom line).
You can flood the market with a side effect-laden drug for some quick cash if you want, but consumers will eventually figure it out & punish you as your cure rating drops & your drug starts losing money.
My only criticism of the game so far is that it lacks a planning stage where you can lay out your production lines in advance.  I had to repeatedly switch between the Ingredients & Cures tabs to work out how to develop a level 3 cure, and keeping track of the machines that I needed quickly became overwhelming.  In the end, I'd go to the Production tab to place a couple machines, then back to the Ingredients & Cures tabs to figure out what machines to place next.
A planning stage that tells you the concentrations/catalysts of imported ingredients (from the Ingredients tab), how to get to the cure (from the Cures tab) & the concentration/catalyst of the drug as it exits each machine in the planned line would be incredibly useful.  Then click a button to commit the entire thing, and you're done.
Also, when I'm deciding which machines to upgrade, it'd be very helpful to know how many of that machine I have across all my production lines.  For now, I can scan the lines to get a rough idea, but this is another example of mental gymnastics that the game could eliminate.
Big Pharma is a game that I wouldn't hesitate to pick up on sale.  I'll be following this one for sequels/expansions.
(This review was for version 1.00.04 of the game.)

The thing I really love is how you can freely go to warp speed and explore, and random events pop up that you can investigate.  It's all very quick and fluid.
You may get tired of the music pretty quickly.  It's great music and sets a nice tone at the start of the game, but I muted after playing awhile.
Basically, I highly recommend this game.

Definitely a let-down after the high standard the original GRID set. They made some neat features like tracks that change as you move through them, AI that doesn't rubberband back to you, and larger cities, but it was in vain since the game was not as fun. I think the original GRID was a little more arcady but it added some character. As I played GRID 2, I felt it was lacking something; I couldn't race how I wanted to.
Also, the story was overdone and a little too cheesy. In GRID 1, the player was a low ranking driver hired to compete against Ravenwood. Slowly, they got better until they were racing in global races as opposed to small local events. In GRID 2, you start out street racing, get "recorded," and then get "famous" through internet videos and social media. To me, it was a bit of a stretch and I prefer the simpler, more generic racing story.
TL;DR: Overall, GRID 2 was fun but it did not live up to the original's standard. It didn't feel right and I thought it was too restrictive. Wait and see about Autosport.

I purchased this game on sale, and after playing several days back to back, I would say that I am glad I did not pay full price for it.
I had seen it in the store for some time and I was very excited to purchase it at a reduced price. The game looked amazing, a compelling story line, crafting, scavanging, survival. It looked emotive, and it is.
The art style of the game creates a very fitting atmosphere, as does the soundtrack.
Overall I can say that I have mostly enjoyed the time I have spent playing so far.
However, there are considerable drawbacks.
As far as I can tell there is no tutorial scenario or instruction of any kind for the game (please let me know if I am wrong so I can read it). This made the first hour (at least) of gameplay much more challenging than it should have been. For example I am still unaware how to unlock more backpack space, if you can even do that.
Additionally, after about day 7 of survival the game just... loses something. You come to realise that this really is the game - all of it. Wake up, feed your survivors, send the night guards to sleep, make sure theyre not cold or sick. Wait for 8pm. Send one person to one of perhaps 12 locations to look for food or materials. Yes, the avoidance of conflict at the beginning of the game can be pretty nerve-wracking but after you have weapons the danger loses its edge a little.
Overall, a really good game, the concept is awesome as is the art and music. The story and actual game progression just lacks something.
TLDR: Good game for casual play at sale price. Little underwhelming after the hype.

The best video game I have ever played hands down. I have played through this countless times. It's perfect in every way and form. The solo campaign is lengthy with plenty of variety in environments. You'll sneak around cargo ships, apartmetns in NYC, and Japanese villages as the ultimate spy. Chaos Theory offers vast amounts of options for every level ensuring plenty of replay value. The graphics, while obviously old, still hold up pretty well to todays standards; with reflective surfaces, lots of realistic textures, and an AI system that is so much fun to mess with. The music, written by Amon Tobin, is fantastic and some of the best original soundtrack work for a video game I've heard. This is a game that you just NEED TO PLAY!
The coop mode was amazing when it was working. It was at least 6 more missions that you could play with a friend and there were even some unique abilities you could do with your partner, like throwing him/her across hallways to knock out guards, or climbing them like a human ladder to get into higher windows. The servers aren't available anymore as far as I know, but I'm sure if you try and host one with your friend you should still be able to play it.
The versus mode is a totally seperate game that's very creative and loads of fun. However! Be warned, this game is highly competitive and the players that are still playing online know the maps inside and out. It's best to play this mode with your friends until you get good enough to play against the 6 or so players that are still playing this online. Also, since the game's versus mode runs on an old engine, the lighting doesn't work anymore with new Nvidia video cards. There Is a fix if you go into the steam communtiy hub to fix it, but if you don't do this, the mercenaries flashlights won't work; which is not good considering you need the flashlight to see in the dark to find spies.
Anyway, this game is a must play for anyone who's ever even had the slightest interest in video games... and considering you're reading this on "Steam", I'm almost positive you have some interest in video games yourself. So buy this game.. now.

Finished my first game all the way to the end of the war. So I shall write a short review on my thoughts of the game. First of all I find the game's artstyle to be very unique and beautiful in its own way. The game has multiple characters to choose from, each with their own strengths and flaws and so a different party will require different strategy to pass through the days. Each decision you make will have an impact on the characters, good or bad, and these will affect the morale of your party. The game has multiple events that require you to plan accordingly such as season change, gang of looters and so on.
One thing that I find weird is that people you harm while scavenging never recover the health they lost even when you re-enter the same area on a different night. Another thing to take note is that armed bandits or thugs never replace the brothers they lost when you take them out (Eg: You take out a thug guarding the entrance of a building, come back a different day and the entrance will be guardless. The other thugs still guard their specific areas). Would be better if they make the guards be more alert after one of their own goes down and the people can recover their health just like the players.
Other than that, I find the game enjoyable as there is a good amount of things to do in game and also every game you start feels different from the last which gives it a very high replayability value. Would totaly recommend this for people who love strategy games.

I know a lot of people wanted this to essentially be a remake of Alpha Centauri... but it's not.  As long as you don't go into the game looking for that, however, it's a great game.  It's a little on the short end for Civ games... you can finish a game of Beyond Earth in about half the time of a game of Civ 5.  Then again, I'm also playing Civ 5 with two expansions adding new technologies, wonders, and game mechanics, and it's been so long since I had the base Civ 5 game with no expansions that I feel that even that isn't a valid comparison.
The one valid point I will make, though, is that it's really hard to take the Civilization brand into a future that hasn't yet happened.  Playing factions in a futuristic game just doesn't have the resonance of playing factions that are developing through the history we've already experienced.  You don't have that moral quandry of whether you react to the events and technologies of history the same way as our ancestors, or the feel that playing a civilization a certain way is upholding the tradition of that civilization.  That said, very few people play Civ as a roleplaying experience... so this might not even apply to most people.  But it was the most interesting and compelling issue I found.
Aside from that one playstyle quirk, this is a very good Civ game which manages to make combat a bit more dynamic and enjoyable through upgradeable units and the like.  It plays very much like Civ 5... so if you liked Civ 5, you'll probably like this game... and if you didn't like Civ 5, you probably won't like this game.  Once it's had a couple expansions, it may even take its place as my favorite Civ game so far (that spot is currently held by Civ 5).

DFO has a very long and interesting history. It was originally a game licensed to Nexon. However everyone on the internet knows how bad Nexon NA handles their games and customers. Because of them a lot of good games have been dying by their hands. The main cause which made this game die is that Nexon kept updating it that made it so player can play all the time. There was no stamina bar or anything which made it easier for botters to exploit the game which ended up killing the game's economy and making it unplayable for people. Despite people's pleas to fix the game Nexon just shuts it down saying it was no long popular anymore which was untrue as there were so many devoted fans to it and for years DFO lie dead...
Until it was picked up by the makers of the game Neople who had so much support from the player's fan base and the game was getting back on its feet which is proof that the game is popular to deny Nexon's claims. Even Neople said so themselves that Nexon handled the game poorly.
Now for a whole year since this game has been alive it is now on steam and because of the memories and good times I had this game I'm upvoting it. Yes I am biased because I love this game. There isn't a game like it (Maybe some but this one was the first and is the best and does it right.) but I wanted to share my thoughts and opinion on just how good this game. The people that only says bad things about for stupid reasons like graphics or what not are not needed. This game is that good that it doesn't need people that doesn't appreciate it.
Now enough of the tale of DFO I'm going to review it. And trust me its not all fanboyism positives.

A lot of classes to choose from and more to come through incoming updates.
The company is better than Nexon and most others and gives us continous updates.
A large community.
Fast-pased and actiony.
They made it very easy to grind for your characters.

It's a old fashioned beat-em up game in the form of a MMO.
CONS:
It can easily be reptitive. But thats with most games.

PvP is not balanced. Everything is gear based and classes have advantage over the other. But if you have skill it doesn't matter what class you use. (Sort of. I'm not a expert on every class.)
Classes might as well be considered genderlocked even if there are male and female counterparts the classes are different from small to big to completely different in general.
Neutral: (Good or Bad depending who you are, but it plays a importance of the game)
2D graphics. If you care about graphics rather than how fun the game is. That is quite shallow. (Sorry its true)
Stamina system. MANY people complain about this system. However it is very important to the games health to prevent botting programs. Its how it died when Nexon got rid of it and people still don't understand this.
Can't use Auction house till 45. This is just a minor problem but Neople had to implement this since botters were still exploting the game through the Auction House. However getting to lvl 45 isn't hard if you like playing it. And most things you wouldn't have made much money as a low lvl character in the first place.

I've been playing MapleStory since its initial release here in the US, and I sincerely wish that I could say great things about this game since I have so many fond memories of what this game was and the potential it had, but unfortunately I can't.
This game has continued to warp itself into a twisted system for sometime now it's nearly impossible to really pinpoint when it happened. MapleStory focuses so much on just catering to the instant gratification aspect of human nature that they neglect to develop the team-play aspect of the game at all. It used to be, you needed a certain number of EACH job to get quests/bosses conquered but now you can either SOLO bosses and/or quests or just fill an expedition with all the same class and get the job done. The main reason for this is because MapleStory is so caught up with creating new classes that overpower its predecessors without focusing on gameplay aspect. Everyone wants to be the same class of character simply because it can beat out the rest with little to no effort and it is because of this that the economy in MapleStory fails as well. With so many websites to buy mesos and gear from, it's really hard to find anything affordable from other players at all.
Everything about this game simply doesn't nurture any long term desire to stick with this game. There is no Team aspect like there once was, Market prices have escaped the realm of reason, and Nexon just keeps feeding this solo-play craze which simply defeats the purpose of an MMO all together. There is no sense of community here anymore, which really is a shame.

As always with a game being this old without having a steam release, don't look at my hours played through steam.
I've played this game on and off since 2010, and it has changed publisher's hands and developed so much over the years. DFO has had a very rocky lifespan, especially in the eastern regions due to shady business practices by dishonest publishers. The games very faithful playerbase trusted  said publisher and this trust was abused many times.
However, I think in the middle of last year, something wonderful happened. In the verge of total death, a little wonderful company called Neople picked up DFO from the absolute ruin Nexon (oops, I said it) reduced it to. Neople is definitely not a Blizzard tier developer/publisher but they have been very reliable over the past year with the direction they are taking this game. They have made promises and kept them, and have put in quantifiable effort into listening to feedback from their playerbase and are acting on it. The result is that a year after their takeover, DFO is back into its old 2009 era golden ages with a solid community and stable publisher.
This isn't a game for everyone, and I think I am too much of a casual to really go indepth about the games problems (minuscule, but valid issues). I will however tell you that if you love the art style you see in the previews/trailers/ screenshots, this game 10000% delivers on the promise of polished old school arcade style action, with content that has been developed over 10's of years. You can easily play this game for thousands of hours and never have to pay these developers a cent. (Although, if you love it, it'd be nice to!)
Overall, excellent game with a publisher you can actually trust. Go get it and sink some hours (this Steam new player event looks juicy af btw)
Cheers!

NOTE: This game was given to me by the developer for review purposes. This did not influence my review in any way.
According to its Steam store page, Stellar Stars is a "Multiplayer Online Roguelite Arena!"
Graphics - Stellar Stars has retro pixel graphics, as seems to be all the rage with indie games these days, and in some games they're really good. Unfortunately, in Stellar Stars they're mostly dull and a bit ugly, with bland colour palettes.
The title screen is quite nice, and the introduction to the "Challenge Story" mode is sort of charming for the first few seconds, but it goes on way too long, and the humour falls flat after the first mild chuckle.
Sound - Sound effects sound like old 8-bit sounds: the sort you'd hear in a game from the period this retro title is emulating. Music is better produced, but with a similar theme. Both are suitable for this title, but I wouldn't bother buying a soundtrack if one were available.
The sound in the too-long introduction is terrible, with text being preceded each time with a distorted bass thump that had me muting it until the game proper had started
Gameplay - Stellar stars plays like an old 8-bit or early 16-bit platformer, but unfortunately not a very good one. Your little character -- whatever it is supposed to be -- moves around in the air like he has jetpacks mounted to his body, and when he's on the ground he reacts like he's on a high-powered hovercraft. It's ridiculously hard and frustrating to try to do precision jumps on the normal levels, but once you hit ice, you may as well just stop playing. This game has the worst inertia and friction I've seen in any platformer.
Controls are via keyboard or controller. I tried both and suggest that you ignore the little screen saying that a controller is optimal -- sure, you have a bit more control over where your shots go and you can shoot upwards without jumping, but left and right controller sensitivity is way over the top and you'll find yourself flying out of control often. The keyboard controls are a bit more tame, but still extremely slippery.
To make controlling your 'thing' even more frustrating, every time you attack the game gives you a little pulse of force in the opposite direction: shoot once or twice on an ice platform in particular, and over the edge you go. And the icing on the cake is the poor collision detection, making tight jumps between platforms an exercise in RSI.
The game is played in a series of one-screen levels, or arenas. In single player, you kill all the baddies, collect the powerups, and move to the next level. The game claims that it is a 'roguelite', but I disagree. Yes, it has some sort of procedural level generation, but since each level is made up of half a dozen platforms and some enemies from a pre-defined pool, that hardly qualifies as 'roguelite' in my opinion. Oh, and the procedural generation will sometimes generate a level that you simply can't beat without taking damage: there will be an enemy or two on a tiny platform on one side of the screen that is blocked from access or attack other than jumping onto it and hoping you kill them before they kill you. Since health pickups are not guaranteed, it basically becomes a game of attrition.
Unfortunately the collectibles are not explained, and even after playing for an hour and a half I couldn't tell you what all of them do. There's a very limited tutorial (part of the introduction I mentioned), but it's too busy trying to be funny to explain anything useful. I managed to get my fireball spell to Level 2 twice, but I don't know how. The other two spells (a purple grenade-like thing and a more powerful version of your starting attack) stayed on Level 1 no matter what, as did the starting attack.
The game supports local and online multiplayer, too. The online multiplayer has five servers / regions: USA, Europe, Australia, Asia, and Japan. I'm not sure when Japan ceased to be a part of Asia. Unfortunately, I can't describe what multiplayer is like because I don't want to submit anyone I know to the pain of playing the game locally (especially not at the price they'd have to pay for it!) and I was unable to find any online games on any of the servers. I did notice two annoyances that have become quite common with indie games with online multiplayer: you can't change your in-game name (it uses your Steam profile name), and there are no server statistics available, so you have no way of knowing if anyone else is even logged in.
Finally, although the game has now been released, I encountered quite a few bugs in my 90-odd minutes of torture:
- weird black bar over bottom portion of the screen, hiding the bottom platform and everything on it (had to quit to desktop and reload)
- game sometimes freezes, requiring task manager to get back to the desktop to restart
- poor hit detection: can occasionally kill ghosts inside platforms, leaving spawned collectibles inside platforms
- broken text on level up screen after destroying first boss
- two characters to unlock for 50 and 99 stars both always say need 50 more or 99 more stars, regardless of how many you've collected (presumably it needs stars earned in multiplayer, but it doesn't say this anywhere)
- in-game text could do with a proof reader
Pros:
+ Procedural level generation (but, see below)
+ Steam achievements (but, see below)
Cons:
- Controls are abysmal
- Mostly ugly pixel graphics
- Still very buggy
- Powerups / collectibles are confusing
- Very overpriced
- Procedural level generation produces more frustration than replayability
- Steam achievements are all multiplayer, and no one is playing
I was interested and even a bit excited to play Stellar Stars. That interest and excitement died fairly quickly after starting the game, and I couldn't even bring myself to play to the two-hour mark.
Not recommended unless you're a masochist and have masochist friends to play with, and don't mind paying a premium to do so.

Like most of the current reviews on show for the game right now, I am a long time veteran player for years now. Neople wouldn't let our existing account be linked to our Steam accounts and I have a pretty good idea on why but that's neither here nor there. If you feel more comfortable watching a video instead of reading a review, you can go to this link:
Anyway, Dungeon Fighter Online (DFO for short) is a 2D side-scrolling beat-em-up RPG that's been out in Korea for ages. It's one of the biggest competitive games played overseas and boasts a very dedicated playerbase in both endgame PvE and competitive PvP. They still host yearly competitions for big cash prizes in Korea for PvP tournaments based on this game. While it's success is booming there, it's life has been pretty tumultuous here in the states. Without going into details of its history, I'll say that the game is very niche. You have to really enjoy beat-em-ups and side-scrollers like MapleStory, Ragnarok, Elsword, Rusty Hearts or DarkBlood to truly appreciate the beauty of this game. The game looks and feels pretty dated but what it lacks in beauty it more than makes up for in content and diversity.
While a lot of MMOs like to focus on grinding levels, this game is more in tune to Diablo where your overarching goal is to obtain endgame equipment to beat endgame raids. There are enemies to beat, EXP to earn, levels to gain and skills to learn; it has everything that other MMOs have. But what this game does extremely well is the sheer diversity of characters it allows you to play. You are able to choose from 13 different classes, each with it's own set of skills and unique abilities. Each one of those classes branch off into 4 separate subclasses which play even more differently than their class counterparts. Some of the newer characters only have 2 subclasses but future patches should add the remaining 2 with ease. Leveling up is extremely streamlined with the Scenario dungeons, where the game literally walks you through the main quests and you go from dungeon to dungeon with ease. This takes away one of the key elements of the game very early on to newer players which is teamplay. Scenarios are designed to get you to endgame as fast as possible. While I understand that the overarching achievement of the game doesn't lie in leveling, it shouldn't be brushed off as a trivial pursuit. But that's my opinion; roast me for it. You are limited to how long you can play by the FP or fatigue point system. You are entitled to 273 dungeon room runs a day but the game will throw at you multiple FP potions to give you some more runs. If you get bored of a character, you can always make a new one without a hassle.
Everyone is going to have differing opinions on the endgame content. No one denies that it's RNG based. No one denies that you will need to grind for months to get your gear. No one denies that the time to acquire these items can be EXTREMELY slimmed down by pouring in a LOT of money in the game. The argument comes in to whether these policies in place limit the gameplay or artificially and unfairly increases the replayability of the game. This bleeds into discussion on whether the game is Pay-To-Win, which is a relevant question for just about any Free-To-Play MMORPG in the market nowadays. I'd say the game is two-fold. It's either Pay-To-Win or it's Time-To-Win. You have to decide whether your time or your money is more important because you'll spending either of the two to get what you want (more than likely, it will be both).
The PvP aspect is a pretty sick joke. While there is a competitive mode that you can take part in, not everything is as fair as it seems. The game runs on a P2P (Peer-To-Peer) networking system where you aren't connecting directly to a centralized game server but rather connecting directly to other players playing the same game. So if you're playing with someone from overseas, BOTH of you will feel lag. Even if you're playing with a neighborhood friend, if they have crappy internet, BOTH of you suffer. This bleeds into PvP a LOT. I'd say it's the partial reason why a lot of new players and even a ton of veteran players don't even bother with it. This leaves a lot of noobs to go up against very experienced players and leaves no room for improvement. Even if the network is working beautifully, PvP hitboxes and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t class skills will leave you frustrated and probably at a loss. This is coming from a veteran who used to frequent PvP a LONG time ago.
The game is extremely small. So small that the developers won't bother giving us figures on how well the game is doing. Check the DFO Facebook group, check the DFO Twitch, check any of their social media and you'll see just how small the game is. Even entering the game you'll start to realize how few people actually play the game. This is in comparison to other MMOs of the same type. As such, most of the community knows each other either through friends or just acquaintances. A lot of the people that play are extremely helpful and are willing to help newcomers however they can. There are, however, ♥♥♥♥♥tains all over the place. You'll be able to tell them apart pretty easily with how they carry themselves and what they say. If there is one thing I'd suggest, stay away from big guilds. They are the bane of the game. Most big guilds won't bat an eye to the new playerbase. I'd suggest joining a smaller guild willing to accept the new players. While low on funds and materials, you'll be better able to make friends and get along with people willing to help. Some of the big guilds, without naming them, are extremely toxic and your best bet is to stay as far as you can.
At the end of the day, its a Free-To-Play game. You are spending only your time to try out a game you might fall in love with. I've had my fair share of history with this game. It's time to have yours.

I absolutely adore this game, for both its gameplay and its personality. It's a difficult shooter, especially at the harder levels, but never unfairly so; there's frequent checkpoints, no "gotcha" death traps, and the bullet-time and multi-jump mechanics make for some really elegant dodging once you get the hang of them. Even the death screens are friendly and encouraging (not to mention varied enough so you won't get sick of the same Game Over screen too much).
A lot of folks have commented on how short the game is; I'd personally use the word "concise". It gets done what it's after in a timely manner, and adding too much more would just feel like padding. Same goes for story: the game gives you just enough so that you know what your character is up to, then takes a step back and lets the gameplay take center stage until the final act.
All in all, this is a really awesome game, with a nice balance of challenge, fairness, and character. Much recommended.

Interesting game, but a bit long and tedious.  Game could seriously benefit from faster speed acceleration than is currently available.  The lack of an area selection tool to move or delete sections of production line is also a noticeable negative.
The pieces all have set shapes, which is part of the puzzle element of creating drugs.  But this works to the games disadvantage as well.  You end up with such chaotic and ugly lines of production that you lose some of the joy and pride of accomplishing a difficult creation.  I'd rather have the option of choosing between multiple shapes for each device.  It would also be very nice to feed one device directly into another without a conveyor belt.
Later on in each mission, you have a large amount of ingredients and production lines.  There is no nice clean link between the screens that show ingredients, production, and your outputs.  It would be extremely helpful to show something as simple as "You are buying 90 of these per month.  This ingredient is used in 3 outputs".  This also doesn't belong on the giant graph/screen on the right once you click on an ingredient.  It should be in the descriptor block for each ingredient.
Click on an ingredient, drug on the cures page, or on one of your drugs under the company page, should show you where on the production map those items are being imported or exported.  This would alleviate some of the tedium.  Or at least on the production map you should be able to zoom way out, and still see the ingredient and output icons that you can see while zoomed in.  Finding one light pink pill on a jumbled messy map is annoying.
If you want a puzzle game, go play Infinifactory.  For an economic sim game, the lack of reporting and inspection into how things are going are lackluster.  For a casual game, each level just takes too long.

What I love about this game is that 2K took a risk.
They took a relatively large risk in terms of the story and it backfired; this was that the game didn't have a major plot twist unlike the other two in the series.
The story is simple and that's why people don't like it as much as the first one, but I really enjoyed the simpleness of it; it gave emotional value that the first one didn't and I generally cried at certain parts of the game.
Yes I see why people didn't like this games location due to it being set in Rapture again but it gave me a feeling of familiarity where I no longer felt like a fish out of water (pardon the pun) but someone that new the ins and outs of how the game will play out and what the world will be like.
So this game isn't a worse version of Bioshock unlike some people would lead you to believe but it is a fresh return and a new take on the world. Go into it with an open mind and you may just fall in love with the characters and story like I did.
P.S. Play the first Bioshock before Bioshock 2 just so you are introduced to Rapture with the intended feeling of "What the ♥♥♥♥ is going on here?"

+ Surprisingly enjoyable gameplay. You will want to keep digging further and further to find rarer elements, and eventually find Dark Matter to save the world. It's a nice combination of exploration and a bit of strategy as to how you progress in upgrades and what path to take.
+ Environmental dangers like meteor showers add a nice mix to the gameplay
- Once you understand the mechanics of the game it becomes extremely simple. Basically you find 1 column you want to drill on and then "Hold S to Win" while resurfacing each time your inventory gets full.
- There's different types of mining ships to buy, but there's really no purpose to them. The first ship is all you need to beat the game.
- Lacking content, it takes about 15minutes or so to beat the game once you understand what you are doing. Not to spoil anything, but the ending is very abrupt and unrewarding. (Watch my Part 2 video to see me finish the game)
- The hazards in this game are not very threatening. You can literally just drill your way threw explosive lava over and over again as your health slowly regenerates over time.
- Just a personal note, but the main menu looks pretty awful in my opinion.
