Big Pharma is obviously a business management sim, but it has some unique things going for it that distinguish it from other types of business management sims and give it a unique hook.
First let's discuss the normal business management aspects. You run a company that makes drugs, and there are essentially three areas of the company you have to manage. The first is that you need the space and the equipment to make the drugs, which means you will need to spend capital to purchase floor space and then you will need to spend more capital to purchase machines to go on that floor space that are used to make your drugs. (There is a LOT more complexity to this part of the game, but we'll get into that later.) The second area is research, which is pretty much just an unlock tree. You pay an initial flat rate to hire a scientist and then also pay each scientist by the hour. The more scientists you have on payroll, the more quickly you'll rack up research points, but that obviously gets expensive, so you need to balance with your income. Research unlocks new machines, new shipping methods, access to new drug recipes, ability to file patents on your recipes, and more. The third area is exploration, which is a tree similar to the research tree. In this area you pay a flat rate to hire explorers and then also pay them by the hour. You deploy your explorers to search jungles, deserts, oceans, etc for new or rare ingredients. By discovering new ingredients with new properties, you have access to new recipes that can be used to make a variety of new drugs. Explorers also have their own research points which you can spend to reduce the purchase price of ingredients and reduce your cost of materials.
These are the basics. Know that you will always have rival companies that are manufacturing and selling drugs in competition with you, and if the rival company's drugs are of a better quality than yours, they can eat up your market share (i.e. you will make fewer sales and earn less money due to your competitor stealing your customers). In the early modes and difficulties, competitors are a breeze to deal with. They can be more of a menace in later modes, though, for sure.
Okay, so what is the unique hook? The unique hook lies in purchasing floor space and machines and then assembling production lines. It is a complicated PUZZLE. Bear with me, because this gets a tad complex. Every ingredient you have to work with has four effect slots, and those four slots are filled with effects. The slots can either contain a curative effect, a negative effect, or simply be empty. The easiest ingredients to work with tend to have one curative effect and one negative effect. The more difficult ingredients have one curative effect and three negative effects. In addition to these effect slots, each ingredient also has a CONCENTRATION value that can be anywhere between 1 and 20. The higher the number, the higher the concentration. Each of the effects in the four slots has a random concentration interval assigned to it, and the effect is only ACTIVE if the concentration falls within that interval. For example, if the ingredient has the curative effect SOOTHES COLD that is active between 11-14, and the negative effect CAUSES CONSTIPATION that is active between 5-12, and the default concentration of the ingredient is 12, then THAT means that both effects are active in the ingredient, so you have to put the ingredient through a machine that will change the concentration so that the curative effect is active and the negative effect is not active. So if you change the concentration to 13, it is still within range to soothe colds, but it will no longer cause constipation. Get it? Still with me? It gets even crazier.
Okay, so obviously there are machines that can change the concentration value of an ingredient to alter the effects. But sometimes you have ingredients with three negative effects and it is literally impossible to deactivate all of the negative side effects, so then what do you do? Well, there are also machines that can shake up the order of the effect slots, and machines that can swap effects between two ingredients. So if you're clever, you can swap negative effects out and positive effects in. In some situations, you can even create super drugs that have multiple positive effects! The problem is that it can require a lot more machines to make these crazy drugs, which is not only more expensive to purchase the machines, but each machine also has a per-use cost as well, so it is in your best interest to have as few machines as possible. UGH. DECISIONS.
There are other ways to deal with negative side effects as well. For example, you eventually learn that not only does every effect have an active range, but every effect also has a "sweet spot" number, which is a specific number between 1 and 20 where the effect is 100% effective. So you can research your own drugs to find the sweet spots and improve your drug quality, which is important so that your competitor doesn't steal your buys with better quality drugs. And of course there are some interesting technologies you can unlock that don't really pertain to concentrations or effects but are still highly useful in other ways. There is really A LOT in here to learn and figure out.
Oh, and don't forget that you actually have to manually place each machine on the factory floor, rotate it, hook up the conveyor belts yourself, etc. Sometimes you have enough funds to set up a production line for a new drug, but you're out of floor space because you built too many huge production lines and you can't fit the new one in there. (Discontinue a line of drugs to make room for a new one? DECISIONS.) So there is also a spatial puzzle element of using the fewest machines possible, laying the conveyors to actually complete the circuit, arranging your machines and production lines in such a way that it doesn't get in the way of future building and/or allows you to upgrade or expand the current production line later as new ingredients become available.
There are lots of different difficulties, modes, and objectives to play. There is even a sandbox mode where you can get all machines, all tech, and are given infinite money, so you can experiment with the machines to figure out what all of them do. (Some people may be confused about how the mixer works at first, so having a safe place to test and observe it is helpful. Combining the mixer and shaker is an advanced gameplay strategy that is difficult to understand or use without a bit of practice and experimentation, so sandbox mode helps with that as well.)
Mods are available from the dev if you want to change up certain aspects of the game. For example, some people (including me) don't think it makes much sense that by default it is impossible to move conveyor belts without selling them and rebuying them at a loss, so you lose money for just correcting/moving conveyors (which is not the case with machines). So there is a mod to make conveyor belts free, which I recommend. (Though what they should have done for best balance, IMO, is just make the buy/sell price the same.)
Tutorial is well done. It is very hands on, but also easy to skim through quickly for those who have little patience and just want to get down to business (i.e. me).
Highly recommended for business sim lovers---especially if you like the idea of having some headscratching and puzzling thrown into the mix. You REALLY have to plan with this one.

I've put in a lot of hours in this game. I am also a small streamer that streams this game on Twitch to help it gain interest. But I paid for this game and expected more...
The game grows on you until you get punched in the face by it's issues.
**Update October 5th**
With the latest update, this developer has decided to make building in the game more difficult by increasing resources required AND having to use the Forge to make materials just to build walls. Instead of sticking with more basic materials like stone, they have forced the player to farm precious stone, combine that with regular stone in the Forge and create bricks one by one. What use to take less than 10 seconds to build a wall, now takes over a minute...for one wall.
So instead of adding real content to the game, the developer is adding grind to end game base building. Turning the only thing that was enjoyable in the game as it stands...base building...into a job of endless grinding just to build basic end level structures.
In addition, the developer community manager decided to turn on the community,  deleting posts and banning players posting their negative feedback about this latest patch. Hardly a game you want to invest in given the lack of direction, lack of content, and treatment of their player base.
**Update August 21st**
The developer has changed the Raid system and introduced Siege Spells. These are the only spells that can damage base walls now. However, the shields and turrets are still not effective for base defense and can be damaged by normal character spells.
I still stand by my review as it's fair and will hopefully give players an idea of what they are investing in.
**
- If you are a base builder and enjoy pvp, stay away. You can build amazing bases but there are zero defenses you can put in place that help fight off base raids. Shield domes that do nothing, turrets that do no damage to high level players, top tier rock walls that can be melted in seconds.
- The higher level spells are so overpowered that players and bases on PvP servers have no chance. (**See Update Above**)
- The resources and 'treasures' in the game are so easy to obtain that storing them away in your base hardly matters. Raiding has no purpose when all the resources are easily obtained. Raiding is only to destroy, and it's way to easy to do that right now.
- PVE? There are only like 10 mob varieties in the game. And they repeat across the map, just have more HP and deal more damage in the 'higher' level zones.
- There is currently no real objectives. No dungeons(just caves), no neutral NPC hubs, no purpose other than explore a small map and fight repeated mobs that respawn in a predictable pattern and timeframe. There is a leveling system and skill tree, but you can only use those skills to fight other players and have a challenge. The AI mobs are not a challenge.
There are public and private servers. You can rent your own server. No solo play unless you password protect your own, private server.
There are plenty of server issues that still exist as of this review. You will also get a couple restarts of the official servers daily to clean up issues...and respawn chest and resources...Yes, that doesn't occur naturally all the time.
Overall, 6/10. I hope it improves as it has some great core gameplay elements.

An immersive, ethical game, This War of Mine tasks players with managing the survival of a band of survivors trapped in a city under war.
Players will have to walk a delicate line in order to maintain survival conditions and balance morale.   Robbing a helpless family might allow your survivors to last another week, but at the cost of low morale for a few days as the survivors contemplate their actions.  Players can continue to push their groups to desperate measures, eventually finding that their team has become hardened, jaded war criminals...if their psyches can handle the journey.
The music is minimalistic and bleak, captures the emotional scene very well.  The graphics are dreamy and sketchy. I felt that the pencil sketch effect helped create a war journal vibe.
I ran into a few glitches in the game that didn't hurt the experience.
This War of Mine benefits from playing this game slowly and deliberately.  I appreciate that this game absolutely rewards cooperation with other civilians and punishes a "guns blazing" playstyle.  Unfortunately for replayability,  I finished the game feeling drained, which is perhaps what the developers wanted.

If you're looking for a game that makes you feel empowered or rewards you for creative thinking, look elsewhere. This War of Mine is a brutally honest examination of life as a civilian in a modern conflict zone. Your characters will have to deal with desperate hunger and thirst, crippling illness and injuries, and crushing depression made only worse by the mental trauma the war inflicts every day.
I think the best example of this is one incident that killed my first playthrough. I had heard of a random event where you came upon a soldier about to♥♥♥♥♥♥a civilian woman and had the opportunity to intervene. When I got this event, I put on my hero's cape and rushed up behind the soldier to bash his head in with my shovel. The soldier turned around, saw me, and shot my character. She died. She was carrying all of my medicine, all of my water, and my only trade item, not to mention my only shovel. She was also the one who had been holding up the spirits of my entire group, keeping them from sinking into depression. The game doesn't give you a chance to rest; immediately it was the next day and I had to deal with keeping the group from falling apart because my character had died and my supplies were all gone. I had to deal with the realization that I really had no way to help that woman, and that if I had been a coward and just let her get♥♥♥♥♥♥♥I would have survived and possibly even gone on to live out the war.
This game is challenging and mature, and incredibly insightful. If you're sick of the super-soldier portrayal of warfare in Call of Honor: Battlefield, give this game a try.

Dungeon fighter Online has had quite the journey beginning with Nexon and ending with Neople. Neople (the actual developers behind the games popularity in Korea) have taken great care improving everything from in game channels, interface, revamped fighting system, translations, customer support and honestly the list goes on. The game isn't what it used to be before and that's a good thing since it is no longer plagued by gold bots that inflated the game in the past. There are plenty of classes to choose from that have also been reworked to the point where it doesnt matter what class you pick since they are all viable end game. A fatique system made its way back into the game limiting the amount of time one can play (156 dungeon rooms) per day, BUT there are PLENTY of WAYS to INCREASE your fatique by using pots that refills the ENTIRE 156 fp points and using other pots that can be used after that as well. It takes a few hours to get through 156 fp points and you'll be lucky if you even use the whole bar end game since dungeons are harder, longer and require more diversity in team to run them more smoothly. Steam has added many more players to the game so finding a party shouldn't be difficult by any means and events are always running to ensure your leveling experience is quick and fun. It is completely possible to reach level cap in 1-2 weeks casually and prepare for endgame content. Although my time says 0.1 on this game, I have been playing on the original client for more than 2-3k hours and still come to this game from old nexon era to neople era. It has improved and is ready to show that. Game is updated every two weeks with events and is taken very well care of by neople who love the game just as much as it's fans. I hope you enjoy your experience!

--Incoming wall of text so get ready for quite the read if you're really indecisive about this game, TL:DR just give it a try and see how you like it, otherwise these are just me explaining certain things that will turn beginner players away that aren't properly explained by the game itself--
Now a few things to note first and foremost: This game as an Energy (Fatigue) System. And there's a reason for that: in Korea to limit how much to play in consideration for someone's health etc. but you can easily just create more characters to keep playing if you're just that in love with the game. Now I've played this game for countless hours so to finally see it back on steam with Neople now I just wanted to give it a good word.
Again the Fatigue system is going to turn off you and a lot of new players and there are ways to counter it with characters, but the game also provides you with ways to restore your Fatigue Points with in-game potions you can use once a day. And Neople has events all the time so if you follow some of them they give you cash shop items that EXTEND your maximum fatigue so you'll have more than you know what to do with.
The FP system also helps combat against gold bots. I mean if you log into DFO and compare it to any (korean) MMO you'll see the difference with how many players the game is filled with vs naked bots flooding common areas. Sure 1 or 2 sneak through the system but neople acts fast to getting rid of them
---whew-
Okay technical junk aside that i know most newbies complain about, lets get to how I feel about the game and this is going to be somewhat biased but bear with me here (haha bear pun)
1.This game has that retro-arcade action feeling in it's gameplay and the gameplay just varies so much. It can be fast paced inputting skills to get off a combo to do massive damage or just using an 1 click AoE spell and watching with joy the havoc you're dealing or maybe it's a bit of both depending on which class you make. The gameplay just boils down to "How fast can you kill this thing without it killing you" but it's not always like that. Most of the lore/story is text-based so you know how in quests it's just "I need help go do this for me". Well in this case it is but isn't this. The game gives you a mini intro on the character you picked which shows their "backstory". Ultimatey you embark on this quest and it leads you to many different places. You could care for the lore or not but it's definitely worth the read when you piece things together and are a big lover of stories. There are a bit weird grammatical or translation errors but you can make out what they generally mean.
2.Yes this game does have in-game transactions via Cash Shop, but I managed to do fine without spending a single dollar on the game. Remember Neople throws out events all the time so chances are, half the event rewards are cash items that you can get or maybe even event exclusive so get on those. Also there are people in-game who DO sell the ingame cash currency "Cera" for in-game gold and the players in the community have collectively agreed to doing this because a player bought the Game Card that supports the devs so it's win/win. Person A gets the gold they need. Person B gets the cash currency they want. And the Devs are supported by Person A's cash
3.Also note MOST cash item stuff is just inventory/cosmetics. There's another thing which which DOES grants stats but the stats are pretty miniscule compared to what you'll be getting in-game so it's all just a teeny tiny boost is all.
4. If you think "Ugh I have to make Alternate characters just to keep playing this game, i'm done" don't because believe it or not this game has 30+ classes with unique playstyles so if anything this game encourages making alts because there are many playstyles out there to play and try out and have fun with. (And the korean devs are STILL pumping out content how cool is that???)
In conclusion this is just the basic things that turn beginners away because yeah, upfront in your face. All that stuff does seem gross, but if you give it time then it becomes really enjoyable.

Currently, I'm undecided if I should buy this game while it's on sale, so hopefully this review will help me (and you) decide it's value
First of all, a little history of the franchise in the 21st century.
It got off to a rocky start with vanilla Civilization III, the game full of bugs and half-cocked ideas that was universally panned by gaming publications expressing their regret, calling it "the end of an era". Usually around this time a few patches are released and developers quietly move on, indeed that is the smart option. We know now that history didn't play out like that, and through carefully designed patches and expansions became one of the greatest strategy games of all time.
Until Civilization IV.
The thing with Civ IV is that it came off the heels of Civ III, so it was rife with expectations and uncertainty. How can Firaxis, at this time their only claim to fame Civilization, create a game even better than Civ III? Well they did, and I will never forget how happy I was as a ten-year-old getting my still favorite videogame of all time. It sparked my love of history and people at a young age, how they shaped history. The Civ IV magic made what some called "the greatest game of all time" or at least the greatest stragety game. It took another two expansions to get fleshed out, but by the end their was some credence to those titles
Ok, so Firaxis pulled two rabbits out of their hat. Big whoop. They can't possibly be considering anothrr Civ game, especially since you just can't top Civ IV. Whatever they release will be a dissappointment.
When I first saw gameplay footage of Civ V I thought just that. I liked my four squares, stacks of units, and older gameplay, and once I let my stubborness go I gave the game a crack when it was on Humble Bundle. From then on I'm as addicted to it as Civ IV, but for different reasons, and for me there is a magic in the franchise because of it.
So Firaxis did it three times in a row. Like...♥♥♥♥♥♥ When was the last time this happened... Halo? CoD? But those never garned such titles by critics or love by fans, only sales numbers (which in many cases they justly deserved).
So then Beyond Earth happens. This is where is gets a bit tricky.
See, the game itself is quite good. But in other ways a step down in the franchise, and make no mistake this is no one off: it is part of the main Civ franchise. So we have to put it up against it's brothers in the realm of greatest strategy games of all time. Since everyone else mentions features the game exceeds or lacks at, I'm simple going to be analyzing the game itself through the lens of history.
Lessons to be learned from the franchise:
-Firaxis is notorious for having the vanilla version and the final version totally different. Beyond the Sword and Brave New World totally transformed their respective titles, and I would argue for the better. I love both Civ IV and V, but I found myself playing their completed predessecors more because they were the most fleshed out.
-Second not is that Beyond Earth is still a Civ game, meaning that Firaxis will not stop until it lives up to the other titles, much like they did for Civ III and for some people Civ V. Let's see what Rising Tide takes it to.
-Lastly, the game has been overcharged at launch. Especially for a Civ game, its somewhat skimpy on content. Seriously, it's probably the least replayable in it's vanilla stage, so it definitely shouldn't be $40-$50, that's just astronomical. But it's on sale.
And to answer that question... I still don't know. If you see it in my library then you'll know. For now I'll recommend it.
Hope this helped you guys.

This...is not the game I was expecting. However, it does what it *does* do very well.
It lies at the midpoint of real-time strategy and play-at-your-own-pace.
It's very quick to start a game once you've done the tutorial, to begin making money. At that point, you start to work on a more complicated drug, researching machines and ingredients and continuing to make money. Eventually, you work on a greater drug.
Laying it out requires planning--the game pauses so you can do that without losing time or money. It's very challenging, but in the way that requires you to think about what you're doing. It is not a game you play in bits and pieces--it is, however, the kind of game that's easy to learn and challenging to master. Getting the right cures, side effects, and concentrations to end up with the most profitable drug requires patience and spatial planning--and maybe a notebook and pen to keep track of everything.
Great fun, though. Pretty sure I played for almost two hours after I meant to go to bed.

First off, this is a great game, I would definetly buy it if I were you.
The physics model is a perfect balance of arcade and simulation, much better than GRID 2, which was like driving on soap. That makes this game very fun and playable with w,a,s,d and arrow keys.
The car selection is huge, you get everything in between hot hatches and formula 1. Touring cars, muscle cars, hypercars, you name it, they have it.
The graphics are great, obviously not the best in the world right now, but still insane.
The frame rate is very constant, I dont have the best PC ever, only 6GB of ram and a core i5, but it still runs at 40-50fps pretty much no matter what I'm doing. I cant say the same for games like need for speed.
The track selection is immense, granted, some of the tracks are just variations of the same track, but it's still difficult to run out of places to race.
Multiplayer is great as well, impact ratings keep all of the jerks out of the race and let everyone have fun without being killed by some idiot driving on the track backwards.
However, there are some flaws. For example, when GRID autosport says you are going to drive formula A, or formula 1, it gives you an indycar instead. Indycar and F1 are NOT the same thing.
Another flaw has to be the DLC, which has been a problem for all of the GRID games. There is so much of it, and none of it is free. You want an extra car? Better have $5 lying around.
This also effects multiplayer, half of the time the party leader is using DLC that you probably dont have, and there is usually no other party to join.
The cokcpit wiew is super blurry as well, not a big problem, but still something I want to point out.
My final thoughts? Still an excellent game. DO NOT listen to the people who say you are better off with GRID 2, ive played the game before, trust me, you want this one. Although I do recommend buying it on sale, the GRID series tends to be on sale more than most racing games on steam, so I was able to get it for 10 bucks. Also, if you are looking for a racing sim, go buy asseto corsa, do not buy GRID.

I previously gave this a non-recommended because of rubber-banding, but after playing it more I have to revise my opinion.
For whatever reason, Codemasters decided to put rubber-banding in for Touring Cars, but the other 4 disciplines have no rubber banding. I'm sure it made sense to someone up there...
Ignoring the rubber-banding, this is a pretty good racing game. The four disciplines feel nicely different in the way they drive, making changes to the set-ups in your cars now finally actually makes a difference in the way they handle, for the first time ever there are practices and qualifying, so you don't just always start on spot 9-12, and you can adjust the race lengths from normal to X2, X3 and X5, which is pretty cool.
Street racing is as cool as it was in Grid 2, Open Wheel is fantastic fun, and the drifting is longer than in Grid 2 where it was waaaaaaay too short.
There are some bad things too. The graphics engine, while running smoothly, is getting really long in the tooth, and they basically copy-pasta'd something like 60% of the tracks from Grid 2 just straight into this one. The AI is still god-awfully terrible and will happily plow into you if you happen to be driving on their racing line (seriously, ♥♥♥♥ you Nathan McKane!) essentially forcing you to drive weird lines so as not get rammed off the ♥♥♥♥ing road by them.
The Endurance discipline is a nice idea on paper, but in reality the whole "you have to worry about your tires" gimmick just makes you drive ultra-careful which is just plain boring. Coupled with the fact that even at X5 length you only race during night time, but that night time is now just basically a "slightly darker day" versus the absolute terror of seeing NOTHING at Le Mans in the first Grid, and it's just a boring chore of a discipline to play through. Racing should be about balls to the wall driving at your limit, not carefully entering and exiting corners so that my stupid tires don't give out too soon.
While there is no stupid "You must gather social media followers to advance races!" crap in this one, there still isn't the sense of team ownership / deciding on sponsors / buying cars etc from the first game, and I can't figure out why they refuse to put that back in. Here you still just drive for teams with crappy team mates and often crappy cars and it's disappointing.
Finally, the in-game commentary has progressively gotten worse from game to game to the point where here it just constantly repeats itself (does hearing a "standings update" that tells you your ten points ahead of ravenwest in the overal team standings sound like something you want/need to hear every lap? No? Well, you'll still get to hear it for 30 laps in Endurance Also, enjoy hearing the commentator count down every minute during practice. "7 minutes left! 6 minutes left!") and never actually gives you any helpful info. The best thing to do is to just turn it off.
All in all, it's enjoyable to race in 3 of the 5 disciplines, it runs smoothly, and you can definitely tinker with set ups to get the cars to drive the way you want them to. If you like not-too-overly-simmy racers, this is worth picking up for $10, but I expect Project Cars to blow it out of the water. (or at least I hope it will.)

As others said, this is a one-man job, so we do need to cut some slack.
This game is a sort of mini puzzle game encased in a shiny cover.
The major challenge in the game is to rotate buildings to create an assembly line of drugs, while keeping in mind that the structures can only be rotated, not flipped. (that, while often annoying, is a huge part of the challenge)
* On some levels, it's pretty difficult to gain the Master rating on a level, which does add to the challenge.
* Nice and clean graphics and music choice by the developer.
* Randomized game effects, ingredient names, and maps add a very distinct and appreciated character to the game.
Some rough edges --
* The tutorial is very winded.
* The game text is written in British English with some rather unusual phrasing, which makes it a bit harder to understand than could have been otherwise.
* The game is just a touch light on features. Some modding is possible by editing some data files, which are formatted in non-compressed JSON. If full modding ever gets added, it should become much more interesting, though.
* slow UI switch between panels makes for a slightly annoying experience.
* It even has a memory leak like the big boys (after playing for hours).

I would be wary of reviewers that invest 5 hours or less into this game. The Advanced Mode's machines, along with the Centrifuge from Intermediate, radically increase the ways in which you can manipulate ingredients. It's also much harder to make and maintain a large profit, especially since competitors play a much greater role in the Advanced Mode. You'll need to start utilizing some hidden optimization tricks involving things like the packer or crossing belts with machines that have a cycle time greater than 1. So while dead-simple machine placement will get you through the Beginner and some of the Intermediate Scenarios, reaching Master in the Advanced Scenarios requires a lot more thought.
The negative reviews for this game have some merit, but the game doesn't promise anything more than it delivers. What this game does, it does very well: designing and optimizing production lines, anticipating what the market for a drug will bear, deciding what ingredients and machines to research or upgrade, all while balancing a budget that is very tight early and expands greatly over time. It's a beautifully-animated game that presents a relaxed puzzle atmosphere and gives you almost all of the information you'll need up-front.
Let's get some things out of the way, though. Sick people are abstractions, which is honestly what I'd expect from most Pharmaceutical companies. The larger the market for a cure, the greater the relative price and the more of that cure you can produce without tanking the price. The market can increase or decrease as a result of random world events, increase naturally over time for infectious diseases, and decrease as people are cured. A cure that's particularly potent will fetch a much higher price, but you may eventually be left without a viable market for that product.
The available cures and how they're upgraded are static. The starting concentration of an ingredient has a fairly narrow range based on the range of the Level 1 cure. The number of plots available for purchase, and the sockets within each building layout, are predetermined. On the other hand...The ingredient order is random, side effects are assigned semi-randomly, the building layouts you get are random, and the market for each cure is random within a small range. This can make or break the profitability of several cures, but the Level 1 cure of every starting ingredient is profitable and smart research choices can dig you out of some terrible early setups. Even a terrible cure can fetch a profit, although it can be much lower than you'd get from a perfect cure.
Anyone who says that the Competitors are pointless was playing on one of the easier difficulties. The competition presents a real challenge in Advanced Mode, as you have 3 competitors that all have the same early options that you do. Different AI companies prioritize different things, but they'll usually go for the more profitable cures and cures that can fetch high ratings (ie, no side effects). You have to be smart with your market choices in Advanced because the AI will very quickly oversaturate and tank the price for several cures. Anticipating what your competition will do is a big factor in your success. Patents in particular can really help you or really screw you over in the short-term, although they're fairly easy to work around, but you can do the same thing to the AI. Mucking with the AI's profit margins can really slow them down, giving you a chance to reach (and patent) the very high-level cures before they get a chance to ruin your market.
Sometimes you can make just plain bad choices, but usually there's okay options and really great options. There's almost always something you can optimize more if you put thought into it, and if you're shooting for a certain level of revenue or profit you'll be shifting around production lines a lot. I used to hit patches where I'd just need to wait, but now patch 1.01 added a much-needed 5x speed option!
Personally, I love this game. The progression has a level of predictability that may put some people off, but the random elements that people keep complaining about actually keep things fresh.

The reviews for this game on Steam are generally negative, and that is unfair. This is a free to play game, that does feature strong incentives to spend on microtransactions, and that is, indeed, hatefull. I am the first to agree that something is very wrong in the industry right now regarding the f2p model. However, I believe a game should still be judged by how good a game it is in its own right. And this match 3 game is, in that regard, quite spectacular. The implementation of the original puzzle quest design is great, the look and feel of the game is pleasing and professional (it looks way better than puzzle quest 2, and better than most games of the genre), and there is a deep strategic level to the gameplay, which is quite surprising. Moreover, the use of the Marvel IP is clever. There is a pretty nice story going on, which is tied up with events on the comics, with the intentional cheesy but great dialogues that are a staple of the genre. Collecting your favorite heroes from Marvel universe is a fun activity in itself. There is a good variety of heroes, from both X-men and Avengers comics, alongside playable villains and rarer heroes (Punisher and Invisible Woman, for instance). Each hero play different, with obvious dps, tank and support roles, so that finding a team that works well together, and the right way to level them so they will interplay efficiently, is an interesting challenge. It delivers on all its promisses, being both a good Marvel game, and a good, a very good indeed, Puzzle game. It's microtransactions scheme is a big flaw, something I wish I would never encounter in any other game again. Unfortunately, that is where the industry is right now, and it is killing otherwise great games.

The AI is all over the place - an area will be devoid of enemies for a period of time, only for a group of 10 enemies to come running out of nowhere trying to get... somewhere?  Once they get there, they just stop running and start wandering the woods at a random point.  Sometimes they run right by you on a mission to go wander aimlessly, other times they all decide they want to fight you.  In order to see an enemy's level, you basically have to get within its agro range which is particularly annoying when you find that you're severely outclassed, but don't worry, dart through a couple trees and they'll probably leave you alone.  Or two shot you.  Who knows.
There doesn't seem to be much correlation between a creature's level and your ability to defeat it.  I've killed many enemies that are much higher level than me.
The spells feel... clunky?  Not responsive at times.
Servers lag out for no apparent reason relatively frequently, and the basic features in the server browser just don't work.  If you play on a server, REMEMBER THE NAME because history doesn't work.  C'mon, this is super basic. Inattention to simple things like this makes me believe that the game is not ready.
The crafting system is easy enough to understand if you've played any sort of MMO or really any game with crafting.
The graphics are oddly grainy, and I don't see a way to improve that despite having a pretty decent setup.  All of the settings are maxed.
You can tell the developers put a lot of thought and effort into certain elements - building is particularly cool - you aren't limited to giant boxes in this game.
Some of the controls are a little awkward or unintuitive, but not terrible, and you can remap most of them if  you're so inclined.
The talent "trees" are pretty straightforward, though can be somewhat limiting in early game.  The first few levels feel REALLY grindy.  I find myself building a house and killing anything that comes near just to advance my xp, which may be intentional.
This game is better played with a group, where each person has their own set of talents.  For example, not everyone in your group needs to spend points on learning how to build, so you could have a builder, while others spend their talents on crafting or fighting.
I could definitely see this game growing to something truly interesting and engaging.  It just isn't there quite yet.  (Hence the early access I suppose).
Would I recommend? Not yet.  Not at $25 anyways.  Worth picking up and holding onto if it goes on sale again.
I'll keep digging deeper to see what else there is, but that's my initial feeling after playing for a few hours.  If they continue to develop and add on, which it seems like they intend to do, my tune could easily change.

Disclaimer:  Yes I have used the microtransactions and have invested money into this game, but I did so not out of a feeling of being underpowered to enjoy the game, but after nearly 60 hours of game time.
Ok, that out of the way, I have to say that I really enjoy Marvel Puzzle Quest.  If you can just set aside the microtransaction part of the game, there is a lot of game here to enjoy.  Once you get to know the basics of the heal mechanics as well as learn the abilities of the characters in your stable, it becomes highly strategic and addictive.  You will want to get engrossed in the cycle of fighting through the "campaign" missions to earn recruitment drops in the hopes of upgrading your stable.
Once you have your "go-to" team, you'll take place in the daily challenges which are something like a-synchronous matches with other players where you earn points toward a reward.  The more points you accumulate through battling other teams, the higher up the ranking ladder you climb, but the higher you are, the more you are worth in points to those below you.  These "tournaments" can become highly addictive as you constantly battle and check your standing, and the instant feedback is pretty gratifying.  Its also pretty intimidating when you see other players that have level 100+ characters.  But I just placed 1st in a tournament with only level 40 or so characters, so it can be done without being ridiculously overpowered, hence the strategy.
The other cool thing is the variants of the powers and the characters, and a feel of wanting to collect them and get them leveled up.  This however is where my only complaint comes in.  Your roster size is limited by a slot system.  And you have to pay for slots using the in-game "hero points" currency.  Depending on how you play and how well you do in the events, you may come to a point that you have more waiting recruits, not enough slots, and not enough hero points to unlock new slots.  The game gives you 7 days before recruits you earned expire, and that may or may not be enough time to earn enough hero points to fix them in your squad.  It is the only "micro-trap" that I have seen really.
All in all I have over 170+ hours on the game now, and I would gladly recommend it to anyone.

I rarely finish games. My Steam library is littered with dozens of games I’ve started but never finished, games such as Dust: An Elysian Tale and Bastion which aren’t bad games by any metric, but didn’t hold my attention long enough for me to complete them. As such, I feel obligated to give a positive review to Rebel Galaxy, which, while by no means flawless, managed to hold my attention for over 45 hours.
Rebel Galaxy is a space trading and combat simulator. In this respect, it is similar to Elite: Dangerous. Rebel Galaxy is not an Elite clone, however – it differentiates itself in three major ways. Unlike Elite Dangerous, which focuses on dogfighting, Rebel Galaxy is a game about capital ship combat. Rebel Galaxy, unlike Elite: Dangerous, also has a campaign. On a less complementary note, Rebel Galaxy is set on a 2-dimensional plane while Elite Dangerous has full 3-dimensional movement.
The first thing I noticed when I started Rebel Galaxy was the music. I wasn’t sure of the genre, but a quick search of the Steam forums indicates that it’s probably Dark Country. Some elements of the music reminded me of the Ballad of Serenity from Firefly, which was clearly an inspiration for the game. I enjoyed the music, but it is clearly not for everyone – I showed the game to my parents, and while my mom loved the music, my dad hated it. Fortunately, there is an option for those who dislike the original soundtrack – the external launcher allows the player to swap .mp3 and .ogg music files for the game’s original music and even to specify the conditions under which they play (combat, docked at station, etc.).
Once I got past the menu into the actual game, I noticed that the graphics are good for an indie title. The texture quality is not that high, as is obvious when you switch to precision aiming mode while controlling a turret, but the camera is held at a fixed distance from the ship and the lighting effects are good, so the game usually looks nice. The art direction is also impressive. All the ships and stations look like they belong in the same universe, with a used, industrial, utilitarian aesthetic which helps with the world building.
At the start of the game, you start off with very little money and the need to upgrade your ship to progress in the campaign. This need continues throughout the game. It is therefore very important that there are interesting ways to make money. Rebel Galaxy offers 5 main ways to earn credits: mining, exploration, trading, bounty hunting, and mission running.
Mining is probably the most boring of the ways to earn money. If you’ve played another game in the genre, the system will be immediately familiar – you click on asteroids highlighted by your scanner with a mining laser equipped, and when they explode you get marketable resources. The only difference between Rebel Galaxy and most other space games in this respect is that there is a piece of purchasable equipment that allows you to target specific parts of the asteroids to get more resources. I found mining to be boring, but it is a relatively safe and efficient way to make money.
I found exploration to be more fun, but it is only a viable way to make money if paired with mining or trading. While at warp speed, asteroid and debris fields are visible. If you enter one of these fields, you get a small amount of credits as part of an “exploration contract”. What makes exploration worthwhile is the possibility of finding mineable asteroids or cargo containers full of valuables in these fields. The cargo containers can also contain ship upgrades, which is what makes exploration exciting for me. The amount of money you get for finding these fields is so small, however, that it is necessary to sell the contents of the cargo containers and mine the asteroids for this to be a viable career path.
Trading is fairly standard. You buy goods at stations where they are cheap, often due to special events, and sell them where they are expensive, again often due to special events. Prices fluctuate over time and there appear to be systemwide fluctuations in price. If you enjoy the trading systems in games such as Elite, you will probably enjoy trading in Rebel Galaxy. The only major issue I have is that the game never really explains how the economy works. There is a (!) symbol indicating whether a special event is altering prices, but the game never explains what effect the economy and government type of a station has on price and availability of goods.
Bounty hunting is a good way to make money in the early game. You can bribe the bartender on a station or hack a message transponder while in space to determine the locations of pilots with prices on their heads. When you arrive at the indicated location, you must destroy the target’s ship, at which point, you receive an immediate transfusion of credits. The hostile ships you run into during missions and while flying around the system map can also have bounties on them, but the methods I described are more reliable ways of finding bounties. The bounties don’t really scale enough for bounty hunting to be a good source of income in the late game, with one important exception – pirate lords. Pirate lords are powerful enemies with large bounties and often valuable cargo whose locations are indicated on the system map. They don’t spawn often enough to make a career solely off killing them, however.
Mission running is how I made most of my money. There are a large variety of different mission types ranging from running a blockade with valuable cargo, to defending a friendly craft from waves of enemies. They can be quite lucrative, with endgame missions sometimes paying out over a million credits. The missions all involve some form of combat, however. I enjoy mission running, but escort missions are a pain because the AI will crash into other ships and warp into asteroid fields.
Given Rebel Galaxy’s focus on combat, bad mechanics in this area would ruin the game. Fortunately, combat is where Rebel Galaxy is at its most innovative. While most other space combat simulators base their combat systems on World War 2 dogfights, Rebel Galaxy’s combat takes more influence from naval warfare in the Age of Sail, with ships firing broadsides and even ramming each other. This influence is likely why the game takes place on a two-dimensional plane.
Sadly, the story all these mechanics service is forgettable. The writing is mediocre to the point that I couldn’t care whether any of the characters lived or died. Furthermore, the human characters' voice acting was awful, with actors donning ridiculous fake accents to deliver lines with a complete lack of emotion. I can forgive this, however, as the story really only exists to direct the player and give the player interesting battles.
If Rebel Galaxy was a full price AAA release, I probably wouldn’t recommend it. However, I purchased it on sale for $9.99. For that price, or even for the full price of $19.99, it is a great deal. I have seldom put this many hours into a game at this price point. It is not without its flaws, but it is worth buying to scratch that desire for a Firefly-inspired space simulator I’ve had ever since first watching the show.

If I were to describe this game in two words it would be; MISSED OPPORTUNITY, the game was knocking on the door of greatness but seemed to back off just to make release.
The game does a wonderful job of simplifying the typically overengineered elements that accompany this type of game to make it enjoyable for casual fans of the genre but unfortunately it went overboard in some aspects that there is more or less only one way or build to play the game at later levels. The fun is generally in the early levels when you have to trade, steal and kill for every last credit to scrape enough another gun for your rickety old ship.
Also despite its size the game is very shallow though it does a good job of covering this us via mechanics and multiple skins. While you do have seven star systems to explore on a given playthrough each is virtually the same as the other save for the appearance of higher level adversaries and purchaseable gear. Lore is non-existent, story events are dull and linear, zero cinematics, races are virtually identical to one another save for a few pieces of equipment and ship designs and factions and NPCs don't really matter beyond the gear they sell or the quests they give. You have zero impact in the universe and neither does it really care about you.
One thing however that can be said to be perfect about this game is the soundtrack. The choice to go with established Delta Blues and Country artists instead of make pretentions at musical composition was a smart choice. The song list perfectly encapsulates the feel and attitude of the game and if Blizzard is listening THIS GAME IS WHAT A STARCRAFT MMO SHOULD SOUND LIKE!
That said despite its shortcomings I did have fun and I am on my third playthrough. An imperfect but fun game is still a good game.
P.S.: Alas what could have been, especially considering that this game was allegedly the prototype for a Star Wars space RPG before EA killed it.

I've never taken the time to write a review for a game, maybe I'm just too lazy.  However, after reading some of the reviews posted for Rebel Galaxy I felt I had to speak out on the game's behalf.
1st thing: This is not the best space sim ever created but it isn't trying to be.  it is simplified into an easy to pickup arcade experience.  Chiefly, your ship basically moves along a 2D plane, you can move in 360 degrees on that plane but your ship does not fly in true 3D as you could in real space.  Other smaller fighter ships can move above or below you but your ship and every other 'Capital' class ship move on that 2D plane.
This works because of the way space combat is implemented, being that your main weapons are 'broadside'.  (Think of any old pirate movie you've seen where one ship fires cannons out of the side of their ship at another ship and you'll have the idea.)  Admittedly, I thought it was hinky at first myself but I gave it a chance and I am glad I did because I really enjoyed the game.
If you can get past the above-mentioned then you are most of the way there to being able to enjoy this great game.
2nd thing:  If you don't enjoy figuring out economics like where you can buy low and then sell high, you probably won't enjoy this.  However, if you like figuring out where you can buy 'Pure Water' for 2000 a ton and offload it for 92000 a ton.. well let me say I love that kind of business and this game doles out the buy-low sell-high experience like few others I have ever played.  Not to mention the fact that while you're playing trader you have to fend off hostile forces, can take on missions to kill pirates, be a pirate yourself, help out citizens or help the pirate cartels, and different factions give you access to different ships.. I mean there really is a little something for everyone here.
3rd thing:  I have seen some reviews here whining about the graphics, something about the color pallete choices and bad voice acting....  Idkwtf these people are talking about.. I think perhaps they should learn how to calibrate the colors on their monitors properly or maybe invest in new ones because as I have played this game it is often pretty just to look at space.  I'm not sure what people expect.  As for the voice acting, it isn't stellar but it isn't bad by any stretch, besides who ever played any game because someone told them it had the best voice acting they'd ever heard???
4th thing:  You play a game because it's fun, and anyone that enjoys a good story, trading or simply a different kind of space combat should enjoy this.  Here you get a great story line, the opportunity to step into someone else's shoes and experience something you could never otherwise experience, and a great visual and auditory experience.
As you can see I was able to get over 200 hours enjoyment out of this game, because I just revelled in trading and missions, taking my time on the main campaign: learning the systems where to buy low and sell high, killin' pirates and anyone else I wanted to.  Along the way I got the best ship outfitted with the best weapons and then finished the main storyline.
Which is the one drawback to this game... If you just rush through and complete the main missions as quickly as you can it will all be over too quickly.  It's worth the full admission price but if you're skeptical, get it on a sale, they happen often enough, but get it all the same because good times await you!

**ATTENTION: REVIEW CONTAINS SPOILERS OF GAMEPLAY MECHANICS, DOES NOT REVEAL STORY ELEMENTS**
I am a gear head. I love driving and wrenching on vehicles (or really anything mechanical) whenever I'm not playing games about driving or wrenching on vehicles. When I first saw this game I had very high expectations even though it's not yet fully developed. The concept was interesting, the trailer was enticing, and the brief snapshots of the game that I viewed through game reviews were very promising.
PROS:
- Initially fun and strikes your curiosity. This alone is enough to grip your attention for at least an hour.
- Simple and fun gameplay when functional.
- Simple and clean graphics that are easy on the eyes.
- The game has a lot of untapped potential.
CONS:
- The Laika 601 is a painfully unreliable car (even for a "jalopy"). This car reminds me of what you would get if Chrysler, Jaguar, and Trabulant put all of their notoriously awful engineering together into one expensive mess of a vehicle.
- Only a few of the car's parts can actually be manipulated which leaves the mechanical aspect feeling very incomplete.
- The Laika handles awfully on any surface and is almost undriveable in the rain at any speed.
- Money is hard to come by when you are constantly repairing your Laika and parts/upgrades are expensive and do little to enhance the look and drive of the vehicle. Although they make some improvement (mostly aesthetic), the difference in driveability is hardly noticeable.
- Gameplay is easy to pick up on, but will leave you feeling burnt out after a few hours.
- Even for a game that is still under development, Jalopy is very buggy, and often unplayable.
The FUN aspects:
- The game is a driving game and does a good job of centering the gameplay on cruising around. There are no distractions like having to take care of your character (you know what I'm talking about; that constant need to eat, drink, go to the bathroom, and shower on a video game...).
- Collecting items is fun as you never know when you will stumble upon a box or what you will find inside of it.
- Having certain items return to a specific spot (like the wallet in the dash compartment) turns out to be really convenient when you drop them as it leaves you with less clean up and you don't have to return to a location to find a lost essential item.
- The vehicle controls feel engaging without being cumbersome. A few of the essential features all have controls that are simple to use and easy to access which allows you to keep your focus on the driving.
- Occasional parts cars from which you can source extra parts and sometimes upgrades.
- Repairing the car is simple and straightforward which is nice since it's something you'll find yourself doing every minute and a half.
ULTIMATE VERDICT:
Jalopy is a fun game with lots of potential, but has a lot to be improved upon. There is a lot of fun to be had with this game, but unfortunately, there are a few of the gameplay mechanics along with bugs that really ruin the game. I have a budget gaming PC, but have never had trouble running any games before; however, I had to play with lots of the initial settings just to be able to play it and not deal with crashing on the menu or right before the tutorial. The driving aspect is present, but feels more like work than a game. I initially thought that the bad handling was part of the game, you know, because it's a jalopy, but after I fully upgraded all of the available mechanical components, the car still drove like a bumper car with 2.5HP lawnmower engine.
Ultimately, I do not recommend this game. I bought it on sale, and if you find it for sale then go ahead and grab it for a few hours of fun; however, if I purchased this game at full price, then I would definitely be feeling buyer's remorse right now. I will watch for updates and see if the game developers take advantage of the game's potential, but for the moment, I am going to set this game to the side.

With great expectation and epic trailers, the Sid Meier's Civilization: Beyond Earth have been released. Well, we all know what happens when expectation is too high.
Sid Meier's Civilization V was a good game. Maybe not the greatest but its always fun to play like a board game chess. So as this one. Although, this have changed a lot and not much at the same time.
The first thing you'll notice is the UI. It's quite complicated and it's even confusing if you have played Civilization V because the HUD and minimap location has been totally changed. A good new is key shortcuts mostly do the same thing frm Civ V. (e.g. do nothing = spacebar)
Gameplay in general haven't changed much. To build city, find resource, use resource, war, and victory. so what's the change?-the game greatly depends on how the player wants to play. In other words, the player can literally customize its own country like nobody else. This was one thing I liked about the Civ: Beyond Earth.
To be honest, these little upgrades and additional features makes what this game so different than Civ V. It's like Civ V with a lot of mods and plug-ins. Some models and sounds were exactly same as Civ V.
In a nutshell, if you really really liked Civilization v. Then this game will be also fun for you. If, however, you didn't really liked Civilization V, then this will be also boring.

Sidescroller, resource management, war themed survival game. This looks similar to Deadlight, but lacks those large environments you go through (sidescroll) and explore.
You start off in your safehouse, a large house filled with rooms, abandoned furniture, loot and garbage that will help you start off. Once you run low of basic materials and food you have to venture outside for more supplies. There are locations of interest you can visit each night from the map screen.
Once there, you explore fairly small level, usually some house, store or apartment building for resources and loot. You can also encounter friendly and hostile NPC's, and depending on your actions you can sometimes trade with them, talk or simply kill and take their possessions.
Every action in game has it's consequences, killing someone will result in characters depression and decrease how good he/she functions. You start off with 3 survivors, and can get more if one of them dies. Your survivors can get sick, die from hunger, wounds or simply freeze to death if it's too cold.
You can build different kind of contraptions that will help you survive. From basic beds, chairs, heaters to rain water gatherers, herb gardens, radio and much more. Throughout the game you will find and hear small parts of story, that will give you a rough picture of what is going on. Also each survivor has his/her own story that changes depending on your actions from day to day basis.
Visually game is similar to Deadlight, with it's own twist. It's very punishing at first, and will take a while to get a hold on how things work, but otherwise is nice little experience.

Big Pharma is a ...Well, lets just say it outright, it's not a game about being a large scale megacorporation producing a massive amount of drugs and cornering the market. It's not a simulation of medical pills and pharma companies, and it certainly is not a game about the overall management of such a company or the simulation of such a thing.
It makes promises that it can not keep. You will get little strategy, severely abstracted simulation, and very limited management. 'Big Pharma' is not about anything big at all.
Instead, it is a small scale game that is essentially a puzzle about optimising chains of machines to produce a desired output, in a randomised building area of random size, with random ingredients that have random effects. If you like that, then good for you. You will probably enjoy this one, but for the rest of us who are after the other 'features' it proclaims to have..
The simulation is basic to the point where I wonder if it is a simulation at all. Diseases have a set number of sufferers or a set cycle/increase of sufferers and your management is limited purely to the supply lines, machines, and conveyor belts. Everything else is abstracted to the degree that I wonder why it was even included in the game, and many times adds nothing except a timer you need to wait on before you can continue working your belts.
The challenge, and main gameplay is more alike a puzzle.
Fit machines in the (random) building you have to have your (random) ingredients produce an optimal effect for maximum profit. Nearly all the gameplay is about optimising your conveyor belts and machines, which will be frustrating to you because the machines come only in one form with 4 facings. You can not make a symmetrical and effective supply line, and conveyors can not go over or under eachother. You get a limited amount of (Randomly placed) input/output areas to connect to, and often you will not have space for just about anything more than a basic machine.
Employees never have to walk in, out, or do anything in your building, they are merely an animation that is part of the machine. Research and exploration happens somewhere else. You never see your scientists or explorers except in a menu where you send them out.
If this game was only purely the production tab, was honest about its size and content and somewhere between 5-10 dollars, then it would be great. But as it currently stands I just can not reccommend it for its price.
The conveyor belt optimising puzzling is nice, and I will likely play it a few more times just for that, but that is all there is to the game. There is no 'improving the lives of millions', there is no 'getting rid of disease', there is no real management or simulation of a 'pharmaceutical conglomerate' here. The challenge scenarios are jokes, the rival corporations are jokes, and the whole 'business sim' part that it talks about in the "About This Game" part of the store are jokes.
This is a conveyor belts puzzle with shiny graphics, get it for that if it is ever at a 75% or even 50% sale, but as long as it stays above 10 euro/dollar, I recommend avoiding it.

Without any further delay, I present to you my review of Big Pharma.
As a big time fan of management games, I couldn’t help but to take a look at Big Pharma, as it looked like it had everything it needed to be a great game. I couldn’t have been more wrong. It isn’t a great game. It’s a fantastic game. In reality, I should be playing right now, making some medication to cure everyone that doesn’t like the game.
Not only will Big Pharma test your personality, it will also test your ability to efficiently organize a factory. There aren’t any shareholders to please, but there’s always the need to be the best, and save everyone, or at least keep their wallets.
From preventing your opponents from producing a certain medication due to your patents, or even be stopped by your opponents with those same patents, to building massive lines that enable a super cure, you’ll find everything you need to have a good time right here.
There’s not much you can’t do in the game, except releasing diseases to help you improve your sales (there’s a suggestion right there!), so even if you’re having a bad day, you can always start the game and give all your customers bad blood pressure, or headaches, or anal leakage…
Bottom line is, Big Pharma is a fantastic management game, that offers some challenging scenarios, with some puzzle components, as well as need for a carefully planned development plan for the more challenging scenarios.

Bloodline Champions is an underrated game made by Stun Lock Studios.  It currently doesn't receive much support from it's developer, mostly because they're working on Dead Island: Epidemic, but that shouldn't stop you from playing this wonderfully exciting game.
It's a 3v3 format played on very small maps.  No creeps, no grinding for cash to make your Champion stronger, you just go in and beat the crap out of the other players.  Matches take upwards of 5 minutes so there's no huge time committment.  It's brilliant in its simplicity.
The only real issue, and it's a rather large one unfortunately, are the servers.  The servers are of poor quality and lag spikes and packet loss are frequent and can sometimes even make the game unplayable.  Even with this rather large flaw the game is still worth playing.  It's free after all and if you're looking to kill 30 minutes and get lots of games in it's totally worth it.

For veterans: They added a directional dash! Which you can spam constantly! You are SO FAST now! And you have a sword if you want to go full ninja mode. For newcomers: If you enjoyed Doom/Doom II, Painkiller or Serious Sam this is a pure, combat-oriented game in a similar style. Beautiful and moody neon-lit cyberpunk environments funnel you through linear levels, from one set-piece arena battle to the next. Modify your weapons to suit your style of play with branching upgrades in order to inject some variety into combat. Two of the game's shortcomings are it's difficulty and repetition. You'll be shooting a variety of robots non-stop, and little else. There's no puzzle-solving (outside of secret hunting) and no forced story exposition.
Oh and secrets, secrets, secrets. You are plenty rewarded for investigating dead-ends, exploding hidden walls and hopping between balconies to get the most upgrade points possible.
Great game, I enjoy playing it with friends. I recommend it to everyone!

Citadel: Forged with First is a wizard themed sandbox game that lets you build castles, tame animals, fly, pvp, but not much else. While I enjoy building in this game I cannot recommend it in its current state.
The game is very poorly optimized, I run on a gtx 970 and even on the lowest setting the game can not maintain 30fps, and some players with 1080's have performance problems, which is completely unacceptable.
There are also countless bugs that make the game frustraiting or even unplayable. While they should be expected in a early access title obvious ones, such as the server list not functioning properly, should have been fixed before the game went into the early access program.
I do not beleive the player base is substainable considering the state of the game, and blue isle studios may have missed there chance at a successful start up by going into early access before the game was ready.
The combat in the game needs a lot of work. Many spells don't work at all, or are unbalanced, and the game only lets you use two hotkeys per weapon, making your combat options feel very limited, and breaks the pace of the game if you have to go through menu's to change spells in the middle of combat.
Building is fairly enjoyable and works on a grid system where peices snap into place, This can create some nice looking houses but limits your options of where to place objects and walls. Scaffolding and supports are built autimatically when you place a floor peice, however they will often be done in a way that is visually unapealing or hangs above terrain, and can be frustraiting to touch up. Anything that can be angled in different directions is difficult to place, instead of a key to rotate it, the direction is based on what part of the tile you are looking at, and feels very clunky.
I Think it's a cool game.

On the one hand, I don't recomment the Redux version of this game because I think the original is simply better, on the other hand though, five years are not gonna change the fact that Hard Reset is a very niche game. Getting the original is really only worth it, if you're into very, very tough games. It's one of the most challenging FPS of recent years, while still being fair and very well balanced (except for a few parts of the DLC), in my opinion.
Hard Reset Redux, however, kind of breaks this core aspect of the game, by adding quick save (at all times!), Shadow Warrior's movement mechanics and lowering the overall difficulty of the game. While this might open up the game for a broader audience, it does so at the expense of what makes the original Hard Reset really special.
That being said, Hard Reset Redux still offers very fun and explosive (literally) gameplay and with the more dynamic movement mechanics it's highly enjoyable in its own way. Bottom line, if you're just looking for a really cool singleplayer FPS, get this Redux version; if you want a super tough challenge, buy the original instead. And, of course, play them on at least Hard (I strongly recommend Insane, though), to get the most out of 'em.

As an experienced ARK player, i've found this game to be quite interesting.

It looks and handles like a survival game, but all the trivial tasks like eating, drinking and resting are removed so the player may focus on the more fun parts of the game. I really enjoy that decission.
At first, the skillpoint distribution system might seem overwhelming but it doesn't take long to get the hang of it.
The building system is quite intuitive and enables the player to create grand structures and castles with relative ease.
Getting the materials to build is usually a boring and menial task, but also this part has been made relatively quick and easy to handle. Need wood? no problem, just point at that tree 50 meters away and use your extract spell!
I've played around 20 hours at the time of writing this, and i fully expect to be investing hundreds, if not thousands more!
I'm looking forward to seeing first hand the improvements and new additions to the game while it's being developed.

Chaos Theory is probably the best of the Splinter Cell games when it comes to stealth and espionage.  It doesn't have the same "badass" feel as Conviction, but here you're more about NOT BEING SEEN than looking cool.
The game is mission-based and although each mission has several objectives, only the primary ones are needed to complete the mission.  How you complete your mission is very open-ended and there are often multiple paths and ways of doing things.  You can be as ruthless as you want, deciding whether or not to kill people (or simply avoid them entirely).
Despite having been released in 2005, the game still looks impressive.  The controls are complex and some people might have a learning curve to get over, but please stick with it. Unlike lots of more recent games, Chaos Theory allows you to not only save (both manual and quick saves) whenever and wherever you want, but name them as well.
All in all, I suggest playing it if you like stealth games.  If not, don't bother.

Goodbye My King:
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
Being a King can be a cut-throat business. You have to make sure that the people of your kingdom are well-fed, have plenty of entertainment, and that they worship your strength when you conquer new territories. However, you can’t please them all; there are always people who watch closely every step you take in the eventuality that you make a fatal mistake.   And you just made one . . . Goodbye My King!
Goodbye My King is an action / puzzle / stealth game where you take control of the booted king who has to recover gem fragments from his old royal chambers, and reconstitute the three gems on his crown to claim back the throne.
As you land on the main menu, you’ll be welcomed by a soldier who’s sharpening his sword sitting alone in one of the castle room. From here, you’ll be able to choose one of the nine languages available and select to play the first level of the three chapters available. Each chapter has five stages to clear, and the aim is to successfully stealth gem fragments located in the royal chambers until you reconstruct a stone. When you finish each chapter, the reconstructed gem will be placed back on your crown.
However, it won’t be as simple as you would expect. First, you have to find your way into the castle which in some stages can be interesting; just remember where your parents used to hide the front key to the house when you were a tadpole (that’s a great hint). Then, you need to search every single room for useful items to get you into the royal chambers. On top of that, you have to make sure that the imposter king doesn’t see you or he will bash you up if he manages to catch up with you. But that’s not all, he has soldiers at his disposal and they too can grab you and throw you out of the castle. You’ll find hints here and there in the form of paper drawings which will show you where to go and what to do. As you progress to another level, you’ll find the castle with more rooms and floors. In regards to the puzzles, they are pretty simple.
Graphically the games looks good. I think that the controls need to be better especially when you try to interact with objects in front of you, and the AI could also be better. There are a few bugs, but bear in mind that this game is currently an early access. However, I did enjoy the first five levels. It was fun to try to avoid the imposter King and steal fragments from his bedroom.
Positive:
~~~~~~~
-	Nice graphics
-	Fun and easy to play
-	Combination of stealth, action and puzzles
-	Well-designed levels
-	Achievements
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Few bugs here and there
-	Controls need to be tweaked a bit
-	No trading cards
I must admit, I had fun playing this game. I wanted to be the King again and I wanted my castle back!

It's Civ. What else can I say? It looks like Civ, it feels like Civ, and it plays like Civ. There really...isn't much else. Don't get me wrong, the seven hours I played were fun, but it all felt a little bit...meh... Like some others have said, it felt a little like I was playing a really amazing Civ 5 mod.
Units: They exist. All the basic units are there. You've got infantry, LAVs, artillery, ships, the whole works. You can customize them a little when you upgrade (2 options), but from what I saw, there's also a lot less freedom with promotion. You can only choose between an instant heal and a 10% boost to unit stats. The Affinities all have unique units, but I never got to see them. The orbital units are interesting, and fun to use.
Buildings: Also exist. Some improve energy output, some improve production. All the usual stuff, with a few cool sounding uniques for the Affinities.
Tech: The tech web is awesome. There's a lot of depth, and a lot of different approaches the player can take. Might be a bit confusing for people not used to strategy/nation-building games.
Culture: The trees are a lot longer, but there's fewer of them than in 5. I didn't like or dislike the changes. As for Affinities, they're a straight progression with no freedom at all, and there aren't as many perks to get.
Aliens: They're Barbarians from Civ 5, except straight from the depths of Hell. There's a lot of them, and their attacks can really hurt weaker units.
Factions: The leaders seem a bit boring, but I found the ideas behind the factions themselves quite interesting.
Overall: Good for people just starting on Civ, or for really die hard fans who don't mind playing something similar to the last game. If you're looking for something new in the series, this isn't it.               7/10
