For those confused, the Global version of DFO has been out for a little over a year now. It was only recently that the game was added to steam, hence the swamping of reviews with deceivingly low playtimes.
The game was originally published in the west by Nexon America, who blamed the game’s playstyle and outdated graphics for its lack of popularity. They let the original localized version of the game die a slow and horrible death, with almost of year of absolutely no content, and little to no events.
Fast-forward to 2015 and the developers themselves, Neople, decide on a whim to try publishing a game on their own for the first time. As you could probably expect, there were rocky beginnings, but solid communication between the developers and the game’s loyal player base helped the game grow more than ever.
There are a couple aspects I’d like to touch upon on my review, and I apologize in advance if this turns out being longer than I expected. I’ve been around DFO, and in and out of its respective foreign versions for around 7 years now. My first contact with the game being with the Japanese version’s Open Beta in 2008. I saw screenshots of the game on a website called
felt I needed to try it right away. The 2D-Sprite/Arcade-esque design and flashy skills looked so damn cool to me. Which brings me into my first review point:
Graphics:
If you’re a fan of 2D sprite-based graphics, I honestly think the screenshots you’ll find on the steam page will speak for themselves. The game’s been in development for over 10 years now, and now with proper widescreen support, the game looks (to me) as sick as ever. Along with the recently added widescreen support is as an in-game texture up-scaler option, which basically follows suit with many GBA/etc emulators in sharping out pixelated edged to create crisp, high resolution sprites. Needess to say, it looks incredible on 1440P monitors and above. (Said option can be turned off and on at will in the options menu).
The character and world design pretty much hit a soft spot with me as well. I think Neople’s most recent marketing attempts really try to push the anime-y aspects of said art direction, but I don’t really think that’s its main appeal. Everything from NPC character design to even the loading pages for each area are vivid, and more than anything, unique (Look up artist Paristo). Before you realize it, you’ll lose yourself in the world and its lore.
Story:
Not so strong. I mentioned in the previous section that the world is engaging, which it is. But it’d be a lie to say that storytelling is the game’s strong point. Very recently Neople introducted the Scenario quest system, where basically you steamroll through dungeons, watching cutscenes and reading NPC dialogue. It’s interesting for me, to some extent, but more often than not you’ll probably find yourself mashing space to clear dungeons and spend your fatigue faster.
Gameplay
DFO, at its core, is a side-scrolling beat-em-up reminiscent of old classics like Streets of Rage and Final Fight. Take that, and add in keyboard-based play, fast/stylish combat, and countless skills. That being said, it’s still a “Korean” MMO in the sense that progression = grind, normally in the form of daily quests, but the core gameplay is so fun and satisfying that you won’t feel it matters.
There is a large variety of classes. I think like 44 in total sub-classes. Each basically plays completely differently (even the male-female counter parts). So there’s enough diversity to keep you engaged for a very long period of time. I actually think the game encourages having many characters, as you start with a whopping like 20-something character slots, and fatigue limitations are per character.
There is a fatigue system, which resets daily. If you’re willing to accept that fact and try the game out, you’ll understand that it’s not really limiting at all. There are fatigue potions basically given out through so many outlets like weekly events events and alchemy that you don’t actually feel limited at all. Come end-game, you’ll actually feel like having to finish all your fatigue is more of a hassle because you want to spend time working on so many different characters.
PvP (no fatigue necessary) is sadly a dead horse for the most part. It’s really freaking fun but due to the game’s netcode, it has pretty much been abandoned by majority of the playerbase. (It’s still going on strong abroad through, youtube search “Action Tournament” and “DFO F1”).
Connectivity:
DFO’s netcode is based on P2P. Meaning that there is no server related connectivity other than that of logging in, and doing stuff like inventory management. The farther you are with your party mates, the more you will lag. Given that this is the global version of the game, you can imagine this being a pretty big issue. That being said, I’ve never really had too much problems personally in my day-to-day gameplay connection-wise. If you play with the same people, and no one has like, cardboard box internet, you’d be fine.
Music:
Look up “Chasing the Moonlight” or “Final Pursuit BGM” on youtube. If either of those two click for you, you’re in the right place.
Community:
As with most MMO communities there are ups-and-downs.  I think for DFO’s case in particular, people can become really toxic and quick to snap because they love the game, and are so close to it so often. In particular if Neople makes a certain decision or announces X coming out next month instead of Y, there will always be people that flip out. Not to mention the sea of misinformation around the web sprouting from inexperienced players or people that assume they know how the foreign versions work.
With all of that aside, however, the developer Neople is very open with the community, has bi-weekly livestreams on twitch, and basically always acknowledge the community’s concerns and complaints very quickly. Game-community wise
and the DFO sub-reddit are the main online hubs for information and message board’ing. I think if you’re a new player, or are just curious to find out more about specific classics, systems or even future patches, it’d be a good idea to hit up either of those two sites. Basically everyone around loves the game, and will answer your questions (A lot of jokers around too, of course).
Guilds will be the reason you stay for sure. There’s a lot of guild specific content, and etc. I won’t go into detail since I’m sure you’re familiar with most of it, as most MMO players probably are. I can’t really speak for other guilds, but I recruit new players into mine regularly and level new characters together and stuff. Since most of my to-do list is daily-gated, I find myself spending a lot of time just hanging around or chatting with friends/guildies in town.
Cash Shop:
Most of anything you can get from the cash shop is either given away through regular events or purchasable with in-game gold. There are hundreds of avatars you can use to dress up your character, and the package deals that are offered at all times can be bought off the auction house. That paired with dyes, and you can really go crazy dressing up your character for hours.
One irk of mine, though, is that avatars, once purchased/opened, are untradeable. This is something specific for the global version of the game, and that I think is pretty garbage, but know it makes sense from a business standpoint.
But yeah, I wrote so much, but I’m pretty sure no one will read this in the sea of reviews. Just know if there’s one guy out there that can write this much for no reason, this is probably a game worth trying out.

This War of Mine is very different to your copy and paste war games and story driven games. This War of Mine centers not on the people fighting the war but to the people who are trying to live and survive in the war.
Although it may look simplistic, honestly, the decisions you have to do will make you feel down for the rest of the game. There are choices but with those choices are consequences.

The strangely titled retro platformer Bleed from Bootdisk Revolution was released recently on Steam but has been available DRM free and on XBox Live since 2012. Featuring a cool pixelated purple-haired heroine dual-wielding pistols, you can make sure this game got my attention and getting it for my birthday from a friend, I had to try it out. Is it worth buying or is this indie game just another retro platformer in the sea of retro platformers? Let's find out.
The story in Bleed isn't exactly complicated stuff. You're basically sent out to kill some ex-heroes who have turned into villains somehow over time in order to become the new ultimate hero. The game does have its own unique humor though and contains several references to oldschool platformers and clichés. I particurarily love the level and boss descriptions and the main character has a ton of personality as every time you die, she will utter a comment about how she died, often pertaining to the level or enemy you fought. The story is pretty basic but sufficiently quirky to make it a bit unique although the gameplay is obviously the focus of the game.
The game plays a lot like the old classic Megaman games although with its own spin on things. The basic goal of each level, which can be played alone or co-op with a friend, is to make it through to the end and killing everything in your path, using your abilities to survive the hazards and enemies that come your way. The controls are gonna take some getting used to, especially the jumping mechanics (which confused me a bit at first as your double jump is controlled by aiming it). You're given two weapon slots and start out with dual pistols and a rocket launcher (two of my favourite weapons in any game) although as you complete each level you earn money you can use to buy new weapons and upgrades and you can change your weapon loadout at any time during the level, which expands your inventory slightly. You're also given a slowmo ability which comes in handy during certain areas and boss fights and it can be upgraded to last longer by giving you more energy, and a health bar which can be upgraded and you have infinite lives so losing is not that big of a deal, respawning you in the room you died. This is a godsend because this game is really challenging, even on the Easy difficulty. I really recommend not playing on anything but Easy when first playing this game as even that mode seriously kicked my♥♥♥♥♥on several occasions, especially since the controls feel a bit awkward at first and take some getting used to.
Once you have beat the game's 7 levels with the last one basically being a boss run, you can play through those again on higher difficulties or attempt some harder modes such as the Arcade mode (playing through the game on one life) or Challenge mode where you fight 3 bosses simultaneously on one screen. You can also unlock other characters by completing the game on other difficulties so the game does have some replay value although for me the game felt a bit too short and with not enough differences to warrant repeated playthroughs. I would've loved the ability to play more than just 7 levels personally.
The graphics are pretty decent, sporting the retro pixelated style you can expect from a retro platformer so there's not much to say about it. It feels deliciously 80's though with a lot of purple and pink used and a pretty broad colour palette. The game has a pretty good soundtrack although it just didn't stick that well with me for some reason. The main theme is pretty much the only memorable theme from the game in my opinion which is a shame. I just didn't feel the soundtrack stood out that well for me.
So overall, how good is Bleed? For me, the game is pretty average and kind of gets lost in the sea of retro indie platformers these days. Although I enjoy the style, especially the dual pistols and just the fact the game has a badass heroine and a quirky story, I found it way too short and way too difficult to really get into. The controls take some getting used to and even then I just can't find much replay value. It might be something I have the odd craving for now and then but I can't see myself playing this much.
SUMMARY:
STORY: 5/10
Largely forgetable and just there to serve the gameplay, although a bit quirky.
GRAPHICS: 7/10
Colourful retro graphics, but nothing you haven't seen a million times before in other retro platformers. If you like this style, this game is probably for you but for me it just feels a bit above average.
GAMEPLAY: 5/10
Difficult controls take a bit getting used to giving the game a bit of an unfair difficulty level for beginners and it will take a while to get into. It's a decent platformer though and the gunplay is fun. I will have to say it's a very short game though, the only replay value is there if you somehow feel the need to play through the same levels over and over.

This War of Mine is a game about civilians trying to survive in active war zone. It's split into two segments, Day and Night. During the day, you manage a group of survivors in a mostly derelict building. You have them dig through rubble, fix holes, barter with other survivors, build things to make the building more liveable...basically just living day to day. Then at night, you send 1 person out to scavenge around the city. You start each game with a party of 3 survivors; random events might have up to 2 more asking if they can join you.
Different survivors have different traits. For example, my current party of 4 has one person who's good at cooking, one who's good at bartering, one who's good at sneaking, and one who's fast.
Part of the game's challenge is trying to manage multiple aspects of the survivors lives, like their morale, their fatigue, their health, their hunger...basically everything about a person's life. For example, if you send the same person out to scavenge two or three nights in a row, they'll get overtired. If you also have them rob people all three nights, they might get so sad they'll lose hope and commit suicide.
The game has a crafting system. Your items of this sort are mostly generalities; for example, if you want to build a radio, you might use 3 sets of "Components," 3 sets of "Parts," and 2 sets of "Electric Parts." Or if you want to filter rainwater, you first need a collector, and then you use some of your "Components" to make filters for the collector. You might also make multiple filters in one go, and use some of them in a moonshine still. Or if you need to make a knife or a pistol for your scavenger to take for defense, you might use some "Weapon Parts" and some "Components," Different items are made at different stations; you might build a bed with a standard workbench, while you would need a herbal workshop to process tobacco into cigarettes for bartering.
I've never lived through a war, but the game developers who worked on This War of Mine did, and that's why they made it. It's one of the most depressing games I've ever played, and yet I keep coming back to it, albeit just in little increments.

I've played this game since nexon's closed beta. Since then the whole world blew up. But it's still pretty good. It's an arcade brawler psuedo-MMO. I say pseudo MMO because it's basically somewhere in-between a co-op multiplayer focused game like Payday or Warframe and a full MMO like World of Warcraft. There's an economy, there are guilds, there's an overworld where you can see other players, but all the fighting is done in instanced dungeons. I prefer that because it allows it to be a bit more challenging and execution heavy than a 'real' MMO. It's got a really wide variety of classes to choose from, a massive amount of content thanks to being like a decade old, and a combat system that's easy to pick up while also having a lot of complexity. It's free to play dragon's crown, basically. Except it came out before dragon's crown.
Now, there are some problems with DFO. It's run by some korean guys in a company called neople, and bless their ♥♥♥♥ing hearts they try their hardest at this but they're more or less running a korean game with korean design and korean ideas but hosted in NA/EU with an english translation. This leads to some parts of the game looking like really cheap pay to win scams when they actually aren't. I'm going to dedicate the rest of this review to try and show why various systems in the game that look absolutely awful are actually not that bad.
The first hurdle you're going to have to jump is the fatigue system. Basically you get X amount of FP every day and once you run out you can't play anymore until tomorrow. Most people probably see this and flash back to ♥♥♥♥♥♥ mobile scam games that let you play for 5 minutes then ask you to pay for more game time. This isn't DFO's case, though. You can't exactly pay for more FP. You can pay for some stuff that extends your FP, but it's not that big of a deal. There are really two things you need to know about FP. One, if you manage it well and stack FP pots, do the fatigueless dungeons, etc, you can play the game for a really really long time without running out. Especially on weekends which have extra FP. Two, FP is per character. So you can switch to an alt and reset your FP entirely. Which means you can, technically, play forever. And even if you're hard maining a character you want an alt. Because having an alt gives so many bonuses that ignoring them is stupid. They give you flat stat boosts depending on how many decently leveled alts you have, you can send them on missions to generate some loot, and you can summon them as supports in dungeons.
The next thing you might notice is that avatars give stat boosts. Just know that you can buy rare avatars (ones with increased stat bonuses) for a not entirely unreasonable price off the auction house. Or you could get the current box set of advanced avatars (slightly worse stats than rare avatars) at usually a pretty dang reasonable price, and that often includes a pet and a special title. So it's a weird system but it's not that bad.
It's worth saying that there are some legitimate problems with DFO. PVP is awful right now- and you might think "well that's 90% of MMO's" but DFO used to have really, really good PVP. It's just really neglected on the DFOG server and I wouldn't recommend playing it for PVP. The other problem is that the late late late game epic grind is pretty bad. Basically the only way to get the best gear (epics) is to play hell mode, the only way to play hell mode is through demon invites, and you can get those through various in-game means (events, drops, auction house, mileage shop [which is basically a weird alt currency that you get passively for completing dungeons.]) What I'm getting at is this game is really RNG. That's all MMORPG's, especially korean ones, but I'm just giving you fair warning. Of course you don't have to worry about that at all for a long time, so the only reason this would affect you is if you get really, really into it. Also, good news is that chronicle or legendary gear (neither of which are that difficult to obtain) will very literally get you through 99.9% of the games content. There is all of one area that really genuinely requires epic gear. It's called anton. I'm 21 and I've been playing this game since I was in junior high. And I have never actually run anton. I almost don't want to. Running Anton at this point would be like an ancient Greek priest climbing mount olympus only to find out their life has been a complete lie. There's just no way it's worth the grind. It's also worth saying that the developers seem to be trying to make the end game at least a bit less grindy. They're just not doing it fast enough.
Basically just play the game and have fun and you won't regret it. It's a fun game. Experiment with different classes, figure out which one you like best, play the game until you aren't having that much fun with it and come back in like 6 months to see what's new. That's what I do, and it's lasted me a literal decade of off and on play.

I've been playing this game on and off since the Nexon beta days back in 2009. Neople has done an amazing job at bringing this game back from the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ that was Nexon. Really fun game the only beat'em up MMO you can find these days. You'll be complaining about the fatigue point system early on but once you get high level you'll be wondering how much longer it'll take to use it all up especially if you play multiple characters. Having unlimited fatigue back in the Nexon days was probably the worst decision ever because gold farmers/sellers were everywhere. I should also mention that there is literally no gold seller spam in the chat like you see in many f2p games, Neople is doing such an amazing job combating that.
The good
-Neople listens to the community they even stream and talk to us on Twitch on Thursdays every 2 weeks to let us know what's going on
-Always have great events going on that can benefit the old and the new players
-Huge variety of classes
-Constant game updates which will get us up to date to the Korean version, I would say in 2017 we would be caught up which was an impossible dream back in the Nexon days
-Cash shop isn't pay2win, you can buy most cash shop avatar boxes with gold
The bad
-Endgame gear you'll be grinding and praying to RNGesus, I would compare it to something like an ARPG end game grind like Diablo or Path of Exile
-PVP isn't as lively as before because Global server+p2p=bad connections but you can still find a few good matches once in a while. Honestly this is the main reason I started playing this game but it went downhill because Neople isn't doing any kind of updates for PVP for some reason
-Sadly there are some classes that are better than others with equal gearing but in the Korean version they are slowly fixing and balancing classes
-Cash shop CAN be pay2win to a certain extent examples: buy & sell avatar boxes for gold which in return gets you more chances at RNGesus to get the best gear, basically you'll have to be spending somewhere in the $100+ or even $1000+ to even consider it being pay2win at that point
-Inventory slots and safe slots only purchasable in the cash shop but Neople give these out during events often
Overall it's one of the best f2p games I've played and am still currently playing. At the rate we're going the game will just keep getting better. Thank you based Neople.

War of the machines.
First person shooters are starting to come back en vogue. With the recent successful reboot of Doom and Blizzard stepping into the arena with Overwatch, the genre is seeing some of its best action in years. Hard Reset was a game that came and went without a lot of people noticing, but it is also the game that put developer Flying Wild Hog on the map, and eventually led them to create the excellent Shadow Warrior reboot. Now the game is getting a second chance on consoles with Redux bringing a new visual coat of paint, rebalanced action, and even some new enemies and weapons.
Hard Reset is a student of the old-school design of shooters. The action is fast, there is no reload button, and the best strategy is going to be circle-strafing. This is also a campaign-only shooter, and a short one at that. There are leader boards and a new game plus option, but once the brief campaign is over, I felt little reason to go back for more.
MSRP: $19.99
Platforms: XB1, PS4, PC
Price I’d Pay: $14.99. I got the game for 85% off so I paid $3.00.
There are only two weapons in the game, each with a dedicated button for switching between. Instead of offering an arsenal Hard Reset instead gives players attachments to their weapons, essentially making them new weapons. This is a neat idea in concept, but in execution it becomes cumbersome fiddling with the weapon wheel to switch between the shotgun and machine gun attachment when dealing with enemies. I ended up finding one that worked for most occasions, and stuck with it.
The enemy variety is also slim. The Redux version does add some new types, but a large bulk of the game is spent mowing down the same collection of robotic foes. Their AI is also simple, spending the majority of their time simply bum-rushing players, which is of course standard for shooters of this type, but also feels dated. The strategy to take them down never changes, so I guess it is good the campaign is brief, as the repetition sets in quickly.
The shooting feels good, but the lackluster enemy design doesn’t do it any favors. Also for a console shooter I recommend turning off aim assist. It really got in my way more than it helped. The biggest issue I had with the actual game play is that it was rarely satisfying to take down an enemy. Bullets don’t have a good impact when they hit, and none of the guns or attachments feel fun to shoot. The game quickly devolves into a shooting gallery in the most mundane way.
The story of Hard Reset is told during loading screens with comic book panels dubbed over. Nothing about the story is memorable; the characters are boring, and even the game recognizes players would rather be shooting. When loading is complete, a large swath of text blankets the screen suggesting the proper action: skipping the cut scene.
At least the world itself is pretty to look at. It is a futuristic, neon-lit environment where it always seems to be dark and raining. Visually the game looks great and runs at a solid frame rate on consoles. It is a pretty game, which is easily one of its most impressive features.
I wanted to love Hard Reset Redux, especially after coming off Doom, which had scratched that 90s FPS itch I have almost annually. There just isn’t enough here to satisfy. Gunplay feels weak, enemies are boring to kill, and the world wears out its welcome quickly. Nothing about this game is overly offensive to the senses, but it just never stands out from the pack either.

Not terrible, and not earth-shattering, Hard Reset Redux is a decent first-person shooter.  Very BladeRunner-esque with it's environment, it's very physics driven, with a highly destructable environment that you can use against your enemies.  Runs smooth and flawless on my R9 290X averaging around 200fps once vSync was taken off at Ultra Settings.
Probably my biggest complaint is that it seems far too easy on Normal mode.  In my first couple of levels, I made mistakes that should have cost me a checkpoint reset several times, but I scraped on through with not too much trouble.  Health and ammo was lying EVERYWHERE in the levels, making stocking back up and staying alive almost ridiculously easy.  Some of the bigger enemies take forever to kill, while their hits to you seem mostly meaningless.  Admittedly, I haven't played on hard or anything else, but I feel that Normal shouldn't be a cakewalk.  Some battles seemed easy to predict, and combat almost became wooden at times ... run backwards, keep the mouse button pressed.

I really enjoy this game, and would recommend it to anyone who likes puzzle games. It is a free-to-play model, which may frustrate some, but I found it to be no problem, since the basic gameplay is solid enough to warrant a decent playthrough. Admittedly I have not played a lot in the PC version, since I started off with Android, but I find this game to have a decently attractive presentation.
Graphics: The character designs are interesting, and the animation is decent, especially for a free to play puzzle game.
Concept: This is basic puzzle quest, except there are up to three characters on each side per battle instead of one. The leveling system is a little odd, since leveling your characters requires ISO, but leveling their powers requires covers, which can be bought or won in game. Some covers are aggravatingly hard to get, but it shouldn't stop anyone from enjoying the game, because the lack of leveling one hero's powers does not break the overall experience.
Sound: Overall, the sound design is good. I wouldn't say it was amazing, since the music is repetitive and generic and the sound effects accompanying each power can get old once a certain power is used multiple times in a battle. The sound won't win any awards in my book, but it is decent enough to not detract from the experience of playing this game.
Replayability: This game is really replayable. The basic concept is solid, and the gameplay, although it relies a bit on luck, is addicting and engaging. Levels in the game can also be replayed for different rewards, which encourages another playthrough. In most games, backtracking is considered a chore, but in this one I find it to be worth while, since the main gameplay is fun, and it is not to tedious or necessary to complete further levels in the game. In other words, it is optional to those who are completionists, or who are looking for something in particular.
Grade: 8/10 (Honestly, a number cannot truly describe an experience, but I am including it for reference and a quick glance to see the sum of the parts I have described.)
I hope all find this helpful in determining if this is the right game for them.

Don't get me wrong, I enjoyed the 63 hours I had with the game. Collecting plants, using interesting spells, getting to fly! But overall, It was a terrible experience. Either its PVE or PVP, having to constantly worry about your base or being attacked out of nowhere is just to frustrating, not to mention time consuming if something does happen. I know some of you will say, "but its a survival game, that's how its meant to be played." I understand that, I do actually enjoy the survival aspect of games, and its a really cool idea on paper. What I don't enjoy is if it's level/gear based PVP. It creates an unbalanced field of unbalanced combat. In no way can you tell me its a good game mechanic when a level 60 attacks a level 5. And I actually never encountered much of this myself, its all the people who start out (arguably the most populated server at the moment) and gets completely stomped by extremely higher levels. This makes it practically impossible to even progress and PLAY THE GAME. Also the fact the building bases offer no protection whatsoever doesn't help the matter. Contrary to the fact, I actually want this game to be good! I love medieval fantasy, I love survival games (when they're fun to play). I want this game to be a HUGE success. I'm sure the developers are doing their best to fix and update the game, I mean heck, its only been 18 days since it released. So I have confidence in the developers that they will undoubtedly improve the game. I hear they are going to create a whole new system for raiding bases. That's the good direction that the game needs, and its refreshing to see the developers respond so quickly. But in my honest opinion, they should ditch the level system (possibly gear too) and make it pure skill based combat. Or at least give new players a chance to get started so they can fend off higher level enemy players. With that said, I wish the Citadel Team the best of luck in creating the potentially great game that it could be.

Wow, where to start. Okay, first of all, not a bad game, but you'd expect that, considering what it so obviously (blatantly?) copied from. This is FREELANCER, with a fresh coat of paint.
The gameplay is almost exactly the same (different factions with rep you raise and lower, a bunch of different systems and stations you travel between via jumpgates to trade/mine/encounter random enemies, and a bunch of different ships to unlock and upgrade with parts you buy and find).
Even the plot is very similar; You're handed a Space Macguffin right at the start of the game, you're not told what it is, and over the course of the plot you try to figure out what it is while everyone else tries to take it from you. I can't say much more without spoilers, other than to say that the rest of the plot, even the conclusion, are almost exactly the same, too. The same kind of threat, the same solution to end the threat.
The only real differences, are two things:
One, there's a somewhat dynamic economy that causes commodity prices (but not equipment prices) to fluctuate (more could have been done to make this intuitive to the player, however - I feel like when you find loot in a dynamic economy game, it should be reasonably easy to ascertain  what kind of station you can sell it at, to get the best price, and in many cases I found that not to be the case. I found myself just randomly station hopping, hoping that the next one will give me a good price. There are mechanics that seem to be intended to help you in this regard (such as finding a hackable object that will give you system-wide current market prices), but it's cumbersome and slow and so you end up not using it.
Two, instead of the game being a 3d, fly-anywhere-you-want kind of experience, you and every other 'capital' ship are locked to a single plane, to facilitate the 'broadside' naval-style combat system. Where Freelancer was a game about dogfighting with some capital ships thrown in, this is a game about capital ship combat with some fighters thrown in. Which is cool and enjoyable, as a fairly wide variety of weapon options keeps it interesting for a good while as you learn what works and what doesn't for how you like to play. Also facilitating this is that there seems to be no risk to trying out different things - if you buy a piece of equipment and find you don't like it, it seems you can sell it back for full price at any station at any time. Which is also really good, because some equipment seems really useless, and some ships are, too - pro tip: the best ships are the ones that are shaped like boxes, with all of their turrets located such that they can almost always fire at an enemy no matter where it is in relation to you, and the fact that lasers never miss an enemy as long as they have line-of-sight on it makes them hands-down superior to every other weapon type.
Now for some bad things:
One, this game was obviously made for console kiddies, and is obviously obviously made to be played with a controller. The camera responds poorly to a mouse, it's difficult to use precision aiming with a mouse, and the game really suffers from what I call "One Button To Rule Them All" syndrome, where one button is used to perform several functions based on context, and what ends up happening is that you hit the button expecting one thing to happen, and something else happens instead, which is very frustrating.
There are other problems like this, too - when you want to dock with a station, you normally hold down this button, but you'll also dock with a station by bumping into it (which often happens by accident). You'll be hailed by a plot-related character, and if you don't manually accept the hail within 10 or 15 seconds, the game will force you into the conversation, even if you're in the middle of a fight. (Yeah, hold on guys, I know we're in the middle of a massive space battle here, but I really need to take this call. ???!?) There's just a lot of little stuff like this that makes it feel like the game treating you like an idiot.
And finally, there is a ridiculously overpowered npc starfighter called the Schizo II that suddenly starts appearing late in the game, that absolutely wrecks anything it manages to hit, including you, even if you have the best equipment in the game. This stupid little fighter plane has more firepower than the biggest, baddest enemy dreadnoughts you'll face, and it's just... really dumb and not fun. The first couple times I encountered them, I actually thought the game had glitched, because I went from roflstomping everything in my way, to suddenly going from 100% to dead in literally 3 seconds, before I had any chance to react to what had knocked me out of warp.
So, tl;dr, I can't recommend this game unless it's on sale (which it fortunately was when I bought it). It's worth a few bucks for a some laughs, the nice soundtrack, and mostly good gameplay, but it ends up leaving a bad taste in your mouth with its odd combination of, sometimes it's annoying you by holding your hand, and other times you find yourself wishing it held your hand a little more. That and, of course, the fact that it's basically a ripoff of Freelancer...

This is a pretty good Hitman game.  It's a shame that it wasn't structured like the other games in the series, where each level is a replayable entity on its own, but that doesn't stop it from being good and well worth your time.  Rather, you play through it as one long narrative, where each level blends into next.  There's nothing complex or especially meaningful with the story but it does its job well in giving the protagonist a reason for pushing forward while entertaining the player.  However, that's also its weakest point.  My enjoyment with hitman games has traditionally been about finding new ways to complete a level, ie: assassinating the target in different ways.  Here though, you don't always have a target.  Sometimes the point of the level is to evade enemies pursuing you or to get to a given location.  It's fun and well realized, but not necessarily classic Hitman.  I can't fault the developers for wanting to go a different direction with their property instead of just rehashing the same thing.  While I wouldn't call this a mistep, I would say it is misguided.  Still, overall very good and worth playing.

Altough the game starts out as fun for the first few hours, the huge uphill-grind became apparent to me when I entered the second system and realised I had to upgrade all my weapons and equipment to 'Mark 3' putting me back at square one when it came to fighting and that the grind I had to endure before was going to continue once more. It made me realise the next system was going to be 'mark 4' and that I was going to have to do the exact same thing in a pretty much similar system with almost similar enemies as in the first two systems.
Rebel Galaxy gets a few things right: pretty graphics, good music and a fun premise. Unfortunately, it also gets a lot of things wrong: your spaceship can't go up or down but smaller spaceships and objects can and the way the game makes you aim (by firing from your portsides) this makes for some rather chaotic fights where you'll be wondering what's going on in front, behind, or on the other side of you (or even  below or above you as fighters can move on a 3D-plane).
Luckily, you can switch to your (auto-aiming) turrets that will actually also do fine without your intervention. This does mean that every ship pretty much plays the same. Yes, you can ram enemy ships if your ship is fast enough but it really isn't all that effective on a 2D-plane.
You can choose between trading, running missions for any of the factions, following the storyline, mining or wandering around aimlessly hoping for random encounters. There's not much else to do. Mining does not yield significant results, trading is very difficult with an interface that doesn't keep good track of what station needs what and the missions are endless fetch-quests where you will spend a lot of time flying to and fro, continuously being thrown out of warp because of some object or another. After having been thrown out of warp for the umptieth time, I decided it was not for me.
When you do finally arrive at your destination there's a good chance that you will end up facing such a formidable foe that you spend the next 20 minutes kiting each one of them or not even damaging them at all because their shields regenerate faster than yours do and because of the way the broadside combat works, it's impossible to keep an eye out on all those ships.
Everything in this game is convoluted: scanning enemy ships requires you to pause the game, keep the mouse button pressed and then do the same for each and every ship in the area. Your radar does not automatically detect objects, you need to press F every so many seconds for them to show up on the map. You can not tell your weapons to prioritize targets, they will do whatever they feel like. You can, however, tell them to ONLY shoot at certain targets which means if you want effective prioritization, you will be pausing the game. A lot. Your wingman is nigh-on useless as he'll just fly off and do whatever he feels like. You can only hire one wingman and you have no control over his ship load-out nor is it very clear what kind of ship he offers. The only indicator of strength is the price you pay for him. Or her.
Maybe if you have more patience or really enjoyed the endless flying around in Eve, this is for you. Some people call it the next Freelancer and although it is definitely Freelancer-inspired, it doesn't capture any of its beauty nor difficulty. All the systems look the same, the factions have no ideology to them and there are no awe-inspiring ship battles where you fly above and through metal carcasses. Everything plays out the same way and the auto-aim, although great for controller users (so I've gathered), doesn't really make it a very good keyboard/mouse-game as you'll be constantly looking portside since those guns can not be AI-controlled and thus need to be fired manually. Yet, they still auto-aim which removes most of the skill requirements for landing good shots. Just move in close enough, keep the right mouse button pressed and voila. Even fighters will be shot down by these guns.

Hitman: Absolution is a game developed by IO Interactive and published by Sqaure Enix and is the fifth game in the Hitman series. As the enigmatic Hitman, you must use stealth and tactical problem solving to enter, execute and exit your assignment with minimum attention and maximum effectiveness
It puts you in the role of Agent 47, a shadowy assassin who is equally capable of slipping in and out of target locations un-noticed, the game provides a wealth of memorable situations you will talk about years down the road
Hitman: Absolution is a very good game, the game offers the main campaign and offers single missions (or contracts) that look interesting, in which you can even design your own missions and publish them, but these are all based on the campaign locations and persons with the parameters changed
Hitman: Absolution has nice graphics with some good stealth action with moderately good combat action for the impatient and apart from the overall "bad guy turns good" story, it has a good plot
The game offers 20 chapters with diversified, intertwined and exotic locations with many ways to meet the objective including hateful villains with even more hateful lovers, partners, family members and incredibly very satisfying ways to kill them and surprisingly, no bugs or crashes whilst I played
I highly recommend Hitman: Absolution. I loved the great locations and the characters!

This game has been eating up several hours a day as of late (just what I need as exams grow ever closer), and it's difficult to describe just what makes it so fun.
Pros:
The matches are short and action-packed. Losing max-health as you get damaged is a great and unique mechanic to prevent the game from lasting forever along with the PUBG-like wall that closes in on the match after 2 minutes.
There are, as of 11/22, 23 characters who all feel very different from each other. Choosing 5 battlerites out of 10-15 for each character can compliment different play styles and keep things fresh and exciting.
The number of rewards you get, especially early-game, keep you playing as you can easily obtain a dozen or so new skins or avatars to play with. If you get something you already own in a chest, you earn tokens which allow you directly buy a desired skin.
Playing with friends is great and their servers have definitely improved since they launched f2p.
Cons:
While each character is unique, there are a few shared abilities that make the game kind of wonky.
Counters are activated by melee and projectile attacks, but sometimes, these include abilities and even ults and vice versa.
Barriers like Raigon and Bakko allow these melee characters get in your face and beat up on you without you being able to defend yourself, and usually ends up with you harming yourself.
There are some connectivity and group issues that I have encountered with my friends that requires us to disband and recreate our party. An easy fix, but an unnecessary issue.
Overall, Battlerite has tons of potential with its own take on a MOBA-like gamemode in the works. I have immensely enjoyed it thus far and hope the devs keep working and improving every aspect of their already magnificent game.

I can't believe I just played this game for more than 8 hours straight.. Always wanted to pick this game up when it came out but couldn't because
of regional restrictions..
Though 8 hours may not be a lot for this game I think it suffices to write a first impression. I can't imagine the rest of the game to be that much different anyway.
It's a pretty typical 'Korean' MMO; take that as you will. After choosing from a diversity of interesting classes, the game starts out with a nice class-based intro. But then it slowly descends into your usual endless chain of quests with a story and dialogue that's even less compelling than my grandma's diary. I quickly found myself skipping through it because not only does it feel dragged out and trivial; it often pops up untimely, interrupting the pace or obnoxiously obscuring the reward screen. Having never played this game before, it's a bit overwhelming when the game presents you with NPCs and   a crapload variety of items that you're not familiar with. And that's probably what you'll be going through for at least major part of the game.
The game does feature a fatigue/stamina system which some may think is awful. I don't find it to be that much of an obstacle (yet) unless you really want to focus on just progressing one character. That said, the game does encourage playing multiple characters for bonuses. Fatigue is separated between characters and seems to be pretty lenient but it's still a limit to your gameplay per character.
But a Korean MMO is of course nothing without it's obligatory cash shop filled to the brim with items that make your DFO life easier and cosmetics that cost more than your wallet is willing to spend. Due to lack of further knowledge regarding the game's mechanics, I won't cry out P2W.. but it really wouldn't come as a surprise if many of the available items are. And that basically sums up my most prominent gripes with the game.
Because in spite of all the above, it's a really fun brawler. The controls are tight and feel very good for the fast-paced/spamfest combat. The sprites and animations are superb and the flashy huge skills really makes combat feel like an over the top scene from an anime out of your wildest dreams. Paired with a banging soundtrack to boot, it makes for a very enjoyable experience. And truthfully, that should be the most important aspect/biggest reason to play this game.
I haven't dabbled in multiplayer yet as I find the singleplayer experience (so far) to be more than satisfying. The servers are located in the US but from my understanding MP seems to be P2P which can be a nuisance when playing with people from other regions. That's about all I can say about it, as I don't care for looking more into it until I (want to) get there.
So in conclusion, I'd say it's a F2P that's definitely worth a try.

Super long review incoming. Apologies in advance.
I've played a good amount of DFO when it was still published by Nexon out here in the west (1000+ hr). Then, when it failed due to a series of abysmal desicions from Nexon NA, I kept playing by playing the chinese localization (the korean one's a bit trickier to get into) and put thousands of hours into that version, and now I'm definitely putting thousands into this version. Do not be fooled by the lack of achievements (they only respond to steam specific accounts and I'm using my pre-existing one might get to it later) and hundreds of hours; a good portion of me is DFO. I say this perhaps to give some weight to what I have to say about this game, as I'd like to see this game get bigger but I'd also like to be honest about the game, for the new Steam crowd that's genuinely interested and doesn't want to depend on sugared up reviews or meme nonsense ones.
I like this game a lot but the PvP frustrates me by way of this version's technical limitations and I get burnt out from the PvE frequently. In my opinion this game isn't for everyone. I'll do my best to describe in short what the game is and if it sounds like something you'll like, take a shot at it, and if it doesn't sound up your alley...it probably isn't. You can still give it a shot though, given that it IS free!
The game itself is a 2D MMORPG where you travel through dungeons and fight mobs in a beat 'em up style. Levelling up characters unlocks new active and passive skills and once you've hit the level cap of 86 (an odd number I know, we'll be getting 90) the endgame is built around farming for certain quest equipment sets between Chronicle sets from puzzle filled Otherverse dungeons, ancient Legendaries, and eventually Epic gear from Hell modes, which is most likely your best gear but their chances of dropping are entirely random. While your epic gears don't drop you can try your hand at some of those other equipment sets that can be guaranteed - you just have to farm for them. Alternatively, you can try levelling other classes to see if you like other playstyles. In some near future we should be getting a raid, and another will follow a while after. The game adds some mandatory pacing with the fatigue system: most dungeons require FP to run and once you're out you're limited to some little side dungeons (only a couple runs a day) and PvP, or you can work on other characters as each character has its own FP bar. If the limitations of Fatigue upsets you, know that it's for the better - it was one of the things that killed old Nexon DFO.
In regards to the Pay to Win discussion...It sort of is, but not excessively, and not in the way that you'd think. The cash shop is filled with a bunch of helpful little tools and some nice avatar packages that'll give you a notable stat boost alongside a fresh new look. You will never have to spend a dime to get these if you don't want to. Neople events are very generous. I have not spent a cent on this game and I have plenty of cash shop items and avatars. Beyond the events, some players sell KK cards for in game gold, so if you have nothing in particular you want to buy with gold but want an avatar package, you can buy KK cards with gold, or the packages themselves since they're tradeable. The reason the game CAN be P2W is that those who sell KK will get a lot of gold, and they can use that gold on Demon Challenges; the material you need to run hell modes and try for epic gear. So, really, they spend real money and just get more chances at epic gear than normal, and they'll have some spare gold to do all the fancy stuff with their gear to make it as good as possible (enchanting, reinforcing, that sort of thing.) That's about it, really. The grind can still take forever and it's nothing that can't be accessed without money. Plus, if you don't care too much about the endgame and want to just experiment with different classes and/or play PvP, none of that will ever have to matter to you.
The last thing I want to talk about is PvP. Within the last few years of my life I've found myself getting quite involved with competitive Melee, Project M, and am picking up new fighters constantly, but I've neglected PvP in this game until sometime last november. As it turns out, this game has a PvP system that is a lot more solid than most other MMOs in my opinion, and it is very successful in korea, with PvP streamers being common and big budget sponsored tournaments being held. But if you find that you might like the PvP in this game...things are...unfortunate here. This game isn't built for enormous regions like North America. You can notice it in PvE as well in parties, but not nearly as well as PvP. The game uses peer 2 peer, which, in the source location, south korea, is amazing. Here, however, it's terrible. Two perfectly decent ethernet connections can struggle. Beyond that, PvE is this game's moneymaker, and in some ways PvP is at its mercy; despite certain stat rebalances for the sake of balanced PvP, gear can make notable differences in PvP, and you're handicapping yourself unless your character is at least 80 something.
HOWEVER, there are a good number of silver linings and if you know how to approach PvP you can still enjoy it pretty well. The use of epics are frowned upon in PvP and community/official tournaments ban them, so you don't have to worry about getting them for PvP. All you really need are halidom sets, which are easily obtainable, especially with some recent content additions. Also, this is something I should've mentioned earlier but levelling up characters, as it may come off as tedious, is incredibly easy and quick compared to most other MMOs, and I swear every day levelling becomes easier. That being said, it can still wear on you, especially if you want to PvP with multiple characters, but even further still, getting those levels and gear will be a non-issue eventually, as the source version in korea recently got a huge PvP update including an option to make characters solely for PvP, which immediately starts them at 85 with proper gear and everything. In terms of connection, just find people that you have fun practicing with/have a good connection with; you WILL find some unless your connection in particular is bad (no WiFi, please). If you want to look for any PvP guilds to scope out the community for them, there's SRK, PVP!, Symbolic, Airbears and Effortless. There's others, I'm sure, but I see those guild names the most in practice. On that note, if you want to really enjoy yourself and get better at PvP, go to the practice channels, where you can host rooms. Ranked channels offers a queue. The ranking system's integrity is unfortunately recognized as poor due to connections and bugs, there are no gear limitations, and the little bonus stuff you can get in there aren't really that worth it in this version. If your PvP experience is only ranked, it's gonna suck, and I think that's unfortunately why PvP isn't as big as it could be; ranked turns a lot of people off. But if you hang around practice channels and attend community held tournaments - which are currently scarce but will likely pick up in the near future - you could really enjoy yourself.
In short, the PvE aspect can be P2W but not excessively and you can get by spending nothing easily, there's a lot of content to explore, and the PvP can be quite enjoyable but with this version's limitations you gotta approach it the right way. Expect getting burnt out by the PvE unless you're an MMO monster and the levelling grind runs through your veins. Despite all the game's very obvious shortcomings I love it. I didn't touch on it before but it looks and sounds perfectly good. I dig the rockin soundtrack (especially the older tracks) and the spritework is pretty solid. There honestly isn't any game quite like this one. It may or may not be up your alley, but it's free. If you've got some time to spare, try it out. You might like it!

Long time player here, I have followed DFO since it's Nexon days. Have been there since Nexon's beta phase, to full release, through the eventual closure, then it's reopening under Neople. It will never cease to amaze me that the current team at Neople (11 employees) has done such so much more for the game than Nexon ever has.
But what is this game? The best way to describe Dungeon Fighter Online is that it is a side-scrolling beat-em up RPG, that also happens to have MMO elements in it.
Dungeon Fighter Online is a fantastic game to come back and play at the end of the day, when you just unwind, and beat up hordes of enemies with flashy skills. And boy does DFO do it well. Heavy weapons, ghostly possession, bare fists, DFO has a little something for everyone. This is backed up by the massive character roster, with each individual character subclasses having at least 20 unique skills. And if you're a speedrunner like I am, the prospect of running dungeons faster and faster keeps me coming back. While it is marketed as an MMO, partying and playing with other people is surprisingly optional. Almost all of the content in the game can be tackled and completed on your own, though bringing a friend or two will certainly help. If you're a person who likes their own quiet time, DFO will never force you to party up, to complete the majority of the content.
Of course, being a free-to-play game, DFO employs a cash shop where you can get flashy goodies. An event package, usually being the most economical bang-for-your-buck package, will run at around $28. These packages are can also be sold in the in-game auction hall for in-game currency as well. Other more “important” items, such as inventory expansions, can be completely bought out for less than $5 dollars. These items provided offer minimal benefits to general play, and are often given out for free during events.
However, the game is by no means perfect. There are many reviews that complain about the state of endgame gearing and equipment, which are partially true. Some of the best  endgame equipment can only be acquired from a random loot table, which may take several months to find, based on your own pace. However, the developers have taken note that the non-Korean market has a much lower tolerance for these types of grinds, and have systemically lowered the effort needed to acquire such equipment. In addition, extreme endgame content (think on par with Borderlands OP8+) has been continuously been toned down so that such an equipment requirement isn't needed. Apart from the equipment grind, DFO's playstyle mantra is to make smaller chunks of playtime over a longer periods of time.
In short, DFO is still what it is listed as. If you liked sidescrolling action games, give it a try. If you were a fan of the arcades and games like River City Ransom and Streets of Rage, give it a try. If you like dressup... give it a try, but prepare to spend money. If you like to call down orbital lasers on unsuspecting mooks, give it a try. If you're looking for that small bite of action you can come back to every day, give it a try.

Very engaging war game, at least the first couple times you try.
Your first 3 times trying to play through will be a very engaging survival game with heartfelt highs and lows with a overcasting shadow of uncertainty behind you at all times. Even when you score a huge stash of food and parts, you quickly realize how temporary your supplies are, or fate may strike you and all the materials you got to build a better workbench are meaningless now that your friend is dying from being fatally wounded by robbers.
The stealthy "scavenge" missions are really tense at times when you are trying to evade inhabitants, and often left me with a great sense of pride when I snuck out or ran away with a hush stash of great stuff. However, at times you realize that the AI of the opposing scavengers are often flawed.  There was a time where I was caught sneaking into a person's house, but they said that if I left, I wouldn't be killed. However, the only way to interact with other people is to trade with them, or hurt/kill them. There is no way of communicating "Ok let me leave your house, but I have to go some pathways to get to the exit first" If you're there too long they'll start shooting you.
Ironically where I find this game really stumbles is when you are really trying to win after those first failed games. You start to see the same exact character thoughts from several different characters. Additionally, there is no interaction between survivors minus the times where you click the "cheer up" button when someone is depressed. However, I really do like the day by day updates in every person's bio that give a little more detail into their thoughts.
Overall, I actually felt this game was fantastic, the highs are high and the lows are low. After my first attempt to survive a month (and a half or so), I watched my two final characters sit in fetal position at different points of the house with a "Broken" status effect after one of their survivor-mates was killed attempting scavenge food. The evening came and the girl survivor left in the night, leaving my lone male survivor all alone to survive. The next day, he was killed trying to find food. The screen fades, and a message says that everyone died, and a genuine sadness filled me after I invested so much in the survival of these fictional characters. You do start to lose that after more playthroughs, as the game becomes more of a game to be conquered, but that first playthrough made my investment worth it.

At its core, DFO is a Beat'Em Up sidescroller in the lineage of Streets of Rage or Turtles in Time. Skills use fighting-game style inputs to control attacks, and ramp up from the simple punch strings of the old Beat'em Ups to the giant supers from fighting games.
There are a ballpark of around 40 subclasses spread across 14 player avatars, most of which play as different from one another as a traditional priest and a warrior, even when they start from the same player sprite. The player classes control and feel radically different from one another, allowing options for whichever playstyle you like. Many of the gameplay options I don't see utilized in other games, such as the Battle Mage: a close/mid ranged spear user who can put elemental properties on her strikes in quick succession, allowing for customized fighting game-esque combos to acheive specific results like directional knockback, movement slow, or damage debuffs. Skills are unlocked progressively like most MMOs, and the build-up can feel a bit slow for some classes. A max-level character will often have around thirty skills, some of which being passives. Usually you've spun up to a good expectiation of what gameplay will be like by level 40.
Being that the combat allows for much more tight control than theme park MMOs, I find the gameplay they pull off to be much more exciting that the "stand and shoot it" that MMOs using the holy trinity of healer/tank/dps can sometimes fall into. Current DFO starts off quite easy, sometimes painfully so, but at the highest end there's content which requires at least the coordination and precision of a complex MMO dungeon. At the time of writing the max player count for one dungeon is four, but the Korean version we draw content from ramps up to 20 player raids. Difficulty levels are primarily unlocked by beating a dungeon on an easier setting, and at a low level you'll be moving on to the next dungeon or outleveling beginner content so fast you migh not see how interesting combat can be at first. It makes leveling alt-friendly, but it's not a great way to introduce the game's strengths to new players.
PvP is great, given that it's built on fighting game principles. It's one of the few games that's ever added a z axis with any measure of grace, and does so by creating small arenas to run freely in instead of locking characters facing opponents like most fighting games. Many attacks can cross the z axis, either moving your character or by having a big hitbox, and it's a major factor in pvp. As well, a skill cancel system exists, allowing for fake outs and quick combo strings.
There's a sea of junk to buy if you want to spend real cash. You don't need any of it. Thankfully, almost none of it follows you into combat. There's a bit to beef you up in PvE, and they've removed its effects from PvP (a failing that used to be a big critisim of the game). Purchases exist primarily to give you convieneces or to allow you to play dress-up.
The UI is a mess; the stuff you can do in the overworld is too much to handle. There are so many features and systems that even I can get lost sometimes, having played since 2009. It's best to find a guild who can point you in the right direction if your head spins. They've been adding♥♥♥♥♥♥to the game for a decade, and they don't seem to ever remove systems that have become redundant.
Another failing of the game is its advertising. Lately they've tryed to shoot for an anime-roleplaying branding, and this steam launch is no exception. The gameplay has nothing to with that, it's just fighting monsters up and down. If that turns you away I really can't blame you. There are plenty of fan-service looking characters, but they only exist to punch a dragon in the face. I can't imagine who'd be drawn to this game to "play [their] anime world" and stick around once they saw gameplay. Sorry if it turns you off, acutal fanservice is minimal in game.
Overall, if you like tight mechanical fighting games and have any interest the player-driven aspect of MMOs, it's probably worth a shot for the cost of free.
I recommend this game, nothing short of mind-blowing, a true work of art.

Now that I have spent some time playing this game and seeing what it has to offer I would like to write a little review because I believe this game deserves as many positive reviews as possible.
To summarise, this game has many pros with a few cons that can be easily changed as long as the developers take the time to read the community's comments and take into account the feedback they are reciving.
Things that I think the game is doing well:
*The art style. The game is very pretty and enjoyable to look at, it also manages to deliver a great atmosphere making this game very relaxing to play.
*Fun RPG elements. Being able to upgrade your car and being able to change the way it looks makes the game exciting and fun. This small RPG element makes you keep coming back to the game.
*Interesting travel system. Being able to select your route is a great feature as it adds a difficulty element to the game. People with more confidance in driving games will enjoy trying to steer their car in terrential rain and have the chance to break road laws while trying to avoid oil spils and pot holes.
Things I believe could be improved:
*More areas. So far there are a few different routes however they can only take you to two different locations. This can make the game boring quite quickly as you will find yourself driving to the same town every time you want to sell or buy something.
*Graphic options. This is a small point but it's worth mentioning. Personally I found the draw distance to be very annoying as I could only see 10 feet ahead of me before seeing fog and this is NOT during the rain. I run the game on fantastic with AI traffic maxed out however I can see a lot of graphical bugs and things that could be improved.
*Money making. Making money in this game is very boring and repetitive. The only way to make money is to sell goods from your own garage or goods you find in crates on the road. Making money in this game is a very slow and annoying process and personally this is the biggest problem for me.
Things I would like to see in future updates.
*More AI. The town, roads and petrol stops feel very empty. I would like to see more cars on the roads as I think it would make the driving more difficult giving you an extra thing to dodge. I would also like to see people walking around in the town as currently the main town gives me a very strong Silent Hill feeling.
*New weather system. I found the rain in this game to be too harsh as driving your car during the rain is in my opinion too  difficult. I think a good thing to add would be a winter route that adds ice to the roads as currently driving through rain feels just like driving on ice.
*More customization. I understand that the customization is not what this game is meant to be played for but I still think there could be more. It would make the game a lot more fun if no two cars looked the same.
Keep in mind that this review is for the pre-alpha state of the game. I understand many things will change but this review is just here to give ideas of improving the game. This is also my opinion so not everyone will agree.

Hard Reset Redux is the graphical and gameplay upgrade to Hard Reset for the PC and consoles. The 2011 game was notorious for being really difficult because of the limited movement and hard hitting enemies that are bullet sponges on the higher difficulties. I loved the old game because of its' fast paced action as well as its unforgiving gameplay, despite its' faults.
I played the Redux on Insane and have just started the Exile levels at this time of writing.
Overall it is a decent update gameplay wise, but there seems to be a number of things that I feel are pointless or don't really integrate well. I'll start with the changes I noticed that were good:
The Redux is also moderately easier than before; the game seems to tolerate alot more mistakes and I have only died twice so far.
These are things I think are negative or pointless changes:
I have also encoutered a bug where the game would alt-tab and say it crashed, but it actually didn't and was able to continue like normal. This didn't happen in the old game but it did in Shadow Warrior. There have been mentions of becoming frozen at the upgrade machines but I haven't experienced that.
All in all, I'm sorry to say but this Redux hasn't really done anything groundbreaking. There have been some good changes but I feel they do not warrant a whole new remake of the original. If you liked or hated the original and loved Shadow Warrior then try it out and form your own opinion on it. If you haven't played the original, you'll probably find this alright, but I recommend you grab the original first. However, if you are a Hard Reset purist or just hate the idea of remakes like this, then don't pick it up (except if you can get the discount)
As for me, I think I'll stick with the original.

to the point of not even being comparable.
- A nice hybrid mix between RTS top world and RTS management in the dungeon world. Everything here is reminicent of Dungeon Keeper except for the lack of first person view. 3 tiers of upgrades for units, many upgrade trees using 3 different rooms, as well as 3 different races (one requires
DLC). Basically there's a lot of 3's.
- Fun and explains much about how to play the game. Although the references start to get cringey after the dozenth time. We get it. You like LotR and Harry Potter.
- Compliments the game perfectly to the point where you don't really notice it, which is a good thing.
- This is honestly what makes or breaks games like this. The original Dungeons had a god awful interface which just brought the whole game down. This game does everything right. Hotkeys for buildings, everything condensed into one area of the hud. It's great.
- Here's where they dropped the ball. No lobby system, poor quick match, requires you to search the forums or steam groups to add players in order to play anything more than 1v1 on the same gamemode and map. I bought this game on discount and found myself finishing it twice in a row just so that I could see both story lines. It's surprisingly addictive, with the continous hunting for better ships and equipment. The battles and pretty much every aspect are barebone and offer very little strategy and depth. The game usually holds your hand, offering help in navigation, autodocking and so forth.
+ The world of Rebel Galaxy feels alive. You see different factions fighting against each other pretty much everywhere. Traders send distress call for help. Satellites wait to be hacked in a small quicktime game and give away precious information.
+ Ships and equipment don't lose value. You can sell them for the price you paid. That allows the player to test every ship and extra as he sees fit and just give it back with nothing lost if it's not to his liking.
+ The graphics are nice. Very detailed ships with a decent damage model. The music is great and I enjoyed the many different songs. Just don't stay in a starbase for too long, of it will keep repeading a single song over and over. A few other minor drag downs are:
- overall bad AI, gets stuck during missions and has problems with pathfinding.
- severe balance issues in difficulty. Some enemies like the tiny Schizo fighters tear apart even the strongest player ships in the blink of an eye, potentially making you lose any progress
- speaking of which, you can only save in starbases and when leaving the game. Not inbetween.
- bad collision model with planets and especially the small moons. They look as if they are far away and the next moment you crash into them. AI traders do that a lot (and even the merchenaries sometimes), leaving cargo all over the place.
- while the battles are quite entertaining in general, unlike most similar games you can't fly up and down. That severely limits your options, especially when things are going bad and you need to get away.
- Trading and asteroid mining seem interesting at first but loses any importance and meaning once you get to the later star systems and earn 1-2 million credits just for a single mission.
