So recently in the steam winter sale over christmas I picked up Hitman Absolution. It was at a price of I think £5 at the time. I completed it within the night I got it and i just wanted to do a quick review on dis♥♥♥♥♥♥..
Graphics: The graphics are suprisingly great for a game that was out in 2012. I ran it at Ultra settings and got over 60 frames so altogether not bad... The colours within the game blend very well.
Design: The layout of the game is great especially the weapon selection system. You are able to hold around 6 items including 3 Melee weapons. For stealthy users, you can use the garrote which is a wire that you can strangle the opponent silently with. Or for others who like to go loud, shotguns may interest you as this game is packed full of interesting weapons to experiment with. Hitman works in the way of if you kill someone who isn't the target, you will receive minus points which affect your score at the end of a mission. This is the punishment for going on a massacre and no, you ain't Eric Harris :)
Gameplay: Enemy AI in Hitman is smart enough to be interesting, but not so smart that it’s unpredictable. While in disguise, characters in the same uniform will only take an interest if you’re somewhere you shouldn’t be, and if you’re discovered enemies will search hard for you and this can be a pain if you are trying to do something stealthily. There are clever crowd dynamics so that you can lose yourself between them and at times causing chaos – though you might not be scored quite so highly. Even combat is well-handled, with solid cover, aiming and targeting controls and a close combat system that allows you to be free with your punches.
Story/Summary: (I copied this from wiki cus cba with doin dis lmao kek)
Set after the events of Hitman Blood Money and Hitman Damnation, the game begins with Agent 47 detailing his relationship with his handler Diana Burnwood whom he had trusted until she, without explanation, betrayed the International Contract Agency (ICA) by sabotaging their funding and database, using the subsequent confusion to vanish. After the ICA is reformed, 47 is tasked by his new handler, Benjamin Travis, a high level official within the ICA, to kill Diana for her betrayal and retrieve an important Agency asset; a teenaged girl named Victoria from her mansion in Chicago, Illinois. 47 sneaks into her mansion and shoots Diana. Rather than finishing her off, 47 comforts his dying friend and asks her why she betrayed the ICA. Diana discovered Victoria was genetically-engineered to become an assassin for the ICA. Not wishing to see Victoria suffer the same fate as 47, she betrayed the ICA and escaped with her. As Diana's final request, 47 agrees to protect Victoria, for which Travis brands him a traitor.
After 47 drops Victoria off at the Rosewood Orphanage to hide, he contacts his informant, Birdie, for information about Victoria and the ICA, which Birdie agrees to provide once 47 has assassinated a crime boss in Chinatown for him. After cutting the barcode tattoo out of his head and giving his Silverballers to Birdie, 47 is informed by Birdie about a man named Blake Dexter, head of Dexter Industries, a home defense system company, who is staying at the Terminus Hotel. 47 sneaks into the hotel and learns from a conversation between Dexter and his secretary Layla Stockton in his penthouse that Dexter is planning to kidnap Victoria and sell her to the highest bidder. However, 47 is knocked out by Dexter's bodyguard Sanchez. Dexter, realizing who 47 is, kills a hotel maid, frames 47 and leaves him to die after setting his penthouse on fire. 47 manages to escape the hotel, and is then hunted by the Chicago PD. After escaping the police, Birdie sends 47 to kill Dexter's informant Dom Osmand. After Dom is killed, Birdie calls 47 for help as Dexter has hired thugs led by a criminal named Edward Wade to find him in order to discover Victoria's location. 47 heads to Chinatown and kills the thugs searching for Birdie only to discover Birdie has already been captured, and immediately heads to the orphanage, learning that Birdie has betrayed him by revealing Victoria's location to Wade so that his life may be spared.
47 manages to arrive at the orphanage just as Wade and his men attack. 47 mortally wounds Wade but Victoria is kidnapped and taken hostage by Lenny, Dexter's son. Learning where to find Dexter from a matchbox found on Wade, 47 heads to the town of Hope, South Dakota, where Dexter rules the town due to his PMC's and the corrupt town sheriff, Clive Skurky, who is under his pay. Retrieving his Silverballers, 47 takes out Lenny's gang, the "Hope Cougars", who were planning to kidnap Victoria from Dexter and sell her to a rival weapons company. After interrogating Lenny over where Victoria is, 47 can either kill Lenny or leave him to die in the desert. Arriving at Dexter Industries HQ, 47 sneaks into the company's laboratory, kills the scientists who examined Victoria and destroys their research data on her. After killing Sanchez in an underground cage fight, 47 recuperates at a hotel but the hotel is attacked by an ICA strike team led by "The Saints". 47 eliminates The Saints including their leader, Lasandra Dixon. Angered over this failure, Travis heads to Hope with a large group of ICA operatives to kill 47 and find Victoria.
47 manages to find Victoria under the Hope Courthouse jails but is subdued by Sheriff Skurky. As Dexter tortures 47, demanding to know where his son is, he is informed that Travis wants Victoria back in exchange for $10 million and leaves. 47 manages to escape into the streets of Hope, just as the ICA takes over the town. 47 chases Skurky to a church where the sheriff tells 47 that Dexter is heading to Blackwater Park in Chicago, before 47 kills him. In Chicago, Dexter and Travis attempt an exchange for Victoria for $10 million but the deal turns sour when Travis refuses his part of the deal and Dexter takes the money anyway. After reaching the top of Blackwater Park, 47 kills Layla and finally Dexter himself, after the latter had tried to escape with Victoria on a helicopter. In Dexter's dying words he offers an apology to his son and his money, leading a disgusted Victoria to throw the $10 million on his body before leaving with 47.
A few months later, Travis and his assistant Jade Nguyen arrive at a cemetery in England with an ICA crew to find Diana's grave as he has suspicions that Diana might not be dead. 47 is there as well as he recounts the letter Diana gave to him. In the letter, Diana reveals Victoria was created by Travis's funding without the knowledge and approval of the ICA higher ups and tasks him to eliminate Travis. After eliminating Jade and Travis's elite bodyguards, 47 confronts Travis himself after injuring him in an explosion. As Travis rants at 47 for wasting Victoria's potential for the ICA, he asks 47 if he really did kill Diana to which 47 responds "You will never know" and kills Travis.
It is later revealed that Diana survived and Victoria is with her at her mansion where 47 watches them from his scope thus revealing that only he knew all along he hit Diana with a shot that would not be fatal. The game ends with a message from Diana to 47 welcoming him back to the ICA and thanking him for his help. This also reveals that the story from the end of Blood Money to Absolution was all one daring hit contract on individuals within the Agency by Diana and executed by 47 to protect Victoria and terminate the assassin cloning project. In the epilogue, Detective Cosmo Faulkner of the Chicago PD, who has been tracking 47 since the Terminus Hotel fire, is having trouble discovering 47's identity until Birdie offers to help him for a price.
Extra Information: There is an extra campaign mode called "Contracts" Where you can make your own contract and allow people to play them. You can also play other peoples.
Conclusion: Overall this game is great. Buy it famalam

This is an awesome indie title to crave your need for fast-paced gameplay, without the hassle of a thousand loading screens or overly complicated storylines. Bleed is a side-scrolling run-and-gun shooter, best enjoyed with a gamepad (I used the Logitech F710, and it worked beautifully) for maximum enjoyment. It satisfies "the itch," even if you didn't know you had one.
While the controls seem strange at first, once you get used to them you will have an absolute blast. Wryn (the main character) is an army of one, capable of dashing through the air multiple times, slowing down time, and utilizing an arsenal of weapons (pistols, RPGs, laser rifles, you name it) as she dodges and destroys her way through each level. All of the movements feel fluid, and it is easy to make snap judgements on the fly to avoid incoming projectiles and the like. Whevever I died, I didn't blame the game; it was almost always a mistake that could have been avoided with better play, which encouraged me to try again.
I can say without a doubt that after the first playtrhough, (which doesn't take very long unfortunately with only 7 levels) I was ready to go for round 2 on the next difficulty. Every second is a rush, so a 5 minute session will be just as fun as an hour-long one. While this indie gem may not keep you occupied for more than a few hours at a time, expect every moment to be a rush that will challenge what you're inner run-and-gunner is made of. Two guns up!

I was worried that Big Pharma could turn out to be either too "casual" (like many cheap "tycoon" clickers), or too messy (like games that pretend to be serious, but just throw a bunch of random events at you at increasing pace - Theme Hospital, I'm looking at you). Luckily, that's not the case.
There's far enough depth to raise the game well over the "casual" category. At the same time, its elements are completely transparent, so it doesn't overwhelm you with complexity. It could rather overwhelm you with opportunities. If you enjoy putting your brain to some work, this is a game a doctor would prescribe.
Shortly, it perfectly touches the same strings that was touched by good old tycoons you are fond of, adds a surprisingly relevant puzzle element, and flavors the mix with good city sim's spirit of careful planning & continuous improvement. For details, look below.
PART 1. MAKING DRUGS
Your goal is to create medicines and make money of them. A complex, profitable medicine usually consists of several components. Making such medicine usually takes many steps: starting an initial mix from a single ingredient and processing the mix through the chain of machinery, changing its concentration and adding other components (in specific order and specific concentrations). Each ingredient has some positive and negative effects. Effects are not just simple "+" or "-": during different processing, each effect could become stronger or weaker, or changed to another, or be removed at all. A mix of several ingredients, as you can guess, is even more complex and could end as many various intricate compounds.

So, making your products is not a straightforward task: there are many methods to make different pills for the very same illness, with various effectivity and side effects. Every production step costs money, so your new creations are usually a compromise between love for humanity and love for money. Plus, when you carefully planned all processing steps and finished your future production line design, you need to fit it into your precious factory space (which is sometimes a puzzle itself).
Plus, you start with a limited set of ingredients and the most primitive machines, so your first drugs are cheap and will not provide for too long. To advance into new delicious markets, you need to jump quickly into expensive research, which cripples your feeble cash flow. And when each of yourr products finally comes to market, there's another story to tell....
PART 2. MAKING MONEY
You can estimate the market size and common price level of drugs for specific ilnesses. So, you can estimate your profits and risks of entering chosen markets, and pick out the best opportunity. You carefully look for needed ingredients and improve your technologies to make the product with minimal cost. Better quality can get you a hefty price bonus. But your product is not evaluated instantly. Only real applications show how good your creation turned out to be. So, only after time, statistics shows how effective the drug is, and how many side effects it caused. The price can fall dramatically if the medicine performs poorly, or causes far too many unpleasant experiences. Wrong formula? Your problem. Does demand for raw materials drive their prices up? Your problem. And don't forget you're not alone here. If your competitors saturate the same market with their products, and prices go down, guess what? You got it. Your problem.
What's better: to reach after the tastiest pie with a risk that, in a year, every company will also be biting it? Or to look for stable but safe haven in a sector no one is looking at? To rush into selling an untested formula on industrial scale to make some quick money? Or to test all effects in detail and get the best product and ideal production line that will feed you for years? To flood the competitor's market with cheap alternatives to cut its profits (cause I can, baby)?  Or to use the same precious factory space for a new experimental drug? Your choice, and... yeah, your problem.
"5 hours of gameplay" reviewers usually stop at, or even before, this point. People with more patience realize, unexpectedly, that Easy scenarios pack is a well-hidden tutorial extension, and that single "competitor" actually was a yawning guide in disguise.
PART 3. MAKING ENEMIES
When you move to second scenarios pack, dusty gnomes inside your PC are finally convinced that you got used to the rules, and things start to get serious.

The whole new dimension of opportunities: research tree is exploded twice. Equipment which no one has shown you before. New level of formulas you can't even imagine creating without a pen and a paper. Vast number of ways to go. Tremendous amount of things to look into.

The whole new level of warfare: margins are thinner. Side effects' combinations are more sophisticated and widespread. Rivals that, you know, look smart, have different characters and can painfully stab you (and each other) in the back. Wow, now I can patent drugs! What, now THEY can patent drugs?!

Dungeon Fighter Online was released over 10 years ago in Korea. It was one of the last 2D sidescrolling MMOs to be released. It took a long time before Nexon finally secured the rights to publish the game in NA, but they ruined the game with their cash shop and never really had stable servers, resulting in a very poor game. Desptie its problems, it is probably the best of the 2D sidescrollers. However, that isn't saying much when your competition is games like Grand Chase and Elsword. Those games are very simple with a severe lack of available skills compared to Dungeon Fighter Online.
The game itself is a 2D beat em up, but it's also an MMO with character levels and skills. As you level up, you earn skill points (SP) and eventually TP (don't know what it's short for). SP allows you to learn new skills and power up old ones whereas TP is much more limited, but they empower select skills further, allowing you to become even more powerful. One of the good things about the game is that you can redistribute your skill points as you wish and there is also an auto allocate button in case you have no idea what you want to do. Some of the more powerful skills require an item known as Clear Cube Fragments that you can obtain from dismantling items. This seems to be a way for players to dispose of common items.
There are several classes available: Slayer, Gunner, Mage, Knight, Fighter, Priest, Thief, Dark Knight, and Creator. Each of the classes have an advancement quest available at level 15 that lets them specialize in different skills. You get the option to change the class for free again one time, then it costs 100k gold or so the second time. Not sure for third, but it gets more expensive each time. A lot of the bigger, flashier skills and abilities are not available until beyond level 30 with a significant power spike after the first awakening. Skills can also be chained together. You can use shortcut commands to do it or you can set them to hotkeys. Memorizing the shortcut commands can allow you to do much more skills than you have room for though.
There are two class upgrades called Awakenings. The first one is available at level 40 though you probably will not be able to collect it until much later in the game. The main problem of the first one is that you have to collect a ton of Cube Fragments. If you have not been dismantling most of the equipment drops you find, you will not have enough for it and will have to grind until you do. The Second Awakening is much more problematic though. Even though it is available at level 75, the enemies there are strong enough to one shot you and they frequently have super armor on so that you cannot do anything about it. You have to defeat enough enemeis to collect 30 tokens from that area in order to unlock your Second Awakening.
The game itself is mostly not grindy. The quests and main story give plenty of experience and you will rarely encounter a point in which when you have to grind to unlock the next dungeon. However, the game's fatigue system artificially creates grind, which will be addressed in the complaints section below.
Later in the game though, the enemies start to have cheap shots. For most of the game, whenever enemies have super armor, you can usually use a "grab" type skill to cancel them. If you hit them enough times it will also break. However, at level 80, this suddenly changes. Enemies with super armor stay with it. Grabbing them does not cancel it. Hitting them does not cancel it. You have to let them play it out. A few boss enemies are also able to move three dimensionally while using skills while you are only able to move two dimensionally. Some are even just flat out invincibile during their skills that flood the entire room. There was also a story boss that inflicted bleed and poison at the same time and would instant kill you if you did not grab the nearby 50% hp/mp heal spot.
PvP is also broken because of the same cheap shot problems as above. The chaining of skills basically turns PvP into whoever can do better combos can win and there's very little that someone can do once they are caught in an attack.
The major problems in the game come mainly from its fatigue system. The fatigue system is a system used to halt player progress by ensuring that they can only run a certain number of dungeons each day. Each room you enter in game costs 1 fatigue point. Early dungeons in the game have about 8 rooms while later in the game, it can go up to as many as 12. Optional areas in the game are used for grinding and are much larger. This also means they cost a lot more fatigue to play.
Fatigue itself turns the game into a massive grind. In order to earn additional fatigue points, you have to earn Mileage Points. You get 1 Mileage Point per dungeon that you complete regardless of its length. However, even with Neo Premium (you get some from events, but its an item mall thing), you only get 273. This sounds like a lot until you realize the average dungeon will only last you about 2 minute 30 seconds (3 if your class is slow, even shorter if you're willing to burn Clear Cube Fragment skills to instant clear rooms). The early game ones will usually at 2 minutes. You'll get about 3 hours of play time unless you play alternate characters. It's a terrible way of addressing the problem and its the same system that Final Fantasy 14 had to drop before it even went to 2.0.
You will also have problems acquiring non-story equipment in the game because of the fatigue system. The story gives you fairly decent "rare" quality gear for progression. The better items require crafting and here is the problem. A lot of items that drop are bound to the character they drop on, not the account. That means if you earned a rare item from a boss, you can't move it to another. At least the four that I did collect from story bosses did not let me trade it even though it says bind on account. You have to dismantle these and unique quality items in order to craft the higher end items as well.
Another problem fatigue causes is the massive pileup of side quests. Side quests give you things like titles that you can equip for bonus stats. The problem is that a lot of these side quests are grindy, which means you have to waste huge amounts of stamina in order to acquire them. On top of that, when you unlock the quest, you will have already out leveled the area and will be able to move on to the next one already, making it even more pointless. The only ones that might be worth unlocking are Hell Mode Dungeons because they have a better chance of unique and legendary loot. Hell Mode Dungeons are a problem though because they require another item called Demon Invitation that you have to grind for in high level, high difficulty dungeons to unlock. They make you grind for a chance to get better gear, but the fatigue system itself inhibits the ability to grind for better gear.
The second problem is the lack of gold sinks. Gold is available in large amounts from simply grinding and selling items. However, there's very little to actually spend your gold on in game. Equipment and items sold by the NPCs are garbage with quest equipment being better and the highest level available potions capping off at level 26. You can buy some dungoen passes for a million gold for some of the daily dungeons, but there's not much to really spend it on. Making higher quality items from the scrap items you collect in the dungeon is barely chump change and the higher quality items that you need for crafting only comes from dismantling. Gold is never really actually taken out of the economy since you will rarely buy anything from the NPCs. The result is massive inflation and high level items costing a hundred million or more gold. Sadly, you cannot grind for it because of the problems stated in fatigue.

Very engaging war game, at least the first couple times you try.
Your first 3 times trying to play through will be a very engaging survival game with heartfelt highs and lows with a overcasting shadow of uncertainty behind you at all times. Even when you score a huge stash of food and parts, you quickly realize how temporary your supplies are, or fate may strike you and all the materials you got to build a better workbench are meaningless now that your friend is dying from being fatally wounded by robbers.
The stealthy "scavenge" missions are really tense at times when you are trying to evade inhabitants, and often left me with a great sense of pride when I snuck out or ran away with a hush stash of great stuff. However, at times you realize that the AI of the opposing scavengers are often flawed.  There was a time where I was caught sneaking into a person's house, but they said that if I left, I wouldn't be killed. However, the only way to interact with other people is to trade with them, or hurt/kill them. There is no way of communicating "Ok let me leave your house, but I have to go some pathways to get to the exit first" If you're there too long they'll start shooting you.
Ironically where I find this game really stumbles is when you are really trying to win after those first failed games. You start to see the same exact character thoughts from several different characters. Additionally, there is no interaction between survivors minus the times where you click the "cheer up" button when someone is depressed. However, I really do like the day by day updates in every person's bio that give a little more detail into their thoughts.
Overall, I actually felt this game was fantastic, the highs are high and the lows are low. After my first attempt to survive a month (and a half or so), I watched my two final characters sit in fetal position at different points of the house with a "Broken" status effect after one of their survivor-mates was killed attempting scavenge food. The evening came and the girl survivor left in the night, leaving my lone male survivor all alone to survive. The next day, he was killed trying to find food. The screen fades, and a message says that everyone died, and a genuine sadness filled me after I invested so much in the survival of these fictional characters. DFO is, quite frankly, one of the best games I've ever played.  I played during the turbulent Nexon years.  I lived through it closing and stumbling through the Chinese version.  I played through the open alpha and finally now, where Neople, the original developers, publish the game globally by themselves.
And this is the best version of DFO we'll ever get.
My Steam says 6.4 hours, but over the course of the game's lifespans I've easily sunk 750+ hours across a bunch of characters.
Pros:
Character classes are all fun to make and play, as each 5 levels gives you new skills to toy with and combo with.
Plenty of character slots to use, with more given out for free all the time.
Biweekly events to help players get useful items like life tokens, safe upgrades, even avatars and equipment.
Neople is extremely quick to respond to the playerbase when issues arise and compensate very well.
PVP is a blast.
The XP curve is so much better now, and Scenario dungeons make the once-awful grind mighty doable.
Co-op with up to four players, or PVP with up to 8 in 1 on 1 matches or all-out brawls.
You can play dress-up.
The official anime is absolute garbage, but it's so funny to watch as a result.  Spot-the-anime-cliche!
You can get most cash shop items from events or from other players.
A point shop where you get points for running dungeons/from events/rebated from cash shop purchases, which you can use to buy helpful items and a limited range of avatars.
Lost Treasure keys actually drop fairly frequently, compared to never seeing a key fragment drop ever in Nexon days.
Extremely moddable.  You can replace background music and even the sounds the characters make.  I have the old Nexon English voice packs, plenty of old dungeon music, and my Mechanic's Combat Robot blasts Darude - Sandstorm instead of its original song every time I crit.
SKILL RESETS ARE FREE AND THERE'S A SKILL TREE!  SCREW YOU NEXON FOR MAKING PEOPLE PAY TWENTY DOLLARS FOR A DAMN SKILL RESET
Gold is fairly easy to obtain and costs for leveling equipment isn't prohibitive.  Hell, Epic quests pop out equipment for your characters every 5 levels.
Extremely controller friendly.  I have Xpadder set up with a PS2 controller and use the game's input commands system to activate most of my skills.
It's not Mighty Number 9.
Cons:
Fatigue.  A lot of people complain about it, but it's a necessary evil to help protect the game's economy, which is actually still pretty healthy compared to Nexon days.  Still, it can be a bummer to get to a new dungeon or brand new skill and have to wait or use a fatigue potion to play with it.
Only can make 2 characters a day, which is only really a con before you have enough alts to deal with fatigue if you want to play more.
Avatars are untradable, except in the special packs that other players can buy and sell.  You have to cash shop or point shop these.  Dammit nipple I just wanted a shirt for my Slayer.
Some classes don't do as much damage as other classes as easily, this can be kind of discouraging.  Ranger is weaker seeming than Launcher, for example.  Though Ranger is still absolutely fun as hell, and got a buff/rework recently that makes him better without a reinforced weapon.  And, if he gets a powerfully reinforced weapon, he can easily outdamage the Launcher late-game.  Play what you enjoy, not what the community says is good.
Connection in PVP is pretty important if you wanna get real competitive.
The people that buy global chat megaphones are either selling things or absolute idiots.  It can be funny, or it can be grating.  At least Megaphones are now 2 Mileage points instead of the...what, $5? they were in Nexon.
If you want the absolute best equipment ever for facerolling PvE content, you gotta beat the odds of winning the lottery five times in a row.  That said, you can do plenty fine with a good set of Chronicle armor and a nice pink weapon.
The game does not tell you about Quick Rebound.  For the sake of God, pick up Quick Rebound.  It's in the top bar of skills in the skill window.
The constant flow of events can be overwhelming; Just remember you DON'T HAVE to do all of them if you don't want.
All of the stuff in the game can be daunting to new players, but it gets easy to understand after a few days.
The game doesn't automatically enable Tutorial mode for new players.  Do yourself a favor and hit O, then navigate to System and enable Tutorial mode.
The Global chat is NOT indicative of the community.  Come find us at
for help and info.
If you like beat 'em ups or fighting games, give DFO a shot.  If you're like me, you'll fall in love instantly.

If you want a true Dungeon Keepers style game then this probably something you will like, and the campaign mode brings back lots of good nostalgia. Definitely worth a play so i will recommend the game based on its campaign.
However the longetivity & large flaws of the game are made strongly apparent by it's Skirmish mode, which mechanically fails to function. If you want to purchase Dungeons 2 to build large dungeons and defend them for as long as you like then i DO NOT recommend Dungeons 2. The information below will explain why for those who are interested:
---
Problem #1:In skirmish mode the game encounters a game-killing problem. Most if not ALL of the Skirmish maps offer very little gold, so little gold in fact that you arent even able to complete enough research and facilities or upgrades you need to win the game or even pay your minions with. I had a map where i only had 1 Infinite gold node, and i could only mine it from one side, meaning not enough income for the game to continue.
Skirmish mode maps are designed to last longer than Campaign levels, yet offer a severely limited amount of gold far under what is required to complete the goals, meaning you cant really accomplish anything and Skirmish mode comes across as broken. Endless Mode is for people who enjoy building or just defending their dungeon, but because of the lack of gold on the map, yet again it is not possible to enjoy this mode forever.
No gold = the games cannot continue.
My message to the devs is to make all Gold money tiles provide an endless supply of gold. Only 4 minions can mine a Golden vein at a time so i do not understand why the developers made the gold amounts so limited.
Problem #2: In order to play the game in any difficulty higher than Normal, you have to have played the maps to the point that you already know where all the resources are in advance, even though shroud in this game is supposed to be an important element. This creates a huge rush early game in order to get your build down perfectly or you just fail every single game, leaving you with limited choice, and limited build options.
In short, the entire game becomes less RTS and is ALL ABOUT trail and error, killing the mood to play once you realise how poorly tuned enemy waves are.
---
Graphics: 5/10 - Medium quality models but this does mean that the games hardware demands are small, so most of you should have very little problems running the game 'graphically'. The game however seems to have optimization issues and seems to use the CPU very inefficiently, leading to a lot of framerate stuttering particularly with digging and selecting units in the dungeon. I use a AMD FX 8150 (8x 3.6ghz) so i cant understand how i could be having any CPU issues.
Sound: 6/10 - The Narrator does a great job (apart from that jab at JonTron which was not cool if it was intended to be funny) and the rest of the games sounds are fitting but not great quality.
Music: 1/10 - Sounds like cheap stock music which can barely be heard throughout the whole game. Sorry guys but i have to be honest to the reader, this was really lacking from your game.
Gameplay 6/10 - Plays similar to Dungeon Keeper 2 and it's quite fun going through campaign mode, but has huge Economy and balancing problems and clearly is missing a great deal of polish and a severe lack of skirmish maps to keep you playing after the campaign. This highly diminishe sthe value of the game.
Average game.
If the economical game-killing problems were fixed, enemy waves properly tuned and the music was given a large improvement, i would say this game is capable of a 9/10 but with the DLC's containing very tiny map additions along with the announcement of Dungeons 3, i sense Kalypso company are simply piggy-backing off of the Dungeon Keepers name, and want the cash more than want to make a deep Dungeon Keepers classic revival.
The Ultimate Evil here is Capitalism.
Questions:
Q. Is it worth £25? (the current british sale price)
A. Considering how short the Campaign was and the polish needed in this game, no. i would buy this at £15 maximum.
Q. I love Dungeon Keepers, should i play Dungeons 2?
A. Yes if you can get this game on a deal, but do not expect to be playing this game for a long time, there's nowhere near enough longetivity and content to keep you playing long, which is a real shame. 12 hours playing casually (and very defensively) and i had finished the main story. I would estimate the average gamer would beat this game in about 8 hours.

Note: Jalopy is an Early Access title. The version reviewed was current as of the date of this review.
In Jalopy, you play an unnamed person living on the outskirts of Berlin, going on a road trip through the beautiful European countryside in your newly repaired Laika two-stroke automobile. The old jalopy breaks down often, so you'll need to be handy with a spanner, and it needs near-constant attention: fuel, oil, wiper fluid, tyres, ... . If you don't keep on top of maintenance, you'll end up stuck on the side of the road. And if you don't find any way of making money on your trip, your meagre savings are sure to run out before you reach your destination.
The graphics in Jalopy are functional rather than beautiful, much like its portrayal of the Eastern European landscape in which it is set. The game is rendered in three dimensions and played from a first-person perspective, but the game world is made up of very-low-polygon models and plain-coloured textures, though with some nice dynamic lighting. The plain and rather blocky graphics have some appeal, but it doesn't take too long for the drab landscape to become a bit boring. This may well be the developer's intention, given the setting. Speech bubbles from characters are a bit too big and intrusive for my liking, but again it's a deliberate style that's been chosen, and they work well enough.
The standard Unity graphical detail settings have been retained, accessible only from the Unity launcher, and not in game. I haven't noticed any performance issues at maximum detail.
Sound effects are quite variable in quality. The engine sound is very weedy, but suits the old jalopy quite well, I think. Rain sounds are good, and other cars sound fine. Tyre sounds, though, are terrible. The first time I went driving off road in the wet I had no idea what that weird sound was supposed to be until I noticed the car sliding out.
There's music on the radio in the car. It fits the setting well, but isn't really the sort of music I listen to for enjoyment, so I tend to turn the radio off instead.
There are no voiceovers for characters in the game; everything is done in text.
Jalopy starts with a brief tutorial; you wake up in your sparsely furnished garage / apartment to find a man (a friend, presumably) presenting you with an old car that he has acquired: a two-stroke Laika 601 Deluxe, the jewel of the East German car manufacturing industry. It's lacking one door, and wheels, and all of the important components from the engine bay, but other than that it's ready to go!
The tutorial guides you through installing all of the parts in the car (you have a well-stocked garage for just this eventuality), and then throws you into the game proper. You're given a car user's manual and a map and off you go on your pre-determined tour of the countryside, with $100 to your name. The tutorial doesn't really give you any information on what you're supposed to do in the game, though, so be prepared for trial and error and a few false starts.
The locations you visit each time you play seem to be the same, but you're given a choice of three different routes. I think the roads you follow are procedurally generated to a degree, or at least the events that can occur on the way must be, as they haven't been exactly the same each time I've played, but they are definitely very similar, so the building blocks must be very large or limited in placement. And the game seems to be structured to force you to stay in a motel each time you reach a destination, as border gates are only open during the day and time doesn't advance unless you're on your journey.
Jalopy is played from a first-person view, and I had a bit of trouble getting a sense for the size of the car while driving. There's partial controller support, but it's still a bit clunky, so I ended up playing with the recommended mouse and keyboard. WASD controls your character's movements as well the car's, and the mouse controls looking around and interacting with the environment, including activating or deactivating the car's various features. The rest of the controls are far less standard, and can't be changed (or even examined) in game; you have to quit and use the Unity launcher for that instead. Oh, the limit of three held items makes inventory management tiresome and frustrating.
Car control is okay, but not fantastic; a controller's analogue stick should be much better here than the recommended keyboard and mouse, as the digital nature of A/D keyboard steering is not very realistic or enjoyable. When it starts raining or you're on dirt roads, though, your dry road tyres wear quickly, and when it's both raining and dirt roads, the car turns into a wet noodle. It's rather unrealistic, but adds a welcome change, and a reason to buy different tyres.
I really like the idea of Jalopy, with its rogue-like elements mixed with its tongue-in-cheek attitude, but at the moment there just doesn't seem to be that much to do. You pick a route to your next destination, keep an eye out for boxes on the side of the road that you can loot, try to fix your car (if you have the tools) when it breaks down, which seems to happen once on every section of your trip, and then fill up with the essentials when you reach the next town. There's only very limited interaction with the few NPCs you'll find, and the road sections that make up most of the game tend to blur into each other after a while, with the graphical style that seems charming and unique at first eventually becoming a bit bland and dull, and virtually unpopulated.
It's buggy, too, even though it's been in Early Access for just about a year now. The developer is still active, and many of the bugs may be addressed with time, but at the moment it's rather unstable. The worst issue I've encountered is a game-breaker, with the game deciding to let me remove items from the trunk, but not replace them, or put anything else in. This is a long-standing issue that was first reported in the forums last year, and given that it prevents you from being able to store or transport anything in the car, it's a big problem. I also had a game-breaking bug where I couldn't do anything at a border checkpoint; the game wouldn't let me pass my papers to the gate guard, but I also couldn't start the car or get out.
Other gameplay issues I've seen are less serious, but still annoying, such as other drivers speeding up behind you to crash into you, leaving you with a fine to pay. There are some weird graphical problems, too. The tutorial man is wearing a jacket with weird textures. There are holes/cracks in geometry in some places, and the smoke and dust effects look bad in the game's plain style; some transparency would really help. I also noticed something very weird with the moon at night, where it seemed to be hidden behind something, and the sun rises in front of the distant mountains. Oh, and why does my car make dust clouds that float leisurely away on the breeze in the rain?
Pros:
+ An interesting idea, with understated humour
+ It's sort of fun
Cons:
- Very buggy
- Hard to get into
- The world seems very underpopulated, almost deserted
- Some control issues
- Some graphical issues
Jalopy is rather like the jalopy in the game; it's a bit hard to get into, it's pretty rough around the edges, and it often breaks down.
There's an interesting and unique game in there, but at the moment it's hidden by gameplay and graphical issues. Still, I'm looking forward to seeing what Jalopy will become as it finishes its journey through Early Access.

I got this a while back in a Humble Bundle, and recently decided to actually try it.  If I had known how good it was, I would have played it earlier.
Yes, it has a lot of features from your normal space exploration/trading/fighting games.  But there are some pretty notable diffirences, like how the economy is easier to get a grip on and how combat is on a 2D plane.  Now, that last bit might sound like it reduces the complexity, but it actually doesn't, it just saves you from motion sickness.  Broadside combat and presenting the right facing make it so that while it's 2d, there's quite a lot of depth to it.  Normally these sorts of games turn into "get the biggest ship or hauler you can get", but thanks to broadside combat positioning is hugely important.  I've had a blast running around in light little corvette, simply because I can dictate the engagement and prevent myself from taking damage in the first place, and survive longer than expected because I can flip my facing easily.
Turrets add another complication to combat, and can either be directly controlled or left to auto-target using parameters you've set for them.  Thanks to how turret position varies between ships, and thier nice placement as "relevant but not the main focus", otherwise similar ships like the Icarus and Baraccuda play entirely diffirently.
And if you find that a ship or weapon isn't fun to use, all ship modules and ships sell back at your purchase cost.  This makes it so that you can experiment as much as you want in the game, and modules carry over between ships.  This also means that the only way you can back yourself into a corner money-wise is with poor trading, and thankfully trading is also pretty straightfoward.
The econ portion's also better than average, with helpful information displays and randomly occuring events that have obvious and easy to track implications for the market.  Even a combat focused player can make a lot of money running supplies between a station having a Market Glut and another one about to get invaded.
The storyline's a bit sterotypical, but honestly these games aren't about the story.  It's about doing what you want, and this game's great at that.  Oh, and also has a pretty well done soundtrack and it knows when to change the tracks pretty well.  Even though I'm not generally a fan of this sort of music, it really works in the game.
Overall, a really good game.  I'd consider it worth getting at normal price, and if it's on sale just go ahead and buy it.

Buy this game when on sale with DLCs included. This game has a lot of potential, but is underdeveloped. It could be a nice Civ game with a kick♥♥♥♥♥story line, but still not there, especially with the latter.
Gameplay: Affinities are well integrated into all aspects of gameplay. The tech web is a fresh addition to a system that has been practically unchanged since Civ2. Aliens are kinda cool, but need more depth. You now choose the upgrades of your units.
Biggest problem (edit:is now corrected) - AI does not react to the new concepts, making the game incredibly easy as of now.
AI will ignore affinity techs until late game, meaning you just need to do two quests, get lvl 3 of random affinity and crush the entire map with upgraded units. The fact you get free upgrade to all units immediately after it is available also contributes, but AI is the bigger problem.
Like in all CIv games, AI doesn't really care about your victory progress, it pursues only its objectives. This is still valid here: you can go on a domination streak, the other Civs will not rally against you. You can place a Mind Flower smack on the border with a Purity Civ, they will ignore it. Considering that 3/5 victory types in this game are to build and hold a planetary wonder, this has to change.
For the first time in Civ game health (hapiness) is simply a nuissance. March through the map, -45 health, who cares?
Story: Again affinities. Everything revolves around who you choose to be. Storyline-wise, these three choices feel very logical and distinct, as they are core in everything Sci-Fi. The sponsors' and leaders' background has integrity. There are a lot of flaws in the details, however.
Most of Civilopedia is nonsence ("Memetwork" - 9gag is now a world wonder). Half the technologies feel like you are researching the same thing, too much random meaningless words thrown in. Unit upgrades lack description. Orbital stations lack description. What the hell is this Great Mistake?

Hello my friends, I see that several of you have already Wishlisted this game, but have yet to actually purchase it, and the game has been on sale more than a few times before now.
However, If you're still considering whether you should buy this game, or have simply forgotten that it was on your Wishlist, then I would wait until it's on sale for 75-90% off.  For while the game has some really nice artwork, the gameplay is very reminiscent to most base-managing platform survival games I've already played, and even some that I haven't gotten around to yet.  The first couple of hours playing this game were a lot of fun, and the story while not very original or unique, is good enough to see you through the first campaign, though after that I'd just about had enough of the game.  It's definitely a play once and then forget all about it kind of game.
I've returned to the game now to try and aquire the five Achievements that I'd missed out on in my first playthrough, but despite the time gap between now and playing it last, well... the game just felt really bland and overly tedious.  Thanks to another Players Achievments Guide however, I was able to aquire three out of the five Achievements that I needed in a very quick and timely manner.   I however made one very brutal discovery, one that wasn't mentioned anywhere on the Store Page.
Two Achievements can only be aquired by purchasing the DLC.
You're probably thinking that this is a good thing and that Achievements often do come with a DLC more times than not, however those other games only add the Achievements once the DLC has been purchased, whereas this already includes them, but forces you to purchase the DLC to unlock it.  In other words, you cannot unlock 100% of the game without emptying you pockets just a little bit more.
Not that it's really the issue here, but the DLC is for a charitable cause, and why is that not the issue here?  Because if we start endorsing pay-for-Achievements now, it won't be long until we're doing it in a few more games, then some more, then most, until finally almost every game is a "buy your way to glory and prestige" game.
I would've have given the game a 5 out of 10 and probably skipped out on giving it a Review since there's no sideways thumb or leveled palm.  However, paid Achievements while still making it 5 out of 10 game, means that I cannot sincerely recommend this game.

TLDR version: I played this game during the free trial, having played a lot of Sid Meier's games before, including Alpha Centauri. This game feels like an updated version of that one, but it pales in comparison. If they'd simply updated AC's graphics, that would have been a better game. I had it on my wish list, but have now removed it, it doesn't seem to be worth my money or my time. So, not recommended.
Long version: I had this game on my wish list and saw that it was on discount, so I was about to buy it when I noticed it was already available for to play for free for the weekend, so I downloaded and installed it. That went well, which was about the best experience I've had with this game, it basically ended there. The first thing I noticed was that factions feel really bland, there is no background on them when you select one, so I basically chose the one that seemed to match the girl from the intro, to give me at least some feeling of immersion. I chose an option that would allow me to select a landing site from a larger area, but still ended up with a completely landlocked first settlement, while I had really wanted one on the seaside, to allow me to build ships. Then I started to explore and expand. Since I didn't feel like slaughtering the aliens, I avoided that for as long as I could and they left me alone. Great, I thought, the game takes into account how I act. But a few turns and cities along, they started blockading a coastal city, that began to starve, attacked and killed a settler and sank some of my ships. I was then forced to defend myself, but my units were easily defeated, even at the normal setting I had selected. Furthermore, the tech tree forces you to choose a certain course, or else certain units won't be available to you at all. This even though the tech tree is already pretty limited. To sum it up: the game forces you to act a certain way, limits you in what you can do and will probably always end up with you having to fight the Aliens, just like in AC. I hate being railroaded into doing things a certain way. If you're going to tell me how to play a game, just make it into a movie already.
Diplomacy, as in many of these games, is laughable. For instance, when an AI who wants something from me, like permission to pass through my territory, it ends up demanding stuff in return, stuff that I don't want to give them and have no incentive to do so. At most, it is only willing to promise doing me a favor in return, without telling me what such a favour would entail. But it is the AI that wants something, it should make it worth my while! If you're not willing to do that now, what reason do I have to believe you will make up for it in the future, when in a few turns we may be at war? Judging by that irrational behaviour, sooner or later, they will all irrationally go to war with me when I become too powerful, even if we've been BFF's forever. Disclaimer: I didn't bother to keep playing to find out for sure.
I also got the feeling that certain things, like units, cost energy, even though it doesn't say so anywhere, as I started to dip into my and was forced to make certain choices to address that, but nevertheless still kept going into the negative immediately after upgrading my reactors and stuff in an effort to compensate. So not only was the cause of the problem unclear to me, forcing me to make give up on options that would otherwise have been preferable in an effort to address that situation, the solutions was also only very temporary. I feel a lot of information is lacking or not easily accessible in the Civilopedia, so I can't make informed decisions.
All in all, I feel it is not even worth even the discounted price of EUR 20,- and am glad I held out until now. I feel it would become either boring or frustrating if I'd kept playing, even with certain mods. If I'd already bought the game, I might have kept playing, just to try and get my money's worth, but right now, I don't see the point of shelling out even half the full price just to keep playing a game that is such a disappointment. Sid Meier is a genius, but I really wonder how involved he was with this product. Maybe they just slapped his name on it and were done with it? It seems to me he would have invented new stuff, tweaked things, instead of lamely ripping off his earlier work and doing that in a bad way. This game, if anything, is worse than Alpha Centauri in every way except graphics. Steam Workshop support may mean some of these issues can or will be fixed, but I hate it when a publisher relies on the community to fix the flaws in their own game. I really dislike the trend of producing Alpha or Beta releases, making them available for paid early access or preorder and then not delivering on the promises made or even completely abandoning the game shortly afterwards. The only way I see to stop that, is to try and avoid jumping on that bandwagon as often as possible. It allows publishers to get away with shipping a shoddy product and then not fixing the obvious problems before moving on to the next game.

Bleed is a 2-D stage-based action platformer with a mouse-aimed weapon system and a unique "bullet time" mechanic.  The player can activate bullet time at will to slow down the entire game, making it much easier to dodge attacks and aim their own.  However, bullet time only lasts a few seconds before requiring a recharge, forcing the player to constantly choose where to use it and for how long.  Combined with a fully-controllable triple air dash and a range of very different weapons, Bleed offers the player a wide variety of options for plotting their own course through the game.
APPROXIMATE LENGTH
1-2 hours, though replays will unlock more things
PROS
(+) Game speed is fast without being TOO fast
(+) Sprites are dynamic and give a smooth feel to the game
(+) Bullet time lets the player set their own pace through trouble sections
(+) Plenty of unique bosses
CONS
(-) Levels are depressingly short and just a formality in between bosses
(-) Bosses die too quickly
(-) Bullet time isn't NEEDED for most of the game and can feel underwhelming to use
YOUR MILEAGE MAY VARY
(?) Unlockable characters are more of a "challenge mode" than a different playstyle
OVERALL
Bleed's premise is a whole lot of fun and shows great promise, though it fumbles in execution by just not having enough substance, and by not making free-form bullet-time as cool as it sounds.  This isn't a deal breaker, but potential players should be wary about setting their expectations too high.

DFO is, quite frankly, one of the best games I've ever played.  I played during the turbulent Nexon years.  I lived through it closing and stumbling through the Chinese version.  I played through the open alpha and finally now, where Neople, the original developers, publish the game globally by themselves.
And this is the best version of DFO we'll ever get.
My Steam says 6.4 hours, but over the course of the game's lifespans I've easily sunk 750+ hours across a bunch of characters.
Pros:
Character classes are all fun to make and play, as each 5 levels gives you new skills to toy with and combo with.
Plenty of character slots to use, with more given out for free all the time.
Biweekly events to help players get useful items like life tokens, safe upgrades, even avatars and equipment.
Neople is extremely quick to respond to the playerbase when issues arise and compensate very well.
PVP is a blast.
The XP curve is so much better now, and Scenario dungeons make the once-awful grind mighty doable.
Co-op with up to four players, or PVP with up to 8 in 1 on 1 matches or all-out brawls.
You can play dress-up.
The official anime is absolute garbage, but it's so funny to watch as a result.  Spot-the-anime-cliche!
You can get most cash shop items from events or from other players.
A point shop where you get points for running dungeons/from events/rebated from cash shop purchases, which you can use to buy helpful items and a limited range of avatars.
Lost Treasure keys actually drop fairly frequently, compared to never seeing a key fragment drop ever in Nexon days.
Extremely moddable.  You can replace background music and even the sounds the characters make.  I have the old Nexon English voice packs, plenty of old dungeon music, and my Mechanic's Combat Robot blasts Darude - Sandstorm instead of its original song every time I crit.
SKILL RESETS ARE FREE AND THERE'S A SKILL TREE!  SCREW YOU NEXON FOR MAKING PEOPLE PAY TWENTY DOLLARS FOR A DAMN SKILL RESET
Gold is fairly easy to obtain and costs for leveling equipment isn't prohibitive.  Hell, Epic quests pop out equipment for your characters every 5 levels.
Extremely controller friendly.  I have Xpadder set up with a PS2 controller and use the game's input commands system to activate most of my skills.
It's not Mighty Number 9.
Cons:
Fatigue.  A lot of people complain about it, but it's a necessary evil to help protect the game's economy, which is actually still pretty healthy compared to Nexon days.  Still, it can be a bummer to get to a new dungeon or brand new skill and have to wait or use a fatigue potion to play with it.
Only can make 2 characters a day, which is only really a con before you have enough alts to deal with fatigue if you want to play more.
Avatars are untradable, except in the special packs that other players can buy and sell.  You have to cash shop or point shop these.  Dammit nipple I just wanted a shirt for my Slayer.
Some classes don't do as much damage as other classes as easily, this can be kind of discouraging.  Ranger is weaker seeming than Launcher, for example.  Though Ranger is still absolutely fun as hell, and got a buff/rework recently that makes him better without a reinforced weapon.  And, if he gets a powerfully reinforced weapon, he can easily outdamage the Launcher late-game.  Play what you enjoy, not what the community says is good.
Connection in PVP is pretty important if you wanna get real competitive.
The people that buy global chat megaphones are either selling things or absolute idiots.  It can be funny, or it can be grating.  At least Megaphones are now 2 Mileage points instead of the...what, $5? they were in Nexon.
If you want the absolute best equipment ever for facerolling PvE content, you gotta beat the odds of winning the lottery five times in a row.  That said, you can do plenty fine with a good set of Chronicle armor and a nice pink weapon.
The game does not tell you about Quick Rebound.  For the sake of God, pick up Quick Rebound.  It's in the top bar of skills in the skill window.
The constant flow of events can be overwhelming; Just remember you DON'T HAVE to do all of them if you don't want.
All of the stuff in the game can be daunting to new players, but it gets easy to understand after a few days.
The game doesn't automatically enable Tutorial mode for new players.  Do yourself a favor and hit O, then navigate to System and enable Tutorial mode.
The Global chat is NOT indicative of the community.  Come find us at
for help and info.
If you like beat 'em ups or fighting games, give DFO a shot.  If you're like me, you'll fall in love instantly.

Its resource management, life-sim and exploration mechanics are simple. Each day plays out in two phases. The clean split between day and night creates the steady metronome that keeps you pushing through This War of Mine. You're tasked with feeding survivors, ensuring they get a good night's rest and looking out for their physical as well as mental health.
Systems This War of Mine's are designed to push you towards moral quandaries, where you're trapped by basic human needs, and shown how they can so easily corrupt otherwise upstanding people.
Like a grim version of The Sims, players click around to move characters and on icons to assign tasks such as making food, building, clearing rubble, rifling through resource points or administering aid—either medicinal or moral. All of this is reliant on having the appropriate resources, which are gathered at night when a character can be sent to scavenge while the others sleep or stand guard. Locations include abandoned squallers, schools, hospitals, churches and more. Areas with more valuable resources are either inhabited or defended, while the safer places yield less.
Everything outside line of sight is enveloped in a fog, giving the exploration real tension. Walking is silent but slow, while running comes at the risk of making noise, denoted by emanating circles of sound. Enemies emit these same tells, as do rats scurrying around. NPCs that hear the sounds or spot you in their line of sight will investigate, The defenseless cower, some propose a barter, others respond with deadly force. The slow, deliberate pacing accentuates the languishing, oppressive atmosphere.
This War of Mine is one the most thematically interesting games.

Okay, if you own Hard Reset, or you own Shadow Warrior, and thus get the crazy 85% discount, ignore everything in the review, go to the "Buy now" button, and pick up the game. At the silly cheap price it's being offered at, they're offering you a gift of a very, very good game, which has been refurnished in their newer engine, with some much needed gameplay tweaks, and some optimisations and additions, for less than the price of a coffee. You would be a complete lunatic not to pick it up for the price offered, or flat broke, but it's -easily- worth the pittance they're asking for the update, and makes the Metro Redux package offer look a bit absurd in comparison.
Hard Reset was a -great- game when it came out, it was unashamedly old school, it didn't even have a crouch button. But it's laserlike focus on good gunplay (it had a shotgun that made me happy in ways that should be illegal) and excellent visual design easily marked it as one of my picks back at the time. It's aged well too, mostly because the engine it rested on was a very well optimised one for the PC platform, you could pretty much run it on a toaster and get good looking results.
Which may beg the question - Why the "redux" update? A few reasons. One - Cybersword. You get a melee option in case you were lacking enough tools as it is. Two, they've integrated the DLC in much more cleanly, so it now presents a much tidier experience. Three, they've updated the engine to give even -more- scalability and at the top end, an even shinier presentation. They've also made some adjustments like deciding the whole stamina system could die in a fire, and therefore allowing you to dodge and run around at will, this is entirely for the good by the way, the game needed that adjustment.
As before, this is as pure a shooter as it's possible to get, you go charging from place to place shooting everything that isn't you, the graphics are great, the sound is rich, and the enemies are unforgiving. Granted, this isn't DOOM, but it's a very good "AA" tier take on the topic, and it very definitely holds its' own as a game which for half the price, will easily give you a lot of entertainment for your buck.
In effect, for new buyers this is the "Definitive" presentation of Hard Reset, made ready for the console crowd (and to them I really do recommend they grab it, it's a great experience), and for people on Steam, this is definitely the way to go, because they'll get the version of the game "as the creators intended", a sort of Director's cut if you will. With all the rough edges sanded off and all the best parts made even better.
A good way to look at this is as the "Director's cut" of Hard Reset, it's been given the treatment that the developers felt it deserved, and for current owners, they're getting the finalised version at the cost of a cup of coffee, so there's no reason to feel slighted. For new buyers, this is the version to get, and as a result, I've very little hesitation giving it a solid pair of thumbs up. This is a very, very good "AA" first person shooter, and deserves your time, and your trigger finger.

I wanted this game to scratch the same itch as games like Infinifactory and Factorio, but I found the game to be a bit of planning and then a whole lot of waiting around.
The goal of maximising your profits meant that I would pause the game as I planned out each build chain, and then when I finally unpaused, all I could do is sit and watch for a long time as either my Scientists or Explorers gathered more progression for me, or I earned enough profit to pause the game and build something else.
Also the lack of a planning mode/phase meant that I would waste money after I build most of a production line, only to find out that either I miscalculated or ran out of room. Hard Reset is a very good FPS, which while claiming to be "retro style" is closer the likes of Painkiller or Serious Sam than to Doom.
Just so we're clear, I really liked the original Hard Reset as well as the Shadow Warrior reboot, and got 100% achievements in both.
However, this Redux version a little disappointing. They decided to ride on Shadow Warrior's success and to take elements from it to add them into Hard Reset : the player is now able to dash in all 4 directions and can use a katana (acquired around 2 hours into the game).
Just so we're clear on the new content, we're talking moves that are directly taken from Shadow Warrior, with the same animations.
There are also new "human" enemies, but we're talking about reskinned version of previously existing enemies, the "human looking" robots, which were dreskinned with some human skins we could already see in the game... It does feel very cheap.
They also changed a few combat situations by swapping some enemies here or adding some there. Some of that includes enemies from the old DLC added to the original levels. This is the good part of this version, if you enjoyed the original, it is worth replaying it just for those new combat situations... However,  only about 1 or 2 fights per level got changed! This is very light!
Now the issues this version brings up.... Originally you could not dash, and you could only sprint forward. Now, not only you can dash in all four directions for as long as you want to, but that dash is a lot faster than the sprinting (sprint move which has therefore become completely useless).
The good thing with the dash is that it makes the game faster paced.... The bad thing is that the enemies AI were not updated in consequence of the new moves. The enemies are still designed with in mind, a player who can only sprint forward and not at a great speed...
The result is that this new dash move allows you to outmaneuver every enemy very easily. MANY of the game's enemies have attacks which are based on rushing towards the player, but now, you can easily dash in any direction to get away.
In the original game, the fun and skill of the game came from predicting the enemies attack and reacting quick enough, but now you can simply f**k around not caring so much, and get away from most situation with a couple of simples dashes.
As for the katana, it can become useful against rusher enemies and in close-up situations. However, the original game's balance is based around managing two different ammo types, using one not to run out of the other and vice versa. A huge part of this balance and ammo management is screwed because the katana doesn't use any ammo at all, and lets you get away with bad weapon management...
In other words the balance of the game has been completely screwed, and it requires a lot less skill to be good at the game.
If you have never played Hard Reset, play the original game first. Then play Redux if you like the game enough.
Recommended for fans of the game only.

Note: Jalopy is an Early Access title. The version reviewed was current as of the date of this review.
In Jalopy, you play an unnamed person living on the outskirts of Berlin, going on a road trip through the beautiful European countryside in your newly repaired Laika two-stroke automobile. The old jalopy breaks down often, so you'll need to be handy with a spanner, and it needs near-constant attention: fuel, oil, wiper fluid, tyres, ... . If you don't keep on top of maintenance, you'll end up stuck on the side of the road. And if you don't find any way of making money on your trip, your meagre savings are sure to run out before you reach your destination.
The graphics in Jalopy are functional rather than beautiful, much like its portrayal of the Eastern European landscape in which it is set. The game is rendered in three dimensions and played from a first-person perspective, but the game world is made up of very-low-polygon models and plain-coloured textures, though with some nice dynamic lighting. The plain and rather blocky graphics have some appeal, but it doesn't take too long for the drab landscape to become a bit boring. This may well be the developer's intention, given the setting. Speech bubbles from characters are a bit too big and intrusive for my liking, but again it's a deliberate style that's been chosen, and they work well enough.
The standard Unity graphical detail settings have been retained, accessible only from the Unity launcher, and not in game. I haven't noticed any performance issues at maximum detail.
Sound effects are quite variable in quality. The engine sound is very weedy, but suits the old jalopy quite well, I think. Rain sounds are good, and other cars sound fine. Tyre sounds, though, are terrible. The first time I went driving off road in the wet I had no idea what that weird sound was supposed to be until I noticed the car sliding out.
There's music on the radio in the car. It fits the setting well, but isn't really the sort of music I listen to for enjoyment, so I tend to turn the radio off instead.
There are no voiceovers for characters in the game; everything is done in text.
Jalopy starts with a brief tutorial; you wake up in your sparsely furnished garage / apartment to find a man (a friend, presumably) presenting you with an old car that he has acquired: a two-stroke Laika 601 Deluxe, the jewel of the East German car manufacturing industry. It's lacking one door, and wheels, and all of the important components from the engine bay, but other than that it's ready to go!
The tutorial guides you through installing all of the parts in the car (you have a well-stocked garage for just this eventuality), and then throws you into the game proper. You're given a car user's manual and a map and off you go on your pre-determined tour of the countryside, with $100 to your name. The tutorial doesn't really give you any information on what you're supposed to do in the game, though, so be prepared for trial and error and a few false starts.
The locations you visit each time you play seem to be the same, but you're given a choice of three different routes. I think the roads you follow are procedurally generated to a degree, or at least the events that can occur on the way must be, as they haven't been exactly the same each time I've played, but they are definitely very similar, so the building blocks must be very large or limited in placement. And the game seems to be structured to force you to stay in a motel each time you reach a destination, as border gates are only open during the day and time doesn't advance unless you're on your journey.
Jalopy is played from a first-person view, and I had a bit of trouble getting a sense for the size of the car while driving. There's partial controller support, but it's still a bit clunky, so I ended up playing with the recommended mouse and keyboard. WASD controls your character's movements as well the car's, and the mouse controls looking around and interacting with the environment, including activating or deactivating the car's various features. The rest of the controls are far less standard, and can't be changed (or even examined) in game; you have to quit and use the Unity launcher for that instead. Oh, the limit of three held items makes inventory management tiresome and frustrating.
Car control is okay, but not fantastic; a controller's analogue stick should be much better here than the recommended keyboard and mouse, as the digital nature of A/D keyboard steering is not very realistic or enjoyable. When it starts raining or you're on dirt roads, though, your dry road tyres wear quickly, and when it's both raining and dirt roads, the car turns into a wet noodle. It's rather unrealistic, but adds a welcome change, and a reason to buy different tyres.
I really like the idea of Jalopy, with its rogue-like elements mixed with its tongue-in-cheek attitude, but at the moment there just doesn't seem to be that much to do. You pick a route to your next destination, keep an eye out for boxes on the side of the road that you can loot, try to fix your car (if you have the tools) when it breaks down, which seems to happen once on every section of your trip, and then fill up with the essentials when you reach the next town. There's only very limited interaction with the few NPCs you'll find, and the road sections that make up most of the game tend to blur into each other after a while, with the graphical style that seems charming and unique at first eventually becoming a bit bland and dull, and virtually unpopulated.
It's buggy, too, even though it's been in Early Access for just about a year now. The developer is still active, and many of the bugs may be addressed with time, but at the moment it's rather unstable. The worst issue I've encountered is a game-breaker, with the game deciding to let me remove items from the trunk, but not replace them, or put anything else in. This is a long-standing issue that was first reported in the forums last year, and given that it prevents you from being able to store or transport anything in the car, it's a big problem. I also had a game-breaking bug where I couldn't do anything at a border checkpoint; the game wouldn't let me pass my papers to the gate guard, but I also couldn't start the car or get out.
Other gameplay issues I've seen are less serious, but still annoying, such as other drivers speeding up behind you to crash into you, leaving you with a fine to pay. There are some weird graphical problems, too. The tutorial man is wearing a jacket with weird textures. There are holes/cracks in geometry in some places, and the smoke and dust effects look bad in the game's plain style; some transparency would really help. I also noticed something very weird with the moon at night, where it seemed to be hidden behind something, and the sun rises in front of the distant mountains. Oh, and why does my car make dust clouds that float leisurely away on the breeze in the rain?
Pros:
+ An interesting idea, with understated humour
+ It's sort of fun
Cons:
- Very buggy
- Hard to get into
- The world seems very underpopulated, almost deserted
- Some control issues
- Some graphical issues
Jalopy is rather like the jalopy in the game; it's a bit hard to get into, it's pretty rough around the edges, and it often breaks down.
There's an interesting and unique game in there, but at the moment it's hidden by gameplay and graphical issues. Still, I'm looking forward to seeing what Jalopy will become as it finishes its journey through Early Access.

I have enjoyed this game, though I am not sure it is worth the full purchase price (I got it free from Humble Bundle).

Fabula Mortis is a first person shooter made with Unreal engine, where you battle versus bots or other players for glory on a 4 different maps. As far as I can tell there is no story mode, just good old pvp.
You can choose from 5 characters + a locked one (not sure how to unlock it, my guess - leveling).
Rouge - the chick with the double revolvers - good from a distance as the iron sight is pretty accurate.
Alice - the machine gun chick - your typical spray and pray character, can have grenades.
Vlad - the melee dude - wolverine style in your face slice and dice - lightning fast.
Wolf - the dude with the flamethrower - the Firebug, can drop tar and set it ablaze.
Rob-o - the C3PO canon launcher - slow, but 1 shots people :)
The unlockable character is called Wild Card and can slide on the ground - that's all I've gathered from the Steam description.
There is character progression in the game - you level up and you gather coins from kills - 25 for a headshot, 50 for first blood and 100 for a kill. Coins and levels persist through character swap. You need level 10 and 10000 coins to unlock the secondary ( and I expect the better) weapon/armaments for each character , so 60 000 coins to unlock it on all six (600 frags). There is a skill tree for all of your characters, that provides minor upgrades like longer power up duration and less respawn time, and then one individual tree for each character, where you unlock the secondary armaments, taunts, grenades ...
So on the available 4 maps you can play the following match types :
Deathmatch, Team Deathmatch, Training Day, King of the Hill and Bodyguard.
Deathmatch and Team Deathmatch are pretty straightforward, in Training day everybody starts with Alice and as you gain kills you progress and swap automatically to the next character, King of the Hill - on of you is the King, everybody on the map can see King's location and whoever kills the King becomes the new one - points are awarded for being the King. Bodyguard game mode is like a team Deathmatch, where one of the players on each team is VIP and only VIP deaths affect the scoreboard, the rest of the team are expendable ;)
There are quite a few power-ups in the game in form of a different colored ball on the ground - armor, damage, big jump and a few others. At first it's hard to get, what the power up exactly does - I would love to have them all listed and explained somewhere. I would also like some Steam achievements and trading cards - to round up the game experience. The maps are fairly different, but only 4 - let's hope more will come in the future. The controls are tight and fully remappable, the combat is fluid and satisfactory, unless you're the victim :p The AI is definitely not the brightest, as it mainly reacts when shot upon, but it's good to have in the mix for more action ;)
The price tag is a bit high in my opinion, as there are free to play alternatives on the market that offer the same, if not better, experience, so I would recommend only to buy the game, once it goes on sale.
TL:DR you can watch my gameplay video, where I play as the victim in Deathmatch mode on all 4 maps
