SHORT VERSION:
AI: VERY BAD.
Content: less Than Civ 4 with no expansions
UI: Unorganized and confusing as hell even after tutorials.
Graphics: About on par with Civ 5, textures aren't quite as good, but with the obnoxiously limited zoom, you don't notice it.
Trading: bad, you can only trade specific amounts of things for specific times that you can't change.
Multiplayer: handicaps from bad features aside, its usual civ.
Singleplayer: Don't care, came for, what should have been, the lasting content, AKA multiplayer.
Combat: bad, no unit stacking plus poor movement and quick healing make it near impossible to kill anything, and thats just on the default difficlty.
LONG VERSION:
Thanks for the free day of play. Now I know why NOT to buy the game.
Took a few hours to do a multiplayer match with a friend to realize this is a trimmed down game based around a movie I didn't watch, and after playing the game I REALLY don't wanna see it.
This game has less content than Civ4 with no expansions the tech tree is shamefully tiny, there's only a handful of actual useful units, ages are basically out the window, there's a handful of civilizations to choose with a handful of meaningless perks each, surprisingly the buildings are about what you would expect from a Civ game.
The AI intentionally try NOT to kill you, and doesn't really try at all for any sort of victory in general.
The trade system occasionally lags the entire match for a few minutes if you trade any significant amount, insult to injury you can't actually modify how much you're trading, I had to trade my friend 4 times to get him 20 power a turn from my surplus of 27. And then I had to do it again every 25 turns because there's no time frame you get to choose from besides that.
Even so, with my help, he tried to spend the entire match Intentionally dying, and only got stronger because the AI are just that bad, had this been a REAL Civ game his corpse would had been used for their new carpet within a couple turns.
Meanwhile I tried winning, a culture victory is a pain with very little to generate culture, science is the same thing with a new coat of paint from the other games, the other victories are all about the same too, so I tried to do domination to try and have fun, boy was that a lie to myself. With an inability to stack units and slow speed it was a struggle to kill a single unit, let alone a city guarded by an airstrike drone for every person stupid enough to buy a copy of this game, on occasion I could get in a cheap shot, but was never actually able to kill a city or harm it for more damage than it could heal in a turn. Eventually turned to a cultural victory, the slow but assured win, my friend couldn't take it anymore and just quit, a few turns later I gave up myself because there's no fun in a victory without any challenge.
Any review site that actually gave this a good review either has shamefully low standards, or a equally low price to buy a good review.

The game started off with showing how terrible I am with taking care of other people, especially with scarce necessities. It shows what necessities needed by the playable characters monologue. Items can be found, crafted and/or upgraded, and through the items' descriptions you learn what to acquire to manage this. From this you venture into the unknown realm of this war of yours. Continuously throughout the game you learn through punishment, i.e. death, sickness, depression and/or wounds. Never assume that getting that particular item through scavenging and/or fighting toughs will be appreciated, as most aspects in the game aims to question your conscience and/or morale. Graves will appear, monologues will fill the air with self-doubt, depression is the mistress that reigns the sheltered characters.
I sat there, thinking that I had it all figured out, I knew how to make these people survive. When suddenly it became clear to me, I know nothing. Even the ones you take in, shelter, feed and nurse back to health might backstab you. Whilst helping NPC’s might gain you some items, it will allow the characters to feel some pride with their own morale.
Friend or foe? Only through enough trials and retrials will you see the complex outlay of the map and the different scenarios encountered. And, sadly, not even then you’ll know the right choices. As there are none, there’s only survival.

All BioShock games are amazing in their own way. The first has its amazing opening that sets the stage of one of the most atmospheric shooters ever made. Infinite has a beautiful world and character development. BioShock 2 has the gameplay. It was the first to allow the use of a gun in one hand and a plasmid in the other. This made BioShock 2 a lot more action-oriented than the first, while maintaining a SLIGHTLY less interesting/less mysterious Rapture, but still an engaging setting. Fighting your way through the mutated denizens of Rapture takes a bit more cunning this time around, and the expanded Plasmid and weapon upgrade system allow you to tackle combat in more ways than one. While you're putting one of the finest FPS games ever made in your cart, make sure to snag Minerva's Den, one of the best pieces of DLC ever made.
While my favorite BioShock may be the first because Rapture was still mysterious, there is an argument for BioShock 2 being the best that is just as valid.

I have been playing this game for over six years on and off, way before it was on Steam. I have really seen the game grown over the years, for better and for worse however it seems it has been for the worse.
As Nexon releases updates, they have added many new classes that outclass and overpower the originals. These new classes are usually much more flashier and stronger than the orignals, making them more popular. The new classes can often solo bosses, something that use to be impossible and defeating the purpose of teamwork.
Through several updates, the game has also become much too easy to level up, unlike how it use to be. Also, Nexon has made the game very pay-to-win like. Often people who have the money to spend on NX have the better equipment in game from the equipment enhancment system.
As the game advanced, Nexon has made many changes which altered the game drastically. One of these changes made in game world feel much more smaller than it use to be. Many and almost all of the maps have been compressed into compact versions, making traveling very different than it use to be. The game world use to be much larger and you could get lost in it and still have fun.
Finally, Maplestory has been a host to many bugs/hacks/down time. The game has been hacked many times, often causing damage to the econonmy and forcing server rollbacks. Hackers seem to also be quite common, seeing as a hacker(s) posted the login ID's of over 50 thousand players, including myself. The also game has more than a few bugs that can affect gameplay or quests, forcing unexpected maintenances.

Although the game centers around Wryn, and her quest to become the #1 best hero in the world, the controls are the star of the show here, with your character's movement being separate from aiming. This allows for the pacing to be pretty intense, and you'll want to just keep running and shooting down enemies without stopping. Keyboard and mouse controls take some time to get used to, but plug in a gamepad and something magical happens. Running, double-jumping, slowing down time, and dodging bullets left and right all become as easy as pie.
The game itself is hard as HELL, but the act of making it through mobs of enemies without a scratch is incredibly rewarding. At about 2 hours (and 6 levels), the game is short, but it doesn't overstay its welcome. There are also a bunch of unlockable weapons, characters, and challenge modes, so the game welcomes you to replay it in order to hone your skills.
And there IS local co-op as well, which is a very nice addition. The second player controls a red-headed Wryn, and can drop-in/out at any time. Though the game was clearly designed around a single-player experience, co-op is extremely fun and a great way to spend the afternoon with your friend.

Update: Marvel Puzzle Quest has changed a lot since I wrote this review. Mostly for the worse. While I do still enjoy playing the game it is largely because I already had a decent force before a lot of the changes were made. The company repeatedly ignores their fan base and makes changes that make the game increasingly hard to play without paying and really expensive if you do pay. I'm going to list the notable changes since this review was originally posted.
The Good:
1. The ever increasing roster size keeps collecting covers interesting and gives reason to come back to the game.
2. PvP seasons: The company recently introduced PvP seasons. These are month long event that keep track of players as they partake in PvP events. The top rated players get fantastic rewards.
The Bad:
1. Shields: In Marvel Puzzle Quest PvP events run on a points system. At first glance it is simple and  fair. In fact it used to be fair but shields have all but ruined the accessability. For every round you win you gain points. If you lose a round you lose points. This is fine. Being that PvP is actually Player vs. AI player people must be able to challenge computer versions of other players. When a computer version of yourself wins or loses you also gain/lose points according. This has always been annoying but for the most part fair. However, shields allow a player to spend a decent sum of money in order to protect themselves from point loss. In otherwords free players quickly lose points from their AI losing but they can't make those who pay lose any points. This makes it very hard for free players especially when first starting off.
2.Gold Characters: Gold characters are enhanced versions of other characters. This essentially means the developers got lazy and wanted to release a new character but didn't feel like designing new character powers. While that alone is annoying it is tolerable. What isn't tolerable is taking a character and nerfing him because he is "overpowered" and then release a stronger version of the character right after. For anyone who joined late and doesn't know this is exactly what they did with Thor.
3. Boost Changes: Boosts were an easy way to allow free players to stand a fighting chance. A player could buy boosts with Iso(in game currency) in order to assist a strategy using what are otherwise weak characters. However, boosts have changed so that in order to buy the useful ones you must spend hero points(premium currency).
4. Healing Changes: In Marvel Puzzle Quest you have always needed to wait for your characters to heal after battle. How long you have to wait varies depending on character level. You have also always been able to pay in order to heal instantly. While this has always given paying members an advantage, it wasn't outrageous because within a couple hours your characters would heal. However, the company has recently made it take longer for heroes to heal making the game even harder to play for free.
The Ugly:
1. Pay to Enter Tournaments: These are occasional tournaments that have an entry fee. The prizes to be won in said tournaments are outstanding. The winner gets one of every cover in the game. While I like the idea of large tournaments that have a little risk to them I don't like how these particular tournaments are set up. I'm fine with an entry fee but the fee should be in iso. I personally think there should be an entry fee somewhere along the lines of 5000-10000 iso. This is a decent amount of currency so there is a big risk for the players but it is entirely in-game currency so it is accessable to everyone if they are willing to save up for a while. Unfortunately the tournament entry fee is in hero points, so it once again favors those who pay fairly significantly.
2. Alliances: Alliances, are this games version of a clan. All events have alliance rankings in addition to individual rankings. All members of the top ranked alliances get prizes. Alliances had the potential to be a great addition to the game. having a community to play with and talk to as well as getting additional prizes for doing so is fantastic. Where the game went wrong is in Alliance sizes. An Alliance starts with 5 player slots. However, the alliance leader has the option to buy additional slots up to 20. Of course to buy these slots you have to spend Hero points. So only the alliances who pay ever win events because they have a larger player base. Adding an additional slot to a guild isn't cheap either; additional slot cost as much expanding you roster size post 20 heroes.
So would I recommend this game now? Maybe, it is really hard to say at this moment due to the fact that I started out so early. I do believe it is possible to do decently well while being a free player but I am rather biased because I already had a large army. Furthermore, at the rate which D3/Demiurge are ruining the game within a month it will likely be totally inaccessable to any new free players and possibly even veteran free players.

Big Pharma is a great game for everyone who likes planning, tweaking, optimization.
Your task is to manage a pharma corporation by producing and selling drugs. To get the job done, you´ll find your self searching for the required ingredients that can be processed and transformed into almost endless varieties as you increase or decrease concentration, add ingredients to produce new treatments and upgrade their effects.
To make things more difficult, almost all ingredients have side effects that you may remove, weaken, avoid (by manipulating concentration) or just accept as a necessary evil - but beware, strong side effects will lower your drug rating and value.
To make matters more complicated, your factory equipment cannot be placed neatly into straight assembly lines - each machine type has its own layout and creating complex chains will indeed be a puzzle game. And things usually don´t stay in place once you add new options to your arsenal - I find myself frequently redesigning my factory layout to optimize it according to the newly unlocked machines (which you can research).
All the while, different scenarios and settings require you to work towards a variety of different objectives, from just making cash to delivering a super-drug with high value.
To sum it up:  This game makes you think! If you like complex problem solving tasks, this is definitely your game.

Jalopy’s another fine title riding the commie wave of nostalgia...and I’m not being sarcastic at all. There’s a palpable need for games to fill up that niche and at the same time, offer something entirely different from most simulators on Steam. Released almost one year ago (and still in Early Access) by an enthusiastic developer that has kept supporting and updating its first Steam project, Jalopy excels in recreating the hardships of moving from point A to B, in a beater that belongs in a museum if not directly in a junkyard.
Coincidently or not, your nearly literal nostalgic trip starts in a garage next to a junkyard. It’s June 1990, you’re in the GDR (German “Democratic” Republic) and just several months away from the official Reunification of Germany. As you can imagine that’s not a topic or set of locations, used often in video games. Yet you play as a nameless and silent protagonist whose job is to help out his Uncle with certain errands which shall eventually culminate in a journey all the way to Turkey. The latest update for Jalopy allows players to reach Bulgaria, so the final destination has almost been implemented.
Not much in the sense of a storyline, but you won’t really have time to bother about that since the true protagonist in this game is none other than the titular jalopy: Laika 601 Deluxe. In real life this would be the Trabant 601, if not for some truly ironic twist through which using in a video game even the name of a defunct Soviet Bloc brand, somehow represents copyright infringement. Isn’t capitalism nice, comrades? So yeah, it’s a Trabi. A real cult classic of a car that became a symbol of the GDR, simply because it was the most affordable car around and there weren’t many alternatives, in terms of personal vehicular means anyways.
Also known as the “Spark plug with a roof”, its chassis was the only part made of actual metal. The rest of the components were a mix of plastic and recycled materials. It would have been a green thumb/hipster dream car if not for the notoriously underpowered two-stroke engine. Fun fact: that’s same motor which had been used to rotate panzer turrets, two decades before the Trabant was first manufactured. Yes, East Germans fitted a car with the shoddy engine of a tank’s main gun. It’s no surprise that reaching 80 km/h (49 mph) is gonna be a rare sight. Don’t expect 100 km/h, except when going downhill.
Unity Engine assets which are skillfully used in conjunction with a minimalist aesthetic. You might say Jalopy has a “large pixel” graphical style to it, yet the shapes have been streamlined enough to bare no resemblance to Minecraft on wheels. Performance was mostly as expected. No problem running the title maxed out, 4K & stable 60 frames per second. A couple of crashes to desktop were encountered when exiting the game and the only texture glitch I found, was related to the rare occasions of gathering dirt as the car passed pot holes and puddles. Dirt texture for the Laika’s grille would “float” behind the car. It’s a title still in its Early Access stage so I won’t judge it too harshly from a technical perspective.

Jalopy sadly, lacks severely in the sound department. No voice acting whatsoever when interacting with NPCs and not even a lot of background sounds either, apart from the engine noise and other mechanical auxiliaries. The Laika’s radio plays a repetitive tune and no options there, other than to switch it on or off. Silence is not golden when you’re driving down the highway. A retro soundtrack comprised of German songs if nothing else, is in dire need of being included in Jalopy.
You might mistake Jalopy for a car repair/assembly simulator in the vein of My Summer Car or Revhead. It’s true that repairing the vehicle is an integral part of the gameplay, yet the journey and the efforts undertaken in reaching your destination, are far more important than the car maintenance aspect. No matter how careful you might be driving, there won’t be a dull moment in Jalopy. Something shall break down like flimsy clockwork and since this shall happen in the middle of the road most of the time, be prepared to pull over frequently. It goes without saying that carrying spare parts in Laika’s trunk, is crucial to your success. Buying car components and even upgrades, won’t be as straight forward since the in-game economy can be abused to the point at which your errand runs become unnecessary.
The lack of a proper progress saving system means that no matter when you quit the game, Jalopy shall take you back to your home garage where stock car parts are always respawned. This might have been a good thing for players still getting accustomed to the fail rate of  Jalopy’s components, yet the fact that these parts can be sold for a hefty sum, translates in economic imbalance and outright cheating. The wares come in many shapes and sizes (they occupy vital space in your car’s trunk) and can be also found along the highways, for some reason. Booze, sausages, cigarette packs and several other commodities which are your main source of income, depending on where you buy and sell them. Contraband is simulated in the sense that as you pass through the borders of certain Eastern Bloc countries, some goods are prohibited over there.
Curiously, no matter what route you pick up on your map and even what direction you choose to drive towards, you always seem to reach your objective. It’s like the proverb: “All roads lead to Rome!” except that instead of Italy’s capital, you go from one gloomy communist scenery to another until you shall reach Turkey and Istanbul in a subsequent update, I presume. Some landmarks are included already and they offer the needed visual diversity that is not present in the towns and roads themselves. Motels, gas stations and shops are a lone driver’s best friends and you can bet that they’ll offer you the needed support since Uncle is mostly used as a guide/tutorial more than anything else.
The car repair segment is not as fleshed out as in similar simulators mainly because the Laika 601 Deluxe isn’t a complex car to begin with. You won’t have any trouble learning the ropes in half an hour or so. From there onwards, is gonna be a smooth ride. Or not, since you will constantly compromise between the wares you need to sell and the spare parts you need to carry for emergency repairs in the middle of nowhere. Driving & fixing the Laika is easy and the dashboard is richly detailed but still missing the option of manual transmission. In the Trabant’s case, the stick shift would have been placed next to the steering wheel. Automatic transmission in this particular car model is both anachronistic and technically infeasible. Alas it’s being used just for the sake of simplicity and I understand it but I still hope the dev team shall include a proper manual gearbox method eventually.
Jalopy is decently priced for the unique experience it offers but I agree it needs Achievements and Trading Cards as well. A quality indie title on Steam deserves nothing but the best support from its developer and growing fanbase. If you want a small taste of automotive communism minus the real life downsides, grab Jalopy now or wait for a Steam Sale if you’re a stingy would-be comrade.

Hard Reset gets a graphical and engine update, along with some gameplay updates. And at the discounted price, in particular for Shadow Warrior owners, you get a reasonable old school FPS action at its core. The gunplay is fun with most of the weapons, as there's a satisfaction you get when tearing an enemy apart with bullets. There's specific area damage that means you can tear apart an enemy, leading to enemies to claw toward you with one claw, slowly but surely. And at first, it really does a good job of giving that old school feel. The problem is that, it stays around a bit too long. Don't get me wrong, if you like the basic action of the old school FPS, it's here. It just doesn't do enough in the variety area to keep up the action, and it'll fall into a slog. The difficulty has been reduced a bit from the original, and that detracts from the game in the end. There's a lot of little annoying things about the game: as new additions push the game to be even easier for no reason, while questionable design decisions regarding controls (f1 and f2 to switch guns? Really?) don't make a lot of sense. Luckily, it's the price for those Shadow Warrior owners in particular that really sells the game here. It's a niche purchase for FPS fans in the standard case, but at that 85% discount, you get a bang for your buck, and you really can't ask for more then that.

Note: The multiplayer mode is active, though I couldn't get a decent ping to any servers to play on them (I live in Australia). So this review is for the single player content.
Homefront is a collaboration of various gameplay elements you've probably seen in any modern-set FPS. Most of which is executed well with a few complaints here and there. Visually, the game looks decent most of the time, but some places are glaringly missing the same level of detail as others. Animations are definately the weakest point of the game with some amateur-level displays of scripted sequences. Right from the beginning of the game, you can notice it as vehicles pivot on their center.
Gunplay is solid, though the guns felt a little on the soft side and the AI is not great, but it's passable.
The story is fine. It had a few interesting moments, but shallow character development and logically-questionable actions detach you from any sense of involvement. It's not a bad game by far, but it's lacking in a lot of areas to reach a full experience that's worth dropping a moderate amount of money on.

If you are a fan of Clint Eastwood westerns, TV shows like Firefly, blues music, Mount & Blade, and naval battle games, there's a high chance you'll like this one.
Rebel Galaxy is a fantastic, simple spaceship sandbox game, where you can be a trader, bounty hunter or even a pirate. And there's nothing stopping you from being all of those at the same time! I would classify this game as a "Mount & Blade lite". Apart from the story missions, you can decide which tasks you want to take on, and in what order. Slowly upgrade from one ship to another, and build your reputation with different factions, in the end getting access to their ships and equipment. For a price, of course.
The soundtrack consists of an amazing collection of Dark Country songs that really set the tone of the game. However, if the genre isn't your cup of tea, the songs can easily get on your nerves, especially because some songs seem to play more than others. I LOVE the soundtrack, but after hours of nonstop playing, some of the songs have a tendency to get annoying. Until you launch the game again the next day.
The gameplay itself is fairly simple. While you are flying in a space ship, the big procedurally generated maps are essentially a 2D surface. You cannot fly up or down. Only forwards and backwards, and naturally any direction inbetween. Now that may seem weird for being a game set in space a totally 3D environment, but the gameplay is quite similar to naval warfare. Think of the combat between the capital ships in Star Wars, where the opposing ships fly side by side so they can unleash their broadsides at each other, instead of the combat in Star Trek, where the ships are flying over and under their enemies while trying to murder each other. I have no problems with the combat system, but one could expect a game set in space to play differently.
Also, as a side note, if you are an achievement hunter, these achievements are perfect. No weird tasks required, most of them will unlock by just playing. There is, however, some grinding to do, although nothing major.
Honestly, Rebel Galaxy is one of my favourite games. It's by no means perfect, I've had a few crashes here and there, and constantly forget to save the game (which is automatic, but only happens when docking at a spaceport) which can result in a lot of lost progress. But the game fills that certain niche, that certain feeling that many other games can't satisfy. It's a unique experience that I've yet to find in a different game. Totally recommended.

Hitman: Absolution is a really well made, fun game and it’s packed with a variety of different content. The levels cover a lot of varied locations which contain some fun and immersive scenarios. The story 'cut scenes' are kind of cheesey and the characters are a bit dumb. The game runs great at 60FPS and I had no problems at all with the performance. If you wanna see my specs, I have them listed on my profile.
The gameplay styles are very well balanced, as it plays well either stealthily or as a third person shooter. There is a really satisfying gameplay mechanic, that kind of bridges the gap between the two styles of play. There is also a whole built in ‘challenges’ system with unlockable stuff and a multiplayer aspect too. All this content is well implemented and adds tons of replay value.
I also played the Sniper Challenge add on and I enjoyed that even more than anything in the main game. It has it’s own built in challenges too, some of which are really detailed. In fact this extra content is loaded with cool little details and it is very immersive. I definitely recommend that you play this part in addition to the main game. As it’s one of the most enjoyable pieces of extra content I’ve ever seen. Over all Hitman: Absolution is fantastic and it's one of my favourite games.

Big Pharma is essentially a game where you are able to spend your money on parts such as "evaporators" and "dissolvers" in order to create new medications that will essentially give you more money, to spend more parts, to get more money, to spend new parts etc. This game has an endless cycle of "spending money on parts" and "gaining more money", just like the games "Rollercoaster Tycoon" and "Holy Potatoes! A Weapon Shop?". Other than giving specific goals to reach, such as gaining $1,000,000 in revenue in 10 years, this game really has no point other than to keep you in the "endless cycle", which is why I cannot give it a "thumbs up".
However, If you are the type of person who loves these kinds of games, then I will tell you that there are many aspects to consider, including:
-Research
-Finding new Ingredients
-Getting Loans when your bankrupt (which many games do not allow you to do)
-Upgrading standard Migraine Pills to something even better
-Upgrading Equipment
-Competitor Companies (AI companies, not multiplayer)
Even though Big Pharma is not my preferred cup of tea, it may be of interest to people who like the game I just described above.
Happy Gaming

This may be a "Free To Play" game, but like most of the lame flash games you see on Facebook, this game heavily revovles around micro-transactions. If you're not familar with the abusive nature of micro-transaction dependent games, then read some of the more in-depth reviews (like the ones with 4+ paragraphs) to get more details. The only positive thing this game has over the flash games on Facebook is that:
1) the game doesn't lag as much as the ones on FaceBook,
2) this game won't force you to spam all of your FaceBook friends, &
3) it has characters from the Marvel franchise.
As for the puzzle game itself, I find it infuriating! I am not merely saying this because I am a poor loser. I get my♥♥♥♥♥kicked all the time in MOBA & fighting games, but I can still enjoy those games. When I make a mistake in those games, I can usually see alternative moves that could have been made & understand how the consequences of the mistake could have been avoided.
In this game, when you destroy blocks, new blocks will fall down to replace the destroyed blocks, sometimes the replacement blocks will just conveniently share the same color & coinciding create a chain reaction, doing massive damage. I am not talking about the pieces that are already on the board & merely fall down. I speaking of the new pieces that weren't on the board previously. Because of this, destroying block on the bottom half of the board is usually more advantageous then destroying the block near the top edge of the board.
Unlike most puzzle games, such as "Tetris", there is no preview of the new incoming blocks that appear from the top of the game board, so there is no way to prepare for them, offensively or defensively.
Many times, chain combos will just happen by accident & sometimes for massive damage; sometimes for you, sometimes against you. This can be a HUGE reward that is being giving out, not for any brilliant strategy or careful planning, but just by sheer randomness. Unless one team is heavily more over-powered than the other, without a preview of the next set of falling blocks, the outcome of the match relies too heavily on luck. You might as well be playing a slot machine.
I'm still gonna play this game though, just because I'm as much of a sucker as those who do play slot machines.

One of the best management simulators to come along in ages and ages.
There's a lot of complexity here and there's a bit of a learning curve, but the tutorial covers the bulk of what you need to know. Unfortunately, the format of the tutorial feels pretty lazy to me and it suffers for that. Namely, it's rendered almost as an in-game manual. The game really needed an overlay-style tutorial rather than "OK, now click this widget, whose location on screen we will now describe in words instead of just pointing at it." But that's seriously the only criticism of this game I've got and it's easily fixable if the developers wanted to put some time in on it. It's also an issue that you'll quickly forget about once you start getting the hang of things.
So basically, your job is to make drugs. Drugs need to cure things. Ideally with as few side-effects as possible. But critically, you need your drugs to be profitable. Everything you do to remove side-effects or analyze the ideal mixture and concentrations for your drug ingredients introduces processing costs, which lowers your profitability. Meanwhile your competitors are making drugs that may target the same conditions. If their drug has fewer side-effects, demand for your drug will drop, and with it, the price you can charge for it. Suddenly you have to go back and do all the work you maybe skipped in the interests of profits because your terrible drug was properly recognized in the market as terrible. Unless of course, you patent your drug. Competition sucks. Nobody wants competition.
You also have some interesting processing challenges around parallelizing the right parts of your pipeline while working within spacing and arrangement constraints. Actually, that's pretty much the core of the game. It's probably one-third budget management and two-thirds arrangement puzzle game that heavily informs the budget management aspect (bad arrangements are unprofitable).
I'll be playing this one for quite awhile.
Honestly, I could also see this game as being quite workable in a multiplayer format and I think multiplayer might be pretty fun. Since the game is moddable, it might even be possible for the community to supply that functionality. Who knows?

This game is extremely refreshing to play, as it stands out from a lot of other games out there. It plays like a twitchy platforming bullet-hell shooter.
The controls are a bit weird at first, but manageable as you play more (XBox controller: Left Stick move, Right Stick fire, Right Trigger jump, Left Trigger slow-mo, Left/Right Bumpers toggle between weapons.) If you're in the air you can "dash" a few times by hitting jump.  KB/Mouse should work as well. Aiming at things far away is difficult with controller and probably easier with mouse, but the platforming and dodging is probably harder with KB/Mouse. I have no idea, but keep that in mind.
So the key to the game is activating slow-motion, and jumping/dashing to dodge projectiles. You have infinite ammo, and can purchase additional weapons using points acquired from playing the game, or unlock weapon variations by beating the game. You only have to manage your health and energy bars, but there are upgrades you can purchase to help out.
The game has 7 levels that get progressively harder. The action never stops as you're always fighting between "screens" of enemies with mini-bosses and bosses thrown in frequently. A playthrough on normal difficulty took me ~80 minutes. It is extremely easy to die, but there are checkpoints at every new section. There are no lives, so you can beat the game through repetition (think Super Meat Boy.) The more deaths you get, the less points you get, etc.
You carry two weapons at a time but can swap out while paused. There are tons of additional weapons to unlock, all with their own style of use, but basic dual pistols are kind of all you need for the majority of the game (although Shotgun helped me a LOT.) There are also additional characters with slight variations in playstyle, but they require beating the game on normal/hard/veryhard.. So if you're dedicated, you can spend a lot of time in this game.
I thought this game was awesome and well designed in all categories (except perhaps story :P)... but again, you probably won't like it if you don't enjoy any of the following: twitchy platformers, bullet-hell shooters, dying frequently, playing as a girl.

There's more to this than meets the eye.
First off, if you're somehow "disturbed" by someone running around and violently murdering basically anyone and everyone, up to and including mercilessly stabbing innocent people while they whimper for their lives, this isn't for you. If you also can't see past the deliberate edginess and enjoy an over-the-top murder spree, this isn't for you. If you're looking for something more meaningful than completely unabashed violence, this isn't for you.
This game is basically Postal if it were designed by every death/black metal band ever. It's gloriously sociopathic and sports some surprisingly fluid design for its admittedly narrow scope. The animation alone is brilliantly detailed, and the gritty film noir colour scheme is made very striking with a much more powerful engine than one would usually expect from an isometric perspective game. The lighting really helps to set a bleak mood a-la Sin City, and the soundtrack is appropriately dark as well. The fully destructible environments also bring some degree of satisfaction that can only come from being in a power fantasy that turns you into a walking apocalypse.
The gameplay is a bit more sophisticated than it may seem at first. Granted, you start out slaughtering people who are all but completely defenceless, but as time goes on, you have to plan your approaches and learn to retreat when necessary. Not Important might be a complete murder machine, but he's still one guy against many, and running and gunning without making use of your environment is a free ticket to a game over screen. You need to use cover, engage in hit-and-run, approach with caution, and make use of chokepoints if you want to make the most of your gory psychopathy. (Newcomers be warned: this is essential when you encounter a very sharp difficulty spike late in the game.) One particularly interesting mechanic is that normal civilians, who are usually helpless against you, can occasionally turn vigilante, pick up a gun, and start defending themselves.
That being said, the game isn't perfect. Some people might not be entertained by such an exaggerated character, a persistently homicidal mass shooter, but then some people just haven't found a piece of heavy equipment with a strong enough engine to pull the stick out of their backside. If anything, the sheer carnage brought on by a ludicrously overacted cross between Postal Dude and Nathan Explosion is hilarious. In more relevant issues, load times are slow. Really slow. This reviewer has played it on a high-end PC with solid state drives, and it has taken as much as a full minute just to get to the main menu even after numerous patches from the developers. Gameplay-wise, Not Important isn't exactly the best marksman, and there's some degree of RNG involved in shooting anyone further than melee range. The AI is rather simplistic and prone to some odd behaviours such relying purely on swarm tactics, blindly firing at you regardless of anyone being in the way, trying to shoot through unbroken scenery, getting hung up on scenery, endlessly running around scenery, and repeating the same voice line ten times in a row in the middle of a firefight. Fortunately this doesn't happen often enough to impede the slaughter.
Bottom line: if you want to return to the glory days of shoot em' ups and twin stick shooters where the objective is raising hell in a hail of bullets with no regard for morality, this is a fine way to spend your time. It's a delightfully violent breath of fresh air away from the modern trend of video game writers' masturbatory forays into moral quandaries and social commentary, and it's obvious that the development team had fun every step of the way. If anything, Not Important is one of the most egalitarian video game characters, because you will kill

This game was a little bit of a surprise..  I don't usually get much into tycoon type games, though I have fond memories of Theme Hospital from a few years back, and I guess Rollercoaster Tycoon, so my experience isn't great to compare this to others in the genre.   That being said, I find this game a great deal of fun.
There are two core elements to the game;  a Logistical puzzle, and, a decent strategic/business simulator.  I'll cover these separately.
The first part is what you mostly see in the pretty screenshots - you need to construct assembly lines that transform raw biological substances (insect parts, plants, etc) into finished pharmaceuticals.   There are a good number of different medicines you can manufacture and each one has vastly different requirements.  You need to purchase a variety of machines to transform the product as it moves along the belt from the 'in window' to the exit.   Some machines strengthen effects and some dilute them.  Other machines are used to combine two ingredients, to analyze a finished drug, to modify or rearrange effects, and to package the final product.  All of these machines have different 'in' and 'out' slots that will need to be matched up via conveyor belts in the correct order.   At first this can be a little daunting and frustrating, especially when you attempt to 'upgrade' a drug to a more powerful version, and some trial and error is required.   That said, it's great fun once you learn the basics, and quite rewarding when you smooth everything out.
The second part of the game is the business sim.  This is probably standard fare for these types of games, but again I'm not experienced enough to provide a good comparison.  In order to succeed you'll need to carefully manage your expenses - buildings and expansions, machines, drug ingredients, research, and exploration all require money, and while you can take out loans, this will quickly sink you if you don't have steady cashflow coming in.   There are competitors who are trying to make a profit as well, and deciding which drugs will provide the best returns can be a challenge.  You must invest time and money into research in order to unlock better machines and make your existing ones more efficient.  You also must send explorers out to discover new substances that can be transformed or combined into new types of drugs.  Random events can have impact on supply and demand as well, so it pays to keep an eye on news popups.
There is a good tutorial, which introduces you to game concepts as you play so you don't get overwhelmed.  After that, a series of 'missions' of advancing difficulties keeps the game fresh.   I can't speak to the replayability of the game as I'm nowhere near completing the core missions yet, but I believe there Is a sandbox mode once you've mastered all the basics.  The missions themselves can take from 15 minutes to a couple hours, depending on the difficulty and how focused you are.
Big Pharma's art style can be described as cartoony and colorful.  It really reminded me of a less silly version of theme hospital, but aside from the graphics (and upbeat music) there aren't may other similarities between these two games.  One nice feature is the ability to 'paint' your factory - with various primary hues and patterns.  This could be useful to customize different product lines or processes on each line, or just pretty things up to your own tastes.
I recommend this to anyone who enjoys casual business sims and puzzles.  Big Pharma succeeds well at both, and I found it well worth the price of 24.99, though I was fortunate enough to get it on sale.

Recommended for the fact that there aren't many Dungeon keeper styled games. out there.
So... where to start..
I wanted to Love this game.. I wanted a game that built upon and improved Dungeon Keeper 2.
I finished it in under 16 hours and don't see myself playing it again.
In no particular order of thought about the game.
* MEMES and references. Mostly the Narrator... if I could turn him off. I would have.  Excessive references to Game of thrones... also Insults by the narrator to HURRY UP AND FINISH THE LEVEL.
* Minions Count against your Population.. So you have to decide between a strong workforce or strong broke army.. or half and half in a way..
* Population cap = Feels like a crutch to slow/stop the player from fielding a Huge army.
* Feeding/Keeping minions happy = Once beer was setup.. ignored it for rest of the level..
* Base = Stripmine to find gold spots.. ( You can easily scan the locations of gold buy click dragging large areas that minions can't mine. just look for the slightly jagged areas and you can spot where gold is. )
* Base Defence = Setup 6 to 10 explosive chests in a 3 wide tunnel and it takes care of all attacks against your dungeon.
* Narrator. Sounds Exactly like the Stanley parable narrator.. so just felt as a joke.. and not as a dark moody game.  also before I found the Option to minimize the talk of the narrator. I Alt + F4'd the game due to the amount of insults.
* Game is a "Slow" quick game... Slow as in it takes a while to get the basics up... Quick as in once you do. you don't really have to worry about much.
* You can ONLY view minion stats while they are on the surface.. trying to select them while in the dungeon only picks them up.
* Once you get a working Hospital up... your minions are IMMORTAL.
* I finished the final level.. with 13 units.. and it was easy to cheese.
I could go on... but..
Dungeons 2 feels like a forced comedic take of the dungeon. Lacking a dungeon atmosphere.
Tips for late game.
* when you start the level with 500 gold... spend it to buy 5 minions to get your base going.
* Setup a Small Treasury about the place that you are mining gold.  Build Treasury's EVERYWHERE that your minions are mining gold. or they'll spend most of their time SLOWLY walking to store gold.. even if the treasury if just a few cells. it will save you HEAPS of time.
* Setup a 4x4 Brewery in a spot where you can easily expand it.
* Setup a 4x4 Workshop to research Traps (explosive chest trap)
* Buy a goblin and an Orc.
* Keep mining for Gold... the Minable gold spots actually give less each time, but more gold over a long time. Mine the walls that contain gold and you'll get more.
* Build the mana place and buy one naga.. work on expanding Population
Continue this
when you start the Second population expansion and get it... have about 10 minions. 2 Goblins for only making traps and research.. 4 Naga, 4 Orcs...
Take a force of the 4 naga and 4 orc. (let the orcs tank) and complete an objective and come back to heal..
Keep your minions alive early game.. go out and murder enough to clean up the areas.. come back and heal. .then go finish an objective.  You don't have to worry about being surprised by a large force... the Game Tells you every time the computer sends a force to attack your base...
HINT!!!!
If you setup a force that you only use for going out.. Select them all while they are on the Surface ( won't work in the dungeon)  Hit Ctrl + 1  (game doesn't tell you this). this will set the group. Now while your minions are in the dungeon all rested... move to the surface map.. hit 1 to select the units and right click on the grass outside... the minions selected will walk out of your base. so you don't have to worry about tracking down your fighting units.
Final Quote.
- "Micro-piglets stalk your dungeon - beware."

I'll say this is one mind bending game.
Cons first:
First the interface does need a touch up.  The GUI needs work to help navigate from cure start to cure finish along the lines of what you need to do.  At the moment you constantly have to switch between tabs in the GUI to determine the proper course of action to produce your product, fortunately you can pause the game.  It is a bit tedious to do so and I would like to see something more streamlined that allows for easier production of your cure.
Second, No multiplayer.  You do play against an AI.  The AI's production of similar products  will effect cure pricing and both you and the AI can issue patents to have sole ownership of a cure.  There are world events that dictate supply and demand so it would be great to have multiplayer for the same reasons.  Unfortunately in a multiplayer scenario there would have to be two requirements:  A: Make it turn based to get around the GUI issue, or B: streamline the GUI for faster recognition of steps.
That's it for cons that I see.

I played dungeon keeper 1 & 2 when those were fresh, and picked up War for the Overworld as soon as it came out.  However, somehow this game slipped my radar.
I was reticent to write a review until I had a few hours into it, but I turned it on today and for five hours could not stop.  It's got every feature you would've enjoyed from a Dungeon Keeper game but manages to infuse an ADDITIONAL RTS element to it via the change in how your minions work on the overworld.  Not only are there optimizations for room size, but the rooms, themselves, are upgradeable via research.  Each minion you have can not only be trained individually to a higher level, but can be completely upgraded to another unique creature via a -different- kind of training:  Nagas become queens, which channel heals that are not only automatic within the dungeon but can be manually controlled in addition during the overworld RTS mode.  Goblins become assassins with the ability to stealth and backstab.  You can even continue to upgrade them, RTS style, with a forge that grants individual evolutions such as the ability to have trolls regenerate or improves the critical strike chance of your goblins.  And there are areas in the campaign where specialized units are absolutely fantastic- Goblin assassins completely disable traps in an area, so that the bulk of your cadre can bypass a trap that would otherwise leave most of them on the ground.
The community via multiplayer isn't robust, but the game was released in 2015.  The fact that it was free last week may shuffle that a bit.  But if you enjoy campaign and skirmish missions with a mashup of dungeon keeper and starcraft-style RTS gameplay, and a narrator who memes about World of Warcraft, Lord of the Rings, Buffy the Vampire Slayer, and Supernatural, this is the game for you.  In my experience, it ticks all the boxes, and has made me laugh at least once a hour for the five hours that I played it.

Excellent soundtrack makes whiling away the hours in space great fun.

I'll be honest. I liked the look of this, but the implementation left me a little cold.  I don't think it's a *bad* game, but it's not really my thing, even though it looked like it could be quite a bit of fun pre-purchase.
The driving controls are a little bit horrible. The game is quite slow, devolving essentially to avoiding potholes and crashing to keep your windscreen clear and your vehicle in good repair... and picking things up from the side of the road to help you keep going. You'll stop and rest at motels every now and again, and show your papers at checkpoints.
Graphically it's quite stylish. It's got a definite eastern European flavour (obviously, as that's what the developers were aiming for) and the audio does the job, but I found I wasn't having a lot of fun with it. Having to actually navigate, rather than just follow an unexciting road might have helped mitigate this, but unfortunately navigation is simply choosing a location on your map, and following the bendy road until you get there. No chance of getting lost.
I'm going to not recommend this one. If Steam let me choose "Meh" instead of "Yes" or "No", I'd choose that. It's entirely possible that, if you like this sort of game, you'll enjoy it - a lot of folk do seem to describe it as charming. I'm afraid I found it to be a constant battle with the clumsy interface and a god-awful driving experience. At least wait until it's on special.

Hitman: Absolution is the first in the series that I flat out gave up on trying to play it the proper way and started playing like a cover shooter. The good levels are few and far between, lost in a mess of "cinematic" events and linear boredom. This is a crying shame because the mechanics of the whole thing are a treat and when they work, they do work wonderfully.
The problem with this one is story. It gets in the way. You'll score perfect headshots on targets and then immediately get launched into stupid cutscenes where they'll deliver huge soliloquys before spitting their last breath. All of the characters are obnoxious cartoon idiots, ala the GTA series.
"YEEHAW, I'LL DO A LITTLE DANCE NOW BECAUSE MY MOTION CAPTURE ACTOR WAS TOLD 'GO BIG'! YEEEHAAAW!"
The worst of that is, we're never really given any reason to take this fools gallery as a serious threat. They're just a bunch of pathetic, bumbling clowns in the face of Agent 47's stone-faced murder master. There's also a little girl, who's got no personality whatsoever, but you're supposed to care about her because... Well, who cares. There's a guy with a weird robot hand, possibly because they couldn't think of any other way to make him even remotely memorable.
I think the moment I snapped, the moment my brain decided "Hey, you know what, crack out the guns, let's end this as fast as possible"? The latex bondage nuns. A level that, if you removed it from the game, would have no impact whatsoever on the story. It's just there because... Latex bondage nuns, I guess. Ooh, edgy.
If you skip from Blood Money to Hitman 2016, you will miss out on nothing. This is Hitman as designed by and for those with head injuries.

- Initially have to reference a fair amount of material hoping back and forth between tabs, making it more like work than a game.
- Once you memorize the tech tree and how the different components work, it becomes a logic/routing/adding/subtracting exercise. It isn't what I think of when I think sim/strategy/management. I feel like it is a tad mislabeled.
- The tutorial is rather important, but is a text walkthrough at the moment.....
Pros:
- If you like time sensitive puzzles, this is a great game.
- If you are looking for logic/spacial reasoning work within the framework of a nice looking interface and overall "game-like" goals, this is a great choice.
- The graphics are nice.
- The interface is usable and I have not run into any issues with it yet.
I might want a good puzzle every now and then. However, enjoy playing it for hours on end I highly doubt.
Recommend? Yes, as a puzzle game. As sim/strategy/management? Sorry, but no.

Hooooo boy! And on the same day that I have to put down one of my favorite games they re-release one of my all time favs back onto the store shelves.
Let me ask you, do you like beat-em-ups? fighting games? RPGs? I don't, save RPGs. Let me say though that DFO is a mash-up of these geners done right, giving you a few basic skills to start you off rather then overloading you with the dozens of combos you will learn, they drip feed you over the course of the leveling process. Even a fighting game scrub like myself was, during the early days of DFO's stay on Nexon, fighting like a pro as they allowed me to take the time I needed to learn, memorize, and master the various skills of my characters.
This is what made DFO one of the single most highest grossing MMOs of it's time, with an extreamly loyal playerbase and addicting to the point of even keeping a man blighted with a short attention span stick around for it's entier run, much more on then off.
The biggest con is probably that you don't really get to the meat of your character's playstyle till level 25 to 30-ish. People have a habbit of dropping out before then in favor of another class or leaving altogether. Some complain about the daily energy limit. I have to at one point though now I appreciate the forced paceing. I do feel the heat system worked best, however. The story is fairly typical and to me feels rather obligitory to give the dungeons some justification. the attempts at humor never really got me to laugh, and I do miss the classic dungeons like lorain, sky tower and the bohemeth. Regardless I do still really enjoy this game. It is the best kind of power fantasy mixing badassery with the feeling of working towards that power and continuing to grow. Even after you've attained all of your skills at level 85 and compleated your build, your still not at the end. you still are constantly learning and growing in your usage of your arsenal, the one you have been masterfully trained to use throughout the course of the game.
This game is really something special. It really, really is and it's worth experiancing before the inevitable end.

I was intrigued by the concept of Puzzle Quest and I am a superhero fan. So this game has to be fantastic, right? And it is. The Bejeweled mechanic combined with special abilities works just fine. And the level system for new skills for your heroes motivates. Thumb up! (5 out of 5 Superheroes so far.)
So why no recommendation and only 1 out of 5 points?
1. The game is designed to be slow. Your heroes get hurt in battle and heal over time.
2. Resources are scarce. Whatever you do, you have to choose on what to invest your resources.
3. You get overwhelmed with opportunities. You don't have enough resources to follow each and every path at the same time.
All those problems sound like good game mechanics for strategists. But they are just designed to motivate the player to pay money. I don't have a problem with a free2play game to offer options for payment. But Marvel Puzzle Quest: Dark Reign is pay2win. I tried it quite a while to see some higher hero levels and some more content. But in the end only one thing is certain: without payment you loose.
You loose heroes, because you don't have enough character slots.
You loose events, because your heroes don't heal fast enough, to win enough battles.
And in the end, you loose either money or motivation.
The game creates a highly motivating circle of simple/casual gameplay, challange, success and reward. It creates an addiction for more success. With new rewards you feel confident to beat new challanges. And the more you succeed the more you get. It's addictive.
But the rewards are never enough. And you start to become frustrated.
To be clear one more time: this game is designed to be pay2win. And if you don't pay, it hurts you. It is more than other free2play games for which you need more time to get better. This game makes gifts to you but if you are not good (=rich) enough, it takes them back. It destroys you, until you pay or leave.
It beats you. But not on the common battlefield New York, but in your head.

Amazing game.
If you are looking for a fun and flexible space game, look no further. You coul be a pirate, a miner, a trader, or a mercenary with plenty of wiggle room in between.
Not only is it flexible, but it also has a great ship upgrading system which really does give the player a sense of accomplishment. Buying your first new ship is amazing, and then going on to eventually own a ship which makes you laugh at that purchase is a great feeling as well. The ship flexibility is there as well, with trading focused ships vs. fighting forcused ships, and more.
As for the trading in this game, the dynamic pricing system really works well. Buy low, sell high is a strong principle in this game, and you feel great when pulling into a station that is under attack with a hull full of pure water which is trading at double the price of any other station.
The actual combat works well in the game too. Some may get turned off by the 2D nature of it for the player, but that 2D nature allows for some cool mechanics such as broadside and mines.
On top of all of this, the sound track is amazing and adds a really cool western vibe with the dark country theme.
Overall, it's a great game and I highly recommend it.

This game is totally bonkers. Kooky, wacky, and super fun. I went into this one not knowing anything about the Bioshock universe and what a great surprise this turned out to be. Bioshock 2 is unlike anything I was expecting. I dig it.
A Howard Huges type industrialist decides it would be a great idea to build New York City deep in the ocean, post World War II. The seafloor city he creates is called Rapture. Over the years everyone who moves in ends up going nuts. The citizens find out a sea slug can be turned into underwater super-meth so they end up addicted as 1950s era zombie drug fiends wearing tuxedos and cocktail dresses. And they join a cult. It's kinda rad. Nobody is keeping up with any building repairs so the whole city is falling apart- and flooding. Rapture's underwater city scape is a nice mix of run down collapsing atomic age buildings and colorful exterior seafloor areas. It's got a nice atmosphere complete with a big band soundtrack and lots of corny fifties kitch that works really well in-game. It reminded me somewhat of Fallout 3 with regard to the black humor and goofy vintage advertisements all over the place. On a side note I'd recommend playing both Bioshock 2 and Fallout 3 back to back. They compliment each other well.
In Bioshock 2 you are a weirdo deep sea construction worker with bad breath roaming around in a metal diving suit called 'Big Daddy'. You've got a decade old headache... the underwater bad guys punked you and ripped off your kid. So it's understandable why you are a hater and extra pi$$ed off. You also happen to have some serious telekinetic powers plus a gnarley drill you can gut people with. That's just for starters. Later on you'll pick up a rivet gun, an antique shotgun, a spear gun, and some other odd weapon doo-dads that will put the hurt on hipster brainwashed junkies. Your job is to wreck these jerks and reunite with your little sister. Easy beans, right?
The game has a setup whereby you can choose what weapons you want to upgrade incrementally, but there are a limited amount of upgrades available on each level. So choose wisely. Another interesting dynamic is you can literally make the game more difficult on the fly by triggering more boss fights. Attack other Big Daddies as you encounter them to adopt their kid (little sister), or not. If you do whack 'em and snag their little sister you have another choice available to either rescue them or pimp 'em out and harvest the loot. Rescue them enough times and you trigger yet another boss fight. That's pretty cool because you can make the game more painful with more boss fights and get rewarded accordingly or make it easier and not have to brawl as much. It's entirely up to you how you want to play it. The benefit to taking the long hard road and making it tough is you get loot to upgrade your telekinetic powers. One of my favorites turned out to be Hypnotize. Roll into a room with a handful of junkies wandering around loose and Hypnotize them to start an entertaining prison brawl. You can kick back and snag the loot when it's all over.

It also caters to the more hard core group with its end game and pvp mostly because of the large variety of classes/subclasses and the mechanical skill ceilling.
With DFO Global being run by Neople, the game is a lot less pay to win compared to before. Since its reboot changing the game completely from the lore, dungeons, the characters, the game's economy, and game play balance, the game is a brand new game from almost a decade before.  Grinding has been eliminated by a large margin in terms of leveling in the game compared to before. Good gears are easily achieved, and dungeons difficulty level curve has been readjusted. From my wallet's and mental health's point of view, I love it.
But from the other categories point of view, I dislike some of these changes that were made into the game. In pre-reboot, ALL of the dungeons truely felt unique in its own way and the storyline/region ties them all together to make you care about the lore and story of the game. Dungeon monsters were challenging and requires some thinking and mechanical skill for you to defeat. NPC's were interesting and also unique. But now? Dungeons all nothing more than a push over. Leveling just feels like a chore more than an experience and it's feels like it's only there for you to familiarize yourself with your subclass. Quests are generic and cliche and most will find themselves just skipping dialogues to maximize leveling efficiency. What happened to old Arad and the old NPC's that we've grown to love? Oh they're still there. Just hidden and grouped up in low level areas and areas you would never revisit again. Now, the new NPC's just feels like a generic anime character that's just there to hand out quests so that you can get on with your day. Their stories doesn't matter any more and why should you? You'll be out of this area and be finished with the questline in 20 minutes anyway. What ultimately matter is the grind for end game. To me, the changes in DFO feels like the changes to WoW. Call me nostalgic, but I'd rather be playing the old DFO even with its massive paywall.
Is the paywall gone though? No, it has never left. Like I mentioned above, I've been playing this game in and out for 8 years mostly because when I finally come back to re-experience the greatness of the game, I was turned off by its massive grind for end game once I've reached max level. Nobody enjoys doing the same dungeon
just for that slim chance of aquiring the weapon of your desire. But getting your Epic level gear is just the first part.
is what drives people to poverty. Although it's more towards the most extreme ends of the game, there really isn't much else to do besides pvp or leveling other characters if this is what you're not doing.
DFO has caused me to set a very high bar for other games because of its amazing amount of variety and of its satisfying game play. However, changes to this game has made the game's story line, charaters, and overall immersion crap. Levels are handed out freely. And the end game grind and pay to win nature can turn people off quite a bit. But that's just my opinion of the game. DFO is still very popular across the globe and there's no shortage of end game players that still enjoy the game to prove it. I still give this game a positive rating and people should try it out themselves since it is free to play, should not just base their decisions solely on a random user who reviewed this awesome game. So yes, give this game a try and it might not seem as bad as I decribe it to be for you.

Bioshock 2 may not have the same feeling you get when you enter Rapture the first time in the original, but having the brute power of being a Big Daddy and protectiing Little Sisters makes up for that. You take a whole new look at Rapture, getting to know how it feels to be an inhabitant, who has lived and died in this underwater tomb. Not to mention that they even found a way to improve gameplay by allowing the ability to use plasmids at the same time as your weapons. This increases tactics and strategies, as well as making reloading times less painful. The "one-two punch" explained by Atlas in the original game is much more affective here with Delta. You also get a deeper sense of the lore with 2 by delving into the connection between Big Daddies and their Little Sisters, as well as meeting the mind behind Plasmids and seeing the only mentioned Fontaine Futuristics. One of my all time favorite moments in the whole series happens in the same game as well, seeing the point of view of a Little Sister. Seeing the world of Rapture through their eyes is not only an interesting one, but partially disturbing showing how we candy coat our own reality for children. Plus, playing this again after Infinite has shown me an interesting comparison between this Bioshock theme of fatherhood. Elizabeth to Songbird or Comstock. Anna to Booker. The Big Daddies to Little Sisters. And here with Delta and Eleonor. Overall, Bioshock 2 lives up to the name and has plenty of potential for replay value.
Minerva's Den:
After the adventures of Delta and Eleonor come to a close, we get one final story from Rapture that feels like a great ending to the underwater city. The gameplay doesn't change much from the main game, but you do get a new plasmid and weapon. The plasmid, Gravity Well, is not very impressive and I found myself sticking to the ones I was more familiar with. While, on the other hand, the new Laser Cannon was a fantastic weapon that I thought kept up with being such a powerful being. I used it almost solely, when I could find or buy ammo. The length of Minerva's Den is pretty good at about 5-6 hours for a DLC. Plus, the story itself did a nice job of throwing of few last twists at you before we pulled the curtain on Rapture.

Dungeons 2 is a game developed by Realmforge Studios and published by Kalypso Media Digital and is the official sequel to DUNGEONS
First off, Dungeons 2 is definitely not Dungeon Keeper. With that out off the way, this game is good in it's own right
The first couple levels are basically tutorials and are slow, but if you get past the first couple it does become more challenging. When I first bought this game I had the idea that it would play similar to the Dungeon Keeper games
Your objective is to give the heroes that enter your dungeon everything they want filling their soul meters, then destroy them before they get a chance to leave your dungeon. Using their souls to buy "gimmicks" that you use to fill your dungeon leading the heroes throughout it, and making you more powerful
There is a balance you need to strike to get the heroes happy without having your creatures accidently slay them to soon, and losing soul energy in the process, as yourself the "Dungeon Lord" gets more soul energy from killing the heroes personally
I find trying to build my dungeon in such a way to completly fill the heroes soul bars and leading them to my dungeon heart, where I await them, to be challenging but rewarding
Dungeons 2 is again a mixed bag but I thoroughly enjoyed playing it. Just give it a chance it may surprise you, like it did for me, but don't expect the next Dungeon Keeper

I went into this game knowing very well, that "free to play" usually means "pay to win". Still this game made me angry!
Why?
First off: The base game is great! It's the standard puzzle quest game play. Basically a two player Bejewelled, where each player has life points and each match-3 (or more) is an attack which  reduces the opponents life points.
In this game you play a team of 3 classic Marvel heroes and villains, from the starter Iron Man to Spider Man to Doctor Doom. Each has up to three special abilities, which are quite varied. The abilities are fueled with the tiles you matched up.
So far, pretty classic puzzle quest. And overall that's done pretty well and is fun to play.
What's no fun is everything around it:
You get heroes and abilities by gathering "covers". You sometimes get them during the single player campaign or during the so called "player vs player" events. It's pseudo PvP really, since the oponent is controlled by the AI, there is no way to customize your team and there is no in-game way of communication except via Steam itself. And even then, there is no way to challenge a specific player.
Since it's "free to play" you can also get covers by spending one of the two in-game currencies, which can be bought in the shop or found by playing: Iso-8 crystals and hero points. The former can be used to level up your heroes or buy the cheapest ones. The latter one can be used to buy the better ones or buy an additional slot for a hero. The heroes are distributed into four categories, 1-star to 4-star, and usually you can get multiple versions of the same character in the different categories. The better the category, the more powerful they can become.
To learn a new ability or to make one more powerful, you need to find the cover of the exact hero with that exact ability on it. And did I mention, that you can't choose specific heroes in the shop? Instead you buy them as a kind of booster pack of one. Or you buy them as a booster of 10 and are guaranteed one specific hero. However those are usually even more expensive than the single boosters.
And that's basically the problem of the whole game: You have no control what you get, and that little you get is very, very expensive. And don't get me started if you actually plan to spend money on this game: You can actually get the 2 weakest character covers for 50 hero points each. The "cheapest" amount to buy is 200 hero points for 1,49€, so about 0,40€ per cover. You need about 10 to fully power one of them up. This is 4,00€ for a full power character. And that's the weakest ones! It only get's more expensive from here! Sure, you can get a whole lot of hero points for about 70€. But I would never spend so much money on a match-3 game. Especially since you can get the original Puzzle Quests for at most 20€ here on Steam. And even if you spens so much, it only gives a discount of about 50%!
What makes me angry, is that the developers are greedy ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s and very obvious about it. Play, if you don't want to spend money, but if you do want to spend: spend it for the originals!

Are you that type of gamer that consistently replaces in-game music with your own? Have you lost all hope in the musical taste of game developers? Well, don't put all your money on black yet, 'cuz here's a game with some brilliant music.
And lasers. And missiles. And energy bolts. And, what else, boatloads of space credits ripe for the taking.
Rebel Galaxy is a space game that features broadside combats, evoking the Age of Sails feeling of yester-decade that, for me at least, is an essential component of meaty and impactful space combat. This is further reinforced by the curious choice of limiting all capital ships' (i.e. you and most enemies you face) movements to a 2D plane, an oddity amongst space games for sure, so make sure to watch gameplay footage to determine whether or not it's your cup of tea beforehand.
The selection of weapons, both broadside and turreted, is competent. There's always something specialised in the range of combat that you prefer, and across-the-broad they do feel enough of a sidegrade to not warrant single-minded choices. The same cannot be said for the ship selection, unfortunately, as end-game ship choices are fairly limited to begin with, and there is only one logical choice (the one with the most firepower). Even mid-game choices aren't that numerous, sidegrades, in particular, are too limited to facilitate different playstyles. Not helping is that some of the most interesting ships and weapons are locked behind faction relations or are limited to loot tables, which is a bit too many requirements for my taste, although it does give you a reason to hunt the occasional pirate lords, rare and powerful enemies guaranteed to drop unique weapons.
Of course, it isn't all sunshine for Rebel Galaxy, as there are some more bad points I'd like to address. For one, this game is leaning towards the casual side of the space genre. Combat is a bit too gear-dependant for my taste, meaning grinding better gear contributes too much of a portion to the player's success in combat, in particular when compared to the player's aim (broadside aiming is essentially automatic, and turrets are best left on auto). Enemy AI is functional but basic, and it's easy to employ kiting tactics to cheese victories. The galaxy is sector-based, and each sector is a bit too small and similar for my taste. The story campaign leans towards the short side and does not feature many meaningful choices, which is a shame considering the relatively excellent VA talents. Trading is a side activity at best, with a simple economy and not a particularly robust selection of goods to trade with. Overall, while I enjoyed my first playthrough, there is little reason for a second one.
All in all, I found myself enjoying the combat segments of the game, especially some of the larger set pieces where you, backed by your allies, take on hordes of hostiles, and I can comfortably recommend the game despite its flaws thanks to its modest price tag.

Normally a big fan of the series, but this one feels lifeless.  Perhaps it's because I have over 2000 hours in Civ5, but I don't think so.
There are some good innovations in this; it's certainly not all bad.  Makes one sorry for the binary voting system.  One of these innovations is the usage of the miasma: tiles that you can pass through, but don't want to end your turn on, lest the unit take damage.  Another development to traditional Civ systems that I like is the multi-directional research tree.  I suppose in the base Civ game, such a tree isn't possible because there must be linear progression through the eras.  So there are great aspects to the game.
I think one of the main problems is that the further you get away from reality in these games, the less potential there is for the game to be immersive.  Strangely, even a fantasy 4E game would feel more tangible than this setting.

What an absolutely fantastic game. Probably my favorite of 2015.
The art style is just fantastic and immersive. The 2D point and click is both fluid and easy to pickup, yet complex enough to be engaging and allow you to get better as you begin to grasp the physics, line of sight, sounds etc
This game forces you into difficult choices that really draw you in. Your characters will respond to both the good and the bad. I attempted to sneak into an apartment building , was shot at, managed to kill my assailant just to have his father(?) attack me for killing his son (self defense? or is it) i had no choice but to kill him as well, at which point his wife came out crying for him not to leave her alone and sobbing on her knees next to his dead body. I ran away, and upon returning my character was "broken" and could no longer go on because of what he had to do. That's how intense this game is.
Resource management feels very well thoughtout. You are no superhero. You won't get the crazy base and be invincible. Do you want a stove? Or do you want a bed? You can try to craft a gun, but what if someone gets sick or injured and you dont have the bandages or meds as a result? Scavenging at night can be nerve wracking, and one bad night could mean the doom of your companions.
It has its flaws, combat damage seems random, and once you figure out the backstab routine becomes almost trivial. When you begin to understand the game mechanics and trading system, the game becomes much less difficult - but that feels alright.
All in all a fantastic effort and exactly what i've come to expect and love from well thought out indie games - risk taking originality. Do yourself a favor and pick it up.
