If you do plan on buying this game regardless, for a better experience try pressing escape on your keyboard instead of exit on the in-game menu. Most of my crashes were caused by pressing that. Now, onto the review.
tl;dr: This is a really neat experience, but the stability issues, a few bugs, and the god-awful combat system just brings the entire game down so much that it just wasn't enjoyable for me.
What it does right: I really love what they're going for here. A look into the life of what happens around war instead of just playing the soldiers fighting in it is something I've never seen a game do before. You get to experience having to make extremely hard choices just to maybe have enough supplies to live through the next through days. This game really makes you think hard about what you're willing to do to scrape by. Resources are extremely scarce; I found myself thinking I had enough of one thing just to run out of it the next day. Overall it does a great job of immersing you in the situation and putting you up to difficult decisions, like stealing from or just outright murdering innocents just to be able to survive, or going up against heavily armed thugs or soldiers to maybe see if they've got something you desperately need.
It also keeps things simple, so you don't have to spend ages learning the mechanics of the game, but also isn't so simple that there's no level of complexity you have to adapt to just to be able get what you need through higher level crafting and trading. It's accessible enough to not push you away in the beginning, but has enough depth to make sure you're still struggling to  the end, and in this case it works really well.
What it does wrong: Despite the really enjoyable core mechanics, some things really break this game for me. For starters, the stability is awful. It took me a couple of hours just to get this game into a semi-playable state, as I had to look up multiple fixes that didn't even work, and play through multiple crashes and freezes until I could identify the main problem and try to work around it. Even  then the game would freeze up on the scavenging screen ocassionally, and it still had the chance of crashing on menus that I couldn't exit out of like I mentioned above.
The crashing wouldn't be as much of a problem if you could save more often, but the game only saves after a full day and night of scavenging, meaning that if you crash at any point during, you have to play that ENTIRE day over again. Needless to say, it can get pretty frustrating if you've done a lot to your house or got pretty far in scavenging that day.
Speaking of infuriating bugs, on the very last night I had a bandit phase through two floors and immediately spot me. I don't mean he just ran up to me... no, he literally passed through the floors in a straight line to see me. This really just soured the entire experience at the very end and completely broke any solid immersion I had. This is an eight month old game that is a full retail release. I could forgive it if it was early access, but things like this and the constant crashing are really unacceptable.
This goes onto my next point of the awful combat. If you can, just avoid it completely. It seems entirely random if you or your opponent dies or not, especially if it involves guns. I've had characters just stand straight up from cover before and stop shooting just to get shot to death. The simplistic system that worked so well for everything else makes the combat absolutely awful in just about every circumstance. The only saving grace is leading them into an instant backstab from a hiding place, but like I said in my last paragraph, even this could lead to a frustrating experience.
After everything is said and done and I've completed the game, I could probably forgive the combat and give this game a positive review, but the sorry state of the game's stability and bugs make it an unenjoyable experience. If you have the patience of a saint and want a really good and different experience, you should definitely buy this game. Otherwise you'd probably be better off waiting until the devs can actually fix everything before you spend your money on this.

Shoot-Em Up Fun
The concept is simple really, take one part Devil May Cry, another part Super Meat Boy and a dose of bullet hell shu'mps (and a splash of Gradius for good measure) and you have yourself 'Bleed'. A shoot-em up platformer that sees the lead character attempting to make a name for herself by 'Bumping off' the great heroes of the land.
In order to take down each 'hero', you have to go through each level, each one providing many challenges. This is no easy game, gameovers can appear thick and fast and both the levels and bosses take great delight in throwing as much at you as possible. Thankfully the game avoids some pitfalls by making the controls sleek, giving off a great amount of control, especially when it comes to the games 'Double Jump' mechanic which works more like an air-dash. It can take some time getting used to but once you get the hang of it, it flows quick and fast.
That said, theres not only finishing the game to consider, theres also the score to keep up. Just like in Devil May Cry, every hit you make raises a bonus bar, hitting the top of the bar bumps you up a score level going from 'D' rank and up to S. Getting hit or letting the bar time out resets the multiplier, meaning that if you want to score big, you have to get as much hits in as possible, all while avoiding damage (easier said than done).
In conclusion: An incredibly sleek, stylish and tough as nails platformer at a cheap price point and one thats well worth grabbing and playing through (even though you may occasionally burst into rounds of swearing thanks to the difficulty)

It's a good game, but I can't give it a positive review.  The concepts are awesome and they're off to a good start, but the gameplay just doesn't deliver enough enjoyment.  The game's systems are very complex, and the main problem the game suffers from is the interface.  The information you need to find out in order to make effective choices is arranged in a very arcane and dispersed fashion.  This leaves you with two choices: 1) Play the entire game alternating between Play and Pause, and spend most of the game looking for information while Paused, or 2) Discover all the information you need AND engage in critical thinking while Playing, at which point, the situation will have changed so much that you need new information and a refinement of your original plan.
What this means is, the gameplay just doesn't deliver enough of a hands-on feel so that you feel real control over the game's systems, and over your chosen outcomes.  But it's one of those games that gives you enough tiny little dopamine-buzzers (Dings, music, sounds, green profit text, etc.) to fool you into thinking you're having a good time and keep you hooked.
But after you play for 4 hours, you're just left with kind of a "blah" feeling.
If they made the interface more concrete and less arcane, the game would have a better feel, ie. Player Input -> Logical Outcome.  Then I'd give it a better review.

The gameplay is a perfectly servicable Dungeon Keeper 2 riff with RTS elements spot welded on. I appreciated the experiment of that sort of pitch, if nothing else. The only major gameplay complaint I encountered was that the pacing of mechanics and play was somewhat plodding.
However, the main campaign's ""jokes"" are so atrocious I could not bring myself to complete it. They stunt casted the narrator from the Stanley Parable and gave him a script that half-asses its narration gimmicks at the same time that it quarter-asses Dungeon Keeper's dry, sardonic take on being the bad guy. It is *relentless* in its attempts to make sure you get a joke, even - especially - when it isn't funny. The early levels are a torrent of awkwardly written "meta jokes" every time you do basically anything, making no less than three jokes about event flags and level scripts in the first two levels. It constantly, unpromptedly brings up how lazy its own writing and scenarios are but expects that saying that it's doing the thing makes it funny.
It makes a joke where the narrator says "Insert funny line here" then goes on an annoyed aside about the unprofessionality of the writers. I was so deeply tempted to just uninstall the game right there, but I kept going until I hit a mission written in 2015 that was nothing but an extended series of the laziest Occupy Wall Street jokes imaginable - the title was even just named "Occupy Wall Street". Stadium beer has more punch than the writing in this game, and it's less likely to give you a headache.
If you look up a few videos of early stuff and aren't bothered by the narration, then give the game a shot if it goes on deep sale. It ain't that bad, aside from the slow, slow pacing. But if it grates on you even a little bit, stay the hell away, because it only gets worse.

This review is only about the single player component, whose main campaign I have just finished.
This game was a joy to play. I got it from a previous Humble Bundle if I remember correctly, but I hadn't gotten around to it until I heard many people praising it after the recent giveaway took place.
It takes a humorous approach at creating a universe bashed together from many popular series, and it prides itself on what it is: a modern, chilled-out Dungeon Keeper clone using updated Warcraft 3-like graphics. You're as evil as evil can be, and anyone out there who disagrees (or dares to oppose you) must be crushed to a pulp. In the underworld, you order your minions around generally, deciding what needs to be mined and what should be built, and slapping, er, motivating your minions. In the overworld, you control your units RTS-style to take out enemy spawning points that periodically attack you as well as other mission-specific objectives. There's a few tower defense elements thrown in as well, but I never found a situation where they truly mattered.
It has a fairly low difficulty curve, but I honestly didn't mind it. I played along, sometimes outright wasting time, just to get all I could out of the beloved narrator from The Stanley Parable. He's half the game, in a good way.
My disappointments with the game revolve around two things:
- lack of micro; while there are a few unit specials, it's pretty much about blobbing your enemy to dust.
- weak animations; many of the units feel like they could've had much more polished animations. It broke my immersion as, admiring the graphic style, I was fantasizing about the likely never-to-be sequel to Warcraft 3.
All in all, I'd give it a 7. A good little game worth trying and relaxing with, likely one you'll remember along with the likes of Overlord and such, but not really ground-breaking.

I started playing during open beta after listening to my friends say how amazing it was for the better part of a year. They said it was the best MMORPG out there, that nothing could replace it or match it, it was the god of all f2p MMORPGs.
They were right.
I've played around a few MMORPGs but nothing was as amazingly fun to play as DFO. Granted it's a little hard to get into (I took a break a few weeks after starting), but that's because it's just so far in a playstyle and content realm of its own.
DFO actually lives up to the name of f2p. (It might be worth to note that I've played purely pve, which is extremely solid in DFO. I'll talk a bit about that later.)
There's no limit to how many of your skills you can use (no arbitrary "pick 4 of your skills to use"), you don't turn ugly after a few days because your outfit expired or someth, job advancements don't take more than half an hour to an hour to do, and Neople has interesting and unique events that pretty much make you a premium member just for playing normally. The miles point system and any "play one dungeon to get this item you normally have to cash for" events such as attendance and buddy events come to mind. I've never once felt the need to cash in order to play the game at a semi-functional level or have fun. I could spend money on this game and not feel as though I've been cheated.
As I said before, the pve experience in DFO is solid. Dungeons are interesting and you aren't forced to run the same-looking map 3 times just to get to the next dungeon, because the map changes for each story quest. Bosses are unique and entertaining to fight (that is, if they last longer than your strongest attack, which they tend not to until way later). Soloing dungeons is possible on any difficulty and I never felt the need to join a party except for the rare occasion I ran out of story quests (story quest exp is given to everyone in the party, regardless of if you had the quest). To be honest, it was easier to just solo dungeons because joining a party is usually overkill.
To go through normal dungeons and just reach cap, there's no grinding for gear involved since story quests pretty much hand you everything you need. Or events do. Endgame gear (which is so creative and diverse, it's amazing how cool effects on epic gear are) is very rng- and grind-based, but I only became interested in grinding for that gear because I saw how cool it made my friend's attacks.
As for extra content, there's so much stuff to do outside of main dungeons. Most of it I haven't bothered to touch because I felt no reason to (Mirror Arad, towers outside of ToD, Anton), but it's there if I were to ever get bored and want to explore. A few of the endgame (and recently, Dark Elf) dungeons are gimmicky, but part of the fun is learning the gimmicks. And honestly, I thought they were creative and a lot better than having every boss be killable in the same exact way.
All in all, DFO is a 10/10 great experience and hopefully the steam release gets more players into the game. Although I don't see why getting the steam version is any better than getting it directly from the website.

Even though you can tame creatures, they do not have a use beyond defending, following, attacking, or riding them. This game is NOT like Ark or Dark and light at all in this aspect. You basically tame stuff to have it for the time being.
Most spells are over powered in very overlooked obviously going to get nerfed ways. Beam spells never run out of mana since mana recharges faster than the spell uses. Enemies can be stun locked with beam spells. Telekinsis makes it impossible to put your stuff in a safe place on PVP since anyone can literally rip your house off the ground and shake out the goodies. etc.
The games progress is too fast and too easy at the moment. It took me a hour to go from level 1 to 20 when the cap is something like 60. This was mostly because I could stunlock a monster 20 levels higher than me and kill it by simply holding down left mouse button and walking side to side. You also gain tons of resources in a short period of time which isn't a bad thing but it shortens playtime quite a bit.
This game is very early access and the developers seem to be the kind that put all their ideas in the game whether they are finished or not and worry about the bugs later. There are crafting tables in game for game mechanics that aren't in the game yet, and areas of the map that are just weird and unfinished.
You gain way to many points per level than you actually need for the stuff that is in the game so far. I quit playing when I got to level 20. I was very careful on what I spent points on and it turns out I didn't really need to be. They give you something like 30 points a level when things unlocking every 5 levels that cost anywhere from 1 to 7 points. I had in the high hundreds of points left and very little to spend them on that I actually wanted or was going to use.
Conclusion
Citadel: Forged with fire is a good game. what the devs are doing with it is really fun in a original way, but it's also a very very very unfinished game, and by far not recommended that you pay full price for it in its current state. I recommend adding it to your wish list and waiting a few months for the game to develop more, or for it to go on sale before buying it.

The best parts of the 1984 movie Red Dawn are when a band of small-town Colorado teenagers launch a series of guerilla attacks against occupying Soviet forces. The scrappiness of their insurgency is exhilarating to watch—it's chilling to see high school students hardened in battle against overwhelming odds. Homefront, with a story written by Red Dawn's director John Milius, makes every effort to recreate that feeling by putting us up against another hypothetical conqueror of America: a unified Korea. It nails the atmosphere, but plays it too safe—Homefront is too busy trying to be Call of Duty to make you feel like a wide-eyed Lea Thompson mowing down Soviet soldiers with a heavy machine gun.Shock and awe
That's not to say Homefront doesn't tell a good story. Leading into the five-hour appetizer campaign, the cutscene explanation of how the US was invaded is surprisingly believable, and its depiction of America after years of war and occupation is incredibly detailed. This is a tour of occupied America—you'll see everything from a hidden refugee community to a locked-down metropolis with $20-per-gallon gas signs, starving suburbs with bodies hanging from water towers and horrific labor camps set in repurposed high schools. Moments into the game, it's clear that Homefront's seven missions are an excuse to show off its well-realized fiction. That's what Homefront does right: it made me feel like what I saw was only a fraction of a fully imagined world.
Combat, though, doesn't match the intensity of the story. The action is a mix of sniping, assault, and defense, but it boils down to ho-hum whack-a-mole gameplay that never made me feel like an outgunned, underdog guerrilla. Ammo is plentiful and AI compatriots are invincible. The remote-controlled Goliath tank is fun to use, but only in that it's overpowered and quick to deliver explosions.Warbucks
Homefront's enduring appeal is in its class-based multiplayer modes. It follows the trend of class-based team warfare and unlockable weaponry, but its remote-controlled drones and an in-match reward system, called Battle Points (which you spend to buy equipment and drones), give it a unique feel. The blend of fast showdowns and large, multi-tiered objective-based maps are appropriately chaotic, especially on a full 32-person server. The hefty feel and sound of the rifles makes headshots all the more satisfying, and the ability to pilot remote-controlled aerial rocket drones adds suspense, forcing me to look not just left and right before running between cover, but also up. I also like the way that the Battle Points system adds enough persistence to reward players having a good day without making them overpowered in the next match.Though the multiplayer maps vary in size, I found that the smaller maps provided Homefront's fiercest firefights, especially once drones come into play. My favorite map is set in a suburban cul-de-sac, where I found refuge from the rain of rocket drone fire and assault choppers by sprinting into garages and ducking behind cars. Those nooks are also great places to deploy my own drones while remaining hidden.
I found myself really enjoying Homefront's multiplayer for its polished mechanics and chaos on the battlefield. It's too bad that same ferocity don't manifest in the single-player campaign.

I've spent 4 hrs in a row on this game now. And I have to say I am impressed.
It has some minor occsional server lag, but nothing like the fcked up stuff you get in games like ARK. This delay might have you missing an occasional shot. Something like 1/50 but it is not a constant nagging presence like in ARK. Furthermore it is much better balanced with creatures, lvls, resources, ease of access etc, than similiar titles. The direction the game takes you towards is also more interesting. Sure you have your house to build, and forge etc to make to create items. But this is not a soul draining task, not even if you're doing it solo. And so it doesn't become the real focus of the game. The real focus becomes actually lvling, fighting and actually facing off with monsters etc.
It took me 4 hrs of gameplay before I ran into a crash, which is basically unheard of in the early days of games such as this. Most ppl don't even play for that long at a time.
It has a survival aspect, but that task is not all consuming, it doesn't force you to run around after food, breed livestock, spend  whole days on making houses, chopping wood, taming beasts, tend gardens and do all sorts of boring time consuming  stuff on the side. I don't get why ppl who like to focus on that even bother to play games, they should be working in kitchens, farms and doing gardening instead.
The interface and stats systems are very effectively constructed, and easy to understand unlike some others(I am looking at you ARK, Lichdom, Tyranny)..
This game has done, what we've all been asknig for, for so long. They've taken the best of Skyrim and Diablo 2 and mashed them together. An open world Skyrim with drop-in, drop-out multiplayer/co-op. And ofc given it a decent lvl of difficulty, which is mostly determined by how fast you wish to progress, with a highly functional risk/reward system when you go out to grab the stuff you need to advance.
It is ofc however, not without a few cons:
-It is performance heavy, one of the heaviest games I've played, and I didn't max it out. This is however to be expected in early access withinin such a type of open world game, and it should get better optimized with time. Even as we get better equippment to deal with the demands.
-There is as of the moment, not that many ways to play it. Oh there are still a few, there are 2 Melee paths, 1 ranged, 1 ranged aoe(and I think there was one more type). Aswell as the chance to choose a 2nd complimentary fighting style to embark on as you progress(a bit later into the game). But each of these paths are currently somewhat limited in terms of abilities available, the slight edition of neutral abilities all can use does help a little with branching out, but it still feels a bit stifled. Even with the addition of your pets/familiars added in.
PS. I should however point out once again, that this is another thing that is to be expected this early on, and in some ways a good thing. It means that they're not breaking the game before they've even gotten started, but are slowly testing and implementing new features. I suspect that if they maintain support, they will keep at it and this game will as time passes, see a meteoric rise in the paths available. The game design allows for such a wide range of choices for the developers to create playstyles and build upon all of them.
-Server lags, yes they are relatively speaking minor, but they are still very much there. However, what little there is can easily be solved by playing the game with friends over lan, which is basically what I am really interested in doing. It is the Skyrim version of Diablo single player, where you can switch the server into a multiplayer one when you want, and inv your friends in, into your world. Or for you to join theirs.
PS. Just because you had a bad experience with lag, did you ever consider that this might have been due to the specific server you were on, your own connection service provider, specifically your connection, or even just your computer lagging? Most don't seem to consider these before they start whining. I had a relatively stable 60-89ms delay, with occasional spikes into about 300ms(relatively rare, like I said, about one in 30-50 shots), Not optiomal, but again, much, much better than ARK.
-It does to some degree share Skyrim's fault of repetative combat and unvaried solutions to them. Everything in the game runs on magic, but that is similar to how a Paladin, DK or Fury Druid in WoW uses magic, but still fights in melee. Again though, this is something I hope they will branch out on eventually, adding alternative playtyles and resources, such as rage/fury, spirit, etc.
Considering the updates, and improvments shown, I expect even more positive changes to this game. Please try it, and upvote it. It certainly deserves a better ranking than it has, too many overly pessimistic gamers have dismissed its prospects from the earliest days, thinking it was unplayable back then and like so many would not improve(ARK). But this one did, and it improved a lot, in every aspect. You won't have 3 T-rexes coming and wrecking your home 20min into the game. You won't have 5 crashes in 3 hrs, and you won't have to work for 2-5 hrs to build a medium sized low lvl house and hope that no overpowered starting ground creature comes  along and wrecks your work. Or that unregulated lifeless chinese farmers comes and camps you, and all the resource locations.
This game is far from finnished, but unlike ARK, it actually already works. It is easy to get into, it follows and interesting system that can be expanded upon, And most importantly, it has the potential to completely fill out the role of that game we've all been waiting for since 2011´-2015(depending on when  you realized what a game like Skyrim could be). It already does so, to some extent. I wish the developers will be allowed to complete that experience, and not be shut down just before the finnish line.
So yes, in spite of some relevant but quickly fading issues, I recommend this game.

Since I saw this game was on sale for $9.99 today I decided I should write a review for people looking at this game. First off, I don't think I have ever seen this game go on a 75% off sale, and for the record I got this game for free. GRID Autosport is probably one of the best racing games on Steam in my opinion. The graphics are great, and it runs well on my average PC.

The career mode is very unique, with you playing as a professional racer who drives across 5 different disciplines: Touring, Endurance, Open Wheel, Tuner, and Street. Touring is basically normal racing on tracks all across the world. Endurance is similar, but the races are a lot longer and require you to manage your tires by deciding when to put wear on them and when to hold back. Open Wheel features open wheel Formula 1 type cars. Tuner events are drift competitions set into heats, and also time attack where racers begin in a staggered moving start and try to set the fastest lap speed rather than the highest position. Finally, Street is racing on tracks made in tight city streets with many sharp turns and short tracks. As you progress through the different disciplines you unlock new Season opportunities and get closer to racing in the GRID, where all disciplines are tested in one competition. For events you do not get to choose the car you drive, which some people don't like but I am fine with. The game is structured into racing seasons where you pick one discipline and a season with preset races and cars. Seasons can also feature a special event where maybe everyone drives the same car or something. When a season ends you can choose a new season from any discipline. The game will save your progress between events so you don't have to play a whole season in one sitting. For each season you can also choose a racing team which gives different challenges or offers which give you bonus XP. For example, improve your lap time, finish above 5th position, lead for a lap. Also, for most racing events each racing team has two drivers. You recieve a teammate with a description and stats (however I do not think the stats really have a great impact on them). During the race you can order your teammate to hold their position, push for a higher one, or just have the default balanced approach.

The racing itself is quite good, featuring a penalty system for infractions like going off track and gaining a position by way of that. There is also a replay feature, similar to Forza Horizon where you can rewind the last seconds where you may have crashed or made a mistake. For racers who don't like this feature, you can disable it, and you will receive an XP bonus. There are also other setting you can turn on or off that will increase your XP bonus or lower it. For inexperienced racers I would recommend turning on the driving line which displays the best path to take on the track and where to brake. Now, a lot of the times you can make big gains in races by way of road rage and muscling your way through the competition, I have to admit I do this some of the time. As long as you are on the track you receive no penalty, however if you take enough damage, your steering column, engine, or tires can be damaged.

The multiplayer is fun, one thing is that you have to set your Steam download region to UK-London in order to find matches. From what I've heard this will not affect your downloads and it hasn't seemed to affect me so far. Surprisingly the multiplayer features the rewind function, however it will only rewind your car while everyone else keeps racing, so its really only for big mistakes. By racing in multiplayer you earn money and XP and can buy new cars. There is no customization and the cars you buy are just for multiplayer.

All In all I think this is a great racing game and a steal for such a big sale. I probably would not buy this game for full price however, but if I didn't have it and saw it on this sale I would definitely grab it! Great graphics, good career mode, good multiplayer, nice music.
NOTE: This game like most racing games is best with a CONTROLLER.

Let me preface this review with this: I love the Civ series. I have played civ since I was younger, and I have always thought of it to be in my top 5 games of all time.
However, Civ: Beyond Earth didn't give me the same feeling as previous Civ games did. Civ: BE feels more of an expansion pack to Civ: 5, rather than a
Let's go over some pros and cons:
Pros:
- Runs great on most systems (Played on my 4 year old laptop at medium settings with no lag)
- Better UI when controlling units
- Quicker loading when talking with other Civs
- Ability to trade "favors"
- Cities aren't built in one turn
Cons:
- UI is not intuiative, I feel like I have to look for things constantly
- Couldn't find "Advanced Setup" option (took me about 30 minutes to find it)
- Unit descriptions are not easy to understand
- No Religion
- Very little diversity with "barbarians"
- No semi-linar story line (feels like I was just dumped into the game without any story as to how/why I am here)
- Maps are basically remakes of Civ: 5
- No sci-fi implemented; no original ideas with the theme of the game
Civ: BE just feels like a remastered edition of Civ: 5 - only thing different are the look of the cities and units. I much prefer what Civ: 5 has over Civ: BE.
I would NOT buy this game, unless it's less than $10. As this game stands, it feels more like an expansion/remastered edition of Civ: 5.
Go spend your money on a better game, such as Civ: 5 or Civ: 4, both of which I highly recommend.

Hatred: A game that tries so hard to be 'shocking' and 'conterversial' to get people's attenion ironicly is now forgotten today thanks to it being pretty mediocre and filled with frustation and boredom.
Story: It's suprisingly shallow and unfocused honestly. A game that is centred around in the viewpoint of a mass shooter SHOULD'VE been interesting. A taboo subject that isn't dared to be foused on in all types of medium could've given a chance of this topic to be develed into. The story is you play a mysterious hateful man the game called 'The Antagonist' who decided that he hates the world and want to fix it by killing as much people as he can. That's it. the cutscenes or the dialogues never explains who he is or why he hate people so much. For what i research from interviews from the devs that not giving the anatagonist any personal backstory or exmaplination is intentional and all the player needs to know that's he's crazy. I guess it would have been safe choice, having the game be more of a black comedy with the dark-humor jokes and over-the-top violence rather than serious look on the mass-killings. I imagine the last thing the devs would want to be accused of symapthising with killers.
Gameplay: Hatred is an isometic shooter very similar in vein to the first Postal where the player controls the Antagonist causing destruction and chaos as well as killing as much people as possible. What makes it different from Postal is that the civilans most of the time are defenceless and they can only run away from you unless they can find weapons on the ground to fight back. Besides that it plays pretty much like every other isometic shooter. There's a mechinic to execute people in brutal ways if they are injured and it;s the only way to refill health so you'll keep seeing the same canned animations every single time that will  lose the shock value very quickly. What's annoying about this is, that in a isometric angle, it hard to tell how much you need to fire to injure an enemy and not kill them. At times it feel like a coin toss. While the gameplay is soild, the diffculty is all over the place. There's enemies such as swatt member that are annoying bullet sponges even using a shotgun at close range. Some enemies such as the soilders will destroy you in squads in seconds without being careful and that was on Level 4! And why someone tell me that cars can insta-kill you in ALL DIFFICULTIES, but bullets and expolsions doesn't damage you by compare?
Presenation: The first thing the player sees in the game is the heavy use of black and white filer throughout the game which i think looks great but it is a double edge sword. The good thing is that it help add the mood and grimness that can be the video game equalivent of SIn City. But the problem is that while playing, it is pretty diffcult to see enemies and even your surrounding. Sure on keyboard you can hold the left alt ke down to see red outline of the enemies and interative objects which is useful. But i wish there is a option to automatcially see the outlines in gameplay in the options.
The game runs at Unreal Engine 4 and it is used very well with suprisingly detailed models and enviroments in an isometric shooter where it is unneeded. The explosions used in the game is well-done with buildings shooks and walls beign destroyed realisticly by throwing grenades or shooting explosive canisters. The fire effects from the molotov cocktails and the flamethrower has great physics and detail.
Conculsion: overall it is a medicore isometric shooter in compareing to other games like Hotline Miami or even the first Postal which came out 20 years ago. But at least the game isn't very expensive in full price and can go pretty low prices in sales. One thing i like to mention the small but buzy mod scenes that created some greatmods such as the FPS mod for the game. So there is some replay value for those interested. But even with that i fully lost all intrested with this game by this point.

There’s extremely little that I’m actually able to say about Hatred that won't make me sound like a psychopath, you spend most of your time gunning down civilians and what little you have left is spent gunning down the law enforcement trying to stop you. Back in 2015 when this little gem of a game snuck its way into Steam Greenlight, it ended up getting removed due to the nature of its content. This caused a massive controversy and raised an important question that needed to be answered: does the ultra-violent nature of the game warrant it being removed and essentially censored off of Steam? That’s a complicated question and there’s many answers, but what’s important to remember is that Hatred is a video game, nothing here is real, and as such keep that in mind when I talk about how satisfying the guns are or how impressive the destruction is. Now, the character you play as in Hatred is a bit difficult for me to refer to, considering in the first five minutes of the game he informs you that his name is “not important”, so for the sake of both this review and my sanity I’m going to refer to him as Trenchcoat Tom. Trenchcoat Tom is quite possibly the single most hilarious yet boring and poorly made character I have ever seen in a game before. Obviously if you’re playing Hatred you aren’t exactly here for the story or narrative, considering there practically is none, but even still Trenchcoat Tom’s dialogue is absolutely horrendous, yet simultaneously hilarious. With such one liners as “I’m a man of hate and disgust” and “I never thought it would be so easy to slaughter my whole neighborhood”, you’ll be laughing every time he opens his mouth. On one hand, his cringy dialogue is a refreshing little bit of comedy every now and again, but on the other hand this literally makes the main character a walking joke and I’m still not sure whether his lines are meant to be that edgy or not. Trenchcoat Tom is the only character that you interact with throughout the entire game, unless you count the civilians screaming and begging for mercy, which I don’t. I don’t feel the need to beat around the bush here: Hatred’s character design is just downright horrible. No background, no emotion, no halfway decent dialogue, none of that, just an edgy guy with the vague objective of “If it moves, it dies”.
So, the story’s horrible and the main character may as well be a walking talking edgy ken doll for all the story that he has, but that really isn’t what you’re here for is it? Narrative is absolutely not what Hatred is about, and that’s incredibly refreshing in today’s day and age where developers of games like Battlefront 2 feel the need to include half-baked “stories” in their games just to say they have one. The main premise of each of Hatred’s missions is, with only two real exceptions, kill X amount of civilians and then escape. At the risk of sounding like a soon-to-be terrorist, I actually think that this is an extremely enjoyable objective, and it’s nice to finally be shooting at something that isn’t shooting me back for once. However, that never lasts for long since, as is common in most civilized countries, after you start piling up bodies, the law gets involved. Initially, you only have to take out normal police officers and state troopers, local law enforcement and the like, but after a while you’ll have to deal with SWAT teams and, eventually, the United States National Guard. These are increasingly challenging, which is a good thing, Hatred would be no fun at all if you were just firing on civilians the whole time, and the law enforcement is always there to keeps things interesting. Sometimes you’ll fight a humvee with a mounted machine gun, but I can count how many times I did that on one hand and still have enough fingers left to finish writing this review. One thing in particular that I like about Hatred is the how enjoyable the weapons are to use, every single one has an indescribably satisfying feel to it. There really aren’t too many weapons to choose from, only five or six tops, which is a bit of a bummer but the one’s that are there work so well that I suppose it works. What surprised me the most about Hatred is that every level was extremely fun and furthermore, memorable, definitely not what you’d expect from a twin-stick shooter. I can still vividly remember each level, from the initial neighborhood to the docks, all the way to the military base in the second to last level of the game. Hatred may lack significantly in the departments of narrative and general character development, but it certainly lacks for nothing when it comes to its levels.
Continuing on about the levels, each one is surprisingly large and provides ample opportunity for exploration, as well as many useful rewards for doing so. The main reward that you’re going to be interested in acquiring though is respawn tokens, pretty self-explanatory items. These are acquired only through completing side objectives, with each level usually containing two or three and some containing none at all. These side objectives are critical, as not only are they needed to make sure this doesn’t become absurdly challenging, forcing you to one life per level, but they give each mission some life as well. The side objectives make this world feel more alive because while you’re on your murder spree in the middle of the neighborhood, some guy across town is hosting a party and there’s a politician speaking in the square. Disrupting these events is quite enjoyable and makes the side objectives more than just more people you have to kill, because clearly there’s enough of that here already. On a separate note, controlling Trenchcoat Tom is extraordinarily fluid and generally just easy, which I didn’t expect from a twin-stick, thinking that it would just about force me to use a controller instead of providing proper mouse and keyboard controls. So you’ve heard about the gameplay, graphics, and just about everything else that I can talk about, but yet there’s one glaring feature that you’ll see I still need to touch on: the graphics. The only color that you’re ever going to see in Hatred is red, everything else is going to be various shades of grey. Now, I imagine you could make some theory on how this is representative of life, and that there is no evil, only various shades of grey, but in response to that I would say “Please stop talking” I’m trying to write here. The graphics are unique and I love that they chose something so defining for their game, it really makes Hatred stand out and I love that. What I don’t love however, is not being able to see someone because they look just as grey as the building behind them, or missing an obstructive wall because it looked like the same grey shade that covers the ground. I don’t know if there was a better way to do this, but it has me mixed: it’s extremely unique and sets Hatred apart from other twin-sticks, but it also means there’s going to be some times where you get killed because of it and end up feeling cheated.
Cringey? Yes. Way too edgy? Yes. One of the most enjoyable twin-stick experiences I’ve ever had? Absolutely.

I started playing during open beta after listening to my friends say how amazing it was for the better part of a year. They said it was the best MMORPG out there, that nothing could replace it or match it, it was the god of all f2p MMORPGs.
They were right.
I've played around a few MMORPGs but nothing was as amazingly fun to play as DFO. Granted it's a little hard to get into (I took a break a few weeks after starting), but that's because it's just so far in a playstyle and content realm of its own.
DFO actually lives up to the name of f2p. (It might be worth to note that I've played purely pve, which is extremely solid in DFO. I'll talk a bit about that later.)
There's no limit to how many of your skills you can use (no arbitrary "pick 4 of your skills to use"), you don't turn ugly after a few days because your outfit expired or someth, job advancements don't take more than half an hour to an hour to do, and Neople has interesting and unique events that pretty much make you a premium member just for playing normally. The miles point system and any "play one dungeon to get this item you normally have to cash for" events such as attendance and buddy events come to mind. I've never once felt the need to cash in order to play the game at a semi-functional level or have fun. I could spend money on this game and not feel as though I've been cheated.
As I said before, the pve experience in DFO is solid. Dungeons are interesting and you aren't forced to run the same-looking map 3 times just to get to the next dungeon, because the map changes for each story quest. Bosses are unique and entertaining to fight (that is, if they last longer than your strongest attack, which they tend not to until way later). Soloing dungeons is possible on any difficulty and I never felt the need to join a party except for the rare occasion I ran out of story quests (story quest exp is given to everyone in the party, regardless of if you had the quest). To be honest, it was easier to just solo dungeons because joining a party is usually overkill.
To go through normal dungeons and just reach cap, there's no grinding for gear involved since story quests pretty much hand you everything you need. Or events do. Endgame gear (which is so creative and diverse, it's amazing how cool effects on epic gear are) is very rng- and grind-based, but I only became interested in grinding for that gear because I saw how cool it made my friend's attacks.
As for extra content, there's so much stuff to do outside of main dungeons. Most of it I haven't bothered to touch because I felt no reason to (Mirror Arad, towers outside of ToD, Anton), but it's there if I were to ever get bored and want to explore. A few of the endgame (and recently, Dark Elf) dungeons are gimmicky, but part of the fun is learning the gimmicks. And honestly, I thought they were creative and a lot better than having every boss be killable in the same exact way.
All in all, DFO is a 10/10 great experience and hopefully the steam release gets more players into the game. Although I don't see why getting the steam version is any better than getting it directly from the website.

First, my hours playing DFO on Steam does not accurately reflect the hours I play on DFO client.  I have been playing since the dreaded Nexon days, the laggy CDNF, and currently the hopeful Neople days.
DFO is one of those few games that challenges the normal standard of games.  For example, a tank character (crusader) can go offense, a support character (dark templar) can go offense.  There is no set roles for a class, you are able to experiment with any class, adding variability and improved game play.
Sure there is a limit (156 fatigue points) of gameplay for a SINGLE CHARACTER, but there are ways around it.  For instance, fp potions, making new characters, out of dungeon game modes, pvp.  As you progress higher levels, the dreaded fp limit is virtually existence since you will be too over-leveled to burn all 156 fp.
The game is NOT P2W as most people claim.  Sure people with money gets the good stuff early on (avatars, pets, titles) but Neople cares for the F2P with events that gives those same avatars, titles, pets in future events.  So its not you will never, but you will have the chance to get cash items.
DFO is not a perfect game, it is 2D side scrolling so 3D people will be disappointed, the community can be cancerous at times, and lag is horrible from time to time, but it's a game that tries to make do with what it is given.  It is a game that given a chance, a few days, and an open mind, can become one of those old favorites.

Marvel + Puzzle Quest has got to be illegal.  The substance is so addictive, it's probably regulated by the government.
Marvel Puzzle Quest is pretty much what it sounds like.  It's a Bejeweled-style game with Marvel Heroes.  You pick a 3-hero team and battle against a computer controlled team.  As you make matches, you gain "Action Points" to activate one of the abilities of heroes to do damage.  Whoever wipes the other team wins.
There's a cash shop element, of course.  All cash-shop money can be earned in game.  Purple money is earned pretty regularly, and Gold money is earned by ranking in the tournaments.  You don't need to spend money to get anywhere in the game.  It just takes longer.
The game is updated constantly.  New story events, new tournaments, and new rewards come in two or three times a week.  There's plenty to do.  I do recommend setting up a facebook account so you can gift/receive rewards that come in.  It speeds up leveling up your characters significantly.
Overall, this game is a great time waster.  Give it a try.

- A Space Boner: do you love space? no I mean REALLY love space? well you better, considering how much of it you'll be warping through.
If you have the patience for rather linear gameplay, forgettable storytelling and a lack of cosmetics (seriously, let me paint my ship any other colour than 'Assulted with an angle grinder') Rebel Galaxy is a worthy spiritual successor to Freelancer and similar titles, just don't expect the world for $20... or the galaxy.

You inherited a beat up old spaceship from long lost relative and suddenly you were drawn into an uncontrollable whirl wind that will sweep across the universe in some galaxy changing event! A game is effectively a 90% Space simulation sandbox. The interesting voiced space character make it feels like a cool RPG too with some humor into serious yet light hearted galaxy adventure.
Like X series, Privateer, Galaxy on fire or galaxy ranger this game you can do everything you can do with a space ship. Mining, Robbing, Transporting, Trading, Bounty hunting, and balancing relation between several different factions and basically do whatever you want. Space station offer RPG like choice menu for you do go but you cannot exactly buy a station, build a station or explore a station in First person view like X series.
Combat itself is very weird at first but once you get the hang of it and buy enough automatic weapon it became some very interesting yet repetitive chores. Pausing and weapon switch is a life saver in early game as you try to turn your good shield against your enemy and let your depleted one regenerate.
I know I clocked in at 50 hours for game completion 100% but you will probably spend a bit less than me as I was too drawn in by the sandbox elements and did too many encounter mission and bounties.
Music is the highlight of this game as it’s gothic, western and Rock’N’Roll mixed together. It does get repetitive after 50+ hours of game paly but it’s still quite nicely done.
There are some graphic glitches if you look very closely but it’s mostly beautifully drawn and all character are nicely designed that on par with other AAA space games.
I will not replay this game as the story is linear but sandbox element did make me quite hard to put it down.
Achievements require some grinding but it’s really not that hard to do except pirate lord random encounter but there is a good guide on how to get it easily.
8.5/10 and applaud for this all around nicely done space adventure that all space fan will enjoy.

(Please note that I have played through the remastered version, hence the low hours on record. I have reviewed that version solely for its remastering qualities.)
Bioshock 2 is a worthy successor to its original first game and while it might only boil down to a Bioshock 1.5, there is still enough content and variety here to entertain the fans of the series.
The developers improved many aspects of the gameplay (including dual-wielding plasmids and weapons) which resulted in more fluid combat and overall faster gameplay. None of the fundamentals have changed of course and sure, should I have played the sequel right after the first game, it would have become monotonous towards the end. However, I believe the Bioshock games are really about their atomsphere, taking your time to explore the really well-designed, memorable levels and soaking in every bit of the story as possible. (i.e. Personally, I wouldn't really be able to play all of them back-to-back.)
The magic of Rapture is, of course, a little bit missing and doesn't feel so novel since we are exploring the underwater city for the second time. However, the story is interesting and there are some twists towards the end. Of course, Lamb, the main antagonist of the game, is no Andrew Ryan but the narrative keeps the player engaged throughout the game. I just wish that the writers could have done something new instead of retelling the first Bioshock story with individualism changed to collectivism.
Nevertheless, it was engaging and great fun to play another System Shock-style game and that alone earns my recommendation. While it is not included in the package, the Minerva's Den DLC is also highly recommended as the narrative there is more gripping and contains more surprises.

Ok well this is my first ever review on steam so bear with me.
Right well as you can see not many people seem to like Beyond Earth that much, there are alot of complaints about lack of unit types, uninspired maps and over all just an overhall of Civ 5. All of these complaints about the game hold some truth but that does not mean that it's a bad game. The first time I tried it I didn't like it much, but later on I was confused as to why I didn't like it because before it came out I was super excited for it, so I went back and tried again, you know what it was great fun. The reason for this is that you really need to immerse yourself in the game's premise and setting, when you picture yourself protecting and looking after your fledgling city exploring your surroundings and dealing with the local fauna it really becomes a fun game. The trick is to stop power gaming it like a Civ V game and enjoy it for what it is, not only that I have no doubt that with subsequent DLCs the game will get better, and have more depth than it does now but for the time being we will just have to wait.
Before I give a rating I feel it only right to point out a few issues that may cause some trouble when playing the first time,  the tech web is a bit of a pain and can be a slightly confusing in comparison to the nice timeline tech tree from Civ V but once you get your head round it you should be fine. Another thing that can be a bit of a pain is finding out what all the different resources are when you play your first game as it takes time to identify what resource is used for what building/unit or if its a luxuary resource. Apart from that the game is good and I recomend it just make sure you have the right mind set going in to play it for the first time.

It has a lot of things going for it.  It is a relatively simple RPG that can be much deeper if you so choose to play it that way.  A few things I have mixed feelings about can be a pro or a con depending on your play style.
Guilds - I can't say much here as I am not yet in a guild.  Not sure what you do in them or what benefits they may offer.
As far as I have seen, a guild can only be joined by a direct invite.  I haven't seen a guild list or anyway to join one other than asking in the global chat to be invited to one.  That gives you no way to preview things like guild rank or population, which matter if you are looking for a large, small, chatty, quiet guild.  You can't start your own guild unless you have at least 4 people in your party and they start it with you.  As a mostly solo player, I really don't care for that.  I'd love to start a guild with myself and my kids, but that is only 3 of us.  So, no guild for us.
Villages - Ahhh villages.  I love this feature.  I think it is truly awesome to actively be able to build and expand your village to make it a more productive place to live.  I like that your contributions to the resource nodes are greatly multiplied so you can help fellow villagers that are not online.   But...you need 10 people in your guild to start a village and only if there is space available on the server for a village.  Again, can't do it with my kids.
Housing - House rent is fairly cheap and can be paid a month in advance.  If you go inactive and lose your house, you will lose your spot in the village, BUT the game will archive your stuff so you'll have it when you rejoin and find a new spot to rent.  The housing is rather sadly stripped down though.  You can not enter your house.  It is basically a block in the landscape that you click on the access storage and a few functions.  The type of house you chose does give you a passive buff in whatever skill you chose, but customizing the look of your house is limited to cash shop and there is no indoors to the housing, sadly.
Farming - If you are a once-a-day casual player, farming is a fairly decent way to make money.  You can sell just about any crop back to a vendor for substantially more than the cost of the seeds.  If you like to play actively for an hour or 2 though, farming might be a tad more frustrating since plants mature in intervals of hours rather than minutes.  Still, it is one of the professions you can excel in without battle.
Ranching - OK, call me silly, but I love when my sheep dances.  XD  The ranch is small and basic.  You can start with a single sheep, but exp is gained fairly fast and allows more space and a larger variety of animals.  Each type of animal prefers certain foods to give you the maximum ranching exp, but you don't HAVE to give it to them.  You can simply pet them until they fall asleep and still gain exp.  As if I could deny that cute little chicken asking me for a caterpillar.
Crafting - I personally find the crafting easy.  I think it is nicely varied and well balanced.  I am only crafting up to level 15 so far, since I am new-ish.  Things I like about crafting - no failures.  I don't know if crafting can fail at higher levels, but I like that I have never had a failure in crafting.  If I gather just enough resources to craft my bow, I will end up with a bow.  Not a disaster and trips to 3 different places to gather more materials to try again.  Your recipes tell you exactly what you need.  Some will even break it down further.  Need an Alewife?  Clilcking on it will tell you what level fishing hole you find them in.  No needing to memorize or Wiki where to find crafting stuff.  Something I find odd about crafting is the imbalance in where your exp is gained from.  380 exp for crafting 2 planks, but only 40 exp for turning them into a bow?  However, you do gain mastery on crafted items, so maybe it's like invisible exp.  Doesn't level up your crafting, but does make it better.
Gathering - I think there is a good amount of gathering.  Gathering nodes are clearly marked on area maps.  Again, no need to memorize or Wiki where to get stuff.  Fishing, logging, mining, mushroom hunting, picking fruit and catching insects all serve equal value.  You start with a basic set of gathering tools, no need to buy anything or complete quests to get basic tools.  That is nice.  They also do not take up inventory space.  The tools and the supplies that go with them are equipable, leaving space in your bags for all the other stuff you need.
Storage - Personally, I think there is a decent amount of storage.  You get increased backpack space and vault space simply from logging in daily for the first 5-6 days.  No cash for a 48 slot storage increase?  That's fairly generous in my opinon.
PVP - Thanks the gods, there is none!  I despise PVP and all the hate, bile, and childish petulence that pours forth from it.  Free games with PVP are always pay-to-win and there will always be people whining about it being that way.  PVP is a cash cow for devs short term, but tends to kill games long term.  Those few people that can drop a few hundred dollars a day/week will always overpower those that can't. Eventually, those that can't will leave while those that can will find the game empty and unchallenging and go spend their money elsewhere.  It's a life/death cycle I really hope this game doesn't fall into.  Ever.
Gnogmenting - I think this isn't really explained well enough in game for most people to realize that, in a broad sense, your weapons are where your abilities come from and gear is where your boosts come from.  So, if you find a low level item that has an ability you really, really want/need, DON'T THROW IT AWAY!  You can gnogment it, what most people would call melding, with another higher level piece of gear and choose which abilities transfer to the new gear.  The game will always choose the higher stats from the new weapon, but you get to choose what it lets you do.  Gear can have abilities and runes.  Gnogmentation allows you to customize both of those to fine tune your gear to your playstyle.
Overall, the game looks average, plays average, sounds average. It is easy, forgiving, and even gives you a free mount if you finish the quests on the first island.  Is it breaking new ground?  No.  Breathtaking scenery?  Nope.  Fast-paced-heart-pounding-non-stop-action? Uh-uh.  So why is it a good game?  Because it isn't pretending to be any of that stuff.  It is asking you to be a Villager or a Hero.  Or both.  And you can succeed at it without having to compete with anyone.

Bioshock 2 is a direct sequel to the previous installment 'bioshock'. Set years after the orignal release in bioshock 2 you play as a failed 'prototype' big daddy which i think was a great feature.
Similar to bioshock, in bioshock2 you have to kill big daddy's, and rescue or kill the little sisters. However bioshock 2 expands on this where you can also use the little sisters to harvest additional adam. In every level after saving all little sisters, a big sister will hunt you down which you can kill for additional adam. I like how bioshock2 expanded on this and it gave the game the feeling that you really are a big daddy looking after a little sister.
The new Toxins concept is brilliant and far better than bioshock1. Also hacking was a nightmare in bioshock1 and in bioshock2 i actually loved hacking, it felt fun to do unlike in BS1 where it felt like a grind.
Pros
-Combat is far superior compared with bioshock1
-Guns are more fun to use compared with bioshock1
-Does not get boring near end game unlike bioshock1
-Improved Toxins conecpt
-6 Endings compared with bioshock1's 3 (This could be good or bad)
-Hacking system is wayyyyyyy better than bioshock1's
Cons
-Short game length (less than 10 hours on standard difficulty)
-Bioshock1's story was more indepth and superior
In conclusion i dont see why this game gets criticized compared with the original bioshock. It improved from bioshock1 in almost every aspect. The story is better in Bioshock1 but the gameplay is far, far, far superior in Bio2.
If you enjoyed Bioshock1, you will most likely enjoy this game.

Gameplay in Civ IV Complete and Civ V Complete is better.
Civ BE's shortfalls relative to the sereis are few but important.
1) No flavor. Considering the work put into animating the rhetoric of factions in Alpha Centauri, and in Civ V, the flat and generic presentation in BE gives the impression that it was viewed as a cash grab, rather than a full product, by the studio. The price, thankfully, reflects that.
2) Balance. Civ BE offers the player options that are patently dumb. I mean to say that the options are not real options in any situation. A good metaphor would be adding a button that makes you lose when you push it. Yes, it's an additional choice, but it adds no value to the game.
3) The game did not dramatically change or improve as is common among Sid Meier's spinoffs and numbered games. The differences between III and IV, or IV and V, for example, are huge. Even the changes in V:GNK, and V:BNW expansions were dramatic and awesome. BE, from the player's perspective, is just a reskin with a new tech tree.
If you can look past these three things, buy and enjoy BE. Otherwise, Buy Civ V Complete and experience the best that the series has to offer.

Big Pharma is a tycoon-style game based around pharmaceutical development. It holds the isometric view of classic games like Rollercoaster Tycoon while being graphically sleek. As with its tycoon-style roots, it also contains puzzle elements as the equipment you must use act as puzzle pieces that you must fit together in a fixed amount of space.
Firstly, it's a management simulation game. If you're as big a fan as Rollercoaster Tycoon as I am, chances are you'll enjoy this game just on the style of the game alone.
As for how the levels are set up, there are several categories of scenarios each with their own set missions. These categories range from Beginner to Advanced difficulties, along with Quick Play and Crippling Debt categories, the last of which severely handicaps you if you're looking for a challenge!
When it comes to dropping into a scenario, the building space and ingredients you have at your disposal are completely randomized. This means you can start the game with a nice area to start building in, or perhaps a not so nice area. It also means that you can have ingredients that induce negative side effects or not. But no fear! You can buy more space with the money you have and discover more ingredients through exploring different biomes for new raw materials to make cures to illnesses with so overcoming a rough start is entirely doable.
Exploring for new ingredients is a must as well as researching new methods to manipulate the drugs to turn them into cures. The ingredient system works very well in my opinion. Sometimes you just have to change the concentration of the ingredient to make higher level cures but sometimes you also need to mix it just right with catalysts to make the drug a higher selling product which adds more layers of depth to production.
With all that, there are also competitors that influence the drug market in their own unique way that isn't the same each time you play. Competitors may release the same drug as you have, saturating the market with supply which brings the price of the drug down a little. So release patents to stop them and hope they don't do the same to you!
This game, while simple at its core, offers a great managing experience and varying levels of challenge even within each mission through three different win-states. The win-states are like a "Bronze, Silver, Gold" medal type system which rewards both casual and hectic play.
If you’re like me that wants to try to perfect everything and max out the space you’re given? There's ALWAYS something that requires your attention, requiring you to be ready to do a whole list of things until you end up closing out of the game or pause it to take the dog for a walk. There's no real time to take a step back and admire what you create or take a breather. Even on the beginner levels there are always ways to enhance production, make new production lines, enhance ingredient discovery or research, etc. However, you can choose to take the game slow if you want; there’s nothing stopping you but the goals you set for yourself when you drop in!
Also just a note, this is one of those games that you need to play the tutorial to really get a good foundation on how to play.
If you're still indecisive, I've made a small video series of me playing the game trying to reach master level on the game. I jump right into it and explain how everything works and I believe you'll know if it's a game for you within a few minutes of skimming through gameplay.
Aside from that, have fun making drugs that give people headaches while simultaneously cure migraines!

I've been playing this game since its early beta days back in June 2015. Big Pharma might look like your run of the mill tycoon game, but it is much deeper than that.
The concentration system for drugs, the random ingrediant generation and robust AI compeditor performance (especially on higher difficulty levels) lends this to be a very interesting and *very* replayable game. Sure the random nature might mean that the available ingrediants are awesome in one game and suck in the next...but since everybody in the game plays with the same pool of ingrediants, the challenge is to make the most of what is available.
This is also a part puzzle game as you try to figure out how to cram your more and more complex production lines into a limited space. It can be extremely satisfying to have nearly every square inch of an area filled to the brim with drug machinery humming with their various drug modifying operations.
The tech tree is laid out in a logical but still strategic manner. Researching techs takes scientists and keeping scientists employed is expensive, so deciding which techs to go for in which order is important. Given the variable ingrediants each game, you aren't going to always want the same path down the tech tree each game. Not to mention you have to weight the options of leaving your scientists idle, which generates research points that are used to upgrade your equipment (making it cheaper to operate) or use them to research new techs, giving you access to brand new equipment or other discounts.
If you are a fan of business tycoon games at all, this game is for you. It is absolutely worth the price of admission.

If you do plan on buying this game regardless, for a better experience try pressing escape on your keyboard instead of exit on the in-game menu. Most of my crashes were caused by pressing that. Now, onto the review.
tl;dr: This is a really neat experience, but the stability issues, a few bugs, and the god-awful combat system just brings the entire game down so much that it just wasn't enjoyable for me.
What it does right: I really love what they're going for here. A look into the life of what happens around war instead of just playing the soldiers fighting in it is something I've never seen a game do before. You get to experience having to make extremely hard choices just to maybe have enough supplies to live through the next through days. This game really makes you think hard about what you're willing to do to scrape by. Resources are extremely scarce; I found myself thinking I had enough of one thing just to run out of it the next day. Overall it does a great job of immersing you in the situation and putting you up to difficult decisions, like stealing from or just outright murdering innocents just to be able to survive, or going up against heavily armed thugs or soldiers to maybe see if they've got something you desperately need.
It also keeps things simple, so you don't have to spend ages learning the mechanics of the game, but also isn't so simple that there's no level of complexity you have to adapt to just to be able get what you need through higher level crafting and trading. It's accessible enough to not push you away in the beginning, but has enough depth to make sure you're still struggling to  the end, and in this case it works really well.
What it does wrong: Despite the really enjoyable core mechanics, some things really break this game for me. For starters, the stability is awful. It took me a couple of hours just to get this game into a semi-playable state, as I had to look up multiple fixes that didn't even work, and play through multiple crashes and freezes until I could identify the main problem and try to work around it. Even  then the game would freeze up on the scavenging screen ocassionally, and it still had the chance of crashing on menus that I couldn't exit out of like I mentioned above.
The crashing wouldn't be as much of a problem if you could save more often, but the game only saves after a full day and night of scavenging, meaning that if you crash at any point during, you have to play that ENTIRE day over again. Needless to say, it can get pretty frustrating if you've done a lot to your house or got pretty far in scavenging that day.
Speaking of infuriating bugs, on the very last night I had a bandit phase through two floors and immediately spot me. I don't mean he just ran up to me... no, he literally passed through the floors in a straight line to see me. This really just soured the entire experience at the very end and completely broke any solid immersion I had. This is an eight month old game that is a full retail release. I could forgive it if it was early access, but things like this and the constant crashing are really unacceptable.
This goes onto my next point of the awful combat. If you can, just avoid it completely. It seems entirely random if you or your opponent dies or not, especially if it involves guns. I've had characters just stand straight up from cover before and stop shooting just to get shot to death. The simplistic system that worked so well for everything else makes the combat absolutely awful in just about every circumstance. The only saving grace is leading them into an instant backstab from a hiding place, but like I said in my last paragraph, even this could lead to a frustrating experience.
After everything is said and done and I've completed the game, I could probably forgive the combat and give this game a positive review, but the sorry state of the game's stability and bugs make it an unenjoyable experience. If you have the patience of a saint and want a really good and different experience, you should definitely buy this game. Otherwise you'd probably be better off waiting until the devs can actually fix everything before you spend your money on this.

I have probably played a few thousands hours of this game prior to the current Steam release.
If you enjoy side-scrolling beatem-ups, you will probably enjoy this game.  It has a large roster of very different classes to play.  Each has plenty of flashy skills.  You'll be able to find playstyles you like ranging from strength vs magic users, ranged vs melee, combo-heavy DPS vs large AOE burst (and inbetween), and so on.
2 major concerns most players might have: Is it pay2win?  Why am I limited by the fatigue system?
The Store items do give you advantages, however you can generally earn these as free players.  I have not spent any actual money on this and I have plenty of avatars, many months of all the contracts, and plenty of other Store items.  The developers have provided MANY events with chances to earn plenty of rewards including frequently giving Store items.  The pay Store items generally allow you to get slightly more powerful faster but you can usually do just as well as a free player if you put in some of work.  I think this is a completely reasonable way for the devs to make money.
Initially, with new characters, it's likely you will be limited in the daily play time by the fatigue system.  However, as you reach level cap, it becomes quite hard to use up all your fatigue as dungeons take longer to finish.  I find the variety of character classes to be the strength of this game since I can change playstyles so I don't get bored.  I have a huge roster of characters at this point and I never run out of fatigue.  I don't have any problem playing as much as I want.  Some players might have 1 main character that they play nearly exclusively.  If that's how you play, there are many ways to get more fatigue.
This is a fun game.  If you give it a try, play for at least a few days.  Take advantage of events.  The community is occasionally a bit salty (as any community) but is overall very friendly.   The devs are a small team adapting this version of the game from the larger Korean version.  They seem to care quite a bit and they care and listen to feedback from the users.

Bleed is a bulletstrom arcade game for 5 euros.
You're Wryn, a teenage girl with pink hair who wants to be the best hero in the world by defeating the biggest and nastiest beasts. So that's it for the story, but you would only play it for the gameplay of course!
As a bulletstorm you'll need to move fast and hit things as fast as you can. The level design is very well built with so many traps, different situations and are well-paced. Enemies don't vary much but they do the job and the bosses smash you to pieces! You can only carry two weapons at a time but in-game you can switch to another set but it's annoying that I can't simply change weapons with the number buttons. This is a PC game, you shouldn't go through this trouble of the two-weapon system.  Many of the weapons are generic, however, they're fun to use nonetheless.
Once you finish this short game, you can replay the different locked characters and difficulty modes. The difficulty modes in this games don't just make the characters harder to kill, they change the spawning and the behaviour of the AI. This is how games should differ their difficulty modes, not just making the enemies bullet-spongy.
The score system is nothing new but it's good. The more you kill, the higher is the classification level. Try not to die so many times and also don't suck! When you finish a level, use the points you got to buy linear and uninteresting upgrades.
Bleed has a pixel cartoony artstyle which I  very much like. The colours are very livid and are enjoyable to see.
In conclusion, for a small duration and fun arcade game, Bleed does the job very well and I recommend it!
