Started playing 2 months ago (on the non-steam edition).
Stay with the game, and you will start to see a game that involves learning to efficiently kill (and loot) large groups of monsters (DiabloII/Path of Exile style) with an emphasis on control/not getting hit because later monsters, player-like enemies (APCs), and bosses can punishingly hitstun/juggle you for poor control/missed mechanics.
This game is published by the development team themselves. DFO has had a long and hard history: First published under Nexon, a terrible company whose greedy practices ruined the game. Undignified with the wasted potential of a game they worked so hard for, the development team bought the game back from Nexon and relaunched it themselves. As you can imagine, that made a world of difference, and now they are the 3rd largest MMO in Korea.
Like DiabloII/Path of Exile, large amounts of time can be spent exploring builds/classes, but more so thanks to the massive roster of 42 different subclasses and a system which encourages alts.
End-game difficulty is partially under your control as lower difficulty classes allow for more forgiving gameplay, while many "fixed" classes (damage primarily scales int and skill point investment) have far easier gearing requirements allowing those with more limited time to still play and be desirable for group content.
A major design strategy that helps keep long term interest is tons of events, with ~7 new events every month offering generous rewards that frequently include cash shop items like costumes, inventory/safe upgrades, character slots, and premium plus. Major content updates every few months makes this game feel like an invested labor of love than other notable korean f2p/p2w grab and runs *cough* blade and soul *cough*.
The game may start off questionably though, as you will steamroll through scenario dungeons (For basically the first 50 levels *Hint: Try to unlock Hard Mode Scenarios ASAP*). The levelling process is more designed for veteran players to get to end-game as quickly as possible, though the story and lore is surprizingly interesting and makes the levelling process a lot more fun if you take the time to read the lore.
So come enjoy this game with us!
There's a long time dedicated fan-base over at reddit and DFONexus, so it's highly recommended to check those places out for tips and newbie guides.

I have only played 8 hours of this game so i have not even experienced the entire content the game has to offer but i can say that this game is highly addictive, and highly recommended for all those who are fans of simulation/management games.
The aim of the game is to take ingredients and alter them in order to create cures for specific illnesses and then sell them to make money to make more cures etc etc.
The game has a very steep learning curve, especially in relation to the later tier drugs that involve mixing. Getting these to work in a fluid manner (maximising profits) is quite challenging and requires a lot of trial and error so i highly recommend after the tutorial loading up the mode which has all the research and drugs unlocked so that you can play around and learn how to create a fluid setup of the machinery and adapt to the different building structures (there are only a few so even though its completely random you will get familiar with each one eventually).
I did read alot of reviews before purchasing this game and a few mentioned the randomness of the drugs you recieve at the start of the game and size of the building being annoying/limiting the ability to play the game. However i dont think this is as much of an issue, the game seems fairly balanced and gives you plenty of time to complete scenarios regardless of the spawn. I can see the spawns being an issue if you are an achievment hunter who wants to complete all the levels on master (the time limit is much much less), however this can be worked around if you just restart the mission a few times so in my opinion the randomness is not a big deal for those who read those reviews and got worried that the game is broken.
I also especially like the addition of a "global economy" aspect in relation to the competing companies whereby you need to ensure that the drugs you make are better than theirs by fine tuning them or you will not sell as many units loosing you money or manufacture ones that the ai have not considered thereby creating your own monopoly of the drug (can also be done by patents).
Also a must have are the mods for this game, only ones i have found so far are the ones supplied by the actual Big Pharma website, they are very useful (example free conveyor belts).
Overall, great game, very challenging and i can see many hours of my life being eaten by it.

I've played Dungeon Fighter since its open beta days when it was published by Nexon NA. I've played many MMOs in the time I've been playing video games, and this is by far one of the best. In a sea of WoW clones and other subpar attempts at MMOs, this is the game I keep coming back to.
Dungeon Fighter is one of the few MMOs that attempts to try and be a GAME instead of a mindless auto-attack grinder. The story too is a bit interesting, albiet with some poor localization peppered in there (at the time of this writing I haven't seen if the localization has improved.)
This game isn't without its flaws however. Since this is an MMO, you will need to grind for better gear. Dungeon design can be a tad bland as well. Monsters seem to just "exist" in dungeon rooms ready for you to kill them. You won't have many dungeons were mobs come rushing into a room, jumping from the background or foreground. It's Beat'Em up staples like those that would only improve the typical PvE experience.  My last gripe are scenario dungeons. You'll be working your way through scenario dungeons into the early-mid 80's. These dungeons are FAR too easy. If there were an option to set all scenario dungeons to hard or higher from the get-go, I believe things could get interesting.
Overall, if you're looking for a break from the usual point and click MMO, give this one a shot. If you grew up playing NES and SNES Beat'Em ups I would say likewise. Realtalk. EVERYBODY has their own definition of what the phrase "pay to win" means. The best way to find out is to obviously play the game but the next best thing is to just state facts and let the individual decide for themselves..
Longtime DFO player here, playing global since the pre-alpha test and played Nexon DFO since their beta to when Nexon closed servers.
The following are facts about DFO:
-Epic rarity equipment is, with few exceptions, the best in slot equipment in the game for both PvE and PvP.
-Some classes can perform very well with ♥♥♥♥♥♥ gear, others struggle even with full epic sets. Class balance is a big deal but epics are still probably going to be your BiS.
-Epic rarity equipment is primarily acquired in hell mode dungeons.
-Hells are resource gated via demon invitations, players can buy more demon invitations via challenges for gold.
-Neople condones the selling of cash shop items for in game gold as an indirect method of purchasing gold with real money.
-With the exception of some very lucky individual outliers, the majority of the players with the best equipment in the game have spent large amounts of real money in order to finance the hells necessary to acquire it.
The following is an opinion of mine:
-Hells are really boring. Even if you do decide to whale it out and max your credit card for hell money your life at endgame is going to be running the same four rooms of the same dungeon by yourself ad nauseum for weeks/months on end.
The facts are facts and don't let anybody tell you otherwise, If somebody tells you that you can farm anything you want without whaling they are lying through their teeth. You don't even need to take MY word for it, just visit the convenient hell mode simulator at
and see for yourself just how likely your average player is at getting an epic set with the amount of invites they can reasonably gather.
Do you define p2w as "being able to buy the BiS gear DIRECTLY from a cash shop? Then DFO isn't p2w, enjoy your stay in Arad.
Do you think p2w is "people who spend lots of money are stronger than those who don't"? Then DFO probably falls closer to the p2w side for you.
Point is, "p2w" isn't a black or white dichotomy, it's sort of a spectrum individual to everybody. Kind of like autism.

I'm going to say yes to this game, but i'm on the fence because of 1 or 2 issues with PVP which i'll get to later.
If you're into Ark, Rust, or any survival game where you need to build a base, you have that here. Definitely find a group to play with because you can't get every skill unlocked, not even close, and currently it does not look like there is a way to reset the tree.
You can tame creatures, which consist of things like bear, wolf, elk, gryphon, dragon, to name a few, but in order to keep them loyal you must farm to build up their time limit. Yes, once you have them, if you ignore them they will disappear. They start with 30 min. loyalty, and early on you can only increase this by 4 hours per item, stacking the time to as high as you want which is a really easy farm I might add.
Base building is ok, but wood wont last long, it takes a tier 2 weapon roughly 8 minutes to get through a door or wall, so my recommendation is what it always is for games like this, more doors, more floors, fake chests. One of the draw backs to building is the larger doors, which only have 5000 hp, as opposed to the 27000 a small door has. This kind of forces you to put a fence around your building, if you want minimum defense for your animals as they cannot fit through small doors. " DO NOT " put them in your house, they will fall through the foundation, and chances are they won't always pop back up when you put them on follow.
Regardless to where you are in the world, if your pet is on Stay / Defense, he will try to run to you if you get hit, so he needs a pen!
If you are on a PVP server at this point, griefing is pretty bad. You cannot access another players chest while in their building without destoying their Throne chair. Smashing the chest just causes the chest, and all of the items inside to go away, which only takes about a minute to do. If they find the throne, that can also be destroyed in a minutes time, and once that goes, all of your chests can be accessed. The worst part about this is now they are free to steal the entire building by putting down their own chair. Chances are you're being raided by someone with a better base already in which they might leave it, but I havent seen that happening. A structure with no claim means you can modify it, such as going into build mode and simply destroying all the foundations. Good bye base.

If you are expecting anything but an arcade racer.. well.. you will be dissappointed. Although not as bad as the later EA games, it is extremely casual.
It has a couple of things going for it:
The feeling of speed is actually really good.
Unfortunately, that is the only good thing about it.
On the downside there are several more points to be made:
Firstly: Why is there no cockpit view? I have no words for how bad this is.
Secondly: The AI. Well, calling them AI would be stretching it a bit. They are as stupid as they can be without imploding the whole known universe.
Thirdly: In some events you get disqualified if you so much as touch another car. That would be fine if that rule applied to the AI as well. Without any penalties they can charge into you as a mad elephant on meth.
Fourthly: The physics. This is a real problem as you will spin out in a ball of petrol flames if you get hit (or try to hit) by another car. While you ponder over your wreck and where the hell you will get the money to fix it and how you will explain it to your wife, the AI will just continue as if nothing happened.
Fifthly: Rubberbanding. This was an annoying feature of GRID and apparently they couldn't keep their greasy fingers of the "insert rubberbanding"-function. Altough not as apparent and bad as in GRID, it is still very present. Unless you lead by some 5 seconds, expect to be rear-ended by the guy you overtook and you haven't seen the smoke of for minutes. Suddenly he's there again like a bat out of hell.
Sixthly: The cars. I have at the moment of writing some 30 cars I've won but they are just a sidenote. You can paint them but that is it. Oh.. change the wheels. Yay! They.. fill.. no.. purpose.. at.. all. Once you have the Golf R there is no need whatsoever for any other. Unless you are forced to use it or you are in a vehicle challange.. which will win you another car you will never use. It makes no sense at all.
Seventhly: Car textures and resolution. Seriously? If you for some reason blows the hood of the car (which happens a lot..) you will be surprised by a low-texture engine that looks like it was stolen from Carmageddon. Yep, that is how bad it is. Guys, really?
There are probably more stuff that annoys me, but these are the ones that I could think of right now.
If you can find this game on a deal for let's say 5 Euros, buy it. Otherwise? No. Save your money and buy a better racing game. There are too many annoying things going on here for me to enjoy it. And I really tried, believe me.

Informal Review from an ex Esports writer!
The Good:
* Core gameplay mechanics are solid (skill based/fun/fast paced). It's like a more action-oriented Blade and Soul. I was very pleased with this aspect of the game.
* Characters all have unique playstyles, which vary in difficulty and theme (shooter, hack and slash, fighter).
* You get to choose 2 characters to unlock for free (forever) when starting the game.
* You can unlock characters without having to spend real life cash.
* You can buy creative/funny skins to customize favorite characters (similar to the classic MOBA business model).
* You can choose to unlock all characters for $20.
* Fairly well designed, you can tell that Codebrush really had a great design team working on this game.
* Because of the small playerbase, you'll often gravitate towards playing on the most popular server with the lowest ping. This  can kind of create a sense of community. Think like old school Counter Strike days.
The Bad:
* Lack of characters to choose from (there's like 10), and you often end up facing mirror matchups (eg; both teams have X character)
* Unlocking characters without cash takes a while (about a week of solid playtime; think LoL without daily bonus wins).
* Leaderboards are based on things kill k/d ratio over an actual matchmaking rating.
* There is no match making.
* Some balance issues. Tiac and Elika are literally unstoppable if they get within melee range, and Elika can just aoe stunlock anyone within range by simply mashing buttons.
* Needs polish, some of the skill animations are annoying and not fluid (like Hyde's grounded R, why can I cast it on the run  while jumping, but not while grounded? having to pause for the animation is annoying). The camera positioning can get messed up when turning quickly. Just small things like this, they wouldn't keep me from playing, but it would make the gameplay feel much more fluid.
* The rank progression system is pretty much meaningless.
The Ugily:
* Incredibly small playerbase. You'll be lucky to find 20 other people playing on servers in your area.
* Servers outside your area have high ping. For example; I'm in seattle, so I'd have to play on designated Seattle custom servers that had < 50 ping. If no one else in Seattle was playing, I'd have to find the next closest US server and play on that, which usually jumps me to > 150 ping.
* The game doesn't feel finished. There isn't a ranked game mode, or even matchmaking for that matter. It's very bare-bones, you open the 32bit client and are presented with 4 options; Tutorial, Training, Network Play, and Shop. The "Network play" is basically a list of custom servers that people jump in and out of (think custom hotjoin games in GW2). Very casual, but there's always 1 or 2 significantly stronger players running around dominating everyone.
Overall, it's a great game. A real diamond in the rough for PvP gamers. I think this is what Forge WANTED to be, but fell short of. I hope Codebrush (the developer) will figure out a way to finance the game so that it can be polished and brought into the mainstream market. -Even if they have to go to a publisher (I hear NCsoft East isn't too busy right now, they might be looking for a new project!).

12 hours in this game, here's what I have to say:
GRID Autosport brought quite a lot of elements from the first GRID (and also TOCA if older players recognize), although discipline classes sound a bit generalized.
First of all, let's address the handling. GRID 1 has an arcade-like handlings with in-game tweaks to alter the characteristics. GRID 2's handling is perhaps the most infamous one; the TrueFeel handling feels too Chris Harris, being slidey as if the car does not have traction control. Autosport, meanwhile, has a sim-like handling and perhaps accurate to real life (but I would suggest full-fat sim racers such as Assetto Corsa for full sim), for example (assuming traction control is disabled in this game):
* FWD cars understeers if you press the throttle deep in corners
* RWD cars will spin out if you apply full throttle before you clear the corner
* FR cars (engine in the front, rear wheels driven) has inferior handling stability than MR (mid engine, rear driven) cars
* And other handling traits that makes the in-game cars handle just like in real life
Graphics is great, set everything to ultra and you have one nice eye-candy. Car selection, while it is not diverse as the first GRID or TOCA, is quite good, and a cherry topper on the Autosport's graphics.
Discipline and AI: while the other discipline is a bit straight-forward, I would touch on the Endurance discipline. This is where all your capability, thought, and car control count as one screw-up can lead to mounting problems. In addition, this is the most challenging and scariest discipline according to myself, as I struggle to maintain my position while two Ravenwests constantly buzzing on the back in the middle of the night. With TC and ABS off, it is indeed nerve-wracking and daring. AI meanwhile, can pose quite a challenge (especially the Ravenwest team) but the teammate might be useless.
In-game music/sounds is great, I should give thumbs up to the menu music. It's so calm and makes you forget about racing pressures.
Aside from the praises I can give, I have a mixed feeling on the cockpit view. If the cockpit view is meant to be blurred to create a focus on the track, I can give a thumbs up, but if it meant to hide low-res textures, it's not good.
To sum up:
+ Sound
+ Realism
+ Handling
+ Track selection
+ Graphics
+ Car selection
+ Challenging discipline and AI
+ Sleek Menu interface
- Cockpit View
- Useless teammate
- Inability to create your own team, and forced to drive for others, as I melodramatically refer as mercenary racer.
Bottom line: GRID Autosport is a beautifully-produced simcade. Despite not being Codemaster's highest masterpiece, it clearly shows that Codemasters is still capable of producing quality racing games.

It hurts to rate a game in a series I enjoy so much, but I wouldn't recommend this game if you're a returning Civilization fan. Below I'll list the bad and the good.
THE BAD
1. The game feels like a skin/mod for Civilization V. It felt all too familiar too soon. I was especially disappointed that the same strategies for Cvilization IV and V still apply to Beyond Earth. This is the core flaw in the game, as it gets boring quickly and thus has no staying power.
2. The maps are boring. Nothing unique in the alien world, just different names for the same tiles.
3. The DLC adds components to the game that should have been included at launch.
THE GOOD
1. The affinity points are a fresh addition; however, the amount of units are still limited.
2. The new tech tree provides a more engaging visual when teching up

I do not recommend this game for anyone who is annoyed by extremely tutorialized baby-proof gameplay.
The game simultaneously tutorializes itself, preventing you from doing stuff except for a very specific way, and chastises you for not doing stuff. This is all done through the narrator, who, though funny, starts getting grating when they as chastising you for something you are actively doing.
:::::: PARAPHRASED EXCERPT FROM THE GAME ::::::
Narrator: "The Supreme Evil went to research a guard room."
ME: Currently fighting off an attack.
Narrator: "After a long pause, the Most Evil of Evils went to research a guard room"
ME: Haven't got a goblin for research yet, mining some gold to buy one.
Narrator: "The extremely lazy evil put off researching a guard room for an extremely long time becuase he doesn't want to win."
ME: ?????? WTF chill out, I was digging for gold and ran into a spider cave.
Narrator: "Have you ever actually PLAYED a videogame before? I'm just saying that my grandmother could have beaten the game by now. All you have to do is click on the research button, and if you can't figure it out, there are some tutorials for people like you."
:::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::
So it's kinda funny, but it's also patronizing because the game practically forces you to do this one thing (you can't do much else until you've built a guard room. can't go to the surface, can't beat the level, can't progress), but at the same tiem, incessantly nags you into building the guard room. Might as well take control of my mouse and do it for me at that point.
They really should have toned it down about 15 notches. I've played Dungeon Keeper before, I know what I'm doing, please stop telling me literally exactly what to do every ten seconds, I think I've got a handle on this extremely complicated concept of "kill stuff, don't die".
Overall it's fun so far, but not quite fun enough to make me recommend it to my friends.

I've always had some apprehension for playing BioShock 2. This is a bit of a forgotten entry in the BioShock series. Even when the trilogy came out remastered, I chortled as several "professional game critics" said that they only played an hour of BioShock 2 but could guarantee the game is good.
And, you know what? I'm honestly appreciative that Steam game me BioShock 1 & 2 Remastered for free! I can waste about 20 hours of my life playing them again with slightly better graphics.
Yeah, don't expect me to review those anytime soon. This is the best I'm doing right now.
BioShock 2 is the slightly silent sequel that came out shortly after one of my favorite video games of all time, BioShock. Yahtzee gave it a scathing review and even put it on his bottom 5 of 2010, while IGN and Gamespot gave it some positive reviews. But that's an entirely unique occurrence with a new game release.
However, after a while of playing Yahtzee's favorite and least favorite games, I can now definitively say... I actually disagree with him. It's not very often that I do, but I don't think this game is anywhere near as bad as he claimed it to be.
Then again, it's not as good as IGN would try to sell it as either. I think I'm somewhere right in the middle with this game.
BioShock 2 looks the same as BioShock 1. You've got Rapture with all of its decrepit watery horrors and some new enemies and features thrown in, but I what I really appreciated were the new tweaks in the gameplay. Combat is much more fast-pasted and fun than BioShock 1 because you can wield your plasmids and weapons at the same time and hacking has now been significantly shortened to help you take control of stuff much faster.
However, I think the morality system took a dip in this entry. In this regard, I do agree with Yahtzee a bit. In the first BioShock, you just had to choose whether you wanted to save or harvest the little sisters. But in the sequel if you choose to save the little sisters... you have to find a body with ADAM on it... and defend them from waves of enemies until she harvests the dead body properly. I didn't realize you could just choose to save her at the nearest hole in the wall, because the game taught me that I should do the first option to gain more ADAM (which you do), but it's tedious as all hell. It feels like level-grinding. And it can be extremely infuriating when you die and spent all of your bullets and money so you'll have to go back and earn some money before you try your hand at harvesting again.
Along with all this... the story isn't that great. When you're a sequel to my 4th favorite game of all time and one of the most critically-praised games of the previous games of the decade and you don't have the writer of that game to assist you, obviously some corner will get cut. I honestly didn't learn anything spectacular or new about Rapture that I had already learned in the first game.
And Sophia Lamb was far less of an interesting villain than Andrew Ryan was. She's all bark and no bite. She keeps taunting you but only sends her waves of followers to take you down, and the final level is absolutely abyssmal. There's no boss fight. Just more waves of enemies and then it's over.
I don't agree with the people who claim that BioShock 2 has an emotionally-investing story. I was honestly playing BioShock 2 because of the enhanced gameplay. If you like BioShock enough for the most surface-level reasons, then BioShock 2 should easily whet your appetite. But as far as its story goes, it doesn't hold a candle to the original. I'm giving Bioshock 2 a 7/10 with a hesitant recommendation.

When I bought this game I was hoping for a nice platforming experience that I would be able to complete in a reasonable amount of time.
Now that we have pretenses out of the way, this game is quite difficult, and not always in the best ways. The levels quite quickly get to the point where they are pretty large. Normally this is a good thing in platformers, but I was sometimes left wandering about in this maze of platforms that vanished behind me, wondering if this lower path I kept trying to get past would eventually get me to the door, or if all of my attempts at getting past these obstacles were meaningless. All the while, platform vanishing kept me at a pace I didn't feel comfortable with leaving little to no room for error, and forcing me to preform tasks with the controls I was not yet comfortable with. Not to mention that so little of the story is gone through between levels that you forget what is even going on.
Too be fair though, the mechanics are nice, 'boss' levels are put in, and secrets are hidden to reward you for exploring the levels, but unfortunately, the disappearing platform mechanic makes it a pain to explore levels because more than half of the platforms you jump on end up disappearing by the time your are halfway to the next one, effectively punishing exploration.
And the global cycles just add on to the punishment. Vanishing platforms are fine, but when a third of the platforms you want to jump onto will kill you if you don't wait for it to turn off, vanishing platforms become the bane of your existence.
Now, maybe I'm just terrible at platforming, but to me all these things added up to be an experience that I didn't really enjoy, being too fast-paced and punishing.

First of all it's not tiny in terms of gameplay time. I personally put in more than 25 hours into it. But it's not for a single playthrough. I have to mention though that there are only 7 levels broken up into smaller sections. I played some levels many times. But more on that later. Let's start with what this game is about.
This is a fast-paced 2D side scroller with a lot of weapons, awesome game mechanics, variety of enemies and it requires some skill to complete it. There are numerous achievements to unlock some of which require hard training. Others are surprisingly simple but require you to read the description of the achievement to get the idea of how to unlock it. As for the graphics there's not much to say but it's nice and pretty in its own way and the art style is consistent and corresponds to game's theme.
This game is about a girl which I appreciate because I like games with female protagonist. So this girl wants to be a hero but there are some heroes already and her task is to defeat them and become the best hero of all times. She got herself a list of those heroes and set to work. And to 'work' your way through you'll need weapons a lot of weapons. And you'll be able to unlock more of those as you progress. I personally was able to find something to match my playstyle and you can switch between weapons which is very handy when it turns out that in order to beat a boss you need a different gun. But that is not to say that you can beat the boss only with a certain gun. It's just that for some players in some cases one is better than the other. But I found the double pistols more than enough in most cases.
But this game in not just about the guns it's also about stylish and acrobatic combat. And that is probably what won me over right away. Once I got into first level I tried it and I was amazed and felt very cool. And being stylish also allows you to increase the rank up to an S-Rank. And that's what made this game even more entertaining. To keep your rank at high level you need to keep shooting and being stylish. Not to mention that having that rank up during boss fights is what gets you majority of the achievements. So I haven' talked about how exactly you're getting stylish, have I? You can boost yourself and fly through the air for a short period of time and then do it again. So it's a bit of Matrix-style there. This gameplay mechanic is very important because it allows you to dodge projectiles, avoid being hit by enemies, escape certain death when you're about to fall into a pit after being hit and more.
Now that we've talked about the variety of guns let's talk about variety of enemies. And there are many different ones and they don't feel repetitive. But you may find some of them being similar when they're trying to match or rather to give you a sense of what the boss is going to be like. There are mini bosses as well which I appreciate because they do a great job of preparing me for a boss battle. So when I meet the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ my reflexes are ready and I already trained my projectile-avoiding skills. And speaking of bosses they're very fun to deal with and give you sense of achievement.
So what else did I do to keep myself entertained? I played it 3 more times so I beat it on every difficulty level. Which didn't seem impossible in contrast with other games where  very hard means that you only do it if you spend entire year training. But maybe it just me when it comes to some games. But again, in this case it felt very hard but not harder. I haven't tried it in arcade mode even on easy and I don't really feel like I'm going to because I died to many times. However I may fancy that one day.
At this point you'd expect some sort of conclusion and there it is. I conclude that this game is awesome and bring joy to your everyday life by being crazy fast, fun and balanced. You can argue that it's too short and I may agree with you. But it's cheap too so no regrets on my side

Prog.1 is a short precision platformer, like Super Meat Boy, who's main idea is keeping you moving by making platforms disappear after you touch them.
It's a neat idea, and well implemented, with good visual cues for things disappearing and reappearing, though the graphics are a bit on the small side, so some people may have a hard time seeing them.
Unfortunately, the controls do feel a bit off. Maybe because there's no momentum, which takes some getting used to, maybe something else. Still, I did mostly get used to it, and it certainly could have been worse.
Frustration-wise, I'd say it was mildly frustrating, so not bad for the type of game.
The story is fairly basic. The few short cutscenes have a nice style, but there's nothing really substantial in the less than 5 minutes given to them. Sadly, no skip button if you want to redo levels later.
The game is short. If Steam's right, it took less than an hour for me to complete all 48 levels. There are some challenge modes, 100 lives/1 life mode and double-jump (easy) mode. I may have beaten 100 lives first time round, but I don't think I'll go back to do it officially.
Overall, despite some issues, if you're keen for more precision platforming, this may very well be worth a look, though I wouldn't spend much.

-Some classes can perform very well with ♥♥♥♥♥♥ gear, others struggle even with full epic sets. Class balance is a big deal but epics are still probably going to be your BiS.
-Epic rarity equipment is primarily acquired in hell mode dungeons.
-Hells are resource gated via demon invitations, players can buy more demon invitations via challenges for gold.
-Neople condones the selling of cash shop items for in game gold as an indirect method of purchasing gold with real money.
-With the exception of some very lucky individual outliers, the majority of the players with the best equipment in the game have spent large amounts of real money in order to finance the hells necessary to acquire it.
The following is an opinion of mine:
-Hells are really boring. Even if you do decide to whale it out and max your credit card for hell money your life at endgame is going to be running the same four rooms of the same dungeon by yourself ad nauseum for weeks/months on end.
The facts are facts and don't let anybody tell you otherwise, If somebody tells you that you can farm anything you want without whaling they are lying through their teeth. You don't even need to take MY word for it, just visit the convenient hell mode simulator at
and see for yourself just how likely your average player is at getting an epic set with the amount of invites they can reasonably gather.
Do you define p2w as "being able to buy the BiS gear DIRECTLY from a cash shop? Then DFO isn't p2w, enjoy your stay in Arad.
Do you think p2w is "people who spend lots of money are stronger than those who don't"? Then DFO probably falls closer to the p2w side for you.
Point is, "p2w" isn't a black or white dichotomy, it's sort of a spectrum individual to everybody. Kind of like autism.

It was pretty fun to learn how to play the game, but unfortunately, they had to add a timer. "But you do realize you can click the timer to stop it." Oh yeah, sure you can, but you only have 5 ♥♥♥♥in secs to do so. I'm not trying to think about a timer. I'm trying to think about what my next move should be. I'm trying to STRATEGIZE! When my turn comes up, and after I draw my card, the first thought that pops into my head shouldn't be, "Oh, I gotta stop that timer so I can actually have time to think! Sure would be a shame if it wasn't there!"
There's no point to it and these aren't tournament matches I'm playing. Hell, even if I WAS in a tournament and there WAS a timer, there's no way it would only be 5-20 secs long! This isn't a game where you have to be quick in your head and fingers, like DotA, LoL, CoD, Starcraft, etc. Card games such as this are like chess. While there is practice and pre-game preparation to be had, when you are in a match, there is no pressure for time. You can take almost as long as you want on your turn to strategize your next move so you can make the least amount of mistakes as possible.
So while I enjoyed learning about MTG and hope to play it again in some other form, I will not be playing Magic Duels. Remove the timer, then I'll reconsider.

Quick disclaimer: DFO is not hosted by Nexon NA anymore. It is self-published by the developers themselves, Neople. What this means is that the game is actually receiving a lot of care this time, regularly receiving updates and being constantly showered with events. It’s nowhere near the sorry state it was in back when DFO was hosted by Nexon NA, and that doesn’t appear to have signs of changing anytime soon.
Pros (Ranked in terms of strength):
#1. DFO’s gameplay. The game opts to have sectioned areas for its locales, rather than a massive sandbox where you can go anywhere you please. In the dungeon sections, you can solo or have an up-to-4 person party. When you’re in a dungeon, it plays very similarly to old-school games like Final Fight, Streets of Rage, Double Dragon, etc., but so much deeper, and when you’re in a party (especially in endgame), much more chaotic… in a very good way.
Whether you want to solo or party up is completely your choice, since while you do get benefits from being in a party, the game does accommodate for – and even encourages – solo play. Even if you pick the hardest difficulty for a dungeon, the game will scale itself down slightly to make getting through areas feel less like you’re hitting brick walls over and over. There will be situations in DFO endgame where you are forced to solo and party alike, so DFO welcomes any style of play and encourages exploration of both.
There are a ton of characters and classes to choose from in DFO. Some play as how you would expect, some differ slightly or vastly from their counterpart, some play outside of the box of the game established norms, and some just break the rules of the game’s mechanics entirely. The amount of variety here is staggering, and you’ll be hard-pressed to not be able to find someone you like playing as.
#2. I’m going to give you a few concepts: Fighting games. Beat-’em/slash-’em-ups. Retro games. Do any of those appeal to you in any way? Then you need to give this game a look, because that’s what DFO is: A homage to old-school beat-’em-ups and retro fighters, all wrapped in a well-made MMORPG package, and it’s free to play. 2D sprites in a 2.5D world, able to jump (but not platform) and move in eight directions, able to do 3-4 basic attacks and a glossary of skills to do some sick combos, all with the complimentary mechanics that RPGs give you, such as status effects, crit and damage multipliers, etc. You know the drill.
#3. Good lord, the events and updates Neople churns out on a regular basis. Since the beta of this game’s revival, there has not been a single moment where there hasn’t been at least 5 events going on. There’s always something to do outside the norm of the game, some event-exclusive reward to hang as a trophy, many event-consistent rare or cash shop-only items the game practically showers you with, something to make leveling tons easier,  something to help you get that much closer to your ultimate weapon… I could go on and on.
#4. I love this game’s soundtrack. Definitely in the top 10 of my favorite video game soundtracks. It’s primarily rock and metal, but DFO throws isn’t afraid to throw in some orchestra, electronica, pop, or even rap in the mix. I honestly don’t think there’s any bad songs, and I could count how many songs that could be considered “average” on my hand. I’m confident you’ll find something in this game that will hit you in the sweet spot and get you hype to play every time you boot it up.
#5. A very brief history lesson about the CS of DFO back during during its Nexon NA run: It was garbage. It’s very easy to be better than garbage, but regardless, Neople’s customer support is soaring leagues above Nexon NA’s. My experience with them has been very pleasant so far. They will usually respond to you in a matter of days, or worst case scenario, about a week. They’re very helpful and will work with you in fixing any issues, so don’t worry, ♥♥♥♥♥♥ things will actually get resolved this time.
Also, don’t think the reviews on DFO’s store page are lying to you. Neople is actually overwhelmingly supportive of both its game and its playerbase.
Cons (Ranked in terms of woe):
#1. I’ll be clear, DFO endgame is really fun and entertainingly challenging, but the biggest grievance is getting the ultimate endgame gear for your character/class of choice. There’s two types of said gear you typically want to shoot for: Epics or Legendaries. The drop/craft success rates of these can be painfully low, but compared to older builds of DFO, the accessibility of attempting these tasks is so, so much easier. However, your odds are still stacked against you heavily. You have many options, but they’re all very difficult, so pick your poison and stick with it.
A word of reassurance, though: Once you overcome all the painful obstacles and get all the awesome gear you need for your class, you will basically become a God. Everything will pay off and you will obliterate everything that stands before you, no matter how hard it is.
#2. Now, this is a part of the game that doesn’t bother me personally, but I’ve seen a lot of people complain about this over the years, and some who wouldn’t even play the game because of it: The Fatigue Point system, or FP for short. Fatigue is a bar right along the top of your bottom UI, and it tells you how much you can do in the game until it runs out and you can’t play with that character anymore.
There are ways to circumvent fatigue, such as having multiple characters to play as once the fatigue of one runs out, or single-use FP potions that restore some or all of your fatigue, or having a Premium Contract (DFO’s premium service) active which gives you 2x the maximum fatigue. However, the fatigue for your character will eventually run out no matter how long you prolong it, and you’ll have to wait for the reset time to come up before you can do runs with them again.
#3. This is something about DFO I really wish wasn’t a problem. DFO doesn’t have an option to hide megaphone chat. Texts from megaphones appear no matter what chat channel you have up, nor how many chat options you disable. It’s extremely unfortunate, since a small revamp of how the megaphone chat works can easily fix this issue. Sadly, players will have to deal with the disruptive yellow text that appears in their chat boxes on a daily basis. The content of them is 50/50, the good being simple trading requests, guild recruiting, or silly comments. The bad, though, can expose players to really toxic and ignorant subjects, soiling the reputation of the DFO community. All I can really tell you is to ignore it as best you can during the bad times.
#4. DFO is a F2P game, so naturally, it’s going to have some systems in place to get you to spend your money. It’s not the worst out there, but it’s not the best either. If you want more inventory space, bank space, etc, you’ll have to pay up. The good thing is, though, as I touched upon in Pro #3, Neople is always showering the playerbase with rare or cash shop-only items. You may not be able to trade paid currency like in Warframe, but you at least have a high chance to get whatever you might need through an event going on, or an event to come later.
#5. Despite being a low-tech game more about efficiency that grandeur, the game still has a few technical hiccups. I’ve had issues where after I start up the game, the game will have very brief moments where it freezes, then resumes as normal, the frequency of them fading to 0 the more I play. I’ve also had times where, extremely rarely, my game would just suddenly crash. I can’t really offer an explanation for the latter, but I know the former is because the game is still loading in assets after starting, and it’s apparently a problem shared amongst most players.

This review is done on an Early Acess build. Updates and fixes should solve some things stated within.
ArcheBlade is quite a unique take on the MOBA genre and it feels pretty solid in its current build. Apart from slight bugs and a few distasteful map designs, ArcheBlade has a way of bringing me back again and again. Yet each area may need separate sections to get a better idea of the grand scheme.
Characters -
Variety in character design really makes the MOBA genre stand out and making sure that each one brings something new is a must have to keep games like these thriving. From numerous hours of gameplay, each character seemed to be generally fleshed out. Not one character really seemed to have complete control over the game and the playstyle of the respective character seemingly forced ways of approaching fights. Rather than a hack and slash type fighter, each character is capable of turning around a battle in their favor. However, currently the character pool seems a little misplaced. While playing, I felt the urge to play a classic swordsmen but only to be given a tank type whose attacks were too slow paced to keep up in large scale fights. I found myself going for objectives and defending them than really  attacking anyone, as the mobility of others was far greater and left me spinning araound in circles 'till I died. There was only one magic type character that I saw that had  potential but rarely gets played due to a visibly weak skill set.
Maps -
ArcheBlade has 8 current maps which have 4 map specific gamemodes embedded into them. These consist of Deathmatch,TeamDM, a Domination variant, and a round based arena. The maps themselves are very well done artisitcally yet can be a bit incovenient to play on. A few of the maps I had the opportunity to play on were easily campable. Some were also prone to "snowballing" and this made it difficult for either team to make a comeback. One map in particular has a large hole ranging from the top of the map, down through the rest of the floors within the level. Although an interesting concept, some areas around the pit were very easy to fall through. Me and a few friends found ourselves falling time and time again because of poor world clipping in this particular map. The map also encouraged jumping into the pit to obtain health capsules that were placed in an arc to direct the player to a safe landing. However, in the midst of battle, jumping into a pit is a last ditch effort to stay alive. Miraculously ending up in the arched path to health and safety was nearly impossible unless planned.
Other notes -
ArcheBlade is a very fun and engaging game and I will come back to it in future updates. But I do want to get across a few ideas for improving the game. One thing I would like to see is a new gamemode specific to ArcheBlade. Although tried and true gamemodes in new games can make the game enjoyable, innovative gamemodes can bring a great experience to an already great game. Another would be more fluid movement controls and the ability to move while attacking. Some characters are capable of this already yet a few fall short due to a lack of mobility while atacking. Being stuck in place in a fight can lead to certain death, which can cost you a game or two. Making attacking animations run while moving can improve some characters usefulness in battle.
All in all, I'd say try this one out. It is definitely a game to look forward to and in it's current state, it is very fun to play. If you're into mulitplayer fighting games and can learn character mechanics fairly quickly, this should be right up your ballpark.

Don't waste too much time on this game.
There are some good things about it! Some of the scenarios are genuinely fun, like the last match in Liliana's Origins storyline - but there are too many things that are broken to make playing worthwhile. What finally convinced me to give up on it was the match against Baral's Lieutenant in Chandra's storyline - every time I cast a Fire Elemental, the game crashed.
This wasn't the first issue - in the tutorial, there would be a pop-up saying something like "Block the attacking creatures," when there were no creatures attacking. (I did eventually get the tutorial to work by quitting the game and re-launching.) The sound seems to be messed up, occasionally becoming very loud or very quiet for no discernable reason.
Besides the straight-up bugs, there are some serious design issues - there's a timer for phases, steps, and resolving effects, but it doesn't stop when a spell or effect is added to the stack, meaning you have to have very quick fingers if you want to respond to a spell your opponent casts. On the other hand, the timer always stops when it gets to the "declare blockers" step, even when you don't have any valid blockers. Previous "Duels of the Planeswalkers" games had an option to auto-pause for each step/phase/spell cast, but that is no longer an option in this incarnation.
Basically, despite the bugs, this game might be fine for new players. It's free-to-play, and it might be the "gateway drug" you've been looking for to get into MtG. However, if you're an experienced player or want to take a more strategic approach to the game, "Duels" is NOT the way to go.

Disclaimer: The hours played is not true, ive been a part of Dungeon Fighter Online since the days of Nexon, and have probably sank well over 3k+ hours into it
Dungeon fighter Online is one of the most unique experiences in gaming i have found.
Blending an Arcade Beat-em-up Action-packed game with an MMO environment, DFO is in its own unique world. Now, its worth keeping in mind that this game is not for everyone. However, this game scratches an itch no other games are able to get to, and it scratches it well.
This is by no means a perfect game, as there are issues that arise. but the amount of pros that exist definitely outway the cons
PROS:
-Gameplay. Dungeon Fighter Online has numerous characters, several subclasses for each, and hundreds of skills in general. Each character will feel different, play differently, and will be a unique experience in its own right. Not only that, but the combat system is absolutely energetic, with smooth transistions between skills, and is an absolute blast to both play and watch.
-Community. Honestly, finding a great community is what makes this game best. There will always be bad apples in games, but 90% of the community is friendly towards both newcomers and veterans, and are willing to help out and participate in any way they can. I highly recommend finding a good guild to join, as it makes the experience of playing DFO 10x better.
-Developers. Neople are miles ahead of what Nexon did with Dungeon Fighter Online. Every employee seems to be passionate about the game, And with keeping it as up-to-date to the Korean Version as possible. They truly care about the community, and are always looking for constructive criticism and advice from the community to make Dungeon Fighter Online the best it can be.
Mixed:
-Graphics. Now, this is by no means a beautiful game. It is stylized in the old-school Side-scrolling Arcade games, pixels and all. If you are looking for an MMO that is absolutely gorgeous, then this is not it. That being said, what are gorgeous are the animations. The skill animations in this game are absolutely bonkers, and feel as powerful as the damage they do. It is definitely not a pretty game to look at in terms of base graphics, but the animations truly make up for it.
-Arena. The PvP in this game is a ton of fun, as it is with most fighting games. It is absolutely a blast to go in and play against friends or guild members, and just duke it out. However, PvP  has had multiple issues lately, including some scripters/hackers, etc. Once the issue of Hackers is resolved, and some adjustments are made to the ranking system, The PvP system will once again be amazing to participate in.
Cons:
-Grinding. If you think youve played an MMO where the grinding was the worst, and thought "nothing could be worse than this", you are sadly wrong. It is worth noting that the level grind that used to exist is pretty much all but gone (except for levels 55-70. ♥♥♥♥ Ghent). However, the end-game particiation grinding is the worst that I've ever seen. The worst part about it is that most of the end-game gear is pure RNG. For some people it takes just weeks to get most end-game itemizations and gear, while others (like myself) have been grinding for well over 8 months and still have barely scratched the surface on what is needed. While leveling is much better, the grind to late-game is one of the absolute worst, and truly needs to be addressed.
All-in-All,  the sytle, gameplay, and grinding will not appeal to everyone. BUT. for those that do, it will be a truly unique experience found nowhere else in gaming, and will keep you hooked and wanting for more. While there is still some polishing and attention needed to be done, there is a reason why the korean version is considered one of the highest-grossing MMOs of all-time. 8.5/10

Where do i begin?
-Physics-
The Physics in this game are completely different from the past games, they are more like a simcade
Its not Assetto Corsa or Project Cars kind of simulation level but it still has a little touch as a Simcade game.
-Cars-
Haven't heard of half the cars in this game and didn't know they existed, surprised me a lot. just like Race Driver GRID back in 2008, full of surprises!
And of course the detail in the cars is insane in terms of damage and such.
-Tunning-
I always wanted the customization at Autosport since 2008 and i finally got it!
Finally i can set down force, suspensions, brakes bias, differential etc the way i always wanted!
I can upgrade my engine, clutch and more stuff under my hood! insane!
-Tracks-
A huge amount of tracks in this game, all around Europe, Asia, Australia, America and more based on real life. as good as it gets they are big as well.
-Graphics-
Beautiful graphics, and my pc is not amazing and i still manage to run it on high with a 16:9 resolution and get a really good fps. so i'll admit, the game engine is as good as it is since always!
-Car Sounds-
Obviously not the only game which has really realistic engine sounds and definitely not the best one.
But they are great and i love them, and they make me wanna boost my corsair all the way to 100% volume.
-Multiplayer-
Compared to GRID 2, this game finally brought back the wide space roads from GRID 2008 which means multiplayer is actually playable without having the whole lobby totaled at the first few corners.
Match making is nice too, i can find races fast and easily without too much pain and also have a voice chat feature which is nice.
Weekly/Daily multiplayer challenges are cool too.
And i love the fact that i can buy whatever car i want again whether its a brand new car or a used car from "ebay".
Just like the old days in GRID 2008!
-Controller Support-
Supports joypads, gamepads, wheel, keyboard and everything you can dream of.
The game is also very balanced so its very playable with keyboard as well for a simcade.
-Camera-
Good to see the rewind feature is still here, very useful indeed!
And the replay feature after finishing a race also has an option to hide hud and upload on youtube directly from the game.
Also has various cameras positions which is cool as well.
The only down sides of this game i could think of are:
-A broken cockpit cam
-Can't make my own team and hire my own team mates
-No drifting mountains like the old days.
But overall, i'm glad codemasters listened to the community and its requests and gave us most of the things we asked for.
We were also introduced to Drag which is brand new to GRID which is cool as well!
8/10 from me, i really want those drift mountains.

Marvel Puzzle Quest (MPQ), is a mobile device port for steam. Is that necessarily a bad thing? I don't think so, but it is something that you need to keep in mind when looking at the UI and graphics. It also effects the pay system, and since this is a F2P game, that's something people tend to focus on. So let's start there:
Can you play MPQ without spending money? Yes. Will you be competitive... well, mostly. Let's talk about what real money gets used for: You can purchase the two types of in-game currency with real money. ISO and Gold. ISO is used, mainly, to purchase boosts for use during combat and to spend to level up your characters. It is the common currency of the game and is earned pretty easily. Gold can be used for a number of things. You can purchase additional slots to hold more characters (you are limited to 4 characters at the start and the prices for additional slots increases the more you have), you can purchase some "super-boosts", you can purchase health packs, and you can purchase additional covers for your characters. Do you "have" to purchase these things? Nope. You do earn some gold through normal game play, and many people (myself included) have found that if you focuse your purchases you don't really hit a wall for a very long time.
Let's move onto the gameplay itself. MPQ is a tile matching game that is themed around the Marvel Comic Universe. You swap tiles on a grid board to make 3 or longer chains of the same color/shape (think Bejewelled), you then score a hit dealing damage and (in most cases) generated Ability Points (AP) of that color. Each character that you have selected (three) will have different abilities both passive and active. These abilities are often fuelled by the AP you generate from your matches. Pretty simple. There is an entertaining amount of depth in selecting which team you want to bring to an event, and finding good synergy between character abilities is important.
The characters are leveled up by unlocking their skills. Skills are found by getting random drop "Covers". Each cover has one skill associated with it. Once you have used that cover to train the character in that skill it will increase the "Current Max Level" of the character, you can then use ISO to increase the level of the character. Every level increase raises the max Hit Points of the character, the amount of damage they do and the effectivness of their skills. Once you have unlocked the first level of the skill you can use Gold to increase the skill level (this is the main form of Pay-to-Win that you see in the game, but is limited by the fact that you have to have the base skill first to buy it).
Health of your characters is the delaying factor in playing. Not only are you doing damage to your enemies, but they are doing damage to your characters as well. Their health will increase back to max over time, but with high level characters this can take several hours. If you take your three best characters into a match that is over their head and get them all killed, this can mean that you don't get to play again for a few hours... unless you use Health Packs. Health packs allow a character to return to full health immediately. You earn health packs over time, one every 30 minutes, but could buy additionals for Gold.
The game provides some basic "PVE" missions to get a feel for the game and earn some basic covers and boosts, but the main part of the game that allows you to progress is the "PVP" duels and "PVE" events. Events rotate every few days and give opportunities for rare and high end rewards, but competition can be tough and some events require having certain characters to participate. Duels are a staple way to put your team against another player. The duels aren't really PVP though, because the same AI that runs the normal missions just uses the team, not an actual player.
Long and the short of it: I find MPQ to be very entertaining, something that I have spent many an hour with and am perfectly happy to keep playing. There are issues, some bugs that break events and some exploits that people have found that can let them rank up super fast, and there are concerns about Pay-To-Win, but overall I can say that if you are looking for a casual time waster, this does the job rather well.

Beyond Earth needs to leave Earth behind.
One of the best features of Alpha Centauri - this game's spiritual forerunner - was that it wasn't just a rehash of Civ2. Its factions weren't just civilizations, even if they carried clear influences of them: they were aligned around ideologies and megomaniacal leaders with clear agendas and personalities. It gave me people to root for and against, making my ultimate victories more satisfying. By comparison, Beyond Earth offers me a bland pantheon of nondescript leaders from civilizations I've alreay played to death in Civ1-5. And I don't care if you've introduced the Slavs and the Brazilians: give me the Hive versus the Morganites. Give me Provost Zacharov and Lady Deidre Skye. Give me rivals with some personality.
I should also mention: I hated Civ5, as much as I tried to like it (it lost the epic feel of Civ4). But the reason I kept trying to play it was that it was beautiful, with amazing renderings of landscapes and an art-deco UI. The terrain of Beyond Earth, by constast, is dark and ugly, covered in clashing greens and oranges that make me think I've landed in the trash heap of a prior civilization. That may give it an alien feel, but it's not an alien feel that makes me want to do anything other than find a different planet to conquer.

e: Changed review to Do Recommend based on latest update. Many of the issues noted below have been resolved and a number of nice new features have been added, including the completion of the tour circuit allowing travel back home through the countries you passed in your journey. This game is starting to shape up into something really pleasing to play. There are still a couple minor and sometimes aggravating bugs still but they are much less prevalent and ruinous. I will leave the previous remarks in for now.
Original Review:
Jalopy is currently an Early Access title with a great concept and solid aesthetic, if you like the idea of fixing up and maintaining a car, with satisfying interactions and an intuitive and unintrusive UI between world and player that is generally pretty neat. I really do like the game, however the EA state of the game as it is, is not ready for primetime. You must be willing to deal with some issues at this stage in development, and some of them are real buzzkills.
The Good:
Driving has a nice springy feel to it but analog inputs are not fully working yet. There is a lot missing from the game at this point in time, but it is worth noting what is there so far. There is an interesting procedural generation engine in place that can make many unique town combinations, and some interesting roadside features and discoveries that may turn up, but overall the levels are maybe a bit too bland, more variety and alternate paths (there are some) would be nice. The music is good, the atmosphere of driving in rain with the lights and radio on is sublime at times.
The Bad:
The biggest problem with the game and the reason why I cannot currently recommend the game to the average buyer, is the frequent and inevitable bugs that can affect your save file, rendering your sometimes rough journeys a total loss when you get home, and find your upgrades missing. Many physics and stat glitches exist to the point where it is not really possible to explore the content of the game to your satisfaction, as many acquisitions will often be wiped from your inventory, car build, and even garage storage. The save files and general data handling in the game needs a complete overhaul, it is a buggy mess.
Bottom Line:
So, if you like the concept and are willing to chip in to support the game's development, as I was, with no regrets, then consider checking Jalopy out. Otherwise, to anyone wishing to get a solid playable game for their money should avoid this game for now. It is neat, it is pleasing at first, but it has a number of hidden disappointments and frustrations that will find you if you try to fully explore the game.
If the save corruption issue were addressed I would be able to recommend this judged as an Early Access title, most of the other bugs are not game-wrecking.

Bleed is an action packed shoot em up indie platformer sacrificed in hell and resurrected in heaven by Jesus himself. This game by developer Ian Campbell brings incredible gameplay with illustrious graphics to another level where it kicks you off the edge whispering into your ear “don’t die.” With these words of wisdom ringing in your mind you pick up the controller and begin one of the toughest fights of your life.
Its games like Bleed that from the moment you watch the trailer you know that it isn’t too far from your hard drive. Unlike many of those games on that hard drive, Bleed sets itself aside from others of its genre with several different elements such as the ability to slow time at the touch of a button. Bleed also leaves a lot of the main characters abilities and stats up to you, this is done through the shop that you are able to visit prior to each level. During each level, you are graded depending on how creative you are with your gameplay, and awarded coins conducive to the grade achieved at the end. These coins are what are used to purchase each upgrade and are vital to this game’s progression.
The heroine of this game is Wryn, a girl with a big dreams and an even bigger arsenal. Your goal as Wryn is to become the ultimate video game hero, and in an action packed bid to claim the title for herself, she must take down the greatest heroes of all time. Bleed is focused on stylish, acrobatic dodging and fluid, challenging gameplay, where Wryn will have to use those abilities to kill hordes of enemies, endure backbreaking obstacles and overpower inventive bosses. Her bitter sarcasm after every tragic death leaves you with a personal vendetta against each level, not to mention a bruised ego.
I give this game 5 broken controllers, because even on the easiest difficulty setting Bleed is more challenging than prying the crack pipe out of Whitney Houstons cold dead lips. The weaponry in Bleed focuses around heavy artillery, starting you off with twin guns and a rocket launcher. By gaining coins throughout each level you can buy new weapons such as a flamethrower or even remote mines. No need to worry about bullets, Wryn seems to have an extended clip with more rounds than the hero of your favorite 80′s cop film. Bleed is fast paced, combined with an intuitive sense of time along with an attention to aiming making gameplay one of a kind.
Offering an EXTRAS option in the main menu extends gameplay making Bleed’s replay value higher than most. With two different modes, Arcade & Challenge, Arcade Mode can be unlocked by beating the story mode, and Challenge Mode consists of fighting bosses complete with your choice of arena. Bleed has a multiplayer option that is available anytime during the Story Mode of the single player campaign as well. Two times the power can sometimes be a burden if you can’t keep up, but also provides the effectiveness needed to complete your objective. Also, each different level is replayable in whatever difficulty may suit you. This way you are able to purchase each of the upgrades and fully experience the game, taking down anything that may come in your path.
After playing the demo and then buying the game during the Steam summer sale, in true Bleed fashion I give it a B+. Bleed catches the eye, paired with addictive gameplay and intuitive dynamics it is destined for success. Although a tough one, this game is a joy to play and even better with friends. Endless creativity at your thumbs, there isn’t a bad thing I can think of when it comes to Bleed. Needless to say, the game is beautifully designed and creativity “bleeds” out of every scene, making this game well worth the buy.
Graphics: 7/10
Playability: 7/10
Story: 5/10
Challenge: 9/10
Replay Value: 7/10

Have played a lot of this game before it reached Steam. It has a very tycoon feel to it while being very puzzle like in the builds. It currently has 35 different challenge senarios that all have randomly generated buildings and ingredients with randomly generated possitives and negitives each time you start a new challenge so you can very much play the same challenge over and over and get an entirely different play through each and every time. The machines mechanics are for the most part well expained though there are some things that you learn by just doing.
And say you don't like any of the scenarios or have beaten the master rank (basicly gold in a gold/silver/bronze rating system) of all the scenarios (which would take a long time to do even if your great at the game)  custom game has a ton of customization to it, choose anywhere from 0-3 competitors, 5-15 randomly generated ingredients, where you start with 2-5, how many catilist there are and their side effects, victory conditions of total revenue, operating profit, within x years, x products with atleast x profit or value or level, minimun cure rating, total products, and pay off loan, which you can combine in any fation, so say you want the winning condition to be where you have to have 3 pills that all make atleast $1,000 profit per pill produced all with atleast B cure rating within 15 years with no competitors, you can do that. You can also set what research you (and all competitors) start with and even what research is disabled in the game (so say you don't want anybody to be able to make patents you can disable patents).
Then you get into settings like map size, event frequency, loan interest rates, plot cost, research speed, scientist saleries, scientiest hire cost, explorer saleries and hire costs, analyzing speed, patent speed, patent cost, cure market size, cure profit margins, starting money, starting loan, ingredient prices, process costs, build costs, research point accrual speed, ingredient point accrual speed, cure rate, infection rate... and all of these things don't have just like 5 settings, they are all sliders that have many many settings even if its not good at informing that well (for example plot cost you could set to where it says low and the first land may cost $500, but then you set it again in low but slightly in a different slider cost and now it costs $480 or $620 for the first one.
Between the randomly generated buildings, the randomly generated ingredients, the number of custom challenges with 3 ratings that are fairly challenging to get the best rank on, and the sheer customability of custom games, you will find that this game is very replayable even doing the same challenge or even same custom game settings because even with the exact same custom settings the buildings and ingredients are randomly generated each time which also means what the competitors make which effects your profit margins also changes each time. And can be as challenging or easy as you want it to be. And even as quick or long as you want it to be depending on how you set all the custom game sliders and victory conditions.

I've been playing Big Pharma via a non-Steam version and have been really enjoying it. I'd played at least a dozen hours before the 1.0 release and have been very please with how the developer has not only been regularly updating the game, but also responding to community inputs and making changes based on them.
I'd have to say that it's partly a puzzle game, in that you have to build assembly lines that require some planning and tinkering to fit them in the available space and also to spend as little money as possible. And you have to research more efficient (abet more costly) production machines that take up less space.
It's also a business sim, in that you buy resourses, process them and then produce a product. This is done very well in the game because you don't have to stare at spreadsheets, instead you can just mouse over the production lines or your company page and the appropriate info is right there. And it's very easy to understand where you are making and losing money, in fact I'd say that this game is one of the best examples of how to make a business sim right.
And the other nice feature that I like is that the game is composed of a number of scenarios/missions, most of which have three different levels of victory, and you don't have to unlock any particular mission to play any other of them. Plus there's also a custom game mode, where you can alter all sorts of criteria and conditions, and a free build mode where you can just make assembly lines and geek out on that.

Not Earth shattering but it's pretty decent. It can best be described as "chill". I don't know the ends and out completely. What I will say if you're and aging MMOer looking for something a bit slower in pace and casual this is a strong choice.
Basically, if you want something close to traditional to tide you over until Pantheon this is a great choice if you are exhausted of WoW, Rift, and other more traditional style mmos. This seems to have some of that community-oriented styling Pantheon is talking about except it's obviousl more casual. So log in, Kickback and relax... Until Pantheon comes and ruin our lives!
Update(now that I understand the game better): I admit it. I'm a crafting hater. Crafting is stupid!  Yet, somehow I find it enjoyable in this game. How did they achieve this? Well, the crafting is very much inter-dependant. If you are working on one skill you are gaining materials for that one and another. They also, wisely put centralized areas where you can just go, gather materials and craft. There is also NO PASS/FAIL. If you make it, you made it. The way the system is setup is: One day you will probably spend your session crafting(I never thought I would spend a play session in a MMORPG just crafting.). Other days you'll quest and move along the story.
PVE: Is largely solo and basic but it works. It becomes much better when you get more skills. Combat is not "Twitch". I would say that speedwise it's pretty close to FFXIV.
Community: Super-friendly. Even I'm geting in on the act. It reminds me of early WoW when as a healer you  would see someone fighting and just decide to throw them some heals(nowadays you just get a "lol" whisper). Someone described the game as  PHP: Players Helping Players. That's an accurate assessment.
PVP: May it never rear it's head into this relaxing underrated gem of a game(unless it's on a seperate server and the buff/nerfs are kept separate from the PHP(hehe) servers).
Shop: I spent money. You don't have to. You don't have to because you aren't really "racing" towards anything. The major bosses are events or Elders that in some cases can be solo'd(not Event Bosses). Because of the "Rebirth" sytem there will be opportunities to  group for low level players and higher level members in the community will even show up to help you from time to time. I grabbed a 3 month subscription and some enchants just because. You are playing just to move the story forward, largely. The High level Gear will come as long as you put in the work. Money just speeds up "aquiring" various materials which just moves things along faster. There is no PVP so I'd be hard-pressed to call that pay-to-win(what are you winning exactly? lol). I would say this shop is the closest I've seen to "I like this game so I'm gonna spend some money".
Tips and Tricks: Auto-Clickers don't seemed to be frowned upon. You should get it if you can. You will however earn Motes of Yorick which can help you "Mass Produce" i.e. Crafting 50 items in 1 click. As far as Crafting is concerned try to keep your crafting equal or higher than your Character Level( I'm personally trying to keep my crafting 5 levels ahead so I can spend more time questing).
Criticism I don't mind the graphics or gameplay(which could be considered "old" by some people's standard). My lone criticism is while the game is somewhat soloable I would like to see a better LFG system.

A swell online beat-em-up with a vast plethora of diverse classes encompassing many playstyles and roles in party play; it competently showcases excessively fun 2D graphics and gameplay in its aged game engine, but stylistically so.  A streamlined leveling process with mildly interesting lore through various landscapes guides you to max level 86 in a week for invested veterans to two or three for new players.   Please understand this review is relatively simplified and generalized, but hopefully it is able to better inform your decision.
Akin to many MMOs however, do expect the honeymoon period to end to reveal the classic wall of grinding.  Repetitive daily progression gating, and the optional endgame obsession with minmaxing and obtaining best-in-slot (BIS) equipment through expensive RNG. These processes can take from weeks to months and years to realize; so, if you're looking for a game to become dedicated in, be sure you understand and accept these mechanics henceforth.  If you're into that though, DFO does have a decent amount of endgame content, from entry-level gearing in Oververse to Anton where party composition and boss pattern knowledge is required (with the raid variant that requires five simultaneous parties coming soon™).  It currently does not really have any single challenging endgame area where you can farm for tradable gear and gold to accumulate wealth with great efficiency and consistency.
No doubt though, if you have a friend to run casually together as an old-school brawler type of game, DFO is a great candidate for scratching that itch for free.  It is also equally viable to casually drop in and out of, and likely part of the overall intended design.
This review will now focus and describe its prevailing pay-2-win and microtransactions systems.  I would recommend reading through other peer reviews to have a better sense of gameplay and general mechanics who would describe it better than me!
Caveat emptor from my prospective, DFO is a P2W game, but the majority of game content is oriented toward free players.  The most important aspect to note here is that Neople's small international team quite readily offers the more mild contract microtransactions through events; it is not unusual for an active player to accumulate hundreds of days worth in contracts after good events.
Cosmetically, DFO offers a lot for players to dress their individual characters. Most of these are offered in packages that can be purchased with real money or usually bought off the auction house with in-game gold; however, contracts and other useful items and equips are often included with the bundle.
The main criticism lies in what is essentially openly-facilitated real money investment into gold currency; as described above although not limited to, avatar packages and other microtransactions such as lost treasure raffle prizes can be converted into in-game power.  Examples include buying a liberation weapon for a fresh level 86 character that would otherwise take several weeks in grinding dailies, and buying endgame RNG (hell mode) admission materials to obtain BIS gear.  While free players can still obtain optimal gear and are not paywall locked, undoubtedly those who pay can reach their set endgame at a far greater accelerated pace than anyone else.
Overall however, you won't generally won't directly feel the adverse affects from such systems existing aside from PVP.
