"Dungeon and Fighter" - that's the name of the game that got its first release in Korea eleven years ago, and would turn out to become one of the biggest, most popular MMOs in the world.
Featuring action packed, 2D combat, based on games of the old, DnF stood out among all the other MMOs in the market, and that is perhaps one of the main reasons it became so popular around Korea and other regions.
In the U.S, the game was originally released as "DFO" under Nexon, who promptly ran the game into the ground not too much time later. Soon after, Neople, DnF's developer in Korea, would publish the game themselves under the name "Dungeon Fighter Online Global", with a much improved service compared to the days of old.
While this version may not be as popular as in Korea or China, it nonetheless still is the same game that any fan of classic games like Double Dragon will be able to enjoy.
The game differentiates itself from other MMOs with its unique gameplay: there are 13 classes in total, with almost all of them being able to branch out into different subclasses. Each subclass is, in turn, completely unique amongst each other. For example, the Male Slayer can become an Asura, a blind swordsman who uses light-based attacks to cleave through their enemies, or the Soul Bender, a shadow-based subclass who can put circles on the ground that debuff all inside them.
Combine with that the fact that skills are initially unlocked every five levels, keeping things fresh and allowing you new ways to go through dungeons; the old but still good and detailed graphics; the actually decent story, and you have an addicting experience that can hook anyone, with even oldtimers being able to level several different characters to cap and still enjoy a new experience everytime.
Not all is good, though. The game is eleven years old, and thus shows its age. Whether it be in some animations, balance or mechanics – such as the FP system, which isn't actually bad, but can be discouraging to some new players – some things may simply be a little outdated to someone who has played other newer games.
Despite its flaws, however, DnF and its English version Dungeon Fighter Online Global is still an amazing game that is matched in its gameplay by few MMOs in the market today. Its publisher, Neople, is much better than Nexon, and has even successfully managed to control goldsellers, a feat few companies could be proud of.
As someone who was skeptic when I first heard of this, I've now personally poured thousands of hours into this game. If you're someone who may be in the fence whether to play, I recommend you give it a try and play it a couple days, even if you may not like the FP system at the beginning. Trust me, you may end up loving the game after all!

Dungeon Fighter Online (DFOG) is a American/European port of the Korean version, "Dungeon and Fighter" (KDNF). DFOG is very different from Nexon DFO (ran 2010 to 2013), it is now in good hands of the Neople team. Although not as much content as the Korean version, DFOG has most of it.
I highly recommend you to come back. It improved greatly with more content:
- Level cap raised from 70 to 86.
- More Dungeons
- 2nd Awakenings
- Awakening Quest is much easier to accomplish
- Scenario feature which helps players get back into action easier.
- EXP curve is lower
- Frequent Events almost every week
- Not hosted by Nexon
- Old Pre-Gent dungeons are somewhat gone and replaced with New dungeons
- Widesceen support
- Female Slayer and Knight classes
I won't deny it, there is somewhat pay-to-win elements. Most of it is buying packages which include auras and Titles which boost stats. But you can still get the packages/titles without using real money using the auction house. You can also buy "Contracts" which lower the level requirement to equip Items and raise skills, but these are time based and don't last well long term. Everyone has a chance to get these items though. You could buy them directly, but they can also be obtained from frequent events and "Lost Treasures" (aka. Crate and Key system, but can also be dropped from enemies.)
(Known as FP) where it
. Yes, it is frowned upon today in the gaming world, but it
(Keeps the economy intact).  Even the cash users are limited by FP, sure they get more FP but everyone still limited. It's not so bad since you can create multiple characters so you can play more. It does motivate people from creating new characters since each character has their own separate FP usage. the Just keep in mind you can only create 2 characters per day. And once you have many characters, you can pretty much play DFO all day.
The Difficulty at the first 5 areas (not dungeons) is very easy. As you could just wreck the monsters and breeze through. However at the Gent dungeons (Level 55+), the difficulty start ramping up to where more effort is required. The community likes to call the dungeons 70 and below "Tutorial" to the real game as an example.
Semi-end game dungeons (Otherverse/Ancients dungeons) are very gimmick based.
The soundtrack is top-notch. The music varies from shredding guitars, sorrow violins, and orchestra.
Overall, 8/10 game. Not perfect, but the game is still fun to my eyes. Sure, there is limits to how much a character can play per day, but the side-dungeons (Costs no FP) and Events (Bonus FP) make up for it.

dungeon fighter online is a 2.5d beat em up dungeon crawler rpg , you pick your class, advance your class, and then level up obtaining new skills and equipment along the way to max level
what makes this game so special to me though, is just how many classes and subclasses there are, and of course the majority of the classes are completely different, although there are similarities between male/female gunners and fighters, but even then their classes play differently from the other gender
another really cool feature about this game is the really unique pvp. when you're not fighting the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t summoning classes high skilled pvp matches can be insanely difficult and fun
on the downside pvp in this is insanely broken with lag being a massive problem, as well as the pvp community being very small
dear new players: do not be afraid of the fatigue system! it is only a real limitation towards new players, as you become a higher level you will understand just how much slower you actually use the fatigue system, and even if you still continue to play that much there are plenty of items to regenerate it. neople will also surely be giving plenty of items with the steam release for all the new players so that they don't run out of fatigue
as for leveling, it is fairly simple as all you really have to do is do scenario dungeons (which are given to you by the epic questlines), and occasionally doing circulation dungeons (one of the normal options) when you run out of scenario dungeons. as for partying, it is very easy to level up quickly with scenario dungeons so usually you don't see many people partying until later in the game where scenarios might not be enough to level up. hopefully with the steam release, with the increase in players more people will be able to party together for fun and whatnot
one of the large problems with this game however (although it can be compared to other mmorpgs), is the insane and massive grind to fully gear your character (varying from class), as it is locked behind essentially daily quest walls, and RNG walls
really though, you shouldn't let this get in your way, don't let the end game tier lists restrict you from whoever you want to play, there are so many classes for you to try out that eventually you will find one you enjoy and ideally will stick with it. all that matters in the end is finding that just right class

tl;dr bretty grett
+
Around 42 different subclasses and counting, each boasting either subtle or very different playstyles, meaning there's bound to be a playstyle that suits every kind of player.
+
Events usually cycle out every 2 weeks and patches appear anywhere from 2 weeks to every month, meaning content will remain fresh so as long as you keep playing.
+
In addition to variations in gameplay thanks to the different subclasses, end-game loot can dramatically change the way you play, allowing further customization to cater to one's playstyle.
+
While the playerbase is more on the small side, finding a group/guild with people willing to help you out won't be a issue. There's a small vocal minorty of bad apples, but ofc there's gonna be some in every game.
NEUTRAL:
~
Like many Asian MMOs, the main objective of the game is to acquire/upgrade gear in order to move into the next tier of gear, a process which can take anywhere from a couple days to months.
~
The levelling process is more like a "tutorial" phase where you learn the ropes of the subclass you're levelling. A lot of the upcoming patches are focused towards adding more tiers of gear and extra content to those who are level-capped.
~
Each character can only be played as long as they have fatigue left, which is lost whenever you enter a dungeon. Afterwards, you can't play on that character until the next day.
~
Some premium items, such as aesthetic avatar packages, are bought with real money but can be sold to players in the in-game Auction House with gold. However, gold is a lot less effective at getting gear than hard work, so take it as you will.
~
There's some PvP content where you can battle against others to climb a ranked ladder, though there are some flaws which are listed later.
~
A lot of content is either locked behind a daily limit or gives diminishing returns after enough runs. This can quickly set up a schedule for players to follow and can get tedious at some points.
CONS:
-
A lot of gear is less locked behind completing hard dungeons and moreso behind a random number generator. Some players can gear their player up quickly with enough luck, while some may never see their end-game fantasy. While there's a lot of features that heavily mitigates this issue, both current and future patches, it's still a prominent issue that tends to be thrown around a lot.
-
- Although the servers are intended for a global audience, the game still uses a peer-2-peer system when connecting with other players. This usually makes it so that harder content is generally reserved for friends or guildmates rather than pubs, and severly cripples PvP.

The limited amount of hours listed on my Steam playtime can't even begin to show the hundreds of hours I've sunk into Dungeon Fighter Online. From the days of Nexon up until now, I've stuck with this game through and through, and no matter how much time I spend away from it, I always end up coming back.
Dungeon Fighter Online is a free-to-play MMORPG action brawler that draws inspiration from beat-em-ups like Double Dragon or Streets of Rage. The game is based almost entirely around PvE combat involving stylish combos, flashy super moves, and a whole lotta button pressing. The gameplay of the game is incredibly addictive, and I always end up coming back to see what absolutely crazy move I'll end up unlocking on the next class I play.
Speaking of classes, there is a GIGANTIC amount of variety in Dungeon Fighter Online. 14 classes, each with their own number of subclasses, totalling up to 52 different kinds of characters you can end up playing. Each subclass is unique, sharing barely any moves with their fellow subclasses, meaning even two people playing the exact same class can have entirely different experiences. All in all, it's incredibly worth it to play multiple characters, both because of variety...
... and because you can only play a limited amount of time on each character a day. You're limited by Fatigue Points (FP), which goes down every time you enter a new room in a dungeon. Once you're out of FP, you can't play that character anymore. Because of this, I'm sure a lot of Pay-to-Win accusations are going to get thrown at DFO, but allow me to be clear; DFO is not Pay-to-Win. DFO is Pay-to-Convienence. You can certainly advance through the game quicker by spending real money, but it isn't going to give you any inherent advantage over somebody who goes completely free-to-play, especially when you consider that DFO gives out the paid content like candy in certain events.
All and all, DFO is an incredibly fun and addictive game that I would highly recommend to anybody looking for a major time killer. Don't let a bunch of people who played the game for two seconds flat and swore it off convince you not to give it a try; you just might like it.

MY BIGGEST IN DEPTH REVIEW EVER! I previously reviewed Grid 2 and I will start with a familiar sentence those who read my grid 2 review will know. Codemasters, my dear old friend. I have been a loyal supporter since Colin Mcrae Rally 2.0, stretching from V8 Supercars 1, 2 (Xbox) to TOCA Race Driver 3 and even the Formula One games (My fave) Its only fair I review GRID: Autosport. In a nutshell, its an improvement over GRID 2. OK LETS GET INTO IT! Again I shall start with the cons.
-Cons
First the AI. Easy to catch, bloomin hard to keep them behind you. It seems there is a rubberbanding effect here where the cars behind get a performance boost when you pass, especially the top drivers (looking at you Westley). Rubberbanding provides a challenge to the player but it kinda makes it frustrating all your effort catching (even on hard difficaulty) suddenly goes to mud because the AI suddenly go faster. And on the subject of AI they REALLY get aggressive out there. For example in Open Wheel (more about classes in the pros!) It is supposed to be NON CONTACT. But they do not leave space, and I found myself getting spun when they slam into me in the breaking zones like im not even there or they re-pass on the inside and clip my rear wheels with their wing. THis is a long paragraph for a single con.
-Damage. This is a pro and con. Its more about the AI damage. They don't seem to have any issues with damage. I went the wrong way, smashed head on into an AI at over 200kph and sent him flipping through the air. When his car righted again he just continued although he did have a lose wing and cosmetic damage... he finished 5th... SO work there needs to be done.
-Multiplayer. Again... I cannot for the life of me find a public match. Inviting my only other friend who plays the game is ok, but sometimes hes not always avaliable to play. This needs to be fixed. It happened on GRID 2 as well.
OK CONS ASIDE!! Lets get into the really great pros.
-Classes. The best thing about this game. Different choice of cars. Its obvious not every one likes the same race series. I hate Nascar, I love Formula One. It is great to see you can choose 5 different choices, from Drift to Open Wheel to Touring etc. It is the best thing about this game, and it brings me back to my V8 Supercars years.
-Damage. Much improved damage on this game, parts come off, or cause your car to pull to the left/right, even lose a wheel, and manage to keep on racing (Put this in F1 2015 pls? k thx) although some pit stops would be nice/
-Career. A big con. The intro introduces you to the mechanics of the game with a 2 lap intro race which is good to get up to speed and you can select which class to start/end with maybe open wheel, or drift any category you want.
-ONBOARD CAMERAS. YES. DRIVING CAMERAS. T-CAMS. ITS WHAT WE DREAMED OF. AND WE GOT.
-Custom races. This is a great feature. Any class, any track, any team. Up to 3 events each with custom lap amounts, practice and qualifying and setups!!! Whats best is the first race can start from qualifying spot, but the second race can start from reversed 1st race position (finish 1st, start last, finish 2nd, start second to last.) Its great!!!
-Graphics. Only one word Amazing!
Overall a great game for any racer out there. Easy to use with my g27 wheel. HIGHLY RECOMMEND~~!!!

If like me you don't mind throwing down 20 bucks and taking a punt on an EA game, I highly recommend Citadel.

This was an old game for old computers back in the old days. I am so happy it was released on Steam. It was the same world, graphics, and style as the first game, just with more rides, scenarios, and the ability to create a huge park from scratch.
You can create your own roller coasters, of which there are dozens of types. Making your own roller coasters so they have high excitement and lower nausea and intensity can take many hours to master. Weaving them around each other and underground, as well as adding scenery can help. It is great fun to see your park bustling with happy guests.
The graphics are dated and the game does have limitations, such as with the camera and the landscaping, but the most enjoyable parts of the game are done extremely well and these limitations, while they do reduce the final score, are not game-breaking. The parts done well and the main point of the game are the park building, the themes, the rides and roller coasters, and the sound effects. Oh, you can also get a little crazy and have a roller coaster start on an incomplete track...
It is a time sink that will eat up many hours of your time. Before you realize, it is 2am and you have to work at 8 later that morning. Then you think about making a roller coaster, are thinking of cool names for your rides or are thinking of just how you will build your custom park from scratch. Games that make you think about them while you are not playing them are the ones worth playing. Time well spent.

This game has some visual style trying to present itself as something original and  retro-style with some stylish low-resolution assets. But actually all asssets just look like a placeholders. It's boring to look at. Everything is dirt brown and dim. Retro style is there just to somehow justify a simplicity or primitiveness.
The game is designed very badly. Right now there is no system or concept being developed step by step following a set road map. The development actually stuck with implementing different new game features with no vision how to combine them into something fun and playable. Thus you end up with an ability to sell your car's engine and then teleport back to your garage to install a new one. Or primitive tire system when shops will sell you a single tire rather then a full set.
Trading game subsystem lacks any kind of idea behind it and simply ineffective and not fun. It's way more efficient to sell your car's engine and teleport back.
Car handling. It just doesn't feel right. It's not intuitive.
Game lacks in-game help and descriptions of it's rules. Little insight you can get trying to read tips on a loading screen. If you read fast enough.
The idea of a road trip behind this game is great. But scenery lacks diversity, and goals are vague. Ideas worth dollar a dozen. What matters is vision and implementation.
Bugs. There are plenty. They are being fixed. Yet, most of them are game braking and annoying.
So, it's a "Not recommended" for now. Wait a bit for this game to grow up and mature.

BioShock 2 had the daunting task of being the sequel to one of the greatest video games of all time, but sadly, lacking a Sky-Hook, didn't reach the same heights as its big brother. My major complaint with BioShock 2 is what made the original so groundbreaking and memorable; the story and characters, in particular, the specimen known as Sofia Lamb. This is by far one of the most unthreatening and wearisome antagonists I have fought against, complete with an incomprehensible philosophy that has been forced in due to the overwhelming praise of Andrew Ryan. However, Ryan is a well-written character with an unambiguous philosophy who commanded a formidable presence throughout the original game. Lamb's confused ideals are simply there because it was the core of Ryan's character, not because they are interesting or challenge the player's own views. Due to the story revolving around Sofia Lamb it too takes on the same characteristics; boring, soulless and desolate. Despite all this, BioShock 2 still manages to be extremely fun thanks to its energetic gameplay that serves as the only improvement from the original. If you're solely revisiting Rapture to maim and murder, this sequel is impossible to pass up.
Very enjoyable, but not a worthy successor.

What's good about HL2 Deathmatch - is all about physics and gravy-gun, and the ability to flood the server with multiple Freemans running around. Or cooperative maps, where you fight through some location filled with respawning monsters, hoping on the backup from the rest of your team.
And now comes the bad part. For one, there are no (absolute zero) chances to find yourself a good team. There are no skilled players, as there are no application for their skills. The weaponry, that were so good in the single-player, aren't really any good for multiplayer arena FPS. That means totally random gameplay. You can die every second, or dominate with dozens of kills - it's not matter anything.
So no, if you're not having some friends who will play with you there, I don't recommend to starting this one. Other Valve products, like Counter Strike and Team Fortress, are much more capable to entertain, and provide decent gameplay.

I remember first playing this game about 8 years ago.  I went under the name "Sharp-Shooter" at the time, and it was my first experience playing an FPS with other players.  Unfortunately, that experience would turn out to be a bad one.
Many of the weapons in this game require little to no skill to use, or have a secondary fire that requires no skill.  With many of them, you can be very vague with your aiming and yet be rewarded with ridiculous damage (usually an instant kill at full health).  An example of this would be the secondary fire for the pulse rifle.  Anyone who has played singleplayer Half Life 2 knows that this is a fairly large orb that rebounds off of all surfaces and instant kills any target it hits regardless of current health.  Well, in Deathmatch it is no different, but this is a problem for two reasons.  The first being that there are other weapons, such as the primary fire for both the SMG and pulse rifle, which have been nerfed considerably in this game compared to the campaign game.  The reduced damage meant that you had to keep your aim on target at all times for the best effect which requires concentration and practice.  The orbs having no reduction of any kind therefore makes this unfair as anyone could take down someone skilled at using the primary fire with no effort at all.  The second is that the orb's ability to rebound everywhere means that there is little chance of avoiding it, and the user could get kills without so much as seeing their targets, or even knowing where they were at the time.
But that's just one example.  And yet the majority of the community somehow convinces itself that every weapon in this game is equally as hard to use as everything else.
So do I recommend this game?  Well, not really.  If you are looking for a fair and skill-based game, this is not for you.  It forces you to play in a way that requires no effort,  which if you refuse to do as I did, will leave you with the stress of losing constantly regardless of how hard you try or how skilled you are.  Then again, like with anything, it is still up to you.

I'm trying to keep the in-depth review as brief as possible, but it's very difficult...there's so much to say about this game.
You start, grow, and manage a pharmaceutical company. You control every aspect of it such as production lines, research and development, budget (purchases, importing ingredients, payroll, cost of production), meeting market demand, etc. This is a pharmaceutical tycoon game and it gives you plenty of options and features to run the business as you please or win a scenario as you please.
Designing the production floor is like a puzzle...but I really hate using that word. It's not a puzzle game. You have to make use of the space you are given (which is a lot so far for me) and plan workflow, but it's much more than that. There are options upon options to consider  The game can be very complex at times, but it also allows the player to keep things simple if they so choose.
There are 8 Scenarios with 5 missions each. Some missions are specific, some are rather broad.  There's also a custom game feature and a free build option. Together, they allow the player to really play as they want. You can develop highly sophisticated medications or you can deal with simple production lines. It's entirely up to you!
Unlike many indie games, particularly with early access but not exclusive to them, this game is extremely...I mean extremely polished. Everything was very well thought out and organized. Key features were included yet nothing seems to exist that doesn't need to be. ALL the necessary fundamentals you'd expect are here (rare for many games today unfortunately), but many are done exceptionally well and are thus, quite noteworthy.
Examples...
Lastly, one of the biggest parts of polish which was noticed...was the lack of any bugs!  I am despearately trying to find some. I know some have to exist. But I so far, have failed to discover any. The game runs smooth and there are no bugs that break immersion or stop gameplay.
The dev did what most other devs do not do today it seems...he focused on QUALITY. He put a substantial amount of time into the game PRIOR to released. He focused on giving customers a QUALITY project to enjoy by making sure the details were there but also that the game works as it is supposed to. He demonstrated that he actually cares about his own game, his own work.
Novel idea huh? Give the players a quality product they expect to have?
First of all, this is the work of only 1 developer. He, like most devs used outside sources for assets (graphics, sounds, effects, voice), but 1 guy is the brain behind this game. Very few games can be pulled off successfully by a single dev and this one was.
He also is very active in his communication with customers (his own forum, social media, and here at the Steam forums).
I am still struggling to find something. I honestly am. I've not experienced anything negative about this game yet.
The only thing I can see wanting to change, is a part in the last tutorial which discusses maximum strength analysis and how to implement it to upgrade a medicine's rating. To me, that's a bit fuzzy. I tried to understand what was being described and how to pull it off, but didn't understand it. That could just be me though. Regardless, it does not prevent the mission from being completed. It just means the user, or me anyway, needs to ask for clarification on the forum.
High quality game, extremely polished, plenty of options and features, a lot of variation, NO BUGS (so far). This game will probably become one of the standards of quality that gamers will compare other games to (like many compare other ea games to Prison Architect or Kerbel).
In a sea of poorly designed games from devs who don't seem to either care about their products or have the knowledge to make them great...and with the current gaming community's frustration level at an all-time high due to the abundance of bad games and ripoffs coming out on Steam...let this game refresh your faith and trust in the industry as it is proof that high quality games CAN be delivered and some devs DO care about their project and their customers.
If you enjoy tycoon style games, do yourself a much deserved favor and GET THIS GAME NOW! You will not regret it (especially with Steam's refund policy of course - but you won't need it).

So I've been playing since the early access non-steam beta came out and I've put about 30 hours into this game before this release and I honestly have to say while I like the idea it has some really bad core problems that all stem from it's use of luck.
Basically this is a puzzle game with a enormous amount of randomness thrown into it and those are two things that rarely work well together. The game is more or less about completing scenario's with tiers of set goals and two months ago I made a rather long post on /r/bigpharmagame that explained why it's not done very good well overall.
The short version is basically everything you need is random. The amount of space you start to build in is random, the drug effects you start with are random, the effects on those drugs are random, the order you unlock new drugs is random, the products your competitors will make are random. The only non-random things are how much money you start with and your overall goal for the scenario. Which leads to many many MANY unwinnable situations, e.g; It's possible to play a scenario were you have to produce certain medicines within a certain time period and random chance will put the drug you need so far down the research list that there's no possible way to even get to it let alone produce anything with it before the time expires.
To put it into something that most people would understand; pretend your playing StarCraft 2 but the amount of SCV's you started with was random, so was the amount of vespene geysers, mineral patches and how much was in them.  With me so far? So YOU might start with 2 SCV's, 4 vespene geysers and 3 mineral patches, while your opponent starts with 10 SCV's, 2 vespene geysers and 20 mineral patches. Now ontop of that also make all the unit costs and research a random number as well. Do you see why this is bad now?
It's basically a requirement to restart a scenario over and over again til you get the space and favorable drugs you need if you plan on getting anything but the bronze completion. Even if you get a favorable start, you still might need to end up restarting anyway because you may have had 2 of the drugs you needed for the 3 pills you had to produce but sadly #3 is the very last one your explorers can find.
Overall it's what killed the game for me. If there was set drugs with set effects with set starting positions on the board then I wouldn't have had nearly any of the complaints I did. But overall you spend more time restarting then actually playing the game unless your content to bust your♥♥♥♥♥for bronze the whole way through, riding the waves of luck.

I played dozens of hours of this game while it was in development and it's been one of my favorite games of the year! I'm happy to see it's now on Steam!
Big Pharma is a very unique game. It's best described as a tycoon/management game, mixed with a logistics puzzler or "product chain" puzzler, such as SpaceChem, Infinifactory, or Factorio. Your goal is to create and sell cures ranging from cough suppressants to cancer medicine. The creation process is done through a network of machines and conveyor belts that tinker and transform the potency of raw ingredients into the desired cures (often combating undesired side effects).
Often just figuring out how to make a good product is an excellent puzzle in itself, but it's made even more challenging by the ability to perfect the potency of a drug, mix multiple beneficial effects, and remove unwanted side effects. On top of that is a whole financial layer, including an ever-changing market of supply (how much raw ingredients cost) and demand (how badly a cure is needed), further complicated by the competition of rival companies who can drive up ingredient costs, compete for similar cures, and even try to patent certain drugs to prevent others from selling them temporarily. All this is mixed with a large research tree and an interesting procedurally generated list of unlockable ingredients that need to be researched and experimented with in order to advance your company.
Sound complex? It is! This game is not a casual experience. As a management game, it strives to be more similar to older "Tycoon" games of the 90's and early 2000's, where succeeding financially is a genuine challenge and there's very little hand-holding when it comes to how to get there. At the same time, the game is definitely in the same vein of puzzle games like the aforementioned SpaceChem; a production puzzle game with no single "right" answers, but millions of wrong ones. Arranging the differently shaped machines and placing conveyor belts is as tricky as trying to figure out the correct combination to make the desired product. But, like the best  of both of those genres, as hard as they are, Big Pharma is actually very easy to learn once you wrap your head around its new ideas, and the payoff is countless ultra-satisfying "I'm a freakin' genius!" moments. The most important thing to note? The tutorial is NOT optional for a new player, and since it's a bit of a wall of text, I imagine that might put some people off.
In terms of aesthetic, I absolutely adore the game. The music is absolutely perfect for the subject matter, the UI is one of the cleanest and most functional I've ever seen, and like most good factory-themed games, seeing your products  move down conveyor belts and through wacky machines en mass is an absolute delight.
My only worry with the game at the time of writing is that it might have released just slightly too early. For the most part it's fully functional, but there are still a few bugs here and there, and it felt like the balance of things like competitor productivity and patents were still trying to be worked out when the game was released. So far, I've found nothing remotely game-breaking and it's definitely more functional than many things released on Steam, but I'm sure it still could use a few patches (there's also whispers of modding support that might expand the game in the future).
Overall, Big Pharma is definitely my kind of game. I'd say it's a must-buy for anyone who likes production puzzlers like SpaceChem or Infinifactory, and a good buy for those who have fond memories of old Tycoon games (with a thematic boost to anyone who loved the game Theme Hospital). Those who want a more casual experience may want to look for something simpler, but for anyone for a great brain-straining puzzle and interesting management game, Big Pharma has your cure!
tl;dr
+ Great open-ended logistic puzzle gameplay
+ Lots of depth, with a good tech tree, many machines, and tons of cures and side effects
+ Procedurally generated factory layouts and randomized ingredients make each game feel unique
+ Great music and lighthearted aesthetic
+ Very challenging with many different ways to succeed
+ Interesting business simulation with fluctuating markets and competing companies, adds a new layer to the financial aspect of the game.
- Complexity may be off-putting; tutorial NOT optional
- Minor bugs, might still need a few balancing tweaks

Its Magic the Gathering and its free. So that is a good thing in my book. It is somewhat grindy Free-to-Play but it does not have a totally random card draw system, but rather after buying a certain number of packs from an expansion you are guaranteed to have all the cards. I also like that system.

When there was only one expansion the game felt somwewhat boring because of that. With more expansions being out now there is more variety and that is good. It also means that new players have to catch up on more cards to acquire and thats where the negative aspects of a Free-to-play game comes in:
You either grind or pay. You can play this game perfectly fine without doing either, but you will be limited in your deck and card choices.
Overall I enjoy being able to play Magic the Gathering for free and online. This is not an amazing adaptation but it is serviceable.

This is my 2 hours into the game review - where I'm wondering if I should keep this or ask for the refund...
The game is kind of like Freelancer... but NO 3D CONTROLS.  I am disappoint.
You can't roll the ship, which means if your turret is under the ship and whatever you want to shoot is over the ship, all they have to do is stay up there and you can never hit them EVER.  I guess you have to change turrets, but that one turret will never see line of sight to a target if it's over the ship.  The game has a distinct "these are just boats on the water, only it __looks__ like space" feeling to it - which is true except smaller enemy and allied ships and missiles do leave the plane that capital ships are in, enough that they can avoid some of your turrets.
Other than no roll or diving, this game is like Freelancer.  Build up your ship and so on.  The gameplay can be some fun.
The camera is really weird (in broadside mode trying to see where you are shooting at is very twitchy) - but you sort of get used to it.  Broadside mode is maybe the strange new game mechanic that I've never seen in another space shmup, and possibly why they didn't implement rolling.  So it's Freelancer minus rolling plus broadside cannons.
Here's a breakdown of all the features this game has:
- There are space factions that either like your or hate you and your actions affect their demeanor toward you.  If you do pirate missions, eventually they will start to like you (which might make civilians hate you, though there might be ways of making everyone like you).
- The ships are upgradeable.  Sell your stuff.  Buy better stuff.  Repeat.
- There are missions.
- There is a commodities market.  You can mine ore and sell it somewhere.  Or buy stuff that's cheap and jump to several systems away to sell it at a higher price.
- There's a story.
----EVERYTHING ABOVE IS IDENTICAL TO FREELANCER AND X3----
- When travelling at warp speeds you might come right up on an asteroid and drop out of warp and need evasive maneuvers Scotty!  This is a nice feature.
- There is at least one "hack the system" mini-game that is offered occasionally.  I won't spoil it - it was a nice surprise.
- Another "chase the convoy" mini-game is pretty fun too.
- There are broadside cannons.  When using the other cannons the camera acts one way, and when using the broadside cannons the camera acts a different way.  Deplorable camera behavior may well be what holds this game back the most -- it can be very annoying and you only notice it when you're in the middle of a fight and have better things to worry about than how to get the camera to point in the right direction!
- This is a more casual 3D space sim.  You can't roll.  Dammit!  And you can't dive.  The physics are okay, but certainly casual.  Things that were possible in a real 3D game aren't available here -- everything happens in a 2D plane because it has to.  If you liked X3 you might like this - but if you like this, there's a far better chance that X3 might be too difficult with its tons of features.  This is a very simplified 3D shoot-em-up (shmup).
- If you try to use a controller (rather than keyboard+mouse) you'll know why there's no roll!  This game was designed with a controller in mind apparently - but the learning curve for the controller is sky high -- EVERY button on the controller is used up, and some you even have to go through menus.  It's not very intuitive compared to keyboard and mouse.  YMMV.  But after the learning curve I'm finding I like the controller better.
- The commodities don't serve any purpose other than to sell them, and there is some description providing background text.  So some rare commodities that show up in price lists seem interesting to try to find, and maybe learn more about them - but because they are just sold anyways, it's not a big hook.
- There is good music (if you like it).  I even liked it for about 5 minutes.  Then I shut it off.  Then I turned it back on.
- Generally the flavoring is really good, and maybe what makes this game worthwhile.  Some of the commodities are funny, along with the voice acting which is all alien gibberish.  The artwork and graphics are "stellar".  Get it?  Stellar?  :)  The tone is very western, which is why so many reviews mention Firefly - certainly has that vibe built in which is nice.  Space should be a wild west.  Actually, compared the Freelancer the flavoring crushes that game.  Remember the corny bar scenes?  They are here too, but much more refined, and it's a noticeable improvement.
After playing this for over 10 hours (almost all in one sitting) this game is pretty enough, and interesting enough to be a good choice if you like this genre.  It's a little grindy, but the grind is broken up well with the storyline and mini-games.
The grind leaves very little reason to try to get the biggest ships (that would take many days of play to access).  At this point it seems the devs gave up on trying to provide more compelling gameplay elements - they could sign off the game as finished.  It's a little unsatisfying reaching the mid-game and knowing the story will just provide more tutorial examples, and there will be more grinding and that's all that remains in the game.

All told, I can't count the hours I've spent in Arad. Either because that data is long deleted or it's just too much.
Perhaps it's this perspective that leads me back here. Not only have I been recommending this game since before the Curiosity rover laned on Mars
, but I can tell you honestly that the game has
.
The leveling process has been revamped and is now sublime, one of the best experiences in gaming. No dungeon repeats and most every one presents some interesting challenges or mix ups on the strategy needed to overcome. For example, early on you'll encounter the Chessboard of Despair, which features a room of super-armored rooks that charge, naturally, all the way across the battlefield in a straight line. Unless you jump or use some ability in response, you'll face a heavy hit. Part of the fun of the game is realizing which spell or positioning or strategy will avail you the day.
Every class is viable, unique and, what's more, every class is
. Fly around with irreverence on a broomstick and smack people with a giant flyswatter, or launch an invasion of mechs to cloud the skies, or wrestle your enemies by flinging them around the arena, or whatever else you can imagine.
And the graphics are lovingly and thoughtfully drawn. While many modern gamers may initially balk at the sprite graphics and smaller resolution of a game made in 2004, ten minutes of play will quell any concerns. Plus Minecraft happened. From simple slashes to cataclysmic ults, everything is presented sharply and clearly and everything looks great.
Just make sure to turn down the opacity of your party member's abilities...
Furthermore the publisher is no longer Nexon but instead the developer, Neople, and Neople actually cares. The community interaction, events, action taken against hackers and scammers, and even this release on Steam all show that they honestly want the game to be a force in the West as it is in the East. There's just too much here for a lifelong fan of side-scrolling brawlers and eastern RPGs to ignore, but I've always loved it at arm's length.
The crushing RNG of endgame was once unbearable, now is discouraging, and soon (from the changes to endgame gear on the Korean servers and the generous DFO Global events), will be manageable. Ten years late to the parity party, but take your wins. I endured Hell for years so you don't have to.
That's a funny joke, you'll get it later.
PvP is in an awkward place. Long gone is the normalized Fair Arena, and any hope of entirely balanced PvP. Though you can enter at lvl 35, there's no point on pressing the P key until level 85 with appropriate gear. Furthermore, expensive advanced avatars can be bought for in game gold or real money and do provide an advantage, triggering some concerns about P2W, though those are mostly ignorable due to the way combos work. The P2P nature of the game also makes lag an inevitability in the West while it's largely an afterthought in Korea.
That said, I jumped in for a few quick matches on my Sword Master intending to play Overwatch after, and left three hours later to watch videos of high ranked Korean Sword Masters on Youtube. Not only is addictive and entirely skill based, meaning you always want to improve, but it's plain fun.
Finally, people may have qualms about the pay structure of the most popular MMORPG of all time (no seriously, look it up), so to assuage your P2W concerns, let me remind you the game is old. Anything you may be scared about has been deemed okay by 500+ million players, including us in the West. There are very distinct moments in DFO history when unacceptable practices snuck in (Kiri's Promise) and were justly smashed by community outcry. The situation has long since stabilized.
Nowadays you can certainly drop thousands of dollars to rush to end-game gear, but everything that you'd want is also available through grinding or just casual play as well. Most people spend money to buy cosmetic items before anything else, but even those are routinely sold on the AH for moderate amounts of gold. Believe me, the monetization of this game is among the most fair F2P in gaming, and the rewards for events and just playing will get you to the endgame.
The bottom line should be clear: Dungeon Fighter Online is undeniably fun. For MMO fans, for beat-em up fans, for hundreds of millions of people all over the world. Any concerns are minor and pale in comparison to the polished, well-oiled fun machine.

MapleStory was one of the first MMORPG titles I've had the chance of playing, besides Runescape Classic (which was a looong time ago).
After a revisit of this game (after many years of on and off playing), as well as THOUSANDS of dollars spent, I cannot say I am willing to recommend this game.
FIrstly, MapleStory is one of the few 2D side-scrolling MMORPGs that try to mix 'cute' and 'breathtaking' together, and at times, they do it very well. Some landscapes are huge, the original lore and locations were very well done, and one can be trapped in the game's beauty for long periods of time. Heck, even getting lost in that game was fun. However, with the changes as of the last two to three years, a lot of the beauty has been lost. In order to cater to the broader generation of players who demand instant gratification, they have changed out most of the old expansive locations and replaced them with compacted versions - so that players can traverse the world much more quickly. However, by doing so, they've stuffed all the game's content into the newer maps, which makes most of the world appear small and claustrophobic.
The music score for this game is wonderful. Whether you're inside the forests of Ellinia, or exploring the depths of Ludibrium,  the background music really amplifies the mystery and beauty the game world is trying to become.
The original MapleStory had a handful of classes, and each of them were unique, but overall balanced. Now, each large 'class update' seems to focus on newer 'Hero' characters, most who severely outclass the older counterparts in terms of damage and flashiness. In fact, there are so many different 'Heroes' nowadays, it saddens me to say that you'll rarely run into the older classes anymore, except in the case of Legacy worlds.
The Cash Shop isn't all too great either. In addition to the standard cosmetic items and EXP boosts that one would commonly find in Free-2-Play MMOs, there are also items which give you in game currency, some which would offer you lowered failure chances when upgrading items. The latter gives players who spend a huge lead over players who don't, and this is made obvious by the overly high prices those items fetch on the marketplace.
Combine that with a marketplace that doesn't let players open one without forking cash (and depending on how much cash you're willing to spend, it also determines whether you'll have to stay logged in to sell items)(players are only able to trade, so they'll have to solicit people in the market entrances) and a bad support team, I truly cannot recommend this game to anyone. MapleStory's golden days are long gone, and what's left is a carcass of what was once a masterpiece.

I have played more racing games in over 20 years than I could ever remember. While not the worst racing game I have ever played, It is a long way from the best.  Controls and handling of the cars is not really an issue except to point out that keyboard players should expect to be at a disadvantage.
The main problems are the AI, the lack of visibility and the atrocious in car view.
The AI is following the same principle that has been used for a few years now. That is they are "heavy" meaning you cannot ram them and expect to see them suffer much. Unfortunately that the same does not apply in reverse, and you will often find yourself losing many positions or even out of a race after being hit by the AI. What make it worse in this game, is the AI generally doesnt see you or care. They will maneuver to overtake on a corner, then  switch into your lane after a few seconds, regardless of where you are. This only applies if your are not drift/sliding around the corner. In this instance you do not exist and that will blindly drive right into you. If by chance you get t-boned and stuck on the front of thier car, then race over. They will not stop to let you off, and will happily push you as far off the track as they can go before hitting a wall or running out of momentum.
Visibilty in this game is not something you will notice much as the graphics are quite nice. The problem does become apparent on the more technical circuits though. The issue is you can see a lot of scenery, but very little of the road ahead. In many places the corners are hard to judge as you can not really see a far as you should be able to. It is like an artificial limit on the draw distance. Using the best line feature can help, but if you cannot see much of the road, you wont see much of a line on the road either.
Now for the in car view. Its there.... partially. This is absolutly the worst view I have EVER seen in a car game. Not only do they further restrict your view by making you feel like you are to small to look over the dash, but the whole interior of the car is blurred W...T...F!!! Bonus xp for limiting views to incar only, but not worth it.
People who played Grid 2 online are in for some good news. You can buy quite a few cars in this game without having to play online for 100hrs. Bad news is there are now something like 50 catagoeries, so you will still get stuck having to use loan cars until your 100hrs is up.

People have complained that they only get around 20fps on low settings with a fairly good PC, that strikes me as odd because I have a completely average computer with my graphics card only being a 2gb variant, meaning I get bad fps on average in almost any game I play. For starters, by taking a normal mana potion, you will regenerate more mana than you spend. This is a very simple and much needed balancing attempt by the game devs, think about it this way, if people could fly indefinetly with no cost whatsoever, they'd be raining down death on everyone, this game would be the ultimate griefing cluster♥♥♥♥.

After playing Grid 2 and having mixed, mostly-positive feelings, I was hoping Autosport would win me over. It did not. I'd definitely recommend Grid 2 over this game, and if you've already played 2, don't bother with Autosport.
My biggest problem is with the driving physics (which are similar to Grid 2). I get that it's an arcade racer; that's fine. But the cars don't feel like they have 4 wheels contacting the ground. They're more than just "floaty". They are kind of like cardboard with a pencil stuck through the middle. When you turn, the car seems to pivot around its center (you can feel the rear wheels swing out). So I'll brake before a turn, start turning in, and keep traction through the turn. But while doing this, the car has pivoted and feels like it's drifting... but I have traction?... it's a bizarre sensation and just feels "wrong".
As a comparison: Project Gotham Racing was an arcade racer that nailed driving physics. Even though PGR was arcadey, the cars felt weighty and had momentum. You could feel the road under the wheels and could tell when you made little mistakes. Very satisfying to master. Grid's physics don't have that magic at all.
Beyond that, Autosport's career mode is dull. My experience with Grid 2 was that, in spite of the poor physics, the career's trickle of exciting tracks and cars kept me playing. However, I do not feel this in Grid Autosport. Your career progress is only portrayed through menus, and everything (everything!) boils down to filling XP bars. Gone is the illusion of building up a racing career, gone is collecting cars, gone is my garage. For the first few races I was actually confused: "what is my GOAL here?" It turns out: I don't need to win, I don't need to beat my rivals, I don't need to finish objectives. I just need to play enough to fill XP bars up.
Couple that with the fact that most of the tracks are straight from Grid 2, and I'm left super disappointed. It's a shame because I've always liked Codemaster's Colin McRae and Dirt series. I want to like this game, but I can't.

This lastest installation of the so called "Sid Meier's" brand of civilization-style games is unfortunately not very good.
First of all, the intgerface is a mess, it's drowned in little miasma clouds, and green and purple details of the alien planet, and fails to clearly provide the basic information - where the enemy units stand, where do you stand, where are your trade routes, how much health the unit has, and so on. The information is there, but you have to dig for it too hard. EU4 style overlays would go a long way here.
Next, the AI is incredibly stupid on the tactical level, it does not withdraw mortally wounded units, it does not understand tactical placement, and it compensates with rather heave cheating which I am not very fond of. You will see huge armies amassed in time you clearly know would not be possible if the opponent played by the rules.
Diplomacy, traditionally, has very little sense. The computer player demand obscene trades that are never even remotely fair, so it's best if you treat this portion of the game as non-existent.
Lastly, you don't feel like a ruler, you feel like an overworked administrator. You don't have much say on how your society lives, what laws it obeys, and instead your tasks center around building road here, a solar panel there, main on that hill, and so on. Thousands of mundane tasks, slow progress, bog of meaningless decisions.
I strongly recommend Alpha Centauri instead - if you can swallow the ugly graphics.

This is a game from 2002 on Steam. Whilst it is a great game, it is clearly not optimised for modern computers. The game is very buggy and will crash when clicking on some menus, and even Alt-Tabbing out sometimes (the Windows Display Driver stopped working). Trying to save the game caused my game to completely lock up (thank god for Ctrl+Alt+Del). Changing compatibility mode to XP may cause the problem, and when you can actually get into the game, it is heaps of fun. But the fact that playing the game without that is like driving a car on the verge of death is dissappointing.
UPDATE: I found a way to get the game to completely work consistently. From the game's directory, install the Autorun. This will also install the game to an Atari directory in addition to the Steam directory. On the executable, run in compatibility mode for Windows XP SP2. Then, from the Save menu in-game, change the resolution to the max. Not only will the game look better, it should run better and be more stable (no more game crashes from Alt-Tabbing).

When Bioshock 2 was announced, it unleashed a shock-wave of excitement throughout the gaming community; its predecessor had been a monumental success, and people could not wait to see what the sequel had in store. Born three long years after the original title, it's safe to say that Bioshock 2 did not disappoint in terms of gameplay, visuals, and setting, although many fans agree that the plot and characters are not quite as memorable as those from the first installment.
The game begins in the year 1958, two years prior to the events of the first Bioshock, and shows the main character that you play, known as Subject Delta, patrolling Rapture with his Little Sister, Eleanor. Some events happen, and the game fast forwards ten years later to the year 1968 (not 1970 as the store page misleads you to believe). Subject Delta, also known as Johnny Topside prior to his conversion into a Big Daddy, has set out to find Eleanor, who is now a young adult in her teens. Time is pressing, however, as the longer a Big Daddy is away from his Little Sister, the higher the odds of him slipping into a coma are. There's but one problem standing in your way, a highly manipulative and slightly insane woman named Sophia Lamb. She has replaced Andrew Ryan as the main antagonist, while Augustus Sinclair helps guide you throughout Rapture through radio messages.
Yes, you read that right. This time around, you get to play as an actual Big Daddy; arguably the most appealing feature of the entire game. You can also take on other Big Daddies to take their Little Sisters, and you can protect them as they're harvesting ADAM from angels. After letting the Little Sister gather from two angels, you take her back to her vent and choose to either harvest or rescue her. Harvesting or rescuing Little Sisters has an impact on the end game cutscene, and there are a total of three different endings. New to the tried and true Splicers and Big Daddies are now Big Sisters, which wear much of the same gear as a Big Daddy but they're much slimmer, quicker, and deadlier.
Another improvement to the gameplay is the ability to wield both a weapon and a Plasmid at the same time, where as in the original Bioshock you had to constantly swap between the two. However, there's a huge glitch in the game that causes your left arm, which is the one that uses Plasmids, to disappear until you either die or get talked to by Eleanor. There are also a new assortment of weapons, such as the drill, grenade launcher, and speargun, and there are a mix of new and old Plasmids to enjoy as well, 11 in total.
Bioshock 2 feels a lot more linear than its predecessor, as there aren't as many non-essential rooms to explore. However, the lush environments and fantastic atmosphere more than make up for the overall closed maps. A huge feature, aside from being a Big Daddy of course, is being able to occasionally venture outside of Rapture, onto the ocean floor. The oceanic scenes and moments spent underwater are beautifully crafted, and make you realize just how small you are in comparison to the immense structure that is the city of Rapture. The Art Deco style has been down-scaled in this installment in lieu of a more steampunk style, which ends up coming full circle in Bioshock Infinite.
One thing that really brought this game down was the inclusion of a multiplayer element. I'm not even sure if the servers are still active anymore, but I did play some multiplayer on console when the game was brand new. Like most games that should stay as a single player experience but don't, the multiplayer was terrible and mostly consisted of death matches between Big Daddies and Splicers. I'm not alone in my distaste for the multiplayer element, as you will see most other reviewers also scorn it as well. This 'feature', however, has been dropped in the Bioshock 2 Remastered version.
Is Bioshock 2 better than the first game? Absolutely not. It's nowhere near as memorable in terms of story or plot, but the gameplay is where this title really shines. Playing as a Big Daddy is satisfying in every imaginable way, from the killing and being able to use a drill, to protecting Little Sisters and helping them harvest ADAM. It's the experience that fans would've been continuing to ask for until we got it, but luckily 2K had the foresight to just go ahead and do it. Sophia Lamb is definitely not as charming a villain as Andrew Ryan or Atlas, but she does have her moments. It's a worthwhile experience for the fan of the Bioshock universe, just don't go in expecting as gripping of a tale.

Having played this game in (pre-Steam) alpha and beta for over 150 hours I can say ... it's amazing!
So, what is it about?
- Create a perfect, smooth running production cycle
- Are you going for a cheap medication, try to appeal the mass-market, make a quick buck?
- Do you want to perfection it, research side-effects, minimize them and improve?
- Beat your competition by patenting the big cures? Maybe YOU are the guy curing Ebola, getting rich and famous?
- Research new ingredients, new cures, new machines, new developments, new production methods
- Send your scouts and scientists on month-long missions to find that rare beetle somewhere in the Arctic ice or learn how to use that new technology you need to unlock a fourth or fifth level of an ingredient.
- Expand, start with new ingredients, new cures, do it all over again!
It's a sandbox game and feels a lot more like Transport Tycoon or Infinifactory than Theme Hospital, you have your input (a plant, an insect, any kind of biological source), you refine it, mix it, filter it, strengthen or weaken specific effects, create a smooth running cycle with dozens of machines or steps in between, then export it as a medication in various forms. Pills or syringes? All your choice. Then you get rid of the side-effects, mix in other incredients, improve, get your A+ cure out and feel proud!
Play with or without competition, maybe you just like to make it look good and not fight with other companies? Your call!
If you like games like Infinifactory / SpaceChem or Transport Tycoon you will love this game.
If you expect a simulation where small changes can affect the outcome on the long run you will love this game.
If you expect the humor of curing patients like you did in Theme Hospital, this game might appeal, but wont fill that need.
Overall it's a big recommendation if you like slow moving steady games, it'll often take hours to set things up well-running, and it's all about patience.

I have to say, when I first started playing this game I didn't expect much because of the low price tag (I bought it when it was on sale).

The gameplay and the bosses remind me of Megaman, and I think this game is pretty much on the same level as Megaman 2 (the only Mega Man game I've played *cough*) when it comes to having fun playing the game.
All in all:
pros:
The controls are really smooth and once you get the hang of them you really start to enjoy this game.
Really well designed stages and bosses
The various game modes are also super fun to play if you want the extra challenge. (Arcade mode and challenge mode)
The difficulty settings

neutral:

The story: Honestly: it's a platformer, it doesn't need to have a great story. The great humour makes up for it though.
cons:
It could be a little bit longer. If you're fast, you can play through this game in about 1 hour (I have also seen some speedrunners getting <15 minutes) . Honestly, this is not a huge flaw, the games is still fun to play.

I used to play MtG when I was a kid, back then 9th Edition was just out and there was a lot of hype about it, although playing online for me was nearly impossible due to very low internet connection speed (we had a 256 Kb/s connection back then iirc), didn't really have much real life pals to play with so I kind of forgotten the game. Gameplay is very dynamic and smooth, tutorials explain pretty much every aspect of the game perfectly (you even get free coins for going through it), you get some free cards to play around once you complete the story line. I could say that maybe matchmaking is sometimes a bit unfair, sometimes it just feels like your opponent has the superior cards and there's nothing you could have done to win, but the more you play, the more gold you get, the more boosters you can get and you get more experience overall. All things considered, I give this game a strong 8 out of 10, there are some things that could be improved, but the game is constantly moving forward, a new patch just came out a few days ago and it brought some healthy changes to the gameplay. I was waiting until the March 2016 patch to write this review.  I felt it would be fair to give Stainless and WotC the extra time to produce a passable game.  Sadly, this has not been the outcome.
Magic Duels is a game that has so much potential, that it fails to even approach.  Free to play card games are generally well recieved in the video game market of 2016, and the amount of money that well made ones make is staggering.
However, for some reason there seems to be a lack of desire or funding on the part of WotC or Stainless, or both, to put together the nessecary resources it takes to produce a functional video game.
Magic Duels has the shell of a great game, but once you look inside you see the blemishes.
Numerous bugs still permeate the play experience.  The netcode is slow and frequently does not match players correctly.  The game does not allow players to accomplish things that they should be able to do in a game of Magic (such as Transforming a planeswalker with an activated ability in the second main phase).  The shuffling algorithms seem off.  The game doesn't even teach the correct rules of Magic, instead making stupid conscessions in the name of simplification that instead only serve to misinform.
I really, really, really wanted to write a positive review of this game.  I was waiting for the March update and resting judgement until they had a chance to get it released and tuned up.  I have given WotC and Stainless every chance to remedy this buggy mess of a game.
Unfortunately, considering the current state of the game, I cannot reccommend anyone play this game, unless you are completely desperate to play Magic on your PC and you don't have the money to play MTGO.
Not recommended.

I don't have a vast experience with mmorpg games, but there are some pros and cons I can list for this game.
Pros:
-The community is extremely friendly. People are respectful and love to help each other. You will find a helping hand every time you ask for advice
-If you enjoy cartoonish graphics but are sick of anime-like games, you will love this.
-The game's music is pretty.
Cons:
-Crafting: Okay fine, this could be a pro if you're the type of person who likes to spend some time looking at recipes, finding mats and all that, but in my opinion the crafting system is a bit complicated. There are items you can use to speed up this process but it makes it grindy (which leads me to my next point) and at some point you're gonna feel forced to spend real money to get them.
-Grinding: prepare to grind a lot for mats. The game has around 7 professions but can't just focus on one of them because you will need to do A LOT of crafting in this game and professions will give you the ingredients you need for the recipes. Sure you can go ahead and buy them from other players and some might even give them to you for free, but since I started playing, my fellow guildies told me to work on all my professions and keep them around the same level as my character, which I did, but go bored in the process. Specially Farming and Gardening are a pain in the butt.
-Events: Okay... so I played this game for around 500 hours and had the opportunity to participate in 3 different events, which I found to be VERY Repetitive. It's like doing the same event every time but with different prizes and different themes. Killing the same mobs every 40 minutes for days, relying on the drop chance to get the items you need to collect in order to obtaing prizes and, once again, crafting A LOT. Let me add I played almost every day and never got to obtain any of the prizes they were offering.
Neutral:
-Story: The story isn't bad but it's nothing out of this world. I'm going to be fair and say that after playing The Lord of the Rings Online, you can't help to have very high expectations.
-No PvP and depending on your personal preferences, this could be a good thing. I guess it helps with the game's healthy community, but I wouldn't say this is necessarily true since The Lord of the Rings Online also has a great and friendly community and does have a PvP system.
To conclude: I would recomend this game to anyone who's not familiar with mmorpg games and is willing to step into them, since it is fairly basic and easy to understand or to elder people or young ones since the community is so nice. You surely will find people to talk to and will have fun in a safe environment.
In the other hand, if you already are used to mmorpg and are the type of person who is looking for a lot of action, This isn't the game for you. Go ahead and give The Lord of the Rings Online and opportunity.

: You inherit a beat up old spaceship from a missing relative. That's the first minute. From there, the game is effectively a sandbox with some light RPG elements. You also start with the stereotypical mystery aboard the vessel, which is your hook into the scripted story of the game. The story itself is fairly light (lighter than my tastes normally, as I love stories), but very fulfilling for a game like this.
: You can do all the things you might imagine with a spaceship: turn pirate, haul freight, do missions, mine asteroid belts for sellable ore and minerals, be a merchant, get various factions angry (or happy) with you, fight the authorities, help the authorities,  wreak havoc on trade routes, explore the galaxy, upgrade your ship, buy new ships, hire mercs, complete quests/missions, etc.
: Combat itself is very engaging, unique, and fun--imagine old school broadsides combat but in SPAAAAAACE. (Apparently the piratical version of Assassin's Creed was the insipration here, so if you liked that, you'll definitely like this.) There are, of course, all manner of automated weapons and systems you can use with various ranges and all that. This is the future after all. Pausing anywhere--including during combat--is a thing, as is saving your game anywhere (some games restrict players on saving).
: The time it takes to complete the core story takes roughly 35-45 hours, though I could see one knocking it out in 25-30 hours if you're fast, play optimally, don't explore, and don't take many side missions.
: Holy sheet the music, man. It's a dark, country-western, hard rock mash-up. Absolutely perfect.
: Space is beautiful. Some elements are a little humble (this is not a AAA game put out by a large studio with a graphics department), but those minor quibbles aside, it's visually perfect.
: I played this on my wall (I use a BenQ projector) with a wireless XBox One controller. Combat in this game works beautifully with a controller and adds quite a bit to my enjoyment level, though the game could work fine with a keyboard and mouse.
:  It's drenched with a strong FireFly/Serenity vibe and should be an easy and safe buy for fans of that. The rest of you should still enjoy quite a bit of fun. Replayability is definitely possible, though I couldn't see playing it more than two or three times. After finishing, the only regret I have is that I had to leave the galaxy so soon. I wish there were a sequel.

I played this game for the Free Weekend, least to say it was a so-so experience.
I like the angle of the game delving into the future, and while the civpedia can be a little bland to look at, the information within is quite interesting.
Drawing more upon the word bland. It is admittedly artistic wise for non-in game features very bland indeed, everything is painted with a shade of grey. Same for the long-term gameplay, the first hour is very gripping of this game as you grapple with the mechanics and marvel at the strange aliens and eat up all the information the game throws at you.
Ok, so i make some solid progress in my first game, even though i played on super easy difficulty for begginers, it was a learning experience drawing upon my CIV 5 knowledge (minimum needed to play this game well) I start up a fresh new game on a different map and it just 'feels' the same, even on ramped up difficulty it feels the same.
Unless im totally missing something, the main jumps on difficulty settings do not matter as it merely changes few factors such as how soon Civ's arrive (in game context you are first to land, and the earlier you get there, the more time you have to set up by game rules) and how sassy and rude franko-iberia (the 'cultural civ') is to you.
To stop myself dragging too far on, a summary.
- User interface is unpolished and unclear - Unable to clearly see the orbital view unless it is pointed out to me or trade routes from UI, same for saying i have no idea where my trade routes go or what slots are open unless i activate it on the map modes which are drum roll please... "hidden in the map with a small cursor"
- Civ's are not as imaginative as thier names, have broad abilities to each that you forget about in game unless you look them up or actively seek to use them.
- Too many bottleneck technologies such as ecology (for removing misama fart gas), and some parts of the tech tree are messy in terms of progress
- Very passive AI for both aliens and other civs if you don't raise a gun at all they leave you alone (my first attempt was actually harmony alignment - (Learn more about it in the game) and i didn't need to kill a single alien, plus i harboured a nest so that they'd go away elsewhere and attack other people whilst i ate all the xenomass resources - win - win)
- Quests are too frequent and powerful with effects that literally buff everything in sight making the game too easy.
Unfortunately it feels more like a very well polished mod for CIV 5, rather than a civ game of its own, and unless i am simply too MLG with my strategies to play the game as intended, other than for one or two incidents ill never feel the true wrath of the godlike siegeworm as it takes away everything precious from me.
Still, i would recommend this game since they are hosting a new expansion soon which will hopefully add more meat onto the bones and make it less convouluted. For the meantime the free weekend is still up so grab it while you can and see for yourself.

A lot of work needs to be done. This game is still very clearly in its alpha stage, and content is lacking. I have a fairly high-end PC yet I still get around 20FPS on the lowest settings. Not good. The grind is very real and, due to the little amount of any real content, you are reduced to the montony of killing mobs or crafting in order to level up.
The building system is easy, fun, and the best part of the game right now. I've seen some very cool structures on my server from creative wooden homes to sprawling stone castles. Another neat aspect of the game is the ability to fly with the aid of tamed beasts, broomsticks, or potions. The fun stops there however because flying drains your mana far too quickly. Despite my negativity I think this game has a great deal of potential. We will see how it holds up six months from now.

To actually get a hero, you'll have to have a comic book cover for them. To actually make said hero practical, you'd will search for 10-13 covers for each hero.
