First, let me say the following in all fairness: 2K tried. No matter what the final outcome, for better or for worse, they tried to make a good game. And in many ways, they did good work on this title. The combat actually feels better than in the original Bioshock, being more fluent and giving you more options. Hacking has been significantly improved as you no longer have to play a mini game endlessly to get it to work. Saying that a quick time event actually improved this issue sounds odd, but I assure you, it is true.
The game also looks stunning. Rapture is simply gorgeous in Bioshock 2. A clear step above from its predecessor in that aspect as well. So visually and mechanically speaking, the game is just fine. If those are the things that are important to you in Bioshock game, I have nothing negative to report to you about Bioshock 2. Unfortunately, the most important parts of any Bioshock game for me, personally, are the characters and the story. And that regard, Bioshock 2 falls flat on its big dumb face.
First off, let's consider the character you play. Supposedly, you are prototype Big Daddy who was forgotten in the bowels of Rapture until you are reactivated and asked to help out. So right off the bat, Bioshock 2 feels like a lazy fan game. You aren't really a character the way you were in the other two games. You are merely a prop that lumbers from place to place while being asked "Isn't it so cool that you get to be a Big Daddy" in the most pandering way possible.
Playing as Jack in Bioshock or Booker DeWitt in Bioshock Infinite just felt right. It felt like you were playing a key figure and participant in the ongoing narrative. Playing a supposed Big Daddy in Bioshock 2 feels downright silly. For one thing - as the great Ben "Yahtzee" Croshaw rightly pointed out - you aren't really a Big Daddy.
As a "Prototype", you can now move at normal speed, use weapons and even Plasmids. So basically, you are a Big Daddy in look only. In function, you may as well be anyone. Moreover, being asked to believe you are a prototype Big Daddy raises the question of why the Big Daddy designers stripped the ability to move normally, use weapons and use Plasmids out of the later models, replaced with simply being able to lumber around at a slow pace and punch things with your drill. The answer is, they wouldn't do that. It's all the worst kind of shoehorning in for the sake of player convenience.
The whole concept of playing a prototype Big Daddy just feels wrong. Rather than feeling like a key figure in the narrative, you feel more like a "Thing" that the designers let you play because Big Daddy + Popular = Delta. Moreover - as Yahtzee also noted - while the designers forced you to lumber around as a supposed Big Daddy, they kept all the game mechanics from the first Bioshock the same. So just as you could as Jack in Bioshock, you can still find candy bars and bags of chips to eat and regain health. But whereas Jack had an actual mouth that wasn't obscured by anything, as a Big Daddy I guess you're cramming it all through your face plate? o_O
Never has a concept felt so tacked on as the notion of playing a Big Daddy. It adds nothing to the narrative and only serves to make you feel a bit stupid as the details noted above begin to erode the immersion.
Another big problem with the narrative has to do with the people you encounter in Rapture this time around. The characters you met in Bioshock were vivid, three dimensional people who were as unforgettable as Rapture itself. Who could forget Doctor Steinman's cries of frustration as he couldn't seem to get his latest surgery victim to come out just right while noting the backdrop of all his previous victims? Who could forget Sander Cohen's blatant disregard for poor, poor Fitzpatrcik as he blew him up for not playing his piano solo in tune?
The problem with Bioshock 2' is that at the end of the first Bioshock, every interesting character in Rapture was either dead or gone (depending on how you play. If you have enough mercy and forgiveness in your heart, you can let the sick ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Sander Cohen live). So with the exception of Tenenbaum - who serves as mere cameo in this one - 2K was forced to come up with their own characters from scratch. The result is the most unforgettable bunch I've ever met in a video game. There is a significant lack of meaning that anyone in Rapture has in this game. The characters in Bioshock all represented something that tied in to the narrative of Objectivism and its ideals. Doctor Steinman represented the medical practice unbound by the limitations of the Hippocratic oath. Cohen represented art as unrestrained by regulation, censorship or basic human decency.
But - for example - In Bioshock 2, you meet Simon Wales... who designed Rapture. ... ... I'm not sure what he's supposed to represent aside from "The guy who designed Rapture". And that's really the crux of my problem with the narrative in Bioshock 2. Bioshock and Bioshock Infinite were all about concepts that were bigger than the games themselves. Bioshock 2 is just a game about Bioshock. And that holds no interest for me.
But now we come to perhaps my biggest problem with the whole thing: Sophia Lamb. This lazy pile of main villain garbage is one of the worst Ret-Cons I've seen crammed into any video game or indeed in any form of entertainment period. This character just doesn't fit in the world of Rapture. And that's even just when the game gets started. To say nothing about the game trying to make us accept that she had been there the whole time in Bioshock, yet was never mentioned once.
Everyone we encountered in Bioshock had a reason to be there. They were all attracted to Rapture in some way because Ryan's ideals and ideas freed them from basic sociological constraints, and they all ran amok as a result. There is no reason in the world why a character like Sophia Lamb would even want to go to a place like Rapture. There was nothing for her down there. And to suggest that she wanted to try and influence Rapture's ideals to her way of thinking and change that world from within is simply laughable, because it would have been such an impossible uphill battle that she - in reality - wouldn't even have bothered.
And it adds tragic insult to injury when we are asked to believe that Andrew Ryan actually challenged Sophia Lamb to a public debate wherein both argued their philosophies back and forth to one another. No. I'm sorry. Just - No. Andrew Ryan would never - EVER give legitimacy and/or equal time to someone with Lamb's ideals! Let alone publicly! Someone who was that much an affront to everything Rapture and Ryan stood for would simply have been dealt with. Not debated.
There's also an inherent laziness to the very concept of Sophia lamb as the villain. It's as if she was created in a 2K board meeting where someone said "What was Andrew Ryan again? Objectivist and quasi-libertarian? Well just make this villain whatever that isn't. Cult leader and pseudo-communist? Sure, there we go, whatever". And then slapped all those traits onto her like a half written bumper sticker. We saw something similar to those opposing traits in in Bioshock Infinite, but Comstock, Columbia and its ideals were all a contrast to Rapture, Andrew Ryan and Objectivism. Sophia Lamb is just tthe opposite of what Andrew Ryan was. So whereas these similar ideas were ambitious in Infinite, they're simply lazy in Bioshock 2.
It all comes across as the laziest kind of fan fiction. And that's exactly what Bioshock 2 feels like: A fan game. If you play this game for mere enjoyment, than it's perfectly serviceable and certainly fun. At least at times. But the narrative is so broken and stupid that it just sin't worth playing for me, or even considering it a legitimate entry into the Bioshock world at all. It's the Star Trek V of Bioshock games. Personally, I don't even count it.

Otherwise, you may be better to wait for (at least) first expansion, which is coming out soon. This was, more or less, true for earlier Civ games (especially Civ5 and less so for others - Alpha haven't even profited from expansion).
What it is?
-----------
Civ5 in space. Bit different graphics, some innovations, but nothing revolutionary.  Factions are bleak, and worse - a handful. Civ5 major flaws are here, too... Diplomacy even uses exact same dialogue lines...
What it isn't?
--------------
Alpha2. With EACH faction wonderfully shade-of-gray, even dark agenda, with highly distinctive gameplay, strengths and weaknesses. With revolutionary solutions, years ahead its time...
-----------
So, in current state I could recommend it to newcomers or people who would like to play Civ5-in-space.
For die-hard fans of Alpha, I couldn't recommend it - they are likely to find themselves disappointed or uninterested, same happened to me with Civ5 - bought it, played 10h, didn't touch it until second expansion (when huge discount influenced the decision). I don't regret it NOW, but it did took 2 expansions to get fixed...
There is also a 'third group', which would have to decide for themselves, since I cannot honestly recommend either - read more reviews, forums, watch gameplay videos...
----------
Will expansion fix it? Well, it doesn't *look* like fix-it-all one, but then again, it's Sid Maiers company. It may surprise me yet... On a positive note, Firaxis seem to be aware of flaws, and it's kind of them to provide free-weekends for a game which received wide negative critics - hopefully, they will do the same with expansion.
Don't get me wrong - I'd gladly pay full price (including the expansion) for a fully fixed game, or Alpha2 remake. Mine 'not-buying-until-it's-improved' decision is a matter of general principles and (likely) stubborness - it shouldn't stop other players.
It's Firaxis game, after all, which means certain standards of quality are present - a trait which most wannabie-4X games cannot claim.
Above was stated clearly which groups of player may like the game, and which may not - at least expansion-less.
As for myself, I'll buy it eventually and probably play lots of it - it's just a question of time.

I remember when BioShock came out, and how much fun I had watching my friend play it. I remember everyone raving about how great it was, and how everyone needed to play it.
However, when BioShock 2 came out, all I had heard of it was "BioShock 2 came out" and nothing else. Because of this, I just immediately assumed that it had been nowhere as good as the first BioShock, and never gave it the time of day.
Then, in 2013, along comes BioShock Infinite, and yet again everyone is going on and on about how great it was, and I figured that it must have lived up to the esteem set by the first in the trilogy, leaving the second to be utterly forgotten.
Come Summer of 2015, and during the annual Steam Summer Sale, I noticed that there was a great deal on the entire BioShock franchise. Remembering how much I enjoyed watching my friend play BioShock, and how everyone raved for months about BioShock Infinite, I figured I'd give it a whirl.
First, of course, I played BioShock, and man-oh-man did I love it. I couldn't wait to hop into some BioShock Infinite gameplay. However, once I began playing Infinite, it didn't take long for me to notice that not only had the game changed almost entirely, but I wasn't having near as much fun playing it as I had playing the first game. I trudged throught the main campaign, and although the Burial at Sea DLCs were entertaining, my overall impression of BioShock Infinite wasn't that great.
Disappointed by this, I then remembered that I owned BioShock 2, and driven by my confusion at how big of a let down Infinite had been, I figured, "What the Hell. Why not?"
I'll tell you why not: if having an amazing time and experiencing a very well-made gaming experience is your trigger, then avoid this game entirely.
Not only did BioShock 2 have the appealing aesthetic of BioShock that Infinite lacked, but the gameplay elements that I loved so much about BioShock had also been restored. If you play games solely for gameplay and you love BioShock, then you're going to love BioShock 2 even more. The dual-wield system present in BioShock 2 allows your character to simultaneously fire your weapon and send out powerful plasmids; a due upgrade, in my opinion, from BioShock's split system, and certainly better than Infinite's system that restricted weapon fire whilst firing a "vigor." Not only is the way that combat is gone about better, but the enemy AI has been noticably improved, and the new, powerful enemy types that enjoy barging in every now and again always keep me on my guard.
And hey, now there's a valid excuse as to why your character is a bullet sponge; his a frickin Big Daddy!
Story-wise the game is very well-made. Some people disliked the main story for being very generic, and I agree that it is a bit bland in concept, but the character develpoment made via audiologs is so deep, that I can't help but love it. Story is mostly subjective, though, and I'm against potentially giving out spoilers to people that don't want them, so I'll end this discussion here.
In conclusion, BioShock 2 is my favorite game in the series. The combat mechanics are amazing, the characters are grabbing, and the aesthetic of Rapture is utterly...mesmerizing. I recommend this game to everyone.

I was waiting until the March 2016 patch to write this review.  I felt it would be fair to give Stainless and WotC the extra time to produce a passable game.  Sadly, this has not been the outcome.
Magic Duels is a game that has so much potential, that it fails to even approach.  Free to play card games are generally well recieved in the video game market of 2016, and the amount of money that well made ones make is staggering.
However, for some reason there seems to be a lack of desire or funding on the part of WotC or Stainless, or both, to put together the nessecary resources it takes to produce a functional video game.
Magic Duels has the shell of a great game, but once you look inside you see the blemishes.
Numerous bugs still permeate the play experience.  The netcode is slow and frequently does not match players correctly.  The game does not allow players to accomplish things that they should be able to do in a game of Magic (such as Transforming a planeswalker with an activated ability in the second main phase).  The shuffling algorithms seem off.  The game doesn't even teach the correct rules of Magic, instead making stupid conscessions in the name of simplification that instead only serve to misinform.
I really, really, really wanted to write a positive review of this game.  I was waiting for the March update and resting judgement until they had a chance to get it released and tuned up.  I have given WotC and Stainless every chance to remedy this buggy mess of a game.
Unfortunately, considering the current state of the game, I cannot reccommend anyone play this game, unless you are completely desperate to play Magic on your PC and you don't have the money to play MTGO.

I am not normally one to write reviews on games. But, I feel this game deserves one.  Villagers and Heroes is a unique game. As you can see, I have many hours put into it. Those hours have been well spent. It has been and will continue to be one of the most enjoyable experiences I have ever had on an MMO.  I am not going to make a list of Pros and Cons. I will just list what this game has to offer and my opnions on it.
1. Unique Storyline and Cheeky Humor- I have to admit that I really got into the storyline and was rather upset when it ended and said it would be continued later. You do pick up a different story later in the game that has many cheeky and funny references to a bra.
2. Quests- Yes, there are quests and most of them are pretty easy and straightforward. Some are harder or require drops that are hard to get. But, in my opnion, the best quests are the ones that are long chains and when you get to the end you feel like you actually accomplish something with all the rewards that came y our way after completion. (P.S. Beware of Pinbone in Sapphira's Lament. Damn goblin will take all your gold if you dont pay attention. But he does have some nice rewards in the earlier ones.)
3. Crafting- Finally! A good game where crafted gear is actually worth something.  The best gears in the game come from a mix of drops, crafted and elder gear (explained a bit later). You even have the chance to craft lengendary gears when you reach a certain level of crafting. I can tell you from experience that it is in your best interests to take a night or 2 off per week to keep your crafting level current with your combat level.
4. Community- This is the biggest part of what has kept me playing this game. I have never come across a group of people so nice and willing to help in any MMO I have played. There is little to no toxicity in here. I think that is mostly due to the fact that there is NO PVP whatsoever here. I realize some people will consider no PVP a bad thing and thats fine. Everyone is welcome to their own opinion. But don't come to Villagers and Heroes looking for PVP. We simply do not have it.
5. Rebirth System- I really like the rebirth system. Every 15 levels, starting at 30, you can rebirth and get an extra permanent 5 talents points to use. Rebirthing will reset ALL of your quests, bounties and combat level. Your crafting levels are NOT touched. You might be thinking what a pain to have to start all over just for a few extra talent points. But when you get into the higher levels, you will be glad for those extra points. You will need them. By the time you hit cap (which is 79 at the time of writing this), if you rebirth everytime you can, you will have 20 extra points to use in your talents. It makes a big difference.
6. Devs who actually listen- Yes, the devs actually listen to the community. They even have a discord you can join to talk to other players and the devs.
7. Villages- Your own house in village where you have your own garden plot and ranching plot to raise crops and animals. I highly recommend leveling your garden some before your ranch. Otherwise you may find your animals asking for something you can't grow yet.
I do realize that this game will not be to everyone's taste. But I do encourage you to give it a shot. I am not talking about 5 mins then saying F*** this. I am talking more than 10 levels. Play until the first rebirth. Explore regions (some are locked behind keys you need to get, but that is part of game.) Get to know the people in your village and guild if you decide to join one. Give this game a good shot. You might find it surprises you. The charm just might overcome any shortcomings you think it has.

Half-Life 2 Deathmatch is the official multiplayer component to Half-Life 2. It released about two weeks after the singleplayer and is stand-alone. It is the successor to the immensely popular and addictive multiplayer to the original game. Although it didn't have the same legacy and lasting appeal as it.
The game includes two multiplayer gamemodes. Deathmatch and Team Deathmatch. Along with a handful of multiplayer maps that were portions of the singleplayer. When I first played Half-Life 2 Deathmatch I remember being a little disappointed since it lacked content and felt like a bit of an afterthought compared to other games at the time like Counter Strike Source and Unreal Tournament 2004.
Indeed the game is mostly known for being full of hackers. Which is unfortunate since it did improve after release with mods like CTF. Half-Life 2 Deathmatch's legacy is now seen in the modifications that were based upon it, like Garry's Mod. If you want to play it today I'd suggest downloading a mod for bots and a few custom maps. It's a relic today, but a playable one. And at 5$ it does give you what you paid for. Nothing more, and nothing less.

People described this game as a mod for Civilization 5 and I can see where they are coming from. The way the game plays and the interface are mostly the same and it has all the same windows (diplomacy, economic overview, etc.). Most of the changes are on the surface level: gold has been replaced by energy, social policies by virtues and archers by rangers.
The main shortfall of CivBE is that is has no character/personality. The maps and menus look bland and your opponents are completely interchangeable. Another thing that's missing is context. You know about Hiawatha and the Iroquois and what a lighthouse is, but you don't know who Élodie is and what a xenomass well does.
All in all, this would have been a GREAT mod for Civ5, but as a standalone game it doesn't compare well to it's bigger brother.
If you didn't play Civ5, play that instead. If you have played Civ5, this feels like a step back.

There are a few things you should consider before jumping to Marvel Puzzle Quest: Dark Reign.
1) Do you mind only playing in small, bite-sized chunks?
2) Do you mind spending real-world cash to continue playing?
If you answered "no" to the first question then have at it. You'll have fun building your deck of characters, leveling them up, taking on new challenges, etc. It's essentially the old Puzzle Quest with a Marvel spin, which isn't a bad thing. It's quite fun if you enjoy that type of game and completing challenges and quest lines is rewarding.
If you answered "yes" to the second question then prepare to be sorely disappointed. You can play this game without ever spending a single cent, but you won't have the best characters, won't have enough storage space for additional characters, won't be able to level them high enough to compete in multiplayer events and will always be running short on health packs. Basically, without spending money on it (and not just once, but regularly) you'll never get the most out of it.

This game combines elements of resource management and building construction along with elements of older RTS games like Warcraft 3. You create a dungeon with adequate defenses where you farm resources and produce units and abilities. In the over world, your units get titles that improve them along with levels after defeating enough enemies. I have heard complaints about the narrator, but I quite like it. The narrator is very similar to the narrator from the Stanley Parable and frequently makes reference to other fantasy tales like Lord of the Rings, Warcraft, God of War, and even some classic rock songs. I cannot count how many times the narrator made me laugh or I freaked out because my dungeon was being invaded during the course of the campaign. The controls are a little hidden, but if you know the basic commands for organizing units in other RTS games you will be right at home. If you want to be the villain in a sarcastic parody of fantasy worlds this game is right for you.

Overall Rating: 6/10
Gameplay Rating: 6/10
Accessibility Rating: 7/10
When you start This War of Mine (TWOM), the main menu consists of one primary button: survive.
At its heart, TWOM is a survival game.  In it, you must guide the actions of a small group of people as they struggle to survive amidst a war that is ravaging their city.
I would recommend this game as a good purchase when on sale.  It is difficult to get started, interesting to play and think about, but ultimately repetitive after you understand the game mechanics.
TWOM is primarily point-and-click.  While you can control zoom levels, the game field is larger than the what is shown at the furthest zoom level out, so you must use the mouse to scroll the screen, which can be annoying.
Each new game puts you in a slightly randomized house with a different amount of resources in each iteration.
The game's economy is interesting and slightly complex, but ultimately quite limited.  The sheer number of different types of items is where the economy's complexity comes from, and the challenge lies in trying to balance what you bring back on scavenging missions due to limited space and the need to have a variety of items.  Once you understand the system, however, it is not difficult to become self-sustaining and to even develop an excess of tradable resources.
Upgrade mechanics in the game are decent, but sometimes too costly for the benefit.
TWOM takes place in a war ravaged (presumably) eastern European nation.  The charm of this game comes from its story more than anything else.  It is possible to simply play the game without getting invested in its story, but why waste the money?
The survivors each have a back story and unique traits that can complement the abilities of others to make a stronger team.  Further, each character reacts to the moral decisions you make as the war progresses and some events are triggered.  TWOM frequently nudges you to consider the terrible impacts of war on the innocent people that live in and around it.
This War of Mine is rated 7/10 for gameplay.  You will restart multiple times, and, after some point, the game's difficulty will fade away, diminishing its overall replay value.
Game options are available before starting a new game, but the menus may be difficult to see due to being low contrast with the background.  Look for the cog wheel in the lower right corner.
Available options are music volume and sound effects in Sound options, resolution, quality, and fullscreen in Video, and localization (language and termperature).
One note is that the game uses a stylized 'Pencil Effect' that can be set to high or low.   This may provide a challenge for low-vision gamers.
+ Dialog shows in text for all speech
+ Key sounds are visualized (those that affect game mechanics)
- It is possible to miss game events that may have an accompanying sound if they happen off-screen.
TWOM is playable for deaf/HOH gamers.  Sound is not required to experience the game, since it uses visual cues to represent when your characters are making too much noise while sneaking around.
+ Limited input required - essentially a mouse-only game.
- No options for altering combat mode, game difficulty, or accessibility accommodations for these events.
This game relies solely on gross mouse control and frequent clicking.  In combat situations, which are infrequent, it may be necessary to react quickly and make use of fine mouse control capabilities.

First, I'm basing my review on the singleplayer, not the multiplayer.  Its a 6 year old game, and in multiplayer, its competing against so many massive titles it really can't hold a candle to, due to budget, tech and gameplay.
In singleplayer, the game isn't bad, but it really isn't particularly good either.  Graphicaly, its fine, but the gameplay is just mediocre, and I'd say its actualy made worse by the story.  The story has a few massive flaws in it.
First, the game tries to take itself very seriously, and offer a realistic look at war.  This would be fine, if it didn't keep switching between being Michael Bay-action-FPS, and something trying to be emotional and artistic.  This drags down both, and takes away from the game.  The action segments feel strange, and don't have much build up since they're switching from an emotional segment.  The emotional segments feel meaningless since you're immediatly pulled out to shoot people.  Making this attempt at making the game realistic ever worse is the inconsitancy and massive plot holes.  How was North Korea even able to grow to be that much of a threat with China and Russia right there to stop them, and even after growing that much, and with the EMP, they still shouldn't have stood much of a chance against the US.  Even dropping both those factors, theres one final flaw.  It feels like you have no impact on the game at all.  You're just a soldier following the main characters.  You have no impact on anything.  Comparing it to another liniar FPS game, Half Life, in Half Life, you are the one getting stuff done.  You launch the satalite, defeat the enemy, ect.  In Homefront, the whole story could have happened without you pretty easily.  Even more because you're constantly following a few NPCs, it just feels like you're watching them experience it, without being there yourself.
As such, I really can't recommend Homefront at full price.  At $10 USD or less, it may be worth it if you enjoy FPS games, but not at full price.

I'm really having a hard time with this one. As a fan of the older games, I really did like a lot of what went into this and some of the atmospheric elements it created, as well as the overall look, tone and feel of the game.
It left me, however, feeling like I do after playing many later iterations of "classic" (relatively speaking) games, like the Splinter Cell or Resident Evil series as other examples: it feels as if studios are constantly being sucked deeper into the pit of action-fueled games, at the expense of what drew an audience in the first place. While this game did have an interesting story and excellent production, it lost a lot of what made the older games (particularly Blood Money) interesting and replayable, namely rewarding creativity, patience, and containing far less linearity. Some linearity is necessary for story, but the breadth of diverse and unobvious solutions to missions was severely lacking overall. Some levels were an exception, but not enough.
This wouldn't have bothered me as much, however, if the difficulty didn't feel so broken. In Blood Money, high difficulty meant enemies would be more wary, 47 would die much more easily (realistically), you'd have less agency assistance, the evidence you left would impact your rating, you wouldn't be able to save, and your map would give you less information. In other words -- you needed to be more thorough, more careful, and generally more creative to achieve higher scores (as an aside, the newspaper at the end of missions was a brilliantly immersive way to give a sense of relevance to the score in 47's world). In Absolution, however, the highest difficulty meant your "point shooting" feature was limited (again, a silly addition to a game that was supposed to be more skill oriented, as it was in Splinter Cell Conviction), there would be no help, no tutorial, no interface, etc. All good so far, and more "immersively realistic" than in previous games. The instinct meter, however, was somewhat broken. The need to hide your face from enemies you're dressed as makes a lot of sense and adds a great element of further disguise. The problem, though, was that it would arbitrarily run out, and this meant you couldn't pass *other* NPC's dressed in *other* outfits without being noticed anymore, or at least not easily.
Again, not so bad if it weren't for the last straw: in Purist or Expert, *copious* amounts of enemies are added. Copious. For instance, the couthouse (according to an online count) has 33 security guards and police officers. THIRTY THREE. In a somewhat rural courthouse. It just feels absurd. Why are there more than half a dozen police officers patrolling the back lot? In the "Attack of the Saints" level there are 46 agency mercs and 3 saints. 49 armed combatants, which is roughly the amount of an infantry platoon. Many of the sections of this level contain troops patrolling what appear to be 10' square sections of an open area, which again feels rather absurd and like a "spray and pray" attempt at making the game more difficult. Rather than requiring creative solutions, playing through these levels on Purist more comes down to memorizing highly specific routes and scripted patrols, angles of throwing objects, and precise timing of changing into disguises in bizarre locations at particular angles away from NPC's. The game becomes more about stealth than about disguise and planning, and not in a fun way the way Splinter Cell was.
Bonus: Why is a sociopathic hick constantly outsmarting 47? He's supposed to be meticulous and absurdly precise, but his attempts to foil the chubby cowboy feel amateurish in cutscenes and the like.
In summary: a well-produced/polished game that handles well and creates good atmosphere, only to have this sullied by poor difficulty mechanics, linearity, and stealth elements that would be more fun if not such an integral part of the game.
TL;DR: Fun game, poor Hitman game. Buy it if it's on sale, and only if you've played Blood Money.

Sure it's a bad Hitman game, but it's also a mess
Hitman Absolution takes a step in the wrong direction with this iteration of the franchise. In an push for more of a story arc challenges, and making it more accessible,  Absolution moved away from core concepts of the Hitman franchise.
In previous games, players were presented with an open world to explore. Instead of murdering everyone on the way to the target, you assume people's identities (stealing their clothes) to gain access to more secure areas until you reached your target and then escape. The highest achievement being a silent assassin, no evidence, no witnesses, no unnecessary kills. So there is a lot of exploration and prodding the defenses with multiple paths to the goal.
Absolution strays a lot from that formula. Firstly, level designs are much more linear. The open world had been replaced by a series of sub-missions. So there is a lot less freedom and exploration. Secondly, while disguises still grant you access to new areas, people in the same outfit can still blow your cover. The leisurely plotting for the path of least resistance is no longer a thing as you are under constant pressure to prevent you from being discovered. Thirdly, there is instinct which is an ability to see through walls, highlight objects of interest and blend in to prevent being discovered. There are no customization with loadouts. Mainly because Absolution is more story driven than other Hitman games, but probably also in part to the scoring system, you cannot customize what items you take at the start of the level. This is simply not the same core concept of design and execution of mission from the previous iterations and it's difficult to see beyond this glaring issue.
For what the game is, it does have some good notes. The voice acting is solid and the crowds of NPCs are pretty amazing. The detail of individual levels is stunning. Sadly the cut scenes look awful. And despite more focus on telling a story, it makes no sense and the dialogue is awful. I do like that they added a scoring system as there was a Hitman community that enjoyed challenging other's speed or coming up with clever alternatives (which is some what served by the contract system).
Individual level designs are limited, and not just compared to the open worlds fans have come to expect. They are small and linear with few options. It's easy to discover the best "alternative path" that avoids most enemy NPCs to absurd levels. Do i duck and roll past 25 roving AI for 5 minutes or take a ladder? Some of the sub-missions are utterly pointless, which is recognized by the fact they aren't even scored by the challenge system. They essentially are quick-time events (QTEs) between cut-scenes.
As for combat, there doesn't seem to be much difference with weapons inside their given class. Yes, they improved the gun play greatly, but the scoring system penalizes you for using it. And since you can't craft your loadout, the effort seems to go to waste. Hand-to-hand combat is terrible as it is a QTE with a shaky screen (while on consules the prompts are clear and easy to read).
The difficulty scaling is simply broken. Once you turn on professional difficulty level designs (already limited) cease to have any sense of rhyme or function. Additional NPCs cripple exploration, alternative routing, and make several playing styles all but useless. I highly recommend watching a purist suit-only run and watch the utter nonsense required to pull of perfect levels. And with the weakening of the disguise mechanic, changing clothes provides the minimal benefit. The most important skill is not accuracy or planning as much as finding random crap to throw to move impassable AI. Sure, 1 or 2 items tosses would be fine, but it sometimes requires 5+ to make it through a single area.
AI detection makes no sense. AI can spot the shoe of a body from 50 feet away, in the dark, on a raining night (through bushes and NPCs). On the other hand, you can sprawl out in a crouch and encircle them and seemingly avoid detection. While they can detect the sound of thrown items, they don't seem to see them. You can use a remote detonator as a decoy or even pick up a thrown object directly under and NPCs feet and toss it again. AI can sense you are in disguise from behind at a distance, while wearing a mask, even a full mascot outfit.
The checkpoint system is broken. It does not save your progress in the level, merely the location. Disposed of enemies respawn and scripted events may have to be triggered again. This can create impossible to pass situations (barring shooting everyone).
The challenge system is a good idea poorly executed. It rewards players for picking up items, or completing side missions in game, or performing certain tasks. But instead of rewarding this as score bonuses at the end, they are multipliers. Also the secret challenges are unlocked as each tier is completed. So a secret mission is kill x people with y weapon. then kill x+2 people with y weapon. then kill x+4 people with y weapon. But doing the x+4 kill resets with ever tier unlock forcing players to replay missions over and over. 1 mission has 12 unique ways to kill an NPC, so for maximum score you have to kill him 12 times, then go back and kill him once more to compete on the global score.
There are also contracts which allows you to replay the level, but this time you set your own challenges and see if others can duplicate your feat. Putting mission designs in the hands of non-developers typically doesn't go well and doesn't here. While some are clever, most fall into 2 categories; 1) simple design to meet achievements 2) ridiculously difficult, manipulate a random event impossible feat. I think the global scoring from the in game levels would have been enough and that tying achievements to online activities for a none multi-player game is bad. You can see the posts on forums looking for people to add as friends and create contract competitions. It's just short-sighted by developers in regards to achievement hunters (though I guess it rewards players for buying the game early).
Instead of making an improved Hitman game, what was produced is a mess of conflicting ideas. Focus on story but not bother to make it any good. Improve gun play, but punish players for using it. Move away from open world and exploration but force replays and time sinks via challenges and unnecessary levels. Move away from open world to cover-stealth then make stealth impossible on higher difficulty levels. Stripe the legendary assassin of his anonymity, power, guile and replace with x-ray vision and precognition.
I cannot recommend this as a Hitman game (since it isn't one) nor as a cover-stealth due to so many flaws in design and execution.

Edit : Seeing the kind of answers and comment I get, I decided to rewrite the
review in a more documented way. I know the game is EARLY ACCESS, and that thumb
down and Negative review could change if the dev correct the issues that only a
few minutes in game have uncovered and if they can erase the very bad "first impression"
they gave me.
First of all, the keybind. If the dev had said "we are in early acces, keybind
will come later", or if they had missed 1 or 2 keybind, that could be
understood. But right now the game has a way to rebind most of the actions you
can do EXCEPT for the most important keybind, the MOVE keybind. We are in 2017,
how in hell could those specific key being absent from a supposed "full key
rebinding option" ? And being in Early Access is not an excuse when all the
others keybind can be changed. To add to the problem, the game don't keep you
from rebinding some key to the move key. In fact it let you proceed and then
just rewrite the binding in game.
Second : The character creator. The actual character creator is lacking a lot of
parameters, and is very poor. I'm not speaking about the 'amount of option' for
the various parameters, as an early access game is bound to have little option
for each parameters, I'm speaking about the huge lack of parameters to customize
a character. No difference in how tall the characters are ? No option present
for the kind of character you want to play. Again being in Early Access is not
an excuse not to have at least the parameters exposed, even if having only 1
option until later in the developpement (like letting players pick if they want
a tall, medium or small body size). If the devs had plans to rewrite the whole
character creator later, then they should have provided 2 basic bodies, with a
clear message in the character creator saying things would be changed later.
Third : Sluggish move feeling in game. The little I moved in the area only got
me feeling like I was moving a elderly guy using his walker to move around, and
not some supposed "hero or healthy character" moving in an environment that
could be dangerous. Having no "good sensation" when moving around in a game is
something that is anti-immersive.
Even if the game is "good looking" in the scenery, it's never a good thing to
see how some "details" are overlooked. As it's just a first "sight" of what kind
of overlooking could happen in others parts of the game. All in all I hope the
dev will work hard and correct those, and give me a good reason to change this
review once more and change the thumb down to a thumb up. So now the ball is in
their camp and I wish that they manage to make a great game in the end.
PS : To those guys who though that telling me to ask for a refund was a good
idea, keep going on every bad review and say so to the players, you will not
help the devs of the games you 'hope to see working'. A game that is in early
access is bound to have problem, and only players who voice about those problems
will give the devs a sign that there is a problem somewhere. Saying "all is ok"
when it's not is not helping the efforts of the dev.

Let me cut straight to the chase.
Is BioShock 2 as memorable as BioShock? Perhaps not.
Is the story as amazing? No.
Is the story flawed in some senses? Yes.
Is it a bad game? No, absolutely not.
BioShock 2 is great in it's own right. It maintains most of the fantastic elements found in BioShock but (in my opinion) improves game-play in several ways.
- Still fantastically atmospheric
- Main story is OK
the story in Minerva's Den (DLC) is incredible.
- Minerva's Den is really worth your time
- One plasmid and one weapon equipped at the same time.
- Hacking system is greatly improved
- Hacking from a distance!
- Exploring is still as rewarding as ever - you'd be surprised how many places you can go
- BioShock 2 is challenging, especially fights with Big Daddies/Sisters
- Main story is not as memorable as BioShock
- You have to fight Big Sisters, even if you choose not to harvest Little Sisters (this makes no sense to me).
- I did not enjoy the multiplayer scene. There were very few players and some players were already at max level. Let me tell you, it is extremely difficult to play against someone with so many advantages. It is a shame because the concept is really solid.
If you enjoyed BioShock I would urge you to give BioShock 2 a try too. Yes, the reviews are not as positive as they are for BioShock, but what really matters is your personal enjoyment of the game. I can say that I certainly enjoyed playing BioShock 2, and I think you would too.

I write this review after having spent a decently long time in this game, for a single play through. I did not beat this game, and I likely won't...after having spent as much time as I have in this, the grind has simply lost its appeal, and that is sadly the biggest weakness this game has.
Don't be led astray, and don't let yourself miss out on this game. It is fun, for a while. The combat is pretty intuitive, if some what simple, the story is satisfactory for what it is, and the game runs great. The issue is that if you are a story driven player, like me, you will run into a problem: GRIND. After 3-4 hours of good paced gameplay, you will find yourself horribly outmatched by your next mission and new enemies...so you fall back and grind for a solid 3-4 hours, completing otherwise pointless missions over and again to earn enough cash to get bigger better guns, armor, shields, ships, whichever it is you need or all of the above. Then you burn through another few hours of gameplay and then have to grind again...and each grind is painfully longer than the last. Personally, I am near the end of the game and faced with a final grind that would likely consume multiple nights...I just don't care anymore. I may come back and finish, I may not.
All that said, I deffinitely got my money's worth out of this game. I had fun for many hours before it became stale, and I am satisfied. IF you are the type of player who enjoys the grind, who loves soaking time to get better and better gear, you may really enjoy this one. If you are simply looking for a few hours of fun playing Space Cowboy (or pirate, if you are so inclined) then you will not regret this. This -is- a fun game, and I do recommend it, you just have to know what you are getting yourself into. $20 well spent.

I had this game on PS4 then got rid of my consol. I saw this on steam and thought, 'Cool a space trading game!' Shortly after loaded it up and playing a while I realised that Rebel Galaxy could be fantastic, but feels kind of meh.
Graphics are good, sound is too. I am very happy that I am able to choose MP3s of my own at specific times. I find hard techno a good sound for battle.
Perhaps I suck at space battles, but I found that I needed to do a sh*tload of side missions to upgrade my ship enough to survive the story missions. It seems quite random. At times 'average' provided a challenge but was doable, and other times as soon as I get close to the target area my shields are gone and my hull is breached.
Perhaps the most disappointing part of the game for me is the fact that the trading aspect is just so random. Not sure if it is explained in a tutorial but I figured out, buy red (low) and sell green (high). It didn't take long for me to get frustrated that no station in the system wanted the stuff in my hold. This leaves me with the feeling that the trading aspect almost seems tacked on.
The AI of mission NPCs is annoying, and many a time my escort mission or fighting companion gets taken out and I fail the mission without any warning.
I like the idea of being able to mine in space. Rebel Galaxy makes this an annoying chore with little pay out. Without doing some internet searching, I seriously doubt the average gamer will be able to make enough money to warrant mining.
If you liked the mining and trading aspects of EVE online - don't buy this game. It will disappoint.
I'd rate this 3/10. If the trading and mining aspects were revisited this could be a great single player game.

I received this game free through the humble bundle offering. I played the game through to the ending. This game is a brain dead shooter experience that epitamizes THQ seeking to push yet another into a then oversaturated shooter market. This was a AAA game that felt like a discounted COD:4. Your allies are idiots, and struggle to open doors, but you can't so you must rely on them. Your allies are two dimensional characters that struggle to understand logic or consider alternatives. You are, yet again, a silent protagonist who says literally no words the entire time for no reason, but who is "imperative" to the story. The game tries to make your character a main character, but you might as well just be another NPC. Your only role in the story is to look at things and shoot them. As soon as you deviate from the strict mission guidelines, the game will fail you and restart you from the checkpoint, despite it seeming that there are alternative options available.
There are moments in which they try to tug at your American heartstrings, but they were unsuccessful, as they were weak attempts to get me to get about characters introduced twenty minutes beforehand. Stuff like mass graves and killing off main characters is only successful if you give the player an attachment to the world.
For the actual plot line, it's incredibly contrived and unlikely. North Korea united with South korea to become our glourious Korea. While this is near impossible, the game then states that the country becomes an economic powerhouse which for some reason dooms the American economy (for some reason). Korea then invades the US and the US is submissive to these powers with no assistance from ally powers. Finally, instead of utilizing American citizen human capital power, they decide that the best thing to do with people who are prisoners, is to have them in labor camps.
In synopsis, the game is not worth buying at any price, and I do not even recommend playing it even if you receive it for free. It goes to show the low quality games that THQ was willing to put out, and why they shutdown. A company that built itself on licensed movie games was able to make an original IP feel like a bad, licensed movie game.

The transition between sublight and warp speeds is seamless, conveying a good sense of size to each solar system. There are some issues with scaling (small/medium craft with advanced weapons survive much better in the same scenarios than larger more expensive craft with the same armament and equipment), and the "precise" aiming mode for turrets is complete trash, swinging drunkenly past where you actually try to aim. Even the general "manual" aiming mode needs work, as it likes to lock on to whatever it feels like. There needs to be a key to quickly toggle between locking and true manual aiming.
The main plot is fun, if short.
This is a solid entry in the genre, and if there were a proper developer's kit I feel like it would attract a great mod community to take the game to the next level. It's been out for around two years and there has been no DLC and I've seen no rumor of a sequel, so that's a bit disappointing. As positive as all the reviews are, I hope sales were good and the developer can go on to produce more in the genre. There are too few space games out there, and few with such a shallow learning curve. It's very easy to pick up and play.

At first, I hated this game. Tiny little bugs that nicked at my OCD, bad fonts, and for whatever reason the leader scenes weren't animated. But, I gave it a chance anyways, because I enjoyed Alpha Centauri. I found lots of reasons to like this game - turn processing was blazing fast, the quests in game gradually develop your colony to your liking (therefore making it radically different than other colonies in all respects, even if one player is using the same faction as you). Trade convoys allow for mutual benefits for any two cities (although, considering the importance, I think it would have been cool to be able to put embargos on a specific trade route, but the current system is more than enough and this game still has plenty of room and time for expansion). There's also a lot of things I don't like - you're not able to see trade routes in the city view, you have to select the convoy or trade vessel that is currently on the route to see, minor UI bugs, bad font and how they use symbolic representations of unit abilities or units themselves to represent military units and buildings in the civilopedia (which I can easily get mixed up as they use the same color scheme and art style). All in all, though, a solid game, definitely worth a try.

Bleed is another one of these modern-day hard-core 2D action-platformers that seem to be all the rage lately. But don't take that as a knock on it. It's actually a really well-made game with some unique elements to it. The primary story mode is comprised of 7 levels, each of which feature a sub-boss, a final boss, and some steep challenges in between. The gameplay is typical fare (jump and shoot), but with some interesting twists. The most notable thing is the shooting mechanic, which is done is the style of twin-stick shooters (shoot in 360 degrees via the mouse or right-thumbstick). Jumping is another key mechanic with a twist - you can jump up to three times, but the jumps are more like dashes in specific directions. So you have to perform the moves with precision and forethought. The final game mechanic is "bullet time", in which the action slows down to a crawl, allowing you to perform crazy dodges, super-precise maneuvers, or get more shots in on bosses. In between levels, you can also buy various upgrades (new weapons, more health, etc) using points you earn by clearing levels (performing well earns more points). The controls are spot-on and the game is very forgiving, having no major penalty for death (at least in the story mode). This allows anyone to eventually be able to beat it if they are persistent enough. Bleed can be completed in around an hour or two at most on normal difficulty (and probably much less if you are really good), so it's not very long, no matter how you slice it. Replay value and longevity comes in the form of higher difficulty levels and an "arcade mode", which tasks you to beat the game with just 1 life (good luck with that!). For those who are into brutal challenges and high scores, there's probably enough here to justify a purchase. But if you're like me, and are now "way too old for that♥♥♥♥♥♥quot;, it's maybe less so of a no-brainer (though I felt it was worth it, regardless). So I would say base your decision on that... If you are into tough platformers and welcome a challenge, this is well worth the money. But if you're more of a casual fan of the genre, take into account the short length for basic completion and decide whether 5 bucks is worth a couple of hours of fun. Overall, the game is solid and has some pretty cool things going for it, so I say it's worth it, but YMMV... I give it a solid B.
Technical notes: I played the game with a gamepad and it worked fine, though it did take me quite a while to wrap my head around the control scheme, which is quite unusual for games like this (left and right sticks for movement and shooting, left and right triggers for bullet-time and jumping). In retrospect, I realize it probably would have been easier to control via mouse and keyboard, due to the precision aiming a mouse provides. I just went with gamepad out of habit for this type of game, without thinking. Both methods definitely work, but this is one of those rare cases where I don't necessarily recommend having a gamepad in order to buy the game. I think it should probably be just fine, if not better, with keyboard and mouse controls only, if that's all you have.

Marvel Puzzle Quest (MPQ), is a mobile device port for steam.  Is that necessarily a bad thing?  I don't think so, but it is something that you need to keep in mind when looking at the UI and graphics.  It also effects the pay system, and since this is a F2P game, that's something people tend to focus on.  So let's start there:
Can you play MPQ without spending money?  Yes.  Will you be competitive... well, mostly.  Let's talk about what real money gets used for:  You can purchase the two types of in-game currency with real money.  ISO and Gold.  ISO is used, mainly, to purchase boosts for use during combat and to spend to level up your characters.  It is the common currency of the game and is earned pretty easily.  Gold can be used for a number of things.  You can purchase additional slots to hold more characters (you are limited to 4 characters at the start and the prices for additional slots increases the more you have), you can purchase some "super-boosts", you can purchase health packs, and you can purchase additional covers for your characters.  Do you "have" to purchase these things?  Nope.  You do earn some gold through normal game play, and many people (myself included) have found that if you focuse your purchases you don't really hit a wall for a very long time.
Let's move onto the gameplay itself.  MPQ is a tile matching game that is themed around the Marvel Comic Universe.  You swap tiles on a grid board to make 3 or longer chains of the same color/shape (think Bejewelled), you then score a hit dealing damage and (in most cases) generated Ability Points (AP) of that color.  Each character that you have selected (three) will have different abilities both passive and active.  These abilities are often fuelled by the AP you generate from your matches.  Pretty simple.  There is an entertaining amount of depth in selecting which team you want to bring to an event, and finding good synergy between character abilities is important.
The characters are leveled up by unlocking their skills.  Skills are found by getting random drop "Covers".  Each cover has one skill associated with it.  Once you have used that cover to train the character in that skill it will increase the "Current Max Level" of the character, you can then use ISO to increase the level of the character.  Every level increase raises the max Hit Points of the character, the amount of damage they do and the effectivness of their skills.  Once you have unlocked the first level of the skill you can use Gold to increase the skill level (this is the main form of Pay-to-Win that you see in the game, but is limited by the fact that you have to have the base skill first to buy it).
Health of your characters is the delaying factor in playing.  Not only are you doing damage to your enemies, but they are doing damage to your characters as well.  Their health will increase back to max over time, but with high level characters this can take several hours.  If you take your three best characters into a match that is over their head and get them all killed, this can mean that you don't get to play again for a few hours... unless you use Health Packs.  Health packs allow a character to return to full health immediately.  You earn health packs over time, one every 30 minutes, but could buy additionals for Gold.
The game provides some basic "PVE" missions to get a feel for the game and earn some basic covers and boosts, but the main part of the game that allows you to progress is the "PVP" duels and "PVE" events.  Events rotate every few days and give opportunities for rare and high end rewards, but competition can be tough and some events require having certain characters to participate.  Duels are a staple way to put your team against another player.  The duels aren't really PVP though, because the same AI that runs the normal missions just uses the team, not an actual player.
Long and the short of it:  I find MPQ to be very entertaining, something that I have spent many an hour with and am perfectly happy to keep playing.  There are issues, some bugs that break events and some exploits that people have found that can let them rank up super fast, and there are concerns about Pay-To-Win, but overall I can say that if you are looking for a casual time waster, this does the job rather well.

One new game mechanic added to the Puzzle Quest system are abilities that effect tiles on the board. Such as Iron Man placing Protect Tiles, that turn the normal gems in to shielded gems to reduce damage to your heroes, or Storm's Attack Tiles that damage your opponent. They still behave like normal gems, in that you can match them to other colors and they'll go away. Some of your enemies also place gems that have a count down timer, and will activate after a number of turns have pasted. Like HAMMER Assassins that will place Sniper Tiles on the board, and will deal heavy damage to your heros after a few turns have passed. This helps you as a player, since you can prevent the enemies abilities by matching those countdown tiles, and removing the ability before it has a chance to go off.
The worst part about this game, is that when your heroes are damaged or knocked out in a game, they will have to recover and this can take up to an hour or more without using heal packs. You start out with a dozen or so, but once you run out, you'll have to pay cash for more. Also, improving your hero is terrible. Instead of earning experience in battles, you earn this ISO-8 currancy, and you spend that on heroes to improve their base health and a few other stats. To improve their abilities, you have to either spend a ton of the premium currancy or hope that you get another copy of that hero. Say you have Captain America, and he only has one ability. To unlock his other 2 abilities, you'll need another Captain America, with that ability, and add his to your hero. It requires too much luck to improve just one hero, and Puzzle Quest's bosses are betting that will pay tons of money to do so.
Yes, this game has a lot of options to get ahead with cash purchases, and these purchases won't go very far, since most of them are completely random. Say you really want Spider-man on your team, then you have to option of fighting Venom to win a Spider-man with a Fantastic Four suit or throw a few dollars at random hero packs and pray he turns up.
I do recommend this game for tablets, since it's best suit to short play sessions.

You can call me a hipster, but I like this one more than the original or Infinite. There's just something about this particular story, these particular characters and this particular Rapture, that was amiss in the other two. While Bioshock established Rapture as a location and told a story of its founder, Bioshock 2 focuses more on the lives of Rapture's ordinary inhabitants, and boy, does it add to the immersion. The storyline is less linear, allowing an option to spare or kill not only Little Sisters, but bosses as well, which leads to one of 6 endings.
The core of the gameplay stayed almost untouched since the original Bioshock, but with some new features. Action-packed harvesting sessions and Big Sister fights are intertwined with the calm and tranquil seabed walks. In addition to previously seen weapons, you have Big Daddy's iconic drill and Rivet Gun at your disposal. Also, you can use both weapons and plasmids in a fight, without swapping one for the other (for me personally it seemed kind of stupid that it wasn't like this all along).
In short, if you just finished Bioshock, and can't get enough of Rapture, get Bioshock 2 in a heartbeat. You won't regret it.
Also, playing as a Big Daddy is beyond cool. 10 drill dashes out of 10.

Pros: Actual deckbuilding, the game is free, the premise of 'planeswalker origins' is more story than I'd have expected from a card game's little 'campaign', it has multiplayer, the AI is reasonably clever, the in-game UI is generally well-made, and the rarity system for card limits is a surisingly good design choice.
Cons: 'Challenges' require use of a dreadful deckbuilding 'wizard', boosters' coin price coupled with the limited availability of coins can be off-putting, very minimal solo content, the only multiplayer available is 1v1 (two-headed giant is advertised, but NOT supported by the network structure), and there are one or two UI nuisances that can render certain games or cards all but unplayable.
At launch, and for a long while thereafter, there was only one type of booster: Magic Origins. Now there's also Battle for Zendikar, Oath of the Gatewatch, and Shadows over Innistrad, IIRC. On the one hand, they excluded a lot of interesting cards from the boosters that they adopted. On the other, they did have the sense to make Origins a strong set, so you're actually still best off getting a lot in Origins rather than having to immediately jump on new sets due to power creep or the like. Still, each booster in-game requires 10 AI wins (5 multiplayer). Seeing as each booster only grants 6 cards, you would need about 100 boosters to finish one of those 4 sets. Which would be 4,000 games of between 5-10 minutes, even with the most aggro of decks. I don't know about you, but in my book, 20,000-40,000 hours of speed running the AI is an ABSURD amount of grinding.
Now, the rotating quests, double coins for first versus win of the day, and one-time campaign bonus coins do cut a significant amount of that if you pace yourself. A quest or two might get you a booster, and a single campaign (there are a decent handful) probably nets you one... but versus isn't really consistent (as only wins count, and it's all 'ranked'), and there is a cap to how many coins you can earn in one day of grinding (a couple hundred-- so don't expect to get more than 3-4 boosters in a day without quests or the like). Most annoyingly, though, the quests are by vast majority those that require you to use 'archetype' decks... i.e. those created by the incredibly poorly considered 'deck wizard'.
On the surface, the deck wizard seems brilliant. No worrying about counting lands by color, it walks you through the usual theme for the dual color you pick, et cetera... Yet, there is no way to veto the wizard's 'suggestions', meaning that you're more often than not forced to throw 8 CMC creatures into your aggro deck, or zombies into your elf tribal, or so on. Not to mention that the wizard has no concept of mana curve, or that the archetypes themselves are rather limited, or that the cards you get with just the starter kit can't properly support any of them...
As an aside, multiplayer does -not- solve this grind, as you -cannot- compete with those who've finished a full set if you're stuck on just starters. The playing field looks to level out if you have any single set complete, which is nice enough, but you're starting off with a huge disadvantage against those who shelled out the money for extra coins.
Speaking of, I can't really recommend purchasing coins as a real solution. I bought twenty or so dollars worth of coins after feeling the game was worth paying into, but it felt like more a matter of principle than significant gain-- the boosters just cost too many coins for too few cards relative to the -actual card game-. Though, the fact that you never get duplicates once you finish a playset does mean that every card you get is guaranteed to go towards completion.
As some random notes, the game uses an interesting ruleset for deckbuilding: common cards are limited to 4 copies of a given card, as per usual, but uncommons have a limit of 3, rares a limit of 2, and mythic rares a limit of 1. This is easily the game's most interesting quirk, as it nearly solves the age-old problem of rare-spam making some instances of pay-to-win in the usual standard formats. Also, the game will skip your main phase instantly if you have only instant-speed cards, which ruins certain combo-plays, along with causing a certain creature to be entirely unplayable. Still, the game's biggest flaw is undoubtedly its lack of alternative multiplayer formats. Two-headed giant is newly available against AI, which means it's only 50-50 whether the game ends in crash and disconnect, rather than an all but certainty as THG games with 4 actual players turn out... which is a shame, really, because strong multiplayer is what could have made this game shine.
---
All in all, if you like card games, there's no reason not to try it. Don't expect much from buying coins, and don't expect a quick route to unlocking cards... and most of all, don't expect the deck wizard to give you anything but an 'okay' deck. That all said, if you're in no rush, it's a great game for some casual AI matches (which have no time limits of any kind), even if the multiplayer is often... iffy.
Biggest Highlight: An AI using Titanic Growth on -my- creature to keep it from activating an on-death ability.
Biggest Nuisance: The new pop-up messages appearing at every freaking victory or deck builder screen now.

Sooo when I first saw this game it was fun and it turned out to be.. but there were a lot of things I didn't like about this game.. and some things I found out about the game.
At the time I dont have many runs ( about 30+ rounds ) and my highest score is around 36.. so yeah.
Tips:
1. Dont ADS. The only time you should ADS is when you are trying to kill the large emojis from a far distance.
2. Shotgun- Best weapon in the game but apperentally it only kills one target and doesn't pierce. 3-4 shots will be able to kill the large emojis
3. LMG ( mounted and loaded ) - Devestating to enemies that follow you. If you find a good distance.. use it but I suggest to use the revolver or somewhat of that source if you are trying to shoot floating enemies.
4. Powerups. There are powerups ( Health, slow time, Sonic speed).. but they are useless unless you want to get shot to death.
5. Jumping. Always Jump. That's just that. Run in a circle path,
6. Reloading: This is also a huge con in the game but mainly it's for the revolver which tends to be the most risky item to use in the game but the most reliable to shoot for floating enemies if you can aim. The revolver takes the longest reload time and if you reload  it takes a good 3-ish seconds ( makes sense though ) and you can't switch to something else in the meantime.
TDLR: Reload in safe places with the revolvers.
------------------------------
PROS AND CONS
Pros:
1. It's actually a good-ish game when you get used to it. I'm a fan of these survival games that you can find your path and perfect it.
2. It's emojis. Die Die Die.
3. Music is nice when playing the game.
4. Sliding ( on the revolver slope ) and jumping mechanics are great.
5. The one map in the game so far actually has a good terrain and the only thing wrong is the stairs on it which should be fixed overtime
Cons:
1. Bullet speed & Spread. I think most guns should have faster bullet speed ( especially the revolver ). The revolver has high damage.. useful especially when shooting floating enemies. Missing your 6 shots because the enemies are moving is too punishing for the reload time. Since you and the enemy are always moving it's very difficult to actually land a shot. The shotgun weapon at the moment is the most broken due to the little spread when shooting far distance. It's fine if I can shoot something up close, but I should not be able to shoot a large emoji across the map and land every shot, killing it in 4 shots ( this should be a job of something like a musket ).
2. Weaponry- Right now, there are 5 weapons in the game: Pistol, LMG ( Heavy ), Shotgun, Revolver, and an Assult Rifle.
Pistol- Decent. I have no concerns about it
LMG- Low spread.. but still balanced seeing how the game runs. Usually I use this on following emojis so no problem
Assult Rifle- I haven't really had the time to find its position but I feel like it's projectile speed is too low for this kind of gun and with the power it delivers I think bullet speed should be faster.
Shotgun- No spread.. Reload time is really fast ( but needed )
Revolver- Slow reload, but compensates with power.. Needs to be basically hitscan.
I think the game should offer more options by having the black crates respawn different weapons.. Maybe gernades too.
3. Powerups- The powerups are good in this game but they are in the middle.. which is chaos once you spend about 3-ish minutes. Basically there is no way for you to heal and the projectiles in the game will kill you because of how many there are.
4. Enemies in general- I'm fine with the ones that follow. The ones that shoot projectiles though are too strong. I'm fine with the bosses but the floating ones ( Especially the vomit ones ) are just too strong with a jacked fire rate.
5. Lack of Options- Motion blur, sensetivity.. some color palate backgrounds make it difficult to see enemes ( Green and Grey ones )
6. Tutorial & grabbing items- It takes about 30 minutes to fully understand how to play the game and learn it.. which for most people can be a turn off about the game. Grabbing items ( mainly guns ) can be a hassle when standing either on or near the weapon crates.
----------------------------------
Should you get the game?
For $2 This game will keep people busy if you like the survival run-and-gun type scenario but the only thing that really sucks is the enemies build up too much for you to handle at the moment. The bullet speed along with motion blur doesn't make the situation better but it is still a fun game once you get the hang of it.
I really liked the game and it is a great time killer if anything.
I hoped that this information has helped you on your decision to buy the game or not. <3

Overall Rating: 6/10
Gameplay Rating: 6/10
Accessibility Rating: 7/10
When you start This War of Mine (TWOM), the main menu consists of one primary button: survive.
At its heart, TWOM is a survival game.  In it, you must guide the actions of a small group of people as they struggle to survive amidst a war that is ravaging their city.
I would recommend this game as a good purchase when on sale.  It is difficult to get started, interesting to play and think about, but ultimately repetitive after you understand the game mechanics.
TWOM is primarily point-and-click.  While you can control zoom levels, the game field is larger than the what is shown at the furthest zoom level out, so you must use the mouse to scroll the screen, which can be annoying.
Each new game puts you in a slightly randomized house with a different amount of resources in each iteration.
The game's economy is interesting and slightly complex, but ultimately quite limited.  The sheer number of different types of items is where the economy's complexity comes from, and the challenge lies in trying to balance what you bring back on scavenging missions due to limited space and the need to have a variety of items.  Once you understand the system, however, it is not difficult to become self-sustaining and to even develop an excess of tradable resources.
Upgrade mechanics in the game are decent, but sometimes too costly for the benefit.
TWOM takes place in a war ravaged (presumably) eastern European nation.  The charm of this game comes from its story more than anything else.  It is possible to simply play the game without getting invested in its story, but why waste the money?
The survivors each have a back story and unique traits that can complement the abilities of others to make a stronger team.  Further, each character reacts to the moral decisions you make as the war progresses and some events are triggered.  TWOM frequently nudges you to consider the terrible impacts of war on the innocent people that live in and around it.
This War of Mine is rated 7/10 for gameplay.  You will restart multiple times, and, after some point, the game's difficulty will fade away, diminishing its overall replay value.
Game options are available before starting a new game, but the menus may be difficult to see due to being low contrast with the background.  Look for the cog wheel in the lower right corner.
Available options are music volume and sound effects in Sound options, resolution, quality, and fullscreen in Video, and localization (language and termperature).
One note is that the game uses a stylized 'Pencil Effect' that can be set to high or low.   This may provide a challenge for low-vision gamers.
+ Dialog shows in text for all speech
+ Key sounds are visualized (those that affect game mechanics)
- It is possible to miss game events that may have an accompanying sound if they happen off-screen.
TWOM is playable for deaf/HOH gamers.  Sound is not required to experience the game, since it uses visual cues to represent when your characters are making too much noise while sneaking around.
+ Limited input required - essentially a mouse-only game.
- No options for altering combat mode, game difficulty, or accessibility accommodations for these events.
This game relies solely on gross mouse control and frequent clicking.  In combat situations, which are infrequent, it may be necessary to react quickly and make use of fine mouse control capabilities.
This War of Mine is rated 6/10 for accessibility.  Mouse controls may prove an occasional challenge for gamers with mobility issues.  The pencil effect adds an aesthetic to the game, but reduces contrast that may be essential for low-vision gamers.

When I started this game, I was hoping for an MMO, that makes a civil option just as viable as a fighting one, somewhat like UO, leading to players playing the roles of the titular villagers and heroes. This is not this game. Instead, the village options are of strictly supporting purpose to aquire equipment and items for adventuring.
As far as free MMO-RPGs go, this one is pretty standard. Paying is for comfort options only, so no part of the game is completely locked out for free players (unless for example you count mounts, which offer only a speed advantage), but the difference in grinding pace can be felt strongly. Graphics and maps are kind of okay, if you don't mind mid-sized single maps instead of an open world, questing is not overly repetitive. Still, there's some signs of lazyness, like the tendency to use standard icons for various unique quest items, quests themselves mostly leaving no change at all (until recently, the biggest visible effect was to remove a fog from a small area, the latest addition to the main quest at least made some NPC build a hut), or my favourite, child NPCs being adult avatars shrinked to 50%.
An aspect, that I would say, could need some improvement, is the fact, that there is few reason to specialize. Players are able and expected to maximize all the civilian skills over time, there are enough points at the highest level to max about half of the fighting skills, and even as a character skilled towards group play, it is possible to solo through most of the game. A bit less omnipotence to strenghten the need of cooperation wouldn't hurt.
So far, I'd say, it's meh, doesn't hurt to play, won't make your day either. Why do I still give a negative review? That would be my reaction to the handling of the new update. In early May, there was an announcement, that a major update is on the way, about which an announcement would be made in early June. A pre-trailer, in film terms. The date came, an internet page was opened, which still did not contain informations, but required "community tasks" to be completed to unlock hints about the update step by step. Those tasks were to make a screenshot of a large group of players (okay), writing short stories and painting fanart (okay...?) and as the latest but certainly not last task to post screenshots on Facebook. Not okay.
Maybe this sort of pseudo-viral campaigning is normal to todays kids, but a game, that pushes me to advertise it, just to get access to a glorified newsletter, deserves a negative vote in my eyes.
P.S.: If anyone is wondering, why I keep playing nonetheless; the player community is a suprisingly pleasant one on the server, I use, especially for MMO-game standards.
