Where is my Heart? is a puzzle platformer wherein the primary gimmick is that all levels are split up into fragments that are generally not connected with each other in a simple, linear fashion. This is somewhat headache inducing at first, but I eventually learned to start steadily traversing around levels, piecing together how they're actually supposed to look in my mind before routing a course to finish them.
On the other hand, there are unfortunately some irritating, borderline luck-based issues with the transformations. One of the transformations is the "Rainbow Spirit", which allows you to rotate the level's fragments by 90° intervals while remaining in the same place spatially. However, if you land even just a few pixels within a wall, you'll die and have to respawn. A similar problem is presented by the Antler Ancestor, whom turns its companions into fireflies that, when you detransform, also turn back to normal. The fireflies flutter around in a semi-random fashion and detransformation isn't instant, so it is incredibly easy for them to end up trapped in a wall or falling to death. Fortunately, the levels that involve detransforming the fireflies in a certain place are very few, but the one that had timing it as its primary puzzle took me an hour to finish without dying and doing so felt entirely out of my hands.
It's not actually necessary to complete levels without dying, and the levels are compact enough that having to respawn at the entrance is only a minor inconvenience. However, there are also hearts to collect in each level as a score, and each death reduces that score by one. Considering the above transformation problems, as well as how each level starts with each of the three characters spawning in one-by-one, and also how there's no quick restart option, I wouldn't be surprised if an eighth of my gameplay time was spent quitting out of levels and going back into them. Personally, if I were to redesign this game's levels, I would have removed the death penalty and also put the hearts in more interesting and challenging places to get to, since a fair amount of them are sort of just arbitrarily placed wherever.
But again, getting a perfect score on every level is optional, and there doesn't even seem to be any reward for doing so — not even an achievement. I'm not sure whether or not I should be upset about that.
Fortunately, as if to counteract all that mess, the aesthetics of the game are super soothing. The spritework is cute and drawn with pleasing, pastel colors, and the soft chiptune soundtrack is so relaxing that I have honestly spent far more time falling asleep to it than actually playing the game. If nothing else, I definitely suggest that you give it a listen

This game is literally a reskinned Civ V.
Like I had heard people say that about it and thought "Oh ok, it must be pretty similar like how people called Fallout 3 'Oblivion with guns' or something"
No.
This is 100% just the base Civ V content with outer spacey looking graphics slapped over it. It's ridiculous how blatant they were about reusing assets and mechanics.
I will say one big change that has been made is also one that seems like it has the most potential, although it's not being put to much right now. Tech trees now have "leaves" and "branches" so can pick between going down a branch and reasearching a higher tier technology, or putting more research into a leaf of technology you've already discovered to get further benefits and upgrades. Ultimately it's not a whole hell of a lot different from just having a larger tech tree with more branches, but it makes things a bit more interesting and leaves room for upgrades that increase speed in reasearching leaves vs branches.
Affinities seem interesting on the surface but are basically just Ideologies + 1.
The ability to pick and chose your starting bonuses seems interesting at first, but really it just means there's only one defining difference between factions and everything else is more homogenous.
It feels like there's even less to do than there is in Civ V when it comes to managing your cities, so they've made up for this by giving you "quest decisions" every couple of turns to make you feel like you're doing something.
I'm sure that, like Civ V, this game will get better once it's got a few expansions under its belt, but for now save yourself the money and the disappointment and buy something else.

Disclaimer: Yes, I know it's EA. however I review a game for what it currently offers, not for promises or potential.
Now, Citadel tries to break out of the mass of survival-sandbox action games by being less survival-y and trying to concentrate on building and combat instead of pushing a button to sate your hunger and thirst every 20 minutes.
However, the game is quite barebones at the moment, unbalanced and really presents some barebones game machanics that, if not worked on and refined properly, will make the game go down the same direction as ARK.
Survival: Now this is up to you, but I enjoy not having to eat or drink or being affected by temperature.
Combat: Easily the weakest part of the game as of now. Everyone is a mage by default, making it less cool to be a mage and has four weapon trees, each one with its own spell tree and some universal utility spells. Each weapon can be imbued with 2 spells, which is not enough. Weapons unlocked from level 1 to 60 are just pure upgrades of one another, not really giving you another possibility than to equip exactly said weapon to become stronger. Spells are kinda just the standard stuff, hurl fireballs, shoot an energy ray or spam magic missiles, the obligatory meteor drop comes at the end. A normal combat situation looks like this: You safespot the incredibly HP-spongy enemies from a safe distance by spamming a spell and gulping down mana potions. Combat is really boring. There's also a melee tree which is completely useless as you have to go close distance and will inevitably get wiped. You also can't attack flying enemies, f*cking you over double as bad.
World: The world is pretty big but does not contain any interesting spots as of now. It's two types of biomes, magic forest and snow and everything looks almost the same on end end on than map than on the other. Caves are all the same, contain some standard enemies and useless loot (which you can't even use most of the time).
Progression: Another big gripe. You get minimal EXP out of harvesting stuff and much more for killing enemies of course. However this game still feels like a korean MMO even with 5x EXP multiplier. You unlock a new spell every 10-15 levels, all armor and weapons unlocked in a higher level are just pure upgrades and do not introduce any new mechanics. Leveling up is a boring, tedious task. Also, equipment has LEVEL REQUIREMENTS, meaning you have to grind your way up to use the good stuff. This makes PvP horribly unbalanced and givesn o motication to loot a higher level cave because you won't be able to use the equipment anyway.
Building: Quite basic, I noticed that this game has NO lighting system, so placing torches will apparently not illuminate dark areas. You have the simple stone, wood and heavy standard building parts and the crafting stations and defenses.
Summing it all up I kinda regret buying this game right now. You can clrearly see that the devs have tried to sell the basic and unvaried content they have as a whole game but there's not enough content and the rough edges are just too apparent.
Now, I am really happy to see that they are on top of the community and I hope to see awesome updates in the future. There is a lot to be done though:
Minor gripes:
- Animations of enemies are horrible, they don't telegraph attacks and just move in a weird way
- AI is even worse than the animations
- Lag, nuff said
As with a lot of EA games, the ideas and promises are great, but it is still to be seen if they finally make something of it.
Until now, don't buy. I think it's gonna be in EA at least for a year more so you can get it at a reduced price every time. But if you want to spend quality time here I advise you to go somewhere else.

I played Puzzle Pirates a decade ago and loved it so didn't think twice before trying out Obsidian. The changes made are good so far but not enough to keep the game thriving.
I can no longer spend hours on pillages playing the same puzzles continuously - the same as with any game I play today - but if you don't stay long enough, you run the risk of being minused in the booty div, making the effort even more pointless when factoring in dub prices. After jobbing for various pillages on Obsidian (where I made the effort to stay for most or all of the journey), I regularly saw jobbers who had stayed for one, two, even three battles and then left minused out for absolutely no reason (they had been puzzling just fine). Since then, I haven't felt compelled to clear more time for pillaging, when my ideal method of playing is likely to be penalised by the community. I am still amazed that anyone should be minused when considering how low the population is nowadays.
The game is very co-operative, which was great years ago when there were tons of players. Nowadays, with just a fraction of the players there once were, I can see no changes made to reflect the need for more solo-oriented play. For example, navy mission pay is still abysmal and while that made sense years ago, there is no reason for it now. The idea is to have as many people online at any given time as possible; if you encourage people to stick around with better navy mission pay (for just one example), they may be more willing to join in with the co-operative play.

Here is my detailed review of the game.
If you don't feel like reading I have a video to help you decide if you should get/support this game
Combat mechanics: Nothing spectacular just a point and shoot kinda game.  But what stands out is the use of spells.  How this work is that you have different weapons and each weapon has a specific spell that can be equipped to it. However you can only equip two spells at a time.  But you can simultaneously equip 2 weapons and switch between them instantly with the G key.  That makes a total of 4 spells. You can mix and match your spells to get the maximum damage out put.
Taming and riding mechanic
I assume you can tame all the creatures  but For now there are only a few thing you can ride. A horse, unicorn,  giant eagle,  fire dragon,  and black dragon. Riding mechanics feels clunky some creatures have really good animation but it just doesn't feel like your riding it. Some creatures are also missing sound effects like foot steps and wings flapping. But then again this is early access and it's only been out a week.
Taming in this game is uneventful. in ark and dark and light you have to battle it out with the creature,  however in this game you just point at it and use the passive spell and wait 2-5 minutes to tame a creature.
The devs also nerfed the tamed creatures before the early access release by a lot since they were OP. But the Nerf was just too much. And tamed creatures are pretty useless in combat. they would definitely need more time to balance this out.
UI.
The UI is manageable it's not the greatest or the worst, but it cae better For example To get stacks in and out of the inventory you have to check the stacks box, and to get individual items you have to unchecke the stacks box. This is annoying but it's not that big of a deal, since you only loose a couple of seconds, and there's more things you can strees about. Also double left click doesn't work for transferring items, you have to use right click or drag it. The UI management is not that big of a deal but I would be grateful if they improve it
Overf all feel- Does this game feel a lot like ark or rust?  Yes and no. This game borrows some mechanics from a lot of it's predecessors but it has it's own unique feel to it. It's actually very fantasy like and you owe this experience through it's music and environment. The music is very medieval and fantasy kinda like what you hear in lord of the rings, dragon age. And skyrim. It actually feels a lot like ESO except more potential! The visuals are very well done,  environment from the different biomes to ruins, castles and, caves feels very unique. You see giants walking around,  orcs trying to kill you, forest guardians, dragon's,  demons and etc you also see players and their warlock towers/ witch cabins. Most of the spell effects are nicely done some are egg but this is all subjective. Most people would love it and some will hate.  You know there's always that someone.
Stability bugs and performance:
Finding a good private server is the key to enjoy this game. Most of the official ones if not all are very laggy. And I've heard because there is a lot of memory leak.  Others say it could also be because of the coding itself there, I don't know there's a lot of speculation. But one thing is for sure, it's an early access so you will get an early access stability. So high latency is to be expected and I've seen up to 1000 Milli second latency in some servers. The server I'm playing on is most of the time on 100+ until the server needs a restart.
Graphics & Performance:
The visuals are pretty good of an indie game,  the colors are vibrant and it really portrays a fantasy world
There are pretty good textures in this game and the spell effects are awesome.
I've heard different kinds of performances, it runs okay for me  but The game Definitely needs optimization but it's not that bad. I have a two Year Old almost three year old system with 3 way sli GTX 980 on an i7 4790k. The game is installed on an SSD. The game doesn't support sli so 2 of my gpu is at 0% usage.  Alright so at first I was getting great performance. However after exploring the map I've come to a conclusion that fps depends on where you are in the map. South of the map for me I'm getting 62 fps consistently going up north I'm getting 35-45 fps per second. I would recommend reading the system spec requirement first before playing, to see if you can actually run the game.
Bugs:
This game is early access and not to mention was just released a week ago so ofcourse there's a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of bugs some are Almost game breaking like when you take a dragon it disappears after a restart or your tame suddenly becomes untamed. So yea there are a lot of bugs but it is still playable. Sometimes though the general population won't experience this bug and just you and a few other people. If that happens don't let it get to you and be patient,  the devs have already put out more  patches or updates than the day-z devs in the past 3 years.
Devs:
Blue isle studio devs are very active that's probably the strongest attribute of this game and why I think this game has a lot of potential. They respond to player's reviews as long as your not shirty about it. But don't expect them to respond to your selfish demands because what you want probably won't be a necessity for them or other players.
What could they have done differently:
In my opinion they shouldn't have copied ark's taming mechanic. Instead they should have put summoning instead of taming.  It makes more sense since it all about magic.  And instead of taming it with a spell,  you can only summon a certain creature after meeting it's pretty requisites like certain rare items.
Also OP spells like telekenesis can still be in-game and can only be acquired through tomes very rare times and they have to be a one time use. Actually adding a lot of spell tomes would add more depth to the game. Like make it a very rare drop,  a treasure chest item,  a boss item,  or a quest item like after you kill 1000 pyramid you get to hve a tome.
Conclusion:
The game has a few unique mechanics like spells and gathering, it also has a fantasy feel to it, which is how it was intended.  But like a lot of early access it is riddled with bugs and has high latency issues.
But these can all be fixed and by the Dev team's attitude towards their player base this can be fixed over time. My opinion is subjective and is hot fact so it's up to you to decide whether you would get it or not.  For me the game has a lot of potential that's why im sticking with it,  because it can reach it's potential by supporting the devs.

Roller Coaster Tycoon 2 is nearly a perfect theme park building experience.
The base gameplay should be rather obvious, but you take control over a blank piece of land or an existing theme park and are tasked with building it up and making it better.  There are many, many maps which have individual goals, sometimes those goals are varied enough to drastically change the gameplay and approach (such as giving you infinite money and telling you to only build rollercoasters), but for the most part the end goals affect the play style very little.
The core mechanic is money.  You buy rides, concessions, and hire staff and balance that out with what you take in.  It's mechanically simple and the choies are normally minor.  The skill level to complete levels is normally on the low side allowing even children to enjoy RCT2, but some of the stages provided me a challenge that required some real planning and thought.
What this game is really about is the parks, and that should be the take away.  No two parks are the same and every person brings thier own stlyle and flair.  From my perspective, the core appeal of Roller Coaster Tycoon is the aesthetic.  It's fun to create parks and make them you're own.  I'll pick up the game just at random beause I have a cool design in mind.  The rollercoasters allow the same level of custom design on the small scale giving the player many oppurtunities to make things how they want.  The core appeal is very minecraf-esque.
Overall, I highly recommend RCT2.  It's a fantastic building experience with a nearly unlimited ammount of hours to be squeezed out, appealingn to all ages.

tl;dr even to scratch the Dungeon Keeper itch, the game just didn’t really hit the mark. Definitely not worth the asking price; anything above 5 is a hard-sell for the execution of a game that fell flat at the best of times, and was just unenjoyable at the worse of them.
As a sequel, Dungeons 2 is far more enjoyable than the clunky mess that was Dungeons. The overwork of the mechanics from hero-grooming simulator to actual dungeon management is far more sensible and enjoyable. Unfortunately, that is about all the definitive good that can be said about the game. The execution of everything else is mediocre at best.
The campaign length ranges from 16 to 20 plus hours, which would have been fine if it was actually fun. Far too much of the game was spent waiting; waiting for the timer to run down, waiting for population to increase, waiting for gold, etc. The initial pop cap of 15 that counts both workers and fighters, who cost 2 by the way, severely cripples expansion rate.
The research to raise the population also required a sizeable stockpile gathered at the slow rate, meaning that there is not much variation to the early game. Often, regardless of the map, it merely involved hiring a few workers, mining all the gold, finding a mana crystal to mine from with a minion that cost 2 as well, not a worker and carrying out the research, fending off the occasional invasion with your 2 POP fighters.
While waiting you do…..nothing, which is the real crux of the issue. You can’t build rooms because the whole point is to gather a stockpile of gold to conduct your research. You can’t explore the Overworld because you often have too few fighters, and losing them would set back your economy since you need to hire them again (initially, you can’t bring unconscious fighters back to your dungeon). For that matter, there is no benefit to exploring. You only ever need to go to the Overworld to finish the objective; there are no resources up there, and since invasions were never a challenge, no need to stop their spawns.
The inclusion of a separate Overworld map that one can enter from a dungeon exit is an inspired inclusion. It adds well to the theme of invading the surface world, and offers a unique layer to the game. Corrupting the land to allow you to use spells on (since most spells can only be used on your territory) was enjoyable….in theory. Not once was I ever forced into a situation that I needed to. For that matter, corrupting the land often involved killing the heroes in battle…which would have been the ideal time to use said spells. What’s more, while the game lets you enter other “dungeons” to fight in, it never really had much weight. I felt more like I was going through the motion rather than an actual invasion or adventure. That could however be a fault of the writing, which leads on to my biggest criticism of the game.
The “humour” of the game probably got me to chuckle once or twice and nothing more. I felt that the game confused references with humour. At its core, the inclusion of references aren’t funny. It’s a list of Easter eggs, no more, no less. The 4th wall breaking by the Narrator was fine but his script and/or delivery was just awful. Considering that the narrator is Kevan Brighting of Stanley Parable fame, I am inclined to give him the benefit of doubt and shift the blame to his script and lack of direction rather than to him. My guess is they tried to be self-aware and parody itself, but were too scared to commit to the idea and instead produced this half-baked execution. It felt like it tried too hard to make itself relevant and “funny” which instead drew irritation and eye-rolling from me.
With a mere 11 missions, 2 factions of 5 units each that play pretty much identical beyond their active abilities, which you don’t really need to use anyway, the game really doesn’t warrant anything beyond 5 dollars, and a couple of hours at best. I may have finished the campaign, but I can’t really say it was worth the hours of waiting. It did however re-kindle my interest, and made me take notice of Dungeons 3, so perhaps one could argue that despite being free, it was a good marketing move on their part.

Overall Rating: 6/10
Gameplay Rating: 6/10
Accessibility Rating: 7/10
When you start This War of Mine (TWOM), the main menu consists of one primary button: survive.
At its heart, TWOM is a survival game.  In it, you must guide the actions of a small group of people as they struggle to survive amidst a war that is ravaging their city.
I would recommend this game as a good purchase when on sale.  It is difficult to get started, interesting to play and think about, but ultimately repetitive after you understand the game mechanics.
TWOM is primarily point-and-click.  While you can control zoom levels, the game field is larger than the what is shown at the furthest zoom level out, so you must use the mouse to scroll the screen, which can be annoying.
Each new game puts you in a slightly randomized house with a different amount of resources in each iteration.
The game's economy is interesting and slightly complex, but ultimately quite limited.  The sheer number of different types of items is where the economy's complexity comes from, and the challenge lies in trying to balance what you bring back on scavenging missions due to limited space and the need to have a variety of items.  Once you understand the system, however, it is not difficult to become self-sustaining and to even develop an excess of tradable resources.
Upgrade mechanics in the game are decent, but sometimes too costly for the benefit.
TWOM takes place in a war ravaged (presumably) eastern European nation.  The charm of this game comes from its story more than anything else.  It is possible to simply play the game without getting invested in its story, but why waste the money?
The survivors each have a back story and unique traits that can complement the abilities of others to make a stronger team.  Further, each character reacts to the moral decisions you make as the war progresses and some events are triggered.  TWOM frequently nudges you to consider the terrible impacts of war on the innocent people that live in and around it.
This War of Mine is rated 7/10 for gameplay.  You will restart multiple times, and, after some point, the game's difficulty will fade away, diminishing its overall replay value.
Game options are available before starting a new game, but the menus may be difficult to see due to being low contrast with the background.  Look for the cog wheel in the lower right corner.
Available options are music volume and sound effects in Sound options, resolution, quality, and fullscreen in Video, and localization (language and termperature).
One note is that the game uses a stylized 'Pencil Effect' that can be set to high or low.   This may provide a challenge for low-vision gamers.
+ Dialog shows in text for all speech
+ Key sounds are visualized (those that affect game mechanics)
- It is possible to miss game events that may have an accompanying sound if they happen off-screen.
TWOM is playable for deaf/HOH gamers.  Sound is not required to experience the game, since it uses visual cues to represent when your characters are making too much noise while sneaking around.
+ Limited input required - essentially a mouse-only game.
- No options for altering combat mode, game difficulty, or accessibility accommodations for these events.
This game relies solely on gross mouse control and frequent clicking.  In combat situations, which are infrequent, it may be necessary to react quickly and make use of fine mouse control capabilities.
This War of Mine is rated 6/10 for accessibility.  Mouse controls may prove an occasional challenge for gamers with mobility issues.  The pencil effect adds an aesthetic to the game, but reduces contrast that may be essential for low-vision gamers.

This game is okay.
Not a whole lot to do other than try to survive.  During the day you work on your homebase.  Build a workbench so you can build tools and weapons.  Upgrade that workbench so you can build a gun and upgrade it some more so you can create bullets.  You can find ingredients and resources at night when you go snooping around like a racoon, or a good ol fashioned cat-burglar.
During the day you can sleep and build and every other day a trader will stop by your pad and you can trade for food with all the crap you collect at night.  Eventually you can start making your own booze and medicines, which can also be used to trade for food.  Food is top priority.  You can't drink water, you need food.
Night time ain't so bad.  Some of the locations of interest have bad guys.  Some are just regular people trying to survive like you.  If you steal from or kill anyone who's not a bad guy, your character will get sad, and if you continue down that path your character will become, "broken."  When that happens they sit around all day, not moving, and there's no saving them from it.  You will be forced to end the day and sleep in bed at night, leaving you open to other cat-burglars that kill you in your paralyzed state.  If you didn't die or become mortally wounded or deathly sick, then eventually you snap out of it and are able to venture out at night with instinct as your guide.  Also, killling bad guys is a good thing.  Sometimes they will say something like, "that priest sure went down easy," or, "let's hit another humanitarian aid again," and this is your cue to kill them.  When you get back home, no one will care that you killed a bad guy.  No one will congratulate you either, though.  Try not to kill or steal from innocents.  But if you must steal, don't get caught or they will kill you.
Fighting is random chance.  Roll the dice.  Sometimes you can sneak up from behind and club them in the head, then shoot em up real good, other times, your character loses the dice roll and you pay with your life.  Your best bet is hide and one-hit-kill them with a knife.
So for the most part, do this until the war ends.  Or whenever the days counter is up.  I lasted 40 days once and the war didn't end.  I lasted 25 days in another game and won.  War ended.
Eventually you learn what you need to create booze, to create meds, to trade for food.
There's no saving your game, so don't worry about that.  It saves every start of day.  And if you do a bunch of stuff during the day, like upragde a workshop and board up a window, and feed everyone and trade for good stuff and have everyone sleep and not be tired for night - then night comes and instead of playing anymore you quit game - it will not save.  In fact, when you reload your last save, it will be before you upgraded anything, before you fed everyone and before you traded.  Quite annoying to say the least.
The game is like a 5-6/10.  I honestly only bought it because it was on sale for eight bucks.

Here’s a list of things I came across while playing this game that are head scratchers or just don’t make any sense.
The survivors know how to make a radio, but no one has the skills to make crude weapons to defend themselves from early raids while you are cleaning out your shelter. The survivors need to collect materials to make a workshop to make crude weapons. Soooo the survivors have the skills to make a workshop, but can’t make simple crude weapons until they can build a workshop.
All the survivors start out with nothing but their empty backpacks. Hmmm
I guess the player is supposed to assume either all of your survivors were caught off guard by an attack somewhere else, but they only managed to grab their “empty” backpacks or all your survivors were caught by bandits as a group and all their belongings were taken nearby, though the bandits let them go free until they reached the shelter. But this conflicts with an early first encounter.
A First early encounter at the shelter immediately followed with a groan from me. A Knock on door asking for help to carry an injured person home from being shot by a sniper. Sorry to hear that, but no I can’t help you at this time, I don’t know you and this could be a trap.
Ohh but wait, after you decline to help you’re told this was your “neighbor”. Oook, how did I the player know you were my neighbor? But wait, didn’t you as the survivors just find this place as a shelter? How is this person your neighbor if you just arrived with not even so much as a 2x4, knife or scrap of food on any of you? ugh
Observation - During play, no survivor is strong enough to lift a table/chair or knock over a damaged wooden dresser and smash it to the ground for wood/fuel, they must craft an axe to break things down to collect wood/fuel.
Observation-When scavenging, you can commonly find rare items like lock picks but more common items like hammers, knives(even a common butter knife that could be used as a weapon) are nowhere to be found. It also appears every radio and alarm clock has been destroyed during the war and one must be made, since you can’t even trade for one, though parts for one can be found.
Observation-How is it that every occupied area around you has people with guns, but everyone in your group is bare handed with not so much as a shiv/knife or a 2x4 when they start.
Items like crowbars break down after repeated use on wooden doors in destroyed buildings. What? I could understand a shovel breaking because of a wooden handle, but a crowbar? Saws are also a one-time use item. wow
Observation- With Ai NPCs, if they have guns It’s always shoot on sight if you try to scavenge a new area with people there. There’s no “hey who are you, get out of here or I’ll shoot” “It’s hey someone’s there, you’re dead” BANG BANG
No chance for “Oh, sorry I was not aware this area was already occupied, I’m leaving”
Observation-How is it possible for an NPC to know you stole something from them if you show up with a different character than the one used to steal? Silly
Why does snow that you collect at your front door need to be melted/purified at your cooking stove when you have a wood heater that is heating your shelter?
The survivors can only send out one scavenger per night no matter how many survivors you have and you can scavenge only one place per night even if you are done scavenging in a short time. If you clean out an area in an hour, you’re done for the rest of the night since you’re confined to that building/area all night. No other areas close buy/next door can be scavenged until the next night even if you have 4 hours to spare, you have to end the night or basically twiddle your thumb for X amount of hours until it’s time to go home.
The game tries to get you to open your shelter up to more survivors for you to manage/take care of beyond your initial starting group. But there is no point in doing so from a survival standpoint unless you want to read their profile/back story. When I became self-sufficient, food was still scarce/hard to come by with just 3 people. Adding more survivors only puts you in a worse position and there is nothing for the extra survivors to do but sit around, always be cold/hungry/tired or get wounded in a raid. If you could actually use the extra survivors to go scavenging, I could see the point in adding them to your shelter.
The survivors can’t go out in the daytime, there appears to be a 24 hour curfew. So for a war that’s been going on for years, there are no temporary trade markets during the day to trade at. Strangely you hear on the radio there are supplies like coffee being dropped off, so why are none of the survivors allowed to leave during the day to get some of this humanitarian aid?
In game time goes by in 10 minute increments, with each increment occurring in less than 10 seconds, somewhere around 8 seconds. So if you do have stuff to do, you need to do it quickly before 8pm. The problem with that is that it takes one of your characters 30 game minutes to walk up 1 flight of stairs or go from one floor of your shelter to another. So if you want to go up 3 stories in your shelter to build/make/break something, it will take you 1 and a half game hours to walk up those stairs. This does not include time to actuallty build/break your item. Crazy stuff.
I completed the game in 42 days without killing anyone simply by concentrating on becoming self-sufficient, there’s no need to kill any NPCs unless that is what you want to do or risk. The worst thing I did was steal some supplies from the old couple.
While the message the game is trying to send is a good one and the charity part is appreciated, the actual game play is unrealistic and is incredibly repetitive after about day 20. It would be even more so if the crime wave did not occur to mix things up after day 10. Don’t be lured in by the massive amount of recommends and wait for a sale, the $20 is too high for the limited amount of content provided.

Okay.... I am trying to take a deep breath and calm myself before I write the review...
Here is the truth.  I LOVED this game, so why would I rate it down?  The artistic value of the game is to be revered.  The game-play is fun, addictive like crack, and balanced all the way through.  It is a survival game that makes you care for your characters because with a little extra thought, proper preparation, and a careful use of resources, the game can be the PERFECT challenge all the way through.  Not so much that you put it away from dying all the time, but just enough so you feel that you can learn from your mistakes when you take the wrong person looting and get him/her shot, push too far into a bandits' base for loot and  get someone killed, or become a bandit yourself and watch your characters hate themselves for it.  It all works!  So WHY in god's name am I rating this game down.... SIGH.  I will tell you at the end, because the ending is is why I am now jaded.
This game has this unique blend of survival and platformer elements.  The combat is a little wonky, but this is not an action game.  This is a survival game that pushes your moralities to the limit: do you send off one of your characters for a day to help your neighbors who in the past have shown you kindness, or do you turn your back and keep to yourself so you can keep your base safe while looting?  Killing is not taken lightly in this game.  Most of the characters are not fighters.  They have never shot at anyone before and you must weigh how stressful it will be on them to out-right murder a person for his/her loot.  sometimes it might be best to come back from a night of looting with a bag half full and a heart that is not broken.
The characters themselves are all full of life and special in their own way.  One or two are trained in combat, and do not feel the pressure of killing so long as they  are not killing innocents.  Some are good cooks, others are handy-men that  use less resources to build and craft with.  Others can keep children calm and tend to wounded while others are small but stealthy, making them ideal for nightly looting runs
Looting is done so well.  Your characters feel no pain from looting bandits, but question themselves for steeling from an elderly family.  The stealth mechanics are solid and intense at many times.  I managed a play-through without ever shooting at anyone. (apart from defending my base from bandits.  Can't be controlled and it doesn't affect your characters depression)  I chose to help all  who asked of it, but stole when I needed to as long as I did not leave someone for dead by doing so, and yes there is a difference between taking what you need in this game, and taking everything, and your character will reflect on that.  Limited backpack space and time turn scavenging into a strategic race for time as you decide whether or not to bring a crowbar and lock-pick, or save the space and only take what loot is easily accessible while scouting out threats, bared and locked doors and piles of obstructing rubble that can be cleared on a succeeding night.  Rubble that can be moved without a shovel,  but will take a lot of your precious time if you chose to do so.
Keeping your team rested and fed feels just right, and the amount of given resources is remarkable.  Too big of a team means that more food will be needed than can be provided.  Too small and your base will be raided while you are out looting and sleeping.  Choosing who sleeps at night, who sleeps on a bed or off a bed, and who sleeps during the day can't be taken lightly.  Wounded characters will take rest, first-aid, and time to heal.  A few nights passed that I had to keep everyone at the base and be frugal for a day so the group could recover.
The bartering system is well thought out.  There is a traveling tradesman that will show up every few days with goods that can be exchanged for home made moon-shine, home grown vegies, looted and self-made meds and anything else you want to trade.  You can also take specific items with you on  "looting"  runs to trade with the military, other survivors and even bandits.  Each group seeks different items, and you are not likely to come home with a full backpack, but you will have exactly what you set out for, and some times that is more important.
There is also a winter that you must survive.  OMG was it intense.  Keeping enough fire wood burning to keep your characters healthy while still having enough to cook food and craft pushed me to the limit more than once.  I was taking an ax to furniture just to keep the fires going.  Brilliant!  The winter is not too long and comes on at a nice pace so that you have time to trade for or scavenge what is needed in time build a heater for your base. (hint: UPGRADE IT EMEDIATELY!)
And lastly, the DLC for this game is heart warming to say the least.  It doesn't add much content to the game, but %100 of the proceeds goes to the War Child charity, and that's just groovy.  The dlc adds some wall-art to the in-game levels.
Now... After so much praise, why did I rate this game down?!
I WILL TELL YOU WHY!
I worked my tail off keeping my crew alive!  I helped EVERYONE that asked of it.  I killed no one, and only stole when I was desperate, and even then I took only what I needed and never left anyone to die.  I brought in a character in need when he asked and he survived with the rest of us to the end....  THE END!
The war lasts 45 days max, some people don't like this, I don't mind it so much.  It can end some time before that, but its random.  If you have built a radio, it will keep you informed of whats going on.  INCLUDING THE WEATHER!
Day 44 roles around.  I have mastered my team and have prevailed through dozens of bandit attacks, and winter included.  I have an outright stock pile of weapons, ammo, food, supplies, crafting tables, trade goods, and FIRE WOOD.  The forecast from the radio, which you will see in the screen shot, called for "warm days ahead."  Winter was about a week in the past at this point and there is only one winter in this damn game!
I leave my base on the 44th night to do some light looting because I wanted to pass the time and grab some last minute stuff in the case that there is some end game fight or something.  I leave with  "WARM DAYS"  in the forecast and a thermostat that reads 20 Celsius.  That is hot for this game, it starts around 15 C. --- An adventure in wide-open spaces ---
Rebel Galaxy puts you in the boots of a space-faring renegade just looking to make a buck at the edge of the known universe. I mean, yes, you're estranged aunt mysteriously gifted you her old ship which was weird, and she also left you in possession of an alien artifact which, wouldn't you know it, happens to house an ancient A.I (don't they all) and you should probably look into that at some point -- but you also have to stack that paper! The main plot can be safely tackled at your leisure while you put time into building your personal net worth and outfitting the ship of your dreams. How you do that is up to you. As a kind of spiritual successor to Freelancer, Rebel Galaxy allows you to make your way through life on the rim anyway you like. As long as it involves shooting people.
At every space station there is a mission board brimming with contracts from the various factions in the game. You can run drugs for a criminal cartel, bust up a pirate siege for the militia, provide some armed backup for the merchant guild, or pick up shady dead-drops for a cloak-and-dagger agency. Of course, let's not forget the most classic of all fictional space-faring economies: the glamorous world of asteroid mining. While there is plenty of outward variety in contract types, almost all of them will result in an inevitable shootout. Even the mining. Especially the mining. This is my ore and you can't have any of it. *pew pew*
Yet, despite my many complaints, Rebel Galaxy did put a smile on my face. It's an ambitious little game that regrettably tries too hard to grab something out of its reach, but what it does get its hands on is excellent. The combat is spectacular, the atmosphere is charming (prolonged exposure to the soundtrack aside) and while there isn't as much depth to the game's systems as it would like you to believe, they are fun to poke and prod at when you get tired of blasting people with your lasers. Rebel Galaxy is the kind of game I'd want save for a rainy day when all I want to do is set my brain on auto-pilot and lose a few hours watching pretty colors and dreaming about being Han Solo.

I played a demo of this game at the very first Indiecade in Culver City, and was immediately struck by the unique puzzle gameplay.  You see only fractions of each level through a kaleidoscopic collage of windows, and you must navigate your three companions to the end gate using the limited information you are given.  There's something beautiful about the broken-up aesthetic, and it creates a mixture of both curiosity and hesitance as you prepare to cross into the unknown when you reach the edge of any given window and can't see where your character will end up next.  Even more exhilarating is when you are given the power to rearrange the windows and cross from one to the next at will (although this mechanic is limited to certain levels, depending on the design of the particular area).
The creators seemed to realize the best way to solve each puzzle is often to take a leap of faith, crash into some spikes or a pit or water, and add that new bit of info to your mental map of the complete level.  So with unlimited lives and time, you are free to enjoy the lovely pixel art and soothing ambient music at your own pace.  For the completionist, there is the added challenge of collecting all the pink hearts in each level without dying, which brings some measure of frustration but also accomplishment once you get them all.
"Where is My Heart" is easy to pick up and play in small chunks, and I find myself returning to it now and then to enjoy this unique gem all over again.

Red Risk is a very solid little game, in which you fight as a modern gladiator (up to 3 players on coop) against infected and (heavily) mutated creatures.
You might struggle with the controls at first, but will find out after a while that they actually make sense. Kite (drag along) your character with the right mouse button, and fire or hit with the left (target must be in range). No need to click that much, just keep the left button down and aim at the closest enemy. Reload your gun with R (not in the manual). Space bar for some extra fighting power.
(I highly recommend Jason and his axe to start with. Again, keep the left mouse button down and aim always and only at the closest incoming monster. Do not re-click, he will do all by himself. Use Space for a 360 spin all 3 seconds. Don't run when you are surrounded, just aim.)
The game is easy and casual, one tournament takes about 15 minutes. Find friends in the forum for coop! Select different characters, higher difficulties and other maps for new challenges!
The graphics are sweet, with some unique ideas, but of course, don't expect it to be a 50 USD game!
Also search the Community Market. Red Risk has some cool items there. Look at the cards for steam leveling.
Have fun !!

For me, the story is an important part of a game. Homefront had an interesting story, however, it did not feel even close to complete. Honestly, I got to the last mission (I didn't know it was the last mission at the time) and thought, "This is where the story's going to really pick up." I figured that after that mission the game was going to kick into full gear, I actually thought that I was just finishing up the introduction to the game and it's characters. To my great disappointment, however, the credits rolled after I finished that mission and I felt very unfulfilled.
The gameplay was fun, but even I could tell that it was far from optimized. One of my main gripes with the gameplay is the cover mechanic. If you run up to a barrier and crouch behind it, most of the time your head is still exposed, making the barrier useless. This made finding cover annoying at times because when I tried to duck behind anything I could still be shot. The actual shooting mechanic works fine, there's nothing special about it, but I don't have any complaints about it either.
I'm not really someone who cares much about graphics and so I found the graphics to be perfectly fine. However, if graphics are very important to you, then I'd recommend you watch a few youtube clips and judge for yourself if it will bother you.
There was nothing wrong with the music, but it didn't stand out either. I couldn't tell you what type of music this game had; even though I literally just finished playing it. That's not really a bad thing, however, as background music is really just supposed to keep the game from ever being silent.
I experienced quite a few glitches for such a short game. Many times you'd see enemies popping in, or simply disappearing. The game crashed on me once or twice, and I've had no end of trouble trying to get the game to stay in full-screen mode. The game is fully beatable, but those few glitches really are annoying at times.
I will say this, for the short time the game lasted, I did have fun with it. I wouldn't recommend paying anything above $5 for this, as I honestly feel like this game wouldn't be worth it. However keep in mind that I don't play multiplayer, so that may add a bit to it if you're into that. So to sum up, if you can get it free, or at a large discount, go ahead and pick it up, but don't go out of your way for it.

After almost 40 hours and over 300 races in the solo campaign on this game on hard difficulty with my gamepad, I have to say: this game is probably one of the best in the genre that I have played of recent on the PC. I thoroughly enjoyed both Grid 1 and 2, but I put 20+ hours more time into Autosport than I did the first 2, and for good reason too.
This game has great diversity in both cars and tracks. On top of this, it also has 5 disciplines: Touring, Endurance, Open Wheel, Tuner and Street. So whether you're into drifting around a track to score the most amount of points, or endure a 12 minute race without burning your tired out, or just want a straight up race, this game offers a lot for fans of the racing genre. Plus, there is a free DLC available for the game that allows you to play a demolition derby mode, much like the previous game in the series.
As you race in these various disciplines, you will earn XP and will gain levels based on a) how many races you participate in, and b) how well you do in those races. Once you have reached level 3 in ALL disciplines, you will unlock the first Grid Series Championship event (level 6 = the next and level 9 the last). This will take upwards of 30 hours to achieve, which is why I put so much time into this game. And I enjoyed the ride (no pun intended) :)
So, if you enjoyed the previous games or have played other racing games such a the DiRT series or even popular racers on console (e.g. Forza), then I'm sure you will like this game, and hence I definitely recommend it! The car physics are a bit of a cross between arcade and simulation too, so if you weren't a fan of Grid 2 and adored the first in the series, you should try this one out. Plus, in the solo campaign, there's no purchasing of new cars nonsense. You simply pick a team and get given cars to drive in (which, personally, I preferred!).
Enjoy! :D

Get ready for crashes! Crashes on startup, crashes on joining a server, crashes once you load into the server, crashes when you load in more terrain. Wanna run up and smack an enemy with your axe? Get ready for a brief freeze wherein the enemy gets a couple free hits on you! Falling off the side of a huge mountain? Who cares! There's fall damage but the terrain is so poorly designed you'll rarely get hit with it. Don't kill any monsters on the side of a slope if you want to be able to loot their corpse because they'll phase right into it. Every enemy no matter how big runs faster than you and some like to start fights then simply run away from you. Real fun. Best part is when the huge giant or forest guardian is chasing behind you and its dead silent. What? Too cheap to add footstep sound effects?
There is minimal options for character customization. You can't rotate your character in the creation screen or zoom in and the lighting is AWFUL. Wondering how your character would look like with Green eyes? Don't bother, both eyes are completely glossed over with black anyway. For men there is Head type, 4 options. Facial structure is linked what kind of hair style you get. Want long hair with a different chin? TOO BAD. Men then can choose a beard, again 4 options. Now you can change your hair color, skin tone, nail color(????) and eye color. And that's it. For women you have head type, but this doesn't change your hair this time. Again 4 options and they're all unattractive.Then you have your hair style, 4 options. Want to see what the hair looks like from behind? No chance. Then you get the same color options as men.
Crafting system is shallow and boring. Interface is clunky and awful. The level banding is ridiculous with high level monsters within a few minutes walk of the safe zones for new players. Enemy variety is minimal and there is no real difference between most of them. Giant=Forest Guardian. Boar=Wolf=Bear=Orc=Sprite. They all use melee attacks and do nothing interesting, they just look different. (except the orcs with crossbows who just run away from you and are much faster than you. Having fun yet?)
Don't put your respawn stone too close to other objects! You might end up respawned inside of one while you lose the chance to get your loot back. There is no commands I could find to get yourself unstuck.
You can get different spells but only two can be bound on a weapon at any given time. You can switch between 1 other weapon bringing your total up to 4 spells. If you are out of mana tho and need to melee you have to use the v key which is very awkward in combat. Your second weapon will be relegated to support spells anyway. The different spells are mostly the same thing just with a different color/look. The cast animations are stiff, ugly and choppy.
You can get things like mana and health stones that you can put in your base. Know what fuels these stones? MANA. I HAVE TO FEED MY MANA STONE MANA... SO IT CAN GIVE ME SOME MANA. *insert gif of guy's head exploding*
Placing building tiles is horrendous. Nothing ever goes where you want it, items don't like to rotate and navigating the menus is blech. Trying to delete a piece you misplaced? Make sure you are pointed PRECISELY at the piece you want to delete because there is no clear indication of what you are about to destroy. You're really too cheap to make a piece light up when the player hovers over it under delete mode?
I'll give the leveling up system SOME credit. IMO it's faults are that basic stuff, like forges, Workbenches, etc need to be unlocked. More powerful versions I could see having to spend points on but every player should get basic access to these. Not to mention storage chests which also need to be unlocked and you need to be a certain level before you can even spend the points to unlock the storage. The strengths of the leveling/unlocking system are that you customize your character pretty well and there's usually something to look forward to when leveling. A goal to strive for and a shiny new toy at the end of it.

I've tried the game from the play-for-free weekend event. Bit over 10 hours into it now. I'm not a big CIV fan mind you but I actually liked Alpha Centauri, the Beyond Earth Predecessor from Sid Meier looong ago (less predictable/boring if everything is alien in my eyes).
I'm torn between recommending it or not and decided to recommend it as it is a pretty addictive game I think for people who are really into Civilization - but if you are just into it for nostalgia from Alpha Centauri and otherwise rather not much of a military-strategy-simulation player ... I'd probably stay away from it.
First of all there is no tutorial really and the encyclopedia raised more questions for me than it answered, the UI is too complicated and unintuitive in my opinion (sometimes I have to click the queue for adding a unit, sometimes I can change it from the city screen, weird things like that).
It is a very complex game but the victory options are not explained upfront, so I spent quite a while doing counterproductve things as I did not know what would allow me to win. In the end the game was lost because nobody on the map (single player) made it before the maximum number of turns ... go figure. And I had been building something that was useless as it only made sense when following a certain victory goal. And I mixed up affinities because I did not understood the impact of affinities from the tiny introduction blurb. Etc etc. Lots of those things.
So if you want to play and enjoy it, there is probably some real manual somewhere and you'd better study some ...
I'm personally not tempted to replay with the knowledge I gained through the first run/game, so this counts as minus in my book.
That being said: there is lots of feedback/interactions/synergy from all kinds of game elements and the game is clearly something that can be played with high skill and likely lots of rewards then. My better half usually loves these micro-management-combat-focused games where you need to learn a lot about details and mechanics and manage many different factors correctly. But while he watched me for quite a while playing Beyond Earth and has played CIV before he is still not interested to pick up this one. Says the diplomacy is too limited and it isn't different enough from CIV.

Despite the temptations of the obvious play on the title, I'll say only that
is... not very good.
At the outset,
looks like a very impressive indie title.  Space is beautiful.  Asteroids are varied in size, shape and colouration.  The music is impressively professional.  The planets in the background are downright breathtaking.  All this means, unfortunately, is that the developers showed excellent taste in Unity assets.
The stuff that's original to
doesn't measure up to the quality of the Unity store elements it employs.  The English writing is clumsy and stilted -- suggestive of a bad translation.  The term "quasar" has been appropriated here to mean something completely other than what quasars are, which is jarring.  The voice acting ranges from occasionally adequate to significantly less so.
Gameplay is uninspired.  You collect "quasar" popups while dodging asteroids.  Ship controls aren't great, although the addition of mouse control improves it somewhat.  Asteroids, though they move at different speeds, all move in an exactly parallel course from right to left -- unless you use a special ability, which will cause them to briefly move in the same way from left to right.  Bosses dump you briefly into a bullet-hell game, and then you're back to dodging and collecting.
To be fair,
is
cheap.  Given that it's only asking a couple of bucks, what do you expect, right?   But the cost of playing
isn't just the pittance of cash it wants; it also demands the time you take to play it.  And the time you'll spend on this bad, clumsy, unfun game could be far better spent elsewhere.
ultimately reminds me quite a bit of games by reviled developer Digital Homicide: you take enough pretty assets that the game will look good in the screen shots, you price it so cheaply that people will be willing to take a chance on it, and then you don't need to worry about whether the gameplay is actually any good.

I usually only post reviews after spending 100 hours on a game but it is sale season and I can help save some money.  This is a great addictive game.  I loved Puzzle Quest 1/2 and this is better than both.  I even like the Marvel stuff, and I am a huge DC fan.
The meat is that you do not have to spend anything to enjoy this game, technically.  Just be prepared to put in lots of time.  I compare it to an online MMO, much like original WOW was for me.  It took me almost 2 years to max out the game.  Here nowhere near that kind of time but it will take some time, and WOW wasnt free either.  I have no problem chipping in a few bucks to support a company and game I like.  Programmers and developers need to eat too.  I do like the way they level up the heroes with random "covers" which is how you get your powers.  You can use in game coins to shortcut this but they are rare and you should spend them wisely.
It is not pay to win, but pay to shortcut I would say.  You don't really compete against anything but the game anyway, even in  PvP.  PvP is handled really interestingly.  You don't fight a person directly but their team run by the AI.  It took some getting used too but gives you loads of opponents to take on.
It has tons of events where you can get new and unique characters.  Basically you match colored gems to get action points, which in turn, allow you to use your various powers, e.g. Iron Man's Repulsor Blast costs 10 red AP, so match 10 gems and you can fire off a blast.  If you ever wanted to play with some great characters and fun gameplay that wont tax your dexterity too much, this is it.
I have read a few negative reviews and I feel everyone is entitled to their opinions, just remember that many of them haven't even played a full hour on this game so weigh those opinions accordingly.  There are even daily rewards to help you along, in the form of new characters, powers for them, tokens to get characters, etc.  It is a game looking to make money and since I support capitalism, that is fine with me.  I do not have even close the top tier characters but I have 16 at the moment and look forward to levelling them all.
If you liked Bejewled, Marvel or even Dr. Mario (yes I am that old), give this game a try, it costs nothing but your time.

This game is similar to that of a flash game where you mine for gold and have to buy soldiers to protect your miners and eventually defeat the oponent that is doing the same thing.
Differences lie with... everything.
Units: There are 5 different units, each has their own purpose in the dungeon like mining, gathering mana, tinkering, or forging. Each type of unit also has their own upgrade to an even more powerful version of that unit. Besides that, each unit can later have upgrades specific to their class, an upgrade for everyone, and/or you can level up specific units if they live long enough.
Dungeon: This is the home that you live in and defend. There are pockets of gold everywhere that you need to mine but you can also create your own custom dungeon each level with different rooms to do all kinds of things. How you build the rooms affects how effective each room is and your idle units will typically upgrade walls which will further increase effectivness.
Idle Units: Jeez, depending on if they've been paid or not, idle units will either happen buy the room your store money and take some, harass other units, or actually motivate them. The devs put some tender love and care into this.
BATTLES: So when you want to attack the opposing forces you need to bring your units above ground. Once above ground the game runs like a typical "War Hammer" or "Path of Exile" where you control your units from above. Each different class of unit has their own abilities you can use in combat by selecting the class from the selected units and using the skill you want. When you do this it doesn't matter what unit you selected, all units of the same class are thereby selected and their mana is collectively used to activate skills.

A side scrolling shooter with bullet time... who would have thought? Wryn is on a quest to become the best hero of all time. Her solution? Take down the heroes of the past first! That said, the game's learning curve is pretty steep and the strange control setup doesn't help. This is one of the first shooting games I've played where the right trigger is not for your guns but is instead for jumping. Thankfully, there are upgrades and additional weapons to be had that can make the game go a lot smoother.
Lastly, my favorite touch was Wryn's comments on if she dies. There are not many but they range from shock to outrage to letting you know that she'll respawn in just a second. They're nice enough to take the edge off of defeat and make you dive back in for more.

Greetings as always!  I bought Rebel Galaxy a year or so ago and requested a refund; the game just seemed a bit bland at a glance.  Time passed and I started reviewing games; I wanted to go back to some of these games I passed on so I picked this up during the previous sale.  So what does Rebel Galaxy provide:  An epic narrative?  No.  Deep mechanics that take hours to master?  Nope.  An expansive game with hours of entertainment after beating the game?  Nah.  So…Do I regret the purchase?
No Controller here:  The premise of this game is a 2d pane arcade space combat; you heard me right; aside from some of the AI smaller ships (known as fighters) there is no verticality in combat or travel which at first felt kind of odd but I quickly found I loved the design for an arcade style game.  To continue this theme the game centers on broadsides (side facing guns) and turrets.  The game will control the turrets (at a lower efficiency) unless you manually manage them but the game will not use the broadsides automatically that, and navigation, is up to you.  You can do missions both repeatable for various factions and the story.  If you were pushing you could probably end this game's main story in less than 10 hours but I took my time over the course of several play sessions (due to a reason I’ll state in my criticisms).
Cowboy Drifting:  The game has an amazing soundtrack, let me start there.  One of my friends actually bought the soundtrack solely because he was watching me play; I just wish the game didn’t seem so shy about it.  Many times the audio effects go over the music and the game seems to focus on instrumental tracks during quiet time and lyrical tracks during combat…which is odd to me.  The games visuals are amazing as well including the particle effects, ship designs and even the avatars for the NPCs you interact with.  The game carries a mesh between a western sci-fi with comic style 3d models.  I would have loved to see more story and background but the game’s visuals just came to life for me.  Especially Steve, he’s pretty awesome and we are good friends…but to you, you have to call him Stephen.
Don’t Rescue Space Slaves:  The game does have its share of issues, one of the most annoying parts I had was how quickly the game felt like a grind during longer play sessions; this really can’t be helped.  I feel the game is meant to be an arcade style game meant for shorter play sessions so I took frequent breaks to do other hobbies.  Your turret controls are annoyingily limited as you can either let them do what they want or tell them to only do one thing (focus my target, shoot fighters, shoot capital ships, etc.) and I really wish I could have set a priority list.  I would have also liked more diverse ship types; don’t get me wrong some of the ships were unique (Scarab is awesome) but it left me wanting more; where are my carriers or ships without a broadside or only a broadside, etc.  The game could use a more thorough explanation when it comes to the ‘under the hood’ as the game play is easy but found myself going to the wiki for specifics on mechanics.  Oh and your mercenary really needs to stop flying so close to suns and killing himself.
With all that said, I enjoyed the game and recommend it to any spaceship combat fan out there looking for something with a bit of a casual arcade feel.  Yes things will annoy you (sometimes the difficulty spikes for reasons) but overall if you pick up the controller (or keyboard) for an hour or two I could very well see this game being worth full retail.  With how old it is; you can’t go wrong with just waiting for a sale however.  Enjoy and make those pirates taste the black.

3.2 hrs after starting the game, I've completed the main storyline.  That's about it really, there's nothing about this game that I can say is good, but it's not a horrible game either.  It's just ... a waste.  So much so that I would consider a refund if I had bought it.
Before I start, I have to say that I did recieve this game for free.  Also, I was looking forward to it since I've always wondered what the hype was about way back when.  Turns out that the hype was for Homefront Revolution, and not this game, its predecessor.  Found out very quickly that this game was a failure jack-of-all-trades type.  Why?  Because this game feels like it was trying to be everything that modern FPS shooters were during those day, but fails hard in it's interpretation.
Story:
Linear, generic and short.  It was super easy to get into it, but never held my attention.  Yes, it has some great moments that do provoke some emotion, but even those moments/oppertunities are wasted.  The people that you meet and interact with in the world may as well be robots.  Just when you think that there may be some meaningful conversation or dialog, nothing.  It's just cut off with some gritty "oh well, let's move on" bs.  The story felt like a rushed copypasta version of something from COD mixed with Wolfenstein and Spec-Ops - The Line (the latter two had much better games that came out after Homefront but still).
Graphics, Audio and Game stability:
Pretty good for the year in which it came out but nothing to set it apart from any other similar games that came out in that time period. I had some issues with game crashes, UI and Objective reminders.  Wouldn't say the game was all that stable, but I didn't play the hours needed to confirm this.
Gameplay:
Felt slow and clunky.  Movement felt slow and lazy, and same goes with shooting.  Lots of the mechanics are similar to the COD series, but worse.  There was an okay amount of guns, but not many gun types, and not many oppertunities to find and use certain guns.  I mean, you have C4 but you won't have the oppertunity to use it in a gunfight, which is 99% of the game, and grenades are dodgy to use/throw.  The game is very linear, go there/do that kinda stuff.  Sure, there might sometimes be another slightly better way to get to the objective or do the objective, but it's negligible stuff.  Most of the time you're just following the moving objective that is your invincible idiot teammate.  Don't really need to think for yourself with this game.
To sum everything up, it's short, boring and generic.

A really fantastic, quick, little game. I have never played anything like it and I loved how much it made me think to solve the puzzles. These kind of puzzles that play with what you can and can't see can feel just impossible sometimes, but there's a really great balance here. Whenever I found myself stumped it never lasted more than a minute or two, and then the layout of the puzzle becomes clear and you get that great feeling where you can see every step to the end after trying to figure it out for a while. It does become significantly more difficult about halfway through but I got used to it. And, I was surprised by how quickly I got used to rearranging the broken map in my head. If spatial reasoning isn't your strong point though, this will probably be quite difficult.
The art is adorable. The sound design and music are great and create a very relaxed atmosphere that doesn't distract you from the puzzle but rather draws you in.
My main complaint would be that the parts where you use the rainbow spirit to flip the screen around can feel a little tedious and try-fail try-fail sometimes. But, that feeling never lasted long and I pretty much always ended those levels feeling very satisfied.
Overall, cute, cheap game that is well worth your time. Highly recommended.

Probably the best paced racing game of all time. Most games start out where you either pass licenses, or like this one where you race with a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ car at first. The difference is most games go on from there as a "Then do whatever" after your first race. GRID 2, however, takes you on a journey as a sports car driver. Reminescent of the days of Porsche Unleashed, you're a driver that needs to be competitively aggressive to promote a world racing event. You go out of your way to challenge drivers from all over the world in an attempt to get the most amount of publicity possible, so more and more people go to the racing league, and more fans pay for the show.
This game has the BEST racing game mechanic I've ever seen called "Flashback". You have the option to reverse time on a limited basis if you royaly screw yourself over. This is very awesome with the race variety where you can't see the map and the road not set in stone, it's different and goes on differently for as long as the timer is up. So you have a pretty good chance of miscalculating a few turns and NEED another option other than "Restart the Race". In easier difficulties this can also be used to your racing advantage, Went left and got cut off? Rewind, go right!
The cars aren't plenty, but provide enough variety for me to not complain and I'm used to Gran Turismo. The cars handle differently, and weight+power+accel+top speed are the only statistics that matter, and they make an actual impact as each car I've played handles differently. Cutely enough though, they made every car as if top of the line engineers built them, so american cars are in the same playing field as the rest and don't handle/perform like a fat 50 year old with erectile dysfunction as they do in real life. The game also doesn't corner assist as invasively as other games do. You feel like you made the turn in your own right and not just because a turn was coming up and you pressed the turn button. It's hard to describe, but seriously it's a really great cornering system with a lot of variety in turns, almost a strategy system to it.
The game provides optional multiplayer, but also compares your times with friends if you're in career mode. It doesn't destroy your privacy like some up-and-coming racing games.
The maps are very awesome, from top tracks of the world to awesome highways you may have seen. The roads have been widened though, to accomodate for high speed driving, unlike other games where there is no sense of thrill.
Difficulty is handled VERY well in this game. Drivers in 2nd and 1st drive like maniacs so you have to earn the position even in the easiest difficulty it adapts to your playstyle/driving and slows down cars infront to still provide an advantage. (IE crash more, they will go slower, but clever enough so you can't wall ride past everyone). The cars behind you will drive aggressively unless you're in first in easier difficulties, after you achieve first and outmaneuver the competition they will not likely catch up anytime soon unless you REALLY mess up.
The variety of events is pretty awesome. Not just a racer. There are drift events, passing events, elimination events(if you're familiar with burnout series), timed trials of course, and pole catching.
The only complaint I have is that I thought the story would go dark somewhere in career, but it didn't. It's fine that it didn't, it would have been kinda weird if it did, but would have made it super interesting. That's just personal though and in no means something people would want other than freaks like me, lol. Most people are perfectly fine with racing being the only exciting part. Not saying completing the story wasn't exciting, but it was very predictable, so less exciting than if it took a turn where you had no idea what the crap would happen.
Thanks for reading my review!

I've played a fair bit of WIMH, and while I like the art style, and the concept of the game, It's just too hard to make any useful forward progress.
Let me start with the good: The art in this game is very nice. From the pixel-art style to the subtle transformations animations, coupled with the ambient sounds and so on, it's all very nice. As well, the concept of the game is very good. You're given a sort of fragmented level wherein you try and collect hearts.
The big problem I have with this game is that if you should die at any point, you basically lose your progress on that level. I.e. if you want to get 100% completion of a level (colect all the hearts), if you make a single error, you have to restart the level. I'm not a massive fan of that.
Also, in a lot of cases the level will rely on trial and error to complete it. Given that there are part where you can figure it out using logic, I don't think that making the player resort to trial and error to figure things out is a good approach to take in your level design.
So, it's an okay game, but I really think it needs some changes to be truly a good game.

It's a proper keyboard-only port of a PlayStation mini (PSP, PS3, Vita game). Although it's been made available in various bundles, I've never seen its price drop on Steam proper for those that are holding out for a sale.
The only actual goal in a given level is figuring out how to get from start to finish, and anything else is entirely optional. There are no enemies, there is no time limit, and you have infinite lives. You can collect hearts if you want to, which you will lose each time you fail. The level-select screen lists the highest number you've collected in a single run, which is a goal you can work toward if you want to. Although there is one achievement tied to collecting these hearts, there is a single level where this can be earned easily.
The game features 26 levels in the main game plus 4 "bonus" levels. Each level can be solved in a matter of minutes, giving at least an hour of playtime. Some levels may of course take longer to figure out, and collecting the hearts without dying can multiply your playtime substantially, I thought the fragmented screen mechanic was used well enough to hold my interest, although there were at least some bits pertaining to collision that were frustrating.
The developers (which took 3 years to port to PC/Mac) promised a Linux version back in 2014 which I think is as likely as this game going on sale, so if you're on a non-Linux box it may be worth checking out if you're looking for a quiet, low-stress platformer with an interesting twist.
