Overall I have played Puzzle Pirates for roughly eleven years. Dark Seas is a bold attempt to revive a dying game and in all respects it did get a lot of people involved on one ocean, though with no change to the issues that drove the game to die in the first place Dark Seas cannot and will not be a success long term. Don't get me wrong, I've met some of the greatest friends I've ever had through puzzle pirates. Some of these friends I have known since my first years as a player. The game is an incredibly tight knit community, however, and that causes some major flaws for newcomers. Puzzle Pirates has always been a fairly niche title, though in my younger years I remember huge crowds of players at once there are now maybe 100-300 players in the game at any given time, a little more if there is an event. This is a number based around Dark Seas, not oceans still existing on the former client. My original ocean now never gets more than 8 players at a time.
The best way for me to describe this game properly to players that may be new to the title is to arrange this review in a pro/con list. These are the experiences I have had, others may have had different.
Pro:
- Puzzle Pirates has always been unique in the manner that everything you do is in the format of a puzzle. You will not be able to jump into this game with a typical MMO experience and succeed on hack-n-slash. It holds very true to it's name. You will be expected to perform well at various puzzles and tasks, even in 'combat,' which is similar to a co-op PVE puzzle or PVP which is much harder to master as a new player. If you want to get better at these puzzles it can take time, you will want to look up guides (luckily youtube is your friend there) or practice heavily.
- Freedom. Whether you want to pillage for some quick cash and then try to make it rich playing card games with other players, run a shoppe and make money by making items for other players through puzzles and employee help, run a crew, own and furnish a home, dress up.... choices are quite open to you. Note that Dark Seas is a new ocean and thus many of the more expensive houses and buildings are not currently available, but in time they should be if the ocean maintains users.
- A truly interactive community. IF you can break through the barrier of being a new player you are likely to meet some truly incredible people here. Do not be fooled-this game can be a very social environment. Engage in conversations with your crew, with other players in card games and pillages, etc. You will eventually find your own group, just don't give up hope if people are wary of a new player. Most players currently don't think Dark Seas will ever attract new players due to the game itself and may not be very willing to aid if they don't think you're really a new player.
- Puzzling variety and complexity. You won't be doing match three bejeweled all day. Each puzzle has it's own quirks to learn and master. While you may be great at one you may do poorly at another. Carpentry is a block puzzle involving placement of Tetris like tiles while rigging is a process of building the largest combo of pieces for each turn. While at a slow pace these puzzles can be very easy it can take time to build up the speed and accuracy you need to perfect your scores. As you rise through rankings the puzzles will add in additional pieces, rules, and perks to keep you on your toes.
Cons:
- This game will not be changing or improving anytime in the forseeable future in my humble opinion. The original client was released in 2003 and aside from some changes over the years the game is a near carbon copy of what it has always been. Don't expect big changes to the user interface or any stylistic adjustments. Most of the players still hanging around are here because we enjoy the nostalgia and I personally feel that any company to take rights to this game will not want to risk losing loyal players by changing the appeals that keep us here.
- Graphics are nothing special. Really, if you have looked at this game in the screenshots, what you see is what you get. It is a simplistic game originally intended for kids. If you want HD graphics and cutscenes this is not the game for you.
- Minimal base character customization. When creating a new pirate you will be able to choose from a handful of basic hairstyles, a few skin tones, a name, and some starting clothing. Later on you CAN change your clothing. Certain holidays like Halloween release special masks and some hats like the wig will give moderate hair or head changes, but that is it. IF your ship in a sinking area does in fact sink you have a minimal chance of getting an injury (for instance, a peg leg or a hook hand or a starfish on your face.) Most of us really love these and look forward to getting them, but it is rare. I've sank numerous times since this ocean started and never got my first injury so far.
- While NOT pay to win this game has a risky dubloon market. Dubloons can be bought with real life currency or earned by exchanging POE (regular money) for a dubloon. However, the dubloon prices in exchange for poe vary by the supply and demand. In esscence this means that the people holding the most wealth have a heavy influence on your ability to rise in wealth as a free player as well. When oceans die out dubloon prices inflate like nothing that should ever occur. In my old ocean dubloons went from 3k poe each to upwards of 49k each. This makes it very hard to purchase items as items bought from shoppes have a delivery fee that consists of a certain amount of dubloons.
Pro/Con Neutrals:
- This game is a time investment. If you want to play be prepared to put in several hours at a time. If you join a pillage you are expected to stay for several battles at the very least. I've been in sea monster hunts running up two or three hours at a time. If you leave before you end the pillage or smh you will very likely be blacklisted from future outings with that crew. This is great if you really enjoy the game but can be stressful to a new player.
- Unspoken rules are common with the community in this game. Just as you're expected not to ditch your ship on pillages you're also expected to as permission to board a ship in your crew, it's common to be expected to wish other players good luck before card games and almost always good game even if you lose, etc. There are many things you will pick up on over time, but starting out may be a little confusing until you learn the things players consider required or common courtesy.
- Adult jokes. This game started out as a children oriented game... years ago. We have all grown now and most are not shy about making jokes in games or chat. If you are not comfortable with those things you can mute people, but it's up to you.
- No leveling, only skill raises, and skill can be lost if you begin performing poorly at a puzzle again.
To wrap this up I simply want to say that while I absolutely DO recommend this game, new players are very likely to be lost or quickly lose interest. There are many more pros (and cons) once you get into the game, but for a newbie it's important to just realize that what you see is what you get.

With a name like "Bleed" you'd probably expect something really gory and over the top, like "Hotline Miami" or that one scene in "Pulp Fiction" where Marvin gets shot in the face. There is some blood here and there, but it's really not that prominent. A better name would be "Shoot" or "Dash". Personally, I feel that the best name for a game like this is "Brief Awesomeness" due to short length and enjoyable gameplay. "Bleed" is a really fun shoot-em-up with some pretty tight controls (Albeit an unusual control scheme from a gamepad perspective. Good luck with a keyboard.) and a good sense of humour. Unfortunately there are only seven levels so you can finish it in no time at all. The only way to make the experience last longer is to be a lousy player who keeps dying or trying to unlock all the achievements. Nevertheless, "Bleed" is enjoyable for the amount of time you spend with it and it has got some replay value. It's currently 10% off and I think it's worth the current price. As for full price... I'll let you decide.

Great theme doesn't save this game.
Thematically this game works really well and I feel that this has led people to ignore that as a game it in fact fails in most areas. It goes without saying the theme to this game is 10/10. It really achieves what it set out and that theme does a lot to bring a tension to this game.
Yet the controls are awful, combat is a mess and the poorly executed roguelike elements renders this game an exercise in frustration.
With Characters being one shot killed at times, controlling things through sketchy clicking and relying on autopathing is just skirting with disaster all the time. Imagine playing any stealth game with just a mouse and you will get the idea. It often feels like a quick reflex game with no way to actually use your reflexs because the controls are just terrible. Point and click stealth action in a permadeath environment is awful.
Combat is just as bad, melee is click on enemy and watch your character swing hoping you kill them before they kill you. Stealth kills are I guess okay just the same click with a different icon. Ranged weapons are a disaster, attempt to get behind cover in the most finicky clicking possible and then shoot by clicking. The whole time you will wish you were able to do this with a keyboard.
Avoiding the stealth and combat is quite difficult. Crafting barely turns a profit from raw materials (You can just barely buy back the raw goods from selling the end product) and relies on you scavenging the materials. This leads to the economy of the game being pretty unrealistic and in many ways removes the peaceful option (though it is mostly possible it becomes vastly more effort than other strategies). In what world is a bottle of moonshine about as valuable than the water and sugar it took to make, especially during a severe war. Rolled cigarettes are about as valuable as raw tobacco.
The economy of this game is entirely unrealistic due to being made arbitarily difficult. Buying guns and ammo is not difficult mid game but want a hatchet though and you are often completely out of luck. A shovel for sale is rarer than a gun in this game. A metal workshop is easier to make than a vegetable garden. Rolling a cigarette is more difficult than making a radio. At the start building a bed is fine but boarding up a window take upgrades. Also bandages take pure alcohol to make...  In short the theme and immersion of this game is thrown out the window and replaced with nonsensical rules to create a difficulty that feels incredibly artificial. It's a disaster.
There is very little roguelike execution. Levels are the same with some having NPC variation. Now unless you are using a guide you will be seeing those areas again and again so the pain of losing is enormous. Also the places that appear each game change the difficulty dramatically, which is a poor execution.
This game is actually bad. One great feature doesn't make up for terrible mechanics and controls. There are aspects of this game that are well executed but as a whole package it falls completely flat.

TL;DR: Bioshock 2 is better than Bioshock 1 and you should definitely buy it.
Improvements over Bioshock 1:
-Dual wield plasmids and guns
-More smooth gameplay
-Level 3 plasmid upgrades
-More moral choices
-Your choices having a more detailed impact on the ending
-Better preformance on newer systems
-Some cool new Plasmids
-A few new guns
-More unique gun upgrades
-Deeper exploration between litle sister/big daddy link
-Cool multiplayer (pretty much dead now, but it's there)
Improvements in my opinion (subjective):
-More empathetic main villain
-A better final boss fight
-Cooler companion characters
-I love the little sister defence sections
Neutral:
-Same environment style. Just as good as 1, but we're used to it by now so it's not as effective
-Several Plasmids are reused
Weaknesses to Bioshock 1:
-Stealth is nowhere near as prominant
-A few bits of the story drag (Looking at you, Siren's Alley)
-You'll be swimming in loot at the end of the game, removing most challenge
-Doesn't have a huge twist in it
Overall, this is a game that got alot of bad rep at launch just because it wasn't made by the orignal creators. Still, it's easy to see lot's of love went into this game. In fact, a few of the ideas from Bioshock 2 were taken into Bioshock Infinite. Now, more than ever, it's totally worth picking up for a blast of the Rapture experience.

This War of Mine is the sort of maudlin affair where the more cynical gamer breaks out the smallest violin possible and witters away whilst the whinging occupants of his flat complain every three seconds about hunger, exhaustion or other unfortunate events despite you feeding, clothing and taking care of them better than some of the people in Tory-run Britain today.
For the record, the game won me over, by virtue of its simple characters and emotional soundtrack. Coupled with the sort of color scheme that gives Gears of War fans raging boners, the games main purpose is to lead you through the shattered lives of your survivors, with you controlling their actions a la the Sims. During the day you craft items, ranging from boarding to block up the gaping holes in your Beirut-esque apartments to saws, shotguns and vodka (the last of which is, apparently, a necessity). At night, you go "scavenging," which is code for 'break into some unlucky sods house and steal all their♥♥♥♥♥♥' Now, naturally those living in said homes dont want to part with their stuff, which is where the combat comes in.
The combat is both a great and a weak point; on the one hand your characters are, for the most part, average men and women, and thus have no combat training; thus, in a straight fight, they get the crap shot or stabbed or beaten out of them. That's great. However, if you're inadvertedly spotted and swarmed-which can happen sometimes in very irritating and dubious circumstances- you can get stunlocked and beaten to death with a rebels/other survivors pinkie, which is bad. Hiding from people in doorways somewhat mitigates this, but if none are around you might as well bend over and enjoy the pounding, because they go in dry.
That aside, the game is fun, simple, and a good pickup. I'd say its also a touch overpriced and the constant complaining of your survivors grates the nerves after a while, but apart from that there's little to complain about. And this is coming from a Scotsman, who's entire existence revolves around complaining.

Cons

Suggestions;
-Re-open Charon after questline is completed
-Add planets and orbits to radar and upgrade textures, it would serve to really fill out the game and the space

After completing BioShock 2 and the Minervas Den DLC I think I can now give an unbiased review of both.
BioShock 2 was a delightful journey through Rapture, following the events of the 1st in the series. and taking a new twist on the main protaganist and their motivations.
There was a steady learning curve, allowing you to build a unique set of skills that include weapons, Plasmids (powers) and perks.  The weapons were varied and the upgrades made a serious change to the basic weapon - the shotgun being suprisingly meaty as it became upgraded.
The Plasmids provide enough for whatever playstyle you prefer; ranging from telekenisis to freezing the baddies in their tracks.
The addition of the other perks, meant that hacking and use of the drill in more 'intimate' fights, became as important as each other.
As always the story develops over several characters, providing a few twists and turns I didn't expect, and it's the 'life' in each charater that serioulsy influences some of the choices that come on offer.  You can be mad, bad and a nasty piece of work, or make alternative choices and be rewarded for your human nature side.
I took about 23 hours but did choose to explore and go looking in every nook and cranny (very recommended), but the dying was never so frustrating you wanted to stop.  Some fights lead to several deaths, but a quick swap of tactics and you're out there in the fray again.
Minerva's Den is a decent sized DLC (8 hours?) that tells a completly new story, with no mention of the main game.  This allows the writers to put in different characters and make it a "BioSHock 2 Light", with none of the research side of the main game (it's assumed that you know what Houdini Splicer is etc. but the rules are to just kill whatever is shooting at you, so little knowledge of the baddies is really needed).  You will get many hours of fun and get into some real scrapes along the way.
Graphics are pretty good on a decent system that can throw the polygons around, the water effects (as you'd expect) are superb, as are the particle and smoke effects.
The sound is amazing and really embeds the player into a post-war environment.
All in all a sound 9/10.

First things first, I'll start with the thing that made me question getting the game, the 2D playing field.
The game does NOT play like EVE online, and for me thats a huge plus. I like EVE, the concept is great, but this game is a different beast. By that I mean EVE, and it's combat system, are completely different. This Game plays like a 3rd person shooter, but with the self awareness of being a ship in space. You play it like you are. And like a 3rd person shooter, you walk along the ground. This game plays the same, there is a 2 dimentional plane that you play across. You do not have altitude or height. AND IT MAKES THE GAME PLAY SO MUCH BETTER. If you were in a fighter or bomber, smaller craft, It would completely ruin the feel. But your in a monolithic ship, late game ships are as large or larger than space stations, it would take away from the gameplay. Because of this lack of hight, your just a massive ship taking damage, and evading behind other celestial bodies in space. It makes the game feel better. I thought it would take away from the game, but it makes it feel more real.
Working Economy
It works, and its a good economy, there are events that happen at random on all stations, and it can change the price of anything in the commodity market. There is not however a responsive market, if you flood a system, or buy up one particular thing within the system, the price doesn't increase or decrease. though I suppose if it did, You could totally abuse that for your own gain. That being said, It's a plus. Because you wouldn't need to really play the game, you could just get the best ship available after grinding for cash. I will say there are levels to the factions that represent your level of affiliation, how much you've done for them, and you can only get the best ship in the game by donig that. So you cant grind for the BEST ship in the game.
Still overall I think the economy is great, though doesn't carry as much weight as I'd like. Trading is not viable, your a merc plain and simple. Trading is for extra income from station to station, not primary. That adds to the game's feel. Your a merc not a trader, you play it as one.
Just to commend them, the feel is perfect. The visuals, the gun play, the sound track, im so ENVELOPED IN THIS WORLD AND EXPERIENCE. The characters aren't well built but what you do with what you have makes you feel like a merc with a mission. It's amazing.
Factions
You do not really have a choice to be friends with the bad guys, except for the red devils, maybe. Everyone else just starts off hating you and thats that. You fight them, your the good guy theyre the bad guy. It would have been nice to make friends with everyone. But the missions you take on make you enemies with them anyway, but it would have been nice to see a campaign and a world in which you could make your own desision for the fate of the known universe.
Last but not least is the replay ability. IF YOU WANT TO PLAY AGAIN BUT ROLLPLAY, DISREGUARD.
You could totally play this game again if you rollplay a character and buy ships that arent objectivly the best in the game.
That being said...
It really doesn't exist for me. It's a chain of events as to why. The ships come in almost like stages, every time you get a ship its a giant purchace, duh. But there really isn't much of a choice, there are objectivly better ships, within your price range. You start off with a little weak ship, you make roughly the same amount of money for quests you can do at this stage, and the amount of money you can realistically save, is around x amount. There are ships within that prlice range, but there is one thats objectivly better than the rest. So you buy that one. Get all the weapons armor all that you want, after you have supped the ship up enough, you want an upgrade to your next ship. Rinse, wash, repeat.
The campaign exists and does its job, but really doesn't HOOK you. Though you do want to know the outcome, but thats more because you bought the game and want to see it happen, not because your attached to the characters and hope everything works out for them.
These two things mean I dont want to play the campaign for campaigns sake, there goes that replay factor.
And the ship progression is objective, so I don't want to play the game to take the same path as i did before.
Over all, AMAZING FEEL. Combat, the explosions, the sights, the sounds, traveling through space, its all perfect. But in combination with the campaign, the factions, and the ship progession, it leaves you wanting more, without the guts to play it for a second time.

This game is fun but not your typical rpg to spend a lot of time with atm. More for having some mixture of pvp and minecraftian fun with friends for a little time a day, or maybe your Sunday afternoon.
In the technical aspect, the graphics are ok and fps are stable. The particle effects do not display properly sometimes and the animations should really be reworked, as currently lots of creatures lack animations and 3rd person is not visually appealing. The artistic direction is pretty good though. The AI is not great and so the game doesn’t have much to offer to PVE players. Character responsiveness is not quite there yet, although it is unclear if this is due to the engine or to server stability.
The most important technical issue right now is servers. Most have capacity for 40 players so they are usualy full, and despite the low population cap, they are very laggy when past 20-30 players. A big issue is that you can not use the same character for different servers, and so it is likely that once you logout, you won’t be able to play again with that character for quite a while. Moreover, in this kind of games, server wipes are a regular thing (usually to clean the servers from the structures the players have built so it doesn’t become full of things). So if you are going to play this for character progression, you might want to reconsiderate this.
The gameplay is pretty similar to Skyrim, which is self explanatory. You have a set of 4 weapons: gloves, wands, staffs and melee (like swords etc). Each type of weapon can be used for melee fight but also to cast its own spells, which make a total of 30 with all weapons combined. You can equip a primary and secondary weapon, which means you will have access to 2 sets of different spells, and so the strategy comes down to find a proper combination of two weapons. The game really needs a proper quickbar to equip all your spells, because currently you can only have a tiny 2-slots quickbar per weapon, which means you will only have immediate access to 4 spells. For anything else, you will have to navigate the menu.
Regarding the world, it will be filled with crafting materials that will be used to craft everything you need, from potions to clothing to your magic wand and your home. In my experience, you can build anywhere you like. The world is not as interactive as a Minecraft world, but it is equally stark: no cities, no people, just you your friends and a variety of monsters that you will be able to fight or tame. The game would really benefit with the addition friendly NPCs that have their own life, trade and give you quests (hello Skyrim!).
The lack of content, the bugs and the server stability issues are rather usual in an Early Access game, so we can not be too harsh for that, can we? I think the game is in the right track and so far, I would recommend it.
Now since this is an early access I will list some things that I would like added to the final version:
-A better character creation: height, weight, close details customization (nose, eyes, mouth...) and so on.
-Animations to creatures and reworked animations for players.
-Skill "trees" for the weapons, and not skill "lines". A tree means you have more than one path of skills and by choosing one skill you loose access to another. This makes your leveling choices meaningful and creates unique characters that completement each other.
-Darker nights to make roaming the world at night a lil bit more interesting and scary.
-Waves in the sea (it just looks weird for the water to lack any kind of movement....)
-Friendly NPCs that trade, give quests, and have their own life (they move around doing different activities through day-night). Could even have some secret NPCs that wander the world (misterious mages or whatever) that sell amazing stuff.
-More things to craft: beds that recover your health-mana, furniture just to decorate, boats, trap systems (like minecraft does).
-More utility spells: floating light orb, transform into various creatures, invisibility, detect presence (to detect hidden behind objects and also invisible mages), mirrored images (double or triple yourself to confuse the enemy), astral traveling (leave your body behind and explore the world as a ghost that can not deal damage but can not be damaged either), expell ghosts (to force mages out of their astral form and destroy their mirrored images), massive teleportation (get close and teleport yourself and your party at once), massive barrier (everyone inside gets a defense buff), necromancy (resurrect a dead creature or mage as an alied zombie), firework (could deal a little bit of damaged, but its core purpose is to signal a place), frog curse (turn an enemy into an invulnerable frog for some seconds, he looses control of the character, good for escaping), Pied Piper of Hamelin (produce a magical music that attracts surrounding monsters and puts them in a peaceful state until you attack them or stop the spell), talk with animals (for example if a level 60 character just passed by, they could say "I've just seen a powerful mage"), mirror curse (makes the enemy move in the opposite direction of the key he is pressing), .... you get the idea.
-Group magic - spells that can only be casted by a full party at once and have long casting times but very powerful effects: a meteor, a storm, an eclipse, an earthquake, a blizzard, summoning the Devil...
-Add voice to some powerful spells (I think powerful/casted spells become more epic by adding a voice).
There are problably a lot of things more to add, but I think the thing should really revolve around the immersion as a mage. That's why making your mage unique and have a big repertoire that not only serves for attacking but for other cool things is very important!

Bleed is a fun, polished, and inexpensive twin-stick shooter/platformer with some bullet-hell style elements. Controls are tight but it can take some time to get used to the button layout. Using RT on a 360 pad to jump feels very awkward at first, but after a few minutes it starts to become second nature. The "Slow time" mechanic is used to great effect, allowing you to perform triple jumps and weave through enemy attacks in a graceful, satisfying manner. Boss battles are very well done and easily the high point of the action. The game offers a respectable challenge at the higher difficulty settings but it never feels overwhelming at any point. The story-mode is quite short, clocking in at about 1 hour, but the budget price makes up for it (a couple extra levels would've been just perfect, though).
Overall, Bleed is an enjoyable arcade-style twin-stick shooter with some neat mechanics and a low price tag. Worth picking up if you have any interest in the genre.

"The Gathering" (as one of my friends insists on refering to it) might be the best card game I have ever played. Actually, it is my favorite tabletop game of all time. I have played innumerable games, of both the video and tabletop variety since I was a child, but in my early high school years I was introduced to Magic and despite all the amazing games I loved, I just keep coming back to MTG as my staple. BUT... While the general game mechanics here are absolutely superb, the digital interface leaves a lot to be desired. Wizards of the Coast has always had a problem with that. Despite their 20 year lead on Blizzard's Hearthstone they just aren't competeing. Granted, some of this is due to Blizzard's uber-refined approachability. Hearthstone has "user-friendly" written all over it. Magic is a little tougher a pill to swallow, but once you're in you will quickly recognize the consistent elegence of the mechanical interactions. Sadly this isn't what holds magic back. Blizzard's game software just works. Magic's digital interface has been spotty for the entirety of the decade plus that I've been playing it. This is the best it has ever been and I couldn't give it better than a B-. There is no chat option with your opponent and while I very much appreciate the intent, it is sorely missed on the rare occasion that it would be useful. Not even a pre-scripted message selection is available. And more recently they have started letting through bugs that effect the actual gameplay. It's free to play though, so I would say that you should %100 try it out. Give it a couple weeks before you decide whether or not to put any money into it. By then, you will know.

Right now, we’re in the heyday of the space sim resurgence, with new indie games popping up all the time and heavily funded titles being fleshed out every day.  Rebel Galaxy was one of the higher profile indie iterations that came out of this movement and it gained that notoriety for having a different sort of take on the way combat between ships would work out.  Yet for all of the special things it does, it also encounters some of the same pitfalls that many other space sims try and sometimes fail to overcome.
One of the most interesting parts of Rebel Galaxy is the way that combat works.   Even in the smallest ship you get starting out, all combat works on a 2D plane that has you essentially moving your ship around like a sailboat.  Much like the battling in sailing tall ships of the past, you’ll have to make use of wide turns and adjusting your speed to bring yourself broadside to use your main weapons.   This makes for some very involving mechanics that have you trying to take in to account the status of shields and armor of both your ship and your enemy.  Your ship also has automatically aiming secondary turrets that can be set to track and attack certain targets or just left to default whatever target you’re looking at (which still works reasonably well).  These can also be taken control of directly if you want to aim precisely, though I rarely used this feature.  This combat system is really the meat of the game and what keeps it worth playing when you’ve grown tired of the other generic portions.
To dig in to those generic elements, the game has you warping between stations, missions, and various waypoints on its 2D representation of star systems doing all of what you’d normally see in game in this genre.  You’ll be able to pick up missions that have you beating up enemies of different factions, taking out pirates with bounties, buying and trading cargo, mining, protecting, or just simply blowing something up.  You can also freestyle much of this stuff by warping around taking out enemies with bounties, responding to distress beacons you come across, or attacking anyone you see and grabbing their cargo like a regular pirate.  It is very similar to old games like Freelancer.  This can be fun at times, but it’s always more advantageous (and profitable) to take missions that have you doing this stuff for more money.   One thing that makes free roaming appealing though, is that you can warp anywhere and turn while you are under way.  This makes the action feel much more interactive than in other games where you just fire off to a preset waypoint.  You can travel your own path.
The story isn’t anything too special, but does have a story put together well enough to make the dialogue and cutscenes worth watching.  Much like any open world RPG, you’re able to ignore it for as long as you want without any consequence.  I’m not sure if the scaling difficulty also scales with the story, but in my progression I don’t recall ever having a story mission that extra easy because I took so much time off upgrading my ship and doing other missions.  Rebel Galaxy also features a solid soundtrack that includes bluesy and southern rock songs that sound fantastic and give the game a Firefly feel.  You can sort of get that the show inspired a bit of the aesthetic both in characters and ships being gritty and Western.  However, this soundtrack has many songs that include lyrics.  That is not inherently a problem in game soundtracks, but when lyrical songs are part of the main rotation of music, especially on longer games like this one, you really start noticing the repetition of the songs.  It got to the point that after about 15 hours or so I could not stand the music distracting me anymore and turned it off for some more instrumental music I enjoy.  Playing though the soundtrack without any repeats outside of the game lets you enjoy it a lot more than in the game.
Musical repetition wasn’t the biggest problem Rebel Galaxy had though.  What had me raging was the seemingly random spikes in difficulty in missions.  Even after a bit of research, I’m not entirely sure how the scaling difficulty is determined, but the consensus seems to be that it’s related to the level of your ship equipment.  This means that even a relatively small upgrade of one or two things can mean either a mission becomes a joke or the enemies become so strong you are torn apart in seconds.  The discreet nature of this system made it extremely frustrating, as the stated difficulty of missions (ranging from “Very Easy” to “Very Hard”) may not at all represent how difficult it actually is.  This means sometimes you may just have to neglect a mission (and sometimes a story mission) until you can upgrade your ship to actually finish it – which brings to the surface some other issues like the general repetition of the types of missions you encounter.  Fun gameplay can only hold back the exhaustion of repetition for so long, so when progress is inhibited it starts to chip away at the paint.  Some games can pull of enemy scaling and it works flawlessly, but something went wrong in this implementation.
In the 22 hours it took me to complete the game, there were times I thought this was absolutely wonderful and times I never wanted to play it again.  Prior to completing it recently, I actually stopped playing it for several months after reaching a particularly rough point, and I think someone with less patience (can’t be too many of those) would give up as soon as the newness of the mechanics wore off.  However, taking the game as a whole as I always do, I think it’s worth picking up at the heavy discounts it’s now seeing.  Rebel Galaxy is worth trying out for $6 it has reached recently at the very least, so I recommend grabbing it next time it’s on sale if you have any interest in space sims.  It stands a step above its more generic or one dimensional indie counterparts in the genre while still falling short of the more polished titles coming along these days.

I'll start with saying that this is a beautiful game. The pixel art style is gorgeous and the music is soothing enough so that it doesn't become annoying as you listen to it for hours on end. Unfortunately, in the world of indie games, "artsy" has been done a few hundred times already. For a lot of people, this alone will not be the deciding factor.
Its main feature (shattered screen) is fairly unique, but sometimes it ends up feeling like more than just a simple inconvenience. While it's certainly the thing that makes this game in any way challenging, there are times when it makes a jump that's challenging enough on its own absolutely obnoxious.
The game's main downside is that if you die, you get penalized by making it impossible to collect all hearts in a stage, ultimately forcing you to restart the entire thing if that's what you're after. I'm not entirely sure what was going through Bernie's head when he decided that this was a good idea. To make the whole process even more frustrating, there is no quick restart button or menu option. Every time you wish to restart you have to exit to the stage selection screen and load the stage again, which ends up being a chore after you fail a precision jump by a milisecond for the umpteenth time.
The story and relationships between the characters feel rather shallow. While I don't necessarily need a story in a simple platformer, I do expect something a little more substantial than what Mario had 30 years ago.
Overall, I find that the game did not live up to its full potential. It's worth playing through if you got it in a bundle, but I wouldn't bother paying the full price for it unless you have nothing else to play.

Where is my Heart? is an adorable puzzle platformer that puts you in control of three little monsters that happen to be bestest friends. They collect hearts (the cute kind, not the still-beating kind) to feed to their tree friend, but ♥♥♥♥ up and feed him some black hearts. This makes the tree float away and the entire world fracture into scrambled shards.
As you can see from the screenshots, this makes getting around kind of a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ The main gimmick is that you see the levels from a scrambled perspective and have to figure out how each piece relates so you can navigate to collect all the hearts and reach the exit. If this doesn't sound particularly fun, well, it isn't. Not only does it take a lot of mental bandwidth to keep the levels straight in your head, a lot of the links between pieces can't be established without some guesswork or some oftentimes-fatal leaps of faith. You control each monster one at a time, with a dedicated button to switch between them. They don't jump real high, so stacking them to reach high places and make long jumps is a common task.
Other puzzles include getting the monsters to heart blocks colored like them to bonk and release their heart, and making platforms by collecting specific hearts that are not distinguished from the others in any way. Each monster can also turn into a special form by stacking everyone on a special block. The brown one turns into an elk-thing that can double-jump, and the gray one turns into a bat-thing that can see and step on hidden platforms. But the orange one turns into this cloud-thing that can rotate the level pieces to realign them. What's more, if he jumps before doing it, he stays stationary while the level rotates, effectively allowing him to teleport around. This is obviously the coolest gimmick in the game, but the level design turns it frustrating fast. Levels that center on his power often have you performing complex shifting combos to get him into isolated pieces, and if you rotate him into a wall, he dies.

This game has lost it's vibrance, quality, and community since its first revamp a couple of years ago.
I can't say that the Big Bang update did the game any good. It made it more playable for the casual side of the gaming community, but for players like me, who enjoy the serious and competitive nature of games, has either become apathetic or not able to find motivation to play the game.
To tell you how great the game was before any of this, because it was a really good one, whenever I watch a video that anyone has uploaded about the old versions of Maplestory I will start feeling noglastic. It's not like the more you see the more it reminds you of the good times, it hits me straight on. I remember how I first reach level 30, 70, and 120. I remember how I made friends with people who I am still in contact with today. I remember my first boss run or training party that I was in with a guild who was so kind and had a growing community. Those feelings were shot straight into my heart as soon as I watched a video that was posted by my guild.
What Nexon got rid of that made many veteran and senior players quit or leave the game was it's challenges. The difficulity of leveling up brought many players together, forcing us to make party and guilds to better fare against the monsters that we faced. Making these connections with other players also allowed us to make friends, a bond that both players can feel even through distances. I know it sounds silly but that's one of the things MapleStory taught me, friendship.
I won't say that MapleStory is bad game now, mostly because I still play it. People can still enjoy the game the way it is now. However, players who played the game for longer than a month before the Big Bang updates will understand me on this: MapleStory will never be able to give us that same exceptional feeling when playing. It's time has passed and so have most of us.
Anyone interested in this game can very well try it. It has become more suitible for the casual audience now. I will warn you already that many of the game's feature will force you either to spend tons of time on it, or spend money to at least losen up that time. Yes, MapleStory is what people calls "Pay 2 Win." However it wasn't always like that, it use to be just for extra clothing. You didn't need anything to make you progress through the game with real money.
tl;dr I recommend you to try it if you have never tried it before. If you don't like it then uninstall it. If you're a returning player then I'm warning you, everything is not the same anymore.

I... kind of figured this concept was dead on arrival, and I think I've played enough to know for certain: this was a terrible idea.
The main gimmick is hiding information from the player, for no other reason than to be annoying. A few cases you can vaguely piece together the world but a lot of times it's just pure trial and error figuring out where everything is.

When you start most levels, you have to wait for all three characters to come in from the door, which takes something like 10 seconds, and is unnecessary on almost every level. It's really tedious. Add to that the slow pace of the gameplay and there being no quick restart, and you have got a colossally slow-paced, tedious mess.
I think there's a few shreds of an idea buried in the stack of trash, but I really, strongly recommend not playing this game. 46 hours in seems like a good time to leave a review.
Okay, let's start with the fact that this is an early access game that's been out for a week. I've lost count of the number of patches and updates they put out since then, it's been amazing. This is how early access should be, constant communication from the developers, acknowledgement of feedback, and plenty of patches for fixing reported bugs.
Of course, there are still many bugs in the game, they're working on that. And they've provided a bulletin board on Trello that shows us what is on their radar to be fixed and added to the game. This is pretty sweet, I've played more than a few EA games these guys are on top of it. Sure, it's only been a week and it could taper off as time goes by, but this is a very encouraging sign to me.
Now, on to the gameplay. In a nutshell, it's fun, but not amazing. The spell casting is fun, getting the first broom is a blast, taming your first dragon and flying around at warp factor 50 is so much fun. But it's a grind, there's not a ton of variety in the combat, you're basically just spamming a lot of your bread and butter spells for whatever your weapon of choice is. And the AI is clumsy, so there's not a ton of challenge in it unless you go pick a fight with something well above your weight class. And the new spells are few and far between.
Fortunately, they're planning on adding more spells and weapons (and armor) as time goes on, so hopefully it won't be a 10 - 15 level wait for a new spell or weapon.
Crafting is simple, get X number of various resources, use them on the appropriate crafting bench, and get stuff. You do get XP for crafting and gathering resources, not a ton, but enough to make it worthwhile to set up a bunch of potions brewing or ore smelting while you go hunting for stuff to kill to get a nice little bonus stream of XP coming in.
Building is fun, if you're into that sort of thing (I am). You can make some badass looking castles and you get XP for building stuff too.
One caveat: I play on a server I rented that is PvE only and I only play with friends. So I can't speak to the level of griefing you might run into on a public PvP server, though I do know that they put in a few balance tweaks in the last patch to make griefing less of an issue.
On the whole, I give this a solid 7.5/10 with a ton of potential. You might be a little bored early on in the development process with the grinding and lack of variety, but give it some time to see what they add. With end game boss fights, world events, and NPC towns and vendors on the design schedule, this game could really be something fun in the future.

I was surprised at how decent this was. Looks great, sounds good, and actually plays really well once you get used to the new handling physics. Handles more like Gran Turismo 4 than it does the original GRID, but that's not a bad thing, it's just different. My primary complaint is that all variations of every track are not open to every class of car in time trials. You can only drive hatchbacks on the Okutama Sprint Circuit, for instance. The Grand Circuit is not an option. The menus are nice and sleek, too. I'd rarely make a point of that sort of thing, but it impressed me a lot for some reason.
It's a good game. So far, everything I've driven has been fun to drive, from Open Wheel, to Street, to Tuner, which I can't say for the original GRID (some of the EU and US events weren't very good). Just don't go into it expecting something which is exactly the same as GRID 2, or something that behaves like a proper simulator.

Great game, probably one of my favorite EA survival titles at the moment. I play on an official server that ranges from mid-full capacity, with little very little server issues (as of 8/3 patch). Currently running gtx 1080 ftw and pulling 50-60 fps.
Pros:
-Devs constantly pushing hotfixes and patches
-Satisfying amount of content for age (multiple content releases since launch, 2 I think)
-Community Managers very responsive
-Fun PVP (assuming the servers are running optimally)
-"Guild" system: User created factions are always a plus in my book
-You can ride a f***ing broom (and bomb mf'ers on them)
-Its a pretty game, especially if you dig sunsets and s**t.
Cons (EA cons and just some personal opinions):
-Monster AI currently lacking: One of the main facets that interested me was the ability to tame npcs and have them roll around as your personal goons or gaurd your base when youre away. Kind of hard to do that when they have the intuition of an old french fry.
-Few other issues involving monsters, including damage scaling (I shouldnt beable to 1v1 a level 50 B. dragon at lvl 25) and storage, but im assuming these will be addressed).
-Weapon balancing: PVE wise, all weapons are viable and pretty fun to use, but PVP wise the staff outshines all others.
-Lack of Tutorial or in-game guide: Doesnt really bother me and the game doesnt have too stiff a learning curve, but it may help the "instruction booklet " gamers out.
Overall a pretty fun and entertaining game. Probably one of the only EA games of this genre I would recommend. It has a very promising future if the devs keep on doing what they're doing.

A "free-to-play" puzzle quest with Marvel characters. If that's all it was, it might have been a fun game. There are a lot of issues working against it though. You're supposed to collect cards, but since you only have a very limited roster, you only want to keep the most powerful cards you can find or just stick with the main couple cards you start out with because they're the ones that level up. If you don't make room for them in your roster, new cards disappear. There's no way to measure your roster's progress on leveling up; when you do level a card up, you have to spend the crystals to actually increase the level. Most of the puzzle rounds have multiple rewards (I guess to push "replayability") but evidently the rewards are randomized so that you could play a single round dozens of times but never get all 4 rewards. I don't mind that the cards must "heal" when they take damage during a round, but the more powerful the enemies, the more damage, the longer time they have to heal. Eventually you can only play 2 or 3 rounds before your entire roster is down. So you have to grind for rewards but can't grind because your team's down. If this was a tablet game, it wouldn't be a big deal; on the PC, why play a game only as long as it takes to start it up? Of course, this is all not a problem if you're fine with paying lots of real money for the tokens.

I will start by saying I am a huge fan of the Civ series. I have played since Civ III and loved every game that has come out. That is until this one.
Pros:
- This is a Civ V mod and looks really good
- They tried a lot of new ideas and concepts with this game
Cons:
- Your first playthough you tend to just fumble through the game. No real information or direction given until you research something, or come across something.
- Miasma is a pain! Is a bit difficult to see, and it slows the game down A LOT. I don't fully understand its purpose or function in the game unless it is there to slow things down.
- The Tech Web is not difficult to understand, but overall a chaotic mess. Some work on this is sorely needed.
- Some of the control and visual icons could use some work. Civ V you knew what button you were pressing, or what unit had what veteran abilities. In this game not so much.
- Affinity needs a lot of work. I understand that you go down one of three paths and that each one requires X resource. It is just boring. I expected more from a Civ game.
- Quest Log Display needs some work. Display to the player what is needed at a glance, rather than have the player open it up and scroll down. It is annoying to have to open quest after quest to find out what I need to do. A bullet point underneath them would do wonders to making this interface more user/player friendly.
- The map seems cramped.
- The AI is not very good at all. Predictible and you can outright ignore them with seemingly zero penalty. Before this game came out they said they did work on this AI to make it better. So where is that?
- Favors for the AI players is a unique concept. Yet without any real explanation of what they do they are uselss. I don't care to take the time to find out what they do.
Just like many have said this is an unfinished game unworthy of even the $20 price tag. Hopefully with the next expansion, or more likely the second expansion, this game will be better. Yet honestly I am not holding my breath.

RollerCoaster Tycoon was the first PC game I ever played. I spent countless hours just playing the first two scenarios alone. RollerCoaster Tycoon 2 however, was a game I never played until I bought it a couple months ago. It's safe to say that I love it as much as the original. Don't let my playtime fool you, I've put in at least 48 hours into it through "OpenRCT2." I highly recommend you play it through OpenRCT2, as it adds a bunch of cool features that weren't in the original game such as cheats and multiplayer. Anyways, I'll try and base my review on the original product alone. If you've ever played the original RCT, then it's basically more of that. It builds upon the foundation of the original game by adding more rides, scenarios, scenery, and other things. Your goal is to build a successful theme park in one of the various scenarios. You must build rides that entice guests to spend their hard earned cash. You also have to build shops, stalls, and bathrooms so that your guests can keep their needs high and stay in the park longer. You can build a variety of rides and add a variety of theming around them, but the most involved rides are the roller coasters. You can build them yourself, or choose from a variety of prebuilt coasters. The roller coaster building is probably my favourite part of the game. You can build the best rollercoaster ever, (and find out guests won't ride it because it's too intense) or you can build death traps that fly off the rails and kill your guests. The only downside is that you can't ride them in first person due to technical limitations of the time. However, you can watch guests ride them. Throw in some staff management, path management, and budgeting, and you've pretty much covered most of the gameplay. My biggest gripe with the game is probably the lack of "free building maps." The scenarios are cool, but there aren't as many open maps like there was in the first game. Another problem I have is how there aren't any maps with both a park entry fee and ride fees. This seems rather odd as most real life parks operate with both admission prices and ride prices. Finally there is no fast forward button in the base game. (OpenRCT2 adds some) This can make it a bit dull when you're waiting for enough income to build your next idea. The graphics have aged well. They have an art style that is cheerful and enjoying to look at. My only complaint with them is probably the isometric view. It adds some struggle to finding a good position for the camera to see things. Thankfully the see-through rides and scenery options exist to compensate for the lack of full camera control. I also love the sound mixing. The park is completely silent until you start adding rides with music. It really adds to the atmosphere of your park. One feature I forgot to mention earlier is the customization. It's top notch. From theming your park, to naming your rides, it's great. You can even rename the guests.
Here's a list of the pros and cons for me.
Pros:
-Fantastic gameplay
-Interesting scenarios
-Charming graphics
-Variety of rides
-The roller coaster building
-The customization
-Hours upon hours of replayability
Cons:
-Not as many open maps as RCT
-Isometric view can be a bit confusing sometimes
-Can't ride roller coasters
-Not being able to charge for both rides and admission at the same time (OpenRCT2 fixes this)
-No fast forward button (OpenRCT2 fixes this)
In conclusion, RollerCoaster Tycoon 2 is one of the best tycoon games out there. It’s basically nothing but improvements over the original. If you're looking for a theme park management game, it doesn't get much better than this.

Holy moly, I don't have any playtime on this game on steam because I played it on my xbox back in the day. Let me tell you, this game and the original Bioshock + Burial at sea DLC for Infinite. Together this is the ultimate video game story! This game has one of the deepest, most interesting and emotional stories of all time. I cried at the end of this game when I got the bad ending.
This game starts off continuing from the bad ending for the first game, you have been stuffed into a Big Daddy suit and biologically linked to a little sister, however you are killed and revived in a Vita Chamber years later. Your little sister has since grown up and it is now your task to find her before you mentally deteriorate by not being with her. And while you're at it figure out what to do with your killer who is the sister's mother.
That's all I'll say for the story, the graphics are very pretty and unique but starting to get slightly outdated today. Still no one should play this game for the graphics, this game's charm lies entirely in it's story and gameplay.
Another thing to boast about in this game is the music, boy is the soundtrack for this game solid. The very talented Garry Schyman is back again and created another beautiful score, it's hard to describe how beautiful it is so just go give it a listen on youtube or something. Also give the tracks from the good old days a listen, there's some really old but good music in here. One song I really like in particular is Boby Darin's Beyond the Sea.
So overall this game deserves a solid 10/10. There is absolutely nothing I don't like about this game, in fact there's nothing I don't like about this entire franchise, in my opinion it is the perfect video game franchise. It fits my taste perfectly and all my love goes out to 2k and Irrational Games.

All good things must come to an end - A Player of Bioshock 1&2
Where to start on such a game. Bioshock 1 and Bioshock 2 are both excellent stories as well as games. Bioshock 1 introduced players into a fulfilling story, loot system, and most of all gameplay style that offered countless ways to take on the same levels over and over. Bioshock 2 did it even better.
Immersion, or should I say Submersion into Bioshock 2 is immediate the environment wants you to think your 1000s of feet below the oceans surface in a failed utopia over run by dna mutated freaks....they the developers delivered 100%.
The AI is awesome, its aggressive, maniacal, depressed, and ready to strike out in a any way necessary to be the king of the hill. BS 2 gets FPS so well that compared to many other FPS games its style(s) of combat is nearly unmatched. The plasmid (the games version of magic) system has more than enough variety and when paired with the 8 possible guns, allows the adventurous gamer to try out a bountiful palate of ways to own the enemy. The boss fights and sub-boss fights are not easy on the two hardest modes and that makes for careful consideration, even with a veteran player.
Throughout the game there is 14 weapons upgrades, not all weapons can be upgraded to full, but thats okay some of the upgrades are not necessary or you will find as most do that certain guns attract you more. However: if your interested in playing BS2 more than once this is where the games ability to try out different modes and strategies of attack increase its replay value expotentially.
If you want to get really good at BS2 combat try out the protector trials, there you can get familiar with all the guns and plasmids, which in turn due to the limits the trials set forces you to reconsider alternate strategies of defense and offense.
To talk more of the story is a spoiler, it is a great story with many twisted side stories all helping to reveal the corrosive, deceptive, and parasitic life you could expect as a citizen of Rapture. The era of BS2 takes place around the 1950's and the environment gets that element done so well, you'll be smacking your chops for a burger & soda at the dog n suds after a quick skinny on the beach with yeah yeah and her sock hop friends. More likely you'll be puzzlingly pleased with the morbid stories heard on over 100 audiologs.
Which leads me to add that, the dialogue produced by not only the main characters in the story but also the average splicer thug and various henchmen is extremely diverse, there are the scenes prepared for your to walk up on, and then the random chats heard in the countless places by some desperate brigand searching the place for another fix of adam (the games source of magic).
The DLC Minerva's Den is an excellent story with plenty of substance and allows the player a few more levels of BS2 action and a new weapon and plasmid to try out.
The Multiplayer had some people (about 6 including me) on it as of 08/2017. There are many different MP styles of play, all of them were fun, but with such a sparse community of players it will be difficult to enjoy the MP experience as it was intended.
For some tips on what upgrades in plasmids and guns:
Guns - 14 power to the people upgrades in the game so not all weapons can be upgraded fully. Unless you really love that drill weapon, forget all 3 upgrades. Unless you really really x infinity love that machine gun forget the ricochet upgrades it is the least effective bar none. If you upgrade all but the 4 mentioned you should have 1 or two upgrades left over to haggle with less desireable but still useful gun upgrades.
Adam - You harvest adam by gathering fights and big sisters, as well as these little slug creatuers primarily located in the wreckage and foliage while traversing between cities underwater. These slug creatures give 10 adam a find, so its not much lost if you dont find them all.
Eventually you will get gene slot adam bonus abilities that allow the little sisters to gather longer and get more adam, ALWAYS USE THESE. And if your good rescue and adopt all sisters, the return is a eventual reward given by them. If you want to play the "evil" story arc, harvest the lil sisters....monster.
Electric, Fire, and Telekinesis are 3 plasmids used most often, only telekinesis is worth the level 3 upgrade. Electric, Fire and Winter blast level 3 is a streaming wave that comes out of the hand and guzzles eve so fast its pointless. The only offset is a very late game gene tonic called elemental vampire with recycles some eve back - its not a equivalent ratio.
As for the other plasmids - most are not worthy of level 3, it comes down to situations and preference. Decoy is always level 3 worth - its the best dmg mitigating ability in the game. Security Comm 3 is meh, same with hypnotize 3, and winter blast 3, bee hive 3 being the most situational as it requires the target to be slain by the bees then their corpse becomes a bee hive mine, its very hard to get this mine utilized outside a gather or "hold them off" fight. Your preference and playstyle often dictate what earns a level 3 purchase so consider what your using most and not.
Overall - If you like FPS games, love headshots, explosions, and setting up techical traps to ambush your foes then Bioshock 2 is a must play. My history with FPS games is pretty long, and the Bioshock series gets the action done right. Done right so much it is hard to uninstall such a enjoyable game but with 4 play throughs and 90+ hours, its time to wave goodbye to the citizens of Rapture.

Having played both the original Bioshock and Infinite and I can say that ,without a doubt, this the entry I enjoyed the most in the franchise, despite being considered the weakest in the trilogy.
While the original Bioshock felt more like survival horror, having the protagonist thrown into Rapture as an unknown quantity until the truth is unveil and has to make his final stand against the last bad guy and Infinite`s DeWitt was little more than a gun for hire (and despite the many plot twists felt that way to the end) Bioshock 2 offers a more humane story, less preachy, convoluted and heavy handed, while staying true tot he lore of the series and providing emotional investment, a great achivement given the nature of the game protagonist, the saupport cast , while not descive, is charismatic and pòsses enough character to add to the plot.
Gameplay-wise, it has the same virtues and com,mits the same sins as the original Bioshock, with a few notable improvements though: Upgrades and New Plasmids are easier to acquire, due to a higher to the higher quantities of ADAM that can be obtained, thanks to the new gathering mechanics through the Little Sisters, whch is both original, challenging and rewarding. Hacking has been simplified and is more rewarding endeavor, but more risky at the same time. But still suffers from the tiresome grinding that is required to bring down the Big Daddies, due to ammo and healing items BEING ALWAYS SCARCE, if I can single one perk from Bioshock Infnite that I could give the first two games, would be it`s more forgiving nature: Combat was deadly and you could still die easily, but you would never be in short supply of means of defending yourself.
All and all Bioshock is a great game, a more streamlined expirience which reatins all the charm of it`s predecessor, corrects a few mistakes and adds a more human story rather that "Let`s get the hell out of here!" both Bioshock 1 and Infinite provided. The story of Delta and Elenor is probably the one that sends the most positive message of them all and...you get to play as a Big Daddy =)
By all means acquire if you are into shooters with RPG elements

I honestly wish that Steam had a Mixed option to put as a way to recommend this game because I honestly feel mixed about it. There are many aspects about Hatred I like, and there are many aspects about Hatred I dislike. I overall enjoyed it, and I do see myself playing it more, but Hatred has a lot of infuriating design and gameplay choices that keeps me from saying that this is a good game.
First thing, optimization, pretty bad. Sometimes the game runs smooth, sometimes the framerate will tank and start to chug a little bit. The game also has a tedenancy to crash from time to time. I remember at one point, I got to the Military Base level and every single time I failed, the game would just crash without fail. It doesn't happen every time, but it can and quite possibly will crash on you.
Gameplay is where I'm the most mixed about. If I had to sum up the gameplay, it's fun in some parts, but it's boring in other parts. Your only goal in the game, as seen in trailers, is to kill a lot of innocent people. Shooting is fine in the game as it is a top-down isometric shooter. The Executions, which were the big deal with the trailers, are pretty violent, but I have seen worse. You perform Executions to get health back. Problem, it's very inconsistent. Granted, you're going to have a good amount of opportunities to perform them, but they are so very inconsistent. You shoot a person, and they maybe won't die which will give you the opportunity to perform the executions. It's a very inconsistent way to get health back, and sometimes not very reliable. There's not much weapon variety or even a good amount of variety in each of the executions. The AI is also pretty bad. Granted, civilian NPCs when given the chance will sometimes pick up a gun and try to kill you. However, they will a lot of times derp out, running straight towards you, Mr. Billy the Trenchcoat Edgelord, while you're shooting your machine gun at them. Sometimes they will run in a circle, run in and out of houses. Enemy AI is kinda better, but they are still derpy. I remember a few times I sat in a room, and they just kept shuffling around the building, either not knowing how to get in or they lined up in a single file line where I was and took a horrible shotgun blast to the face when they walked around the corner. There are vehicles, but take my advice, never use them unless they are the ones that you spawn in at the beginning of the level because those will have guns and will absorb a lot of damage.
One other issue is that this game is hard. Infuriatingly hard. I heard that the game was hard even on Easy, and I did play the game on Easy, and it was brutally difficult. I can only imagine that on the higher difficulties, it will make me want to throw my laptop out my window and never use computers ever again. You will be swarmed by enemies constantly to the point of being overwhelmed and you will lose all your health in seconds. It becomes frustrating with the fact that the game has Respawns instead of Checkpoints and you get a respawn when you complete a side objective. If you die and you have no respawns, you're doing the whole level over again. I have to imagine that the only reason why Hatred is so hard is to expand how much time you're playing.
That's another thing, this game is short. As of typing this review, I have played this game for 5.5 hours, but I can guarantee that the game is much shorter than that. The campaign took me about 4 hours to beat, and I can guarantee that I could've completed it much faster if it wasn't with how hard this game is.
That's not to say that this game is completely bad. As mentioned before, it does some fun parts. I see this game as a bit of a stress ball at times, a stress ball that near the end of it will give you some stress, but a stress ball nonetheless. Some moments of it can be enjoyed and I even enjoyed it in parts. Graphically the game is not a bad looker, it's actually pretty good in a lot of areas from the details, fire effects, and just the amount of destruction you can cause is pretty fun to see. There is also, as of now, a Survival mode where you pick one of 3 characters with slightly different stats, choose your loadout, a map, and just kill as many NPCs as you can for points.
Unfortunately that's just about it that I can say about Hatred. It's a short game with repetitive gameplay that's going to get stale quickly when you realize that there isn't many weapons in the game nor is there many execution variations and NPCs are like bullet sponges and a punishing difficulty even on easier settings. It's a good looking game that unfortunately has poor optimization. It's like a 5/10 game, I can't say it's good, but I also can't say it's bad. If I had to recommend this game, I would recommend it for people who want something to just mess around in and be the bad guy or even a challenge. Anything else, I do not recommend this game as I do think that there are much better and enjoyable options than Hatred out there. As much as I did enjoy this game, it's just one that I can't see myself recommending to others or to the majority of people. I do want to see some more games from this developer, as this was a promising first game from them and I would like to see a new game from them. This was just unfortunately a game that fell short, but I think the devs can make something better.

This game has lost it's vibrance, quality, and community since its first revamp a couple of years ago.
I can't say that the Big Bang update did the game any good. It made it more playable for the casual side of the gaming community, but for players like me, who enjoy the serious and competitive nature of games, has either become apathetic or not able to find motivation to play the game.
To tell you how great the game was before any of this, because it was a really good one, whenever I watch a video that anyone has uploaded about the old versions of Maplestory I will start feeling noglastic. It's not like the more you see the more it reminds you of the good times, it hits me straight on. I remember how I first reach level 30, 70, and 120. I remember how I made friends with people who I am still in contact with today. I remember my first boss run or training party that I was in with a guild who was so kind and had a growing community. Those feelings were shot straight into my heart as soon as I watched a video that was posted by my guild.
What Nexon got rid of that made many veteran and senior players quit or leave the game was it's challenges. The difficulity of leveling up brought many players together, forcing us to make party and guilds to better fare against the monsters that we faced. Making these connections with other players also allowed us to make friends, a bond that both players can feel even through distances. I know it sounds silly but that's one of the things MapleStory taught me, friendship.
I won't say that MapleStory is bad game now, mostly because I still play it. People can still enjoy the game the way it is now. However, players who played the game for longer than a month before the Big Bang updates will understand me on this: MapleStory will never be able to give us that same exceptional feeling when playing. It's time has passed and so have most of us.
Anyone interested in this game can very well try it. It has become more suitible for the casual audience now. I will warn you already that many of the game's feature will force you either to spend tons of time on it, or spend money to at least losen up that time. Yes, MapleStory is what people calls "Pay 2 Win." However it wasn't always like that, it use to be just for extra clothing. You didn't need anything to make you progress through the game with real money.
tl;dr I recommend you to try it if you have never tried it before. If you don't like it then uninstall it. If you're a returning player then I'm warning you, everything is not the same anymore.

Welp, a game that got me busy for so long, deserves a long review in turn, so here goes:
As far as visuals go, the game does quite well for itself, specially considering it's not a AAA game. Developers managed to convey the emptiness of space, without making it a dull place with nothing to see. Plenty of asteroid belts, abandoned loot and friend and foe alike to encounter, ships look swell and enemies are threatening.
Gameplay wise, if you like what you do in the first hour, then by all means keep going, if not, refund, because game will be basically more of the same. Main story line, and like 85% side quests fit the "kill X" or "fetch" style of quest, with a few escort missions in between. Not saying by any means they weren't entertaining, they were, but more variety would've been very welcome.
As far as storyline goes, it is both sensate and a safe bet, without being too ambitious. A gadget lost to ages found and recovered, and a struggle with those who seek to possess it; entertaining enough to get you thru the game, yet without any ramifications or input in the matter, a classical storytelling.
Factions and the such, honestly, near useless. If you♥♥♥♥♥♥someone off they're going to attack you on sight, and if you're pals with someone, they won't... that's it really. At least for me, it seemed pointless to befriend the militia anywhere past neutral so I wouldn't have to fight them as well, they don't help you, unlock adittional missions or anything. Guilds do give out certain benefits like extra ships and gizmos, but other than that, it's pretty pointless to try and be pals with anyone.
As for trade, despite developers claiming otherwise, it is currently, almost entirely unused potential. It is absolutely POINTLESS to invest in a hidden caché for contraband, as the prices for such items fluctuate the low to mid ranges, and you can make the same or more credits with legal items. I never once felt inclined to buy contraband items, because the risk was not worth the money, when it could have been used as such a pivotal point of the game: risk dealing on illegal goods, for a hefty return on your investment. Even on legal stuff, devs promise it goes beyond "buy cheap and sell expensive" but in practice, it's exactly that. Events are pretty unimportant, and sometimes a station offering a good "on surplus" will sell more expensive than a normal, no event station.
As for alternative gameplay styles, some people claim to be doing pretty good for themselves as miners or traders; I honestly did not make 1/100 of what I did as a mercenary, via mining or trading, at least when factoring the time invested. In the time it took me to farm enough meteoric diamonds to make half a million, I could have hopped across the system and complete 3 relief missions for thrice that amount.
And finally, replayability, this is where the game loses a lot of shine. You can keep playing past the final mission, but have little incentive to do so. There is no New Game+ mode, no unlocked specials and honestly, once you buy a Dreadnaught class ship, you can literally dive head first into a cluster of enemies, and let the auto-turrets do the picking, all challenge is removed. It would be nice to face new threats that actually carried a risk, not just a "pew pew die" gameplay style.
So, is the game worth it? Absolutely, even at full price. Would I recommend it? No doubt, but like I said, make sure you enjoy the mechanics and if you don't, refund, it doesn't get any different for the rest of the game. Does it need work? Very much, both for alternative gamestyles and replayability. Would I purchase DLC? Bring it on!

ok, I will recommend it but in this review I will be quite critical of the game, because I think it's not a game for everybody.
First, the fun thing about this game is the combat, that's what this game is made for and polished for. The story is acceptable, I have seen worse stories in better games. Everything else is unpolished or bare-bones. I have seen someone saying in the forum that the game is fun but shallow and I think that describes it pretty well.
For specific points (everytime I'm talking about money bellow here it never means real world money):
- Why put faster space travel behind a paywall? Really the time you loose flying through nothing is absolutely boring. Sure at the beginning it can be cool to be in space but that does not last longer than 10 minutes and the fact that you can only fly on a horizontal plane lets the feeling vanish even faster. So the warp drive should be at it's highest setting from the beginning without needing to buy costly upgrades, but it isn't.
- Enemies scale with you, it is not as bad as I've seen in other games where the enemies are always exact your level, you can sometimes get ahead of the enemies. But it's still pretty frustrating when you finally can afford a new ship and then realize all enemies also just upgraded to the next bigger ship.
- I really dislike some missions where you have to go to a specific point and while you got there or when you arrive there you suddenly are surrounded by 30 small ships and 5 bigger ships than you yourself have, I would've liked a more strategical approach to those battles instead of dumping you in and watch you squirm.
- I do like the ship designs but I would've liked if you could've changed some things about it with money, like buying more space for turrets, so that you could get the other juggernauts for example to the same level as the blackgate, so that not everybody ends up with pretty much the same super ship at the end.
- Another point about the ships, it woud've been nice to have a little more variety on ships.
- I dislike long grinding, so I like games where the progression comes natural, that's not the case here. At least after you have your 2nd or 3rd ship you will have to start grinding on missions and bounties or do mining (i can't say anything about mining, because I have not done it since it didn't interest me) to get better equipment and bigger ships. I have seen some ppl saying they went back to or never changed their first ship because then the enemy difficulty also didn't change much, but in my case I want to see and use all these different ships, that's the reason I'm playing.
- The missions where you have to pair warp are broken, you need luck to not get something in your way until you get to the destination, as soon as even a speck of dust in the way, the other ship will just turn around fly back to your starting point and then do the same again.
Ok these are the points I wanted to make, there are still some minor nitpicks but they are so small I don't think I need to describe them in detail here.
So, it's a fun game, the combat is pretty engaging and the different ships do provide some variety, but buy with cation, there are some things that can make the game quite annoying at times.
