Jalopy is part simulator part, rogue like, part adventure, complete fun.
While still in early access it provides a unique rogue like game where you drive an old soviet era car through eastern block europe. driving itself is not the challenge, as with a simulator game, reaching your destination is the challenge, a survival game with no death state, no enemies exept soviet engineering.
You start of in your uncles workshop you get the car ready to do and you are given $100, from there you must travel across eastern europe, maintaining your crappy car, keeping it fuelled, paying for motel beds, you save when you sleep in a motel before crossing the border checkpoint and onwards you go on your grand journey eastward.
It has simple but well stylised art, a great soundtrack that makes you feel like you are in 90's eastern germany, and a totally unique and fantastic experience for any fan of atmospheric survival rogue like. it is hard to explain why it is amazing but there can be no doubt that it is.
The only issue is that it is short 3-4 hours currently on a single playthrough till you reach the end of early access but it is progressing and adding more features and whenever I hear about a new zone I fuel up my Jalopy and hit the road again. if you are willing to play a short game or are willing you wait for more content later this game is 100% worth it for any fan of this style of game.

All of the mechanical changes I am in favor of, and I feel sets Civ:BE up to be a really solid game once a DLC or two are released. As an example:
Happyness changed into health, and the lack of luxory resources to affect it, is a nice change becasue it simplifies the dependancy on starting near and aquiring resources to maintain.
The wonder system seems to weigh much less which I appreciate, making wonder spamming not so affective.
Hovering units helps aid the problems presented by 1 unit per tile.
The technology web (while at first confusing and convuluted) seems to offer much greater flexebility to how you want to play.
The culture is also simplified, but also more free to experiment with, as opposed to Civ 5 which kind of locks you into a certain trait.
The game pace seems to move quicker, and as a whole seems to have cut a lot of the mechanical fluff out of Civ 5, and replaced it with a more solid foundation.
Admitedly, this foundation is rather bare, but I'd expect that so far, and I am okay with this as DLC's to deepen the gameplay are sure to come.

The economy is woven through each system as well. Everything is connected. And its awesome, super well designed game.

____MARVEL PUZZLE QUEST REVIEW____
Upon logging into steam and finding this featured in the store as F2P, A part of me leapt in excitement. As a long term puzzle quest lover I found myself drawn into the universe that is Marvel Puzzle Quest. Instead of having one character, you have up to 3 that switch in mid battle (each character is strongest with a particular tileset). As you match tiles, you gain the amount destroyed as power which you can then use as abilities.
This opened up some room for strategy, in which I would try to think 2-3 steps ahead and plan my attacks according to my characters strengths. The campaign is somewhat lackluster in the script department, with the cutscenes just being the same portraits as the ingame characters. However as you progress through the prologue, you are faced with goons that deploy timed tiles that explode after the timer expires. In certain situations you can be unlucky and not have any tiles nearby, but with careful planning, most tiles can be destroyed before their time expires. Going further into the campaign, these encounters just repeated, with very little varience.
However, there is plenty of varience in the somewhat multiplayer aspect of the game. Instead of fighting other players in realtime, the opponent's party is controlled by the AI, which is rather predictable (always uses abilites when they get appropriate power), but because you are fighting someone else's roster, you think about what strategy they were thinking about with their particular roster. This is somewhat compelling, but the real fun comes in the weekly events. Every week there is a particular event in which you compete with up to 1000 players for a chance to win rare covers. This brings me to my next point: the levelling system.
Instead of levelling like a normal rpg through experience points, you level by collecting the same cover with that particular ability and since heroes are level capped by the amount of covers they have, the more covers you have for a particular character, the higher you can level that character.This hampers progression and you will find that you will level the characters with the most covers instead of thinking about some strategy.  This is where the transactions come into play.
There are two types of currency: Iso-8, which is very common and can be generated by winning each game and awarded by winning particular events for the first time; and Hero points, which can be found in only a handful of stages in the PvE campaign. Conversely you can place in the top 25 in events and earn hero points, but to be able to do this, you need a good hero roster, which in turn requires hero points. Therefore every player will either have to wait 1 week for 50 hero points (hero points are awarded for logging in once per week) or they can choose to pay $1 for 100. At first this doesnt seem like a big issue. only $1 and you can have 100 hero points. However, the more roster slots you have, the more hero points it costs to upgrade. This is one area where the developers aimed their micro transactions at. I am guilty of spending $5 for 600 hero points to unlock a few more slots. I am currently up to 20 slots and have only paid $5 which I believe is reasonable. The other area where microtransactions seem tempting is the recovery time for your heroes.
As you battle, your heroes will get damaged. They will recover when they are not in use, but as you gain higher levels, the characters take longer to recover. For example, a level 1 Iron Man takes only about 10 minutes to fully recover, as apposed to a level 50 Iron Man, which takes 4 hours to recover. The whole aspect of waiting for characters to recover interrupts the flow of the game, which seems like a good idea when you're on the move/on a mobile device. However, this should have been removed with the PC version as most people can just play a few rounds, then they have to wait 2-3 hours to recover. You can instantly recover by using medkits which are somewhat rare, or can be purchased for 50 cents each. This price of 50 cents doesnt seem high, but when you have to do it almost every battle, you start to feel a pinch on your wallet.
One strategy that I believe newbies should employ (and this is only to help progression and to enjoy the game as it should be: uninterrupted) is to set your system clock forward. This tricks the game into thinking that time has passed and your characters will recover the amount of time you put the clock forward. Ignore the events, just focus on the prologue, get through it and level up your characters. Once you have finished the campaign, set your clock back to normal time and use 1 medkit on each character.
This "trick" should not have to be used and it's bad gameplay design to have to resort to such things. However, with all this said, I have put about 100 hours into this game over the last 2 weeks, so they must be doing something right. Think of this game as a CCG with puzzle quest elements. Overall I would recommened this because it is free and you can still get a lot of enjoyment for free.
____Pros____

Half-Life 2: Deathmatch, there is a lot of things to say about this one. The game is perfect and the community, although small, is great, too. You find mostly adults who remember when this game was popular (I was in the gaming community at the time but I didn't play it often) and are actually nice. They aren't "Rekt scrub (lenny here)." The gameplay itself is fantastic and simple. You go on a map either from Half-Life 2 or a community-made map and shoot the enemy, as easy as that. It may sound a little tooo simple but players have came up with strategies on how to do your objective, my personal favorite is the gravity gun and grenade trick (probabally has some name that I dont know about :P) where you switch to your gravity gun after laying down a grenade and launch it at other players.
So, you might be wondering why the game is dead if it has fantastic gameplay and community. Well, the reasons I've picked up on from playing is when Valve removed the bhopping glitch. From what I've seen, bhopping is still possible but isn't as good or efficent. Another reason is that it's old. The game came out in 2004 and according to Steam is actually released a little before HL2 which technically makes HL2 DM the first game requiring Steam, not HL2. Valve doesn't update it unless if it's something like bug fixes. No new content. To be honest, I think that's a good and a bad thing. It's good because the gameplay can't be ruined discluding the removal of bhopping. It's bad because if it's not updated it's almost abandonware.
When I said the gameplay is simple and how players made a way to make it even more complex, I wasn't lieing. There is another gamemode actually that was community-made in the game. It's HL2:DM roleplay. Just imagine Gmod's DarkRP except RDM almost doesn't exist and you don't have a random 6 year old admin telling you what you can and cannot do. It's actually really fun, too, even though it's not as complex as DarkRP. Infact, I never realized how much DarkRP catered around its players until I've played the roleplay mode in HL2:DM. DarkRP is preschool compared to this.
Overall, HL2:DM is an abandon game with fantastic gameplay and a fantastic community.

This game is awesome, yet it could have been the über hot masterpiece of the millenia, if devs would have had put more efford into it. Content is quite little, even though it looks like a lot. This somewhat reminds me of Escape Velocity as if depicted in 3D, minus the depth.
Pros
-Space, the last frontier, and all that crap. Shooting, pirates, traders, looting, ships, equipment, aliens, etc. Drool all over my keyboard.
-Very pretty. Pisses off that I had to put the graphics to minimal to have it nearly lag-free.
-Broadside-battling is interesting concept.
-Nice story. Nothing great - it could've been better, but it was interesting enough to disappoint me with how short it was.
-Interesting music.
-You can add your own music to the playlist, and for different situations as well! Like, in-station, idle, ambient, combat. How awesome is that?!
-I laughed every time my hireling crashed to my butt-shield when exiting warp.
Cons
-Gets repetitive rather fast. Missions, characters, encounters, music, battles, and so on...
-Broadside-battling starts to feel nuisance when your turrets do nearly as much damage, while turrets aint limited to sides. The only reason to use broadsides is the combined damage-output with turrets.
-Battles become boring over time - you fly among your adversaries and let your turrets blast away anything that comes too close, while trying to find a target for your broadsides to fire at. If a ship is too strong to handle otherwise, you just tailgate it and slowly drain its strength - if it's worth the efford.
-With biggest and baddest ship available to you, you can kill stuff that should scare the bejeebus out of you, without breaking a sweat. I went side-to-side with
and pummeled it to pieces with oh so ease. I suppose that should have been the biggest and baddest single foe you can fight with.
-It lacks depth. There's no lore. Things just are, things just happen. For example, in EV, there's description for every freaking station and planet you can land. And there's heck a lot more of those than in RG. In RG, there's only some relatively meaningless info.
-Mining, it's boring as is in general. Here it's also annoying. Fine, getting a single item out of that rock is easy enough, you just select lasers and your aim is forced on a rock, then you just fire. But if a rock contains several items, this wont work anymore. You need to do a PULSE scan (which aint clarified anywhere - you can also do "what it is and what it has" scan as well, which doesn't work for this purpose!) and try to find "special spot" in said rock (if you have a required component for that), and pray Rorath that your aim is true enough to get all those preciouses out of it. Hunting bounties is more worth it, especially when you get past the first solar system. Not to forget that if the rock is below your horisontal axis, you need to be far enough and/or in proper angle to be able to hit that bloody stone.
-This game's controls are designed for gamepad, and it oh so freaking shines. So many things are stacked under the E key that it actually becomes annoyance. And you cannot separate them. So. It is rare for me to find the need to write a review. (Especially not the day of purchase.) Generally a game has to grab me. Rebel Galaxy... has certainly done that. I was skeptical at the outset- a 20 dollar plane-locked space game? Hm. The ad hooked me though, and I finally gave in and bought it.
The first thing I noticed was how GOOD the game feels. The controls take some adjustment- it plays like the ship battles from Assasins Creed 3. But every single time I light up my hyperdrive it puts a smile on my face. Combat is SERIOUSLY fast paced, but flexible.
Missions are about what you would expect from a game like this, but they do pay well. It can be hard to pick a downside this early- this is my first day playing, but I would say that the game does not really help you get established well. It warns you within the first half hour that your ship is crap, but only helps fix it a little. It tells you, briefly, what you should fix. I could see this being off putting for new players. Also- not for children. A fair bit of harsh language.
Ships are wonderfully customizable. Your guns matter- make sure to get ones you like. They can make all the difference depending on your play style. I am a bit of an odd bird with these kinds of things- I like to keep things as far away from me as I can. Until they get too close, then I ram the ever living ... stuffing out of them. With the customization options this games have, I can fill my play style to a T.
Feels a bit like SPAZ 2, for those in the know, mixed with ship combat from Assassins Creed 3. Then given a touch of western feel (mostly in the form of music selection).
TLDR: Screw that, I'm going back to play this game more.
UPDATE: I have now played the game through to completion. I stand by my initial reveiw, but have more to add. Typically I rate a game based on how much time I get out of it, on a scale of worth it, or not. Having dropped 40+ hours in, and still enjoying it, I would easily rate this as worth it.  If I had to pick any one gripe about a generally great title, it would be "unmet potential". This game feels good to play. But there is so much more I would love to do, including, (without being too spoilery) getting my best friend back. I would love to have more access to more ships, and be able to fight some seriously massive foes. Crack starbases outside of missions, if for not better reason than gits and shiggles. A massive, customizeable universe. ECT. If ever there is a sequel, I will be getting it. Had a blast.
TLDR: Seriously this time. With a few touch ups could be a modern $60 title, priced at $20. Has a lot more potential than is met in game, but is entirely worthwhile as is. Worth $20? Beyond a doubt.

Awkward controls, boring player-characters, and uninspired maps. This just isn't a fun game.
-
Most of the controls are done with mouse. You move by right clicking and attack by left clicking. This is extremely awkward, and makes it further difficult to fight. (probably intentional)
-
I tried all 3 characters, and while they are unique to each other, none of them are suited for surviving.
There is a pistol wielder, an axe wielder, and a sniper.
The pistol can fire quickly but does little damage. This is probably the best choice for surviving, but you end up just running around the enemies as they try to corner you firing into them.
The axe is purely melee. They are heavily dependant on the ability to stun lock the enemy. You must be directly in front of the enemy to attack them. Their special ability is a spinning attack, which is helpful when you're surrounded.
The sniper is useless. Semi-powerful shots, but a single chamber rifle. Reloading after hitting 1 enemy when there's a horde after you is time consuming and frustrating. I commited suicide while playing the sniper, just to end it.
-
I didn't continue past the first map, but usually you want your first map to be amazing, so players will enjoy playing in the first place. This first map was awful. It's very small, and has several 'arms' attached to it. These arms are very thin and usually a dead-end. So, running around the enemy is nearly impossible, forcing you to take damage as you try to get around them.
-
While there is a nice variety of enemies to deal with, the overall gameplay is generic and lackluster. The enemies walk towards you, and you hit them until they die. The AI is designed as mindless drones that attempt to overpower you with numbers rather than any type of strategy.
In between rounds, you are awarded 1 token to purchase a survival item. This can be restoring all your health, restoring all your ammo, putting your hunger to 0%, and putting your thirst to 0%. This is never explained, and when first attempting to open the shop, it will state, "You are not near a stand" after a bit, I realized that there are weapon racks near the spawn point. You must be standing next to these in order to purchase items.
Enemies also drop pills that restore health, hunger, and thirst. Though it's 1% per pill, making it almost useless
Just overall, the game feels like it suffers from being too generic.
They need more characters to play as (perhaps toss out archetypes and let people select their own weapons), and better maps (more open, so you can feel like you're not always cornered)

Where Is My Heart is a mind-bending puzzle game where you must navigate levels that have been visually fractured into multiple boxes on the screen.  You control 3 characters who don't have any special abilities but must climb on eachother to succed and specific ones are required to hit matching color switches.  Some levels provide special blocks which let you give one of the characters a special ability temporarily.  Levels are scored by collecting additional hearts, and a perfect score requires no deaths as well as collecting all the hearts on a given level.  I'm assuming there's some sort of special ending for perfecting all levels but I'm not sure I have it in me.
I don't think I've ever played such a disorienting game, and I mean that in a good way.  It's a unique twist on what would otherwise be a pretty simple puzzle game and it works well.  Don't let the cutesy graphics fool you, the game makes you work for your perfect scores, though strangely neither that nor finishing the game are required to obtain all the achievements.
While I recommend the game, I wish it was a bit longer and had a bit more complexity.  It's pretty limited by the colored switch blocks and one special power per character that only appear on specific levels.  If you enjoy a challenge, it's worth a look.

Seriously, though, Jalopy is a wonderful game, even in its Early Access stages.
[PROS]
+ "Semi-open world" (Drive freely during each leg of your trip)
+ Car maintenance system makes Jalopy unique compared to other open-world driving games
+ Radio has nice music
+ Fairly lightweight (I can run this on an i3 with an integrated GPU with 60 FPS)
+ Your Uncle tells you stories to keep you from getting bored while driving (until he got temporarily removed due to his bugginess, but dev says he'll be back by the full release)
+ Your Uncle's shirt also defies the physics behind light
+ Boxes with loot on the roadside provide steady income for you to pay for motel rooms, and...
+ Upgradeable car parts, with different types, color, and brands each providing their own perks at varying prices
+ Other surprises you can find along your trip (and there's probably going to be more as development continues)
+ AI traffic driving habits can be hilarious
+ Three different routes to choose from between each town, and the routes are randomly generated each time you play
+ Your car, its parts, and anything loaded in and on it is saved, allowing you to drive through the Eastern Bloc once again with the exact same car with the same wallet each time you press the "Drive Home" button
+ Impossible to become permanently stuck (Money flows in at a steady rate if you pick up the boxes and sell their contents. Else, you can just go back home and start again while bringing the stock car parts in the garage to sell later)
[CONS]
- "Semi-open world" (Routes generated are based off of premade "chunks", and they're put together to create each leg of the journey, so expect some scenery repeats)
- Object interaction can be kinda awkward sometimes (You can get your car stuck on the corner of a fence post somehow, among other quirks)
- Playing for an extended amount of time (~3 hours or more in one sitting) can cause visual and audio bugs to start appearing
- Vulnerable to cheating devices (Was able to give myself near infinite money with Cheat Engine; whether this is a significant con or not is up to you)
- Game doesn't teach you as much as it should (Probably because your Uncle doesn't ride with you for now, as he used to say dialogue that taught you certain things about the game before he was disabled. Although, helpful signage is increasingly prevalent)
- Handling is a bit awkward with keyboard controls
- No alternator (If your battery dies, you can't charge it with the engine, since there's no alternator. This could change by the time the full release is out, though, and replacement batteries are really cheap at the dealerships)
Overall, I find this game definitely enjoyable. We won't know for sure what the end product will be yet, but based on the progress the dev has made so far, the final game will very likely be a masterpiece. Bought this game for $8, and I have no regrets.

Bleed is a balls-out arcade style run and gun shooter that's honestly not a bad way to spend an evening. Nothing the game does is ever truly remarkable or original, but the near-flawless execution of fundamentals in enemy and level design definitely allow it to stand side by side with all those old-school games that it most admires.
Bleed adds its own little variations to the formula by allowing you to slow down time as well as a triple dash jump that can be continuously aimed. These mechanics, when used in conjunction with one another, feel satisfying and evoke the action-movie flair that the game wants to emulate so badly.
The game's only real barrier to entry may be the controls, which will take some getting used to. Trying to shoot enemies at precise angles while jumping around and slowing down time is quite the workout for your hands whether you're on a keyboard and mouse or just a gamepad. There's also some real balance issues when it comes to all the weapons you can unlock, as nothing ever feels quite as versatile as the twin pistols you start the game with, so upgrading doesn't feel quite as exciting as it should.
That said, Bleed does nearly everything right if you're on the market for a quick-fix action game. It's just the right length to feel arcadey, and you'll probably blast through it in an evening, but my time spent with it felt worth it.

Imagine mixing these things:
+ " Max Payne / Vanquish(xb/ps3)  " Slo Mo Bullet Time
+ " Contra " 2D arcade style with high speeds
+ " Geometry wars " tight controls and evasion
+ retro faith
= Bleed
When I first played this game I was so excited after only the first level that I rather repeated the first level on a higher difficulty because I never wanted this game to end. After 10 minutes I got used to the game pad controls and trust me, the controls are so tight that you can develop a very high level of skill in this game.
The game will force you to pay high attention to evading a huge amount of projectiles flying at you and by making good use of the rechargeable bullet time (slo mo moments) you will be amazed by what crazy situations you can get out of. This is where my heart starts to beat really fast and I just think "did I just... omg... holy sh*t... I don't even..." The Boss fight are very hard and fair and a challenge mode lets you play against most bosses quickly without playing the level (even 3 at a time, good for short sessions).  Story mode gives you unlimited continuous and lots of checkpoints. Arcade mode lets you play the whole game in one life and damn, it was probably the most satisfying moment in my gaming life to beat the final boss with my minimum health.
there are 7 levels and 4 difficulties with 12 unique boss fights.
Controls:
I do recommend to play this with an xbox360 Controller (native support).
Left stick to move. right stick to aim (and automatically shoot with infinite ammo)
LT (hold) activate slo mo. RT jump + dash up to 3 times per jump in any direction.
with dashes and slo mo you can wiggle your way out of many situations.
The Bad:
- Local multi player is not awesome but it makes the game harder since both drain the same slo mo time and the camera only follows one person. I guess it was experimental.
- Also the story is just there to justify the scenes. Don't expect too much there.
- Semi Automatic weapons are not good for the game pad. This could be fixed by a laser pointer (do it plz)
- It is short, but considering that this is a one man dev team game for 5 bucks it is still awesome.
If you like the above mentioned games, then you can be sure that bleed will give you a nice gameplay experience.

is an arcade game. You control a space ship and need to collect as many white orbs as you can before the timer runs out. Meanwhile, a bunch of asteroids are thrown your way. To help you collect orbs while dodging the asteroids, your ship has three 'skills' (special functions). You can:
At the end of each level you completed successfully, which means you collected a minimum amount of orbs before time ran out and managed to keep your ship in one piece, you get a score. A better score means more points to spend in a 'skill tree'. Here you can increase the duration of your ship's special functions and reduce their cooldown time. Every time you get a very good score, you unlock a new type of space ship that you can fly. Better ships reduce the cooldown time of your ships special functions a bit.
Every 5 levels, you get served a 'boss level'. In those levels you're up against a bigger space ship that shoots wave after wave of bullets you need to dodge. If you manage to keep your ship in one piece until the timer runs out, the bigger ship is destroyed and you win.

TL;DR: MPQ is a mediocre bejwelled style clone with addictive team oriented combat mechanics. The game is a harsh grind if you want to play seriously and very difficult if you desire to play it freemium. Play at your own peril!
*2017 Edit: Almost prophetically much of what I've complained about in this past review has been addressed over the last couple years of the game's existence. The addition of the champion system for max level heroes gives you the illusion of usefulness for the endless streams of duplicate covers you will get from your hard earned tokens. Similarly, the addition of command points gives you the illusion of being able to steer the titanic sized ship known as RNG instead of strictly using character tokens. These two solutions are fairly successful, I've never felt more in command of my roster which has grown exponentially. Whereas before it felt hopeless, now there is a semblance of being able to strategically construct my teams. I finally feel like I have a toe-hold and I've been able to begin the ascent to end-game and high level play. The new bottleneck for freemium players comes in the form of roster size. It seems like every month we get new characters which shuffle up the meta, an ostensibly great thing! The downside is that you want to keep everyone you get your hands on which is impossible. You're forced to make those hard and fast decisions of who to keep and who to let go and it can be tragic when you make the wrong choices so be sure to do your research!*
I really enjoy waiting for an hour between rounds while my characters heal... It's bearable at the start when it takes a couple minutes and you can play a few rounds, but it gets steadily worse. The difficulty curve is sharp after the introduction missions, that factor combined with the RNG bejeweled style board means that you'll be watching your heal timer a lot after a failed mission. The demand for cash from D3 publisher is inescapable if you actually want to play the game at any level of efficiency you might need to throw cash at this game.
The game gets a plus for having fun game play mixed with Marvel characters, but there are just too many drawbacks to make this game worth recommending. There is a loose RPG system in which you level up characters by collecting comic books, but it's marred by the fact that it too is RNG based (unless you use money).  Some iconic characters are given to you at the start of the game, but everything you get afterwards is all random and the majority of heroes I've received thus far are terrible or useless. You need to continually advance in the game if you desire better rewards, but any impression of success is stymied when you get your seventh 'Hawk-Eye' in a row or some equally as rage worthy hero thanks to the RNG rewards. This game would be much better if there was a way to slowly work towards a hero comic that compliments your roster, one that you can chose and grind towards. Success would feel much better and the grind would be worth the effort if you could finally piece together your Marvel Dream Team and smite some foes with righteous fury. Instead you're forced to use valuable experience, recruitment tokens, and gold to expand your roster never knowing who you're going to get. I've got a 5/5/- black widow and I just keep getting her comic books, it's driving me insane...
The gameplay is a bit stiff in comparison to previous iterations of the PQ franchise and some attack animations are slow and repetitive. The graphics aren't anything to write home about and everything just feels slow. This game is a step backwards in almost every area and far too frustrating to be worth time or money. Just get Puzzle Quest 2 and enjoy that game, this debacle doesn't do the franchise justice and is a blemish on an otherwise amazing series of games.

Control 1 survivor into 1 location in a night to gather ressources. This can be harmless and therefore purely investigating or with combat/stealth involved. You make choices regarding theft, killing, what to gather and what ressources to leave behind (maybe for the next night?).
Combat isnt easy and unforgiving. Dead means dead.
On occasion you have the possibility to trade and to interact with neighbours (is helping them worth the risk?).
And foremost see how the survivors react to your choices - does stealing from others make them sad? Do they care about that kill?  What about their needs for meds, food or maybe cigarettes ? A very immersive, sometimes emotional but rewarding gaming experience. I enjoyed the game even when I failed (and all died). Which I normally dont.

This lighthearted game aims to be more social and relaxing and it comes at the cost of complex combat and gameplay.
You can almost ALL combat or all of the housing/villager aspects of the game if you so choose. You are only forced into doing the first quest which is killing four weak goblin mobs so you can access the main world of the game. The vast amount of the talkative players can be found in the "World Chat" tab on your chat window and you can easily talk with anyone who's online for help (the game is naturally relaxing so the players are calm and friendly). This essentially summarizes the game, BUT if you want to be able to play the mobile version AND the PC version on the same account DO NOT play on steam. You are unable to use your steam account to play the mobile version for contract/legal reasons.
What the game does:
>Simple combat
>Easily able to interact with friendly community
>Relaxing villager skills and being able to be part of a village
>Cartoon-like world with no rush or pressure
>Able to train all villager skills as much as you want
>Various events (like the Spooky Town event going on now that allows players of ANY combat level to participate in a boss battle where any number of people can help and receive rewards)
>Mobile version for NON-STEAM accounts
What the game doesn't do:
>PvP
>Gameplay beyond cast a few spells or do repetitive clicking to grow/collect materials and make potions or gear
>Allow fast travel between zones without paying for an optional subscription (that only boosts leveling speed, inventory slots, you know)
This game serves well for people not looking for an intense experience and who just want to sit back and grind out a few crafting/agricultural skills (without worrying about which methods are most efficient like in other click-grind games) or just talking and interacting with a welcoming community.

Well, I've put in a few hours on this now, so thought I'd commit a few words here to give my impressions.
What we have here is not a traditional space simulator. There is no three-axis movement by your own vessels, instead you move along the "galactic plane", giving the whole thing a very classic space opera feel. This is accentuated by the choice of graphic and audio design. The bulky ship designs echo babylon 5 and the modern take on Battlestar Galactica, whilst the gorgeous space-scapes and lighting effects feel like direct descendants of Babylon 5 and the Star Trek movies.
The choice of combat along a single plane actually works quite well, giving the battles a naval feel that echoes that of the earlier Star Trek movies.
And then there's the music, a forlorn, western vibe carrying throughout that echoes Firefly as much as it does Red Dead Redemption. All in all, the sense of immersion off these factors alone is fantastic, so how does it play?
Very well, if truth be told. As is so often the case, there is a plot to be followed and plenty of side-objectives to keep a player occupied. These can be straight mining or trading, or can be more comabatative, by taking on various missions or engaging in a bit of bounty hunting (or piracy, if that's your thing).
There's plenty of scope when it comes to upgrading your ships and you'll be doing this a lot. At the end of the day, it is possible to develop effective strategies that will help you take down somewhat more impressive vessels in combat, but there's a limit to this and you will want bigger ships to take down your bigger objectives.
The 2D style of combat won't suit everyone, especially not those who are used to barreling through three-axis engagements from other games, but for capital ship combat I feel it works quite well and it still allows for engaging battles. to succeed will require an amount of grinding, but rarely have I enjoyed the grind as much as I do here.
Frankly, this has risen to occupy the top-cluster of my Steam purchases and I can see myself dipping in and out of this for some time to come.

A few things to note first, I am an extremely old school mmo player, I started with Ultima Online and played various graphical muds before then, I also played old text based muds like Achaea and before then I played bbs door games like Usurper and LORD. Villagers and Heroes released on Steam just over two years ago, it was a semi-unique title with some really fun concepts that definitely piqued my interest, the gathering system was fairly in depth for the type of game it was and the crafting was pretty standard but well done.  The biggest flaw the game had was the energy system that was renamed 'Vim'.  About a year ago the developers listened to the playerbase and removed the system though, which really means a lot.  The idea that you have developers who can improve their game over time without making the older playerbase quit is a pretty huge feat.
One of the biggest advantages Villagers and Heroes has is the developer is an industry veteran, he used to own the company Dynamix making games like Stellar 7 way back in the 80s.  One of my favourite flight sims, Red Baron, was made by him as well.  Villagers and Heroes is also not the original name either, this game used to be a browser game called A Mystical Land, so the idea that he's really kept this title alive by bringing it to new platforms like Steam means he's willing to keep up with the times and make sure this title never dies.
Two years ago when this game released on Steam the new playerbase from Steam made a ton of suggestions and the developer actually listened and improved the game, he removed a lot of the original features that made players feel like it was pay to win because he knows that if you are happy with his title you'll spend money on it anyways, trying to milk players for money is not the way to go.
On October 25th (in three days from now) this game will be released worldwide on Android devices (it's currently avaiable in some areas but not all) which really should prove this is a team that is keeping up with the times.  Sadly you cannot use your Steam account on Android (since an account created with Steam is bound to an agreement with Valve) but this game is now cross-platform to mobile devices and when it shows up on the Play store for NA you will see a huge influx of players.
At the moment there are only a few games that are cross-platform between mobile and PC and I do beleive there are only two on Steam, AdventureQuest 3D and this game, so there isn't much competition in this market.  Albion Online is probably the best cross-platform game right now but it is primarily focused around PvP while Villagers and Heroes is focused solely on PvE.  AdventureQuest 3D is a new title, it doesn't have a lot of content, the crafting is clunky and it has absolutely no gathering mechanics as of yet.  Player owned housing and guild terratories exist in VnH, they do not exist in AQ3D yet.  The maps in AQ3D are also quite small and really doesn't feel as open-world as VnH feels.
With all this being sad though, VnH isn't going to be like World of Warcraft, it's a far more casual style mmo and the mechanics are fairly simple, but it still has plenty of depth to keep a more hardcore gamer like myself interested.
If you check out the title on steamcharts (
) you will notice that it had 2,898 peak players on steam launch and still retained 555 peak concurrent users after 1 month, that's about a 20% retention rate, keep in mind though that the majority of players play using the website client and won't be tracked on steamcharts.  After three months it still had 431 peak concurrent users, which is a really nice retention rate for a F2P title on steam.  After one year (April 2015) it had 163 peak concurrent users which isn't amazing but you'll notice this number actually increased when they revamped the game and removed a few negative features like Vim.
I really can't stress enough though that the majority of players use the official website client so they aren't tracked by steamcharts sadly, so just look at these figures as a general guideline of the health of the game.  The fact that the playerbase on steam has slowly been increasing over the last few months should be a good indicator of the current health of the game leading up to the worldwide mobile release.
If you are looking for a simple game that has guild territory, player own housing, farming, ranching, a good selection of gathering and crafting skills as well as a combat and progression system that is more focused on boss kills over grinding small mobs then you should really look at this title.  If you have children (or in my case a girlfriend) who you would like to play with but you do not have multiple computers then you should take a look at this title.  If you want to play this title on PC and then switch to your android tablet or phone while your out of the house then take a look at this title. It's a very niche title and you will either love or hate it so you might as well give it a shot.

As a fan of games like Freelancer, Endless Space and other space genre games that allow a broad range of freedom, it's been a bit of a dry spell.  Though I am not completely done with the main story line, I am pleased to report - the drought has ended as Rebel Space comes - guns blazing - onto the scene.  And it supports and runs nicely on OSX? Nice.
The game has style, and the storyline evolves really nicely - it gets you into the action, and moves you along at a pace that feels natural.  You don't start out feeling like a newb, but you definitely do get a sense that you are benefitting directly from your experiences as a ship captain in a galaxy full of character and adventure.
Be patient though.  Don't be discouraged if you run into early challenges or even get blown away a couple times.  The game elegantly saves every time you visit a station - and I recommend you do so frequently as new challenges to your ability as a pilot await beyond each new jumpgate.
The graphics and interfaces are acceptable - and I mean that in a very good way.  While they don't introduce any new ground to the space genre, the UI, controls and navigation nonetheless quickly become muscle memory driven, allowing you to focus on piloting your ship.    At first, I thought the 2D plane and forced third person view would render the game arcade-like, and limit strategy and tactics, but frankly, these guys have done an amazing job and tbh, I didn't even realize the combat plane was 2d.
In short, Rebel Space is the old school, choose your own path space game we've been missing for years, and this reviewer hopes the folks at Double Damage continue to evolve this great new franchise.

Over the last few hours of playing this game I have seesaw-ed over if this game is worth buying and putting hours into, and to that I have to say no. Now the reasons behind that are not so clear, I have been playing racing games on PC for at least 15+ years and this one game stands out in its mediocrity.
The physics for many cars are decent enough but drifting is over used and on some cars leads to out right loss of control, also at least in my experience using the handbrake is ill-advised. Unless you drive very carefully you can expect to hit the wall often usually due to the fact that if you brake you drift and if you drift you are not bleeding speed fast enough thus sending you off of your line and into the wall.
I can say that some of my impacts were actually quite entertaining from various spin outs only to face the right direction to my favorite 100ft+ barrel roll and landing on all 4 wheels will little loss of speed, in true James Bond style.
With the nuts and bolts of the cars there is no customization beyond the paint job which will leave anyone more used to the last handful of Need for Speed games of the last 10 years with a sense of "Why bother?". With no upgrades or even basic tuning you loose the sense of accomplishment of pushing your old Mach 1 Mustang to the limit to beat out the newest BMW M3's though perfect knowledge of both tuning your car to the track and driving style.
Now so far in this review I have bashed the game fairly hard in all the same places that many reviews here do, but there are a few things that this game has that I can only wish could be used in other games and other things that the game just plain does well.
The idea of building bit by bit a fanbase and bouncing from sponsor to sponsor as they demand things that you know won't happen is very appealing and I believe adds a LOT to the emersion of the game. The other side of this is you put in your name and see IT in the cutscenes and hear the nickname that you selected instead of hearing "Ryan Cooper" a billion times, it really is refreshing to hear and again lends greater emersion of the driver.
Another thing often overlooked is how the menus behave especially in the middle of the race. What I am talking about is probably the best done race restart sequence I have ever seen. In most games you hit Esc>Restart>*Scroll up/down*>Restart/Yes and then it restarts the race.
Now having to do this process everytime you need to restart a close race because you caught the last turn wrong or the like that extra step of scolling and often the extra second or two of time needed to load that menu even on a powerful computer, can mean the difference between quiting the game for a while or pushing through one more time.
Grid 2 you hit restart and even before the menu is fully loaded you hit restart again and it restarts the race in a fraction of the time of other titles.
The above is really all that can be squeezed out of this game because its not bad and it is NOT an ugly game but it is lacking in the places that these games need most. If this game where $0.99 to no more than $4.99 on the upper most end then I would consider buying the game maybe.

Seriously, though, Jalopy is a wonderful game, even in its Early Access stages.
[PROS]
+ "Semi-open world" (Drive freely during each leg of your trip)
+ Car maintenance system makes Jalopy unique compared to other open-world driving games
+ Radio has nice music
+ Fairly lightweight (I can run this on an i3 with an integrated GPU with 60 FPS)
+ Your Uncle tells you stories to keep you from getting bored while driving (until he got temporarily removed due to his bugginess, but dev says he'll be back by the full release)
+ Your Uncle's shirt also defies the physics behind light
+ Boxes with loot on the roadside provide steady income for you to pay for motel rooms, and...
+ Upgradeable car parts, with different types, color, and brands each providing their own perks at varying prices
+ Other surprises you can find along your trip (and there's probably going to be more as development continues)
+ AI traffic driving habits can be hilarious
+ Three different routes to choose from between each town, and the routes are randomly generated each time you play
+ Your car, its parts, and anything loaded in and on it is saved, allowing you to drive through the Eastern Bloc once again with the exact same car with the same wallet each time you press the "Drive Home" button
+ Impossible to become permanently stuck (Money flows in at a steady rate if you pick up the boxes and sell their contents. Else, you can just go back home and start again while bringing the stock car parts in the garage to sell later)
[CONS]
- "Semi-open world" (Routes generated are based off of premade "chunks", and they're put together to create each leg of the journey, so expect some scenery repeats)
- Object interaction can be kinda awkward sometimes (You can get your car stuck on the corner of a fence post somehow, among other quirks)
- Playing for an extended amount of time (~3 hours or more in one sitting) can cause visual and audio bugs to start appearing
- Vulnerable to cheating devices (Was able to give myself near infinite money with Cheat Engine; whether this is a significant con or not is up to you)
- Game doesn't teach you as much as it should (Probably because your Uncle doesn't ride with you for now, as he used to say dialogue that taught you certain things about the game before he was disabled. Although, helpful signage is increasingly prevalent)
- Handling is a bit awkward with keyboard controls
- No alternator (If your battery dies, you can't charge it with the engine, since there's no alternator. This could change by the time the full release is out, though, and replacement batteries are really cheap at the dealerships)
Overall, I find this game definitely enjoyable. We won't know for sure what the end product will be yet, but based on the progress the dev has made so far, the final game will very likely be a masterpiece. Bought this game for $8, and I have no regrets.

Although I’m usually not a fan of pixel graphics on anything other than arcade style games, I found the art and sound effects of Where is my Heart? very pleasing. The atmosphere the game works to create is very fitting of three little tree spirits on an adventure. The exact story of that adventure is a little hazy as the game tries to tell it wordlessly through the first and last levels and you’d learn more by just reading the steam page description, but the mood is there. Most of my complaints are around the special abilities of the characters. Rainbow spirit if often not as responsive as I’d like to buttons relating to his special abilities and the requirement to jump before rotating yourself out of the puzzle to drop into a new screen sometimes moves you into another screen and your rotation happens from that place instead. Bat king’s ability to find hidden ground to stand on is only useful for him but somehow the hidden holes he finds the others can walk into. Of course, if they stop inside the hole and bat king moves away they’ll phase into solid matter and die. All that said, the game stuck to its cute and childish roots with random amusing sayings from the characters between levels and a lot of effort was put into the puzzles to really utilize all the spirits’ skills and the player’s ability to mentally rearrange the fragmented screens. Clever use of background patterns, made more clear by the pixel graphics, provided ample clues as to how the pieces of the level were actually arranged relative to each other. Overall the game was a cute and short with puzzles that stretch the player’s visualization abilities.

Grid Autosport is very similar to Grid 1 in terms of racing.  Maybe a little less arcady than the first one.  It gives buyers new cars, tracks, and a chance to play on steam servers instead of Tunngle or something.   However, unless you have some friends to play with, you're going to have a tough time even finding a custom game (which is further limited to whether the host/player trying to join have the dlc being used).  I personally like the campaign in the first one more -- I never wound up beating this one.  I like the tracks and the multiplayer mechanics more than Grid 2 though -- which was overall more arcady  (imagine Grid 1 mixed with Hot Pursuit 2).   The corner cutting mechanic is still unpredictable, but better than Grid 2.  I'd reccomend this game only to those who have some friends wanting to race  (lack of player base).    If you're looking for a solo racing game, Grid 1 is just as good of a buy.  The only feature I occasionally play on this game is the weekly racenet challenges.

If you like to complete your games at 100%, this game is not for you.
In each level you have to collect a certain amount of hearts, using 3 characters, but, due to how the game is designed, sometimes you'll end up dying because of something you did not see. If that happens, you lose a heart and respawn, and that, if you are compulsive as I am, means you
restart the level (because you'll only get 9 hearts out of 10, for example). But the game does not have a level restart button, so you have to go out to the menu and choose again the same level. And to make things worse, when you start a level you have to wait for the 3 characters to come in, and they sure take their time to do so.
In conclusion, if you find yourself wanting to restart a level over and over, the game will annoy you really quickly.

A one of a kind game. A marvellous job is done here at making a fine mèlange of mid 17th century piracy, a range of and complex puzzles, and the aspect of multiplayer online gaming together to make Puzzle Pirates... With some serious orientation to PvP naval combat on the Dark Seas!
Totalling a whopping 22 puzzling skills, 11 of those skills being piracy skills; puzzles that are performed whilst on a ship; 5 carousing skills, puzzles and card games that one can indulge in at the inn; and 6 crafting skills, puzzles that are performed at a place of work on land – each and every puzzle within Puzzle Pirates has a unique kick to it, and no two puzzles feel comparable.
A minority of games can make you, the player, indulge in a gratifying sensation of accomplishment when reach a goal or an achievement. Progression in Puzzle Pirates feels like a genuine accomplishment on your side, and that you are truthfully making progress that betters yourself. You’ll start off with the standing of ‘able’ in all puzzling skills, and once you understand the fundamentals about a certain puzzle, it’s all about how you, the player, attack the puzzle to achieve a greater score to be able to climb the standing ladder. With a total of 9 standings ranging from ‘able’, the lowest standing possible, to ‘ultimate’, the highest standing achievement, and while there’s an in-game accolade, a trophy, for attaining the ultimate standing in a certain puzzle, it’s all about that inner feeling that YOU are doing a damn good job of your duty station or shoppe job.
Puzzle Pirates is definitely a game that’s pro-community heavy. Commanding officers of ships need other pirates to work at duty stations to keep the ship operating smoothly, shoppe managers need employees to work and process goods, and crews need to have each other’s backs in this PvP-oriented Puzzle Pirates Ocean. With the in-game economy being 99% player-driven, as simple as it appears, it’s easy to gloss over the fact that Puzzle Pirates is an unexpectedly comprehensive game, from a weaving stall being able to weave hemp into cloth then selling the cloth to a tailoring shoppe only for them to stitch an article of clothing for a pirate to wear; or smithing iron and wood into cannonballs to sell to a player owned ship ready to engage in naval warfare. If the commanding officers can’t replenish their ships with the required stock from the islands distillery or smithies, there can’t be any feasible navy battles to engage in. If there’s no apothecary to concoct dyes or enamel, there can’t be any coloured bolts of cloth woven at weaveries, or any enamel to paint onto swords. Everybody would just be using... Sticks to poke each other during frays. ALL GLORY TO THE STICK.
Regardless if you’re into plundering NPC (Also known as Non-Player Pirate; NPP) brigands and barbarians, engaging in PvP naval combat by engaging other player vessels, sitting at an apothecary and mixing up some dye, running your own shoppe, or just playing a few rounds of Hearts, there’s definitely going to be a place for you that you will enjoy about the Dark Seas of Puzzle Pirates.
There’s so much more to Puzzle Pirates than just puzzling. There’s flag politics, (hopefully soon to be (Because they’re currently disabled)) blockades, construction, sea monsters to battle... Can’t fit it all in this review.
But I’ll tell you that I really hate rigging. A lot. As much as I am terrible at writing reviews.
Play this game, you nerd. It’s great. You won’t regret it.

This is a short game that you can easily beat in a few hours. If you're going for Diamond on every level you'll be in for some ride, though... A ride that's not really worth it. The boss fights (on Diamond) are frustratingly hard, and not for the right reasons. In order to win, you need to combine skilled gameplay (good) with memorization (not that great) and some luck (bad). This would not have been so bad if the controls were better, but they are not suited for precise maneuvering. Many good bullet hell games will let you slow down your movement by holding a button, but ShipLord doesn't let you to that, which means that you'll crash into projectiles that should've been easy to dodge.
A lot of the time I felt like I died not because of error I made but because of flaws in the game. Sometimes astroid formations are nearly impossible to dodge, and sometimes astroids spawn just as you pick up a point at the edge of the screen. Oh, and points sometimes spawn inside of astroids, making them hard to spot until it's too late. If you're unlucky they will spawn at the opposite side of the screen, thus not giving you enough time to pick them up unless you use "Energy Collector".
The graphics, story, and voice acting are all below average, and there are a few grammar and spelling mistakes in the game. The game would've been better if it were in 2D and it would've been better without any story or voice acting, though that's a minor complaint.
I give this game a 6 or a 7 out of 10. It is not entirely without merit, but there are so many better games out there, and unless you really like the genre I recommend you skip it. I had some fun with it, despite how frustrating it could be at times. It might be worth picking up on a game, but it's a very unpolished game that has a lot of flaws.

When I first got this, I thought it was a Bullet Hell Asteroids clone where I had to collect things and could upgrade my spaceship along the way. However, upon playing I was disappointed and here is why:
Pros:
♦ Decent Graphics for what it is (Not phenomenal, but decent enough for the indie game it is)
♦ Has amazing voiceovers (Not the best voice actors, but it still has voiceovers unlike some other games which is a major positive)
♦ Great Concept
♦ Easy Steam Achievements for just playing the game (If you can get through the whole game, the achievements are gotten for just beating the games)
♦ Trading Cards
♦ Controls are changeable (This is good as you can assign any control to any button)
♦ Sound and Music fitted the genre (Seemed decent enough for the game)
♦ Devs seem nice (From what I've talked to them)
Cons:
♦ Tagged as “Bullet Hell” when your ship can’t even shoot (This is terrible as your ship can’t even shoot and the only time you face bullets are against a boss and there is only three of them)
♦ Poor hitbox (The radius at which you can get hit by anything seems way off)
♦ Background of levels interferes with the actual game (Numerous times I thought background asteroids were actually part of what I had to dodge)
♦ Played the first four levels and got a score of 112-113 in each level. (I found this weird because from level 1 I was maxing the “Decrease energy orb spawn time” and the “Decrease energy orb collection time”.  Therefore, I should have been able to collect more orbs as I progressed, not the same amount. This makes me think those two upgrades don’t work)
♦ Game seems more luck than skill based (This is because the asteroids spawn in randomly and depending on where they spawn, depends on if you can collect the energy orbs)
♦ Game is very repetitive (Nothing seems to change except the bosses, every level has the same timer, virtually the same asteroids and difficulty doesn’t seem to increase or work properly due to being RNG)
♦ Difficulty is a problem (I say this as it seems to make the game scale in difficulty the Devs have just increased the size of the asteroids. This means due to the randomness the asteroids spawn in, sometimes it's impossible to dodge them if numerous big asteroids fly towards you when your shield isn't up)
♦ Ship Cooldown reduction when you unlock new ships doesn’t seem to do anything (I’ve got the 4% cooldown reduction ship and I could collect the same amount of energy orbs in the time it took my shield to cooldown, as I could with the 0% cooldown reduction ship)
♦ No hotkey to restart a level (This is annoying as you have to press Escape to bring up the Pause Menu to be able restart the game, you should be able to restart without needing to bring up  the Pause Menu)
♦ When you have to pause the game you have to use the mouse to resume (This is bad because when you click to resume, wherever your mouse pointer is your ship will automatically fly there causing you to hit whatever is there. This can easily get you killed)
Overall, due to the poor hitbox, repetitiveness, upgrades seeming like they’re not working, the difficulty issue, the amount of luck over skill needed and the fact that there are way more cons than pros, I therefore can’t recommend this game unless major improvements are made.

Magic Duels Origin started off on an extremely bad foot. Game breaking crashes, limited card selection, and a bad quest system that only worked half the time. Recently however the game has seen some improvement, keyword some. The quest system is varied but when you receive the quests still seems to be sporadic.With five different card sets you can make halfway decent and varied decks. Overall I enjoy it for that Magic the Gathering itch and if you are wanting to play Magic for free or to see if Magic is the card game for you and don't mind dealing with some occasional problems then go ahead and give this a try.
Pros
Free to Play Magic!
Very centered around learning how to play Magic so great for beginners.
Quest system and getting gold is easy enough to get at least a pack a day and you can spend real money to get more packs as well.
You can get gold without ever having to play another person.
Two-Headed Giant format is available and always a fun alternative option of playing magic, and you can earn gold this way as well.
Cons
Crashes often and there seems to be a very slow response time by the devs to fix problems.
Limits cards based on rarity(3 uncommons, 2 rares, 1 mythic) so making a real life deck isn't possible more often than not.
While it's advertised that there are hundreds of different AI opponents it tends to feels like 1 deck with slight variations and they seem to get the exact cards each game. I have once played a white green deck retrying 4 different times and 3 of the 4 times they got the exact same rare card(keep in mind you can only have 2 in a 60 deck). This happens so often that either I am the unluckiest man alive or it's coded to rig the game for the ai to have "preferred" cards in their hand. Update: I have noticed 2 distinct decks for the ai now! One is a hyper agressive red deck(always fun to play against /sarcasm) and then the tri color, mish mash that I mentioned before.

Since there are sooooo many bad reviews, just because the people wanted a 1:1 copy of Dungeon Keeper, I decided to write a fair review.
This game is far from being bad! Sure it is not a 1:1 Dungeon Keeper Clone, but it doesn't even try to be a direct copy of Westwoods Old School classic. It is more a combination of Dungeon Keeper and Warcraft. The Dungeon building phases are fun, but after you get the hang out of it, they get pretty fast too easy. The battles on the overworld are fun, too. But only if you like games like Warcraft with a strict amount of units. Both placed in one game is a good combination and gives this game a nice touch. I liked the campaign very much, sure it was too short for such a game, but still it was definitely fun!
But don't get me wrong. There were some points in the game, that really made me angry. Like the missing managment of the Snubs (Imps). If you had a trap and the entrance the little ones immediately run there just to repair it. Which caused a  big problem, because there were still enemies. The snubs ran there, dropped the traps in their hands and run away. Since they didn't reach their position new snubs started to run there. After a couple of seconds the complete amount of snubs tried to reach this one trap at the entrance. None of them was working on gold mining or any other job, that had to be done. That was pretty annoying.
Still this game is far from being bad! So I decided to give it a positiv thumbs up and you should, too. But be aware...it is NOT a 1:1 copy of Dungeon Keeper!

So what is Where is my Heart?  Is it a platformer?  Is it a puzzle game?  Well, it's a little of both.  Okay okay, so that was a generic opening, but it is what it is.  Where is my Heart is unique among puzzle platformers in that the levels are broken-up into fragments.  As the player explores to the edge of one segment, they must watch the rest of the screen to see which segment the character will be navigating next.  It's a little bit of spice that makes what would otherwise be a bland and straight-forward platforming game into a puzzle, almost in the literal sense as the player is required to look at a jumble of pieces, and try to make-out the greater whole.
Story-wise, I couldn't tell you what's going on.  I remember reading a quick summary on the store page, but the game itself doesn't make much mention of it, and that's fine.  During the game, the player controls one of three members of a monster family.  One looking like a Domo wannabe, one orange thing, and a vampire, because of course there's going to be a vampire.  The player must toggle between them to navigate the levels; using them as stepping stones to reach higher ledges, or unlocking character-specific locks that reveal a passage elsewhere on the level, and even forming a sort of totem to turn the top member into a special spirit beast.
Yes, each member can turn into a special spirit beast, and it's often required to do-so in order to complete the level.  The brown monster turns into a forest spirit that can double-jump, allowing him to reach higher platforms; meanwhile the other two members of the family turn into spirits so that he can take them with him.  This allows the player to reach areas that would otherwise require someone to be left behind after being used as a stepping stone without needing to leave anyone behind.  The orange monster turns into a rainbow spirit that lets you rotate the segments while she remains in the same spot on the screen, thus allowing her to skip around the stage (though it has its risks if the player tries to "teleport" into solid ground, or stays in a space without a segment).  Finally, the gray monster (the vampire) turns into a bat spirit that can see hidden passages and platforms that he can use so that the other two can use him as a stepping stone.
The levels are short, but sweet.  It's a case of quality over quantity, allowing the player to focus on a smaller playing field while trying to figure out how to navigate the heroes to the end goal.  Every level has two goals.  The first is to simply get each hero to the end goal, and the second goal is to collect all hearts without letting anyone die.  The first goal is oftentimes simple enough, where some of the levels will really stretch the player's mind to figure out where that heart with very little context clues in its tiny segment might be hiding in what would otherwise be plain sight if the level wasn't broken-up into scattered segments.  The only real hassle is that once the path to the end goal has been opened up, it can feel like a bit of a chore having to manually walk the other two characters over there to finish the level.  Some levels require the other characters to take a new path, but for most levels it's just selecting the next character to walk the same path three times.
What few faults this game has are out-weighed by it's over-all charm, so I can definitely recommend this game to anyone looking for a good puzzle/platformer.

Definitely recommend this game.
It's filled with cute 8-bit music, lovable characters and an easy to follow storyline.
However, the game is rather difficult as the levels go on. As well as the challenge they have throughout this game, I've found out that every time you die, your way out (a tree) eats black hearts, which of course are seen as a bad thing. Eventually the tree becomes miserable, though I haven't gotten so far as to find out what happens when they ingest too many corrupt pumping pixels.
A little later in the game, you're able to add all of your little characters together to create one with special powers. There are specific boxes that you can jump on in different levels. With these boxes, your characters must jump on each other as a tower and make sure a certain colour is on top; (The game itself will guide you with this).
The boxes that I've encountered so far are pretty neat. One of them requires the orange character to be on top. This turns him/her into a flying white cube angel that can rotate the map, but will deteriorate if left outside of it for too long.
The other box, I'll leave you to figure it out.
All in all, I really enjoy this game, even as someone who usually isn't into these sort of styles. It opened me up and did NOT have me wondering where my heart is! :-)

Im glad I decided to not buy this back in 2011 when it first came out. Single player is under 5 hours long. The sound is a bit buggy and leaves a lot to be desired. I think one of the most annoying things has been the fact you have to press E to get up a ladder? Who even does that? The gunplay is a cut and paste of Call of Duty, right down to the little "X" when you land a hit. I get this is a now almost 8 year old title and CoD was huge when this was made, but come on guys? Really? The shooting isn't quite as polished as it should be. Movement feels sluggish and labored.
Graphics wise, this is about par for the course in 2011. The textures are okay, but the overall scheme of things feels very bland, and repetitive. While the enemies were noticable, there were times it was hard to see them. The urban landscape was a nice touch. I also did like the fact that it did not take much to kill you, making it feel like you really needed to play more tactically than other titles of the same genre.
THQ did release a couple more of these, so I am hoping they fixed some of the minor gripes with this. This would be a solid title if it wasn't for the glaring rip-off of the CoD series.
I do admit, I have not played the MP part, so this review should be take with a bit of salt. My only guess is the MP is pretty much what you would expect from any FPS title of the time.
Edit: I did get this free from the humblebundle deal going on right now. I love free games, but even free it was still pretty bad. The blatant cut and paste of CoD kinda killed it. A very solid racing game indeed. It comes highly recommended from me. Codemasters have been perfecting their racing games for many years and this one is perhaps the best, I think since TOCA 2. Brilliant car physics for both the open wheelers and the tin-tops. A great damage engine, the graphics are the best yet in the Grid series. If you like arcade style racing and or doing your car up with shiny decals and nos look elsewhere. This is a serious racing game. Not as serious as R Factor but it does suit someone that is a fan of motorsport and understands the sports subtleties. For me its a good thing, but for a NFS fan it might not be so. Although there is a nod to arcade racing with the 'tuner' and 'street' classes this Grid title also gives back more to the anoraks than previous incarnations.
Where the game is a real winner in the longevity stakes; is the online mode. I have had some dramatic and close races online with some serious game racing competition, you are able to run nose to tail and dice to the flag.
The AI are pretty good. Probably one of the best AI in a racing game although they are no match for myself of course they can fight back and hold their line. One of the things I find an issue with many racing games AI is that they are too tentative when attempting to overtake. Not shy in this game however!
The Grid series was for me a little pretentious in places. Especially Grid 2 where it seemed almost every car could only driven with an annoying arcade style drifting style. Not so here. Just like real racings its all about braking, taking the apex nicely and getting the power down fast out of the corner minimising wheelspin. You can even adjust the setup so this can be done smoother although that aspect is fairly simple this is surely a good thing to everyone except a car mechanic.
The handling on most codemasters racing games is very good. The rally style handling of the Colin Mcrae games really was spot on and they have always seemed to have a good grasp on that aspect of racing since. Where GTA and Forza often seem to suffer from box-like understeer or wild oversteer you can really get a nice feel for most of the vehicles in Grid. Realistic or not they are satisfying to use.
You will however get more than a hint of deja vu if you have bought the previous Grid games. This is more of an update of the previous incarnations than a new game. For me though for the price you cannot argue. The game bears the name of a popular motorsport magazine and herein lies the key difference in the Grid series that makes this one stand out. The racing is a sober and realistic (without being too realistic). They have stopped trying to copy Need For Speed and actually produced something reminiscent Codemasters great racing games of old. As a bit of a purist I wasn't sure about the rewind feature, although on reflection I think its actually quite handy. Especially in a long race against the computer cars (where you would have had to restart the race on older games).
There is a wide selection of cars and tracks on offer. I think this is where the game progressing from the earlier titles comes in handy, since much of the old content has simply been given a lick of paint whilst new machinery has been added on top of that. The tin tops and open wheelers both handle characteristic to their class. Such great tracks as Spa, Brands Hatch and Hockenheim are all beautifully rendered.
The damage engine much like previous Grid games is very satisfying. The only game that I recall that comes close to its level of intricacy is on of the recent GTA games. You can enjoy some epic and frightiningly realistic looking shunts. Here is also where improved technology in the visual department is beneficial. The sense of speed is more tangible than ever and when you do get it very wrong you thank your lucky stars its a game and you are not inside the roll-cage!
I am not a moaner and realise you don't always get what you want in life. But if I had to criticize this game I would probably say I would have liked a few more real permanent circuits (even if that meant less fictional street circuits.)  Also to complete career mode you have to total every class of racing in the game. Certain classes I like and certain ones not so much so they became somewhat of a chore. I also think the endurance class was quite interesting but they missed an opportunity to put in much longer truer enduro racing with pit-stops. Pit stops were one of the reasons TOCA 2 is one of my all-time favorite games.
Overall this is a game for race fans by race fans and they have done a tidy job.

I grew up in Yugoslavia and then in what was left of it - Serbia. My family's primary vehicle until last year was a Yugo. We used it for a total of 27 years.
Jalopy deals with a complicated and extremely depressing time of the Eastern bloc and Balkans. Having a car like a Laika wasn't about customization, it was about having a cheap car that broke down all the time and you had to create a Frankenstein monster by mixing and matching various off-brand or generic parts from other, better vehicles. Adding flaming decals to a cheap car was a clear example of the time: showing prestige on something cheap and pathetic, because that's all you could get.
Jalopy isn't a depressing game, but it's a very good timepiece. Travelling somewhere else felt nice, soothing, because you were surrounded by the beautiful vistas of the region. Going to a shop felt depressing because they were empty. You wonder why every gas station doesn't have spare tires, but that's what it was like - you were lucky to find basic things. The cities are cold, the motels are bare (and the toilet can't even flush), the border patrol sometimes takes ages to check your papers, making you wonder whether you did something wrong...
But in all of this, it does the gamey things of giving you loot in boxes left on the road, letting you find abandoned Laikas with spare parts, scrap yards with mini puzzles to solve and rare parts inside. It does this, because everything you do lets you make your Laika better, more reliable. Because something as silly as making a horrible car be less horrible was the type of absurd solace people found back then.
It's not about pimping a ride, making a silly car, surviving in the wilderness, or anything like that. It's about capturing a moment in time, the state of millions of people through gameplay of mundane activities.
If that's something you can appreciate and think you can enjoy, Jalopy is the game for you. I can't wait for the full release.
