Before anybody wonders about my Civilisation lineage, I have been playing the series since the original on the Amiga and so I have had to live through the good old phalanx beating a tank.
When you start the game you are presented with an introduction video that is well animated and narrated. This adequately gives the background of the game.
The menu is basically the same as in Civ 5 and so veterans should easily be able to navigate through the options.
When you start a new game is where the similarities between Beyond Earth and Civilisation V start to differ. As I like to tailor the games and have more choice in how I play I always choose to set-p the game and not to just start.
You have to choose a sponsor for your mission, each has a different bonus, there is a choice between 8 sponsors.
Once you have made that choice you move onto choosing what type of colonist you brought along. These again have different bonuses e.g. +2 science to each city or +4 energy etc, there are 5 choices for the colonist.
Next you choose the space craft that brought you here, again there are 5 to choose from with differing bonuses. These bonuses are for the immediate start of the game and are for when you arrive on the planet, from seeing the coast line to having a larger drop area for your fist city.
After that you choose the cargo you brought and finally you choose what planet to land on from a list of options which you can reload and it is just really the same as choosing what world type, as in continents, archipelago and the like.
You can further tailor your game by choosing the advanced set-up.
Once the world is loaded, you get to choose where your first city is located, unlike Civ 5 you are limited to a few tiles as you do not have a settler as such but a choice of where to land on, you get to build settler units later (called colonists). I find this a little strange and possibly there should be a wider choice as after all you were in orbit and so could just continue to orbit the world to find a better site to land on. The world looks the different from Civ 5 but also the same enough so that you can figure out what things are.
I find that the tech tree is slightly confusing as it is based upon a web pattern and not the linear left to right from Civ 5 and so at first glance it can be a little overwhelming. Hovering over each tech node and the associated unlocks give sufficient detail to allow you an understanding on what this node will do when researched.
Production is easy to work out as the buildings have well defined icons that show what they will provide and hovering over the buildings will give more information on the build cost and maintenance.
As turns progress you will receive quests, for instance I found a resource pod and a quest appeared that I had to find 3 resource pods, completing these quests give rewards and you even get to chose an outcome of the quest which gives different rewards depending on the choice.
The game has culture like in Civ 5 and when you reach a number of culture points you get to choose a virtue, these fall along the same lines as the social policies from Civ 5 but there are only 4 different trees to choose from which have 3 stages to each tree and contain multiple nodes per stage. These virtue trees give differing bonuses and when you unlock a number of nodes you gain additional bonuses. I would assign these as the poor cousin to the social policies as I find that they are not really expansive enough for me.
You have a smaller choice of units, but as the game does not cross the ages then technological advancements would not be as aggressive as in Civilisation and so the unit pool would be less.
You are able to upgrade your units when you reach different affinity levels, some upgrades are when you reach X number of levels but later upgrades are when you reach a specific level in a specific affinity.
These 4 different affinities are unlocked through the game and the bulk of them come from the technology that you research. For example your basic soldier can be upgraded to a brawler if you choose the harmony path, a sentinel via purity or a disciple via supremacy. These different upgrades grant different bonuses to the unit.
I have been annoyed by the diplomacy spamming from the other colonists requesting my resources, I have said no and that should be the end of it....maybe if I destroy them it will shut them up.
This game is different to Civ 5 but it is also similar enough so that you will be able to pick it up if you are a Civ veteran.
I do not feel that the game looks as good as Civ 5 as the colours are generally dull and some things are harder to distinguish, especially the unit damaging miasma when it is on grass hills.
I would like to say that this game is worth getting but, at the moment, I am not overly enjoying playing is. Beyond Earth has not captured me like Civ 5 had and still does as I do not feel the good old "one more turn" pulling at me.
Is it better than Civ 5?
Now that is the main question and I would have to say no. To me Civ 5 is still the best in the series to date.
For this I would not recommend this game.

Half-Life 2: Deathmatch is basically Half-Life 2 multiplayer, with custom made maps in Source SDK and a few members within the community still playing.
Now, this is the story all about how. Atratzu life got flipped-turned upside down. And I'd like to take a minute, just sit right there. I'll tell you how I became a red splat on the side of the wall.
Half-Life 2: Deathmatch suddenly appeared in my steam library, I believe it was recently added to a bundle that I've purchased (specifically, with my past purchase of Half-Life 2: Episode One). Half-Life 2: Deathmatch used to be a very large FPS community which started after the huge success of the Half-Life 2 series. But because Half-Life 2 is only single player, the community asked for a multiplayer competitive game, and valve delivered.
Half-Life 2: Deathmatch, controls EXACTLY like Half-Life 2. Which honestly I always thought I would be alright at a Half-Life multiplayer FPS, but it's been a long time since I played through all the Half-Life 2 games, so my skills were quite rusty.
You have the same weapons, but the maps/servers are customized. I joined and played a Free for all, and a team death match. There is still several active people playing the game, at the end of one game people were actually congratulating the person who got first!
I'm not sure if it's because so few play the game that they're all a tighter knit group, or I just found the one small patch in space time where people are still friendly, but it was nice to actually play a few rounds with some people who aren't screaming little kids swearing and speaking profanities they cannot comprehend.
 To be completely honest, I haven't been on a FPS craze for a long time, the game has aged the same way as Half-Life 2. If you ever wanted to play a multiplayer FPS of Half-Life 2 there are plenty of servers, many are empty, you could even figure out the technical know-how to set up your own server and own maps.
I actually probably have used source SDK more then Half-Life 2: Death Match. It's a shame to see a community shrink so much, but props to those of you who keep playing one of your favorite games, don't change and keep on shooting!

BioShock 2 is essentially more of the same from what you got in the first game, which isn't a bad thing at all, albeit this time with a different narrative and protagonist. In this game however, you play as Delta, one of the earliest Big Daddy prototypes on a mission to rescue his little sister, it features some familiar faces from the first game and it's set a few years after the events in the first game.  I think the story is really good for a sequel, and wasn't expecting to get engrossed into it as much as I was, but by the end of this game I wish there would have been more, but for what it's worth, it tells a great self-contained story.
The gameplay has also been changed up, in the sense that you can now use plasmids and guns at the same time, much like in BioShock Infinite, which I think makes the gameplay better than the first. The hacking system has also been changed up, and instead of being whisked away to some minigame, you now have to hack things in real time.
The environmental design in this game is still great, although since it's been a few years since the first game, there is more stuff like coral littered around Rapture, the water effects have always awed me. Although you do start to notice its age in certain regards, mostly when it comes to the textures, which can range from okay to pretty awful, but hopefully the remasters will remedy that.
Anyway, if you were a fan of the first one and want to get more of Rapture, or if you're a fan of shooters in general with a good story then I'd recommend this. You can usually find it on sale for relatively cheap.

Seriously, I can't handle the emotional and moral pitfalls this game forces you through. The choices you have to make to ensure your rag-tag group of survives lives just to see another day. But that just makes me want to play it even more so. Why? Rather than your typical, "Choice A is bad, choice B is good" scenario that most games present you, This War of Mine makes every scenario a moral grey area. Will you survive the honest way, trading and bartering goods between your neighbors, but putting extra pressure on your survivors to make sure they scavenge supplies or else risk trading away their own? Or do you decide to resort to thievery and even murder to get what you need, but in the process risk not only your survivors' physical health, but their mental well-being as well.
Truly a game that everyone should play at least once to experience the feeling of trying to keep a group of people together under extremely stessful circumstances, This War of Mine does an excellent job of providing a feeling of loss, hopelessness, and utter despair, yet at the same time, can provide a sense of accomplishment and camraderie that is hard to find in a lot of current games.

Solid gameplay and theme, but utimately it is a cash grab designed around forcing the user to pay money to avoid grinding some missions for rare curriencies and items.
You will be expected to play or grind for:
- The ability to recruit new heros to play with. You'll start with 3 (Iron Man, Storm and Black Widow) and you'll have one empty slot for a hero. After that you'll need to scronge up their pay currency to add an empty space to recruit any heros (including ones you earn that will expire and disappear if you don't get an empty space! Not to mention you'll earn recruit tokens which allow you to get characters for free, but not the empty space for free. If you don't have an empty space, they are WORTHLESS.
- Abilities and level ups. Character abilties are unlocked and leveled up after randomly earning comic book covers after missions. If you don't get the cover you need from a mission, you'll have to replay the SAME CONTENT to hope you earn it next time. And if you get 2 Hawkeye comics, but one is Classic Hawkeye and the other is Dark Avenger Hawkeye, those are two different characters and don't level up aside each other (not to mention they'll take up two character slots, which remember you're paying for!).
From what I saw, you'll grind up the pay currency by playing the semi-PVP battles. Much like the Marvel Facebook game, you'll fight AI-controlled player teams to place on a leaderboard for the shot at rewards. This isn't as much PVP as it is PVE where someone in the world happened to choose that team. Since this game allows people to gain a lot of power by paying money, the top spaces in the leaderboards (read: where you need to be for prizes) will be filled with 'wallet warriors': people who have amazing teams simply because they paid money. If you want to play this game and fork out minimal to zero cash, expect frustration. There ARE prizes for simply playing the "PVP", but you will need to devote a LOT of time to get the good items.
For example, winning a PVP match earns about 20-30 'Shield Points'. To get the pay currency for free, to unlock all the good stuff in the game without paying real money, you'll need to rack up ~1000 Shield Points. Enjoy the grind!
All in all, the Puzzle Quest mechanics are still solid and the Marvel theme never disappoints, but it is a pay-to-win cashgrab unless you are a superfan of Puzzle Quest and don't mind the grind. In tempting players to fork out cash at every turn, Marvel Puzzle Quest undermines the fantasy of having a league of powerful superheros, which is really the core of the game. I don't recommend this game, but play the game for yourself if you are still curious after my review. It is free-to-play, afterall.

A game that simultaneously compels you to keep playing for hours, and makes you want to shut it off and never come back. The harsh permadeath difficulty, monochrome colouring, and Last Of Us-esque music combine to make a game that has you sympathise with the victims and killers alike, forcing you into moral agony that isn't signposted like in most games, but rather leaves you to ponder raiding the house of civillians for the medicine you need, or trading your only weapon for it in another shelter. If you only steal what you NEED, it's not wrong, but maybe it is, and it's those kind of itching questions that permeate the experience. This War Of Mine presents both war at it's most atrocious and interactive 'entertainment' at it's finest.
The sparse dialogue is occasionally a bit heavy-handed, but the lack of subtlety in some areas is more than made up for in the soul-crushing power found everwhere else. In a year of disappointing releases and little genuine spark, here comes a game brave enough to take on issues both modern and eternal, and powerful enough to succeed.

"A carnival mirror Star Wars wearing a ten gallon hat and sporting dusty spurs and a pair of six-shooters." That is perhaps the most accurate image to paint of Rebel Galaxy, a well-built adventure into a cutthroat universe where the size of one's guns is the most important factor in day to day survival. It throws the player into a pilot's seat behind a vessel which often faces a bevy of pirates and other ne'er-do-wells between points A and B, wherever those might lay and however far apart they may be. Sometimes they wish to bring one to justice for the crime of transporting proscribed goods, sometimes because their friends got shot last week and vengeance is the specie of the universe.
The silent protagonist will need to regularly switch out for bigger and better broadsides (a fun and somewhat uncommon mechanic in spaceships!), turrets, shields, and craft. Their new toys WILL get a workout as well, to a soundtrack that would very well fit a posse of cowboys shooting out their disagreements in a swing-door saloon. As the player explores, they will also come to the realization that the star systems traveled in their adventures are simultaneously massive and easily covered, due to the dual engine nature of space travel in the Rebel Galaxy.
Regarding criticisms, there are a couple. First and foremost, missions involving the escort of a principal (fortunately only required by the main storyline in a handful of places) show that while combat works just fine, certain aspects of the AI are lacking - in particular, pathing around things like planets or asteroid fields. Second, additional variety in martial confrontations would go leagues to making the game from something to really like into something to really love; different ships change how one fights a great deal more than different kinds of broadside or secondary weapons.
All in all, Rebel Galaxy has good asset quality, fascinating attention to detail - the dynamic burn and missile scarring on ships and rock is strangely wonderful - and meticulous work put into making the whole experience bind together into a neat, fun, cohesive six-gunning experience.

In the style of Escape Velocity and Privateer you are a faceless space trucker out to investigate the trouble an estranged family member got into.
The game has incredibly stylish visuals and the emptiness of space is genuinely colorful. I like the feel of the navigation & combat as it is locked to a 2D plane and plays much more like a boat or mech game than a 3D simulator. This cuts down on the amount of controls and disorientation that would come with them. The game is generally light on unnecessary details and is an incredibly relaxing experience to tootle around in.
The RPG piece of the game is streamlined as well. There aren’t ships or upgrades I would consider trap options. You can’t get stuck in a slow moving cargo freighter with no guns. Every ship is better than the last and when combined with the arcadey combat is a much more casual and action oriented experience than the many games that proceed it.
The cargo flipping economic sim component is the weakest part of the game. Finding efficient trade routes and running them for cash isn’t exposed properly in the menus to make sound decisions. For the most part you should be shooting evil pirates during missions or in random encounters and just selling whatever they stole. Because all the upgrades are generally positive and cash flow is constant; money effectively equals exp and the game is paced well to provide steady improvement without the feel of grind.
The music is fantastic. In the same vein of StarCraft II terrans you have truckers listening to space country. I think it nails the tone perfectly but if that isn’t your bag you can tie your own custom soundtrack to the audio queues the game uses for seamless transitions.
Edit: I have completed the game and am pleased with the time spent. It does get grindy during the approach to the end of the game as you have likely settled into a favorite loadout. I recommend this game on a steam sale for a relaxing trip through space.

Where Is My Heart? is a cute little puzzle platformer with a surprisingly refreshing idea. The idea is simple; the level is split up into several little windows all containing parts of the level, and some of them overlapping each other. So if you walk in a straight line you'll appear in a different window after just a few steps (which can basically be anywhere on the screen), all this while still walking straight, mind you. It's a difficult concept to explain and really needs to be seen in action to understand it all. It's confusing at first, but once it clicks it's one of the best and charming puzzle games you'll ever play.
It's short, with its 26 levels (2 hours) of gameplay, because it's also the only way to keep the idea fun and fresh. Any longer and it wouldn't have made such an impact. Well, or maybe less anyway.
There's also a story behind all the puzzling and it too is charming, and even a bit sad. The retro graphics help set the mood and they truly fit this amazing little game. And the music manages to support the game in a relaxing way.
Where Is My Heart? is highly recommended and needs to be played by as many people as possible.

Where is my heart? It's a rather existential question that I wouldn't have an immediate answer to. Perhaps with a loved one, or a place I am or long to be; at any one time my heart could be any number of places or nowhere at all, if I'm feeling especially down. Where is my Heart, the game, doesn't concern itself as much with metaphorical musings or heavy philosophical discussion, but all the same invites a certain curiosity to it. Even when saying little, there's a distinct undertone of the developers hinting at something more meaningful than the journey of a trio of monsters to find their magical tree, which feels trapped just beneath the surface longing to get out.
Before I get ahead of myself, Where is my Heart is a puzzle platformer best summed up as a walk-in sliding puzzle. The world has become shattered, disorganized, split into various sized panes that each show but a part of the whole level. Your objective then becomes one of observation and out of the box navigation, having to traverse an area where walking through one pane rarely puts you on the other side, but instead somewhere entirely different on the screen. It's a hard concept to wrap your head around, even after spending a good deal of time with the game, but as you begin to understand it as a mechanic its brilliance starts to become apparent.
Taken out of context, the levels themselves rarely amount to much, but when splintered into dozens of screens then switched around they become puzzles within themselves. It pushes you to think of abstract paths and tests your memory to remember which panes line up with each other. Adding in a selection of special character powers only adds to the tantalizing challenge, that seems so thoughtfully planned out and lovingly designed. But for all the love and care that evidently went into making WIMH, all throughout the experience it seems almost scared of becoming too clever, or inserting too much personality into the level designs.
The outcome of this is a game that lacks substance. Levels are enjoyable to navigate but disconnected from each other and unmemorable in their own right. When I saw the end after only two hours, I couldn't help but feel like much of the game was a missed opportunity to use such an original mechanic, which never seemed to evolve past what was seen in the first few levels. This doesn't mean I disliked WIMH, but I was disappointed that it made such shallow use of its design concepts, instead playing it close to the chest with a game that's cute but not especially inspired beyond its core mechanic, and as such will likely fade from my memory rather quickly.
All that aside, Where is my Heart is still a rather deliciously adorable adventure that is worth undergoing if you can accept it for what it is. The charming ascetic and soothing audio design goes a long way in making up for its underwhelming ambition, to the degree I doubt I could legitimately hate the game even if I wanted to. Much the same as a children book, it's simplistic by nature even to its own detriment, but still incredibly easy to fall in love with and want to revisit again and again.
So where is my heart? I suppose right now it's being held captive by an enchanting little game that wants so much to love you too, if only for a short while.

Some notes for context: I've played a few different MMORPGs - was on World of Warcraft for a while, also Dark Age of Camelot, Final Fantasy XI, City of Heroes, and Dungeons & Dragons Online.  This is about the second time I've come back to this game, so take the "hours played" figure up there with a grain or two of salt (mind you, the first time was about 2010 or thereabouts, so there's been a while between drinks, so to speak).
To Be Aware Of: if you read a lot of the older reviews, they'll complain about the crafting system, and how it was extremely limited.  This is now fixed - so if you're reading a review which talks about "Vim", you're effectively reading a review for a game which no longer exists.
One of the things which is most pleasant for me as a player of "Villagers and Heroes" is the lack of urgency about the game.  It isn't a game where you can't do much other than grind until you're in the upper echelons of the level rankings (as opposed to, for example, DAoC); it also isn't a game which is (in my opinion) thoroughly dependent on purchased content to make it worth playing (unlike D&D Online).  If you choose to play this game in its "free to play" mode, you can still get a very enjoyable experience without spending a cent.  While it doesn't have much variety in the early game (all classes get to start in the same place, doing the same quest, and there's only one species available - default humans) there's still a lot of options available.
The biggest alteration between the first time I played this game and the most recent iteration is in the crafting system, which is now based more on time and effort than on limited resources of energy.  There are items (which spawn automatically when you're gathering) called "Motes of Yorick" which cut down the production time for large amounts of things (very useful when you're refining raw materials prior to actually crafting), but using these isn't compulsory (you can sit there and grind individually through, for example, turning all your lumps of copper ore into copper pigs one at a time).  This is a massive improvement over the old system (trust me, I've tried both).  There's also clockwork harvesters (occasional rewards from crafting quests, or from the daily "lucky cards" random draw; otherwise, purchaseable for cash through the shop) which can cut down the amount of time which is required for gathering raw materials.
Combat is pretty basic and pretty generic for most MMOs out there.  I'm not a huge combat fan at the best of times, so I tend to be very much about getting through as quickly as possible, preferably with as little damage done as I can handle.
I'm based in Western Australia (timezone GMT +8, which means I'm at least 8 hours out of synch with just about everyone) so I can't really comment on the community.  What I've seen of it makes me think it's pretty friendly, and there's a fairly low incidence of trolling, harassment, and overall nastiness in the global chat.  Most people seem pretty helpful, and there's usually someone available to answer newbie questions without attempting to bite your head off.
Overall, I'd recommend the game for people who aren't after the sort of "intense" gaming experience which can come from some of the more popular MMOs.  If you're just after something nice and pleasant to help you fill up a few hours each night, or let you blow off steam killing off mobs, thumping rocks, chopping down trees, and so on, this is probably a good game to have a look at.  It's pretty playable solo - you don't need to have a guild or a bunch of friends playing in order to be able to do well at the game.

GRID: Autosport is my favourite casual sim, with amazing physics (similar to GRID 1), good AI, great track selection, nice damage system, and beautiful graphics.
Note: I recommend you read the in-depth review below and watch some gameplay videos!
================================================================
I'm writing this review with about 6 hours of play time logged, so keep that in mind.
GRID Autosport is a great game. I has a few downfalls, but overall it is very enjoyable.
Starting with the graphics/visual side, it has some great looking effects and beautiful lighting. Car models look a little on the low-detail side, but its not a very big problem.
The in-car cameras, I have to say, fail. There's no working dials, and very low detail on the interiors. The mirrors don't work either. Depending on what your requirements are, this could be game breaking or just a 'meh' situation. I can live with it, because I'm not a hardcore sim player. It still needs fixing though, because sometimes it is a nice change to play inside the car.
Physics wise, the game is super. It feels great with an Xbox 360 Gamepad, and absolutely jaw-droppingly amazing with a wheel (and I'm even using an old Logitech Momo wheel!). Haven't tried it with a keyboard yet. It's very accessable, but also quite deep. A very good example of 'simcade' handling, and a great improvement over GRID 2.
My old Momo steering wheel worked fine first time, so thumbs up for old wheel support :)
I don't know whether I like or hate the AI. I think maybe both. They are so damn agressive, it makes for some hair-raising, what-the-heck-how-did-I-pull-that-off racing, but also gets a bit rough, and can get on your nerves sometimes if you want to race clean. They'll grind and bump you quite regularly, so get used it it :)
I haven't had a go at Online yet, I'll update the review when I do.
Car list is good, ranging from the VW Golf, to the Bugatti Veyron and Koenigsegg (did I spell that right?) Agera. Like said before, it would be nice to have some higher quality car models, but it's not game breaking.
There are a nice range of tracks, from Bathurst to the original San Francisco from GRID 1 (finally! I loved that track!).
Performance is good, running it all maxed out at 1080p with a solid 60FPS on a GTX 980 Ti and i7 6700k.
-------------------
Pros & Cons List:
+ Nice Graphics (eye candy, track detail).
+ Jaw dropping handling (in my opinion).
+ Supported my old Momo Force Feedback wheel.
+ AI provide a good challenge, and make the races exciting
+ Good car list, nice variety (all DLC included).
+ Nice range of tracks (all DLC included).
+ Good optimization, had no hitches getting it running.
- The car models are not as high quality as I'd like (but lower quality models help with optimzation).
- Interior views are lacking detail.
- AI can get too rough.
------------------
Thanks for reading :)

If you are looking for a continuation in the legendary Civilization Series. Turn away, this isn't it. Not to say it's inherently bad, but it just isn't Civ. I absolutely love Civ V and while Beyond Earth does scratch the Civ itch a bit, it brings a different experience to the table. Yes, the gameplay is shockingly similar to that of Civ 5, but what it brings new is wonderful. An overhaul of the previously named "Culture and Social Policies" is now streamlined and way more useful. New "quests" and major decisions have to be made that influence your "civ" one way or antother- one of my favorite aspects. And finally, the unforgiving alien landscapes. New terrain, such as crevaces, canyons, and the crazy aliens that, at first, threaten your small cities existence. The final major change is the technology overhaul. Instead of a linear tech "tree" from the previous games, the tech section is now organized into a large web, encoumpassing many different things in any direction. While this was daunting and honestly confusing at first, as you progress it starts to make sense. What I have come to enjoy about this style of technology system is that two players could decide to go in opposite directions of the tech web, researching different things and still be competetive, despite each other not having each other's units/tech/buildings/etc. There is a new aspect in Beyond Earth that introduces orbital units. Satellites that can gain a bit more solar energy (this games "gold") to satellites that provide defense bonuses and healing per turn for millitary units. While this is somewhat intriguing, I feel it wasn't fully fleshed out and honestly you can get through an entire game completly ignoring this new system.
The Good: Tech Web, Culture overhaul, Quest Decisions
The Bad: Boring early game, some mechanics too similar to Civ 5.
Overall: I think this would have done much better as a "standalone" DLC for Civ 5, or an "addon game" rather than a brand new $60 game. It feels too similar to pay really anything substantial, but if you do play it, it can be a lot of fun.

The first time I robbed a house with people inside, they were armed robbers camped out in a church. Marko, my scavenger, killed one of them with a knife. He told himself that it was alright, that it was self defense. Neither of us could really say that later when starvation forced him to kill a husband and wife for the food in their cupboards.
This War of Mine is a Rare Gem that every gamer should consider playing. Set in a roughly Balkan setting the game forces players into the roles of civilians trapped in a war zone, or more uncomfortably if you upload your own photo, yourself in the same situation. Scavenging for supplies, fending off hunger, bandits, and even depression just become a part of the daily life.
Few games so effectively marry story and gameplay together, and This War of Mine constantly drives your actions towards the moral questions hanging over the game. To what ends will you go to survive? Would you kill for a tin of processed food? What toll would that take?
Aesthetically the game is a canvass of gray shades, and the soundtrack is muted. While there are a few clunky patches here an there, it's well worth giving This War of Mind a look. Anyone who plays shooters regularly owes it to themselves to consider what the other side of a war might look like.

At first glance, this game was not something I liked or cared for in any general sense. Being an on the rails shooter bullet hell type game without weapons, you can imagine it became incredibly frustrating, very quickly. That frustration amounted to full blown hatred of the game, the 120 second timer, the lack of weapons and only 3 special abilities... but... after about 3 hours of game time, I realized that although I wanted to smash my head against the wall, I was actually enjoying trying to get 100 Quasars on each level (the white orbs you collect to win the level.... you need 100 on each level to fight the bosses). Sometimes the game seems impossibly unfair and about as challenging as walking to the moon on glass shards but when you finally succeed, you feel like you truly accomplished something that not every gamer would be able to do. At this point, I've beaten the first nine levels and I'm on the second boss and I think I've met my match but considering I at first despised this game and now I've come to respect it, I'd say it's worth the money.
Pros:
-Hard, omg it's so hard
-Pretty nice graphics
-Winning feels like ejaculation. It's just wonderful.
-Easy to learn, with abilities that can save your ♥♥♥... a lot.
-Lots of unlockables
-Later levels become insanely fast
Cons:
-Oh my flying spaghetti monster, this game is so ♥♥♥♥ing hard!
-No weapons (you're meant to survive without getting hit, even in boss fights)
-120 second timer. That doesn't sound very long but when you've got about 5000 rocks about to smash into you, it is.
-It'd be nice if there was an "easy, normal or hard option" because this game defaults to ♥♥♥♥ING INSANE
-I know the story isn't a huge focus and from a fiction stand point is fine but scientifically it's like what? No more suns in the whole galaxy? Coooooome ooooon.
Final Verdict: If you like to rip the veins out of your arms one by one using a Toothpick then this game is for you. Bullet Hell types will find a lot of enjoyment here, especially out of the boss fights which really add in variety to the base gameplay. And if you're going to buy this game, don't judge it based on the first couple of playthroughs, get all the abilities and play to the first boss and then judge it. Recommended for the masochists out there.

I never though I would enjoy this game as much as I did.
When I first took a look, it seemed like a whole lot of micro management with a broken morality system.
By the same token, few games have been able to elicit genuine emotion from me.
That said, this game is an instant classic in the steam library and a must have for those looking for a neat twist on the survival genre.  You play as a group of survivors in a war torn city just trying to make ends meet.  You’re lucky if you don't get shot by rebel soldiers or fellow scavengers, and luckier if you get to eat that day.  Go through the day trying to mediate the needs of your own group with that of your neighbors and then journey into the night looking for supplies to keep yourselves going.  There will be moral challenges, yes, but not necessarily any repercussions.  Careful and clever players will find ways to commit crimes with impunity; however, this does not mean you will escape the emotional consequences, as your party attempts to cope with the atrocities they commit to survive in war.  Teamwork is necessary, but others… they are expendable.  Or, perhaps, you value their lives and will attempt, at all opportunities to be good and ethical – good luck.
Ultimately the game is a masterpiece, forcing a set of mind of survival and melancholia with its powerful imagery, music and dialogue.  I’m only about 15 hours in, and I want more; and so will you.
Also, the soundtrack is free and it’s a pretty nice listen.  So, there’s that.

Yay! I ‘m going to review Dungeons 2! Oh those Roman numerals, I decided to put a ‘2’ instead of “II” because those are really just two “I’s” (eyes) stuck together. Why Roman numeral why!
So what we begin with is the main menu. There is a campaign, skirmish, and for all you crazy option loving crazies out there, options. I won’t spoil what happens in the campaign, But I dare do say it’s fun, and funny. A combination I adore, plus you get to be evil. Plus, you’re building a dungeon! How cool is that?! It’s fun to me because I enjoy the carving out your dungeon aspect, hiring units, (once the proper room is build of course,) researching upgrades, (There are general upgrades, as well as unit specific upgrades,) and the mana aspect (cast spells, etc,) Oh! And traps.
And it’s funny...because of the narrator (and the slaps you may dole out to your minions). I have to be honest and say I have read other reviews, and they say, he can be...oh, what’s that word…annoying? Anyway, I found that if you sat there during the campaign, the narrator would remark something witty and funny, and, actually, the narrator tends to say funny words, on scripted spots of the game, (There is a LOT of references to movies and games) . This is a given, You may not like it. I do, enjoy the comments of the narrators wit.
So, you may be asking yourself, “Big deal, it’s another dungeon game.” Yes, but it helps keep it fresh by allowing you play with more than one faction! That is, two factions. Yes, two factions does not seem like a lot, but you can switch them up between plays in the skirmish maps. (There is a third playable faction, but only if you buy the appropriate DLC!) These two factions play somewhat similar with the same goals, but their style differs. For example, Faction ‘A’ requires the thirst of your minions to be sated. You can stock up on beer and store these good for your minions. The other faction, ‘B’ demands that your minions be admired by your basic workers, something that cannot be stocked up upon and must be dealt with as the minions needs arises.
There’s not a lot of skirmish maps to play with, unfortunately. There is DLC for that too. Also, I don’t believe you can make your own maps. It may have to do with how the overworld ‘evilfies’ as you rampage across the surface. It would probably be hard to design a way to allow the freedom of map making while also having changes of the map being ‘evilfied’. Like say, if I hypothetically created a map on here, some things may not ‘evilfy’ correctly. There’s integers to worry about, there’s zones, actions, boolians, true’s and falses, parameters that must be set, flags, and the different doodads that must be placed appropriately when creating a map to ensure it all works when things get all evil looking on the surface.
There’s not a whole lot I dislike about the game. Sometimes the hand can be picky on what it picks up, it takes a bit of practice. There is no way of prolonging enemy waves of coming into your dungeon, (unless you kill them before they arrive,) it’s ether fight or die when they come. It usually starts out with two or three pitchfork presents, then works up to stronger units attacking you as time progresses.

I recommend this game, but not at its full 20 euro price. I pi!cked it up for 7,50 and consider it money well spent, at 20 euro's this review would be a thumbs down.
The game alternates days in which you can build, maintain and exploit your shelter and nights during which you run out to scavenge for food and components. Combat and stealth during these nights are implemented in a rudimentary fashion. There are also 'moral choices' but they don't really attribute to anything. You (as a player) can choose to feel bad about robbing the elderly or about killing thugs, but there's very little incentive to avoid these situations. The characters feel bad, but if they do get depressed or sad, there's many different buttons to push that can solve this.
The reservations stem from many small odd design choices, rather than any major flaws. Example: the inability to make potable water from rainwater by boiling it (allowing you to generate water by spending fuel, essentially). Example 2: the scavenging quickly becomes monotonous and predictable. The game is actually pretty easy if you have an eye for this type of gameplay.
I guess you're expected to feel bad about many of your actions, as a player. However, after killing an elderly couple in cold blood and stealing food from a hospital, my four survivors just sat around playing their guitars and one day later they had forgotton about all the horror. That sums it up really: there's too many weird and poor gamey mechanics implemented for the game to have any real emotional impact. And on top of that, the gameplay becomes repetitive quickly once you figure out the paths of least resistance for all basic requirements.
For all that, I had fun figuring out how to work it, even if it didn't last too long.

The game is an arena shooter and your goal is to survive all 10 levels of each match, there will be regular enemies and some bosses that can be pretty difficult to take down. It can be played in single or in multiplayer with other two people. The latter option is recommended even if there aren't many people to play it online, it's better to have a friend to play with.

The soundtrack features a death metal theme that fits perfectly with the game's atmosphere but gets repetitive being the only song you can listen to.

There are way better games available but I'll recommend it for the trading cards and the achievements.

Easy-win guide for new players here:
Go for a stove and beds at the begginning and just loot materials. Don't always go for food and don't be scared of starving a little bit. Just care more for the sick or wounded guy. Then just craft a hatchet and start killing everyone in your way. That's how I finished the game in the hardest possible mod.
Also, don't always help the people who comes to your door asking for stupid stuff.
To avoid getting your guys depressed, leave the easier places to sneak in to later. First, go for a hatchet. Secondly, kill a civillian with a gun and take his gun. Thirdly, steal some stuff and just wait for your survivor's to recover from everything. Then kill some heavy armed bandits and get their AK-47. Finally, attack at the millitary base. At this point, you are going to lose at least 1 person in your group so just send someone avarage and clear the way for your real badass soldiers (Roman, pavle, marko) After you clean the military base, steal all the AK-47 asap because they diseppear if you leave them on dead bodies. At least, try to remove them from the dead bodies and place them on the ground. Then steal all the ammo as soon as possible because *winter is coming* :)
Survive the winter by selling those AK-47 and using your infinite ammo which you got from the military base to protect yourself at night.
When the winter is over, it's going to be very easy to finish the game. You will have every kind of stuff in your house.
Best combo (you probably cannot select these guys at the begginning) : Roman, Marko, Boris and the stealthy chick (I forgot her name)
Boris: early game op / Stealthy chick and Marko: mid game usefull / Roman = Khal Drogo in late game. Killing machine!

I don't care much for most puzzle platformers; I usually feel they're too basic, or contrived. So understand my feeling when I say that this game is a labor of love, and that it shows in every facet of its design, right down to the oddly (somehow) unique pixel graphics.
The premise is simple: you have three little monsters, you control them one at a time, and you must guide them each to the exit of each level. There is no time limit, and no serious penalty for death; they simply respawn at the entrance. But here's the tricky bit; the world has become fragmented, though not necessarily broken. You can see the full picture, it's just that the full picture is muddled and confused, with pieces going every which way in no discernible order. Simply reaching the exit of each level becomes more complex, as even a straight pathway can take your monsters to every corner of the screen, or worse, numerous corners all at once.
Each monster has a specific color, which may be required when activating a block or, as you'll later discover, special abilities. Each monster can transform into one of three specific beasties, each with their own special ability necessary to complete a stage. The only one I'll mention is that of our orange monster, who transforms into a bird(?) of sorts and has the ability to shift the fragmented world in a clockwise or counterclockwise direction. For the other monsters, this matters little, but for her, she can remain still, while the world swirls around her, allowing her to move to entirely different fragments that may have been unreachable otherwise.
To reach each end, you must gather a number of hearts strewn about each stage, thereby opening the door. But as you progress, this task slowly becomes more complex, as mechanics more complicated than jumping ledge to ledge are uncovered. The way these mechanics present themselves is a big part of why I enjoy this game so. See, it's never spelled out for you; there isn't a mid-level tutorial message or loading screen hint giving a dry description of how hitting a switch opens doors. The game simply presents you with the opportunity to touch and experiment with things, and these range from the simple (hitting a block with the correctly colored monster) to the complex (learning to properly manipulate the world's fragments). What makes this game special is that even the simplest mechanics are so often used in different and unique ways between each level. I often felt impressed by the simple brilliance of many of the layouts, and how so many of them would educate and influence your actions in the next. It quickly became intuitive to take what I already knew and wonder,
or,
.
Each level presents the challenge of gathering every heart without losing a single monster even once, rewarding you with a special heart symbol and, on occasion, an entirely new level. Majority of games, I wouldn't care for such frivolity, but the very clear dedication that went into making each and every level stand out as a unique entity makes the practice of perfecting every single one of them feel very, very worthwhile.
At the time of writing this review, I've completed what I suspect to be over half of the available levels, and I do plan to complete the rest before too long. Should I make any new discoveries in that time that I feel just
to be in this review, I will be sure to make note. That's just how good this game is. I very much want to fully complete this title, and experience every last ounce of thought and love that the developers put into making it. And as someone who typically feels indifference towards these types of games, that says a lot.

Man, had my characters not get reset from previous stages of the game (like back in the days when it was "A Mystical Land" and not Villagers and Heroes), I honestly would've never stopped playing. It was the only reason I left the game in the first place. I lost all of my items, my characters, as well as my friends that I used to group up with to farm bosses with (I powerleveled with them like CRAZY). After the first reset, I tried to get back into the game. I just couldn't. It was like getting sick from your favorite diner. I just couldn't go back to it. Until now.
Today, on September 18th of 2016, after numerous years, I've finally decided to get back into the game and try it again. No, my characters were not brought back, BUT my enjoyment of the game was. There wasn't many people on at the time I was, but those that were on were relatively friendly, just like the people I played with back in 2011. Aside from the people, the graphics were improved by a LOT (not to the point where they're like Crysis 3 graphics, but to a more vibrant and colorful point than once before), the lore of the game has been extended and is a bit more intriguing, there's a ton more items, there's now player housing, mounts, and even more than what I had mentioned.
Will I be getting back into this game? When I get more free time on my hands, absolutely.
Do I recommend the game to others? YES! Bring friends with you! The more people you have with you, the more fun the game is! If you wanna play with me sometime, please don't hesitate to add me as a friend and message me!
To wrap things up, I just want to say that I'm glad I revisited this game after so many years of avoiding it. Coming back to it now after so long just feels great. Hopefully soon I'll be back to where I was before my characters were all reset.

This game was a fun romp is the best that i could put it.
The music made this game for me, I normally think of electronic music when I play space games but the swamprock/dark country music really worked to make you feel like a small guy trying to find his way in a big scary galaxy. The combat was an arcadey style which focused around its broadside, naval combat system, which was only possible because the game was played on a single plane. The single plane is a huge downside, everythings laid out very flat and I guess this might be a good thing for people who are disoriented easily but not my cup of tea. The other major issue I had with the game was the progression system. Each system you go is progressively harder, the ships are all progressively larger. In the starter solar system the largest ships you fight are light frigates, 3 solar systems in, you're fighting some of the same sized ships from the previous system but also huge juggernauts with massive health pools. The objecitves are usually these huge juggernauts so if you want to play a light frigate youll have to skip ahead and deck yourself out with gear from 2 or 3 systems ahead. Yes thats right, even the equipment progression is forced by each solar system. All of these severley neuters the "open world" feel that the game was supposed to have. Combat becomes a chore, making money becomes a chore because it gets boring. This leads me to the third thing i dislike about the game, even the mining becomes a scavenger hunt. With how fast the lasers overheat, you're left getting a mediocre amount of low quality ores or scavenging belts to find 1 or 2 asteroids that contain 2 or 3 pieces of higher quality ore, gold or diamond.
Pros:
- An open wold feel, make money how you want (scavenging, pirating, mining, trading)
- Dynamic trading economy, based on random events that occur in the stations in each system
- The naval style combat
- Music, the music made the atmosphere in this game, reminisent of firefly or the terran cinematics in the original starcraft
Cons:
- Only able to travel on 1 plane (no verticle movement)
- Felt too much of an arcade game
- Linear progression system
- Ship variety and playstyle is lacking
- Fruitless mining
In all, I can recommend this game when its on sale, its a simple game in the guise of a better one. Despite strangulation by a linear progression system, the music and and unique naval style combat make it worth a try.

This game perfectly sums up the dark era of first person shooters.
Gameplay ripped straight from Call of Duty? Check.
Interesting premise and potential squandered by horrible writing and gung-ho idiocy? Check.
4 hour long story? Check. (The 5 hours I spent in-game was in MP. I have completed the story when it first released on Xbox 360)
Super linear and set-piece driven, but nothing unique to add? Check.
Tonal inconsistencies between showing the gritty, horrors of war followed by over-the-top supersoldier nonsense, and characters acting childish? Check.
The most abrupt, sequelbait and unsatisfying ending known to mankind since RAGE? Check.
The singleplayer is terrible. Absolutely terrible. It is not worth your time unless you simply don't play First Person Shooters, like many positive reviews here.
As for the multiplayer? It's a whole other story. Now, surprisingly, people say it's half-decent, if not good.
No. No, it's terrible. Probably the biggest cluster♥♥♥♥ I have ever experienced in FPS hell, and is an absolute travesty.
It's in fact, the WORST of Call of Duty and Battlefield combined.
With Call of Duty's over-simplified gunplay, aim-first design, and rich-get-richer problems, combined with the open maps and conquest mode being ripped straight from it. The Elmer's School Glue that fails to hold these termite-ridden popsicle sticks together is the Battle Point system, AKA, the only thing unique about this entire game.
You have to "earn" your vehicles, in other words, basically exponentially perform better for already performing better. Get kills and destroy stuff, you get to get more kills and destroy more stuff (easier). And it's not hard to earn these points! They're not streaks, they're not earned with teamwork, they're not earned through time. You earn Battle Points by merely killing enemies and destroying vehicles and drones, as it builds up in your point bank. Just a few several kills in this long, cluster♥♥♥♥ match can get you a cheap power-weapon.
Essentially, the MP boils down to sniper-fests and explosions from helicopters, drones, UAVs, tanks, etc. You are not given effective tools to eliminate these vehicles in a timely matter and everyone will be spamming these throughout the match since it's so easy to earn them. I should know, I was getting wanted 5-stars left-and-right, as it's so easy to go on 10+ kill streaks when you have basic reflexes and awareness.
That's really all there is to say about Homefront. There's nothing good about it. It's not even average, it's legitimately a sorry excuse for a game that had this much marketing behind it, but also a sorry excuse for a First Person Shooter in all aspects. What little there is good about the game (Sound design, I guess?), ultimately does not matter with design this bad.
And I cannot find any valid reason from a hardcore gamer, that this game is worth anyone's time.

- The world is quite repetitive. The roads all look the same, houses by the road side look the same.
- The map gives no indication where you are at any given point in time.
A few tips:
When you exit the vehicle to trundle along in search of parts or shops, NEVER forget your wallet.
Gather as much sellable goods as possible, you WILL need cash. Vodka bottles are gold.
Stock up on tool kits whenever you can.
All in all, I believe that the game will develop nicely and recommend it for that reason. There is a lot of work to be done, but it is very playable as it is now. Do not expect Euro Truck Simulator distances though.

There's a reason why this game is generally regarded as either being terrible or a giant missed opportunity and that's because it's both.
If you love smoke and mirrors and sleight of hand tricks this game will impress you. If you haven't touched a Civilization game ever this will be serviceable to you even if you're providing yourself a great disservice by starting with this one.
If you're a civilization fan with discerning tastes and certain expecations of a veteran series and veteran developer this game will disgust you. Since at best it could be described as an ambitious fan mod and reskin of Civ V in which you get new, ugly terrain to look at and have aliens attacking you instead of barbarians. Hey, that's different, right?...
To be fair there are some tweaks and "additions" that are ok. Just ok. Nothing great, nothing game changing just something you'd expect from DLC or a mod, really. In fact, most of these tweaks are in fact mods for Civ V that fans already made. Nothing really thought provoking here.
On the most absolute technical terms and virgin eyes Beyond Earth is a serviceable, ok game. It has absolutely NO personality and stabbing your ear with a Q-tip provides better sound effects and the ensuing ringing in your ears is better music than this game provides but from a gameplay perspective if you ignore everything that this series is supposed to be about and what THIS game SHOULD have been about *cough* Alpha Centauri, then this game is ok. Just ok.
If you want the last, newest and good Civ game play Civ IV, if you want a modern, more new user friendly and so combat focused that it might as well be called Risk 2.0, play Civ V. If you want Alpha Ceentauri or a successor to V that makes up for everything wrong V did while being a competent and compelling package in its own right, ignore Beyond Earth.
The real tragedy, though, is that this game apparently sold well enough for them to make an expansion for it. An expansion that I imagine most will praise but wish it was in the base game in the first place...

I've played this game a lot. A lot. Dozens of games. All sorts of high difficulties. Tons of mods. I'm active in several communities that piece apart issues with the game and try to improve on them, so I know a thing or two about the game's shortcomings.
Does it have them? Absolutely. But most of them are behind hours and hours of understanding core game mechanics to know what is and what is not unbalanced. Listen, if you're genuinely interested in Civilization in Space, you'll enjoy this game. If you expect it to be everything Alpha Centauri was and more -- you'll probably be disappointed. If you don't actually like sci-fi and space, you'll probably be disappointed.
The game is a gem for those who can appreciate it though. There's very little wrong with the game and the devs are constantly working to remedy that. I look forward to seeing how the game changes with the upcoming DLC Rising Tide.

The original GRID seemed to nail the balance between a simulation and an arcade experience. GRID: Autosport has a more sim-like feel, which may appeal to some but not to me. The cars feel big and like you have to lug them through turns, yet oddly there's a tipping point while braking where suddenly the car will basically do a 180 if you so much as tap the stick. The braking feels all over the place, probably because the game doesn't convey an intuitive sense of speed: 75 mph feels the same as 150 mph. Regardless, this is a game where proper braking is absolutely crucial, but the game does you no favors. The distance markers are too small, for example, and the announcer is useless. It all adds up to an unintuitive sense of control, and in racing games, if the control isn't there it's a good bet the overall gaming experience is in serious trouble.
I've only played a couple drift events but so far it's a hot mess. This game seems to think spinning your tires = drifting. The sweet spot of control through a turn is almost non-existent. You never get that "let it all hang out" feeling through a turn because going open throttle on even a straight will send you out of control! What were they thinking? But worse, there is no sense of what makes a good drift or a bad drift. There's some vague connection to markers on the sides of the turns but I've done absolutely sh**ty drifts of just tire-spinning and fish-tailing and they seem to score as well if not better than a controlled slide (on the extremely rare occasion the game lets me perform one).
Menus and skill progression, similar to Dirt 3, are terrible and totally uninspiring. I don't know why it's so hard for them. In the case of G:AS it's an extremely minimalist design that could easily have come from an 80s or 90s game, and gives you very little sense of progress, or why progress even matters. The tiers in the original GRID were not a standout but they did the job. Every game Codemasters has produced in the last few years has this sort of wannabe minimalist avant-garde look that also happens to be just passable at conveying information. It's better than Dirt 3's triangles, is about the best I can say.
And Codemasters, it's just a videogame. You don't need to confirm every freakin' decision I make. Do I really want to exit Practice Mode? YES, FREAKING YES!! If I accidentally pick the wrong thing and lose my race, it's not like I just deleted my dissertation or formatted my hard drive. So enough with the stupid confirming. Please Please fire the menu team. They have no idea how to design menus that compliment the rest of the game and they're annoying as hell.
Bottom line: all this adds up to a game that is just not terribly fun to play. It's not a horrible game but in both real cars and car racing games, the crucial make or break element is that intangible feeling of driving excitement. Racing is supposed to be edge of your seat type stuff, and this doesn't feel like it at all. It just feels mediocre. Glad I got this on sale but unless future Codemaster game reviews are overwhelmingly positive, this is likely my last purchase.

While it won't last an impression as deep as the first Bioshock, this sequel does exactly what a sequel should: maintain the core gameplay of the original and fixing/improving on what didn't quite work while keeping what does work. Combat feels just a tad more dynamic because of three major improvements:
1. You permanently dual-wield a weapon in your right hand (fired with M1) and a plasmid in your left hand (fired with M2). Not having to switch just makes it that bit faster to use plasmids.
2. The research camera now gives you a minute in which to fight an enemy as creatively as possible, and rewards you based on how many strategies/weapon types/plasmids you used.
3. Hacking can be done remotely with special darts, and the minigame now takes place in real-time, with a meter that you have to stop in the right area. Because of this hacking while in combat is easier started but harder to finish, and overall more strategic.
There is a greater variety in enemy types (such as the absolutely frightening Big Sisters), each weapon now has a third upgrade that unlocks after the first two are applied and adds some kind of very special effect to it... Countless little improvements that all add up to solidifying the gameplay. In terms of gameplay, Bioshock 2 is definitely superior to 1.
The writing in general also feels more solid, although it has less twists and turns than in the original. (It still has its fair share of them, of course). That said I would not necessarily call it "better" than Bioshock 1, but I do think 2 has a much more solid finale, and the moral choices you made along the way matter a bit more (but are still largely irrelevant, unfortunately). You do get more moral choices as well, but there was one in particular where I felt that the developers' idea of what was morally good and evil in the context did not quite match up with how I felt about the choice. It's the hazard of a black/white moral system.
Overall Bioshock 2 is just a very solid game and if you like the first one, you will like this one too. I can really just sum up 3 gripes I have with the game:
1. As I mentioned, one of the moral choices feels very gray and what you consider morally good may not be what the game judges it as.
2. The game is very unstable and crashes a lot. Save frequently or wait for the remaster update, that might fix it.
3. Bioshock 2 also delves deeper into the backstory for even the first game, but unfortunately contradicts some of the new lore from Bioshock Infinite: Burial at Sea in the process. So I'm afraid that the game itself is no longer a part of the canon.
Finally, I would like to just quickly address Minerva's Den. I haven't actually finished this chapter, but what I've seen of it felt even more solid and it looks like the writing is going to be very interesting as well. I'll update this review with my thoughts about that once I finish it.

I started playing Dungeons 2 then stopped after a few missions, it just wasn't gripping me.  I also always felt rushed, you also always have this feeling that you're about to run out of gold by next pay day and scramble to keep unearthing more gold veins.
I then decided to give it another go this weekend, continuing the campaign where I left off and the game has managed to open up a bit more but now I'm feeling not only rushed, but also overwhelmed.  I constantly need to be doing stuff above ground as well as needing to defend underground, I have to keep the gold flowing which has it's own risks of unearthing spiders and the like.
I have yet to actually build an arena on any map and now I also have a forge to build.  I don't get enough gold / time to research all upgrades in any of the places (tinkerer, forge, mana place) and even if I had been able to build an arena, I'd never be able to use it because my forces are either busy fighting above ground or defending underground.
It's just rush rush rush from the minute the map starts.  I keep getting this feeling I'm missing the "cookie cutter recipe" of how you're supposed to approach every map.  Almost like DOTA, start map, press this key combination to buy these things and get to that specific lane ASAP.  There's just very little "fun" factor and I'm not getting any actual time to "explore" the game.  I've started redoing each map after playing it for 5-10 minutes just so I can get a little "exploration" into the game mechanics.  It feels much like diving into an FPS that has you fighting aliens non stop from the second it loads till it's finished.  You don't actually get to try out the cover system or the vault system because you're constantly overwhelmed and the second you're done killing everything the mission abruptly ends with no option to continue playing in order to explore the mechanics.
I felt much the same way about Dungeons 1, never finished it.  Still, it has that nostalgic feeling that reminds me of many happy hours playing DK2 as a kid which is why I'm trying so hard to like it.
TLDR; Definitely has potential, get it on sale and even if you don't end up finishing it, you should get your money's worth.  Will be buying War for the Overworld in the hope that it'll be the one that will scratch the itch.

This War of Mine is a Rare Gem that every gamer should consider playing. Set in a roughly Balkan setting the game forces players into the roles of civilians trapped in a war zone, or more uncomfortably if you upload your own photo, yourself in the same situation. Scavenging for supplies, fending off hunger, bandits, and even depression just become a part of the daily life.
Few games so effectively marry story and gameplay together, and This War of Mine constantly drives your actions towards the moral questions hanging over the game. To what ends will you go to survive? Would you kill for a tin of processed food? What toll would that take?
Aesthetically the game is a canvass of gray shades, and the soundtrack is muted. While there are a few clunky patches here an there, it's well worth giving This War of Mind a look. Anyone who plays shooters regularly owes it to themselves to consider what the other side of a war might look like.

I never though I would enjoy this game as much as I did.
When I first took a look, it seemed like a whole lot of micro management with a broken morality system.
By the same token, few games have been able to elicit genuine emotion from me.
That said, this game is an instant classic in the steam library and a must have for those looking for a neat twist on the survival genre.  You play as a group of survivors in a war torn city just trying to make ends meet.  You’re lucky if you don't get shot by rebel soldiers or fellow scavengers, and luckier if you get to eat that day.  Go through the day trying to mediate the needs of your own group with that of your neighbors and then journey into the night looking for supplies to keep yourselves going.  There will be moral challenges, yes, but not necessarily any repercussions.  Careful and clever players will find ways to commit crimes with impunity; however, this does not mean you will escape the emotional consequences, as your party attempts to cope with the atrocities they commit to survive in war.  Teamwork is necessary, but others… they are expendable.  Or, perhaps, you value their lives and will attempt, at all opportunities to be good and ethical – good luck.
Ultimately the game is a masterpiece, forcing a set of mind of survival and melancholia with its powerful imagery, music and dialogue.  I’m only about 15 hours in, and I want more; and so will you.
Also, the soundtrack is free and it’s a pretty nice listen.  So, there’s that.

I recommend this game, but not at its full 20 euro price. I pi!cked it up for 7,50 and consider it money well spent, at 20 euro's this review would be a thumbs down.
The game alternates days in which you can build, maintain and exploit your shelter and nights during which you run out to scavenge for food and components. Combat and stealth during these nights are implemented in a rudimentary fashion. There are also 'moral choices' but they don't really attribute to anything. You (as a player) can choose to feel bad about robbing the elderly or about killing thugs, but there's very little incentive to avoid these situations. The characters feel bad, but if they do get depressed or sad, there's many different buttons to push that can solve this.
The reservations stem from many small odd design choices, rather than any major flaws. Example: the inability to make potable water from rainwater by boiling it (allowing you to generate water by spending fuel, essentially). Example 2: the scavenging quickly becomes monotonous and predictable. The game is actually pretty easy if you have an eye for this type of gameplay.
I guess you're expected to feel bad about many of your actions, as a player. However, after killing an elderly couple in cold blood and stealing food from a hospital, my four survivors just sat around playing their guitars and one day later they had forgotton about all the horror. That sums it up really: there's too many weird and poor gamey mechanics implemented for the game to have any real emotional impact. And on top of that, the gameplay becomes repetitive quickly once you figure out the paths of least resistance for all basic requirements.
For all that, I had fun figuring out how to work it, even if it didn't last too long.

I have to say I find this game to be truly amazing. I really don't like mobas, they just aren't my thing. But that is why I love Battlerite. It is an arena moba. There are no lanes, teams are 2v2 or 3v3, and it is just an areana pvp. It doesn't force you to memorize different items or learn which is the best for certain characters. It is very straight to the point, and it is honestly very easy to pick up and play for the first time. By no means is the game dumbed down to the point it isn't worth playing, they have taken just a lot of the monotony away from the moba genre. I don't have a lot of hours clocked in yet, but I know that is going to change very soon. The game is incredibly fun to play, really beautiful graphics, and all around fun champions. To me the real best part is that the matches are 2v2 or 3v3. To me that is the best just because I don't have many irl friends that play PC games like I do, only a handful. I really don't like playing games like this with random people, I feel like there needs to be a strategy going in and composition. So the lower player amounts make it easier to find friends who might love the game too and start playing with them. All in all this is a wonderful game, that I feel is just what the Moba genre needed. I really hope this game does well, and I would love to see more new players (like myself at the time of this review) in the game too.

First off, if you paid more than 5 USD or the equivalent, you paid too much.
TLDR:
So, I'm pretty critical of Rebel Galaxy. Yeah, it's not a AAA title or a realistic space/economic/mining/fighting simulator but we knew that going in. When I compare it to even something free like Endless Sky, I find Rebel Galaxy incredibly lacking in substance and just a shell of intentions to sell a game.
On to the review:
This is a bare bones sailing ship simulator set in space. 2D travel and fighting, silly economics with station events (actually one of the most interactive aspects in the entire game), barbaric ship speed controls that defy exhibited ship design or a semblance to reality, and a ship and equipment selection system that is no different than putting up a security deposit on the ship and gear you want to take out for that day (buy/sale prices are the same). It's great for testing out and playing around with various ship/weapon/equipment tactics but so unrealistic it breaks immersion and lacks any sense of investment or achievement.
I had zero investment in the main story arc or characters because it was too short, flat, simplistic and superficial; something a 5th grader would write ( Mr. Guild leader, don't you have anything else to say? No? Too busy? Then why am I talking to you at all?). The naming convention for celestial locations and named characters throughout were a mishmash of Star Trek, Star Wars and other IP's characters' blended names but it unfortunately came off less as nerd cred or homage and more of a lottery scheme by the lazy. Mining was a joke, Commodity pricing and market mechanics were there to make a bit more or less as you sold your battle loot.
There were topical side missions you could pick up as you progressed through the main story line which was nice and surprised me every time but that had more to do with my low opinion of the game than their quality (same mission, different skin). Rebel Galaxy was also graphically nice with flashy lights and explosions. Faction variation followed distinct racial design formula and there were at least 1 or two different hulls per class of ship for each race. Overall, I love this game. It has been forever since I've been able to play a competent, open ended space exploration title. However, I have some critiques to offer.
The first critique has to do with the way the enemy AI handles encounters where they are obviously outclassed. While they do try to run when heavily damaged, when you hail them, there appears a 0% chance they will actively surrender to you when you tell them to stand down. While I can appreciate that many of these are hardened criminals you are dealing with, meaning they won't be daunted as easily as traders, their behaviour makes little sense. If someone were to obliterate a pirate's capital ship through their shields, the rest of the battlegroup ought to at least be receptive to a chance to live. It becomes rather annoying to even use the hail feature in these encounters since the automatic reply will always be something like "sure, sure, there's no talking out of this one". I found this broke my immersion rather than enhance it.
My second critique has to do with the way saves are handled. As is, you can only save after exiting a station. This is problematic for a couple of reasons. Realistically, there is 0 reason to do this, and it just makes it tedious for longer sessions where you may have to make up for a lot of progress if you run into an unfortunate encounter. If you want to make a restriction on when players save, maybe just opt for not being able to save in combat. Further, while many save slots are on offer to the player, it seems the game uses only one at a time, with no way to access the other slots. It may be true that new games started use these slots, but personally it doesn't appear that that is the case. This critique is also problematic for another key reason. Today, shortly after purchasing my first destroyer, my game crashed. On restart, my save file was just gone... no explanation  as to why, just gone. All of my hardware in my rig is brand new, it's very unlikely that data corruption on the part of the hardware is the culprit, and now 35 hours of playtime appears to have gone down the toilet. I have to be honest, I'm quite dissapointed in this. It's not enough to make me not reccomend the game, but if it continues to occur, I might have to update my review.
Finally, I have to talk about the music in the game. It's overly repetitive, it's annoying, and you are going to want to turn it off. It has it's charm for all of maybe an hour, and then grates on you. While it is worth noting that the devs have allowed for command pathing so you may add custom music, which is great, it still seems really lazy on the part of sound design.
The lack of a multiplayer option is also a bit of a let down, this really keeps this game from being on the same level as titles like Elite Dangerous. Despite this, I still enjoyed the single player experience.
Outside of these critiques, I found the gameplay to be fun, engaging, and simple enough to be inviting to a variety of skill sets, yet complex enough to reward players who want to dive a little deeper in terms of encounter planning, and ship functionality. Additionally, the ability to play the game the way you wish at all points without being locked into being a mercenary, trader, militia member, or pirate was truly refreshing. Numeric Scoring scales are all arbitrary, so I won't bother actually giving a score. All I will say is that if you loved older titles of this kind, like Freespace, this is the game for you. If you are a member of the uninitiated to this genre, but are still curious, I still heartily reccomend this title.
Thank you for taking the time to read my review.

As a gamer, this was my first foray into the FPS series about 6 years ago, and as such I have a bit of a soft spot for it years later. I played it on a number of different platforms years ago, but finally I got the version on Steam just so recently and figured I'd leave my two cents on this.
The overall gameplay, when you first step into it, feels a little off. Controls aren't as tight as you would find in some of the other modern shooters (CS:GO, CoD, Battlefield, etc.) and something always feels a little clunky and unresponsive; it definitely needs some time to get used to, but once you get the hang of it, you'll fly by both the multiplayer and campaign and crush whatever gets thrown your way.
Speaking of campaign, it's short and hasn't aged quite well. You can definitely tell its age playing it in 2017/2018, with the lower-quality graphics and oddball facial patterns on main characters. Nonetheless, the story is peculiar (it guessed a few North Korea-related topics quite accurately, including their missile testing and rise of Kim Jong-Un), gory and harrowing at quite a few points, but gameplay wise it's quite the generic campaign you'd find in a lot of shooters over the last few years.
The multiplayer is quite good. I heard it was overhyped back in the day to be a "CoD killer", but it honestly isn't. Think of it fitting a niche between CoD and Battlefield; the map and vehicle setups are big enough for large 32 player fights, but also small enough to keep a fast-pace sense to the fight. I also really enjoy the Battle Points method used for your "killstreaks" and vehicles; it's nice to not have to rely on maintaining a streak in order to get your rewards and it levels the playing field for mediocre gamers like myself. The points system for perks/utilities is really good and allows for diversity in classes. (You can also tell that CoD ripped off some of these perk names and uses for their future titles too...)
Overall, still a good gaming experience 7 years after its release, but definitely not worth it's $20+ price tag. Worth picking up on a sale, but better off spending your money on another, more modernized and well-supported shooter. 7.5/10

- There is a lack of enemy types. I saw the same 7 or 8 enemies in the various biomes across the map.

Perhaps give it 6 months and check what progress has been made and revise if anyone is still playing it.
