Grid Autosport is tantalizingly close to being great. All the ingredients are there. Impressive technical competency, a large amount of content, outstanding attention to detail in graphics & audio. But it fails at the fundamentals. The driving just isn’t as fun and interesting as it is in Gran Turismo or Forza.
In order to make a track racing game interesting over the long haul, the tiniest details need to be just right. Not only does the underlying physics model need to be complex, but it needs to be communicated to the player just right so they can instinctively feel what’s going on. The camera angle plays a huge part in this, which is easy to demonstrate in Gran Turismo. In Gran Turismo the bumper cam is the defacto way to play the game. The alternative angles, like behind the car, are all hilariously awful in execution. You can’t see properly where you’re going, it’s completely stiff in an almost unnerving way. When you use the bumper cam you can see the car rearing back, diving forwards, tilting to the sides, all in subtle ways which tell you how stable the car is, or if you’re about to spin out etc.
Grid Autosport feels simplistic. It isn’t complex enough, it’s too smooth. It’s almost hard to nail down exactly what it does wrong, because there’s plenty of great arcade racing games which aren’t boring. They’re usually much faster than Grid Autosport. Like the original Grid which met criticism from simulator fans who thought it felt like a racing sim sped up to 200% speed. I loved that aspect of it! When you drive down the same tracks in Grid Autosport at a more realistic speed, you’re given time to reflect on how nothing interesting is going on in the game. In Gran Turismo it’s engaging to drive slow piece of crap cars thanks to the exceptional feel of the physics. In Grid Autosport I’m struggling to be excited about the fastest cars in the world.
The career mode in Grid Autosport is easily 50+ hours long, and I will never finish it. The game isn’t good enough to hold my interest. When I first got the game I played it a lot. Now I fire it up once a month and play it for a hour or two. That’s the level of engagement I get from it. And that’s fine! It has its merits, which make it a nice experience. But when their novelty fades, you’re left with only the underlying game to carry it. That’s where it fails.
Despite this, I’m recommending it. It’s ok! Good enough to grab on sale. The first 10 hours or so are great. It’s only after that the tedium hits you like a ton of bricks.

This War of Mine is a Rare Gem that every gamer should consider playing. Set in a roughly Balkan setting the game forces players into the roles of civilians trapped in a war zone, or more uncomfortably if you upload your own photo, yourself in the same situation. Scavenging for supplies, fending off hunger, bandits, and even depression just become a part of the daily life.
Few games so effectively marry story and gameplay together, and This War of Mine constantly drives your actions towards the moral questions hanging over the game. To what ends will you go to survive? Would you kill for a tin of processed food? What toll would that take?
Aesthetically the game is a canvass of gray shades, and the soundtrack is muted. While there are a few clunky patches here an there, it's well worth giving This War of Mind a look. Anyone who plays shooters regularly owes it to themselves to consider what the other side of a war might look like.

I never though I would enjoy this game as much as I did.
When I first took a look, it seemed like a whole lot of micro management with a broken morality system.
By the same token, few games have been able to elicit genuine emotion from me.
That said, this game is an instant classic in the steam library and a must have for those looking for a neat twist on the survival genre.  You play as a group of survivors in a war torn city just trying to make ends meet.  You’re lucky if you don't get shot by rebel soldiers or fellow scavengers, and luckier if you get to eat that day.  Go through the day trying to mediate the needs of your own group with that of your neighbors and then journey into the night looking for supplies to keep yourselves going.  There will be moral challenges, yes, but not necessarily any repercussions.  Careful and clever players will find ways to commit crimes with impunity; however, this does not mean you will escape the emotional consequences, as your party attempts to cope with the atrocities they commit to survive in war.  Teamwork is necessary, but others… they are expendable.  Or, perhaps, you value their lives and will attempt, at all opportunities to be good and ethical – good luck.
Ultimately the game is a masterpiece, forcing a set of mind of survival and melancholia with its powerful imagery, music and dialogue.  I’m only about 15 hours in, and I want more; and so will you.
Also, the soundtrack is free and it’s a pretty nice listen.  So, there’s that.

I recommend this game, but not at its full 20 euro price. I pi!cked it up for 7,50 and consider it money well spent, at 20 euro's this review would be a thumbs down.
The game alternates days in which you can build, maintain and exploit your shelter and nights during which you run out to scavenge for food and components. Combat and stealth during these nights are implemented in a rudimentary fashion. There are also 'moral choices' but they don't really attribute to anything. You (as a player) can choose to feel bad about robbing the elderly or about killing thugs, but there's very little incentive to avoid these situations. The characters feel bad, but if they do get depressed or sad, there's many different buttons to push that can solve this.
The reservations stem from many small odd design choices, rather than any major flaws. Example: the inability to make potable water from rainwater by boiling it (allowing you to generate water by spending fuel, essentially). Example 2: the scavenging quickly becomes monotonous and predictable. The game is actually pretty easy if you have an eye for this type of gameplay.
I guess you're expected to feel bad about many of your actions, as a player. However, after killing an elderly couple in cold blood and stealing food from a hospital, my four survivors just sat around playing their guitars and one day later they had forgotton about all the horror. That sums it up really: there's too many weird and poor gamey mechanics implemented for the game to have any real emotional impact. And on top of that, the gameplay becomes repetitive quickly once you figure out the paths of least resistance for all basic requirements.
For all that, I had fun figuring out how to work it, even if it didn't last too long.

Given my love for Civ 5 I'm surprised this one didn't grab me too. It's just a tadge dull; lacking the diversity of gameplay that kept me going back to its predecessor. A couple of likes and peeves:
+A few new bells and whistles; I quite enjoyed quest progression, environmental hazards and synergies.
+At it's core it's a Civ game and plays thusly.
-Tech tree is hard to approach. Can very quickly become messy and advisor recommendations appear random.
-Too few civs and setup options, decreasing replay value. Civ bonuses lack impact.
-A lack of sense of progression. Tech advancements in Civ 5 changed your units and cities in a variety of ways as you advance through the ages, from warriors to tanks, catapults to rockets so on etc, and stramrolling an enemy civ way behind your tech level was always a good laugh. Beyond Earth doesn't provide this; as you upgrade your space marines become different space marines, tanks become different tanks.
-No civ specific units.
These are just the main peeves; I could go on but it's 3am, I'm half asleep watching a fairly poop horror movie so should wrap up. Unfortunately at this time it's fairly generic and lacks the magic found in 5. There are better turn based strategies out there. If you're new to the genre it's  may not be for you; try Civ 5. Enjoy Civ 5? Try the demo of Beyond Earth before purchase, but be skeptical as the end game is faaairly dull.
TL;DR I love Civ 5, play Civ 5, Civ 5, Civ...5....zzzzz

Wow, so it looks like the developer deleted my review from the forum discussions page since it won't post here.
Let's try again.  I don't bother saving these when I write them, so here's the condensed pros/cons and overall rating.
Pros:
-Good concept.
-Awesome monsters, creatures and overall solid graphics.
-Multiplayer would be awesome...
-Easy to pick up and play.
-It's not technically broken and glitches are few (i.e. it'll run, it saved my progress, didn't crash, etc.)
Cons:
-Many unfinished ideas (thirst/hunger system, empty inventory screen, etc.)
-No strategy involved.  Enemies just run at you and are easy.  Sheer numbers disguised as "challenge."  Their attacks are all melee or cheap status FX like poison, stun, etc. from which there is no cure from because there's no inventory system even though it has a button!
-Terrible controls.  It's an action hack n' slash with hack n' slash RPG controls (left mouse to attack/right mouse to click and move).
-Huge delay in when you can attack enemies.  You have to target them individually, again like a hack n' slash RPG.  The combat is generally slow, slow, slow.
-Every arena seems to have the same 10 waves of enemies.
-Only 2 moves per playable character.
-For my money, the projectile characters are weak, unbalanced, slow to reload and useless.  If there was multiplayer I could see there being strategy or fun in choosing them but not in single.
-Zero variety in gameplay which gets boring FAST.
-Level up system is worthless (your health caps at 200 a few levels in).
-Game seems to be a month old and NOBODY is playing multiplayer it seems.  That should have warned me.
-Though the 4.99 budget tag seems tempting, I got more content out of the 99 cent Reveal the Deep than this game.
Overall:  3/10

I have played Puzzle Pirates for over 10 years now. If you like puzzles, interacting with others to do missions, build crews to take over islands, this is a great game to play. However, that only lasts for a short period of time. Eventually, you will find this game to be stagnant. The game developers/ocean masters "encourages" you to make suggestions on how to make the game better. But, the majority of the time, your answer falls on deaf ears. You are allowed to create forum posts to give suggestions but then you, out of the blue, you will find that some developer or Om has locked your thread when it is gaining  momentum because someone suggested the same thing 13 years ago and nothing was done about it.
The developers and ocean masters dont care about the game anymore. 10 years ago, we used to have OMs come online and host events, now they sit on their spy ships and read petitions and give you temporary bans for accidentally mistyping a curse word which then causes it to evade the pirate filter.
Developers dont do much to make changes to the game. From the perspective of a former active pirate on this game, they spend their time developing content for the latest mystery boxes, which one generally comes out once a month, and you get 1 mystery box for every $10 you spend on doubloons in the game. Once in a while there is a new puzzle or sea monster hunt to get the players excited about something new to the game. To give you an accurate timeframe, I am writing this in September 2017. The last puzzle that was introduced into the game was Patching, in July 2012. That is 5 YEARS ago. The Last Sea monster hunt to be added to the game was Kraken Hunts, in June/July 2014.
Aside for the lack of the developers to provide the game with new content, there are a few game mechanics that are just disfunctional. In my opinion, one of the biggest issues is the trading system. If you have an item and wish to sell it, you have to tell people on a trade chat while you are online in order to attempt to sell it. If you are offline, you cannot sell your item. This inefficient method of buying/selling items causes your chat to be overloaded with messages and most experienced players end up muting them.
So yea, if you like puzzles, meeting people, feel free to check out this game. But, eventually, the longer you play, you will start to see inefficiencies, and then, because you care, you are going to make suggestions....Then your suggestions will fall on deaf ears because the developers and OMs do not care.

I bought this game and MSC and played them back-to-back to get a brief impression of what each was and which of the two was "better". For me, Jalopy was an easy winner.
Both games are in EA, and both are very unfinished. Jalopy is filled with inaccessible areas, the tutorial drags on and is borderline broken, and the AI is ridiculously stupid. What this game has that MSC doesn't, however, is potential. Jalopy oozes atmosphere, and unlike MSC, there is always an objective to work towards. The driving is servicable, and the trip is broken up by tons of emergent gameplay via the weather system, the way your car dynamically breaks down, the other drivers on the road, and the condition of the roads themselves.
Jalopy takes you on a very interesting trip through the Eastern bloc, with beautiful visuals and pretty nice environments. Your resources are limited, and it always feels like you're running on empty as you drive to the nearest checkpoint. It's almost like a modern day Oregon Trail, except you're taking care of your car instead of a party of people. Deciding whether to stay the night in a motel but lose money and time, to stock up on supplies but weigh your car down, to go a shorter route or to take the longer one with a gas station, all are little choices that make Jalopy interesting.
So for me, Jalopy is an easy choice over My Summer Car. It's like choosing Half-Life 2 over Postal 2, if I had to make a comparison. That being said, do not expect a finished experience. Jalopy is short, buggy, and unfinished, but I will definitely return to the game when it is in a more finished state.

Not sure what all of the hate is about over this one.
It's puzzle quest with a different theme in a F2P format. I didn't think I'd be playing this too much, but I've actually put in a good bit of time. Bit of a mix of strategy and frustration and I have not found the F2P mechanic all that limiting. If you are obsessed with advancing quickly or be able to recover instantly from a loss, yes - sooner or later you're going to need to lay some money down.
As other positive reviewers have stated, develop your free characters - use your game currency for character slots and just play the game. Repeat your missions until you get all of the possible loot - some of the tutorials missions only have 1 reward, however after that they have from 2-4. After the first day or two, you should get 2 free characters from a large pool. I thought I was lucky with 2 uncommon heroes - modern hawkeye and cap, but my son received a rare spiderman and a legendary x-force wolverine.
The event system has a reward structure of its own, and you can win many of the missions even with a new team. Most of the missions I have seen have a pre-assigned hero that joins you for that fight and you can leverage them to help win fights you would not normally be able to pull off.
If you sink everything into 1 character you're going to be sitting around waiting for a long time if they get ko'd in a fight, so try to spread the iso-8 around when your can. Unlike PQ, you do not heal automatically after a fight. Your characters need time to heal up and this is lengthened a bit if they were ko'd. You can acquire medkits which will give you a full heal, but if you are reckless, rely too heavily on one character to win your missions - or just not very good at the game you will burn through them quckly.

The gameplay is so much fun - a great time killer. The same old Bejeweled/PQ basic mechanic of 'matching 3 gems or more' is there, a huge appeal for its fanbase.
Also, with the quests system, there's a sense of progression unlike the old Bejeweled. You actually need to check your opponents level prior to accepting the quest, rearrange your roster, heal your heroes or arming the power ups to make things easier.
In addition to great quests, we also have very decent graphic and badass OSTs. Granted that it's not AAA's 3D levels, but the detailed chars and charming designs are more than enough. The actual Heads Up Display is clear and concise, allowing players to reach the menu they want to use. There's also a simple descriptions to each of heroes' powers so you can understand what you're going to invoke before deciding (since the point placement is permanent and not respecable).
The video options are barebones, but really there's no need Anti Aliasing and those fancy Physx Tesselation whatever it's called options. You can use your native resolutions - at least that's commonly used nowadays - to prevent screen tearing. Well, in my case, it autodetected everything so it's click and play.
Game performance overall is silky smooth even on my mid-end rig. Transitions between scenes are quite short, no boring loading screen that takes ages to finish and so far zero crash.
Now after all good stuffs, here comes the problem, microtransactions. In order to upgrade your heroes within reasonable timeframe, you need to either be lucky with rewards rolls, or grind the best rewarding quess repeatedly, or purchasing DLCs. That's where the major problem is. All would have been a little better if the quest rewards can make up for it so free players don't have to bang against the wall out of frustration.
Multiplayer is missing, but I'd imagine it'd be great to have a match up against other people real time matching gems together.
Great Free to Play game ridden by micro transactions. It's a real shame, the game has a chance to be other FTP killers on Steam, but severely missed it. In the end though, I'd play until I am tired with the brick wall that prevents me from advancing, or bored.

Ok so I've heard a lot of people are having trouble starting it up! Here's what you can do.
open the Control Panel (you can do it by using WinKey+X key combination) go to Programs > Programs and Features, click the Turn Windows features on or off link, find the Legacy components on the list, enable DirectPlay and click OK to install it.
After you have done that, go to your Rollercoaster Tycoon file, should be in something like this....
D:\Program Files (x86)\Steam\steamapps\common\Rollercoaster Tycoon 2
Mines in the D: drive normally its in C: though. Find the .exe and right click it and go to "Troubleshoot compatability" use whatever setting it comes up with. That SHOULD fix it! Hopefully this helps folks because this really is a fun little game to play.

is a swashbuckling spacefaring game featuring beautiful scenery and well-designed combat, but a rather thin story arc. If you are looking for an immersive space RPG with good dialogue and engaging narratives, then this game is probably not for you. The characters never feel "real" due to the limited animation and clunky dialogue, and the plot is entirely linear.
However, the game really shines whenever you are flying about the system in your ship, completing quests and blasting into oblivion anyone that pisses you off (or you get blown up, that happens too). It will be important to note that while the game feels like it is 3D, the player can only travel along a 2D plane, and combat also takes place as if on a flat surface; small NPC fighter craft can and do travel in a 3D manner to cover up this limit to the combat mechanic, so that it still appears like a proper space battle. Combat and flight controls are simple and intuitive, allowing you to dive right into combat from the get go, and you do get tossed straight into the fight from the start.
There are a large number of side quests for the player to complete so that you can gather resources and grind out larger and better ships, weapon systems, components, etc. In general, the quests do vary enough to keep you interested until later in the game. Asteroid mining exists but does not feel rewarding enough, as blowing up enemy ships is a more efficient use of your time. There is also a limited trading/commerce system where commodities are have greater value in certain systems than others, but it seems like a side show and has limited impact, except at the beginning of the game when you are trying to grind out your first couple of ships.
Despite its drawbacks and limitations, Rebel Galaxy does offer great value for what it is. A wonderful no-frills space combat simulator with no pretentions. Veterans of games like Escape Velocity and Endless Sky will appreciate where this game is coming from, though there are some differences such as an inability to "flip" stations by attacking them, or acquiring a fleet of ships (you only ever get one). Oh you remember playing Escape Velocity way back when? Congrats, you are old. If you want to relive those glory days or just want to spend time wrecking things in space, this game is for you.

This game had wonderful narration, a compelling story and neat gameplay. Which is pretty much overshadowed by the utter lack of content, the abysmal AI and the quite annoying difficulty because of it.
Dungeons 2 is basically in competition with the game known as "War for the Overworld" and when you compare the two, this one flat out loses.
Here are a list of things that Dungeons 2 doesn't have, or support.
-Workshop Compatibility.
-Map Editor, and access to all the units, props and environment while in Editor.
-Themed Dungeons.
-Ability to use the "Good" guys and turn them to your side.
-Survival Mode.
-Home Realm. (Plays the part of your MAIN Dungeon)
-Both limited and unlimited variatons of the gold resource.
And yet it's competitor does.
When you go into the main menu for both games, Dungeons 2 has next to no options for anything, and War for the Overworld has a whole slew of things for you to do. Ontop of that, the games narrator's are about equal in terms of humor, comedic timing, story telling, helpfulness, and skill. The Campaigns of both games are fairly close as well from a storytelling standpoint.
(SPOILER)
To addon to the abysmal AI point I made above: From a Narrative standpoint the final battle of the Undead DLC where you bring back the prime evil. The other two aspects of evil are more focused on killing you, than actually claiming the ritual site. Any aspect of evil (Again this is a narrative point) winning, would lead to the creation of the Prime Evil. However the AI actively lets the Good guys win, just so they can focus on attacking YOU. Meaning the AI goes balls to the walls trying to kill you, pretty much avoiding eachother.
This basically culminates in you losing way more often than you rightly should, as the AI is constantly agressive towards you, pretty consistently neutral/passive towards eachother, and lets good win the day, just for the sake of killing you - One of the Aspects of evil, simply because you're the player. Right, thats a gameplay mechanic.
Ontop of that annoying little mechanic, you will lose. A lot. Due to stupid AI shenanigans, and agressiveness. Meaning early on in the missions, you'll wind up being attacked by quickly overwhelming forces, unless you play perfectly. Which is fine, except in missions such as the one described above, you're attacked right off the bat by two enimies on a set path to your base, and one enemy who randomly teleports into your base. Each force being especially difficult to fight off.
Atleast the AI in War for the Overworld are more realistic, and consistent.
But when you come down to it, content wise Dungeons 2 loses by a landslide, the DLC for both games are pretty bad though. Except for like one DLC for each game, Dungeons 2 has a DLC that basically lets you finish the story, and War for the Overworld has a DLC that basically picks up where the games ending left off.
Again though, War for the Overworld has Workshop compatibility, a whole slew of game modes, and an editor. Dungeons 2 has DLC - which do you think is better.
Edit: I just realized that the War for the Overworld team actually replies to comments in their updates, and take feedback and ideas to heart. Holy crap they beat Dungeons 2 so bad.

Credentials: I have been playing and collecting Magic the Gathering since the mid 1990s, this is the second revision of my review for this game, the original was written at 51.2 hours, the 1st revision at 953 and the 2nd at 1234. I cannot recommend this game either now, or when I first reviewed it.
After using my gold to buy boosters to complete sets, I was not given the boosters I paid for. This was made worse by the fact that I paid for my gold with real money.
Numerous cards have been bugged or broken with each release and have been left unfixed for 3 or more months, which has been the frequency thus far, at which the developers release patches, they will not release patches for serious or critical bugs outside of content release patches, so the game stays in a state of being permanently bugged.
The game has a tendency to randomly hang mid-turn when playing vs matches against human opponents online, requiring you to either concede and lose rank, or terminate the game's process and restart the game.
The game on occasion prevents you from stopping the phase transition clock, which can prevent you from casting spells.
Trying to connect to a vs match against somebody online can sometimes take up to 10 minutes, with the game either repeatedly disconnecting for no reason, or hanging in an unrecoverable way that requires the player to terminate the game's process and restart the game.
2HG games experience worse connection problems still and are extremely unstable.
Anti-aliasing and shadow casting in the game has been broken since launch. This makes the edges in game geometry(e.g. cards) jagged and shadows appear as solid black blocks.
This game has suffered numerous security vulnerabilities along the way, some of which still exist despite being reported many times, some enable players to cheat, crash or freeze the game client.
Starting from the SOI patch, they have started to remove cards that are relatively complex to code for them to code(Archangel of Tithes for example), substituting then with another, as well as omitting any such cards from future set releases on a "nothing is sacred" basis, Emrakul, the Promised End; the most important card in the set, was omitted from the EMN release for example.
There are also many minor problems the game either has, or has had that are too numerous to list here.
Their release schedule is 4 content releases per year, aligning with the paper set release schedule, half of the content releases have delayed by anywhere between 1 and 6 months.
They have done little to nothing since release to enhance the game, add features, additional play modes, customization options and so on and have indicated this is unlikely to happen.
Magic Duels has been positioned more as an advert for paper MTG or Magic Online than a game in its own right and thus has little support.
This game violates multiple rules of paper Magic The Gathering. Turn phases do not work the same way, there is no upkeep step for example, which renders some spells less effective, nor is there any way to specify trigger order on the stack, which renders some combos broken.
The game does not permit 4 of any non basic land card to be played in a deck as per constructed rules, instead, card count is restricted by rarity. 1x Mythic, 2x Rare, 3x Uncommon, 4x Common. This causes severe balancing issues to occur, because all of the cards featured in this game, are designed and play tested around the common rule that up to 4 copies of any card may be played.
Set releases are incomplete, they do not release every card in each set, with between a third and a half of each set excluded, this further causes balancing issues and substantially reduces the quality of the content this game has to offer, as many fun, low impact cards are excluded, as well as some of the more popular cards each set has to offer.
The game features a collection of starter box cards from many past and present sets and because these cards have not been balanced, or developed alongside recent set releases; which consist mostly of current Standard legal cards, they can and have caused severe balancing issues that are left unfixed for months on end between updates, this can make the game tedious and repetitive to play. This problem would be substantially less severe, if they invested more time into analyzing the impact the cards in question are likely to have on the format and/or if they more frequently patched the game.
Wizards of the Coast, who own the Magic The Gathering franchise, are notoriously averse to investing in or committing to products that deviate from their core business, which is paper Magic The Gathering. Because of this, Magic Duels does not presently have the resources either financial, human or otherwise to become the successful, feature rich digital trading card game that long term players such as myself know it can be, and until this changes, this game will not fulfill its potential.
There have been recent indications(2015 / 2016) that their attitude towards digitizing their game may be evolving to a degree, but as things presently stand, this game seems to have only minimal support of its owners ergo, its long term future looks bleak, which should be foremost on your mind if you intend to buy content or invest substantial amounts of your time into collecting cards and building decks.
Having devoted well over a thousand hours of my time to this game as a lifelong fan of MTG, I cannot recommend this game, either to players who are new to Magic The Gathering, or to experienced long term players. I'd recommend this game with a few conditions:
1.) If you play do not cash out the starting heroes they give you: Iron Man, Storm, Black Widow and Hawkeye. They all synergize well and if you cash them out before finishing the prologue you may be stuck trying to grind iso8 points to get them back.
2.) The purchasing of heroes, with the exception of Black Widow / Hawkeye is random, you do not get to pick what you pay for which is intentional way to get you to spend money... on a puzzle game. Yep.
3.) Unlocking hero abilities requires acquiring the same hero again or paying $$.  So if you have Hawkeye without his 2 main abilities unlocked you must get the same version of him to be able to unlock it. You could do that with the quests or buy it.
Outside of these mechanics in the game the puzzling is a shared board of gems that you and the AI or human opponents use to gain energy for abilities. There is a bit of strategy to get gems to drop in a 4 or 5 or combo as well as certain heroes abilties use certain colors. To me this is a cool / unique gameplay alternative to each player having their own set of gems.  The gameplay can be very quick but also strategic in that there is no turn timer, so you can try to work out the best option each turn.  For a puzzle game and based on Marvel I think this format is fairly unique and fun, the only downer is:
a.) not being able to pick what hero you purchase or unlock
b.) instead of them charging $4.99 or $9.99 they try to make all their money back in game, which shows.
Ultimately this game could be much more enjoyable with an upfront price tag and less attempts to channel players into spending. I'd give it a 7/10 just on the fun factor, if they made some changes I'd happily pay $9.99 and say this is a 8 or 9/10.

I'm honestly conflicted here. On the one hand, I really love well-designed match-3 puzzle games; I can't even tell you how many hours I blew on the original Puzzle Quest, and I even enjoyed that wonky hex-based Puzzle Quest Galactrix game right up the point where the constant crash bugs♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off too much to continue. Marvel Puzzle Quest: Dark Reign is absolutely the best game they've released so far. You play as an ever-growing band of Avengers characters, smashing your way through H.A.M.M.E.R. forces and supervillains alike, gathering power and taking back S.H.I.E.L.D. headquarters from sinister, interloping bureaucrats the only way you know how: by matching colored tiles in rows of 3, 4, or 5. Players familiar with earlier Puzzle Quest titles will be aware that they tend to go overboard throwing crazy equipment and abilities at you, and Marvel Puzzle Quest is no exception. Before each mission, you select up to three characters to fight on your team, each of which has different fighting styles (reflected in the amount of damage you inflict by matching particular colors) and special moves which you charge up by gathering enough tiles of the correct color. It sounds dorky (probably because it really is extraordinarily dorky), but all the same it leads to surprisingly gripping gameplay; victory can be snatched from the jaws of defeat when you spot that perfect 5-in-a-row of blue tiles, snag it for an extra turn, and then have Black Widow unload Stun Darts into the opposing team, leaving them helpless while you pound their stupid liberty-hating faces in.
The roster of characters is huge, and each character feels thematically correct and unique enough that you want to collect 'em all. Along with the fact that they scraped the Marvel barrel looking for bodies to fill your roster, there are also tons of alternate costume versions of characters. For example, long before you find the Amazing Spider Man (a stun-locking, party-healing defense-oriented character), you unlock the Bombastic Bag Man, one of Spidey's goofier alter egos who instead plays as a Bugs Bunny-style prankster, disabling enemy attacks and swapping tiles around the field as he sees fit. Putting together a well-balanced team with abilities designed around what you're about to face can make the difference between a swift victory and a painful, drawn out death.
On the other hand, the game's got some of the most onerous micropayment systems I've ever seen. There are two primary in-game currencies: ISO-8 and Hero Points. You can gather ISO-8 quickly by completing new missions, or painfully slowly by replaying missions you've already beaten. ISO-8 is spent primarily on leveling up your heroes and upgrading their abilities, and doing so occasionally unlocks new characters. The other currency is Hero Points. These are earned at a rate of 50 per week if you sign in at least once a day every day, and are given out as prizes after completing certain missions. There's no way to farm these, and their primary use is to upgrade your roster size. You can only have so many characters on your team, and buying more slots costs a gradually escalating number of Hero Points. At first this isn't too painful; you can get 100 points for $0.99 in the in-game store, and that's enough to buy two character slots when you first start playing. But the cost rises as your roster expands. I didn't even finish the prologue before it hit 150 per slot, and at that point I had 4 more characters on deck, just waiting to be activated. This wouldn't be that bad, except that unlocked characters expire if you don't launch them quickly, eradicating your earned rewards entirely.
Even if that doesn't bother you, you then need to train your characters to make them in any way competitive. Level 1 characters are generally useless, and getting them up to speed with the rest of your party costs both ISO-8 for levels and Hero Points to rush the process of getting their abilities and level cap up to full power. In theory, a patient player could do all of this by playing at a snail's pace, farming ISO-8 constantly, and waiting for the trickle of Hero Points to add up, but this is honestly not the sort of game that someone dabbles in; it's a brutal time-sink, and the psuedo-multiplayer mode in which you attack other teams and get attacked in return gives you even more incentive to always be playing and buffing and building your team to higher power levels.
If the prices were reasonable, I wouldn't be complaining nearly so much, but the math just gets real ugly real fast. Getting a single character from zero to maxed out can easily run you $10-$20 (depending on how many abilities they have and how high their max level is), and there are many, many characters to buff. You can buy in-game currency at a more efficient rate by buying the currency packs, which come in $9.99, $39.99, and $99.99 (!!!) sizes. When I realized that seeing all the game's content and satisfying my completionist urges would require buying multiple $99.99 packs, I decided it was time to pull the plug. Play at your own risk.

Not a terrible game as the mass of negative reviews may indivate, however, there are some major drawbacks which certain gamers won't get on with.
The Bad:
1) Filled with "micro"payments (not that micro really...) where you can pay to get ahead.
2) Although the steam version was released 5 days ago, you're competing with iOS players who have obviously had a long time to play. They have more stuff, better characters, and there's many PvP tournaments to unlock more, better, characters which are virtually unobtainable due to their inherent advantage. If you were to pay to get yourself competitive, you'd be looking at paying thousands of pounds. Maybe they could have given Steam users a boost, or segregated the communities or had steam only contests so it's at least level?
3) There's a lot of required characters for limited time events. Some are provided for use in certain battles, but I've found limited time games blocked from me because I don't have Iron Man Mk40.
4) There's nothing original here, it's the same old game with some Marvel characters.
5) It takes gold to unlock more character slots. Gold is available in finite amounts from the various single player and PvP events, but frustratingly once you receive a character card you are given 7 days to put it in your roster (either by increasing the roster or destroying an existing character card) else you lose your new character. It appears more characters have been added over time, as iOS players gathered enough gold to boost their slots. As a steam player this is a further handicap.
6) Your characters have health which regenerates over time, but if they're K/O'd in battle, you lose them for an hour or more as they regenerate. You have 5 health packs for an instant revive, and a new health pack generates every 36 minutes. This does allow you to keep going, but you may find as you get into the game you are reluctant to try harder battles because your team will take damage which means you'll have to stop playing for a while. This is more designed for players who have half an hour to kill at regular intervals, rather than someone who wants to play solidly.
The Good:
1) It is puzzle quest, and it's free (sort of) so if you can resist paying, it's not bad.
2) Since the iOS players have such an advantage, you're never competitive so there's less of a compulsion to be right up there. This makes it easier not to pay, and if you enjoy the challenge of being an underdog, it's not bad. Of course, if you're naturally very competitive you'll hate this game because there's no way you can do that without spending a sum which could be better used as a deposit on a mortgage.
3) The game appears solid and bug free.
4) It is simple enough to leave the game running in the background as your team heals when you do other things.
I'd probably give this about 4/10, and would only recommend it to fans of Marvel, casual gamers who like CandyCrush/Bejewelled, and anyone wanting a free to play game who can resist the urge to pay for in game purchases. This is nothing special, it's a run of the mill game designed to milk money from gamers, but it can still be fun.

- Could use some polish. Often, finding the best spot to sell your loot is a pain when a simple extra piece of interface would've solved this issue.
+ Good combat mechanics: think Assassin's creed black flag with a bit more complexity (but still the same action fun)
+ Can't really fault it, it's the fun and fast paced black flag combat with some much better ship customisation which drastically changes the way you fight, allowing for more playstyles and ultimately more combat approach opportunities.
+ Good practical ship customisation, plenty of ugprades, weapons, components to choose from.
- Bad visual ship customisation (literally nothing here)
+ Good world interaction and dynamism. (things that happen in the world affect you, the stations around you, etc. and there's always something happening)
+ Good soundtrack but...
- Very few tracks, becomes bery repetitive with time, however...
+ The game lets you swap around your own tracks instead of game tracks for exploration, combat, menu, etc.
- unlockables are badly tiered and not paced properly.
- So far the story is kinda meh.
+ Not that it matters because this is above all a space exploration and fighting game.
+ A few factions that do things in the world and interact solidly with each other but...
- There are too few, and they lack proper lore and atmosphere. Feels like they pulled out a name out of a name generator and that was it. So far, no faction loyalty quests.
- Side Quests are repetitive and boring. Think Skyrim with a slightly bigger range.
All in all, this game is easily a 7.5/10, even an 8 if you're into more than just the combat and are willing to spend a little time trading.
If you see this game for less than £5 or 10$, buy it, it is definitely worth every penny of that.

Broadsides naval combat in space? Yes please.
Rebel Galaxy does feel a bit like Microprose Pirates! of old: trade and combat on both sides of the law, with vying factions in a frontier-like setting. You can follow along with the main storyline or go off and do your own thing, as you will. There are combat advantages to either a fast and manoeuvrable craft or a heavy battlewagon, so there's no one way to "win".
I was quite impressed by the engine performance of the game - while I didn't have all the anti-aliasing and stuff ramped all the way up, it performed quite well on my aging laptop, in spite of the broad range of visual effects going on.
The storyline is linear, medium-length, and doesn't have a lot of layers to it. I would have liked there to be more of it, certainly, but that's a testament to how much I was enjoying it. That said, it's not a game style that really needs a complex story in order to be enjoyable. It's quite good for picking up, playing for a couple of missions and putting back down again once you've had a good sortie or two.
I got it on sale for NZ$7.19, but in retrospect it was well worth the NZ$23.99 I didn't pay.

Here we have another overhead shooter, and you know what? I'm perfectly alright with that. Shootemups are among my most-played genre, and I'm always on the lookout for something new and interesting. Although a game might consist of standard fare like shooting aliens, zombies, or - in
's case - demons, there's usually a handful of unique qualities that set it apart from the pack. Unfortunately,
stands out by being really bad.
Only a few people are ruthless enough to survive wave after wave of the damned, in the Underworld's favorite game show. Upon starting this game, you'll be prompted to create a profile and choose a character. Each of the three contestants has their own weapon and special ability. If you want to win, my advice is to choose Elise. If you pick either Jason or Walter, and attempt to play alone, then you're almost guaranteed to fail. More on that in just a moment.
Two of the contestants carry guns, which leads to one of the interesting but flawed aspects of
. In order to shoot a demon, you have to be standing still. Aiming is extremely simple, because all you have to do is hold the left mouse-button and drag the cursor on-top of a monster. You can't waste bullets even if you want to. Reloading is also instantaneous as long as you continue mashing the "r" key. The thing is, I don't mind that the contestants can't shoot while moving, nor that they can't be controlled with a "WASD" setup. The problems start happening due to balance issues and poor mechanics.
Elise, the handgun user, is far better than the other two characters, and this can be attributed almost entirely to poor design-decisions. Walter carries a sniper rifle and has to reload after every shot. His special ability allows him to shoot a row of enemies at once. The problem is that unlike regular-shooting, he has to be facing the general direction of the enemy he wants to hit. This means that he actually has to clumsily move to face the enemy, then take the shot. You could fire one regular-shot to help center your aim, but then you have to reload, and then make sure that your finger is not holding down the mouse-button (special abilities are triggered with the space bar). This convoluted process crops up constantly, and will result in you taking a lot of damage.
Jason uses an axe. His special ability is a spin-attack. While this contestant has twice as much health than the other two, he's going to get hurt far more often. Monsters don't actually swing their arms, grab at the player, or do anything that could inflict pain. If they get close enough, then you'll probably lose some life. The axe behaves similarily to the guns, Jason won't swing unless the cursor is hovering over a nearby monster. This disconnected feeling makes melee much harder than it should be. When combat is this inconsistent, your best bet is to stay as far away as possible.
So now we turn to Elise. Her special ability allows her to fire her gun at an extremely fast rate for a few seconds. This ability doesn't have a cool-down period, and it'll chew through the toughest monsters. As long as you keep mashing that reload key, and pressing the space-bar every few seconds, you'll coast through almost every wave.
Alongside the minor creatures that shamble towards you, there are a few elite boss monsters. These abominations have some unique attribute that isn't designed well at all. In wave 6, you'll face an elite that stuns you every few seconds. There is absolutely nothing you can do about getting stunned. Only Elise and her magic pistol has a chance, and things can still go wrong. As I mentioned earlier, players can't move while shooting. If Elise (or Walter) is getting pushed by a monster, that counts as moving. In wave 5, there's a giant fiend that sprays poison everywhere, which you also can't hope to avoid. The wave 8 boss is a giant spider. This creature can stun the player, but it has almost half the health of the earlier boss, which doesn't make much sense. The wave 10 boss is just one long game of keep-away. This cow-looking monster is pretty fast, and he gets a little help from some friends, but he's still pretty easy.
Upon surviving these ten waves, you win the tournament and are awarded points. Said points can unlock new maps. These newer locations have different layouts, but the waves are the exact same. Changing the difficulty just gives most creatures more hit-points. Once you figure out how to survive those ten waves, there's really nothing else to look out for. I suppose playing with other people online could make the game slightly more interesting, but what's more liable to happen is that everyone will be bored. As long as somebody chooses Elise, and abuses her special ability, then the only potential threat is the wave 6 boss.
tries to have a survival element, by requiring that the player stay hydrated and nourished. After each wave, the player is awarded a point, which can be used towards health, ammo, food, or water. You're never going to need to waste those precious points on anything but health and ammo. Your hunger & thirst gauges are easily managed by the copious pills left behind by the undead. I don't mind the idea, but when there's no follow-through, it's just an unnecessary distraction.
Even with all of these major issues, I still have a couple nitpicks to share. As if playing the Sniper wasn't bad enough, most enemies have odd amounts of HP, like 238, 340, and even 105. I'm complaining about this because the Sniper's bullets do 100 points of damage each. I think this guy would be far more effective if the monsters didn't require so many additional shots; having monsters with 100, 200, and 300 HP seems far more sensible. Sometimes when a demon is killed, its corpse can fall over top of other monsters, which stops you from shooting.
I understand that
was developed by one person, and it has some nice qualities like the music and atmosphere. The dancing girls are an amusing touch as well. However, there are far too many issues with this game for me to recommend it.

1st off, I have to admit I watched the trailers and the music they used for them had me hooked and had me amped to immerse myself in a world somewhat like firefly like what was depicted. Of course I immediately looked into that to see if the in-game soundtrack was similar or if it was all one big bullshot, before I made the purchase. The graphics aren't amazing compared to some others certainly, but they work well enough and add somewhat of a gritty feel and atmosphere to the game which all works in it's favor. They've presented space as somewhat colorful, and lively place that isn't necessarily welcoming. Truth be told, in my own subjective opinion the trailers only present half of what you're actually getting. From my initial impression this game actually lives up to the hype... amazing, i know. That being said, the story may have more depth, but the initial hook of trying to find your lost black-sheep aunt seems kinda 'typical' in some senses, but it works for a lead in and it grows from there to introduce you to all sorts(aliens, robots, swindlers, hooligans, etc) as it progresses. The voice acting isn't used for everything so there is some reading involved, but what is voiced is done well which is another step bonus as space games tend to feel like campy troped up amature hour most of the time any more.
I will add a few caveats here though, if you're expecting something complicated and fiddly.. don't. It's big starship battles certainly, and the controls are somewhat reminiscent of perhaps the ship battles in AC: Black Flag which isn't a bad thing. It's more arcadey at heart, although the underlying system is much more than that.. Its just presented in such a way that's very easy to sink into and enjoy in a light hearted way. The controls in general are also very easy and no more or less than what they need to be for this type of title. Played it with a mouse and keyboard but I'm going to be testing the gamepad side of it next, also I noted that on the launcher there was an option to select Ps4 button prompts so if thats the type you're using they've got you covered which is nice and I wish more devs would take note of that.
To be fair I'm not very far into it, but even if it's just a short game there's plent of sandbox content in there with tons of random events some of which feel like they were deliberately put there to troll you; such as mercenaries and other factions spewing out the occasional distress beacon, only to fly off when you arrive... I'm assuming they're trying to bait smaller targets and not necessarily something bristling with guns and the ability to resolve minor disputes with an unplanned sudden finality.
As it stands, I'm already looking forward to my next session. So if you are looking for a good sci-fi sandbox romp with somewhat typical plot, I'd say this is a good one to check out.
I could go on and on about how amazing this game is, but I won't.  I've got to get back to it, play it and thank us later.

EDITED FROM AN EARLIER POSITIVE REVIEW
EDIT 9/29/17: I run a private server (hosted through Vilayer), and promote said server in order to try to do my part to keep this game alive.  According to the Steam chart website, the game is down to a peak of roughly 130 players per day.  It has steadily gone down since release, unfortunately.
My point is that I have tried to do my part (after starting out negatively) to promote the game and get others to play it.
Today, the devs released a new patch that essentially broke the game.  Tamed animals saw their HP nerfed by 90% or so, making them basically unusable for fear of them getting killed by weak, low-level mobs.  Flying speed for all flying types (brooms and potions) was severely nerfed, to the point where my character can run faster than he can fly.  Neither of these things was addressed in the patch notes, so it was an unpleasant surprise logging into the game tonight.
Later, a dev admitted that the flying nerf was overdone, a mistake, and that they would test it "internally" and possibly fix it in a later patch. My claim regarding tames being nerfed was met with incredulity, despite several other posts from players saying the same thing.
Devs said they would be introducing new content almost every week; last "new content" was three patches ago and consisted of an overhyped NPC that was riduclously underpowered (and so, so easy to kill for any level player).  Basically fluff.
I know this is a small dev team, and lord knows I've done my best to support them, but the game is unplayable in its current state.  I don't know what else to say.  Two months in and it appears the devs are out of ideas and/or lack a clear roadmap of how to proceed.  Very frustrating as the game has so, so much promise.
EDIT 8/28/17: Many of the Official servers have experienced major stability issues due to what appears to be game engine/rendering/PhysX issues.  The devs have worked hard to do what they can, and still seem committed to the game long-term.  I'm still enjoying the game immensely, and when my Official server is down, I've tried various private servers to get my "fix."  In the long run, I'm hopeful they'll get the bugs worked out and make this game what it appears it can be.
Original: My first review of this game was negative due to the AMD "low level fatal error" debacle.  Devs *finally* fixed it up and now the game seems accessible to most players.
I've got around 30 hours in-game so far.  FPS isn't where it needs to be, but I have some faith that the devs will get it optimized as time goes on.  One minor troubling thing to me is that the devs seem reluctant to push out hotfixes; we've had, on average, a patch every 5 days or so since release.  Other EA games I've played (ARK, Conan, etc.) seemed to push out hotfixes daily, if not hourly (esp ARK).  These devs don't, for whatever reason, which means that older (existing) bugs persist, and bugs that come with new content aren't immediately addressed.
The game itself is a blast to play, but the grind can be real.  It all depends on how you play the game.  If you're a "prepper" type like me, you tend to grind for mana, mats, etc., to be prepared for cave runs and the like.
I like where the game is now a month after release, and look forward to what comes in the future!

If you thought Civ V on the slowest stting took forever, then THIS will teach you otherwise. The ENTIRE GAME feels incredibly slow. I've seen snails get a move on faster. BACKWARDS! If you haven't played Civ in a while ... don't get this. Get Civ V with all its DLCs and expansions on a sale. It's a way better game and feels a lot more complete.
This entire game feels like it was supposed to be an expansion for the main game. And then cut off and sold seperately.
Just don't. Spare yourself the agony and go play Civ V instead.

After playing a fair bit of a game that is still in development, I think I can give it a review of its current state.
Citadel: Forged with fire is a great game and seems like there is endless things to do and achieve however once you achieve level 60 (which in all fairness is not exactly hard to achieve) and have a proper base built, you will find the game content lacking. There is nothing more after you craft the so wanted end gear which you intitially would think you would need it for higher level content. Honestly at level 30, any mob is killable.
Building in this gaming is great, it really is but the raiding makes it useless. The only way to defend your base is to pray others dont find your base. Once your base is found, enemies can easily demolish one wall in less that 5 minutes making hours of building and thought completely put to waste.
Taming is an interesting concept in this game. The only thing that has a proper use in taming is getting a big dragon later on, otherwise its a complete waste of time. Sure taming has bugs: pets just vanish, cant use the storage properly, etc, etc, but again, keep in mind this is an early access game. It is bound to have bugs, but developers seem to fix a series of them aswell as rethink some concepts which is great.
Gear is another story. Gear in this game is weird, there are magical properties which are basically buffs each piece gives however on items that theoritically give 2+ magical properties seem to be capped at just 1? Not sure if this is simply another bug or if there's actual gear that you can get with more buffs. Looting gear from enemies is the dumbest thing about this game. Sure they drop gear, but the gear you craft which is really, really easy to craft is always better than the one you pick up from enemies.
Sadly, I cannot recommend this game to anyone at it's current state and for what its worth (20$). Some concepts have to be added to make it so theres more we need to worry about and do (hunger and thirst), others have to be rethought (how raiding works). Aswell as a lot of content needs to be added so there's at least something to do later on. Gear drops must be implemented, and the magical properties fixed.

GRID Autosport does a lot to correct many of the issues I had with GRID 2. The cringe-inducing, over-the-top presentation has been toned way down. The narrator and your crew chief speak in a calm, non-irritating voice, and they generally only tell you relevant information. For example, when an accident occurs during a race, your crew chief no longer feels the need to inform you. Instead, you might hear the stadium announcer take note of it over the loudspeaker. It's a small touch, but it goes a long way towards adding realism to the game and alleviating a lot of the annoying dialog that plagued the first two games in the series. The game also doesn't have fake SportsCenter clips or any other such nonsense. The focus here is on the driving.
On the track, GRID Autosport can be challenging, exciting, and frustrating, just as any good racing game should be. I found the handling model to be a good balance of fun and realism. It requires far more thought, caution, and finesse than GRID 2 did, but it's not nearly as punishing as a true simulation. On harder difficulties, the AI offers up stiff competition, and they race each other in a believable fashion. 16-car races offer that perfect balance of chaos and control, and they can be an absolute blast. In contrast, time attack and endurance events offer you plenty of opportunities to dip into that zen state in which you can focus on hitting every apex and shaving off tenths of seconds here and there. GRID Autosport's mix of different racing types do a lot to prevent boredom. When I was getting a little tired of one style of racing, there was always another that I could easily switch to.
Visually, this game is gorgeous. With the high-resolution texture pack installed, car models, buildings, and other in-world objects look fantastic. While earlier Codemasters games often used ugly filters that would wash out colors, GRID Autosport's environments are bursting with color, and the lighting model makes everything pop fantastically. The city stages are borrowed from GRID 2, but I don't blame them, as these are teeming with detail that make them a sight to behold. Famous buildings and landmarks, background details like descending passenger jets, and a nicely modeled crowd all go a long way towards adding to the immersion. For as much as a racing game can have an "atmosphere", GRID Autosport nails it.
If you're looking for a game in which you can slowly amass a gigantic garage full of exotic sports cars, this game is not for you. This game is not Gran Turismo or Forza. Nor is it Assetto Corsa or iRacing. You don't buy cars, you don't upgrade or customize cars, you barely even tune them. This is a game solely about racing, as the title suggests. So long as you know what you're getting into, you won't be disappointed. I was pleasantly surprised by GRID Autosport at almost every turn, and it gets my recommendation for anyone looking for a solid sim-cade racer on PC.

This game is basically a more polished Bioshock 1. It takes place in the same setting (only 10 years later) and you're an old-model Bid Daddy. I find this game to be superiour to it's predecessor in every way: Combat is better, use of plasmids is smoother and more fun, the story is more personal and more compelling, there are actual characters for you to care about and the game actually uses the fact Rapture is set under water. It really looks like the devs took every complaint to heart and fixed every single issue.
Some issues though:
- The story, like in the original, takes a while to kick in. That worked fine in the first game because you had that sense of wonder and desire to explore this ruined city, but you don't really have it in this game since you've been here already. Getting through the first 3 hours or so without much of a story requires a bit of willpower.
- Seeing as you're a Big Daddy now, you have Little Sisters to protect while they harvest Adam. The problem is, doing that is an example of pretty much one of the worst things in gaming: Escort missions. Having to protect someone else from oncoming waves of enemies. Doing this 4-6 times each level feels like a chore.
And sure, you have plenty of traps, mines and turrents to prepare with, but if you do that then the mission is pretty much to stand still and wait, which isn't much fun either.
- While the Drill is f**king epic, it runs out of fuel too fast. I guess it would be a little overpowered if it didn't, but.. what's the harm in that? The shooting mechanics have never been the best part of a Bioshock game, so I see no reason to encourage people to not go full-melee.
These are just a few very minor issues in the overall picture. The game really is immersive, creative and most importantly fun as hell. You get to learn more about how Rapture used to be, how Little Sisters and Big Daddies were created and the special bond they share. But most importantly - The hacking system in this game is not complete sh!t.

You become so invested in this game and the stories of the people you're entrusted with.  There is no quick save or reload when a character is killed.  You are affected by the situations of other survivors, and the choices you make, whether practical, cruel, or compassionate. Events are randomly generated, the harsheness of the environment, the length that events will affect you, and how many days until the war you are caught in will end.  I wanted to cry during one play through because I had heard on the radio that there would be a ceasefire to get international aid into the city. We had little food, were struggling to keep the stoves burning, and I was counting down the days to the reported intervention.  Then the day before, it was cancelled. I was devistated, but there was nothing to be done for it.  A new area cleared up in the city that day, and luckily it had been barely touched.  But just the hope that I had had, that even if it wasn't an end, we would still get a reprieve...It hits you.
This is a game about surviving in a warzone.  A civil warzone to be exact.  Rebels and the military caring little for the people caught in between, and military snipers themselves are a true threat to you. You will come across kind people, cruel people, your survivors will do the best that they can under your direction.  My personal favorite are the crazies.  Some are violent, some are harmless, and rather fun to listen to while you very relaxedly scavenge through a building with them. You are what they have to survive.  And you will find yourself trying so hard to make that happen.

This is a very simple but fun game. On the surface it is simply an arcade ship simulator on a mixed 2D/3D plane. However there is a deeper portion to the game for those that want to look for it. An interesting yet unobtrusive story serves as the impetus for exploring a galaxy populated by interesting characters from a multitude of species with their own agendas and factions as you find your way amongst the stars.
Fans of the game Freelancer will feel right at home in Rebel Galaxy and find many of the same mechanics apply here. You can take on numerous roles to suit your gameplay with an array of different ships and classes of them to suit different playstyles. Everything from nimble corvettes to hulking dreadnoughts and lumbering transports are available to the player who has the cash to procure and outfit them.
The only real issue is that there are a lot of minor controls that are poorly explained and require some player exploration to discern exactly how certain mechanics work. Beyond that the game is quite fun and engaging with a simplicity that means it can easily be picked up for a brief stint and set down again without any disruption.

Published by a Russian shovelware house EHTechnology, Last Tale had a lot to prove, but almost from the start it became very clear that actual love and care has been put into this little platformer.
While created in the Construct 2, the game exhibits none of the sloppiness associated with that middleware.
Unlike Cave Story, a game Last Tale bears more than a passing resemblance to, this experience is entirely linear. There are 5 worlds, with 3-4 stages each, and a boss encounter at the end. To progress, one must destroy all enemies in a level. While most later levels are linear, the first few are more labyrinthine, and might require some backtracking to clear. The first four bosses are really well made and are actually really fun to fight against. Their patterns are distinct and decently telegraphed, so the encounters are challenging but rarely frustrating. The final, fifth boss is the only exception. He's an utter bаstard, and the only way to defeat him is to exploit a glitch in his AI.
The pixel art is simple yet charming, with a lot of unexpected little details. My only complain here would probably be the palette that is far too muted for a New Year-themed game.
The music is surprisingly good as well, though, once again, not very New-Year-related. Most of it is comprised of often somber buzzing chiptunes similar to the ones in Cave Story.
While nothing special, Last Tale is worth the asking price. My first playthrough took me almost exactly two hours, of which more than a third was spent dying on the final boss, but on the whole it was time well-spent.

If there was a "maybe" recommend option, I'd use that instead. The game isn't bad. The visuals are amazing. The car handles reasonably well (I don't care about "realism", I care about a car I can control). Starting off was tough. I only like the occasional racing game, and I used the "easy" difficulty (there's a very easy, a normal, and more beyond that), and there's an option to have damage to your car actually affect its handling or just show up for visual effects. While that's cool, I like easy mode, so visual effects only for me.
The game throws you into a "big race" to start off with no training; I didn't even know what button was accelerate (it's RT on the controller). It turns out that race isn't terribly important and the following race is a test drive which actually tries to show you how to drive. That was cool. It even lets you continue the test drive after you're done - it doesn't automatically take you out of it until you're ready to leave. This made all the difference.
The game is overloaded with unnecessary unskippable cutscenes, and there's a story about getting publicity that doesn't need to be there. I couldn't work out what "getting more fans" does.  After the first couple of races, you have to set up an account etc - the whole process made me feel like I was spending more time looking at cutscenes and in the high quality menus than I was actually racing.
The racing is satisfying when you actually get to it, especially the "rewind" feature when you press Y that lets you fix up any mistakes. This is AMAZING for a player who doesn't race often. You can see what mistakes you made and fix them. It feels like cheating and I love it. There's some sort of limit to how many times you can rewind, or an unseen cooldown or something.
The best races I liked were the 1 on 1 short races, and even the tougher ones were great thanks to rewinding. On one particular race the opponent was really beating me over and over, but I just rewound the race a couple of times and I won. The over-the-top voiceover said how good I was and how I beat them at their own game, and I was all "ya I did".

I have to say, after reading the reviews on this game, I wanted to be impressed. However, after about five seconds of playing on the first course I immediately wanted to stop playing. My biggest issue is that it doesn't handle like a car, nor any normal vehicle for that matter. Everything slides around likes it's on ice, regardless of what I do(did). The one feature of the game that genuinely piqued my interest was the Flashback feature, but it didn't help much to compensate for the terrible physics. It may just be me who encountered this (although I don't see how that's possible) for the short amount of time I played. And when I say short, I mean it. I only played for about 15 mins and was not left with a good impression.
I was also unsatisfied with the camera in such a tight space. I'm not used to racing games, which made it even more difficult to play. Again being on those lines, there was no tutorial (that I saw) about how to play. Granted, they explained the keys to drive and the flashbacks while playing, but there were no tips for turning, stopping, elaborate roads, etc.
On the flipside, I liked the feeling given by the environment and detail put into certain things, such as the amount of damage and debris that could accumulate on the cars themselves. Again, as I mentioned earlier, I really liked the flashback feature. I haven't seen this in many games, and it gave me the ability to see how to approach specific situations from different angles (...literally). While I may not have played as long as some of the other people posting reviews, I hope anybody reading this would take very into consideration all of the goods and bads very carefully. Personally, I wasn't impressed with the game and I find it hard to see more pros than cons, so I'd say try the demo before you get anywhere near that "buy" button.

I've put in more than 2000 hours into the original Puzzle Pirates over its long run. It's a great cooperative MMO where all actions are replaced with puzzles. The game creates a friendly atmosphere with players who want to work together and help one another. There are a variety of puzzles that take different sorts of thinking and reasoning in order to excel. One can contribute and be helpful even if they aren't the best, allowing players of different skill levels to play together. It's a casual, but intensely fun experience with a lot of friendly, sometimes goofy people and well worth your time to investigate.
The tutorials may be lacking for a truly new player, but helpers, whose names are in pink, are always around to answer any questions.

This game is fun, if you enjoy the isometric strategy games as much as I do, but be warned; there's more to it that what you think, both positively and negatively. I highly suggest it, however, to anyone new in the Amusement park tycoon genre, as I think it'll appeal more to you guys.
Let's start off with the cons. Really, I only found one because the game doesn't lag, has lasting gameplay, and other things. However, be warned; all of this doesn't matter if you don't download open RCT2. The game will crash on you, deleting all of yuor data you didn't save, and it does this frequently. I don't know if this is fixed, but I'd rather not try to find out. One other thing that may make you choose the original over this one; the scenarios in this are actually pre-built, and they have some attractions, and clear areas to put roller coasters or rides. That's about it. This game will not dissapoint you if you're into this sort of thing.
Alright, time for the pros.
I would have to start off with the lasting gameplay. Different rides and different coasters are unlocked through reasearch, so you'll have to spend some time not only collecting money to build rides, but spending money to research them. This is a neat little mechanic I appreciate because it makes the game last longer without an obvious barrier, since it allows you to allocate your funds in research.
Another detail I noticed is how different scenarios have different coasters. You can make different scenarios in this game, albeit with a limited pallete. What does this mean? Well, it means you can't choose every single roller coaster and attraction along with every single scenery. This has it's ups and downs. On the one hand, it makes the gameplay sweeter knowing that you can't experience everything in one playthrough. On the other, though, you'll feel limited when it comes to options if you want to have everything from the start. I think you should be able to choose, but it's mainly due to sprite limitations.
Last thing I would have to say is that it delivers. Yes, the graphics are pretty bad, and yes, the rotation does take some getting used to, but for a 10$ game, it's pretty solid in content. As I write this, it is 3.50; definetly worth it. If you aren't going to play it now, buy it for later.
There is one final thing I have to put forward, that goes along with my previous statement; it's old. This game, even if you will enjoy it, does have it's limitations. If you want a low-budget tycoon game, then this is the game for you. It does everything it says it does for 10$ and more. If you're looking for a better rollercoaster tycoon game, though, you'll have to go planet coaster. Planet coaster does everything mention above without crashing, with better controls, more availability, and the fact the camera is 3d makes it better for everyone and more modern. The graphics are great, but for all of that, you'll have to pay over a couple of more bucks. So while RCT2 game has more content, it has less overall than Planet Coaster.
Well, that's all I had to say. If you are new, definetly get this game. If you are looking for a game to play meanwhile, get the game. In fact, there is barely any reason *not* to get the game. Just don't forget to download OpenRCT2 for the crashed :)

Sequel 101: Take the original and make it bigger, better and more violent. Bioshock 2 covers its bases well with expanded gameplay, stage design and enemy variation. The story lacks the surprise twist from the original, but it makes up for it in buckets by simply being a better game.
The original Bioshock was a surprise hit from 2007. It offered incredible atmosphere, a riveting story and entertaining gameplay. All the ingredients for an instant classic. The sequel had a lot to live up and it took a slightly different approach. Incredible atmosphere, an entertaining story and literally riveting gameplay. For the sequel you get to play as a big daddy, the huge lumbering divers on the game’s cover. Arguably the most intelligent design choice for a sequel since Terminator 2.
Bioshock 2 is an insane power fantasy. You play as an armoured badass in the run down districts of the once shining city of Rapture. You are subject Delta, an old cover model and you are called back from the beyond to rescue your daughter from some head-shrink. Yeah, the story is a bit thin, but your motivation is clear: Save your daughter from a psycho and kill, murder and maim anyone who gets in your way.
Playing as the big poppa gives you access to the iconic drill, a rivet gun (earlier pun intended), a huge machine gun, an elephant gun that has no business being fired from the hip, a spear gun taken from the bow of a whaler and a rocket launcher that probably fell of an armoured truck. In your other hand you command the forces of nature to shock, roast and freeze your enemies. You are a one man army and you are not going to let anyone get in your way.
To compensate, the enemies are more numerous and aggressive. You’ll often fight against dozens while also hacking and setting traps at the same time. You’ll also brave gauntlets against an incoming tide of enemies while you defend your little sister helper while she’s gathering valuable power-up juice. The addition of these standoffs is a welcome one and adds some serious meat to the gameplay. Setting traps allows for some really creative tricks. This goes on from start to finish and gets more intense along the way. No difficulty falloff here.
Difficulty in general; Bioshock 2 is quite challenging in its own right. Enemies hit hard and never stop attacking. So even on normal does it present a good challenge (unlike Infinite’s 1999 mode, which was as easy as shooting fish in a barrel.) Furthermore, the city of Rapture looks just as gorgeous as before. Ok, maybe the textures are a bit washed out, but when the place is flooded, everything looks washed out.
One major problem persists the game and that is the stability. Bioshock 2 has a nasty habit of crashing to desktop for no apparent reason. I’m still vexed as to why it happens, but it annoys the living hell out of me and it has me save every ten minutes to prevent losing all that progress. Also, the controls are somewhat of a mess. You’ll have to tinker with them, but its manageable. There’s also a multiplayer mode…which I’m not even touching. I came here to drill people and save little sisters; and that’s just what this game lets you do.

As it is now, after initial play through, it is just a dust collector.
