This war of mine is a fantastic game. It scratched all the itches that I had going into the game from the description. Oh and the DLC idea, amazing.
For those of you who haven't seen yet or assume that it's only one part of the game that is all black and white, it's not. Don't let that discourage you though, the theme alongside the music for this game is perfectly suited and it adds a lot of atmosphere to the game. The whole game plays out as a cross sectional doll house style which works really well.
You are not a solider or hero. Let me say that again, You are NOT a solider or hero. You will struggle, you will lose people along the way and you will despair at the constant dire situations you find yourself in. This game has done an amazing job portraying the struggle or regular people trapped in a war locked country trying to survive. Sure you can try and take people on using force to take what is theirs but you can also try to scavenge and stay morally and literally safe.
This game throws a lot at you in the beginning and it does take a little while to get the hang of all aspects but even once you have (by the start of the third scenario I had the game figured out entirely) the game still offers a lot of challenge especially at the start. Balancing the need for food, security, warmth, sleep, preventing illness and injury as well as treating those issues is a constant for most of your game. Usually you are dealing with multiple issues at once while still trying to get your base up and running.
I've had a lot of fun on this game, I picked it up for around $8 USD during a sale but honestly for me it felt worth the full price. The DLC for this game comes in three different prices that all do the same thing. It gives you an achievement, adds a bunch of graffiti art to previously available locations, these unlock an achievement once you have found them all. Most importantly of all though, all the money from DLC purchases goes entirely to the charity War Child. I couldn't believe it when I saw that, what an amazing idea to make achievements and the DLC go towards a good cause. I bought it and while most people don't care about achievements I'm proud to have both of these two because they do actually mean something for a change.
A couple of little negatives to round up the review. Once you know how everything works the game gets easier, not entirely easy but a lot of the challenge and excitement of trying to figure out the game is gone because you follow a lot of the same principals to getting yourself established. When you have nothing to do in the base it can get a bit annoying to wait a minute or two for the day to end while you just sit there. You can click end day and move straight into the night but you could miss out on a potential visitor to your base by doing this. (1 per day max). The combat can be quite clunky and strange to get use to. Sometime you will encounter a few bugs but nothing game breaking, the worst I had was a random -5 degree day not during winter and 18 fuel for fire disappearing from my inventory.
Overall I definitely got my money and times worth from this game, I recommend it strongly to anyone that this style of game appeals to even remotely. 8.5/10

The key for this game was given to me for review purposes.
Let me start off by saying... Red Risk can be a fun game. However, there are some design choices that I don't agree with and I believe they kind of break the game.
But first, I will start with a list of pros:
1. The soundtrack is pretty cool and I really enjoy it (although the tracks sound very similar)
2. Decent concept; you are part of a game show where you need to survive waves of zombies and monsters
3. Nice dark style (This game isn't called RED Risk for no reason)
Quite honestly, that is all for the list of pros, at least for now.
The cons/suggestions for improvement are as follows:
1. Drops need to have a better indication that they are there
2. The game can really use a "run and gun" mechanic
3. It was unclear how to obtain rank points
4. The basic action needs to be updated... (It would work better if the mouse indicator wasn't the exact spot that your weapon hits. For the axe, left clicking should make you automatically swing and hit whatever is in it's path. For the guns, left clicking should shoot in whatever direction you are pointing. The would make the game smoother and, ultimately, more fun.)
5. Another suggestion... It would be cool if the game kept separate stats for each character as well as an aggragate total for your profile.
6. Animations need to be clearer... (There is no indication that you are getting hurt besides the screen dimming. The monsters don't make any special movement. Also, the character you control isnt very animated either. There needs to be an indication that you are swinging your axe as opposed to using your special ability.)
I will keep an eye on this game to see how the development process progresses. I will update my reveiw as necessary. Hopefully, I can one day give this game a thumbs up!

TL;DR: A solid future setting for the Civilization series, marred only by a loss of the X-factor that made the Civilization series what it is, and a barebones diplomacy and factional interaction setup that requires the Rising Tide expansion to actually become something worthy.
+ A streamlined Civ V formula brought into space and the sci-fi era.
+ A solid forward-telling story of a likely "future scenario" done in classic Sid Meier's fashion.
+ Solid replayability with the three paths you can take to bring your faction to the end, and even mixes.
+ Some carry-over into and out of Sid Meier's Starships.
+ Rising Tide adds a lot to the game, like fleshing out the aformentioned barebones diplomacy and spying systems.
- Lost a lot of the X-factor and character that the original Civilization series had in spades.
- Diplomacy is bare-bones, akin to on-release Civ V without expansions.
- Science-fiction future setting may put off some purists.
- Sid Meier's Starships is a multi-platform (mobile) game and as such is not as deep as Beyond Earth.
- Rising Tide is needed to extend the game beyond the barebones problems it has.

First and foremost, if you don't like puzzles, there is not much here for you, and I would not recommend you play this game.
With that out of the way, I have played Puzzle Pirates: Dark Seas for 450+ hours during closed beta, as well as 3000+ hours on the original version, and I highly recommend it for those who enjoy puzzling, communities of (usually) friendly and well-intentioned people, and a player-run economy that generally knows what it's doing. There are a plethora of ways you can play the game and enjoy it, all without needing to pay out of pocket (though it can make things go faster, it is not absolutely necessary).
Most of the puzzles are simple enough to pick up quickly, but have a lot of depth for those who invest the time in them. While some puzzles are gated by a "paywall of sorts" (such as labor puzzles and parlor games), they are free on certain days of the week, so most players only need to get the necessary badges if the puzzles are particularly fun to the individual. It introduces the puzzles to players overtime, as to not overwhelm them with things to do until they have a feel for the game as a whole.
Moveover, there is already a relatively well-built infrastructure from the closed beta, allowing the new players to not have to deal with the frustrations of an MMO with basically nothing. The economy is currently rather stable, and most items can be purchased at fairly reasonable prices (I personally had a hand in regulating the cloth and clothing markets). The fancier stuff will still cost a bit, but the prices are not overly bloated for absurd profits. Plus, there are enough ships out and about to where most people will have opportunities to go out on the seas if they so choose.
However, I will say that there is a relatively steep learning curve. For better or worse, many of the more active players running pillages/sea monster hunts (SMH) prefer their pirates to be 'elite', which can put a player-made gate on some of the more profitable areas of the game. While not necessarily good for newer players, considering the risks to the ship holder in these excursions (especially SMH, where ships can be sunk), it is somewhat understandable.
One of the more interesting aspects is that, on a ship, every piece needs to work together to succeed. Sailing/Rigging give the ship the ability to move, but can be slowed by a high bilge. Carpentry/Patching repair damage on the ship, which will help to keep the bilge low, allowing the ship to move more efficiently. Bilging keeps water out of the ship, which can be made easier or harder based on how well the carpentry/patching can remove damage. While not directly related to the other 3, the ship can only shoot if the cannons are full, so a good gunner can turn the tides of battle. The battle navigator uses moves from the sailors, cannons from the gunner, and their own intuition in order to damage, outmaneuver, and ultimately grapple the enemy ship. It is like Guns of Icarus, only with puzzles, and on a much smaller scale.

Delivery fees, Labor/Parlor Badge and so forth are all ways to sink the doubloons out of the economy. Luckly you can just buy them from other players for Pieces of Eight, the earned currency. To be honest im tempted at saying this is a really good family game as the puzzle rules are simple enough for all ages and most dont require high execution for the majority of time. This game is pretty remarkable for a EA launch.  The devs have been very responsive and major changes / rebalances have already taken place.
Short review:
I got my $20 worth on day 1 and it's quickly becoming one of my favorite games.  The open world is beautiful and is continually worth exploring.  The biggest strengths to the game are the building system, taming creatures, and the skill trees (need some balancing, but there's a clever variety of weapons, as well as situational loadouts and utility spells).
_____________________
For the sake of review, here's my criticism:
The main funkiller for me was server lag and the need for occasional server restarts, but reasons were diagnosed and solved pretty quickly (Fireballs traveled infinitely, and thus were rendering 99999999m out of bounds).  The devs are open, honest, and responsive to feedback including how the world and objects are rendered, and stability has increased dramatically.  If you're worried about performance, consult other reviews; I've had a solid experience and good fps, but
*FIXED* Telekinesis spell was hilarious; I knew not to get attached to my bases after playing RUST and watching trailers where entire castles were picked up and thrown at a mountainside.  This is a shame because building is the most beautifully done and intuitive aspect of the game.  Even a solo player can make an impressive structure in a modest amount of time.  Instead of living in a 2x2 or worrying about honeycomb door cancer, you have a lot more freedom, and its mostly just a place to do your crafting.  All you really need to succeed in the game is a weapon and some mana potions, which can be done even as a wandering nomad (which I also like).
Hiding your throne (much like a TC in RUST) can add strategic elements to base defense as well.  Early game PvP was fun and mostly balanced as we were all learning the ropes, but mid-game PvP was just telekinesis griefing back and forth.  Once you destroy the throne, GG, you can just delete everything. What will become of the spell, I'm not sure, but I cast my vote for being able to throwing boulders and trees at bases.  Knowing people were telekinesis griefing each other even on PvE servers makes you wonder about the human condition, especially when I giggle inside.
AI is respectable for an open world game; NPCs were laughable placeholders in every other EA title, but these have some life to them; I'd just complain that they're too easy.  Just face tank all the damage, chug pots, or take shots from a safe location.  This is a major gripe for some people, but to me, it exceeded expectations.
Potion chugging is tedious for some people.
++Items exist with mana and hp regen,
--There's only one slot for an accessory *Which is also your broom slot*
I'm not sure how I feel about the progression; the grind was pretty peaceful and satisfying; hitting level 10, level 20, or level 30 is meaningful in the context of your surroundings.  Depending on what you want from the game you might want to play on custom servers with xp modifiers so everyone is on the same playing field.  It's inaccurate to call it an MMO; I like the 40-man servers because you get to know your neighbors and it encourages some diplomacy beyond gunning down nakeds.

My first dungeon keeper style game that I've played.  I did enjoy it a lot.
Plot - You play as an ultimate evil who is out there to conquer the overworld! It's actually a really cool little story, because it's voiced by Kevan Brighting (narrator of Stanley's Parable). It makes it really easy to listen and there's plenty of jokes and references. Some of them are pretty cheesy, but some made me laugh also.
Gameplay - I suppose it's based on classic dungeon keeper games, though in this one you go to the overworld and the game turns into real time strategy. It's pretty fun and it won't require you to be RTS pro, but if you're not careful you could get overwhelmed. The game has missions and it advances through quests inside them. There's optional objectives that you don't have to do, but I still did them cause I enjoyed it.
Graphics - I'm not a sucker for graphics so I won't be too picky. I've played on lower settings as usual on my machine, but I seem to experience lower-ish fps in the overworld. Could be my PC or a little bit of optimization issues? Who knows, though it doesn't require 200 fps or newest equipment to play it without any big problems.
Music - The whole soundtrack was nice and I liked it. Especially when it changes to a nice and peaceful music where the alliance still thrives and to a menacing part when you are building your dungeon deep underground.
Overall, I would recommend this game to anyone that is interested in it and new to the genre (I sure was). Superb voice acting, nice cool story. I think you'll have fun.

This is a short game that you can easily beat in a few hours. If you're going for Diamond on every level you'll be in for some ride, though... A ride that's not really worth it. The boss fights (on Diamond) are frustratingly hard, and not for the right reasons. In order to win, you need to combine skilled gameplay (good) with memorization (not that great) and some luck (bad). This would not have been so bad if the controls were better, but they are not suited for precise maneuvering. Many good bullet hell games will let you slow down your movement by holding a button, but ShipLord doesn't let you to that, which means that you'll crash into projectiles that should've been easy to dodge.
A lot of the time I felt like I died not because of error I made but because of flaws in the game. Sometimes astroid formations are nearly impossible to dodge, and sometimes astroids spawn just as you pick up a point at the edge of the screen. Oh, and points sometimes spawn inside of astroids, making them hard to spot until it's too late. If you're unlucky they will spawn at the opposite side of the screen, thus not giving you enough time to pick them up unless you use "Energy Collector".
The graphics, story, and voice acting are all below average, and there are a few grammar and spelling mistakes in the game. The game would've been better if it were in 2D and it would've been better without any story or voice acting, though that's a minor complaint.
I give this game a 6 or a 7 out of 10. It is not entirely without merit, but there are so many better games out there, and unless you really like the genre I recommend you skip it. I had some fun with it, despite how frustrating it could be at times. It might be worth picking up on a game, but it's a very unpolished game that has a lot of flaws.

ShipLord is a different take on the bullet hell genre. Instead of focusing on combat, the main goal is to collect an energy source for Earth called quasars. Gameplay is mostly dodging asteroids and activating skills to make that task easier. There is a shield that lets you smash through the asteroids, a time freeze, and an auto-loot skill that collects all quasars on screen. Collecting certain amounts of quasars awards points to spend to increase the duration or reduce the cooldown of the skills. Ranking in the platinum and diamond tier on each level will unlock new ships which each grant additional cooldown of the skills. After 4 levels collecting quasars there is a boss round where you dodge the attacks until an asteroid hits them.
This game is rather fun, and the choice to leave out combat makes for fewer things to distract the player. Rather relaxing play. Avoid if easily frustrated. While it has only 15 levels there are bonus levels that are endurance focused with steam leaderboard rankings. This game is listed at about $8 USD and personally I would value this game at $5-6 USD. If you absolutely love bullet hell then this may be a great deal for you, otherwise add it to your wishlist so you can be notified when it goes on sale.

REBEL GALAXY 2017 REVIEW:
PROS:
GRAPHICS: There is nothing like hunting and fighting your enemy while in the backdrop
of a stunning planet or blazing sun. All the ships going by and space stations absolutely glitter. The broadside
battles are simply amazing and seeing the damage on your ship after you have won the batte with scorch marks
holes and sparking remains makes you want to repair your ship and find the next bounty or mission!
GAMEPLAY: If you enjoyed playing Freelancer in the past this is the game for you! Yet is unfair to compare the two as this game is quite different in many ways and is a hidden gem!
The controls are quite easy to pick up and by just pointing your ship in the indictated direction of your mission (In yellow) the on screen prompts tell you what to do from hitting E to go to hyperspace for what direction your next mission is.
BATTLES: If you think you will be flying a tiny ship think again as flying capital ships in this game is truly what sets this
game apart from others in its Genre. The BROADSIDE BATTLES is so well done that at times it leaves you on the edge of
your seat wondering if you will win. The ability to put up a shield for incoming fire and being able to switch guns mid battle is what makes this game so much fun!  DDG could have easily made this game into one that enabled the NPCs to just sit their and fight it out with you as you circle them and easily take your enemy out.
Yet each battle can be unique with some running away and others defiantly going down in a blaze of glory. When you get to the 3 or four way battles then the CHAOS happens and its truly awesome!
STORYLINE: If you enjoyed Freelancer and love Firefly TV series this is the game for you!
The ability to choose your own dialog from being the galaxies ultimate Villain/Pirate to the good
guy will make you want to have two different save files to play good and bad.
VOICEOVERS: You have to give credit where credit is due. We have seen countless games with scrolling dialog at the
bottom that go so slowly our eyes bleed or voiceovers that make us cringe. Yet DDG did it RIGHT!
Each character, from the local bartender, contact, enemy and every alien has its own unique voice and the ability to choose to tick them off or be their friend is a pleasant surprise. The hallarous responses are quite a blast.
There is also a feature in Area Scan that pauses the game and you can talk with the enemy at times. (More Below)
IN BATTLE: Quite a surprise is while in battle the enemy will at times taunt you or when loosing will contact you with different messages. This alone makes you feel when playing the game for the first time that your playing against a real person. GREAT JOB DDG!
TRADING/MINING: Trading is quite enjoyable if you like to conquor the galaxy that way and mining changes things up from the usual gameplay.
GALAXY MAP: Yes I gave this one its own subject and when playing this game you'll understand why. We are all tired I am sure of simply seeing dots and names on a map and thats it. Not in this game! You can scroll right in to see the area from astroids to space stations to give you an idea of what your jumping into. Again great job DDG!!
MUSIC: You will see alot of comments about firefly in the reviews and rightly so, the music makes
the game and is epic. Then again if you dont like the firefly-like music and your not a browncoat than you can mute it.
But either way from the moment you enter the game you feel like you could play for hours.
CUTSCENES: Talking with the NPC either hailing from your ship, talking to the local bartender (Human, Robot, or Alien)
is a treat and the ability to change your mind by telling them off or being the good guy is so much fun.
AREA SCAN: Great feature very few talk about. The ability to pause the game and scan your enemy and see if they have a bounty, what they have in their cargo hold or even which one you want to target first is awesome! There is even an option at times to talk with the enemy through this screen, which will give you a cut scene to them either asking for money for them to leave you alone or to bribe you the other way. Great feature.
CONS:
Badly in need of a DLC!!
GAMEPLAY:  Its been said in many reviews that side missions, random encounters get Repetitive. Yet depending on the player and if one is going from one mission to the next for hours and hours it may seem that way but I have found that it isnt really all that bad if you truly take your time and enjoy the game.
I do agree with many who say that the ships going by are very few, not that we need alot going by in
the galaxy itself but it would be nice at major space stations and jump points to see ships coming and going more to get the sense that their is more than just us in this amazing world. (Ie. Ships coming through warp gates like freelancer)
WEAPONS:  Being able to customize your equipment and weapons would make this game better and more diverse.
2D MOVEMENT: Please dont take this next part as the galaxy being 2D for the game is certainly not that. Yet adding the ability to move up or down would be welcomed and would add another Strategy aspect to the battles.
Conclusion: Absoultely an amazing game! Cant wait for a DLC and if Multiplayer did happen
well this game would without a doubt be on the top of the charts!! 9/10

Hello y'all!
This is basically a game of Space Trucking in a galaxy that has something against truckers, judging by the amount of pirates involved. The gameplay is rather repetative as well, since you'll be doing the same type of quest over and over again.
So why the thumbs up?
- There is something deeply pleasing in driving (ehm, flying) an ever improving Space Truck through ever more advanced pirate fleets, some of which can be pretty darn dangerous.
- The game's soundtrack helps in getting you into the right mindset, to fly through space and truck stuff from one place to another. And if it doesn't, you can change it to something else without hassle.
- The combat can be pretty fun, messy as it is. Welding an opposing dreadnaught into space dust using the blind spot and your 4 front mounted mining laser turrets is also pretty amusing in a "haha, you can't get me and if I'm wrong I'm SO dead" kind of way. (Until you find a dreadnought that features 18 or so rocket ports at what you hoped would be the blind spot, anyway).
- There are quite a few Space Trucks available, most of which have a reasonably clear use for your preferred style of combat.
That being said, the game IS repetative and some of the achievements are a grind. But if you can pick it up at a discount? Give it a go.

Homefront is an FPS which tells the story of a resistance movement fighting back against a near future Korean occupation of the USA.
The game play is a very generic FPS. Pretty much identical to Call of Duty and Medal of Honor; you can only carry two weapons, and four grenades. You will have to swap to different weapons from dead enemies throughout each level as finding ammo is more difficult than you would imagine. None of the enemies use the same weapon...
Graphics wise, it looks nice, but you can tell the game was released in 2011, it looks better than most games released, however it shows it's age when comparing it to more recent titles. The graphical options are wide and you can probably play this game on a potato if you really wanted.
All the maps in the single player are very well designed, sadly you can't really explore because you are constantly reminded to keep following your squad leader. You fight through various different environments such as the streets of suburbs, department stores, and baseball fields, all of which show a disturbing outcome of the quite scary "what if?" scenario from a Korean invasion.
The single player of Homefront will take about five hours to complete; this is pretty short in my opinion, and the game ends on a massive cliff hanger, I would of liked to have seen another two or three more missions to tire up the loose ends in the story. Multiplayer is still very much alive in Homefront, I have only played in a couple of games but I had no problem finding a map full of people to jump into. A lot of the reviews you will read on here will say multiplayer is the strongest aspect of the game, so they can't all be wrong.

I remember putting this game on my wishlist and then promptly forgetting about it. Then, my friend gifted it to me for Christmas, and, oh man, am I glad they did.

If you've played other space traders, you know what to expect. Buy low, sell high. Become a pirate and sell your ill-gotten goods. Kill other pirates and take their ill-gotten goods and sell 'em. Become a Bounty Hunter. Mine asteroids. Take on side jobs. Plenty of ship customization options; weapons, different types of shields. As well as different ships to play around with.
In this game, capital ships can only move left and right; no vertical movement. Fighters, gunboats, and the like can move horizontally and vertically. Your weapons are broadsides, like old naval combat. (Think pirate ships launching cannonballs out the sides) You also have turrets, which you can individually configure. Want the two turrets on the side to only shoot at whatever you're targeting, or only shoot at fighters? Done. I must say, this is one of the only games I have ever played where I actually enjoyed grinding for more money. The combat is that enjoyable.

The soundtrack, oh boy.

Puzzle Pirates is a perfect blend of puzzle app (think Candy Crush) with MMORPG.  The social aspects of the game really enhance the quick and clever twists on the traditional Match-3 type of game.  In Puzzle Pirates, you can join a crew, go on a pillage, furnish your house, ply a trade, and much more, while gaining fame across the seas for your puzzling prowess.  (I'm a fan of the bilge pump puzzle, personally.)  The Lego-style graphics are adorable, and the pirate theme stays family friendly (chat servers convert players' saltier language choices into boating terms like "scupper" and "booch.")  Dark Seas adds a new twist to the game by asking crews to choose allegiance to one of two factions: Shadow or Defiance.  This seemingly minor change dramatically impacts not only PvP but also the importance of islands, which remain in play through blockages rather than becoming overpopulated with permanent shops.  It's an interesting shift for long-term players, and gives new players an immediate sense of community beyond their crews.
I highly recommend Puzzle Pirates: Dark Seas for its broad appeal.  Come, me hearties, and pillage the Dark Seas!

Civ: BE fails to be a true successor to Civ: 5 in just about every way imaginable.  The game boils down to being a reskin of Civ: 5. I could almost take a stab in the dark in saying that there's probably a mod out there that can effectively turn Civ 5 into Beyond Earth.  Interface is pretty much the same, the branching research trees are unimaginative, the units are few and dull by comparison to Civ: 5's ever changing technology and unit types.  Overall If you absolutely love Civ: 5 consider getting this game if it's on sale for a quarter of the price.
PROS
+ Interesting Sci-fi landscapes
+ Starting decisions allow for some extra faction customization
+ Polished sounds and graphics
CONS
+ Poor variety of units
+ Late game tech decisions lack polish and customization
+ Dumb AI (surprised?)
+ Not enough innovation involved to justify being a new Civ. title
+ Feels like a Reskin of Civ: 5

After Hitman Blood Money blew me and other Hitman fans away, there was no doubt in my mind Absolution would only improve the series further.
Except for how it didn't. If you are a Hitman fan and you haven't played Absolution, do yourself a favor and never do it. It isn't worth your time, your money, or your attention. The developers decided to focus on making Hitman modern, which isn't inherently a bad thing. However that meant experimenting with a linear narrative which is where I think they truly ruined the game. Hitman levels are traditionally single maps that reward exploration and patience as you find multiple ways to kill your target. While that is in Absolution to some degree, most of the time I found myself in heavily scripted scenarios. I honestly wouldn't recommend this to non-Hitman fans either, because a) it isn't a good representation of Hitman at its best, and b) HITMAN (2016) is fantastic and is a much better Hitman game, go buy and play that instead.

Similarly to Bioshock, Bioshock 2 has aged fairly well, and the gameplay formula is virtually identical.  There's no disputing that Bioshock 2 is a knock-off of the first game made primarily to squeeze more money out of the property, but it's not at all a bad game.
In many ways, the gameplay is improved from the original.  While variety of weapons suffers a bit (being restricted to Big Daddy-sized weapons except for one oddly normal-sized shotgun), they all enable dramatically different styles of play and feel very distinct.  Being able to use plasmids immediately with a right click, rather than swapping between weapons and plasmids, is another huge plus (and an iteration on the gameplay formula that was retained for Bioshock Infinite.)
Level design also remains solid, and the maps are once again primarily nonlinear and generally pretty large.  The plot is sufficient, and does do a good job of fleshing out more of Rapture - particularly Ryan as he began to circle the drain before the first game's protagonist arrives, and how Rapture reacts to this - although there are some impressively large plot holes they essentially have to shove under the rug.  No matter.
I did encounter some oddities with sound, particularly with gunfire being extremely quiet (to the point that when security bots were shooting me, I was completely unable to locate them via sound due to it being ALMOST silent), and I ran into a LOT - and I mean a LOT - of crash to desktop bugs that would just happen out of nowhere.  I could never replicate these bugs, they just happened randomly.  Once or twice I even lost recent quicksaves and had to retread the past 40+ minutes of gameplay.  I also somehow lost some tonics when I sent them into storage at a gene bank.
Suffice to say, this game still has some serious bugs and they aren't likely to be addressed.  None of them prevent you from playing the game, but it's something to be aware of.
It's a shame the multiplayer is effectively dead.  Then again, at this point, the ideas it uses that would've been novel at the time are probably old hat, anyhow.

The game shiplord has lots of potential. It has boss fights, tons of missions, tons of upgrades to upgrade your ship, and if you live long enough, the game might be really enjoyable. As it stands below:
Story/campaign: 7/10
Graphics/art: 9/10
AI: 10/10 (Simplistic which is why 10)
Functionality: 10/10
Content: 8/10
Gameplay/mechanics: 5/10
Controls/navigation 6/10
Replayability: 5/10
Worth the buy? 7/10
Now, this game has a lot of potential indeed. All it needs is more beginning game gameplay, getting new players hooked, and you're onto something. Surviving though through the first say two missions is not a piece of cake. So here are my suggestions:
1. Instead of making it so you die in one hit, restart the game, implement LIVES or... health? Like you get hit once, you have a chance on living, twice, you go "oh no, one life left!", third, dead. Right now, it is frustrating, especially what I am going to tell you about below.
2. Level requirements. Moving to level 3 requires 71 quars (or whatever they are called). If you don't have 71 quars, you cannot move on, that is it. Even if you get through this level at current alive, you cannot move on and you are stuck. What I recommend, PLEASE make quars a side quest. Say you get 71 quars? You get a GOLD MEDAL or you get 3 new upgrades, then move on regardless. Right now you can't. If you have a rough time surviving the mission and you achieve the 71 or so quars and then DIE... you'll get pretty mad.
3. Shields. Needs some rework or a displayed timer on it or increased time value for how long your shields are up. Right now, you have like two seconds to destroy rocks. If you run into a rock at 2.1s without any upgrades (mind you, you only get ONE per level) you die. Like immediately. The shield mechanic is very wonky and along with the one hit you die system, the shield is more hazardous than useless.
4. Upgrading needs to be reworked. You only have 1 upgrade per level (if you make it with required quars). And if you DO upgrade? It's pretty lame of an increase. Like 1 second recharge of something to .999 second recharge? Or use of shield is increased from 2 seconds to 2.1 second use? Pretty underpowering. Either give the player like 4-6 upgrade points (or maybe an upgrade after every 30-50 quars you get) so replaying levels will be worth it. Maybe add sounds or experience bars for making the player WANT to collect white dots (quars or whatever they are called).
5. The controls. So far you only have the arrow keys. How about implementing movement with your mouse? Yeah? So far, the controls steer you off in hasty directions. Using the arrow keys can sometimes confuse your brain or whatever and I think the mouse integration, even better: THREE movement options, arrows, mouse, AWSD keys would do the trick quite nicely. Especially when your shield is the Q key and right there next to the WASD, very good. Just work on movement a little more if you want WASD and arrow keys really functioning.
If you improve those 5 points, like patch your game, update your game, and make good gameplay out of this, it will double or triple your player base. I know because gameplay is everything, not graphics. And with decent graphics like this, it will make people want to play this game. But not only you have to achieve the 5 points above. If you want to be super famous, you will of course have to do more, but that will be easy if you complete the 5 bullet points above. With all that said, and your content, and your over the top multiple missions, this will be a great game.
Hopefully this review will help the developers. For standard readers, I'd give the developers a chance to improve this game a bit more, I know I would if I was the owner. Is it worth the buy right now? Maybe for 5 dollars. It is worth a look. Will you have fun? Maybe after you get past the beginning, keep in mind though, dedication is key in this game.

The first Dungeons game took a lot of flak for looking like Dungeon Keeper but only being a Tower Defence game. However I still liked it and felt it was a good beginning of a series I fully expected to get better.
With Dungeons 2 that they addressed that but not by just copying Dungeon Keeper, oh no. In this game they put their own spin on the theme by keeping the Tower Defense game in the Dungeon levels, so you where always defending against something (the original Dungeon Keeper lacked that) and having an over world map for you to go forth and conquer.
The end result is a very good Dungeon game that sees you attacked repeatedly as with any good tower defence game and a much needed Real Time Strategy Element involving the surface world.
Add to that the narratives tendency to plagiarize ideas from all over as it blantanty plays the pop culture comedy card for kicks and giggles, you have to wonder, does this actually beat the original Dungeon Keeper at its own game.

I was hungry. We were unable to defend ourselves from the raids that happened almost every night. I was scavenging in someone's home, only doing to others what had been done to us. I was getting a bit rabid, I couldn't find what we needed.
And then I saw him.
He was walking around the house, but when he saw me he didn't try to stop me from stealing. He just kept on looking around the house.
And then I saw it.
He was brandishing a small pistol, the sort of weapon that would surely help us to both defend ourselves from attacks, but also could be used to give us the upper hand in these scavenging missions.
So I waited until he had turned away from me, and I began knifing him. Even though I had surprise on my side, he had a far superior weapon. One shot and it would have been a mistake. It took three tussles to finish him off, and I swiftly looted him and pocketed the gun. I emerged unscathed. Or so I thought.
He'd done me no wrong, but he had something I needed. Or was it wanted? There's a massive difference. I became depressed. His shadow hung over the house when I returned early the next morning. Who was I anymore?
I turned the game off soon after, and went to sleep. I had a dream about the man I'd killed. About how I wasn't any better than the jackals looting my place, and attacking our people. About where my morals had gone. About how great a game this is that makes you ask yourself questions such as these.
I lost the gun the following night. A man with an assault rifle called me a &quot♥♥♥♥♥♥quot; before killing me like an animal. In truth, I was no better than him at that stage.

This is a pretty good Point-and-Click type game, although doesn't seem too story driven as things happen at random as you progress into the game. It does give that war time feel about it when you play it. It gives me a feeling of that WW2 type feel to it of what it was like back then, but as a modern age war thing that's going on. There really isn't too much to it on how to actually play the game, most of it is figuring out what stuff you need to get in order to survive the war.
There are some parts of this game which I do not like. First part is you're starting out with absolutely nothing. If it were really a modern age war that was going on you wouldn't really be left with absolutely nothing to get started on survival with bare minimals just to survive the first few days. For example; a bag with at least 4-5 medkits and medicines as your survival kit and a weapon of somesort as your self-defence, be it a handgun or whatever.
Second part is the time in the game for each day, it travels far too quickly to get a decent number of things done in one day when progressed quite far into the game and having a number of things to make at once just to survive better. Time seems to travel at 5 ticks a second.
Third part, the characters themselves becoming absolutely useless when someone dies unexpectedly due to illness or being killed while out scuraging for items or at the safehouse in the middle of the night. Yes it would be normal for someone to grieve for their losses, but really? You don't need them to be sitting in one spot for the entire day to run out when they could try go off and do work around the safehouse to prepare for the next few days gathering more items. It's really annoying when it comes down to one character and that person sits there being absolutely useless just becuase the other two died at the same time due to whatever reason. -- Also another thing that bothers me is when a character only has a shovel as their attacking weapon going up against an enemy with a knife, the character with the shovel shouldn't be so easily killed or being too slow to fight back against someone with a knife. A person with a shovel wouldn't be so easily defeated by someone with a knife.
Fourth part now… the framerate is rather choppy and could do with some work with optimization to make it better and smoother. I have Intel Core i7-3610QM @ 2.30GHz x4 (Intel 3rd Gen HD Graphics (4000 series)) , Nvidia GeForce GT630M w/ 2GB DDR3, and 8GB RAM on Linux Mint 17.1, games tend to run pretty smoothly on a system like mine at 60FPS.

Rebel Galaxy is a futuristic space battle game that is reminiscent of Colony Wars 3 Red Sun in some respects. There are missions in which you earn credits to buy upgrades. Everything needs upgraded. The ship, the weapons, the hull, the shields, even the tractor beam for Pete's sake. You can explore dozens of different star systems once you have your jump drive. It allows you to use jump gates. You may want to upgrade everything to the maximum before each jump though. There is a story line that is original. You find an A.I. who has a bit of amnesia so you help her get her memory fragments only to discover a much larger plot. This game is addictive. The thrill of gaining enough cash to upgrade something keeps you glued to the screen for hours. The achievements are quite a rush. And you can choose which guild you want to side with. There is even an option to side with the pirates.
There were a couple of things about this game that I did not like. First, it is completely inclined to the ecliptic. Meaning that the combat is not truly 3D. It plays more or less like a surface of the water naval battle. Enemy ships can go up and down but you can not. Secondly, there is lag. Sometimes when I am trying to go warp speed from place to place it freezes up breifly and sometimes it goes slow for no apparent reason.
All things considered I would say that this game is worth buying. It is not a 2D game in case you are wondering. Watch the youtube reviews to see what I mean if you haven't figured it out yet. And although the lag is annoying it is not enough to really ruin the game.  It is a wild ride into the final frontier you won't want to miss. Addictive action, upgrades and an interesting story that you can sink your teeth into.  If you liked Star Wars and Star Trek then you will want to get this game.

Puzzle Pirates: Dark Seas is a new take on the classic Puzzle Pirates game. In this version (or Ocean), the focus is on PvP experience, with players divided in two faction which are permanently at war with each other. There are safe areas for new players to learn the ropes, but once you sail deep and explore these mysterious waters, stakes grow high as you risk losing your ship in an effort for sinking your opponent!
While most of the features remain unchanged from classic PP, this is hardly a drawback but rather a strength. Each activity your perform while at sea or even in land has a puzzle associated, and these puzzles are just incredible. There's a great variety to pick from, and most players will find a few which they love (and a few which they hate!), as they learn how to become ever better. Your skill in these puzzles determines how well you perform your activity, which makes mastering a puzzle really satisfying and useful (not to mention fun).
Behind it's simple appearance, PP has an incredibly complex economic system, where every piece of clothing your pirate wears has a long history before it came to be: cloth has to be weaved, dyes have to be prepared, clothes have to be sown, and the necessary materials are transported in ships which fight off greedy pirates trying to steal their cargo.
The graphics and general appareance suggest an old game (and it definitely is), but at the same time demonstrate how awesome the concept must have been to keep a large amount of players interested over the years. Don't let this scare off new players though, the Dark Seas are a new area just discovered, and even the old salts sailing the oceans for over 10 years started over in here, so there's never been a better time to join the fun!

GAMEPLAY

The microtransactions in this game make the game pay-to-win. As a new pirate, you can sail with the navy which will make around 200 poe an hour. You could possibly join a non elite pillage and get maybe 10k an hour if you're lucky. Or you can buy $10 of doubloons for 150k, which increases the amount you get depending on how much you spend at once. Red Risk is a top-down action game made by Microblast Games (Dead Bits, Overcast, Particula). When I think of hell then flames, go-go dancers, and demonic beasts come up to my mind; and Red Risk fulfilled my image of hell.
You play as one of the three characters, each with specific weapon (axe, pistol or sniper rifle) and unique skill. Red Risk tournament starts immediately as you are thrown into the arena - you have to survive through rounds, while taking care of your health, ammo, starve and thirst (stats are regained at a specific place in the arena for credits you get for surviving).
The developers chosen pretty uncomfortable controls, as you have to use one mouse button to move, and the second button to attack. Keyboard is just used for your special ability and to check your stats.
Even though the game is obviously low-budget and the graphics style is not terrible as you could expect, the animations make it look pretty bad in action. Your melee character will swing his axe like he would be on drugs, enemy characters usually attack just by making weird moves next to you. Those moves might seem funny, but they're actually taking your health down, of course.
Ranged characters in the game play pretty bad, as they share the same controls with the melee character, except they have to reload their weapons. It seems that they are made with thought for the co-op multiplayer, as they are pretty weak on their own, especially the sniper.
As I've already mentioned, the graphic style is not that bad until something moves, and there's also indifferent heavy metal soundtrack, that even for a metalhead might feel cheesy, but it does its job. There's several arenas where you can get access after you level up (by killing enemies in unlocked arenas), so you can expect getting few hours of playtime from this, if you'll be having fun. Also, there are three difficulties that indicate the health and attack of your enemies.
Red Risk, as it is, isn't worth recommending. It's a slighty below mediocre top-down action game with bad animation and uncomfortable controls. Also, another important thing to mention is the fact that the developers are known for permanently lowering price of their games shortly after release, so if you are interested, you still might want to wait. This....is...the best software....I have ever owned.
Seriously.
I use this primarily for Elite Dangerous, and with a little work have created a semi-sentient AI which talks to me and I can talk back to.  However, it can be used for ANY program on your computer, and you can create multiple profiles that you can switch to as you switch programs.
You can try a free trial for 21 days (so at least try it out), but it took me all of an hour to buy this amazing gem.  Knowing what I know now, I'd pay $30 and be happy, as this keeps having updates added to it and expanded.  The functionality is solid, I've had no bugs, even with using some of the "Advanced" features.
Now, to what it does:
VoiceAttack uses a speech recognition engine (usually Windows by default, but this is changeable if you want to do that) to listen to voice commands and perform keyboard, joystick, or controller commands/keybinds/button presses/what have you.  Yes, it even works with joystick motions.  You can set it to also play sounds as part of the command, so if you have community made voice packs for a game, or use a text to speed engine, you can have it talk to you.  Or just play a beep or something.  Whatever you want.  It works amazingly for VR, and it is very easy to get immersed using voice commands.
I can say (in my case for Elite Dangerous), "Eden, prepare for docking." and VoiceAttack plays a sound from Eden (a voice pack dealio I got), reduces my thruster speed, balances my power out to normal, and retracts my docking gear all while I can be doing other things.
All commands in VoiceAttack can be run in parallel or one after the other.  I can have VoiceAttack do multiple commands together, and there are even settings to make sure your keybinds/commands don't conflict with each other.  There is soooo much flexibility, it's amazing.  It's also incredibly stable.  I have not had one single issue, even when I enabled some of the "Unsupported Plugin" features that had warning boxes and flashing lights (jk not really lol).
Now, it can be a little daunting at first, as you have to basically "program" your commands in a very simple synatx, but I found it easy to pick up after an hour.  The documentation is absolutely incredible.  I work in the computer science field, and there are people who's entire jobs is writing documentation who write worse documentation than this software has.  Maybe I just work with some bad people, I don't know, but what I do know is it was written in a way that was easy to pick up for non-programmers and programmers alike.   That aside, the community and developer has some amazing support, and if you have trouble you can just ask.
You can even set up variables, and do loops.  I haven't got it working yet, but I plan on adding a command to constantly request docking permission from stations in Elite Dangerous every so many seconds in the event the docks are all full.  The software is capable of doing just that.
So, would I recommend this?  Yes.  Yes.  For sure yes.

Qualifications: I have played ARPG/MOBA's since AoS / TOB. Played hundreds hours of dota / hon / lol / hots / dota 2. I also played a few games of bloodline champions but didn't find it very compelling, and there were ping issues playing from Australia on US servers.
TLDR Review:  The aesthetics are excellent, the progression system balances the interest of players and the developer ($) fairly, the size of the game is currently less than 2GB compressed, it runs without flaw and the netcode is fast - I am yet to encounter any problems.
The gameplay is overtly simple, but there is deep nuance and complexity hiding behind the simplicity. Timing, skill shots, positioning, area control, movement, builds (loadouts) and teamwork create a broad spectrum for skill and a deep level of strategy.
In addition to being a joy to play, it makes for a great viewing (streaming) as combat has a consistent intensity throughout, in contrast to other MOBA's were it is broken up by periods of farming, death timers and movement.
I haven't had fun playing MOBA's in years, this game has reinvigorated my love for video games and the A-RTS / MOBA genre, time will tell how long it can hold my interest, but I am enjoying the hell out of this game at the moment!
9 / 10 from me, with plenty of room to improve with game changes, new maps and new champions. This is how F2P should be done.
Congratulations to Stunlock Studios - If they were a public company, I would invest, this game is destined for success, and hopefully, it will topple the current MOBA's.

If you like any of the previous GRID games then you will be happy with this itteration. It combines both simulation and arcade racing. There are pretty severe downfalls to this game however, and it does truely ruin the experience.
The singleplayer is a decent experience. It is the typical arcade style menu system in which you choose a race out of a list and take part in it. Compared to GRID 1 it is very simplistic. You simply pick a race, pick a team and go! You still have a team-driver taking part with you on most events and have the ability to change his driving tactics.
All of this would have been great if the AI weren't so clumsy. On the easier difficulties (easy or medium), they are extremely slow and easy to win. Even with inexperienced gamers. However, as soon as you pick a higher difficulty, they become extremely aggressive, ignore the player and drive with the strength of a tank. You will be span off the track constantly.
Having only played online with friends (not publically either), I cannot comment on the entire online experience, but it is pretty good. When the online lobby is first created, players can join fine, the first race is usually flawless. However, oftentimes there will be game-breaking desychronisation issues on some races after that.
One main issue I keep encountering is where the AI will not load for the players properly. The host will see ALL AI, but some most will not move and stay at the starting grid. Other players will either see the same, or not see any AI at all. You and your players can race fine (although unfairly) but the race will never end since the AI haven't even moved from start line yet. There are MORE issues with online, that will most likely never be fixed by codemasters.
In conclusion, I recommend this game IF you like any of the previous GRID games AND if you can get over the constant bugs and flaws with AI and connection issues. It is fun (for the most part) and is ever so steadily improving with DLC. Hopefully Codemasters will at least attempt to fix the online issues before pumping out even more DLC for a broken game.

If you've ever played a "Space Trader" type of game, then you are already going to be familiar with the basic premise of Rebel Galaxy.  For those unfamiliar, the core of the gameplay involves zipping from system to system, station to station, selling your gotten (ill or otherwise) gains, buying upgrades and/or new ships, getting more loots, warp, rinse, repeat.  If that doesn't sound like your cup of tea, then let me save you some time - don't play this game.  For those that are fans of the formula, you won't find many, if any, surprises here, but some solid fun and colorful carnage.
In Rebel Galaxy, you can trade, mine, or bounty hunt your way to fortune.  You will likely do a mixture of these things, but RG places a lot of emphasis on the combat aspect.  It is quite rare not to run into at least one combat scenario on any particular outing, and most (maybe all) missions center around combat.  In the late stages of the game, this has the perhaps unfortunate effect of relegating the basic but interesting trade aspect of the game as secondary gameplay characteristic, with mining becoming a boring tertiary.  I found myself busting open enemy capital ships like pinatas and simply selling loot off to the highest bidder as I bounced between station between my next objective.
Combat is, at first, thankfully decently enjoying.  It's fun to take your little ship, soup it up, and take on fleets that outmatch you.  You can also hire a mercenary ship which gives you, again, at first, valuable support in the early to mid-game.  Your ship operates on a 2d plane, and you try to maneuver your broadsides into position to blast other capital ships, switching to turrets to swat down fighter ships.  Fighters are the only craft that move on a 3d axis.  This keeps combat simple and easy to get into, but also painfully straightforward.  There are a number of weapon combination you can experiment with, but by the time you get into the mid game, it's generally most effective to simply spam DPS.
On the odd occassion, you will find yourself in some entertaining scuffles.  Getting into a 3-way battle where every faction hates you makes for some chaotic fun.  Unfortunately these situations are rare and most battles consist of working away at the edge of a small fleet and spamming DPS on capital ships you can lure out of formation, then on to the next, etc.  You can hire a mercenary, but this becomes a huge waste of money toward the end game when that mercenary that you paid over 1 million credits for dies within 3 battles.
Also, by the time you get to the end game, you will likely be ridiculously over-powered.  I beat the game before I even acquired a dreadnaught class ship, and with top rank equipment I could very easily take on fleets consisting of multiple deadnaughts, destroyers, frigates, corvettes, and swarms of fighter craft.
The main missions and the story are devoid of any really interesting characters.  The humans look like the same 4 white people with different hair and costumes.  The aliens are all the same one person.  No one has any interesting personalities, and are even weak from a cliche standpoint.  The plot is, at best, competent but not remarkable in any way what-so-ever.  The atmopshere of the game is a mixed bag.  The bundled music is a great collection of blues rock, but gets repetetive (fortunately, the game's launcher makes it easy to mix your own music into the game's playlist, something I recommend).  The denizens can't seem to figure out of they're space hicks or space limeys.  The main antagonists are about entirely devoid of any sort of personality at all, and basically just shoot at you whilst screeching angrily.
This review might sound like I'm shooting Rebel Galaxy down as mercilessly as the hundreds of fighter ships I neutron-beamed into metallic space vapor.  This isn't really the case though.  Particularly in the first half of the game where I ran around in a (relatively) tiny Icarus corvette, armed to the teeth and taking on ships three times my size.  It's just that this game could have really been a lot better than it is.  It hits a lot of the right notes, but only in extremely shallow ways.  This made it just "decent" instead of a future classic.  It could have also benefited greatly from a custom skirmish mode that allows players to set up scenarios for theory-crafting or just simply massive chaos on a large scale.  Rebel Galaxy 2, perhaps?  As it stands, it's a solidly enjoyable entry into the space trader genre, but definitely only for fans.

Wonderful game, simple, straightforward, and oriented toward those who love driving, and not just a race game.
You get to build your very one car, upgrading it, getting attached to it, learning what it likes and what it diesn't, trying out builds, refining it's look.
Enjoy hours of driving through wonderful landscapes, as you crank the volume on the radio up and open the window, hope the bad smoke won't come just yet, trying to reach the gas station to get a new repair kit after using the last you had.
Its concept is very simple, and the game feels very simple at a first glance, yet, a simple thing can make your trip a nightmare.
Forgot to fuel up and don't have a fuel can on a 420km long trip without gas station? Better hope you'll make it there or maybe are lucky enough to find an abandonned laika with a spare reservoir.
Not enough money for the motel? Gotta sell some spare stuff, hoping you can get enough to pass the night and will find abandonned stuff on the road.
On the downsides, that game still being early access, a few bugs and crashes are to be expected, but nothing that cannot be fixed with a little removal of the v-sync or setting the traffic AI lower.
Main issue with the "tutoriel", while very well done, nothing tells you about how to gain money, gotta find out by yourself what to do, but it's no biggie.
I spend hours on that game, as short as the full trip still is, as it's missing part of the cities to go to, the randomness and different weathers and lengh of travel you get everytime makes it so I still discover new elements as I try new roads even now.
This game clearly is for those who love idle exploration and find driving relaxing, but for its price, I think it's well worth it, and can only get better with time, as it's often updated.

ShipLord
Space Avoid-er
Just1337 Studio
KupiKey
is an indie space avoid-er developed by Just1337 Studio and published by KupiKey.
You play as the crew of a spaceship, whose goal is to collect Quasar, the only energy source in the universe, while also avoiding the alien specie of Kryp, who is after all the Quasar.
The story is pretty simple and straight-forward, and it lacks any depth, but it doesn't have to have one. Since it isn't the main goal of the game, I'm gonna forgive it for its simplicity.
The game looks surprisingly really good: the design of the ships is neither too detailed nor too simplistic, and the asteroids are mostly varied from one another. The background is gorgeous, with planets rotating and stars shining. However, more than once I confused an asteroid for a background planet, and vice-versa, resulting in my instant death, forcing me to turn off the planets from the Options menu to avoid further dying.
Your goal is to collect as many Quasar as possible while avoiding asteroids. You also have three abilities to use: a energy shield, a force field that stops the massive rocks in their tracks, and energy collection that instantly attracts every Quasar that has spawned. You will also battle bosses, which consists in avoiding their attacks for a certain amount of time.
As you can see the gameplay is very simple and easy to master. It is very reminiscent of some good old space games that managed to be both fun without requiring complicated mechanics and big variety.
The game gets harder and harder the more you play: the speed and amount of asteroids increases, and each boss has a precise pattern that you must follow to avoid being insta-killed.
The electronic soundtrack is pretty decent, and both sound effects and voice acting do their job. For being a first-time developer, it's pretty good.
There are 15 levels, as well as bonus ones, different skins for your ship, upgrades that feel a bit useless, and 9 Steam achievements for completionists. However, I believe that once you've beaten the game, you won't feel the need to go back to it again.
Overall, the game is a good space avoid-er that fans of the genre must play. If you aren't familiar with them, I recommend waiting for it to go on sale, since it is pretty good in it of itself, with some good-looking graphics and easy gameplay.

ShipLord is a side-scroller with a novel approach to level progression. Put simply:
Instead, you must quickly and carefully manoeuvre your spaceship to dodge incoming asteroids and enemy projectiles. You will be rewarded if you collect enough energy orbs along the way too.
Helping you to survive the onslaught of asteroids are 3 abilities: a shield which provides temporary invulnerability, a force field to slow down time and repel asteroids and a tracor beam
that pulls energy to your position. They're all upgradeable too, which is a nice reward between levels. Unlockable ships and bonus levels provide some extra incentive to score highly.
It's simple, addictive and exhilerating gameplay which quickly becomes challenging, not only because of the tricky asteroid projectories (and sneaky ultra-fast moon rocks!) but also due to
the lack of mid-level checkpoints. They wouldn't make much sense here however, because levels consist of surviving for "only" 1 minute or so. Expect to repeat some levels a few times until you learn when and where the troublesome asteroids pop up.
Like the regular levels, ShipLord features inventive boss encounters too. For example, you must defeat the first one without using any abilities. Better hope your dodging skills are well-honed!
Music and sound effects did not have much of an impact on me, but some of the voice acting is done well.
Gameplay is very smooth and it feels nice piloting the sapceship in and around the obstacles while collecting enough energy your nerves can risk going for. The 3D planets orbiting in the background are a pleasant distraction.
To summarize: the presentation is very nice and good attention to detail is evident throughout. Just1337 Studio have conceived an original game and executed it very well. This is only their
first release, so I would keep a close eye on Just1337 Studio if I were you!

When viewed as a sequel to Civ V, this game falls short. I think a lot of us were expecting the full Brave New World experience right off the bat, but I remember what Civ V was like before Gods and Kings, and before Brave New World, and I feel the new mechanics implemented in Beyond Earth are interesting and different. As a stand-alone turn-based strategy game, Beyond Earth holds up well. The sci-fi setting means it's more about making your own backstory for the colony than taking on a pre-established history, so while there are no fun "I just nuked Ghandi" moments, you feel more like the actual leader of the colony, making alliances with no preconceptions of who your partners are.

PROS:
- Cars look awesome from the outside, Tracks and locales are breathtaking when graphics are turned up.

CONS:
- HOWEVER (on the last point) the ST is known for it's ludicrous cornering ability, and i had to upgrade the car and Soften the front suspenstion/stiffen the rear suspension to get the most realistic driving experience one should expect from the ST. I could be biased but the car is an autocross machine and handles perfectly well just as stock.
- car interiors ARE A JOKE. I only play racing games in first person in-car view so as to fully immerse myself in the experience. i hate to compare this to Need for Speed, but if you look at Shift, the interiors, even for the low-end/old drifter cars, are immaculately rendered, and you can look around. in Grid, looking left or right blinks the screen left or right to an un-interior generic side view, giving me no frame of reference because my driver didn't turn his head. In addition, on graphical settings where the cockpit isn't blurred, the instrumentation is blocky and disgusting. at night, no dashboard or other interior lights are visible. Again, i drive a focus, and although the shape of the top of the dashboard is correct (even reflecting *almost* as i would expect when the sun hits it, i'm sorry but at night that console needs to be LIT. So yeah, Codemasters, MASSIVE missed opportunity with the car interior. i can't bring myself to look left or right because what i get is a generic blank view of what's on the left or right because my driver doesn't turn his head like NFS Shift so i have no frame of reference, and the worst part is it's just as well because what IS rendered of the interior of the car is a half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥POS anyway in both texture and polygon terms. Bad bad bad car interior.
That's it, every other part of the game is straight up FUN, with beautifully rendered and presented cars on beautiful tracks and HOLY♥♥♥♥♥♥I'M DRIVING IN PARIS THIS IS SO COOL and the driving is awesomely gratifying in just the right realistic correct way that one can get better at before they know it. Car interiors are disgustingly, DISGUSTINGLY disappointing though. Need for Speed: Shift, i'm looking at the exact interior of a Lamborghini Reventon from radio to seat stitching to AC vents. Grid, i'm looking at something a 6 year old made using Duplo bricks.

Do you play games with so many buttons you can't possibly remember them all ? such as Flight sims, Star Citizen or Elite Danngerous ? If the annswer is yes then I strongly urge you to buy this product as it is quite simply awesome at what it does.
I use this for Elite and Star Citizen and having the ability to tell my ship to "prepare for landing" (the landing gear lowers) or to go into "combat mode" (decoupling) or to "stand down" (the hardpoints on my Viper retract). I really finnd this adds to the immersion of the games I use it with (i'm still working on my VR profiles atm :D )
There are a lot of ready made profiles in which people have added sounds to play when the command applys - Either a voice such as Glados from Portal
or an enntirely new creation such as HICS for Star Citizen
I also use it for a Jukebox in my games as there is a simple feature which will play your music and also make sure that there are no repeats if your list is randomised.
Setting up a new profile is actually quite simple aswell so you won't need to be a complete code wizard to use this - which in my case is excellent as I know nothing of coding/programming etc etc. It isd literally a case of the following :-
1: create new profile
2: edit new profile
3: add new command
4: type in the word you want to say and then click the "key press button" and put in the keyboard command you wish to activate when you say the word/phrase
5: repeat step 2 to 4 for the rest of the commands
6: launch game
7: talk to game
Once you see the editing page you will see exactly how easy it is, The developer of this should be striking deals with Frontier and Cloud Imperium as they compliment each other so well, I can't comment exactly on flight sims ETC as I don't own any but I have no reason at all to think that the process would be any more difficult at all. I am really selling this software short for what it can do so I suggest you take this review as if I had just opened it for an hour and played around a bit - this can do so much more and it is still all simple.

tl;dr: get the OpenRCT2 mod.
Do yourself a favor, forget about more recent theme park simulators, forget about sequels to this game that tried to take it into 3D, this one is the definitive theme park simulator. There's a point at which something becomes so perfected that there's no reason to try to make a better version of it. It rarely happens in games, but RCT2, particularly with the OpenRCT2 mod, becomes the perfect theme park simulator game. After the mod, you have 1080p, 60fps, steam integration. Less crashes than the vanilla game. Autosaving. Quality-of-life fixes. Seriously, just check it out:
The visuals are timeless, look great, and are actually more straighforward to play with on a isometric grid rather than in complete 3 dimensions, especially when designing paths and tracks. Now count in the countless mods for the game, new rides, endless scenarios, porting of RCT1 scenarios, and the ridiculous amount of hours you can spend finishing even just the vanilla game scenarios, you've got a game for the ages.
Sometimes I hear the question: "If you were put in jail for 3 years and had no internet but could choose 1 game to play, what would it be?" This game. The amount of content and time you can put into it is higher than almost any other offline game. What's more, with very simple mods you can also join other players in online play.
As I said, this game has reached perfection due to the community around it. You don't need another theme park simulator. This one is all you will ever need, due to it's incredible depth of features and the enthusiastic open-source community behind it.

VoiceAttack has changed the way I use my computer.  The ability to create completely custom voice commands with custom sound/voice feedback has led me to program profiles for almost every game, simulator and program I have.  It's quite addictive.  From things as simple as playing and pausing Netflix, to complex macros to automate functions, Voice attack has proved useful in so many ways.
It is remarkably easy to use once you get your head around it.  Find the keystroke, shortcut or button you wish to activate by voice, create the command and type what you want to say to activate it. Then add the keystrokes or shortcuts in the order you want them with any pauses you may require, then finish by adding your audio feedback be it a specific sound, a random sound from a directory or spoken feedback.  That's it.
Examples:
Euro Trucker 2 "Attatch trailer"
DCS World "Landing gear up"
Windows "Shut down"
I would reccomend this app to everyone.  It's a great tool to have.  When you bring VR into the equation, then it becomes essential in my view.  When it is awkward getting to your keyboard and having to remove your headset, you can save a lot of messing about.
There are cheaper apps claiming to do similar things but VoiceAttack is solid, functional and reliable.  Highly reccomended.

Best 'BioShock' game released to date-- improving on BioShock's mechanics and giving a straight-cut storyline that frankly allows for more replayability than the first game due the the fact that there's no huge twists that the game rides off of which makes the story boring on repeated playthroughs. Had this been by Ken Levine, yeah, it would have had a huge twist; all his games have similar twists.
BioShock 2 skips the crowd pandering and supernatural drama tv show vibe that Infinite gave us and goes straight back to Rapture for Round 2 and a closer look at the characters of Rapture. Characters from past, deceased or otherwise, are fleshed out in more audio logs which provides a different viewpoint in their motives.
Plasmids take a farily large upgrade as well. Instead of only being able to upgrade damage and appearance of each plasmids, upgrading adds new ways to use each plasmids. If you upgrade to Electro Shock 2, you can create a ball of electricity or ground trap, at Electro Shock 3, you can shoot continous streams of electricity-- and most plasmids are this way.
Guns are practically the same, although reskinned to appear as a Big Daddy variant, with the typical three ammo types and upgrade stations that can eventually make your weapon super-charged.
Overall, it's more technically advanced than the first BioShock game, with an average story that did it's job (and I praise it for), and if you actually played the Shock series in order, is more engaging and atmospheric than Infinite.

Gave this game a good hour of my time before I gave up. Why?
Was it the sub-par graphics? No. I can live with graphics being basic, but they are styled to something I'd expect in an MMO about five or six years ago.
Was it the vast emptiness? Also no. While I was on there were NO other players on at all. So these vast villages and towns felt... dead. But even then, I prefer single player games, so I can live with that.
Was it the bugs and massive lag-spikes? Yes. Falling through the terrain became all too commonplace. Several times I would spend five minutes running a metre due to a lag spike forcing me to re-run it. Also, why so much delay between acknowledging I've hit attack/move/speak/craft/open menu (it makes a sound and graphic when you do) and actually performing that function.
So why the immediate hatred for this game with just a few bugs? The truth is that there are far better free-to-play MMOs out there that nailed down the basics before they decided to get all fancy (Neverwinter, Rift, DC Universe just to name three). Yes, the player controlled villages was a cool idea, whilst every game needs a hook, you should always make a game PLAYABLE first.
Players will forgive an average game that has a good (if somewhat buggy) hook if the basics are playable. Why? They'll stay long enough to give the developers a chance to streamline the hooks.
Players will not forgive a subpar game that has a good hook if the basics are buggy? Why? They'll abandon it before the developers actually improve the game engine.

This game begins with the designing your character - choose wisely, there is no going back on the customisation unless you are willing to pay real money for it.
The talents and skills you choose to start off with gives you a head start in those areas, but they can be changed as you progress or by using a potion. Each style has its own variations and each variation has its own perk, so plan ahead what perk you want for your character. Choose the style in accordance to the perk you want, even if the variation with that particular perk is not available when you start off. You can always buy the variation you want as soon as you have placed your house. Changing one house styles to another cost a lot of gold (120 gold) though, so it's better to choose the right style to begin with and then just buy extra variations to that style, which is cheaper (30-90 gold).

It's a cross between Freelancer and Sid Meier's Pirates! It's like Freelance in the sense that you get to upgrade your ship, trade, be a space pirate if you want and side with a faction. It's similar to Sid Meier's Pirates! as you get to go to outposts which have fluctuating prices of goods, have a bar in which you can get information and hire a merc to work for you and in-game events that influence how much goods cost.
Let's take it part by part:
Gameplay: It's an open world (or open galaxy) 3rd person space combat simulation that let's you be your own kind of spacefarer. Though you're in space, you can only go left or right as there is no up and down movement. There are 2-3 tiers of basic upgrades for your ship in the first solar system, and I think it adds one per system you go into (I'm not sure yet. I've played 16 hours of the game and I'v eonly done a few story missions lol). There are factions and so far, I've only encountered one guild.
Story: I haven't played much of the main storyline so far as I spent most of my time doing side missions and getting money. I'm sorry about this.
Combat: The combat is kinda tricky at first but It's kinda awesome once you get the hang of it. Also, you can travel to the next system as soon as you want and upgrade your ship enough to be really overpowered in the previous system. I have mining lasers that swat around fighters like they're mosquitoes.
Graphics: The developers didn't skip out on making this game beautiful. From projectiles and laser beams to missile and engine trails, the graphics look great. The makers of the game didn't also skip out on the characters here, animating them with lip movements consistent with their dialogue (I really shouldn't be impressed with this but I am because they could've just put in a picture and have dialogue play in the background).
Music and Sound Effects: Sound effects are to be expected in a space shooter but there's a small amount of dialogue that has some popping "p's" during recording. The music makes the atmosphere kinda feel like you're in Firefly (TV Series) and you can include tracks of your own as there's an option before you start the game. There's nothing like having beams of lasers shoot around while you're listening to dubstep.

+ They run events that make the game feel somewhat alive and give you the sense that maybe other people are playing.
- Port from mobile. It works, but it's not efficient. The UI was designed for portrait mode on a phone, so we're better off playing in a tall window. The buttons are massive, but I guess you won't misclick.

- RNG/Loot crate effect. There's some very powerful characters out there, and you might never get them. Every player should be able to assign Lumberg to a floor, but most people who play won't get him.

On the technical side, it looks great and sounds ok. The music though I found it cool in the begining, I muted it afterwards. Also I was not fond of the miniaturised star systems. It made the game world feel too small.
