This is gonna be a long, in-depth review. While I give it the thumbs up, I do so with a grain of salt, and a very big grain of salt.
But for those of you with TL;DR Syndrom, here is a short summary:  The game has graphics that look bad today, but has a good, nostalgia feel, while also giving a nice digital world look. Its a basic and standard MMO, but lacking in some content specifically, content found in other MMOs.
So, to begin with, Im into MMOs. Personally, I am interested in a social MMO, with different aspects to play. Namely, housing, PvE-content, socializing among the community, dungeon runs, RP especially like a knight (like, wearing knights armour, sword, shield, horse) and some PvPing. Yes, I'm aware VnH does not have PvP, but more on that later.
So, really, once you see the game world, and the store page, you'd think this game is just what I'm looking for, right?
First off, the game is pretty entertaining in gameplay. The quests, while the standard, go gather x amount of this, talk to someone, find this, find that, can be rather interesting and entertaining enough. Crafting, while I'm not a big fan of it, plays a major role in you getting the best gear, weapons, etc.
Furthermore, the community is so friendly that they'd simply all agree to craft you whatever item(s) you need/wanted. So it is possible to rank up your crafts at a relaxing pace.
Classes: Its the usual class system that we've seen in all the other MMOs before:Heavy armoured, melee damage inflicting warriors, the OPed archers, the annoying healing Priests, and of course the-middle-of-all-the-classes, the wizard, who is a rather interesting class.
The game is also not p2w at all. There are ways to get market items for free in drops and your daily Lucky Cards. The gear that takes real money, is simply for looks. It shows it comes with no new moves, attacks, or ratings to suggest buying one would give yourself an advantage in battle.
Storage is a problem, but it is so much better than other MMOs, especially SWTOR and Eldevin. There are literally, 28 vaults you can rent, 3 more bags, and storage conatiners you can share with your other characters.
Ultimately, without getting to the end of the game, I can tell you who the final boss will be. No darklord, no emperor, no stone lord, no evil wizard, witches, dark knights, or anything. Storage will be the final boss. The game should be called Storage Wars, as given enough time, it'll cause you tons of problems. So storage is a big time problem, but the storage you start out with, as well as the free vault, will give you a great start. The rest is for once you travel deep into the game.
Something I would like to see added to the game:
Mini games. Somethin to do to pass a few minutes, earn a few coins, and maybe play against another player, like checkers, chess, duel etc. The games could be simple like, memory, side-scrolling and other such little things, VnH themed! It'd certainly help the game. I'd even be satisfied with that to count as PvP.
Now, for the negatives. I'll list them, then explain. As you'll clearly see, this game is lacking majorly in some content that has become the standard in MMOs:
1.No mounts.
2. No PvP.
Yep thats right. No mounts. Now, it wouldn't be such a big deal to me. I could make do without a horse to ride around on. Majorly dissapointed, yes. But not detrimental to the game.
Now, why people couldn't raise aniamals to ride around on, like horses for example, it would fit in PERFECTLY with the game setting. Ultimately, the game is split into two halves: 50% deals with farming, gathering, and just being a neighbor.
The other 50% deals with setting off on adventure to kill Ai monsters. So, raising a colt to a full grown horse wouldn't just make sense, it would only add to the game's depth, adding to the theme of the community working together to build a world, making it more interesting all around! Even Eldevin, who's mechanics, and graphics are much older than this game, has a VARIETY of mounts as well as also being set in a medieval world.
Next, the PvP. Players love dueling it out on the internet. PvP arenas/ zones/ servers can be found just about anywhere on an online-themed game. So why not here? To keep the the community happy, they say. Well ok, I can try to deal with that. I understand that part. Sadly, it has kept me away from really jumping into the game, wanting to spending money, etc. on it. No pressure Mad Otter. Personally, I think that the lack of PvP is really what has also kept this game from becoming something bigger and being able to compete in the MMO market against the giants of the internet.
Finally we have reached the Big One. Housing. Ok, at character creation (best creation I ever went through on a game!)
So at creation, they ask for your house design. They list a few different styles for the outside of your house look. And, once you reach the capital city, right inside, is a guy named Donald. Who is, apparently, in love with the fact that players can own a house. He gives you a quest to go to any village and talk to his sister. The reward: one title to own a house! For free! You must simply choose the when and where! Exciting, isn't it?
So, after settling down on a spot, I buy my house. First thing you'll see is, that there are DOZENS of outside decoration looks, but they cost real money. No matter though, its just whats on the inside, right?
Long story short, there is no housing. All that hubbub about how wonderful they are? Apparently being able to have an extra vault, with access to all your storage areas, is something wonderful everyone should have!
Scam of the game, I call it.
There is talk they'll add interior housing to the game, but no immediate plans of when and it dont sound like the devs are even working on it as of 11/21/15.

With mixed feelings, I'm recommending this game.  Read on for the full review and gamer beware.
Dungeons 2 is a worthy heir to Dungeon Keeper legacy and also throws in some War Craft style RTS gameplay.  The mechanics are incredibly polished and storyline is very tongue-in-cheek but amazingly thought out and scripted.  Anyone who was a fan of the original Dungeon Keeper franchise, or RTS's in general will definitely enjoy this title.
Now for the issues which gave me pause.  Unfortunately, I just paid $30 for a tutorial campaign.  That is unacceptable Kalypso.  I love your franchise and this was a COMPLETE DISSERVICE.  After spending less time to complete than almost any other game I've played, it ended just as soon as it had begun, LITERALLY TELLING YOU 'Now comes the real game', and, oh yeah, BUY IT!  As to why I say it's a tutorial campaign, you literally CAN NOT LOSE!  The entire campaign was designed to familiarize the player with the mechanics and trickled just enough resistance to only slow you down before utterly overwhelming your opponent.  Every level was designed to encourage you to easily research all upgrades and 'sandbox' your way to victory at your own pace.  Also, ala Starcraft, you're given the opportunity to try 2 different factions and the third, which I assume wasn't ready for release, is destined for DLC.  Again, the keyword is "TRY".  Even the Heores of Might and Magic franchise provides secondary campaigns with it's admitedly easy to complete tutorials >_<
So yes, with a heavy heart, I recommend this game, but only bcause of what it could be, not because of the TUTORIAL I just completed.  How about throwing us gamers that purchased this product a complentary, real, campaign?

is already a lot of fun to play in its current stage. It's a small and simple game, not one you'll likely play through an entire night's session (although once I almost did), but one you'll probably want to come back to again and again for another quick round or two.
There are many cute details that make it different from most other driving and racing games in existence. First of all is, of course, the titular car you're driving. It's an old, ramshackle and unreliable car that is quite unpredictable and takes a lot of maintenance. While other games might have you perform chip tuning, adjust your gear ratios or put some embarrassing neon lights on your car, you're going to be dealing with much more basic stuff here. Hope you'll make it to the next gas station with that popped tire, adjust the oil-to-fuel ratio for your two-stroke engine, or decide whether you're going to sell your air filter so you can afford an extra can of gas for the road, just to be sure.
The game has some rogue-like elements, in that upgrades to your car are permanent. You can run into big trouble on any one of your road trips. Run out of fuel miles from the next gas station, run out of money and not being able to pay for a hotel or some essential repairs, and so on. In those cases, you can alwasy reset the game by going back home, and starting your trip from scratch. Maybe next time you'll be luckier, and earn enough cash to afford the next upgrade that will make subsequent trips more successful.
The main game mechanic is about finding and selling goods to finance those upgrades. All along the (randomly generated but linear) roads, it's possible to find cardboard boxes and locked crates containing various basic goods. These can be sold at gas stations and shops in towns, where prices vary depending on what there's currently an abundance or shortage of in the country. This is based mostly on luck, but quite motivating. You're always going to have basic expenses: fuel, oil, repairs, hotels, maybe even fines for crashing or smuggling contraband. But anything you earn beyond that, you can invest in your car. New engines and engine parts, paint jobs, repair tools, or a roof rack for extra storage space are all for sale. On a lucky trip, you might find half a dozen bottles of wine, just before reaching a country that has a shortage of alcohol. And there's your new carburettor!
Graphically, the simplistically rendered environments already look very good, and there's a nice variety between the different country-to-country trips (more are being added). The original soundtrack is one of the game's strong points. And I like how the car's controls are all toggled from the actual cockpit, from lights and wipers to the radio and popping the hood.
Being Early Access, of course there's still numerous bugs that can crash your game or make you lose progress. Still, the atmosphere and "random loot" make this little game already so much fun to play, that it's definitely worth considering already getting it now. The developer is also very responsive, updates often, and is adding many of the suggestions to the game. This is how Early Access should be done!

A lot of reviewers have rightfully dinged the game not running under Win 10 x64. If the game is going to be marketed to an audience with modern computers, it should be able to run without excuses about it being old. My problems were resolved by opening the Add/Remove Programs applet, selecting Windows Features, and enabling Legacy Components / Direct Play.
Sudden Strike’s biggest problem is that it is an old game with old game problems. Path finding is horrible, with units often taking the long way around obstacles and exposing themselves to plenty of enemy fire. Tanks bump into each other, and often advance backwards with their weakest face to the enemy. Supply vehicles collide like keystone kops, get confused, and stop resupplying.
You’re often are presented with large maps with a lot of units to start with, but it’s never explained that you need to take the objectives in the order listed, or you don’t get reinforcements. The enemy troops mostly sit in defensive positions with artillery, and do a remarkable job of killing a lot of your units before they are winkled out of their foxholes. They receive a seemingly endless supply of Tiger and Panther tanks that are ridiculously hard to kill.
In the face of strong German armor and endless troops, you have limited reinforcements that are doled out as you capture objectives. Reinforcements consist of weak armored vehicles and infantry easily mowed down by dug-in defenders. This is the type of game that requires a lot of attention on your part. You command literaly thousands of troops and equipment to accomplish your objectives. These could be any one of seceral battles in the Eurpoean theater to the invasion of Iwo Jima to its defense as the entrenched Japanese Army.
Be forewarned that this is not a 'get in and win the battle in thiry minutes' type game. For instance, in landing on Iwo Jima there are two objectives. Take two seperate Japanese command posts on opposite ends of the island. Your troops land on the beaches and your job is to move them up the beach to engage and take cover. Tanks and halftarcks, etc to follow by the way.
I made plans to take the first objective and fond that you have to keep an eye on your troops because if you fail to do so they take the least path of resistance land/obstacle wise and end up getting slaughtered by entrenched Japanses machine gunners in trenchs along the beach. You have the ability as a bonus mode to call in naval artillery and airstrikes but these come up occasionally and aren't always readily available so use them wisely. As with 'real life' shell or bomb and area where resistance is tough and then advance your troops in the 'cautious' or 'attack' mode. Once you have your troops in cover or trenches you can switch to 'defensive' and have them hold their ground.
If you're looking for long (maybe up to a couple of hours or more) of real strategy battle tactics using riflemen, flamethrowers, machine gunners, officers, medics and engineers supplemented with tanks, halftarcks, jeeps, planes, bombers, artillery both land and naval then this game will give you a true "Armchair General" experience. Not recommended for kids or those with short attention spans or those who play first persons shooters constantly.
Another very similar game is Theater of war. If you've tried that you'll enjoy this one but with even better graphics.

Emerge is an unique 4X city-builder/defender which got crossed with some rogue-lite features!
You'll have to save cities (Or die trying) by capturing/defending territories (An amount is required in each mission) and by doing a special objective (The real condition to win that matters).
I said "rogue-lite" cause you cannot manually save your game, it means you can't "go back" and you create an unique character for each mission. There are plenty of classes, starting bonuses and weapons to choose.
...But i prefer to give you a list of things as we are talking about something pretty big:
_Build defenses (Automated turrets)
_Manage random territories and capture these wisely (Each one gets its own statistics)
_Explore (Random but expected "positive" or "negative" event)
_Random events (The unexpected ones)
_Big amount of loot including items, consumables and weapons (Those last with degrees of rarity of course!)
_Build manufactories into your city (To improve your production, economy and science stats and even more things...)
_Defend or attack territories by yourself, alone or with recruits (Nicely done that action part of the game)
_Level-up system with perks to select (Each class gets its own skills)
_There are a campaign, skirmish and a challenge mode
_Spend your AP each turn carefully, in addition many options can be added on your AP bar.
_Research tree split on 3 branchs (Quite complex as you always want to pick up everything :D)
_More of + 15 types of ennemies to fight (With 3 bosses)
_And even more things you'll find out by yourself :)
First you'll find it hard, unbalanced and too agressive... And then you'll eventually learn (Unlike mostly of negative reviews who found it "impossible" within one hour or less) you'll find SO MANY possibilities, SO HUGE content to discover and unlock. Finally those ways you found firstly insanely tough, you'll laught about next :)
So yeah, i enjoy it VERY much. It's not a game apparently to put on every hands as not everybody gets the patience required to understand it well. But if you enjoy challenges, good replayability, countless of possiblities, then you have to try out that hidden little gem which is
Thank you for reading :)

Theirs something unique about driving a little Laika 601(Trabant) through Europe, Travelling from the GDR, through the CSFR and further. With the changing enviroments and roads turning from the Autobahn to small dirt ones.  ThIs  games not just a simple roadtrip however, you will have to make repairs to your little Laikas 2-stroke engine. Make emergency roadside tyre changes and much more. Along the way you will have to finance yourself by buying and selling. Finding boxes and crates alongside the road that could contain valuable goods. Or even stopping by the scrapyard to salavage some parts for your Laika. Or if you're feeling wealthier then take a trip to the Laika dealership. Buying anything from new engine parts to roof racks, to extra lights, or for extra customization a can of paint or decals to a unique touch.
For a game that is in early development still, it is definitely an entertaining one. Whilst it does have some glitches and bugs that you can encounter along the way such as flipping your Laika onto its roof. Or falling through some steps along the coast. They do not ruin the experience that this game provides. For what could seem a simple concept of a  roadtrip you can tell that the developers have worked hard to recreate both the atmosphere of the late Cold War. With Soviet Ladas and Yugos filling up the motorway. Whilst the little in-car radio plays upbeat but fitting music that only adds further to the experience of chugging along in your little car.
If you've ever wanted to drive an East German car through Eastern Europe during the fall of the wall. Then this is likely the game for you. Or if you want to play with upgrades, economy and all the hassle you will have with your jalopy breaking down. It's a solid recommendation. Sure, it's in Early Access and has quite a few amusing bugs and glitches, just don't expect the whole game to be polished and perfect. As its one of the best games i've seen come out of Greenlight.

BioShock 2 still manages to be my favorite BioShock game AND overall favorite shooter of all time.. but there was so much denial towards this game's existence.. why?
Well as we know, BioShock is supposed to be filled with plot-twists and mind bending story.. that's it.. that's what most people didn't like about BioShock 2, as it's a much simpler "Search and Rescue" storyline set in Rapture.

The graphics are pretty. The affinity system is neat. The addition of quests is welcome.
Gameplay systems are otherwise uninspiring. There is no world council/UN. Aliens supposedly push back against you beating on them, but I don't see it in practice. The quests usually boil down to building a new type of building each time you research a tech, allowing you to choose one of two bonuses.

Supposedly there will be an expansion that revolutionizes this type of game by allowing you to build cities in water! Uh, except that Alpha Centauri already did that and undoubtedly did it better than this unambitious group ever will.
If you are looking for variety in this type of game, do yourself a favor and try out Endless Legend instead.

Emerge: Cities of the Apocalypse
Emerge: Cities Of The Apocalypse is a resource management and real time defence shooter as described on the store page. The whole world here is again ravaged by zombies and as a survivor it’s your job to take back the control of the cities.
You start off by creating your survivor choosing from three classes, gender, name etc. The classes being Bounty hunter, Scientist and Engineer which all bring something new to the combat scenarios. You start out in your stronghold where your main objective lies in capturing new parts of cities and fending off zombies. As you progress, you gain new survivors who are randomly generated and help you in taking control over the city. As soon as you capture a part of a city, zombie hordes try to break in and retake that specific part. At this point, you are given the choices to either forfeit or try to battle it out with the zombies. If you decide to slug it out, you are taken to a real time combat screen where your survivors mow down zombies who try to reach a barricade.
If the zombies are successful in reaching the barricade and take it down, the survivors are forced to flee. In this position, some of your survivors tend to die due to the zombies. For a indie game like this, there is a surprising amount of customization available to the player. From the survivors to the gun types, there are a lot of choices which can be made.
In the beginning the only zombies who show up are your basic shambling dumb ones. As the game progresses and you unlock new and bigger maps, deadlier zombies start showing up in your neighbourhood. To keep up with the increasing number and types, you have to modify your buildings and place more survivors to keep the control of your city.
Emerge: Cities of the Apocalypse is visually quite bland. Honestly, it looks like a flash game which could have used a couple more assets. The sound design is good but nothing exceptional. Also, the game struggles with its gun types where the reloading and recoil is totally baffling which leads to many cheap feeling defeats.
Though it has its problems, Emerge: Cities of the Apocalypse is a well thought out game which has a lot of content available for its asking price. If you like these kind of games or are a fan of zombie defence games in general, Emerge should be good enough for you to sink your teeth in.

This is an isometric style twin stick shooter with a fairly decent story mode and a wave survival mode. You will perform brutal executions on people to stay alive as this is the method in which you regain health, blow up buildings and more in what seems like a fully destructible environment backtracked to a pretty awesome heavy metal soundtrack. The protagonist of this game will explain that he hates everyone and just wants to kill as many people as possible. So yeah, very dark in terms of story as you will be required kill a lot of innocent unarmed people, but also armed police officers and army personnel.
In story mode you will go through multiple level in which you will need to kill as many people as possible whilst working towards primary and optional objectives. There is also increasing difficulty levels for story mode to add some re-playability.
Survival mode is as you would expect with a leveling system and a choice of three characters to use; each with different stats. You will also get a choice of weapons whilst working through the leveling system as well as choice of three different settings in which to survive as long as you can.
Achievements if you are interested will take a good amount of time and will require a decent amount of skill but one achievement requires you to play the game for 50 hours, unfortunately the timer for this is broken and ended up taking a lot longer.
I definitely recommend this game but it is not for the faint of heart. This game is violent, gory and sadistic.

flash game series into a compelling, satisfying and addictive format. I never really played much of
but I did play a lot of
back in 2007, and the sequel on the next year. If enjoy both of these series or at least one of them (like myself), I think you’d enjoy this game. That said, brace yourselves for I have a feeling this is going to be a rather long one…
First of all, I’m going to adress some caveats which are the lack of support for resolutions above 720p and any other kind of video options (the game doesn’t look that great but still…) and no mouse sensitivity options. As far as I’m aware the game seems to be locked at 60 fps. That said I find that one of the weakest points of the game are the visuals and the sounds. The sound effects get the job done but they’re pretty ‘meh’ and they, along with the visuals, remind a lot of typical flash games. If you can ignore these superficial details, you’re in for quite the treat.
The game is divided into 2 different sections, a real-time section and a turn-based section, the latter being the one you’ll spend most of your time on. You’ll be responsible for handling a sector of human resistance in a post-apocalyptic world filled with zombies and, at the same time, your goal will be to explore and expand. In each turn you’ll have a certain amount of action points which you can spend on capturing or scouting sectors, boosting your weapon damage or your research for the next turn, looking for survivors to join your squad or simply just exploring which can trigger certain random events and they can be both good and bad for you. There are also various types of resources which you need, production for building defenses, research in order to shorten the amount of turns it takes to research new technologies, economy which allows you to produce more credits each turn, crystals which are a special type of currency and infrastructure which allows you to capture more sectors.
In order to complete your mission you’ll have to capture sectors by moving your squad over a sector and wiping out the enemies inside, assuming there are any. By doing so you’ll gain credits and crystals, and you’ll also have a chance to get some random loot (weapons, mods, grenades, defenses, etc). Still, having a lot of sectors means your defenses will be spread thin but it also means you can build more improvements which will grant you more resources per turn. Scouting also plays a huge role in this part of the game, in the sense that allows you to know what kind of resources a sector produces and how many enemies are there. At the end of each turn zombies will move, so if you’ve scouted the sector to which they moved to, you’ll be able to spot them. Zombies can also try to capture one of your sectors and, depending on your defenses they might succeed or not. If they do succeed you can attempt to reclaim that sector with your squad, or you can just abandon it.
It is when you directly engage in combat, by either capturing a sector or reclaiming one, that the real-time section of the game begins. This is where the game resembles
. Your squad is placed on the right side of the screen behind a barricade and you need to keep the zombies, coming from the left side, from destroying that barricade. Here you’ll face different types of enemies, your standard zombies, crippled zombies, crawlers, zombies that attack from a certain range, burning zombies, you name it. Of course it may sound simple but in truth you there is more depth to it, each member of your squad has different attribute which you can improve upon leveling up and you can also equip them with various different weapons (pistols, plasma rifles, crossbows, grenade launchers, etc) which play a vital role in whether you’re victorious or not. You can also configure the AI of your survivors so that they target either far or closer enemies, weaker, faster, ranged and so on.
That about pretty much sums up the overall gameplay which is explained pretty well in the game tutorial. Now,
and the first one is the fact that you can’t compare the weapon you currently have equiped with the one you’ve selected on your storage/merchant. If this was an option, it would be much easier to compare the loot you just got with the weapon you’re using but alas. Second and last, the game offers a campaign and skirmish mode but the campaign is pretty much just a set of scenarios and there isn’t really any progression. It would be great if you could carry your team to the next mission and maybe even your research, while increasing the difficulty of the game just enough to keep things from becoming too easy but sadly that is not the case.
might not be the looker or the game to feature the greatest and latest in sound design but it combines 2 elements I really enjoy, explore and expand, and the sort of barricade wave defense that I greatly enjoyed from
.
The game sure is repetitive after a few hours but, for me at least, it has that “one more turn” feel to it, which makes it rather addictive. If you enjoy turn-based games of expansion, conquest and resource management but you also like facing your foes head on in real-time combat this might be something you’re interested in. If during your first 2 hours with the game it doesn’t grab you, you can just ask for a refund but if it does, you pretty much know what you’re getting for the rest of the journey.

Short version: Depressed and Weary survival simulator 2015.
Long version:
If you're a kid, or you've got a young mind, this game is not for you. I think this sold mostly in the 25+ age range. Granted, it does what most games do. Plays with your emotions, strings them like a harp. But it's harrowing. Harsh. It made me feel worried for almost every day I kept my survivors alive because I had to think: I don't know what this place has. I need wood so we don't fall deathly cold in the space of a night, but I need food so we don't starve. But I can't carry enough to properly satisfy one of our requirements, let alone two. Can I rob the elderly couple? Sure, but we'll all know they won't live if we do. Someone wants to join us? I need to stand at the door with stocked, hard-worked food and tell them to stay in the cold. Away from safety. Because I'm worried my own won't have enough supplies if something goes wrong. And the game makes sure I feel the guilt for every decision. I killed a soldier who tried to kill me. Straightforward there. So I hid in the dark and slit his throat with a character, and the whole process had me scared because I didn't know if he could do it, and when he hurriedly and botchedly killed and rob them, and when he came home, he sat on the floor completely broken because it pained him, and it pained me.
It's perfect for the casual adult gamers. But as the giant paragraph states: This is a painful game. You need to play it because you feel like you've understood how much people suffer and what their choices do to them to give themselves the most basic right of survival.

I'm usually super critical of games, specially 20$+ early access titles, but im going to drop a recomend on this title. Here's why:
I fell like this game has massive potential. If you're into survival sandbox types like Ark or Rust this is a must watch for your list. My first day pulled me into a no life 15 hour grind fest. And yes it is a bit of a grind fest, BUT the progression is rewarding enough that it doesn't feel stale or boring. The map is HUGE with plenty of exploring and discovering to be done. Of course there are the various early access problems you encounter with most rushed to market titles. server issues are abundant, the AI is a bit underwhelming, raiding needs huge balances, and more items and spells would deffinitley be a welcome sight.
All of that aside the main reason im actually giving my thumb of approval on this title comes down to a few simple thing.
1) the game brings a whole new dimension and feel to the "survival sandbox" genre.
2) even with the issues it has it still managed to draw me into a no life session consuming an entire day.
3) and most importantly in the 4 days this game has been there have already been multiple patches trying to adress some of the issues i mentioned above. The devs seem to legitamitley care for our experience in this game and seem like they are going to put in the effort to take it where it needs to be.

Lots of fun and its not too complex of a game to get into. Its keeps things simple by locking the game to a 2d plain, and the only thing that can fly in 3d are fighters, which get chewed up by your ships point defences.
Dont expect something super complicated like Elite Dangerous, but if you are looking for a fun game that has all the parts of a great space game (mining, piracy, combat, merc work, and a good story) so its very satisfying for about 30 hours, then its kinda samey like Diablo or any other game where you grind for cash and parts. The story i wrapped up at 30 hours and it was GREAT!! I loved it, not too complicated of a story and it left me wanting a second game, without an abrupt ending that made me mad. Oh did i mention that the soundtrack is a perfect match for this game? Because the soundtrack is a perfect match.
The combat was a bit frustrating to get the hang of, because most of us are used to moving in 3D in space combat, and thats not the case for this game. So the good old maneuver of "roll the ship over to keep the dammaged section out of the enemy line of fire!!" just dosent work, but the ships can turn fairly fast so its not an issue once you get used to it. And since most combat starts with measured and targeted broadsides, and it degenerates into a desperate close range gun battle where you are spamming your guns as fast as you can (accuracy be dammed when the enemy is filling up your sky) i found it to be a lot of fun.
TLDR: Good sumple fun, broadside combat, and an epic sountrack. A game based on Battleship style combat. I dont regret buying this at all, and i want a second game!!!

I've got really mixed feelings about this game. I've seen and played old flash games with similar concepts, They've done it better, by a lot.
It's not a bad game per se, but it definitely need some improvement. If you don't rush certain tech you find find yourself hit pretty hard. To be honest with some tweaks it could be a beautiful thing and offer a lot of replayability. Crystals are too important and not that easy to get for how much they are needed. The scientist class takes the edge off, but leaves you feeling meh. The war chest post mission lets you hold 3 things, but you can only take one in? It's almost always going to be infrastructure. No point keeping a glowing weapon your characters can't use till the end of the map.If characters kept their levels AND your squad that you invested so much in either stuck around (or at least the slots did) I could definitely recommend it. Until then, not so much. Without those factors it just leaves you doing more of the same with some very minor spice thrown in.
In short a major problem with this game is any actual progression, as opposed to temporary progression. It's bad enough that it's not really fun to play pretty quickly. If the author changes that, I'll swiftly change my review, because it only needs very minor things to be good.
A little tip to the author, this is the kind of game that could be absolutely amazing if you opened it to modding. Lots of good opportunities.

A spiritual successor to Alpha Centauri that aims to be different yet familiar to those who had played the venerable Civ-in-space from decades ago. Unfortunately, it falls short of reaching the same excellence of AC let alone surpassing it. Although it has some great graphics (based on the Civ V engine) and uses almost similar mechanics from Civ V, albeit with differences to depict its futuristic setting, the Civ:BE at times feels shallow and seem to lack the depth and engagement of other Civ titles.
An expansion entitled Rising Tide is suppose to improve upon the base game and it is hope that the new content will be able to lift the game from mediocre to awesome. Despite its flaws (other reviewers have already pointed them out so I won't repeat it here), Civ:BE still has potential. It is hoped that Firaxis will continue to support the game by releasing more content that not only improves gameplay but also establish it as a standalone but excellent title that inherits AC's DNA without replicating it.
In short, it is a recommended purchase for those interested in sci-fi themed colony building sims. However, I would only get it during sales as the current status of the game does not warrant its full price.

With Absolution the Hitman series of games got a more streamlined, easily approachable chapter. Another game that comes to mind which made similar modifications to its original formula is Max Payne 3. Both games divided its maps into smaller pieces. Although MP literally has rooms, while Hitman definitely has bigger places to explore. I have to say right at the beginning that my biggest problem with both games is this. I was able to wander around full maps previously, collect leftover stuff and find new places. Now it is mostly gone. Absolution still has some of the freedom, but in the end the number of possibilities were reduced. I am not sure if these games were the victims of the previous generation's (ps3/xbox360) scarce resources at the end of their lifetime as both games came out in 2012. Of course as a PC user I would not accept this kind of excuse.
As for graphics the game looks great. I watched a quick look on ps3 when Absolution came out and while it looks good it really shines on pc. Four years down the line it still makes an amazing job at recreating various places. Cutscenes are pre-rendered, but they use a lot of effects and look even better than in-game visuals, so the method is justified. The characters featured in the story are well-designed, facial animations are expressive. A few scenes, Chinatown for example has a lot of npcs walking around. IO pretty much marketed the game with these vast crowds and for a reason because they look good with decent amount of variety while also run well performance-wise. Sometimes I see lod-changing in the crowd and of course most of the faces are not high quality, but they still make for a believable lot.
World design - which pretty much includes story, level design and most of the content - is mixed. The story is somewhat dumb, but not bad for a video game. Although I never really needed convoluted plots in a Hitman game. They were mostly about sandbox levels with one or more target. Various places featured throughout the game. Chinatown, South Dakota, a hotel in Chicago just to name a few. They are diverse with unique elements, characters and visual style. The whole environment is a living entity, every aspect is part pf the whole. Given objectives can be reached through various ways. You can avoid mostly everyone through stealth or take out a guard to get his disguise. The level design in Absolution is still great, the quality IO is known for is still there but the limitations get in the way most of the time. This time around they went into a more cinematic direction more so than ever. Here I have to point out that this kind of generalization of various game franchises is in my opinion a terrible thing. Publishers go for the easier path and distribute games which are easily marketable and not hard/risky to make thus being very similar. That is why a few previously flurishing genres died out, the Commandos series being a fine example. I have a few problems with this cinematic approach. The story is not good enough as I said earlier, but more importantly it breaks the game. There are chapters where 47 have to evade the police which is not that bad but it is far from the old games' style. I consider these sections a waste of game-time. I want to play pre-planned missions not running around on rooftops and drug-labs while trying to evade the police to avoid massacre. Because when stealth fails there comes the killing.
Gameplay pretty much nails the game's coffin for me. It supports the things mentioned above. I am playing on normal mode as I like to explore environments without being caught continously. That means that when it comes to killing I have no problem clearing whole buildings. Of course you get negative points for every action against any human being besides the target(s). You can argue that the game should be hard to do quietly. There is one big difference however between Absolution and the second Hitman for example. There is no proper save system here. You have to do whole missions at one go. They are divided into smaller segments but it is still frustrating to start over whole sections or kill everyone because of one wrong step. Trial and error still presents just in a worse, more fustrating form. I think that the best Hitman games are all about exploration and retries. Not whole missions, just one situation. You can create a more linear and harsh experience but you will lose the most fun part. You will not do silly things if your precious score depends on it. I did not say a word about the checkpoints in the game, but there is not much to say in a positive manner. There are points throughout the level where you can save your position. When you load back that checkpoint everything resets. This is just plain ridiculous. All your hard work clearing out places what I really enjoyed in previous titles became pointless. In the end the game basically wants you to avoid any kind of contact with anyone. This is a strict stealth game which punishes you if you cannot stay silent. Contrary that it gives you various tools for killing like knife, vase, bone and a damn bong. This is one more thing that would work so well if you could reload save to try out them. To say something positive the mechanics are great. Movement can be clunky at times but overall it works well. There is a cover system. Interacting with objects and doing actions is easier. This makes the game more approachable but these changes serve Absolution for the better.
Sound and music is good. The signature music-style is back with good voice talents. Weapon sounds are immersive and appropriate. The clue sounds are there which hint points of progression. The whole feeling is really give the game a proper atmosphere. You can overhear a lot of talk while you walking around places. Everything is so authentic it is a real shame that the things mentioned above prevent the whole to be experienced.
In terms of content Hitman a decent amount. There are challenges for each chapter in the campaign. These are things like find every disguise, kill target through various ways or more silly ones like find a film and play it with a projector. Completing these challenges will raise the score modifier for the chapter while unlocking various stuff. These things will mostly come to play in the Contracts mode which is a competitive-focused platform for the game. Missions can be created and played in this mode to gain money for upgrades and other stuff. You have to select a campaign mission for this. Published missions have various conditions like pre-determined murder weapon and disguise for each target or basic ones like no casualties, unseen, etc. The earned score is submitted for each uploaded mission so you can see how others fared. You can also rate the given content. Creating these missions are pretty straightforward. You have to do them in real-time. There is a mark option for every npc (not including the basic crowd) which makes him/her a target up to a maximum of three. I thought I will get an editor where I can choose the targets and conditions. This while being easier to understand leaves much to desire.
All in all Absolution for me slipped on the limitations introduced. Were they primarily because of technical problems on previous generation consoles or it was a deliberate choice to slice the chapters into pieces to fit the cinematic approach is does not really matter in the end. I would not consider the game a pure Hitman experience. It is more a mix of Blood Money and any other stealth game around - Splinter Cell for example. As steam's review system is pretty much comes down to a yes or no I have to say no for this title as from where I stand Absolution is a letdown. While being a good game I did not get the wanted experience out of it. I bought a Hitman game, and as that Absolution failed me.

Not bad. I got it on sale and Im glad I tried this before buying the newer and more expensive Grid: Autosport. This is more of an arcade style racer than a simulator. When I think racing simulator I instantly think Gran Tourismo or even Assetto Corsa. Its still a great game but the only tweaking you will be doing to your car is placing sponsor decals and other aesthetics.
All in all, its fairly easy to play. Newcomers to driving games can probably master the controls very soon while seasoned racers will be able to come in and start with a bang. One thing I love, is there seem to be a lot of short races. I was (and still am) a Gran Tourismo junkie. But what I always hated about taht game was in order to complete 100% of the game you had to do the extremely long, marathon style races. Some take hours and hours to finish. Im not sure if Grid has any of those but it doesnt seem to be that type of game. GT only has them because it tries to be a true simulator.
Im not crazy about the focus on drifting with every single car/class. While I dont mind drifting, I think drifting capable cars (and those amde jsut for drifting) fall into a different class than all of the other cars available. Matter of fact, drift cars and that style of racing, belongs to a small minority. But in most racing games now, they tend to add drifting into the game no matter tha car or track style. Well, thats not always the best way to drive a track. Also, your car type really matters when it comes to sliding around. In Grid, so far, Ive even been expected to drift an old Dodge Charger in a "takeover" style race while simultaneously racing against a clock. Well, I may be sliding the rear-end out to get around some turns, but Im not going to be holding a full-on drift. The car is too heavy, tires spin too much, and I wouldnt be able to accelerate out of the turn enough to make up for lost time in the drift. But then here is what makes it an arcade racer and not a simulator...my acceleration and grip coming out the turn (while drifting) was perfectly fine. A real simulator wouldnt allow that to occur.
As an Arcade style racer its great. When properly placed into the category I literally have no complaints. Due to certain graphics and the fact that some of the menu layouts are poor, I would give this an 8/10 in the arcade racer category.
If you enjoyed civ 5, you will like this, if your looking for some new gameplay mechanics, get it, if your new to the series, dont bother.

Okay, so this is my first review i have ever made for a steam game and honestly it is the first game ive really felt i wanted to make a review for. I felt like making a review because so many of the other reviews are absolutley praising the game without giving any insight into the game. So first off i installed this on 6/20 and as of 6/25 i have over 20 hours of gameplay and 2 playthroughs so i feel fairly qualified to give an in depth review.. First off this game is not for everyone. It can get and feel very grindy due to limited inventory space and game does have some odd but not gamebreaking bugs that ive encountered, but nothing major. Basically you start off with 1-4 survivors, depending on what scenarios youve unlocked and such. You start out in a large house that has loot scattered all throughout it and some rubble piles and locks on some doors. The number 1 goal on day one is to loot your intire house. At night you have the option to send one survivor out scavenging while the rest stay and guard or sleep. At night you get to choose which place to go to and loot and some places are more dangerous then others. This is the first part that might start to feel grindy due to finding maybe 60 things of loot and only have 10-17 backpack slots depending on character. During the day as the game progresses you will be visited by neighbors asking for help, other survivors, or the trader. It is up to you if you want to help them out or trade, but it is highly advisable to buy all components and wood from the trader and to always help your neighbors if you can spare the supplies or man power. Also during the day you can have some survivors sleep while others cook and build stuff.
This game can be very brutal and unforgiving if you dont plan accordingly, but if you love loot/survival games then this game is for you. Also i have known about this game since it came out but was originally turned off by the way the game was set up, but i bit the bullet and now this is one of my favorite games i have played. As a side note, i didnt mention combat in this game at all due to it is more of a secondary feature of the game and isnt really the main focus and you could go the entire game without using the combat system, i didnt even know how to use it till the end of my first playthough.
Also forgot to mention the amazing dlc offer for this game. You can basically pay what you want, they have different amounts, but it adds grafitti throughout the world but whatever you pay is donated to a charity so to me it is well worth the dollar to get the dlc.

Wars have a serious impact on people's lives.Things that we have for granted are becoming scarce, hard to obtain. Food , meds , fuel for getting warm , clean water  become top priority for them to survive.A title coming from 11bitstudios a game development company from Poland , puts you in a situation like this and dares you to survive.This war of mine is a 2.5D survival management game.You take control of 4 people who are struggling to live in times of war.
During the day you manage your reserves ,you decide which one  takes a meal, meds or bandages, rests or works by creating necessary stuff like an oven or a bed to sleep.One critical need in the game is their mood, how they feel.There are situations that will broke their mentality and they will need something to cheer them up or someone to talk it out.Every character has a specialty for example he can be good at trading or sneaking.
During the night comes the part of the game that you will go scavenging.First you choose which one goes out and which one rests or takes the shift for guarding.There are 20 places on the map that you can choose to go and find the stuff you need.There are people who can trade or bandits, soldiers and other scavengers that you will have to avoid or engage in order to survive .The decision is yours ,whatever you choose to do will have an impact on your crew.For example i chose to pillage one house where an elder couple where living , i attacked one of them and killed him.Next day my crew was depressed.There is a limitation on how many things you can carry and it varies among the members of your crew.
Time is essential here, day or night it never freezes so you constantly need to take fast decisions.When the night ends and you return back to the refuge there is a possibility of a raid(a good one) where you can loose items or your crew members getting hurt.On top of all of this you will have to encounter the winter when it comes(winter is coming as the Starks say).The game is hard as it owes to be and sometimes disturbing because it makes you feel the grief of war.There is also a fun feature where you can put pictures of your friends when you create a character.
There are polish companies that make serious games, they put a lot of effort and love and its clear on the outcome ,they really gained my respect.

Look, your first playthrough will be annoying as hell. You're going to die and restart...a lot. But it is an arcade style game, so you can't get mad when you lose your respawns (extra lives) and then have to restart from the beginning of the level. On your first playthrough it'll take you awhile to figure out how to do things and how to not die every 10 minutes. But, on your second playthrough, you'll breeze through it inside of an hour. That's what I just did. I came home from work, booted it up, and beat it before I even had dinner. And, I gotta say, the replay is where you're going to get your money back.

That second time playing it though, man it's like a whole other game to me. You're not focusing on where you need to go or how you need to get there and not die, you just know from the countless times you restarted the level. Look, this game is $9 and it's 2 years old. Just get it already. If you're reading reviews about a 2 year old game then you have a serious commitment problem that probably stems from your mother not hugging you or something. I don't know your life story, and I don't care, just buy it already.

For anyone that has any experience in playing video games or especially MMOs, I do not recommend this game.
Graphics:  The photos  look much better than this game actually looks in game.  For the most part it is large empty spaces without much in the way of adventure.  The coloring is very cartoonish with little to no texturing.
Story/Quest Lines:  The story can be rather humorous, however the generic grinding system leaves one rather bored.  Combat can be really buggy.  Mobs sometimes don't aggro immediately.  When ignoring mobs and running away, they will eventually drop aggro but will suddenly come back.  Mobs will sometimes randomly respawn immediately after killing them.  While testing out the archer my auto attack would randomly just stop and I'd have to attack, again to get it working.  Very buggy.
Crafting System:  The crafting and gathering is even more boring, as one can pick from the same tree until you have all of the materials that tree or resource supplies that is needed.
If you are of the younger generation of gamers and have little to no experience with MMORPGs, this would be great for beginners.  Possibly recommended for children (maybe 8 and under) - not recommended for pre-teen to adult.

Another in a string of dissapointments from Codemasters. They used to be one of the top racing game makers. Now, it seems like every year things get worse. The original GRiD was actually quite good except for two flaws: the inexplicable stacks of tires along the walls and the flashback feature. You couldn't see the tire stacks so you would drive a normal racing line, going near the walls, and then BAM you're wrecked. The flashback was a nice concept, but it ultimately failed because it never went back far enough.
The 2004/2005 rally game was the last good one they made. The F1 games were disappointing, GRiD 2 was horrible, and the DiRT series tried but ultimately failed, especially DiRT 3. It was great that 3 brought back more rallying, but Gymhkana 'hoonigan' events, seriously? Games are supposed to be fun, and that's not fun, it's just stupid.
GRiD Autosport seems to be an attempt to recapture some of the first GRiD game's fun factors. It doesn't do that. The controls are snappy, unnatural, and unpredictable. With oriignal GRiD, it was start up and play, Not with Autosport. It suffers, as many current driving games do, from 'current-gen overdone graphics lag,' which is my way of thinking about how developers feel compelled these days to ignore physics and animate each little frame when moving from one position to another at the expense of response time and realism. When it takes half a second for the game to respond to me pressing the button for reverse view, that's a big warning flag. What ends up happening is that the steering responds slowly and then more quickly, not in a linear fashion. This causes you to stop steering (or countersteering) when you see the right time to do it, but by the time you see it, it's already too late and you've overdone it. Then you try to counter (or counter-counter) that which only makes it worse. Thinking it was because I was using a gamepad controller, I tried my Logitech G27 wheel. Same thing. It's an unfortunate side effect of the capabilities of graphics display and engines and such being well beyond the capabilities of developers and the physica processing. Older games don't do that, but every game equating to PS3 and Xbox360 does, along with their PC equivalents.
Yet we keep buying what Codemasters makes so I guess they accomplished their goals. For me, this is the last Codemasters game I will ever buy. Sad ending to a relationship going back to the first CMR game. Fortunately I still have CMR 2005 and play it regularly, TOCA 2 is still a lot of fun, and even DiRT 2 is at least enjoyable, if unrealistic and lacking in relevant driving modes. But having fun is what a game is all about, and those games deliver.

Single player campaign is enjoyable for the most part, the story and the background are solid, but it lacks a charismatic lead character to back it up. You never really care about what's going on as much as what to expect lore-wise, and at the end of the game you can't help but sit there, hoping that's not the ending, which is short, unappealing, and nigh inexistent. It never really takes off, and it feels like you've just played a prologue (a good one at that, mind you) rather than a whole campaign.
Gameplay-wise, mechanics feel kinda clunky, making use of the "CoD" controls, only worse. AI of your partners isn't well developed, they'll block you out of your covers and entrances more times that you'll want to admit. Most of the guns feel the same with different scopes, and the aim is questionable at best. All in all, though, it makes for an above average experience, and surprisingly enough, gunfights aren't bad and they might even feel smooth in motion, despite its aforementioned clunkiness.
Now, if this game had a direct sequel, having it gone through a severe revision of both mechanics and storytelling, I would probably give this a thumbs up, keeping in mind that this is just that, a glorified prologue; but it hasn't happened, and it probably never will, all things considered.

This pseudo-3d combat sim actually had some potential to be good. Like a lot. And it still has some features that are exemplary. However, it has some awful things in it too.
The good:
The music. Like the series called Firefly? It will bloody catapult you right into the feeling. It's absolutely fantastic, and you can set your custom music, separated into 'combat', 'ambient' and other categories, and you can even tell the game to mix the originals and your own. This is actually my favourite feature of the game, it is so simple yet so effective.
Controls (with gamepad mind you). Intuitive, however, you pretty quickly end up "HOLD DA BUTTONZ, ALL OF 'EM". You need to hold X for flak coverage, left stick inclick to use the afterburner, left trigger to aim, right trigger to fire broadsides, right stick to aim your broadsides, so yeah. But still, the controls work smoothly and comparatively easily.
The combat in the beginning. While the game still attempts to be fair, it is pretty fun. Small craft can be taken out by your flak and turrets, larger ones get the broadside.
The bad
"Hey, you go for an Average difficulty mission? How about you get 3 random encounters in the mission area, so you not only have to destroy the 2 light frigates we've sent you to kill, but also 3 destroyers, 9 heavy frigates, about 20 corvettes, and about a 100 fighters, bombers?" And once the random encounters locations are generated, they cannot be changed. So I have a practically impossible main mission in front of me, ♥♥♥♥ you very much.
"Trade system". Components cost about 100k+ once you hit tier 3 (in the first system, there are already 2 tiers, so tier 3 is fairly early, but you have a good understanding of the mechanics by that time) and your cargo can be about 50 units at best. However, you cannot check the prices of other stations in real time, and you can certainly simply buy everything a station can offer in trade goods, and have half the cargo empty still. An extremely lucky trading run can net even 50k, however, you can earn literal millions with single missions by that time.
Pseudo 3d ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. The problem comes, is that some stuff is in 2d, some is in 3d. Asteroid belts are in 3d, but your radar is in 2d, which means if you warp travel, you have no freakin' idea wether you'll get stuck in that asteroid field by the annoying "WARP INHIBITED BY X/Y" (X=stellar mass, Y=hostile forces) every five second, because some asteroids are on your level, some below, some above, some while you could easily fit under/above it, still inhibits warp because ♥♥♥♥you, Enemy fighters, bombers, gunboats move in 3d, you move in 2d, enemy corvettes and above move in 2d. Your flaks only cover your port and starboard, however, if a bomber is shooting at you from your keel, or from the mast (the bottom and the top of the ship respectively) you can only pray that your turrets deal with him in time. Even better, if it shoots you from your poop, where usually no or few turrets face, and your engines exhaust is harmless (however, you can at least turn and face them with your flaks and broadsides then).
Overall, the difficulty spike inbetween tiers is too big (your tier 2 turrets are BB guns against a tier 3 shield), forcing you to farm in the previous system for cash before you can afford proper equipment for the new system. Way, waaay too much farming, and even then, the random events are simply unfair.

Emerge: Cities of the Apocalypse is relatively casual hybrid game of with light elements of zombie tower defense, resource management, RPG. The recurring goal of the game is to secure different cities by reclaiming sectors within the city. Each reclaimed sectors allows for limited construction of resource-generating buildings, either providing much needed production for different types of automated defenses, research points for advanced technology, economy for purchases, or crystals for miscellaneous purposes including recruiting NPC survivors.
Gameplay is sort of turn-based, whereby you spend limited Action Points to do things like scouting or taking over sectors. You may also spend APs to trigger random events, or activate one of several strategic options unlocked via research. At the end of your turn, zombies will move around and may incur upon your territory. When your automated defenses (if you choose ot build any) fail to fully eliminate the invading zombie, you and up to 4 recruited NPC teammates will be tasked to do the dirty work in some defense shooting action. Armed with one of several types of weapons, direct your reticule to approaching zombie hordes to gun them down before the barricade gets torn down and you get overrun. Kill enough zombies and you level up to gain a precious skill point to be put into either combat related skills or non-combat related skills such as increasing chances of finding survivors, or increasing resource production among other skills.
-  It's a fun, casual game that tests your decision making ability and how one adapts to the random situations.
- Other than the moving zombie hordes during combat, everything else is pretty much static.
- The AI of your comrades during combat is rather dubious, especially when it comes them them moving their aiming reticule, which isn't going to as fast as the player zipping their mouse around.
- The random events will eventually loses it's novelty when you have read most of them, and all you are concerned is whether it's a positive or negative events.
- Unless you are used to replaying to unlock perks and such, its get repetitive pretty fast.
The basic premise of the game doesn’t quite change and you are tasked with doing the same thing over and over again with additional challenging conditions, which might lead to gradual waning of interest if you decide to grind maps upon maps in one session. When played in moderated sessions, such as during coffee breaks or an hour or so before bedtime, it provides a satisfying amount of entertainment without causing addictive indulgence. Do remember that Emerge: Cities of the Apocalypse is what I consider a casual game, and while I often have no qualms about buying an indie game and supporting its developer, watching some Let's Play videos convinced me that this was worth a purchase for its price, and it is.

So its been many months since I played Civilization: Beyond Earth, and, sadly, I haven't felt any real desire to do so.
Beyond Earth isn't a bad game. But comparatively to Civilization V & VI, it isn't a particularly good one either. It's an average game. Compared to the fifth and sixth games it just lacks personality overall, and the Sci-Fi nature of the game contrasts too heavily with the historical nature of the fifth and sixth games.
I consistently enjoyed the start of the game and the harmony based aspects of the game, but after a while I simply lost interest in starting new campaigns. So I stopped playing, and didn't get the expansion despite initially intending to.
The release of Civilization VI and the months of enjoyment I've had in it have led me to the decision to update this review.
I
recommend this game overall, but it is not going to give you the level of enjoyment that Civilization V and Civilization VI will.
I don't recommend Civilization: Beyond Earth over the fifth and sixth Civilization games. But I do recommend it as a game in its own right. There is still enjoyment to be had, just not as much as in the other games. If Steam Reviews had some form of 'maybe' or 'conditional' option, that's what I would give for Beyond Earth.

I do recommend this game, because it is a solid foundation for a game that has the potential to be very good indeed. Sadly, it is like vanilla Civ V was. With a few expansions, or at least one, it could become as good, or even better than Civ V. It doesn't have the historical appeal that Civ V does; that's replaced with Sci Fi appeal.
But at the end of the day, this isn't about whether it's better than Civ V or not. It's about whether this game is good or not. And it is, and I do recommend it. I just hope that the expansions in the future make it as good as we all hope it to be. Rising Tides does look to be a solid expansion. So yes, you should get it if you're a fan of the series or the genre(s), but sadly, don't expect it to be as good as Civ V. Yet!
I just hope my faith in Firaxis and 2K isn't misplaced.

When I first saw This War Of Mine, I was pulled in by the idea of the tables being turned.. Rather than another FPS or something similar, this takes you into the lives of the people caught in the middle of hell. People who have to fight and scavenge off others who are just as poorly off, to survive a little while longer and perhaps make it through the war.

By this time, I already was so drawn in that I felt connected with the group I had managed to keep alive for nearly 10 days, their light just barely alive. A while after, a person in my group, Bruno, died from severe wounds after we were robbed by force. The other two, were too broken to even move because they could no longer take it..
With no one left around to console them, it was over, I was done for. I had failed to keep my group alive, their regret of my choice to steal from other survivors breaking them further was too much.
This game, makes you question everything, and opens your eyes to the real hardships and horrors of war. War is a terrible, terrible thing in of itself, and this captures every piece of what it's like to be a poor survivor stuck in the middle perfectly. This war of mine is a tragic masterpiece and a horrible bit of art in every meaning of the word.
I cannot send enough praise to the developers way for capturing this so well.

Having also played Grid 1 to death, I'm quite baffled with the negative reviews, as it seems we're playing different games compared to my experience with Grid 2.
Firstly I have to say I'm playing with an Xbox360 controller, so I can vary the throttle on the trigger (gas pedal).
The cars all handle differently (as they did in Grid 1), but where as in the first game you had to re-adjust your gamepad per car in order to tame it, in Grid 2 you simply learn the car instead.
This makes for a far more consistent experience, and one that gets you playing the game, rather than messing with the right control balance, only to have to change it for the next car.
If you play this on easy difficulty, you'll probably not get much out of it.  However, turn it up to medium or higher, with Damage and you're really getting into the fun of things on your way to mastering the game, and enjoying nail biting races!
Grid 2 is far more about understanding your car, choosing the right ride for the race, and reacting to the track. There are tight time attack races with blind corners, and slopes that challenge you to rethink your breaking point, as your breaking is lighter due to the car lifting off the track a little more...it's subtle, but genious!

In one race mode the track layout changes per lap, throwing a few surprises here and there! It makes for an exilarating atmosphere with other racers breathing down your back. Some of the drivers are also deliberately aggressive! I generally try to avoid them damaging my precious paintjob!
If you're lucky enough that your name is in the audio name files, your car mechanic calls you by it during races, "That crash looked nasty Jim!" and so on! It's a little detail that adds a personal touch.
Personal Rating: Good racing, especially on medium and higher difficulty! Great control with an xbox360 controller. Amazing Graphics and visible damage!
Score Rating: 90% - A solid driving experience!

Okay, so this is my first review i have ever made for a steam game and honestly it is the first game ive really felt i wanted to make a review for. I felt like making a review because so many of the other reviews are absolutley praising the game without giving any insight into the game. So first off i installed this on 6/20 and as of 6/25 i have over 20 hours of gameplay and 2 playthroughs so i feel fairly qualified to give an in depth review.. First off this game is not for everyone. It can get and feel very grindy due to limited inventory space and game does have some odd but not gamebreaking bugs that ive encountered, but nothing major. Basically you start off with 1-4 survivors, depending on what scenarios youve unlocked and such. You start out in a large house that has loot scattered all throughout it and some rubble piles and locks on some doors. The number 1 goal on day one is to loot your intire house. At night you have the option to send one survivor out scavenging while the rest stay and guard or sleep. At night you get to choose which place to go to and loot and some places are more dangerous then others. This is the first part that might start to feel grindy due to finding maybe 60 things of loot and only have 10-17 backpack slots depending on character. During the day as the game progresses you will be visited by neighbors asking for help, other survivors, or the trader. It is up to you if you want to help them out or trade, but it is highly advisable to buy all components and wood from the trader and to always help your neighbors if you can spare the supplies or man power. Also during the day you can have some survivors sleep while others cook and build stuff.
This game can be very brutal and unforgiving if you dont plan accordingly, but if you love loot/survival games then this game is for you. Wars have a serious impact on people's lives.Things that we have for granted are becoming scarce, hard to obtain. Food , meds , fuel for getting warm , clean water  become top priority for them to survive.A title coming from 11bitstudios a game development company from Poland , puts you in a situation like this and dares you to survive.This war of mine is a 2.5D survival management game.You take control of 4 people who are struggling to live in times of war.
During the day you manage your reserves ,you decide which one  takes a meal, meds or bandages, rests or works by creating necessary stuff like an oven or a bed to sleep.One critical need in the game is their mood, how they feel.There are situations that will broke their mentality and they will need something to cheer them up or someone to talk it out.Every character has a specialty for example he can be good at trading or sneaking.
During the night comes the part of the game that you will go scavenging.First you choose which one goes out and which one rests or takes the shift for guarding.There are 20 places on the map that you can choose to go and find the stuff you need.There are people who can trade or bandits, soldiers and other scavengers that you will have to avoid or engage in order to survive .The decision is yours ,whatever you choose to do will have an impact on your crew.For example i chose to pillage one house where an elder couple where living , i attacked one of them and killed him.Next day my crew was depressed.There is a limitation on how many things you can carry and it varies among the members of your crew.
Time is essential here, day or night it never freezes so you constantly need to take fast decisions.When the night ends and you return back to the refuge there is a possibility of a raid(a good one) where you can loose items or your crew members getting hurt.On top of all of this you will have to encounter the winter when it comes(winter is coming as the Starks say).The game is hard as it owes to be and sometimes disturbing because it makes you feel the grief of war.There is also a fun feature where you can put pictures of your friends when you create a character.
There are polish companies that make serious games, they put a lot of effort and love and its clear on the outcome ,they really gained my respect.

Crea is a fun and interesting build/rpg game. Similar to Starbound and Terraria, but different enough to have caught my attention, and entertaining to the point I'm playing this more than the other two. Crea has it's pros and cons, though despite some of the bad stuff, the game is highly recommended.Crea not only has an easy to use building system, it's controls and features are quite easy to handle and understand. This game keeps the who family busy working on fun projects and quests. Crea not only has a built in multi-user feature which allows friends and family to play the way they want to, but it also has a deicated server program which is a huge plus in my books. Storyline is a bit confusing, as there is basically no totorial so have to figure out most of how the game works by yourself.
Now for the cons. Notice I'm putting workshop under cons, when it should normally be a pro? Thats because despite the game being great, the workshop side of the game was written horribly. Don't fine out the hard way, back up your game before trying even one mod. I highly recommend avoiding the workshop portion all together. If you want to try it, you may want to also copy \Steam\userdata\200365626\280520\remote because I noticed the cloud and the backups tend to be off by hours sometimes. It all depends on how you save your game.
Reason workshop should be avoided, is because 80% of the mods do not work, or are outdated. The 20% I found to work on my side, would not work for people connecting. This is why you need to back up before trying a mod. Even testing one out for 15 seconds, the game writes the info down and now that game will forever be looking for that mod you tried out, despite having unsubscrbed from it. You may see only 5 mods on your side, but people connecting will be refused connection because the game will still require them to have the mods you tried out, even if you unsubscribed from it. Which is bad when a mod happens to crash your game which now requires you to have it or no one can connect. So again, back up every time.
Now the huge con in regards to the CREA workshop. Testing out a mod, should be an easy point and click subscribe and that's it. The sloppy coding of workshop takes it a step further. The only thing the game client should be asking you in regards to running a mod, is in what order to load in, and to which games, in case your running multiple servers with different mods. So if it isn't confusing enough trying to get the mods in the correct order, you now have to figure out which ones to highlight, and which ones not to highlight because the mod loads itself in without the need of highlighting it and attempting to do so causes the game to crash, and when your game crashes due to a mod, you HAVE TO RESTORE from backup. No ifs, no maybe's, you will have to restore the game from before the mod crash as that save is now corrupted and unplayable.
Keep away from workshop, unless the game gets upgraded with a better stable workshop system.
