So I've spent an entire day of my life playing Crea and I've got to say it was worth it.
The game obviously isn't finished and in hopes that a dev will see this review, I'm going to list bugs, improvements etc., so this review will be quite lengthy.
Now for pros and cons, starting with cons.
- For the beginner players, this will affect you the second you jump into your first world. The mechanics are... different. It takes a while to get used to having a weapon loadout (W) and a slot for your tool (Q), and spells as 1-9 on your keyboard. This makes for block placing, getting used to (SPACE) as your jump key compared to Terraria, Starbound, etc., quite annoying.
-The devs really don't want you exploring too much, which is one of the big bummers for me, because despite my decent amount of playtime im sure that there are hundreds of dungeons and chests i haven't uncovered because the devs discourage behabior they don't want. But i see the reasoning for this. In a game like Terraria, nothing really stops you from exploring the entire map before you settle down and make a base, which can grant you lots of nice loot of weapons to get you ahead in the game. In Crea, giving the shortness of the game so far, I understand why the devs prevent you from exploring too much early on by making monsters stronger the further you go from your original spawn. Finding this loot early on can set you ahead and snowball the game in other games, and i assume Crea doesn't want that.
-This leads me to my next point. Loot. Although on one hand, most chests being locked is a good thing as it encourages you to fight monsters to get keys, progressing your character and skills in the process, this isn't my issue. What i would've liked to see was more impactful items, and/or weaponry that can't be crafted normally, but found in loot or monster drops. However, Crea unfortunately has nothing of the sort, which makes finding chests less exciting than in other games.
-Bugs. Sure, the game is farm from finished, so rather than me criticizing the devs for these bugs existing, I'm going to list all the bugs i can remember experiencing, in hopes that they can be worked on. (N.B, I played Crea on OSX)
- Fullscreen map is bugged. I don't know if this is a mac only issue, but trying to open the fullscreen map by pressing (M) three times only opens a massive screen of glitched textures, rendering it useless.
- A few isolated grapple incidents where the grapple goes through some terrain. I'm not as mad at this bug as some others may be, because i haven't fallen to my death because of it.
- Dying while fighting the 3rd boss (The one in the forest i forgot his name), causes for your items to be lost completely. No pack left outside the way crystal you traveled to the forest with, and no pack in the actual forest where you died. Lost a 200 quality shield because i put it in my inventory to switch for my bow. F
- A few inventory texture bugs when you try to put a bow in a spell slot. Wierd, upside down inventories pop up when you try to click the bow in the numbered slot.
- Some peripheral features that would make life easier. When using the Imbuing Chamber, Shift clicking should work to quickly place the item directly from your inventory into the chamber. Secondly, Left clicking grabs all items, Right clicking grabs one; It'd be useful if, after left clicking to grab all, you could then right click to
one, rather than having to grab one, then place it.
-SPOILERS!!!
Shortness of the game. Unforunately, just 24 hours of playtime was enough to 'Complete' the game. More than 4 bosses would be great, as once you've killed Sano, you sort of fly through the game. Having to kill the first three bosses once more but harder is a good concept in order to unlock the final boss, and although killing him releases new ores and remna into the world, there really isn't any incentive to continue, which is why the game needs more bosses, or side quests, rather than aimlessly mining and getting stronger for no reason.
-Bows. I really admire the RPG system the devs have implemented and that's what separates Crea from other games of its kind (I'll expand in Pros). However, the Archer 'class' isn't very viable for killing bosses. Even when killing regular monsters, you can't walk around with just a bow in your hand. If they get close you're screwed, so you need a melee. If they fly directly above you, you're screwed, because you can't fire straight up for some reason. So you need a sword or to use magic as a secondary. But with Bosses, bows become obsolete, especially aginst bosses 1,3,4. From my experience, I've been unable to beat a boss without using a sword and shield. The shield is the most important thing when fighting a boss. And when you need to kill the altars when fighting the final boss, bows are useless. Hey, maybe I'm just bad, but the bosses seem very sword/spear and shield reliant, or you have no hopes of surviving projectiles, or the strong attacks bosses have.
-When you start your game, you're just put into the middle of it all, no tutorials, and Crea lacks quite a few tooltips to help you understand why something won't work. The main example would be the Auri Tree, which, if not given much more space than a regular tree, won't let you plant it. However, the game doesn't tell you this, and so I had to look it up online to see what was wrong.
-A wider range of weapons. Crea has 4 main weapons, Sword, Spear, Wand and Bow, with different subsets with swords and spears (rapiers, Broadswords, etc.) Which is great, but doesn't give you any fresh mechanics. It's hard to explain. If you look at terraria, at the start of the game, you fight with swords or spears or bows, but progress to crossbows, axes, guns, lasers, chackrams, ninja stars, boomerangs. A wider range of weapons would be a breath of fresh air to Crea.
-Finally, a minor issue with dungeons. 'Do not kill monsters'. What's the point of a dungeon where you can't kill monsters and improve your skills. Trying to get to treasure without dying is impossible, so you just end up running to find the exit, making it so boring.
-Honestly, Crea is so unique in many ways. First is the skill system. Wow. Honestly a beautifully crafted level up RPG system, where you add points to your stats. Classic. Then is the Talent points, which brings Crea into its own as an RPG. In my experience of games, very few have done what Crea has. Levelling up particular aspects, in order to upgrade stats, learn spells/skills, add to your gameplay. It's mesmerising and really keeps you playing to improve your character in all factors.
-Chaos Crafting. Crea implements a completely unique mechanic when crafting equipment, letting you A) enchant your gear with enchantments dropped form killing monsters and chests, to add to the items stats, and add unique effects, and B) Use the complex, yet entirely unique format of 'Chaos Crafting' to improve the quality of your item. Higher quality = Higher stats, so it encourages you to learn the process of perfecting your craft and polish your items to perfect quality.
-Research. The time i've spent on the Wiki for Crea is probably 1/100th of the time I've spent on the Terraria or Minecraft wiki.  All because of its research system. Instead of having to find what items i need to craft an item online, Crea doesn't let you craft it until you research it, using materials you find in the world. The crafting window shows the recipes and makes crafting easy and unique. Once you research one thing, you unlock the next, and the next, etc. etc. Getting you lost in Crea's wide range of items
-Progression. Crea's game progression is beautiful and keeps you going. By the time you craft one item, a better one is availble.

I've owned this game for a very long time, well before its actual release, so I've been around for a huge chunk of the dev cycle.
At first glance, everyone I've told about this game says the same thing, "Another Terraria clone??"
First off, get that out of your mind immediately. Terraria, while fun, has very little depth in comparison to Crea.
What Crea offers that Terraria does not (as of 1.5.1):
- Actual stats on gear that isn't limited to just "equip this set for an effect"
- Customization options of gear AND skills, allowing you to play and progress your character using more than just "oh my friend just dumped top level gear on me and now I'm at the endgame"
- Random encounters, dungeons (and not just large biome hunting grounds), customizable monster difficulty scaling
- Actual strategy based bosses and not just gear check monsters (they could be improved, of course, though)
- A variety of NPCs that are more than just different categories of vendors.
- Actual lore
- A massive amount of skills, usable by many different builds (not just equip a single weapon and become a wizard/tank/ranged)
- A warp/waypoint system that is fantastic (and also customizable)
- MODDING!  A possible infinite amount of plusses (if only the community was larger!)
Things Terraria has over Crea:
- Larger community
The things that I hope for in the future development of this game:
- Harder difficulty (this might be a minus to some people, but I maxed out my most recent Crea character after about 25ish hours of play, though I can absolutely make the monsters higher level if I wanted to, but there's no progression after maxing some skills and level 50 without mods)
- More bosses
- More skills
- Basically just more progression, like an expansion pack, haha.
Overall, this charming game is definitely worth a buy and worth a ton of hours sank into it.
With modding, this could be an amazing asset to any RP community, even, it's got so much potential from mods alone.

Rebel Galaxy is a very casual space pilot "simulator", all combat is really handled in 2D and mostly resembles sea battles (broadside artillery, all ships except fighters manouver on the same "height") so if you're looking for a serious space-sim it's not for you.
Gameplay consists of main storyline broken up by (a lot) of generated sidequests which get a bit boring after a while since there's only a few types (search and destroy, delivery, defend target, pick up object). Since main story quickly ramps up in difficulty you'll be grinding these quite a lot. Apart from sidequests you can also play as a trader, buying low and selling high, a miner selling resources found in asteroids, pirate hunter looking for bounties or a pirate hunting civillian ships.
As you progress you will upgrade your ship with new weapons, shields and additional equipment, every once in a while buying a new ship.
Pros:
+ Enjoyable space combat (if you dont mind the sea battles feel).
+ Plenty of ships/upgrades to work towards.
+ Decent voice-acting (somewhat repetetive lines from enemies).
+ Multiple ways to progress.
+ Great music
Cons:
- Requires a lot of grinding sidequests to progress.
- Not much depth or variety beyond the basics.

A nice surprise from the Indie market, Emerge: Cities of the Apocalypse is an entertaining strategic zombie survival game.  You won't be scavenging for supplies, directly rescuing survivors, or securing a clean source of water, though it has its own style of gameplay that I have found to be unique and fun in its own right.
Each scenario that you play involves you taking control over a small colony with the goal of expanding and securing the city around you.  You'll be facing off against an ever increasing horde of zombies with new varieties arriving as time goes on.  To achieve this goal, and often other scenario-specific goals, you'll be researching technologies on three separate trees to assist you.  These tech trees will improve your resource collection (cash, crystals, production, and science) and will make your colony more effective at fighting off the encroaching ranks of the dead.
Though much of the game is spent looking down at the city from a bird's eye view, there will be times when you take a more direct approach in defending your colony.  Your character, selected from one of three varying classes, will face off against the zombies in what feels like an improved Oregon Trail hunting mini-game.  A variety of weapon types and skills that can be upgraded when your character and their compatriots level also adds a level of strategy to this as weapons and abilities add a considerable amount of options to develop your own style of play.
All in all, Emerge: Cities of the Apocalypse is an enjoyable game that I certainly don't regret spending my money on.  I would give a forewarning to those who might be on the fence, it does feel like a well designed mobile game.  However, when compared to said mobile games or the flash games that might do something very similar, Emerge does just enough to make those others obsolete on a purely gameplay basis.
I would recommend this game to anyone who is a fan of zombie apocalypse games and is wanting to play one that isn't survival in its strictest term as gamers have come to know it.  It is an enjoyable strategy-lite that I can definitely see myself putting more hours into in the future.

Is this game better than the original?
That's hard to say. It's certainly an excellent game. The graphics remain beautiful, the shooting is great, and the melee combat is an improvement. Is the plot better? For this, I would say no. I'm not saying that the plot is bad, far from it, but as good as it is it simply cannot match up to the plot of the first game.
Also, the villain (Dr Sophia Lamb) is less compelling or menacing than Andrew Ryan. She is still a compelling character, but less so. Dr Lamb represents the polar opposite of Ryan, espousing the view that all should work together and sacrifice for the common good, to the degree where they lose all autonomy and become little more than drones in a hive.
Overall, i would say that this game isn't quite as good as the original, but still manages to be a brilliant game and a sure classic in a trilogy of classics.

You can even fight battles both attacking and defensive in a barricade style like you would've seen in the Last Stand. It's all pretty badass. It's clearly been made by an amateur developer but there is a clearly a lot of effort with a very specific idea in mind and it combines to make one of the more unique zombie games I've played in a while. In summation, I highly recommend this game for the low price tag.

Battlerite is what I call a well done game.
The f2p launch was really successful and with 40k players the game is really enjoyable. SLS made a game that was missing in the f2p list, 2v2 arena with fast gameplay and lots of strategy and skillshots. Also for those who like fashion-gaming there are some sick outfits and weapons and those are really easy to earn as you can recieve rewards from a lot of daily-weekly quests and achievements. The game is really well balanced, and it's really deep since you can use a lot of different strats for every single character. As a longtime Civilization player, I was quite disappointed in this game. If Civilization V was looked at as a simplified update to Civilization IV, then Civilization: Beyond Earth is a simplified, spaceborne version of Civilization V. There are quite a few changes that I found interesting, such as the tech web, but there is so much taken out, like rich player interactions with other factions, it feels flat. It feels like a nerfed skin for Civ5. The interface looks like they yanked out hunks of the game as well. If you win, you get a pop-up that's even more minimalist than the Civ5 win screen. You also don't get the stats at the end to tell you what the demographics were, just "You won. Congrats."
Until they fix some of what's screwy, missing or nerfed, I can't recommend this game. I'd rather play "Sid Meier's Starships".

When I first saw This War Of Mine, I was pulled in by the idea of the tables being turned.. Rather than another FPS or something similar, this takes you into the lives of the people caught in the middle of hell. People who have to fight and scavenge off others who are just as poorly off, to survive a little while longer and perhaps make it through the war.
As I started playing, I thought by the looks of it, it isn't something I can hugely immerse myself into. How wrong I was.
On my second scavenging night, the paranoia of being caught, the anxiety of time not being on your side and the stress of needing to find as much stuff as possible to not have wasted a night is insane. By this time, I already was so drawn in that I felt connected with the group I had managed to keep alive for nearly 10 days, their light just barely alive. A while after, a person in my group, Bruno, died from severe wounds after we were robbed by force. The other two, were too broken to even move because they could no longer take it..
With no one left around to console them, it was over, I was done for. I had failed to keep my group alive, their regret of my choice to steal from other survivors breaking them further was too much.
This game, makes you question everything, and opens your eyes to the real hardships and horrors of war. War is a terrible, terrible thing in of itself, and this captures every piece of what it's like to be a poor survivor stuck in the middle perfectly. This war of mine is a tragic masterpiece and a horrible bit of art in every meaning of the word.
I cannot send enough praise to the developers way for capturing this so well.

Okay, so this is my first review i have ever made for a steam game and honestly it is the first game ive really felt i wanted to make a review for. I felt like making a review because so many of the other reviews are absolutley praising the game without giving any insight into the game. So first off i installed this on 6/20 and as of 6/25 i have over 20 hours of gameplay and 2 playthroughs so i feel fairly qualified to give an in depth review.. First off this game is not for everyone. It can get and feel very grindy due to limited inventory space and game does have some odd but not gamebreaking bugs that ive encountered, but nothing major. Basically you start off with 1-4 survivors, depending on what scenarios youve unlocked and such. You start out in a large house that has loot scattered all throughout it and some rubble piles and locks on some doors. The number 1 goal on day one is to loot your intire house. At night you have the option to send one survivor out scavenging while the rest stay and guard or sleep. At night you get to choose which place to go to and loot and some places are more dangerous then others. This is the first part that might start to feel grindy due to finding maybe 60 things of loot and only have 10-17 backpack slots depending on character. During the day as the game progresses you will be visited by neighbors asking for help, other survivors, or the trader. It is up to you if you want to help them out or trade, but it is highly advisable to buy all components and wood from the trader and to always help your neighbors if you can spare the supplies or man power. Also during the day you can have some survivors sleep while others cook and build stuff.
This game can be very brutal and unforgiving if you dont plan accordingly, but if you love loot/survival games then this game is for you. Also i have known about this game since it came out but was originally turned off by the way the game was set up, but i bit the bullet and now this is one of my favorite games i have played. As a side note, i didnt mention combat in this game at all due to it is more of a secondary feature of the game and isnt really the main focus and you could go the entire game without using the combat system, i didnt even know how to use it till the end of my first playthough.
Also forgot to mention the amazing dlc offer for this game. You can basically pay what you want, they have different amounts, but it adds grafitti throughout the world but whatever you pay is donated to a charity so to me it is well worth the dollar to get the dlc.

Wars have a serious impact on people's lives.Things that we have for granted are becoming scarce, hard to obtain. Food , meds , fuel for getting warm , clean water  become top priority for them to survive.A title coming from 11bitstudios a game development company from Poland , puts you in a situation like this and dares you to survive.This war of mine is a 2.5D survival management game.You take control of 4 people who are struggling to live in times of war.
During the day you manage your reserves ,you decide which one  takes a meal, meds or bandages, rests or works by creating necessary stuff like an oven or a bed to sleep.One critical need in the game is their mood, how they feel.There are situations that will broke their mentality and they will need something to cheer them up or someone to talk it out.Every character has a specialty for example he can be good at trading or sneaking.
During the night comes the part of the game that you will go scavenging.First you choose which one goes out and which one rests or takes the shift for guarding.There are 20 places on the map that you can choose to go and find the stuff you need.There are people who can trade or bandits, soldiers and other scavengers that you will have to avoid or engage in order to survive .The decision is yours ,whatever you choose to do will have an impact on your crew.For example i chose to pillage one house where an elder couple where living , i attacked one of them and killed him.Next day my crew was depressed.There is a limitation on how many things you can carry and it varies among the members of your crew.
Time is essential here, day or night it never freezes so you constantly need to take fast decisions.When the night ends and you return back to the refuge there is a possibility of a raid(a good one) where you can loose items or your crew members getting hurt.On top of all of this you will have to encounter the winter when it comes(winter is coming as the Starks say).The game is hard as it owes to be and sometimes disturbing because it makes you feel the grief of war.There is also a fun feature where you can put pictures of your friends when you create a character.
There are polish companies that make serious games, they put a lot of effort and love and its clear on the outcome ,they really gained my respect.

The game's concept caught my attention as it involves being responsible for maintaining an old vehicle while driving through former communist states in Europe. Earn money by selling goods found in boxes on the side of the road and keep an eye out for the vehicle's part conditions, battery charge, and fuel level as you drive (like a car-survival genre of some sort). You can also upgrade your vehicle's components and add extra parts and paint jobs through the Laika shop. I recommend this game to those who are interested in vehicles especially in the sense of having the responsibility of maintaining one.
As of Sept.3,2016 the game 'ends' at Hungary but you have the option to return home via menu or map and keep your current vehicle & components, credits, and any item stored in the car. Every route (especially the long ones) always provides a challenge and certain 'special locations' not typically found on short, sunny routes.
-To sell items, just equip them and give them to the cashier at the shop/gas station. There's a lever by the counter in case you want to cancel the items you want to buy.
-Accidentally dropped your wallet out of the car? It'll return to your car where it's always stored (glovebox)
-You can always get out of the car and walk to the nearest appropriate shop in case your car breaks down or use the restart/return home option (I recommend walking to the nearest shop because it adds a feeling of realism and adventure)

This game is too amazing for a review..... So instead heres a Wikipedia page of chicken....
The domestic chicken is descended primarily from the Red junglefowl (Gallus gallus) and is scientifically classified as the same species.[19] As such it can and does freely interbreed with populations of red jungle fowl.[19] Recent genetic analysis has revealed that at least the gene for yellow skin was incorporated into domestic birds through hybridization with the Grey junglefowl (G. sonneratii).[20] The traditional poultry farming view is stated in Encyclopædia Britannica (2007): "Humans first domesticated chickens of Indian origin for the purpose of cockfighting in Asia, Africa, and Europe. Very little formal attention was given to egg or meat production... "[2] In the last decade there have been a number of genetic studies. According to one study, a single domestication event occurring in the region of modern Thailand created the modern chicken with minor transitions separating the modern breeds.[21] However, that study was later found to be based on incomplete data, and recent studies point to multiple maternal origins, with the clade found in the Americas, Europe, Middle East, and Africa, originating from the Indian subcontinent, where a large number of unique haplotypes occur.[22][23] It is postulated that the Jungle fowl, known as the "bamboo fowl" in many Southeast Asian languages, is a special pheasant well adapted to take advantage of the large amounts of fruits that are produced during the end of the 50 year bamboo seeding cycle to boost its own reproduction.[24] In domesticating the chicken, humans took advantage of this prolific reproduction of the jungle fowl when exposed to large amount of food.[25]
It has been claimed (based on paleoclimatic assumptions) that chickens were domesticated in Southern China in 6000 BC.[26] However, according to a recent study,[27] "it is not known whether these birds made much contribution to the modern domestic fowl. Chickens from the Harappan culture of the Indus Valley (2500-2100 BC), in what today is Pakistan, may have been the main source of diffusion throughout the world." A northern road spread the chicken to the Tarim basin of central Asia. The chicken reached Europe (Romania, Turkey, Greece, Ukraine) about 3000 BC.[28] Introduction into Western Europe came far later, about the 1st millennium BC. Phoenicians spread chickens along the Mediterranean coasts, to Iberia. Breeding increased under the Roman Empire, and was reduced in the Middle Ages.[28] Middle East traces of chicken go back to a little earlier than 2000 BC, in Syria; chicken went southward only in the 1st millennium BC. The chicken reached Egypt for purposes of ♥♥♥♥ fighting about 1400 BC, and became widely bred only in Ptolemaic Egypt (about 300 BC).[28] Little is known about the chicken's introduction into Africa. Three possible routes of introduction in about the early first millennium AD could have been through the Egyptian Nile Valley, the East Africa Roman-Greek or Indian trade, or from Carthage and the Berbers, across the Sahara. The earliest known remains are from Mali, Nubia, East Coast, and South Africa and date back to the middle of the first millennium AD.[28] Domestic chicken in the Americas before Western conquest is still an ongoing discussion, but blue-egged chickens, found only in the Americas and Asia, suggest an Asian origin for early American chickens.[28]
A lack of data from Thailand, Russia, the Indian subcontinent, Southeast Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa makes it difficult to lay out a clear map of the spread of chickens in these areas; better description and genetic analysis of local breeds threatened by extinction may also help with research into this area.[28]
South America
An unusual variety of chicken that has its origins in South America is the araucana, bred in southern Chile by the Mapuche people. Araucanas, some of which are tailless and some of which have tufts of feathers around their ears, lay blue-green eggs. It has long been suggested that they pre-date the arrival of European chickens brought by the Spanish and are evidence of pre-Columbian trans-Pacific contacts between Asian or Pacific Oceanic peoples, particularly the Polynesians, and South America. In 2007, an international team of researchers reported the results of analysis of chicken bones found on the Arauco Peninsula in south-central Chile. Radiocarbon dating suggested that the chickens were Pre-Columbian, and DNA analysis showed that they were related to prehistoric populations of chickens in Polynesia.[29] These results appeared to confirm that the chickens came from Polynesia and that there were transpacific contacts between Polynesia and South America before Columbus's arrival in the Americas.[30]
However, a later report looking at the same specimens concluded:
A published, apparently pre-Columbian, Chilean specimen and six pre-European Polynesian specimens also cluster with the same European/Indian subcontinental/Southeast Asian sequences, providing no support for a Polynesian introduction of chickens to South America. In contrast, sequences from two archaeological sites on Easter Island group with an uncommon haplogroup from Indonesia, Japan, and China and may represent a genetic signature of an early Polynesian dispersal. Modeling of the potential marine carbon contribution to the Chilean archaeological specimen casts further doubt on claims for pre-Columbian chickens, and definitive proof will require further analyses of ancient DNA sequences and radiocarbon and stable isotope data from archaeological excavations within both Chile and Polynesia.[31]

I purchased and beat Grid 1 and had a pretty good time with it. Then Grid 2 was announced but they said they weren't including cockpit view. That's lazy as hell and I skipped Grid 2. Then Grid Autosport was announced and cockpit view was making a return. YAY! Just recently all of Codemaster's games recieved major discounts. I picked up Grid Autosport and gave it a try. I'm over 10 hours in and while the game is fun overall, there are a few things I don't like. The main thing is that yes, the cockpit view is back, but only sort of. The view is there, but the gauges are a static image, any car that has shift lights don't actually have working shift lights, and then the entire dash is blurred. The rearview mirrors don't even work and they, too, are blurred. There is also the lack of a field of view option.
There is also rubberbanding. It's the strongest in the touring car discipline. You can disable it by deleting a file but that file is tied to the game's anti-piracy system for some reason. This means that if you delete the file to get rid of rubberbanding, the game won't let you save your progress. That's ridiculous and pathetic. The AI is also extremely aggressive and will slam into you when you try to pass them. Codemasters wants this game to have some sim-like elements but won't include a full cockpit view and adds rubberbanding. It's like they want to make a racing game but also don't want to make a racing game.
There aren't a whole lot of tracks present but the ones included do look alright. The cars look nice as well. There's some DLC available (of course) but I'm not spending any more money on this game so I'm not sure how that content is.
There are some positives, though. The graphics are okay and there's no FPS lock. The game runs pretty smoothly. There's a few different disciplines and a decent variety of vehicles. Lots of input devices are supported and there's a nice amount of graphical options and difficulty options. The sounds are pretty good, from engine noises to crowds and track sounds, everything sounds nice. So while the game can be fun, I can't recommend it due to the half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥cockpit view and inclusion of rubberbanding AI. And I definitely wouldn't recommend it at its normal $50 price. Wait a while and pick it up when it gets to $10 if you really want to try it.

Original Review:
Emerge: Cities of the Apocalypse is a new game on Steam that combines a turn based strategy game and a top-down shooter game in one lite horror game. I’ll say despite my few annoyances I experienced with the game, I would recommend it to other people to try out and would say that it is well worth the $7+ it is currently priced at on Steam. For the record, I have spent 8+ hours with this game according to Steam and I have still yet to complete the entire campaign.
-INITIAL THOUGHTS-
I like how Emerge manages to combine multiple genres in one cohesive game. Not only do you have the ability to choose your class and weapons, but you also have the building phase of the game where you are trying to expand your city reach like a RTS game, and you have to stop zombies from tearing down your barricades in the battle phase much like a Tower Defense game. Not only does this manage to combine all of these aspects of gameplay, but it combines them effectively so that it feels natural to the player. If you’ve played strategy games and real time tower defense games, then you will be able to pick this game up pretty quickly once you understand how all the classes work and what things you should research for certain effects.
One thing that bothers me tough is that although the tutorial goes over a lot, yet I still have been unable to figure out how to use modules as intended. While it might be an oversight in the tutorial, the only way I’ve found to access your storage is through either the recruit menu or the merchant menu, neither of which seemed to have had an option for me to use the modules from what I saw. Thankfully though, the tutorial does go over how get recruits, set their AI, and even about upgrading stats and weapons, so the modules are probably just an oversight. Other than that, I say that the game is pretty solid in design, application, and explanation.
-PRESENTATION-
This game functions somewhat as a horror game and it has a very dark atmosphere around it. Visually, I like the use of a pseudo 3D environment to capture sectors of the city and being able to customize the UI was also a huge bonus for me. The UI in general, I found to be nice and user friendly.  The music, in my opinion, was the best and worst part of the presentation. The music and sound effects really helps to setup the dark atmosphere for the game but the BGM doesn’t stay at one consistent volume which kind of ruins it for me. I found myself messing around with the audio several times because it was either too quiet or way too loud and 10 mins or so later I would have to readjust it again. Other than that though, I had no other problems with Emerge’s presentation and I felt that it does a great job overall for depicting a zombie apocalyptic atmosphere.
-ENGAGEMENT/GAMEPLAY-
This game will be engaging for those who are used to playing long Strategy games, for others I feel that interest and wanting to complete a map would be the most engaging factors. Don’t get me wrong, the gameplay is fun and well thought out but on average it took me about an hour and a half, if not longer, just to complete 1 map (and I’m still only on the “small” maps). Of course the time it takes to complete a map will vary on your setup (class, weapon, research, etc.) but for me it was very time consuming. Thankfully, at any time in the game you can exit the game and it will save your progress until you try that map again.
As for gameplay, it essentially comes down into 2 parts. The building phase and the battle phase as I call them. In the building phase, the player has to use action points to scout areas, take over sectors of the city, buy/sell weapons, and other things commonly found in Strategy games. In the battle phase the game becomes more like a Top-Down Shooter/Tower Defense game where you actually have to shoot invading zombies as they try to break down your border and take over your city. This is where your choice of class and weapon are most important in my opinion. While your class does affect things in the building phase, your actual survival rests upon your chosen weapon and skills like any other Shooter game out there. I also like the difficulty increase in the game. As you go through the campaign mode you constantly unlock more and more enemies and encounter different aspects of gameplay you hadn’t experienced before. In short, if you’ve been looking for a game that takes both skill and strategy in order to complete, then this is the game for you.
-OVERALL-
I only had minor issues with the game thus far and I have really enjoyed playing this game. I say if you like Strategy games, Top-Down Shooter games, Tower Defense games, or if you are just a fan of Zombie games in general, then this you should definitely check this game out. I really like it and I hope to spend even more hours playing it.
Thanks for reading, and Happy Game Making!!

is a fun mix of turn-based strategy and realtime defense combat. You aim to capture a certain amount of sectors on the map (and perhaps complete some additional objectives) before the roaming zombie horde becomes too strong to hold off.
Each turn, if a pack of zombies moves into a sector controlled by you, you will be shown how any automated defenses you may have had fared at fending them off, and should there be undead survivors, you can attempt to prevail in realtime combat. Using the mouse cursor, you aim and shoot your weapon, while the keyboard serves to expend combat consumables like grenades or limited-ammunition turrets. Up to four AI-controlled companions can lend their aid in these encounters, while there's also the option to delegate the main character's gunfire to the very same AI logic and solely utilize items yourself. Combat lasts until the player's barricade is destroyed, in which case there's a chance for characters to die fleeing, or until all attackers have been fended off.
All characters partaking in combat gain experience points based on how they perform, and this is also the only regular source of experience points, somewhat necessitating use of the realtime combat to grow in strength (while stronger enemies appear after a certain amount of turns, giving the game a bit of a 'race against the clock' vibe). On levelup, characters can be given another point in one of their traits, which for example enable the use of higher-level weapons or give resource bonuses for the turn-based side of things. Manual actions by the user there, such as attempting to conquer or scout a neighbouring sector, cost action points, which replenish each turn. As far as resources go, there are production points used for the construction of defenses (for the simulated combat phase) and research points that let you progress along a
-style tech tree, as well as economy points that give you an influx of credits every turn, and two monetary resources — credits and crystals.
As far as content goes, there are ample unlocks, although the vast bulk of weapons are already available from the get-go. As the game progresses, you gain many more character classes to use, get starting bonuses or new scenarios, bigger maps, and a lot of different enemies to encounter. Unfortunately there is no character persistence between campaign levels ("areas"), and thus you start anew in the next one, only able to bring one of your items. I typically carry with me one that boosts research per turn, to get a faster start the next time. Gameplay fundamentals are virtually unchanged throughout the campaign stages, and this is a title that prides itself on replayability much more than on diversified visual design.
The game definitely aims at a more old-school audience who embrace a lack of hand-holding, who relish having to find out how to unlock things on their own instead of being spoon-fed the unlock conditions. In that spirit, your power grows at a slow
pace, and the power difference between a level 1 and a level 2 weapon feels truly minuscule.
Weapons are divided into 'hitscan' ones that only hit when your recoil-affected cursor is on the enemy's model, while projectile weapons fly towards opponents. Of the former type, I only somewhat enjoyed the sniper rifle, while the bullet-fed automatic weapons were too inaccurate for my tastes. I ended up strongly preferring weapons capable of harming multiple opponents per shot, namely the jolly crossbow and the grenade launcher. One character trait increases the amount of targets a crossbow bolt can penetrate and immediately became my favourite.
The music fits the scenario's mood very well and reminded me strongly of an older videogame gem I only recently discovered.
Bug reports and feature requests I churned out while playing were responded to quickly and diligently, and from what I could observe, this game is definitely a labour of love crafted over the course of several years by the solo developer.
Due to technical limitations, it only runs at 1024x768 or 1280x720, fullscreen or windowed, and thus might not be very fun on a 4K screen. On my 1080p screen, I played the game in a 720p window and had no engine-related issues. Pressing
will make the windowed game stretch to fill the screen, but everything — including text — becomes notably more pixelated in the process.
As far as Steam Achievements go, this isn't a
— and it doesn't want to be. Dozens of hours are needed to see all
has to offer, and the cheevos mirror this.

Bioshock 2: Taken Edition.
The original Bioshock needs little explanation for its initial success. A curveball in the field of story-based first person shooters, the strong direction and risks it took to shake up the standard makes it an oft-remembered title. Between the success of the original and the ever-so-popular Bioshock: Infinite, it seems odd how much Bioshock 2 comes off as the black sheep of the family. While well-lauded with some minor critiques back in the day, it comes off as an afterthought compared to the rest of its namesake. "Oh, right, Bioshock 2 exists," was my initial reaction when I bought the Bioshock package deal during a sale. As I began playing, I found myself rather surprised just how much more I enjoyed this over its predescessor.
The story starts off with a bang and the plot goes as follows: You are a Big Daddy (and so will be for the entire course of the game) that's on the hunt for his Little Sister. The Objectivist, libertarian "paradise" of the former game has crumbled and given way to a despotic autocracy under the guise of a theocratic Utopia. While the game starts off slowly to ease you in, it doesn't take long for it to find its stride. The first thing I noticed was how much more lively this rendition of Rapture felt. Unlike in the first game where every unique NPC was either behind a glass window or part of a cutscene, you are given the choice of dealing with them as you so wish. Audio diaries abound, the enemies themselves have an incredible amount of lines, everything in general is more talkative. Well, save for the vending machines, they did away with the whole "WELCOME TO THE CIIIIRCUS OF VALUUUES!" schtick for better or worse. It can be a little overwhelming at times, since there were a few times where the intercom would interrupt an audio diary I was listening to or something else of the sort will take over. I won't touch on the ending in detail, but I will say that it's certainly better than the 30 second one from the first.
However, the biggest improvement from the first game lies in the gameplay itself. Long gone are the loose gun controls and odd hit detection for snug shooting and bashing, and with those improvements comes better plasmids, more weapons, and a (thankfully) fun research system. No longer will you have to bust your camera out and take pictures of the enemy - now you get style points for throwing everything at them. My favorite change is the fact that you can have both a plasmid and a weapon out at the same time - you no longer have to switch between the two. The levels themselves are more complex and massive than the first one, which was fairly linear in comparison. One thing I want to nitpick is the fact that you cannot feasibly get every plasmid in the game or upgrade all your weapons, as there are simply not enough stations or ADAM to go around. Outside of that, everything is an improvement.
Graphically, there are some reused assets as to be expected, but the models are sharp and less cartoonish than in the first Bioshock. The setpieces and underwater sections are gorgeous, and as a plus, the textures aren't as muddied. And while the frequency of the old-fashioned tunes have taken a nosedive, the ambience and fight music have been tweaked to be more noticeable and rousing. Too often, video game scores are generic and cookie-cutter to be anything more than a part of an "EPIC GAME MUSIC COMPILATION - THE BEST" Youtube video. On that front, I found myself looking up certain tracks because they were that damn good.
Even so, there are some elements that I did not enjoy. More specifically, the way of gathering ADAM is a chore. You plop a Little Sister down and kill wave after wave of splicers before picking the little♥♥♥♥♥♥back up and going on your way to another corpse. Some of the symbolism thrown at you in the course of the game is about as subtle as a deer looking into the headlights of an incoming semi, and the main villain doesn't even feel particularly rancorous. While you got taunted and jeered at in the first game, the antagonist in this one might as well just say, "Oh dear, you survived again. Oh well, let me repeat my ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t diatribe again, since I am totally in the right again." The last time around, you had every reason to gut the villain. This time, you just go, "Well, okay, good for you." Plus, there are some twists and turns that might catch some people off-guard and be too reaching, but again, that's up to personal preference.
Bioshock 2, even with its share of quirks, is what a sequel should be like. It hits all of the high notes while adjusting a lot of the lower ones. Go get it in the bundle deal, it's dirt cheap.
(Also, multiplayer is deader than a doorknob. If you like your achievements, I hope you either enjoy wrangling up a bunch of friends to play it or altering around some files for those 'cheevos!)

Although less of a departure from the usual basis of a civilization game than I would have hoped, and lacking the elements of real history and growth that had always been a key factor in my own personal enjoyment of the series, this game had many new features and options that could be utilized by all other games in the genre to their betterment.
I was hoping for the ability to hop from planet to planet, running a colonial empire that was many times the size of any previously seen by civ players, instead we were treated to much the same game with added features, but without the history or nations we all know and enjoy watching take power; instead we were gifted with new nations, conglomorations and corporate junctions that somehow came together to head to space. There is little to no explanation to the mythos, and much of the "sci-fi" technology, especially in monuments and special buildings, just feels like it was thrown in to fill space.
Although the ability to choose how this new planet must deal with the addition of alien life is an amazing feature, it is also forced upon you to truly gain an advantage on the battlefield. Although we all came in giant colony ships, there is no technology to send another ship out, or go to another planet. I know we have had five renditions of the earths history, and that it is getting old, but if the game was going to be so similar to civ 5 they should have just added it on as the next step to the end game.
If you enjoy civ games, and the historical nature of them isnt a key to your enjoyment, than this game is great.

I played this game long enough to win once and try a couple of other civs. Then I decided I'd played this game long enough...period.
The colours are very drab and pastel-like, making it hard (at least for me) to really imprint on the map. I can still remember some of the geography of Civ 4 and Civ 5 games that I played years ago, yet I can't remember the geography of maps I played in BE only weeks ago. Everything just blends together.
The science tree is awful. The lack of colours and the spherical/nodal design make the tree more confusing than helpful. The fact that almost every building has a hidden choose-your-own bonus makes those even more confusing than the rest of the techs, and don't even get me started on how many different buildings require specific skills...I had no idea what I was building from one game to the next. The satellite system is also poorly designed and hard to use.
Then, of course, there's the diplomacy...by which I mean the almost complete lack of it. The leaders have absolutely no personality and a lot of what made Civ 5 good is lost.
The AI and balance could also use some work, with explorers happily wandering into death-traps of insects, various creatures easily overwhelming the player making certain play-styles nearly impossible, and worker build choices that would remove or drain resources that were already critically low or negative.
There were a couple of improvements over Civ 5, though. I found the espionnage system far more interesting than in Civ 5, and I liked the idea of leaders offering to trade favours rather than the inane Civ 5 system of "I like you -- can I have 1/4 of your income?" But for the few things I liked about it, there was just an overwhelming amount of things I didn't. I won't be buying any of the expansions...even if they address some of these issues, I consider the game an unfixable flop that won't be made playable by anything short of a complete overhaul.

I regret buying this game for $9.99 discounted, then the song of winter DLC for $15 not discounted.
When I saw the 10 dollar temporary pricetag and dungeon manging preview vid (first dungeon managing game mind you) I was sucked into it's style and unit management very quickly. Installing, then playing the game. the campaign though pathetically a day or two long, had some of the most enjoyable voice acting from a narrative voice I've experienced in recent gaming. Not to mention the fun references and pokes to other well known game franchises every 30seconds.
Now why I regretted buying this; it's hollow, and cheap.
After quickly finishing the campaign I grew easily accustomed to the 'horde' race and was eager to try the demon race. Now being a MAN I simply could not continue playing on normal difficulty. So I ramped it hard, beat a few skirmishes, big whoop. Naturally you only want to try for a better challenge, right? So I skipped very hard right into impossible difficulty. And right there, is where it began to show how flawed the game was built. They knew the dungeon managing experience they were setting to make, however the balancing, difficulty, variance in gameplay, that all fell flat on it's face.
First of all evert single race operates the EXACT SAME, build treasuries, build relax room (brewery, admiration, F.R.P.), build a mana room, build a trap resources room, build an upgrade room, then smash some camps, get your evil up, and upgrade. Rinse and repeat. Only I could repeat it barely twice per race before becoming numb.
AND FUSTRATED, because impossible difficulty is well.... IMPOSSIBLE. Literally, I like hard difficulties bordering on the unfair masicism. But it's just not balanced. I couldn't find a single youtube video that showed someone beating this game on impossible. Why? Because impossible is broken. The first half is always fine but as soon as you get swamped with units that disarm your traps, you lose. You, lose. You have no chance fighting 3 times whatever size your army is as a constant stream without your traps.
Lastly let me talk about the races. 'Horde' being probably the most easiest and simple to play as. Demon's being way too ridiculously weak in the beginning to stand any chance above hard difficulty. And then undead which honestly don't add anything new besides the undead theme of rooms and... some units come back when they die?
Anyway.... this game is just so short, vanilla version includes a pitifully short campaign and just two boring races. And when you try to play the game seriously on a difficult that makes you try, it breaks because it wasn't balanced for higher difficulties and maps. It is such an insult when you finish the campaign and open skirmish just to find NO ORIGINAL MAPS. THEY JUST RECYCLE THE CAMPAIGN MAPS.
It's fun for the first game you play, but just don't buy it. Play at your unlucky friend's who bought it.
EDIT: Oh I forgot to mention? You better turn on 15min auto save or save yourself every 5minutes. I play on win10 and this game CRASHES EVERY 20minutes guaranteed. It WILL crash on you, and it seems to be a lot more likely to crash the longer you go without saving, ironically.

This is a F2P "match three" game built on the standard Puzzle Quest model of "matches do damage." There's also a limited PvP element, as your team is matched up against other users' squads of three heroes.
It's a hugely grindy game, and you are pressured to make IAPs through a mechanic where you're granted new heroes pretty regularly...but they expire if you don't claim them. You're constantly squeezed for slots to keep the heroes, and the in-game currency comes far too infreqently to actually buy slots in a timely manner.
It's not a bad Mavel themed time waster, if you enjoy the basic Bejewled game mechanic, but I can't recommend it if you actually want to collect and play with good decently powered heroes.
Note: I've played both this and the iOS versions of the game.

TO clarify at the start, i am Recommending the Mobile version, NOT the PC version.
I play this game pretty reguarly on mobile and the majority of complaints i see come from the timers for heroes to heal and microtransactions.
The microtransactions were recently inflated to obscene prices on mobile as well but in all honesty you do not need them to enjoy the game, i advise spending Iso cyrstal on levelling your heros and after a couple of lighting rounds and other events you'll amass heroes faster than you can get space to hold them all. Im at 19 character spaces without paying for any 'fun' coins
As for the Timers of health regen, It was originally designed as a mobile game/ gate mechanism to prevent you from playing the whole game endlessly. That obviously does not fit well here on PC, but i spend weeks playing this on the mobile to return each day to play a bit more until i get bored or all my main characters are awaiting regen.
The game itself however is your typical Puzzle quest game! A match 3 gem game where any colours you match are stored for use as Powers that your characters have. The game ends when you reduce the enemy team to 0HP. I won't lie, sometimes you will feel cheated by the game for chaining colours and anniliating your team, but it happens sometimes for your benifit as well. Also some battles are so artifically hard thats about my only legitimate complaint about it. When you come up against a level 230 Venom as an optional mission, yeah you'll skip it but think how your even supposed to complete it as currently most chracters can only reach Lv 141.
But to re-iterate, i really enjoy this game. Even the "PvP" aspects which are just more single player matches vs an AI using another players characters.
The choice shouldn't be about wether to play it or not, it should be about what platform to play it on.
And i choose Mobile.

Homefront looks pretty good and despite the ridiculous plot it sets an intriguing atmosphere, but other than that it has little to offer. For a shooter there’s no interesting or tactical challenge. As you enter every scene, suddenly out of nowhere a large amount of bullet-spongy enemy soldiers show up shooting you frantically and you take cover and shoot them down. You immediately feel it’s done bad. There’s very little room for different approaches, no decent build-up to confrontation, no interesting behavior by the enemy -just the nonstop spraying – etc. When you’ve killed all the enemies in a particular area you move on to the next setting in annoyingly long exposition sections where you can only walk very slowly – only to be made longer because the collectibles (newspapers that give background information) are implemented so poorly. Moreover, many special actions like jumping down a small ledge or climbing something must be done with a use/action key, which you can’t perform before your slow NPC companions have done so. It just drags on and on. And when the gameplay does deviate, it’s so heavily scripted there’s no fun to be had whatsoever – do this, click now, wait, click now or start over. I survived 17 days. This is not a game where dying doesn't matter. I never thought any of my characters would get killed. They all died within a space of 2 days. Katia was killed while scavenging. I though I'd quickly steal some supplies from a house full of armed men, as we were desperate for food and valuable items for bartering to get more bandages. As the night of her death ended, the next morning saw another of my team, Marin, pass away from severe wounds, even though he was bandaged and recovering, or so I thought, in bed. It was the worst night I'd experienced. If this wasn't enough, the third member left the house. He was also wounded, tired and hungry. That left me with Pavle, the 'fast runner'. He was broken, and he would not move, because everyone had died. On the last night of scavenging with him, he was knifed by someone, as I tried to steal some precious food supplies. I was going to quickly run away, but had to run past the Garage owner's son who knifed me. Seeing as I could do nothing, I pressed 'End Day'. I might as well have pressed 'End Game'. Pavle committed suicide. The credits explained he thought he had no chance in seeing his son again, so decided it would be easier to give up.
This game has so much character, and also a huge replayability factor. I was too keen on helping others, so I invited another in to the house at about Day 8. Now I had another mouth to feed, another body to protect. He then fought with another of my team, causing both to be wounded. That did not help matters. I had already messed up scavenging in the wrong locations, not crafting weapons at the beginning to protect ourselves, not building enough beds at the start. I thought I would do well when at Day 6 I knocked an armed guard over the head with a shovel while scavenging with Bruno, because he was about to assault a poor girl who was also scavenging the supermarket. I killed him, and got his AK47 and 20 bullets. But that didn't help me. What helps is food, water, bandages, furniture and warmth. And above all, kinship. Characters can talk to others and build each other up. This is a true survivors' game. A simulation of real survival during wartime.
Do not be put off by the 2D nature of the game. The only game which made me feel as emotional as this game, was The Last of Us. That says something. £15 is peanuts for a game with a soul.

This War of Mine is one of the few survival games I fell in love with as soon as I started playing. While a lot of survival games have some unknown scary thing, or zombies after you, this game is more on realism. You play as survivors stuck in an area that is caught up in war. There is no help, you must survive. You must fortify your base, collect food, survive the cold, make hard decisions, and decide how to spend resources.
What I thought was most brilliant was how you have to consider the morality in what you do since it can affect the morale of your survival group. I also rather enjoyed the art work and visuals the game has, however, I had to keep it on soft graphics since the sharper/bolder graphics where a bit much visually.
The only things I can say about this game that is negative is it can get monotonous in go grab components and wood, go make things, rinse and repeat, oh and don't die like a dog out there. I would not dismiss this game on that point alone. If you like survival games this is definitely worth trying out. I'm glad I did, and I can see they have already done some things to make the game have more re-play value. Hopefully they continue to develop this game in further patches. If they haven't already, having a way to build larger backpacks at a workshop or finding them in game would be awesome.

It's an absolute shame every platform has seemingly done away with star ratings -- though I think I get it, it's a way to drive sales.
Since, I'd recommend this game, but I'd only give it about a
. It's an average game.
The first 20 or so hours of this game are amazing -- though I'd imagine this number might be lower if you accidentally discover what you're supposed to do first, or choose to play in a medium sized world first.
My spoiler-free review is this: this game will feel very familiar if you've played any crafting game before (quickly becoming my favorite genre) -- but, unfortunately, Crea doesn't really offer anything new in the genre. It does streamline certain things (things like weapons and gear do not have durability), and there is a heavy emphasis on fighting -- which isn't a bad thing, except, ultimately, it ends up feeling like fighting for fighting's sake.
There is lore in this game, but it is not presented in a forthright way -- thus there is little-to-no incentive to care about it.
: if you're interested in a quick, 2D RPG-light, crafting/adventuring fix to play with a friend or loved one, I highly recommend this.
But if you're looking for something deeper, look elsewhere. I'm almost 40 hours in, and while I still enjoy it, about 15 or so hours ago the charm wore off, and now I am more or less chasing achievements where fun happens too infrequently.

Honestly a pretty good game! The story is pretty good but the ending felt a bit weak to me. The game starts out slow, as you begin with a can opener of a space ship, and slowly start earning money to upgrade and then buy a new ship. Some people complained it was too slow, however I found it more rewarding to see higher rewards appearing in the mission boards the more my reputation as a pilot grew. As far as combat, the mechanics are all really fun to use and strategize with. There are a variety of weapons with different perks and shortcomings to choose from, as well as variants of shields. One of my favorite mechanics was the deflector, which is essentially a second shield which you have to manually activate. It lasts briefly but can be the difference between survival and a death blow.
I had a couple problems with the game though. One thing that bothered me is that the armor doesn't seem to effectively scale with the size of the ship. I won the entire game with the barracuda corvette, which is a mid-game ship but it is the smallest playable ship class. When I tried to go to a larger ship size (I went from the barracude to the big one that looks like a star destroyer) it was obviously very slow and cumbersome compared to the barracuda, but also I kept getting destroyed because I was a bigger target with the same shielding as when I was a small target. I switched back to the barracuda and haven't looked back since. I know there are armor classes for the different ship classes (light, medium, etc.) but it feels like the shielding should scale as well.
The single most annoying thing in the game is getting pulled out of warp not because you are on a collision course, but because you are almost on a collision course. I can't tell you how many times I got pulled out of warp, had to go normal speed past an asteroid I wasn't even going to hit, and then wait a few seconds for the warp drive to warm up. Huge waste of time for a very very dumb mechanic.
The galaxy itself looked really beautiful, and there were a lot of times when something would catch my eye and I would just stop playing to take it in for a moment, because the art is just incredible. I once saw a dreadnought half shrouded in a storm nebula and if I had seen it outside of the game I would've figured it's that bull crap cover art that companies like Ubisoft like to pull all the time to showcase their "game's" graphics. The one problem I had with the game's art (and I'm not even sure if this is to blame on the artists or just the devs in general) is the size of the planets. They try to make them seem bigger by creating a barrier around them that makes you lose shield health (as though you are heating up from re-entry) but it's especially obvious with the moons, that the celestial bodies in this game are all very small. And I understand why, but it just feels a little cheesy.
All around, I thought this was a pretty good game. Lots of space to explore and strategies to try. 7/10

"I promised Diana I'd keep you safe" - Agent 47
Now, Hitman: Absolution has been criticized for being too 'linear', in the sense that, in past Hitman games (and future, considering HITMAN 2016), each mission was open for the player to decide how to kill which target when and where etc. In Absolution, this is AND isn't the case. I personally, love this game. The story was a step-up from past Hitman games, and it actually explored 47's emotional side.
First off, the graphics. To be expected, the graphics are a HUGE improvement over past Hitman games. This is due to the engine improvement (Glacier2 over the original Glacier engine used for Hitman: Blood Money). The texure details, animations and overall quality has been significantly upgraded.
The gameplay is where this game has taken some flak. As stated earlier, this game is much more linear than its predecessors; this is due in part to the story, which also stated previously, explores 47's personal life/emotions etc. There are, however, some exceptions, which throw the player into an open area and say "here are your targets, kill them in whichever way you choose, so you can proceed".
For example,

That is just one of a few different missions which offer that kind of open, "Blood Money"-esque mission style.
The story is quite good, though I'm not entirely sold on the story overriding some gameplay elements (see above). The story in Absolution is vastly different from past Hitman games, and depicts Agent 47 as the target, being hunted
. Agent 47 is asked by Diana (his handler at the International Contract Agency), to look after a mysterious girl named Victoria, who is later sought after by both the Agency and other powerful parties. The story offers action and emotion, as well as that classic badass "Hitman" feel, just in a 'new suit', so to speak.
Absolution is also the first in the series to introduce 'Contracts Mode' (not to be confused with the third Hitman game, Hitman: Contracts). In Contracts, players can create their own missions (dubbed Contracts), from pre-existing missions in the game. For example, I created a Contract which was set on the second part of the third mission in the game (Terminus Hotel; Upper Floors). In it, I marked three targets for assassination, and then proceeded to kill them in a certain way; I stabbed someone with a screwdriver, garroted someone with measuring tape and broke someone's neck. I then hid all the bodies out of sight, and did it all without changing disguises or being spotted. This means that other players who play my Contract will need to kill those targets in EXACTLY the same manner as me, if they want maximum points.
Contracts Mode is a great addition to the Hitman series, and especially Absolution, as players will be able to satisfy their own need for "Blood Money".
Overall, all things considered, Hitman: Absolution is a good game. From its great graphics and good storyline, to its fun gameplay (even if it didn't quite satisfy that "Blood Money" itch, but I suppose that's what Contracts Mode is for :P ), this game is great.

I think my major issue with this game is the lack of a truly interesting antagonist. While Sofia Lamb was an ok villain and the game's focus on collectivist and socialist ideologies was a clever approach, I never really felt that it provided enough of an in depth view like the first game did. Andrew Ryan's charasmatic personality added a whole new level to Bioshock's plot, and really helped the player understand how the ideas he supported affected the city's destruction. In this one, Lamb sounds more like a generic evil professor, which makes it a bit difficult for the game and player to properly explore her belief system like the previous one did with Ryan. In addition, the game's overall plot played a bit too safe, and didn't really try to add any revolutionary events (I actually thought the DLC's plot twist was a lot more well done). Other than that, the gameplay has improved greatly since the first Bioshock, and the weapons and plasmids offer a lot more varaity to it. If you can get past the rather slow plot and some of the characters, it's still a great game and a worthy addition to the Bioshock series. I just think the first one is a little bit better.

The best in the franchise, Hitman: Absolution brings Agent 47 into a streamlined, satisfying league of his own. Others may sing paeans to Blood Money's non-linearity and Silent Assassin's score (both series highs, respectively), but Absolution boasts the most responsive and satisfying gameplay. The cover-based stealth and multiple discrete mission paths recall the excellent Deus Ex: Human Revolution, and part of the fun of each level is following the breadcrumbs the designers left for players to find and act on - the gun shop level, Birdie's Gift, is an outstanding example. The story comprises the black ops pulp and stereotypes we've come to expect from the franchise, though it's all presented impeccably. Chuckle-worthy black humor abounds, even if it stoops to juvenile levels on occasion.
No, Absolution's not perfect. The score system can at times be infuriating: it's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t that you get a "Spotted" malus while firing multiple bullets through an isolated guard's faceplate. And without getting into major spoilers, the game inexplicably reverses wodges of the plot in its last five seconds. It's an infuriating way to end the series' narrative high point.
Yet, all in all, the game plays very well, looks gorgeous, and sounds great. Buy if you at all giggle at the prospect of electrocuting a man through his urine stream.

First of all, it is one of the most unbalanced multiplayer games of all time. New players aren\'t going to stand a chance because they don\'t know how the game works and all the cheap tatics the experienced players use, and they don\'t have good equipment. It\'s completely unfair. The best weapons I would recommend from my experience are the grenade launcher with any upgrade, except homing grenades, the elephant gun with the quad barrel upgrade for headshots, the crossbow with the rate of fire upgrade, or you could use any other upgrade for headshots. I\'d recommend the pistol with any upgrade if you have good aim. You also can\'t go wrong with the shotty. My favorite plasmids are electrobolt to stun opponents(works great with headshots), Aero Dash to get around faster and to confuse your opponents. Dash can also get you out of electro-stuns, fire,bees and away from turrets. Telekinesis is probably the best plasmid. This game is like Candy Crush, in that you _can_ get through everything for free if you wait long enough, but unlike Candy Crush, where you could keep playing if you passed a stage, Marvel Puzzle Quest forces you to wait, no matter how good you are. Your heroes have HP which persist over stages, and it takes time for the heroes to recover HP. There are some stages where you can possibly go through without losing any health, but you'll get to stages where you just can't prevent damage, so if you want to continue, you'd need to wait for HP to regenerate, and then move on. Paying money is just for 'cheats'; extra EXP, other heroes, instant heals, etc. This game is pretty much unplayable if you're playing it for free.

While it may seem like yet another bad MOBA at a glance, Battlerite will be a fairly new and refreshing experience for a lot of players. There's no creeps, no bases to defend, no leveling up or buying items; just high-skill arena combat. You move your character with WASD and aim skills with the mouse, rather than moving with right-click like a typical MOBA. Either way it's free so you might as well give it a shot.
Good:
- It's free without being "pay to win"
- High skill ceiling and mechanically deep
- Gameplay is satisfying, matches are quick and entertaining
- Developers gradually balance with small tweaks rather than knee-jerk changes
- The rate at which you unlock content is very fair, never feels like "grinding"
- Useful replay system, but viewing them outside of the game would be nice
Questionable:
- "Battlerite" system is underwhelming, feels like the illusion of choice*
- Not all characters available immediately, you must earn them by playing
- Hard for new players to get into - no singleplayer mode, tutorial is misleading
- Many cosmetics look atrocious to the point of destroying the game's aesthetic
- Art-style feels generic and uninspired, very "Blizzard-esque" in a boring way
- Bloodline Champions was better (before it was abandoned, at least)
- Not enough variety in map layouts, arenas feel very samey as well
- Developers added some weird MOBA-esque mode... not sure why
* = Most characters have around 3 or 4 Battlerites that are pretty much manditory to get in all situations, and the remaining choices are decided by the enemy's composition moreso than player preference. Missing certain Battlerites will feel like your character is missing one of their arms: they just don't function properly without them. Before you had to pick 1 Battlerite per round, allowing you to adapt to the enemy's builds, but now you pick them all upfront which makes the system seem rather pointless.

TO clarify at the start, i am Recommending the Mobile version, NOT the PC version.
I play this game pretty reguarly on mobile and the majority of complaints i see come from the timers for heroes to heal and microtransactions.
The microtransactions were recently inflated to obscene prices on mobile as well but in all honesty you do not need them to enjoy the game, i advise spending Iso cyrstal on levelling your heros and after a couple of lighting rounds and other events you'll amass heroes faster than you can get space to hold them all. Im at 19 character spaces without paying for any 'fun' coins
As for the Timers of health regen, It was originally designed as a mobile game/ gate mechanism to prevent you from playing the whole game endlessly. That obviously does not fit well here on PC, but i spend weeks playing this on the mobile to return each day to play a bit more until i get bored or all my main characters are awaiting regen.
The game itself however is your typical Puzzle quest game! A match 3 gem game where any colours you match are stored for use as Powers that your characters have. The game ends when you reduce the enemy team to 0HP. I won't lie, sometimes you will feel cheated by the game for chaining colours and anniliating your team, but it happens sometimes for your benifit as well. Also some battles are so artifically hard thats about my only legitimate complaint about it. When you come up against a level 230 Venom as an optional mission, yeah you'll skip it but think how your even supposed to complete it as currently most chracters can only reach Lv 141.
But to re-iterate, i really enjoy this game. Even the "PvP" aspects which are just more single player matches vs an AI using another players characters.
The choice shouldn't be about wether to play it or not, it should be about what platform to play it on.
And i choose Mobile.

Review for Crea v1.4.9
My guild and I loved this game. We have been so sick of the amount of multiplayer games that are only 4 people max or poorly made/hardly updated. This game felt like an absolute rare find. Looking at the game, we were interested, and after playing it, we were not disappointed. We loved playing through Terraria, so that will be a big comparison I will use.
We began playing Crea, and it was initially a bit confusing, but we managed to understand it quickly with helpful bits of tutorials. I recall going to make my first piece of armor or weapon and being so confused with all I saw, but the tutorial was very good at explaining how the crafting works – and It was cool! Also, the skill trees were a pretty cool addition coming from Terraria. There (currently) are 5 trees: Arms (physical damage), Syle (Magic Damage), Mining, Crafting, and Exploration. All of these trees have its own level that you level up in doing things related to that tree, which was pretty neat. The trees add unique abilities, and overall improve your character. Your character as well has its own level (gained from killing mobs) which allows you to get attributes for your character (intellect, defense, etc.).
The entire play though of the game was enjoyable. I felt like it was a
short, and more content would be a nice addition (more bosses, higher level, etc.), but that does NOT mean this game was lacking. I really loved the “level of detail” Crea had. While Terraria was longer, it did not have much in comparison to Crea mechanically speaking. As well, adding more content I feel is a lot easier than what Terraria would have to do to add similar mechanics to their game, and I can totally see this game getting more content.
Crea seems to be still in pretty good development. Jasson, the developer, loves this game, and has clearly shown he cares about improving player’s experiences. The game gets plenty of updates in short amounts of time, with bug fixes, and improvements. During our play through, we encountered a few bugs (and lets be real – every game has some bugs), which were all promptly replied to within 24 hours, and fixed very quickly. If you don’t believe me about Jasson, go check out his stream and see for yourself – go chat about the game with him while he makes it!
As a group, we’d all agree this game was the best game of this type we’ve played. Crea was fantastic, and I look forward to seeing this game grow more (mechanics and content wise) and in popularity.  Jasson is definitely passionate about his game, and has created a gem of a game. This game should not be passed up! I don’t have an x/10 (as I generally don’t do that), but as a quote from the guild: “If Crea was a 10/10, Terraria would be an 8, and Starbound would be a 5.”

This game captures exactly what it is supposed to capture: The pointlessness of a violent world-hating rampage carried out by someone who hates themselves and sees themselves reflected in the world.  It isn't fun.  Its distant, black & white, and actually somewhat boring.
There is a catharsis to it.  It is one of those little gems in video gaming that proves video games are an art form, because this feels like playing an interactive gallery art project.  It enters the player into a world / world view (a mirror looking at a mirror), forces the player to adopt the character's mentality, and work through goals set for him as he interacts with the world.  Movies are non-interactive, books are open to misinterpretation, painting is very limited.  As a video game, Hatred does what its creators I think set out to do.  It definetly doesn't encourage shooting sprees.  Once you hate yourself and your life so much, no matter what you do and what you acheive, whatever you think your life goals are or aren't, it pretty much doesn't matter.  It just says a miserable spiral of self destruction isn't the world's fault, its your own, and if you hate everything you do anyway that will include whatever desperate final act you decide to commit.  By working through the rampage fantasy it defeats it.
I think Hatred makes a point that is worth understanding and does a good job of conveying it.
