'This War of Mine' is a side-scrolling survival game developed and self-published by 11 bit studios back in 2014. The game's overall theme is based on a war-torn city with player activity focused on civilian survival through scavenging, trading, crafting and resource management rather than direct military action.
The game places you in control of three starting survivors in one of the default scenarios with more  joining as the story progresses. The game starts by scavenging and fortifying a derelict house which will act as the player's base of operations. During the day the player can construct basic survival necessities such as beds, food production facilities and water collecting devices and at night, the player can elect to send a member of the team to scavenge for supplies or trade with known traders in the area. Survive the harsh conditions, defend against bandit attacks, scavenge supplies and keep your survivors sane and healthy until the peacekeepers arrive to resolve the conflict and put an end to the war.
+ Great art style that blends well with the theme
+ Challenging survival game mechanics but...(see CON #1)
+ Refreshing new theme for a survival game (by that I mean, no zombies, monsters or ghosts)
+ Adequate base upgrade and item crafting mechanic (although I wish there were more items to craft)
+ Good resource management mechanic
+ Random events that add replayability but...(see CON #2)
+ Good survivor skill variety but... (see NEUTRAL #1)
+ Morality and state of mind system
+ Good scavenging and combat mechanic that works well with the side-scrolling system
+ Atmospheric with good sound effects and lighting
- The challenge wears out after you get past the learning curve (which is not that steep)
- The game becomes repetitive after a few playthroughs...dare I say, tedious at some points
- No speed up time (only an option to end the day and start the night game)
- Limited construction space in each room of your base
- Some of the game mechanics are highly exploitable
+/- Limited survivor customization
+/- Autosave is too far in between
. This War of Mine is essentially for people looking for an authentic but not too realistic survival experience since it has the basic elements of a survival game while at the same time having the resource management mechanics of simulation title.

While I feel that this game has the weakest story out of all the games in the Bioshock trilogy, I definitely believe Bioshock 2 has the best gameplay. For one, dual wielding has been added, meaning you don't need to wait for your character to switch between having a weapon and plasmid out in the heat of battle. Because you play as a Big Daddy, the game has expanded upon the ways you can collect Adam to upgrade your plasmids. Like before, you can choose to harvest or rescue Little Sisters, but now you can also escort Little Sisters around so they can harvest Adam off of corpses for you. Also, hacking has been drastically improved. Not only can you now hack machines from a distance, but also the pipe minigame has been removed, being replaced with an extremely brief timing-based minigame that will make you want to hack things much more frequently than you did in the original.
This is also the only Bioshock game to have a Multiplayer mode. It's a fun distraction, but it didn't really appeal to me as something I'd wanna dedicate my time towards, especially considering how small the multiplayer community is now. I never was unable to find a server to play on, but that's only because there's often only 1 or 2 servers available. That being said, the achievements in the Multiplayer are not only rare, but easy to obtain, so it might be worth checking out if you're into that.
One final thing I want to point out is the Minerva's Den DLC. This extra campaign is definitely worth picking up, as it's extremely well written and designed. It's definitely better than the main storyline.
All in all, Bioshock 2 is a fun Bioshock experience. That being said, I'd mainly recommend it to people who are already fans of the Bioshock series, as the changes that have been added to the gameplay aren't really enough to satisfy considering the underwhelming storyline. Basically, if you've played Bioshock and want more of the gameplay, play this. If on the other hand you've played the original and want more of the storyline, play Infinite and it's Burial at Sea DLC.

Overall, this game is a great sequel to the original.
It is set in the same city of rapture, but the storyline is pretty different. The story itself offers much more in the way of choice, in comparison to the first story. Due to this, it also seems a bit more meaningful.
The gameplay is modified quite positively. Rather than having 4 groups of 8 genes and plasmids to splice, you can just pick from a selection of 24 genes and 8 plasmids instead, which is great at letting you play the game just the way you want. Also, the game adds the mechanic of Adam collection, which is a much better utilisation of the little sisters than in the first game. There are also some new enemies added, like the big sister, which adds a sort of mini boss fight to each level. The hacking mechanic in the first game was a bit cumbersome at times, but this game simplifies the process. It does not necessarily making it any easier, though.
The artwork in this game is as good as ever, carrying on the run down steampunk look of the city, with some additions in the form of areas where you can walk on the sea floor and see the coral and other fauna and flora. Also, the little sisters and other character designs seem to have made it up past the good side of the uncanny valley, with better voice acting as well.
The only major downside to this is that for some reason, if you are using windows 10, the game will crash when using DirectX 10. You can fix this if you switch to DX9, but then you have ugly muddy textures. This is extremely annoying. It is also worth noting that issues will also occur on windows 7, due to internet explorer. Somehow.
This game is definitely an improvement on the original, and it can also serve as a good one off game if you've never played the original.

I personally think this game is an improvement over its predecessors on every point.
The HUD is perfectly clear. You understand immediately your status, when people is about to see through your disguise, what actions you can do... The controls require quite more keybindings, which can be disturbing at first, but allow for smoother action.
The mission mechanics are more intuitive. Targets have better highlight, tactics are hinted through challenges, a score system rewards the cleanest assassins.
The missions are more challenging. The previous games' omniscient map was OP, honestly. You now have a basic radar, and Instinct. Instinct gives helpful information, allow you to prevent people from seeing through your disguise, and can trigger Point Shooting (or badass mode). The fact that it's not unlimited makes it fairer, in my opinion.
Mission areas are smaller, but missions can actually follow one another, allowing you to keep disguise and equipment. No more pre-mission weapon selection, but this is coherent with the story.
Because, yeah, the main plot is not secondary.

This remastered edition has come a long way from its release. From my understanding the rereleases were initially plagued with crashes. I did not suffer this problem on my PC, using Windows 10. Personally I had more issues just trying to
the original Bioshock than any issues I encountered with the Remastered version. I had one crash in 13 hours of gameplay, and it was towards the end of the game.
Issues aside, this game is great. I played 13 hours of it in the past 5 days - I haven't done been so interested in a game in years. It's been out around 10 years but it plays as if it just came out yesterday. I completed it a few years back and liked it alright, but I loved it this time through. The premise is unique and the story is renowned for its execution and development. Characters are not just caricatures for the most part and the devs do a good job of making you feel sympathy even for your typical grunt enemies found throughout the game, known as Splicers.
Combat is immensely satisfying and allows extreme freedom in approach. It's entirely feasible to beat the game with just the starting melee weapon if you're so inclined. Your character is a Gordon Freeman-type who never speaks, but is connected to the world and characters around him regardless.
All of Bioshock has this incredible feeling around it - it reminds me of reading
as a child. Your character jumps down a rabbit hole into a completely nonsensical world filled with unforgettable characters. Even though it's a linear single-player FPS, I feel like I could play through it many more times and discover things I've never seen before. I paid $20 for all the Bioshock series but I feel like I've already got my money's worth with the first entry already.

Gameplay:
GRID Autosport provides a fun environment plus intense racing to give you the perfect balance between Simulation and Arcade.
The driving model is very good as it's not too challenging but at the same time you can't underestimate it or else you'll be put into a wall.
There are 5 disciplines in this game: Tuner, Street, Open Wheel, Endurance, and Touring.
These 5 different disciplines all bring a unique selection of cars and unique gameplay.
This all works very well in making a fun yet challenging game that can give Forza Motorsport and Gran Turismo fans such as myself the same level of entertainment except on the PC platform.
Codemasters have made a huge improvement to their racing franchises (since the fall of quality aka. DiRT Showdown) by listening to the community and what they want in a racing game.
GRID 2 had a extremely arcade like driving model and lacked many features including interior camera, since then they've taken all the feedback and produced this great game.
AI is extremely well done, they know what they're doing (most of the time) and have proven to be a formiddable opponent at higher AI difficulties.
Also there are many many camera angles to suit anybody's preference.
Story:
This game features quite a flexible campaign to become the best at all 5 disciplines and become the GRID Champion.
It's pretty much the same as Forza in which you choose a series to do and then you do it.
GRID makes this concept more enjoyable by making you pick what team you'd like to race for the series and that team has objectives to complete during that season and certain vehicles picked out for you. You also get a teammate in that series (Beware, They're pretty damn bad) which you control their aggression through 5 stages.
Defend Position, Hold Position, Balanced, Push Position, Attack Position
This makes for very dynamic gameplay as you also have to focus on another AI's aggresion of the race and estimate their stress levels.
Each team has a livery for particular vehicles such as: Kicker's Volkswagon Golf Livery.
The real joy is in the Multiplayer portion of the game.
Multiplayer:
In Multiplayer you have to earn money by doing challenges and racing other players in intense races.
Normally that's all a Multiplayer is? Yeah but not in this game.
The real joy of Multiplayer is managing a garage of vehicles you've purchased and then making custom liveries for them giving a sense of personalisation and pride.
The higher the rank the more range of sponsors you can put onto your vehicle.
You can also make a Club of friends or strangers that has a custom made livery for all members to use.
Cons:
This game would be great if only these four things weren't on this portion of the review.
- Interior is poorly textured and blurred. Originally made so people would focus on the track instead of the interior making
a saddening atmosphere in the vehicle.
- No looking around the vehicle's interior. Another let down but at least 4K users get a great version of the game where
they can see all of the cockpit.
- Blurred out mirrors. The side and rear view mirrors are blurred out and don't actually work at all which is another
saddening aspect of the interior viewing.
- Not many people playing multiplayer.
I hope you enjoyed reading this review and I hope this helped make you decide if you'd like to buy it or not.

+ Visually the graphics of this game look fantastic with a lot of detail and color
+ Filled with fantasy charm and references to Game of Thrones and Lord of the Rings
+ Gameplay is fun, you are essentially managing a variety of minions commanding them to mine gold, build structures / traps, and eventually build an army to take out the humans above while they are constantly invading your dungeon to try to take you out.
+ A unique multi-layered map, meaning that there's an overworld on top of your underworld with an entirely different environment and you have to send troops to and from to complete various objectives.
+ Lots of things to build, upgrades, traps, and a variety of troops
+ An amazing narrator who essentially tells the story through the cutscenes and as you play with some very well written dialogue and some guinuely funny moments. (At one point I noticed him say something like "Is this going too slow for you? Well check out the in-game cash shop and buy 20 gems for $100 to speed up the game by 100% Oh wait....this isn't a free to play game. Carry on")
+ Although the game gets a bit complex later on Dungeons 2 does a remarkably well done job of gradually introducing the player to new game mechanics without the need of any real tutorials or any reading.
+ When controlling units there's a lot of interesting RPG mechanics where you earn exp, can research abilities, find books to upgrade or give units special perks, and strategically mix various units to give various buffs. (example: using a naga to heal from afar while orcs are in front)
+ As you advance in the campaign the game seems to just get better and better
+ At one point in the campaign you get to play as an alternative race with all new units with new abilities, structures, and so on, there's yet another race in the Game of Winter DLC
- You can't rotate the camera it's essentially locked at an angle similar to Starcraft and other RTS games. It's not that bad, but I would have loved to see alternate viewpoints
- The narrator can be incredibly annoying when you take too long to complete an objective.
- You have a low population cap in first few missions at 15, which makes things a bit more difficult than they should. Later on you can increase the cap but you constantly feel limited
- The level before the last of level of the campaign the "A Blood Red Wedding" IS ABSOLUTELY HORRIBLE!!!!!!! Why? Well the length of the mission is far too long inflated by tons of timers. To put it simply every 5minutes you get fight a few enemies and then you have to wait 5minutes to fight anymore (literally you must wait for this stupid timer to tick down) meanwhile you just sit there and stare blankly at the screen waiting and waiting and waiting and waiting for hours...until finally the mission ends. :(

Hatred is a top down shooter in a similar vein as Postal 1 or the SAS Survival Flash games, and unfortunately suffers for it. The basic gameplay could be fun, with basic movement and a dodge roll that allows brief invincibility (supposedly), and weapons that certainly have decent impact for a game in this genre. The story mode is nothing to be proud of, and completable in only a few short hours, but the game has a decent enough survival mode that gives some extra time for it. However, this game is nothing more than a cheap flash game in a better engine with a bigger file size, and isn't worth the price.
Further, there is a glaring problem in the gameplay in that apparently you're not shooting humans, but rather precognizant empaths who know your position no matter what. Maybe it's because it's 2017 and I've been spoiled on games with mediocre but present stealth mechanics like Time Splitters 2 and Perfect Dark, but instead of using the typical vision cones of AI design, enemies will instead know your position at all moments. This wouldn't be such a problem, except for when you get sniped by an enemy that was outside of your visual area because they phased into existance from your opposite side and knew immediately to shoot you through several civilians blocking their way. Want to maybe break away from the action and heal up? Too bad, the enemy knows you're going to do that and they'll head you off. Even and especially if your path is haphazard and confusing, they will find you. What's worse is that enemy units aren't armed with pea shooters, so you will die plenty not because of skill but because of overwhelming AI aggression.

If you run through and take everyone in your way down you just end up waiting at a door blocked by the same fridge over and over for 5 minutes until your squad amble up, have a natter and then slowly unblock whatever was in the way so you can follow them to the next set piece. Gun play is passable, but not great and repetitive due to how the levels are set up. Story is pretty dire, with not much believable to go on, and unlikeable inconsistent characters throughout. If you're looking for more terraria,
This is a charming terraria clone that does a lot to make itself different.
-This game is a lot slower paced than terraria, reaching a feeling closer to minecraft.
-The combat is slower paced aswell, all enemies, including the bosses, all have specific patterns that you can get around by learning their gimmicks, efficiently using the dodge roll,and using your many unlockable abilities.
-The character progression is similar to that of an RPG, you get xp in specific categories while you play the game, meanwhile a main xp bar fills up. you can use all of that to unlock/upgrade abilities and upgrade your character.
-Crafting is a bit more complex, you have to 'research' something before you can craft it, on top of that, you can make your gear stronger than normal by using chaos crafting.
-You actually lose your things upon death, but you can get them back by going back to your death point without worrying about the items despawning, aslong as you have atleast 1 way shard in your inventory.
-Enemy difficulty scales with the local area difficulty rather than constantly adding new enemy variants.
-you get from tier to tier mostly through mining, but it's a bit less grindy to do in this game because one of the gather skills is a built in spelunker potion.
-There's a handful of different biomes.
-This game has a few bugs, but is mostly polished.
-It takes a bit of time to learn the basics of the game.

It's really hard to explain just how bad this game is. My issue was that despite my early misgivings, I kept thinking the game would 'open up' after the 4 hours mark, and so I kept playing. Once I reached the first boss, that was when I knew...
This game suffers from No Man's Sky syndrome.
"What is NMS Syndrome?", you may ask. Great question! It's a special sort of suffering that comes about when a game has just enough intrigue and promise to make you play past Steam's refund period, and then instantly drops off afterwards.
The problems with this game are not going to be fixed without a total rework and transformation into a totally different game, but let me go ahead and spend my time explaining to you just how extensive they are.
This might seem to be a silly thing to start with, but my god the music in this game is the blandest most boring OST I have ever heard. It's tough to even call it music, honestly. This was always my biggest problem with it. Once you realize there is no 'action' in the game and it's truly a slow, plodding, boring experience, the music begins to make sense, but by then you've already lost all hope.
If anything could start to make a dent in the playability of this game, making the music more interesting would be a big first step. Compare this to Terraria, which I consider the gold standard for indie game music. The music changes based on where you are in a planet, and it not only fits the general mood of an area, it also can help set the mood, like when you enter the Dungeon for the first time.
Crea? The bosses don't even have different music. It's the same bland overworld track you've been listening to for 3 hours straight!
Night-time/Day-time? Same music!
Underground? Hey, the music changes a little bit! Too bad it's still boring.

One of the reasons I bought this game was because of the big lauded User Interface upgrade that I saw so much about and how excited people were for it. Guess what?
...it's good. Like, the UI isn't bad at all.
But the control scheme for this game is the worst thing I have experienced barring $0.99 games being resold from 1995 on Steam. I don't even know how to explain this, but here goes.
1. You have two main 'control schemes' you must use. One is for exploration, the other is for combat.
2. Each control scheme has a sort of alternate scheme you can switch from. As an example, you can have a melee/ranged and a magic loudout for your character, then your other scheme will be for exploration with magic spells to detect ore and such.
3. So let's say you're playing with your sword and bow scheme. LMB will likely attack with the sword, and RMB will charge up and shoot your arrow. Want to switch to magic? Maybe you, like me, binded it to scroll-wheel-down. But if you want to switch to exploration mode, with your pickaxe and torches and stuff? That's a
.
4a. It gets better. The buttons you need to press change depending on what mode you're in. For example, in exploration mode, if you have a spell like the 'locate ore' spell on your hotbar in the '4' position, pressing 4 does not activate the spell. Instead, after pressing 4, you have to press RMB to activate it!
4b. But let's say you're in combat mode, with your wands in hand and spells at the ready with Fireball tagged to the 4 slot. Pressing '4' DOES cast the spell! WHAT?!
5a. Your actions against the lower hotbars also change depending on what menu you are viewing. For example, let's say you're in combat mode and there's an enemy coming. You don't have any of your inventory/character/talent windows or etc open, so if you right-click on fireball on your quick menu, it will cast Fireball.
5b. But then let's say that you DO have an inventory or talent menu open... if you don't realize this and right-click on Fireball... it will
! The enymy was already close by, now you have to frantically open up your talent menu, scroll to the fireball spell, drag it to your hotbar, close the menu, then right-click it again to cast it! Oops, you died!
6. This one is more agregious, because of how asinine it is. In Exploration Mode, left clicking removes an object or mines a tile... and right click places one. Further, when you pluck comething out of your inventory, like a crafting table, and you then right click to place it... it doesn't place it! You often have to right-click twice! God forbid you left-click instead, you'll be baffled as to why you can't place this item down.
Oh no! An enemy is attacking! You're in exploration mode underground, and you need to switch to your weapons in a hurry! What do you do? In your panic, you hit scroll-wheel-down, but alas... that switches to your alternate exploration loadout. So you hit your other button and now you're in magic mode... but oops! You forgot to place a torch somewhere so now you're in total darkness! (Unlike in Terraria, you can't hold shift for a split second to illuminate your surroundings with a torch in your inventory)
You quicklly press the other button and swap your loadout to melee since this is CQC, but you're still totally blind. Swinging wildly, you quickly die. Or you try to run blindly, fall off a ledge, and take a ridiculous amount of fall damage.
All I'm saying is that the control scheme in this game is abominable. But even all of what I've said pales in comparison to the next point...
You know what I think makes Terraria great? You can be as good as you want at the game and it's all skill based. Sure, you might only be doing one-damage to the boss with each arrow you fire, but you're still actually damaging him. In Crea, you will often be fighting enemies at a much higher level than you and not be damaging them at all. Let's dive into core gameplay.
In Crea, as you perform an activity, you gain EXP for that thing. You have Arms, magic, exploration, crafting, and gathering.
Arms is your physical attacks and such. This includes melee and ranged weapons like bows. (All right, just bows. No guns or anything cool.)
Magic is obviously stuff related to magic, mostly meaning spells.
Exploration is gained literally by walking around, and boosted by walking in areas you haven't been before, moreso in high level areas. This category also includes mobility upgrades like a double jump and sprinting.
Crafting is leveled by crafting items, researching, etc. It not only allows you to refine items better, but get better sell prices and such.
Gather is gained when you pick up items, dig in the ground, etc. It includes a few 'spells' that allow you to see ore and treasure chests and stuff, plus lots of upgrades for mining speed and etc.
So the fundamental issue with leveling, especially in Crea, is that it just flatly locks you out of everything. In Terraria, double jumps can be obtained by finding a cloud in a bottle, and you might literally luck out and find those in a surface level chest five minutes into the game. In Crea, you're guaranteed 5 hours of grinding before you gain such a simple thing.
But the real issue is what leveling and stats do to the gameplay experience. Crea has leveled zones, meaning the further you are from spawn, the stronger the enemies are, to the point of just one-shotting you. Three of your leveling traits gain you zero combat survivability. The only way to increase your actual player level is to grind in combat by attacking every single enemy you see, and it takes a LONG time.
.......

This game is great for a while with a pretty good singleplayer story and fun driving physics, but it certainly has some (at times) game-breaking/ruining flaws. Although some flaws might draw you away from this game, I would probably still suggest it. HOWEVER: The Reloaded Edition is a true waste of money; half the cars just performance versions of the previous ones, and in multiplayer, (if you can find a game) DLC is almost always disabled. Also, IF YOU WANT A DECENT MULTIPLAYER EXPERIENCE, DO NOT BUY THIS GAME!
PROS:
- Physics (while at times completely unrealistic) make this game for me. They're probably the most fun/realistic of many racing games I've played
- Singleplayer mode is quite extensive and fun, and it lets you use most cars in the game pretty regularly
- Customization might not be the best, and it has a serious flaw (as shown in cons), but it is very expansive for personalizing a car to your liking
- This game adapts to your driving style very well, for example: If you prefer drifting, you know you can overtake/attack opponents at corners very effectively, while using a more powerful car with more traction lets you overtake others on straights
CONS:
- Customization has a very annoying flaw: You cannot use the default liveries of your cars unless you're in multiplayer; in singleplayer the default livery is automatically applied to all vehicles without any confirmation from the player ... This actually ruins customization for me, especially being an owner of the Reloaded Edition and not being able to use the DLC liveries (but meh, the Reloaded Edition was under $30 on♥♥♥♥♥
- The AI in this game is the worst I've seen in any game for years; AI using drift cars act exactly as others using grip cars; each AI has no personality of its own ... In addition, the AI units don't have any apparent awareness of your positon; they commit to their actions regardless of where you are, commonly resulting in them pitting you, ramming you into the side of the wall, or braking before necessary, causing you to crash into them (it is quite obvious that this is not meant to be a feature excused by "aggressive drivers")
- The multiplayer is indeed the worst I've seen of any game; not only are there very rarely players on, and if you manage to find some, DLC is always disabled, and overall its design is terrible: flashbacks (if enabled) have clearly had 5 minutes spent in their design, the AI is even worse (driving absurdly slowly, having even less awareness of you, etc.), players are able to ram you out of the way without any effect to their progress, etc ... AGAIN: DO NOT BUY THIS GAME IF YOU WANT A DECENT MULTIPLAYER GAME!
Despite all these flaws, I would still suggest this game for its pros; it is still a fun game and decent racing game.

I've heard that BioShock 2 is a 'simple shooter', failing in comparison with original BioShock, and I've learned it to be VERY far from truth. This is a great and unique game that actually made me fall in love with Rapture. Some minor
ahead.
The level design is superb. Set ~10 years after the end of BioShock, this game features Rapture that now truly became a sunken Babylon, beautiful and forlorn, mysterious and sad. The small underwater parts are a nice touch, I've always wanted to be able to travel the ocean floor! And the part where you are seeing Rapture through the eyes of the Little Sister is also perfect and very creepy, and it adds to the story a lot.
And the story itself fits the setting perfectly, and is as interesting and rich as the BioShock's one, or even more so (it's hard to judge but BioShock2 had larger impact on me personally). There are more moral choices you make through the game (a man chooses! *wink wink*), and it helps you to immerse into the narrative, and the narrative reacts to these choices (frankly, hearing Sinclair say 'so a tin man had a heart of gold' made me tear a little). The music and voices are very good too.
Gameplay is simply the best throughout the series. You have 8 different weapons/gadgets and 11 plasmids in 8 possible slots, and you can combine some of them (trap+elemental plasmids), and you also use security devices (dear flying bots, Alexander and Diego and Sean and Thoroughfare and Diana and the others I remember each and everyone of you you were my FRIENDS thank you oh I'm gonna cry now), and there are some physical upgrades of various types, and the fully upgraded plasmids felt POWERFUL. The controls and the map demand some getting used to but are handy overall (I hated plasmid/weapon change in BioShock and, though it is perfectly reasonable, having only 2 weapons and a few physical enhancements in Infinite seemed rather restrictive, also, having NO MAP was a nightmare). Some say that guarding Little Sisters while they gather ADAM seems repetitive but I actually liked this kind of challenge - it was fun (with a right touch of nervousness) to prepare the location for the splicers attack using traps and other countermeasures.
Overall, I loved the
atmosphere of the game a lot. There are fewer outright scary moments than in BioShock, but the place itself seems... haunted. Dark, and lonely, and dying, and mutating. Babylon turning into Leviathan.
Play it.

I play this free-to-play, and here's my experience thus far:
Pros: Unrestricted deck building, unlike Magic Origins where cards could only be used in a single deck.  You build a collection, and while a deck building guide is there if you want it, you by no means have to use it.  Its pretty easy to find opponents online, and I the skill level pairings are pretty fair.  They also seem to be adding more card sets over time, with extra story mode content for each set.
Cons: Only six cards to a new pack, which makes collecting new cards very slow.  The story modes are short, and really only give you enough gold to buy a single new pack, and you can only gain coins from them once, so gaining new cards is based heavily on your ability to win online and complete the daily missions.
Overall: I absolutely recommend this game for casual players, those returning to the game after some hiatus, or people who just want to play MTG for free.  If you're looking for a new competitive medium to play in, this won't be it unless you shell out some cash.

Tembo the Badass Elephant (i love this name) is a good platformer. I enjoyed my time with it and would recommend it to anyone who likes these kind of games.
The game consists of various zones, which all have a different theme and bring some new obstacles/enemies. Tembo's moveset is the same from start to finish. Only the new environmental aspects alter the gameplay a bit. This is my biggest issue with the game, there is very little progression.
Other minor negative aspects are, that the camera is sometimes a bit too close and that certain moves are bound to the same gamepad button.
But the flow of the game compensates these problems easily.
It is possible to argue that this game is to short, but if you want to get 100% you have to spend ~10 hours, which is totally ok if you get the game with a discount.

A realistic way of looking at how survivors of war have to struggle daily to survive with little supplies and lots of conflicts and bandits. Winter tests your mettle as low temperatures increase the likelyhood of getting sick and dying while using up precious supplies as fuel for warmth. This game shows how the aftermath of war is devastating and it shows us why we should not go to war in the first place.
First Playthrough: Pavle dies looking for supplies and everyone else leaves or dies. Didn't survive the war.
Second Playthrough: Made my own story. Pavle dies again. Everyone else survives.
Third Playthrough: Made my own story without Pavle and tried out characters I hadn't played with yet. Everyone survives.
Fourth Playthrough: Made my own story and had the ultimate team: bargainer, handyman, skilled scavenger, combat specialist. Everyone lived happily ever after.
10/10 would play again.

Tembo is a fairly simple 2D mix of exploration & fast platforming but the water hose gimmick doesn't gel well with the rest of the mechanics. It feels awkward to use on the fly, definitely killing the pace a bit.
I like Tembo's concept but its execution isn't stellar. I guess it has that in common with Pulseman but Pulseman was more charming aesthetically. You'd never guess this was made by Game Freak.
On consoles the game had performance issues in spite of its simple looks. On PC (& probably PS4 Pro/XbonX) it can run smoothly. On my old gaming PC I get less stuttering than the consoles do but it's still there. Easily playable but not as smooth as a game like this should be.
Professional reviewers complained that the game forcing you to replay levels to earn enough collectibles to progress was padding. It's true that exploration isn't as interesting in a mostly linear 2D game like this. There are times when the path you need to take for total completion requires a leap of faith when there's often some similar looking spots in a level which lead to death.
Many paths also prevent you from backtracking which is definitely not ideal for a game with mandatory collectibles. It's usually obvious when this will happen but sometimes you'll get stuck in a scripted setpiece that shoots you ahead with no way to go back.
That said, finding enough collectibles to unlock the last level wasn't an issue & I don't remember being forced to replay them until I was achievement hunting. The game is quite short though so a cynic might assume the developers did intend to pad it out.
Meanwhile, if you're Achievement hunting, then a much bigger problem is grinding up to 99 lives which more than doubles the length of the game in a mindlessly repetitive way. Probably the most effective way to earn extra lives is to play the first level over & over & over which stops being fun long before the achievement is earned.
Reviewers also noted, or complained about, the game's difficulty but I don't remember it being that hard. If you've played 2D platformers from the 90s this shouldn't be anything new.
Tembo might be worth a look to platforming fans during a sale but there are several similarly priced or cheaper games with a greater amount of more consistently enjoyable content.

How would modern war look and feel like for normal people? That is the question this game is trying to answer for the players. And it does it in a quite immersive and unique fashion.
The War of Mine wants you to "write" the story for a group of citizens, which found shelter in a city at war. You are controlling their actions and are responsible for their survival. They need food, safety and warmth and how you get that is all up to you. You can give the characters their own personality by the way you play - friendly, passive, aggressive or something in between. Based on your actions, the characters will struggle with different type of issues - hunger, depression or sickness. The atmosphere you receive from all that is fantasticly emotional and feels like you are a witness of war.
Not only are there tons of ways you can play out the story for the characters, but there are also many different scenarios for each scene, which add a lot to the replay value of the game. Even if you get through the game entirely, there is nothing that stops you from starting all over and writing another story.
While the gameplay, the atmosphere and the variety are great, sometimes this game can become frustrating because of it. Since you are expecting a realistic behavior at all times, you can get caught off guard by it because it is not the case for everything. For example in reality it should be easy to kill somebody with a knife after sneaking up to him from behind. But that is not the case in this game: They just lose a bit of health, turn around and shoot you. And then you lost a character, just because you expected the game to act realistic on that action. And there is no direct save-load-system to try out such mechanics.
I still highly recommend this game for pretty much anybody. It is surely worth the couple of bucks for the unique experience (even educational-wise) it offers.

Tembo is a refreshed fine 2D action platform game. You control a war elephant to kill hostile aliens and rescue civilians of the earth. The visual effects are overall pleasant to the eyes, expect that the alien soldiers are too small to see sometimes. The level design is nice, making most of the play course very smooth and fluent, like the classic Sonic games (which were also from SEGA).
The game is not quite hard itself, but some check points are placed improperly and may require you to back-track a little for killing the enemies shortly before the check point which are not recorded after your death.
Another minor thing I want to complain about is that the water tanks automatically fill your water supply but render you vulnerable by holding you in position for about 1 second. I got hit a hanful times because of this delay, especially in the last boss fight.
Overall, Tembo offers fun 2D action game experiences for about 4 hours (just clearing all the stages, without completing all achievements) at a reasonable price. Recommended.

Problem with the game is quite serious...
1, Good graphics, textures
2. Enough cars, groups, levels

Now comming to the core issue....
AI - provides good opponents, at least with very hard difficulty, however it is absolutely not consistent. Simply, this is arcade style  and even the producers claim this is supposed to be race simmulator (not driving simmulator) it is very far from race simmulator due to the problem with AI. Even if you keep very consistent lap times (and I mean quite fast ones), you will be catched from behind (inconsistently). For instance, you are keeping the distance against your opponent from behind for couple of laps, at some point he is going to outperform even the leading car for one lap (meaning, when both of you are keeping in the middle throughout the race).
Physics - I simply do not know, rather unrealistic.....very unrealistic. Understeer is not going to be your major problem, you will rather be slippering on tarmac lubricated by high quality Yorkshire butter. Considering F1 2013 comming from the same developer, its highly incomparable.
OVERALL>

I wonder why Codemasters just can not use realism at level of F1 2013 or iRacing, use Racing simmulation features from Grid Autosport and keep graphics at this level or NFS... I have tried many different games / simmulators and it seems that it is rather difficult to get it right. I mean F1 2013  is great, however I am rather Le Mans series or GT fan, I would definately welcome F1 2013  level game / simmulator with GT /Touring /Le Mans cars and circuits. iRacing Asseto Corza, Forza and everything else would become obsolete then...
POST REVIEW>
Being a bit harsh in the previous comments I decided to go through the game once again, just to comfort myself with my opinion about the game. I should not have done it. I spent several hours playing different tracks and cars with focus on racing aspects of the game. Trying different scenarios (going the same car, the very same track with the same settings), plugging in upgrades, w/o upgrades AI was playing tricks on me all the time. I tried two identical races (same car, etc, same position on the grid), first race getting to the podium and setting decent lap times at hard and very hard level, in the second race I managed to improve by another sec. during my fastest lap of the race and improving overall time by 7 seconds during 9 lap race, however there was no podium what so ever.  In certain corners I was evidently faster than AI, AI managed to gtet me either by pushing me out or outperforming me in the straight by two seconds in the final straight. At hard and very hard level, AI is very inconsistent (performance level) and AI is programmed just to make it difficult always, no matter how much you improve from race to race. It seems that AI is set up so that you can not win realisticly, unles you block the opponent AI in every corner, focusing very hard not to be pushed out of the track.  Talking about pushing out / crashing, if AI pushes you out, you are done, if you try to push AI out (unless you hit it from behind and accelerate faster than AI), you will be out again. No mather how hard you crash opponent AI, you can not destroy it, and, eventualy be penalized. This game reminds me TOCA RACE / DTM Driver but this game was released years ago. Based on developers presentation, this is a game and not  a simmulator, and it is supposed to focus on racing simmulation  or something. No way, this game is far from a good racing simmulator / racing game. It fails in driving simmulation aspects as well as racing game aspects. It seems that developers would love to please those who want to play at first, not taking into consideration that many customers expect good simmulation (driving and racing) and those looking for fun first can adapt to simmulator (e.g. F1 2013), however, it does not work in the opposite way.  No matter how hard you try at very hard level, even if you are doing very competitive times AI always adjusts, just to make it more difficult again.
During qualifying I have noted that the game does not measure actual time and distance, at very hard level I was trying to follow the leader of qualification (after 80% of qualification session). I was keeping almost the same distance for over one lap, during that lap my SECTOR 1  lap time was 2nd (which is OK if you are not catching the leader, you stay behind),  SECTOR 2  was still OK  3rd / 4th, however, still keeping the same distance from the leader and pushing still very hard I managed to qualify 12th and the leader improved his no. 1 time. In the following lap I was still behind the leader and the situation repeated. This game does not even profide you decent driving against yourself, this is just for fun and no real driving is involved. Comapring this to DTM 3 Race driver  / TOCA DRIVER, Codemasters should just refurbish old TOCA and leave everyghing else, may be they did, however, TOCA / DTM was better in terms of driving.... it seems much better.
Another issue is qualifying, I have tried to follow an opponent (AI) and I did not have problem to follow (at very hard), in several sectors I was being more than competitive. However, when I detached from the car trying to go for a qualifying lap, Sector 1 - 2nd or 3rd no problem, Sector 2 - 5th or 6 th, last sector I dropped more than several positions (AI does it). Usually, I am pretty consistent being able to run up to 10 laps within 0. 25 sec, however even with my best lap I could hardly do middle. This would be very Ok if my performance against AI in the race would be the same ( I mean worse than AI at the same rate as in qualifying). However, there is inconsistency and it is very serious. If this was supposed to be racing game, it is definately not the case.
If you are looking for fun and you are not used to F1 2013, Asseto Corsa, Forza 4, Gran Tourismo, NFS shift 2, i Racing (even if not being copmparable and you do not have a good racing wheel (ordinary is pretty enough for Grid Autosport, buying Fanatec products or Thrustmaster T500 is waste of penny for this game), I can imagine that one can enjoy the game, however, if you love racing / driving do not go for it.... This game was developed just for business and considering the year of release it is far worse than original GRID (released 2007).  I am very dissappointed by Codemasters because F1 2013 and original GRID are really classics / top notch products.
I am ready to invest more funds (even double), however make something really standing out, I am not prepared for compromise next time.

On it's own, this game is a good game. Good cover system, solid shooting mechanics, good graphics. If you're looking for a good action shooter or a decent stealth game, I can't recommend this more.
But if you're looking for an experience akin to the previous Hitman games, you're probably going to be disappointed.
First off, the level design is linear, not sandbox. This was one of the most defining aspects of the previous Hitman games; having a big environment to explore and discover new ways to eliminate your targets. As a result of this, the elimination stages of the game don't feel as open-ended and explorable, and while there are still creative ways to take out your target, they're much easier to find and pull off.
You can't even choose your loadout before you enter a mission, not even just in the elimination stages. And I say "elimination stages" there because some of the stages don't even give you a target, and instead are just about going from point A to point B, which is disappointing in a
game. The biggest sin of the game though in my opinion is the very flawed disguise system.
Now I'll be the first to admit that Blood Money's disguise system, despite being one of my favourite games, was a bit op. Guards really didn't detect you very often, though I felt that the difficulty of obtaining those disguises slightly made up for it. I agree that IO should have nerfed disguises since Blood Money (something which I think they did perfectly in the newest installment: HITMAN), but in Absolution, if you're playing above Normal difficulty, the disguise system is brutally unfair, because
with your disguise will be able to see through it, and on Expert/Purist, it's near impossible to play properly stealthily because of this. The only way to stop that detection is with instinct, allowing you to be undetectable for a short span of time. But on Hard+, instinct depletes quick, does not regenerate and is hard to get back. Sometimes you may as well not even have a disguise. If you want to play stealthily, I cannot recommend anything above Hard difficulty, or you'll have an unfair experience. If you want to play this like an action game, be my guest and crank it up to Purist if you want a challenge.
There is some salvation in this game for Hitman fans though. The Contracts mode allows you to create your own hits and publish them online, challenging others to beat your score. This is the closest to the good ol' Hitman gameplay this game ever gets, and if you can look past Absolution's flawed disguise system then you could put dozens of hours into this mode.
Again, if you're looking for a good action shooter or an okay stealth game, go ahead and buy this. Even Hitman fans will still probably find some fun here. But if you wanted a proper follow-up to Blood Money, don't let yourself down.

The main improvement over the first Bioshock is the storyline. To me this is centred on the main characters' unbreakable bond to his 'little sister' Eleanor, for which he would do anything to find and protect. There is also a sorrow and sadness to Rapture, the underwater city the game is set in. The ruined state of the city is captured in superb detail, and the glimpses throughout the many windows of the ocean add to this atmosphere. The diaries of some of the characters help to pull you even more into this immersive world.
In Bioshock 2, the enemies were a lot more varied, in both their model and in how they could attack you. Also you could choose who lives and dies out of characters other than little sisters, giving you a greater feeling of involvement in the story and its progression.
The music in Bioshock 2 cannot be overlooked either, and is used to great effect in places to give the 'retro' feel to Rapture. The sorrowful sounding string-quartet in the background during some scenes turns them into truly breathtakingly sad moments.
Now add to all of this the gameplay, which is seamless and natural, complimenting rather than obscuring the storyline and mood of Rapture.
No crashes or corrupted save files for me.

Let me start off by saying I was a huge fan of the original GRID. It wasn't realistic, but it was fun.
So how does GRID Autosport stack up? It has its similarities to GRID but it isn't as good.
PROS
The game is fun and there is a large variety of different vehicle types to choose from. The handling is a bit slippery but it's really easy to handle even with all assists off. This allows you to go around corners at really high speeds which adds to the excitement at the expense of realism.
CONS
The game is NOT complete. The interiors are nothing but blurry pictures. Even at night, you can't see any lights inside the vehicle. What's the point of a cockpit view if you can't even see your own speedometer? The game also lacks content. Sure there are a wide range of different types of vehicles (Indy, Coupes, Touring, etc) but considering how the interiors are non-existent couldn't they have stuffed a little more in there instead of releasing an early DLC? The track selection is adequet. There are lots of famous tracks and a lot of city tracks but the number of different tracks is still relatively low. Finally, the game itself can get quite boring. The campaign is like any other campaign. You win races and you climb up into better and faster cars. The problem is, for the first several hours, you're basically driving the same car on the same tracks. This gets tedious especially since some events require you to complete the same track twice.
CONCLUSION
With games like Gran Turismo 6, Forza 5, F1 2013, and Shift 2 out, it's hard to recommend this game content-wise. The gameplay however is not lacking although it may feel dull at times. The conclusion? This game feels rushed and Codemasters should have spent more time on it.

Absolution has every key aspect of a proper Hitman game: stealth, distraction, disguises, multiple ways of neutralizing your enemies and eliminating your targets, diverse levels and an interesting story. The graphics are nice, the soundtracks are fitting (although not composed by Jesper Kyd).
The one thing I really hate is the saving system, as checkpoints only retain your inventory and mission progress. All civilians and non-target enemies are respawn, wasting the players' time and putting them in though situations. I want good old proper manual saves back, please.
There are rare glitches in challenge tracking and detection by NPCs. Despite the overwhelming number of controls, actions can be ambiguous. Point Shooting seems kind of useless, Splinter Cell did it better with Mark & Execute.
To finish this review on a positive note: the main campaign offers plenty of playtime with 20 missions (most of them divided into multiple levels), further extended by Contracts mode.

You still get spells, though, so it's kinda like having a dungeon lord anyways. This makes it easier to allocate units across your dungeon where they are needed, like at your core when being attacked.
The game also adds in the overworld, which gives you a chance to stretch your legs a bit and attack things with your minions. Balancing attacking targets with defending your dungeon gets a bit tricky at times but is easily managed.
Overall, the game is worth playing. Once you let go of the need for it to be a carbon copy of the first, it's fun and balanced and that's what's important.

I have looked and never found a game like this. I don't really know how to describe it either. It has great real-time space combat that you can micro-manage if you wish to, but the fleet AI is not useless. Three distinct races to choose from, each with a Rebellion variant, so really 6 races. The main difference in the Rebellion variants is the Titan that can be built for each as well as a few research tree exclusives. I have been playing this game since its original release in 2008 and have been happy with each new addition and upgrade. The team behind this game is amazing and constantly working on making a very unique game better and better. In Sins of a Solar Empire: Rebellion you need to build a galactic empire using military force, economic prowess, and cultural dominance. You could build the best fleet the universe has ever seen but if your planets all defect because the enemy has a more pervasive culture it won't do you much good. Equally a great culture that reduces enemy planet allegiance will not win the game for you if you don't have a fleet to take control of a system close enough to the enemy to spread that culture from.
This game has space pirates, peace treaties, beautiful graphics, amazing sound, and enough DLC to keep the learning curve going almost 10 years after release. Watch videos online, and read some strategy to get the best feel if this game is for you. It can be over whelming in many aspects if you have not played earlier, simpler versions. Like any game once you know what you are doing you will get good at it, and fairly quickly too.
Even with no campaign this game has some pretty good lore, and tons of pre-mapped scenarios which serve as a good learning curve and campaign if you just work through them one by one. Who needs cut scenes and character development when all you really need to know is that the galaxy needs a leader, and it might as well be you.

8/3/17 - Review update:  I have changed my review to a 'Yes'.  The developer rolled out a major patch yesterday that fixed 99% of the things I initially complained about below, including my frame rated jumping from sub 20 to low 30's with everything on max.  The game is now playable and enjoyable.
Ok, I really hate to leave this review, but after playing 6 hours I am forced to go negative.  I will change this review when they get some core bugs worked out.  I know this is pre-release and I am hopeful this will be fixed.  BTW, all my play time has been on one official PVE server with sub 100ms ping, usually sub 50ms.
Pro:  Game is awesome, from graphics to UI, to crafting/gathering, etc..  super solid.
Cons:
- LAG
- Disappearing resources due to lag.  You will see them and when you walk closer they disappear.
- Bug that renders you spell casting unusable.  Usually when this happens you have to unbind the spell from the weapon, un-equip the weapon and quit the game.  Sometime it takes 2 or 3 time for this to work. (If you haven't played yet, you absolutely MUST have a spell bound to a weapon or you are gonna be very crippled)
- When you do log in, it can take from 2 to 3 minutes for your base to fully appear (maybe more since my base is so
small).  Again this appears to be LAG
- Takes forever for the 'favorites' or 'history' servers list to populate.  Again probably LAG.
- LAG
So again it is with sadness that I have to go negative here, but the cons are so annoying that they are breaking the immersion.  Your mileage may vary.  If you are on the fence about the game, for now I would say no, but check back in a month and I am sure they will have it sorted out.
If you are cool with solo play, then I would recommend.  You can host your own local server, which does not suffer from the problems I mentioned above.

If you like Moba-style games and want something new to try, then take a look at Arche Blade. This game have a handful of characters for you to play as, each with their own move sets. There's no single button to cast a skill, instead you have to input the right order of commands to perform certain attacks and chain combos to deal the most damage in combat against the enemies. There are multiple modes such as capture the nodes and  free-for-all. For a free game it gives yet another reason to try it out, i definately can see myself coming back to this again and again.

ONLINE GAME PLAY-
Grid2 is pure arcade. The fastest way around a corner in the Grid2 universe is to approach the corner at full speed and throw the car in sideways, sliding all the way around (although this is different to the drift technique within the game). This technique is hard to grasp for some people who are used to real world physics resulting in hugely varied skill levels making online racing boring - no close racing.
I found if I created an online game and invited friends who did not have the same downloaded content as me (even if I didnt select race settings that use the downloaded content) my friends could not join.
I like the in game voice chat. While loading new races it would break up a little, but I guess that's to be expected.
Finding an open online game is near impossible. It is region based, so you cant join a game out side of your region. i.e. I can only join games hosted in Australia.
All of the people I race with are 30 plus, some with families. So they don't play regularly, the problem with this results in a very slow climb in XP points and cash, which allows you to modify your vehicles or buy new ones. In this respect I wish all cars were available from the get go in online mode.
CONTROLLER SETUP -
I use a Logitech G27 steering wheel and pedals controller. I had to download and install the Logitech profile software, tweak settings in there and then tweak settings within Grid2 for the controller to feel 'right'. It took a lot of mucking around and research, which was a little annoying. Once setup, it was great.
In game sometimes the controller would not respond correctly. Seemed like the calibration was lost, but a restart of the game and controller power cycle would usually fix it - annoying if you've just hosted a game and need to quit the session to reset your controller. This would happen to both me and a friend with the exact same controller.
CONCLUSION
Overall its a great game. I've had a lot of fun playing it online with friends.

This platformer from Sega shamelessly draws a lot of inspiration from the Donkey Kong Country series of games and infuses it into the Sonic franchise, but this idea of a giant animal crashing through pretty much everything obviously can't be about a rodent or member of the ape family, so an elephant will step into the role this time.
You are Tembo, a badass elephante with a deep hatred for the color purple. So naturally your handlers exploit these emotions and shower their enemies with peanuts who so conveniently wear the dark magenta relative. This motivates Tembo to rampage through their ranks and weaponry, picking up civilians who are caught in the middle of their bloody conflict.
Tembo has a plethora of moves at his disposal which are all available from the get go. These will be utilized to help navigate the levels and to reduce the influence of the men of mauve. They're not too difficult to pull off: Up, down or forward plus X does something, they do something else in mid-air and right trigger squirts water. Precision is rather important here, so using the D-Pad instead of the analog sticks will provide better control overall, but I still had problems with initiating the wrong moves at the wrong time and dying as a result. This game is certainly not immune to frustration. It is very wise to take ones' time through the game despite the itch to ceaselessly plow through an area. Stopping to smell the roses will yield a secret that might have been missed otherwise, or maybe a killing room will be a bit easier if you take the time to sidestep projectiles. Also, each section of levels has a point gate that is satiated by finding knick knacks and panty whacking bad guys. If you manage to find all of the civilians in a level, you'll get a badge. ooh...

The graphics quality doesn't disappoint. Color palettes vary per stage and the API faithfully supports 144 Hz. Crashing through objects sends out enough particles to appease and frames were never dropped on even my laptop sporting a meager 860M GPU. There are enough polygons to make me happy and wireframes are carefully hidden behind cartoony textures. The comic-book inspired text accents the fine attention to detail while animations both exaggerated and subtle strike an appropriate balance.
The audio has one major flaw. Both the music and sound effects are too quiet. Sega's audio team has made the same mistake that I noticed in Sonic Racing Transformed. Sure, you can just turn up the volume on your speakers, but if you forget that you turned the sound up and went straight to YouTube after Tembo, you might be in for a surprise. Anyway, the sound effects compliment the visual presentation very well and the orchestral score with memorable themes is exactly how video game music should be done. It is quite a reprieve from Bioshock's atonal soundtrack or Darksider's complicated score. Keep it simple. Keep it classy. Thank you Tembo.
For the bottom line, Tembo is a fine game to pick up on sale if you're bored with the rest of your collection. While it is a kickass presentation and high-quality production, it's too short to merit the $15 price tag. I beat it in 5 hours and I suck at life, so you'll probably win the day in about 4 hours. Especially for patient gamers who explore each stage and find all of the civilians as they go. Then you won't have to worry about the point gates and levels won't have to be repeated. Just try not to die, because the killing rooms can be frustrating and so can initiating the midair roll attack at the wrong time. You'll find out what I mean.

Personally, I love this game to pieces, and it's not for my love of elephants I used to have as a kid.
Tembo, The Badass Elephant is an enjoyable little Indie Platformer made by Game Freak and SEGA, two companies I have devoted a lot of my time to when I was younger. It's relatively short, being only 15 or so levels long, but each level is colorful, creative, and has unique puzzles that I enjoyed solving.
Cutscenes are played out like comic books and they are all adorable and very well made.
Tembo has a lot of different abilities, being able to charge into enemies, rocket down to the ground, and use his trunk to put out enemies that are on fire. These are only a few abilities he has, and you don't even have to unlock any new ones throughout, each and every one is given to you at the very beginning. Which I like, but also have a problem with...
Although I praised each level for its creativity, I also felt it got a little repetitive. Throughout the game it's the same thing over and over again, killing enemies, and saving prisoners that are being held captive. I wish that you were able to unlock abilities that fit in with the territory that you were in, rather than getting everything at the beginning, it's like going to a restaurant and getting everything the minute you sit down. It's appreciated, very appreciated, but you kind of want to take the time to think about what you want. Some enemies in certain levels require you to use a certain skill to defeat them (Spraying them with water, ground pounding, etc.). But I had hoped that you would encounter said enemies and wonder how you had to handle that enemy, I wish that you were offered more of a challenge with this game. Don't get me wring, it's pretty chalenging when you get to the final world, but I wish it offered MORE of a challenge, but for the reasons I just mentioned.
But the game is fantastic and I love it. I personally own the game on Steam AND on PS4 and it's worth every dollar.

The stupid drifts from GRID 2 are gone! (Yeeaah!)
This game is now closer to the good old GRID, but forget the handbrake lad, you won't be using it as you would on GRID :)
GRID Autosport's assist are VERY well done, in my opinion. The old GRID assists would allow you do "derp" around with the handbrake, allowing you to go into a corner at full speed and just go around it with a perfect powerslide.
Now Autosport's assists are an "assist". They don't give you the power to "derp" around and win, but they limit your car, in a way newer drivers would be able to feel how the game is, and drive around, but not to get good lap times.
When you get rid of those assists (don't get off ABS so soon though :) ) you'll be able to really get into Hot Lapping, and getting the drifty feel around a corner and therefore going around it faster.
ABS should be the last assist to get rid of. Why? After letting your car oversteer all it wants, getting the brakes to lock isn't a very good idea, so, get those oversteers controlled, and then you can get into the brake locking, and being your own ABS.
Without ABS you'll be able to lose speed faster on a smaller amount of space, and time, therefore improving your lap times.
Now, let's get into the game, not the driving itself.
The career, I found it a bit boring, but that's because of another factor we'll talk about later, and you won't be able to make your own livery ( :( ), but you'll be able to race with real sponsors, and choose the one that you want to race with.
Each sponsor can have a different car, but they have different rewards on XP. You won't need to buy a car, since the sponsor gives you one, or several if other vehicle is needed on the event.
Sponsors also give you different possibilities in terms of vehicle setup and parts to install to improve your car's performance.
Okay, I said the career was a bit boring because of the... Car color :( Nah, the Artificial Intelligence (A.K.A. AI).
This is where the juice gets sour.
The AI is a bit dumb, let's say. I've only raced it on very hard, but I think they act the pretty same on the other difficulties.
I've experienced ramming, pushing you out of the track (into the grass, dirt, W/E), dumb lines on corners, and other "derpy" movement.
The AI is VERY aggressive but at the same time dumb and suicidal (who knows why...).
On the first races I had I found it very hard to get past the Ravenwest guys, their cars are a bit overpowered comparing to yours, and if you don't get them at the correct time, you'll have a VERY hard time, or you'll even lose the race.
AI fails reacting to braking, even to other AI driver's braking, and it's a damn ramfest at the first corner.
Once I saw a Focus Touring car at the Hockenheimring just going straight past a hairpin, and flipping on the gravel (spooky).
So, biggest fail? AI, definitely.
About the online.
Now, here starts the fun. Racing people worldwide! Now that's amazing :)
I'm a HUGE fan of online racing, but not on Sim Racing games, GRID Autosport IS NOT A SIM, it's a sim/arcade as people would call it, and this game fits me perfectly!
They have done a really good thing, so you can point out who's a rammer, and who's going to keep their line and race with the minimum contact possible.
Followed by the online name of the player, comes a plain circle with an exclamation mark in it.
It goes from Orange to White and can have 4 colors.
Orange - Avoid this guy!
Yellow - Contact is common
Green - Contact is possible
White - Contact is avoided
You'll start with a yellow circle, but don't worry, you'll get that to green or white in no time, if you race properly :) (Not like the A.I. ^^ )
I've experienced some lags, like ramming the guy that was in front of me, but I didn't even touch him, but hopefully that's going to be fixed, also my connection isn't a big deal.
Now, on the online you can create your own "Club", and people can apply to join it.
You can create your own livery for your club, just like how it was on GRID 2 :) You can change and paint wheels as well.
But, you'll have to buy your own cars. Don't worry if you don't have it, you'll be able to race anyways, but with a car that isn't your, therefore you can't change it's setup, install parts or repair it. (We'll get there very soon :) )
When you buy your car you'll be able to level it up, and higher the level, you start unlocking setup packages, that allow you to change your car's setup. The higher the package, more freedom on setting it up. Level also unlocks parts to improve your car's performance, but everything will cost you GRID $, but not that much, a race or two can pay those :)
After a race, you'll have to repair your car, because it was worn. It's called condition, and it's measured in percentage, the higher the percentage is, the best the car will react on an impact (more durable), and better it's performance, so keep it always on the 100% :)
The online prices are very good and equilibrated, you can also buy used cars, that are cheaper, but they have more mileage, and more mileage means the more expensive the car is to repair after it being used.
I've never bought a used car, always stuck to newer ones, because on the long-run you'll save more money.

The game is aggravating.... Its designed to be a casual game.  A casual console game. You respawn with no penalty pretty much. Yet they have difficulty settings and like the original the hardest difficulty is a joke. Not in a good way.
If you die, you just respawn to the nearest respawn location. Dead guys stay dead, damage you did will still be there.
What I'm saying is there is no real acomplishment to beating areas. Especially after you die. Because it just dawns on you that throughout the game you will be able to widdle down opponents by respawning and chipping away health. Anyone can beat the game on the harderst difficulty if your cool with repsawning over and over.
What is totally unacceptable is that buttons sometimes don't register. That ice blast  you needed to stun lock that baddie as you reload sometimes doesnt register.
Switching between different ammos and spells is not fluid at all. In the middle of a fight it is really difficult to tell what spell you switched to. Sometimes you will switch to a gun and then only a few seconds of firing later realize it was set to the wrong ammo. It's really hard to keep track of how much ammo you have too. Your gun might stop, you think your reloading as you try and dodge attacks, but really what happened is you just ran out of ammo. The max ammo for guns is really low.
In short. The game is a console port. Buttons dont register sometimes. switching between guns,ammo,spells is clunky.
Its designed to be a easy casual game, but gives you the options to make it more difficult which actually only reveals how broken the combat system is and how unintuitive switching abilities are. Did I mention button presses not registering?
So if you want something with a challenge don't do it. If you want to feel really strong and good when your really not in a game, you might like it.

TL;DR - This is a mostly neutral-to-positive review. While i find it hard to reccomend at full price, i'd still do so.
Okay, first things first, what have you guys done to the name of this game? While it's safe to say the GRID series isn't nearly as closely related to the toca race driver series as it used to be, simply naming the 3rd iteration GRID Autosport sounds off to me. Having to explain to people which GRID title i'm referring to is time i could've spent talking about your title instead.
I have no idea what to say about the carreer mode at this point, so far, i'm under the impression Team Ravenwest is the hot stuff in town, and i'm not having any of it. I'm far too busy fighting it out with the track and the people right in front or behind me. Atleast they've let me play around with whatever discipline i felt like doing without forcing me to do something else for a change of pace just yet.
The handling and physics are pretty similar to GRID2, and while i miss RD:GRID's wacky instant handbrake drifts, i can sorta understand why they went with a slightly less agile approach. However, with every iteration of GRID, the CPU controlled cars seem more agressive and heavy. While i understand driving people off the track to gain the lead has always been a bit of a problem in racing games, CPU Opponents shoulden't be able to effortlessly get me into a wreck just because they don't agree with my driving line.
From a technical standpoint, there's a few graphical glitches when using AMD's CrossfireX, sometimes the grass flickers, but seeing how other games just completely fall flat in this regard i can look past it, since the performance scaling is all right. It doesn't change a whole lot, since even at 1440p, maxing out the settings leaves more than enough headroom to comfortable run this maxed out ( safe from some intel only settings, thanks). While the shaders and effects stepped up quite a bit from GRID2, the environments and roads seem left behind on most tracks, leaving you with an uninspired and uninteresting landscape at times. I have yet to see some of the tracks for other disciplines ( i have mostly seen the circuit-esque tracks at the point of writing), so take this with a grain of salt.

Lets be honest here, people who get this aren't doing it because they want to play vanilla. They're getting it because the game has show itself to be a magnificant base for countless differient sci-fi series that lack RTS games, or at the least fully space-based RTS games.
Want to play a Halo RTS that isn't crap? Get Sins of the Prophets. Want a Star Wars RTS based around space combat instead of planetary combat? You've got three or four mods to choose from. Want a Star Trek RTS? Take your pick. These are some of the most popular options, though their are a few other series that have mods for them.
That said though, the game has been showing its age, ever since launch. It's a 32-bit game, which means that large scale battles aren't happening unless you want the game to grind to a laggy halt. Even with the LAA patch. That Ironclad didn't bother to make a 64-bit version is extremely short sighted - And it's hard to say that they didn't know about the memory issues either, the same thing plagued Trinity. That issue aside though, their really isn't anything bad about the game.
I'd love to see a sequel to this game, but between the flop that was Sins of a Dark Age and the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t that Rebellion Games pulled the odds of this game getting one are slim.

Call me stupid, but I bought this game on trust.
Civ is a fantastic series, with a long and distinguished pedigree, one I thought I didn't have to worry about. I thought "It's Civ, how could they get it wrong? I've been enjoying them for years."
Oh boy!
I have played 16 hours and I've had enough. I got it on sale and I still feel ripped off.  Also it may be worth noting that a good portion of that time was Alt-Tabbed out, looking for solutions/explanations online.
Fact is, there are so many things wrong with this game.
* It's just so BLAND, and DULL, and FORGETTABLE! The Civs, the setting, the aliens, the wonders... everything!
* The tutorial has glaring omissions (leading to having to search the net for an explaination as to, for example, why my explorer unit won't enter a city to resupply his expedition module - it was because there is only room in the city for a single unit. Nice if they could have mentioned that in-game).
* In fact, the majority of things seem under-explained, the Affinities system being another good example and that's a core mechanic of the game!
* There is a corrosive fog (Miasma) which is so visually subtle that I have to rely on tooltips to tell me if its there to stop my units being damaged. It's simly not graphically clear enough.
* The local wildlife is seemingly pointless. they generally leave you alone until you start an expedition and then they flatten your unit.
* Also with the wildlife, the AI civs congratulate you for not attacking them... Sorry, I thought these Civs originated from a world that was systematically pillaged of all its natural resources to the point of the human race having to evacuate to have a future! Apparently a side effect of cryosleep is that it forcibly turns you into a conservationist! Sorry but it broke the feel of things for me, especially when the militaristic Brazilian guy started browbeating me for killing the aliens! Yeah, right! I don't remember being made a pariah for exterminating Barbarians...
* But the BIG one for me was that in a game about building your civilisation, you are penalised for actually doing so. The unfathomable Health statistic, which apparently was meant to replace Happiness from earlier games (presumably in the same way Jar Jar Binks was meant to replace Chewbacca) actually punishes you for founding new cities, even if you are specifically looking after your Civs 'Health' needs. I'm sorry... What?!
Whilst the penalties are not huge, you are left with the feeling that you are somehow doing something wrong.

One of the worst rail shooters I've ever played. It's like a "you're along for the ride" kind of experience. You can literally not do anything yourself.

Then you have these "this neighborhood is peaceful" moments where you kind of want to explore, but the game only lets you walk, not even run, so you lose interest because the game is literally slowing you down.
I will admit the hitboxes are almost solid and the AI is not too bad, but dammit. This game takes every bit of individuality from you. You want to use a particular weapon? Well too bad that you're going to run out of ammo after 10 enemies and noone drops that kind of cartidges. Better switch to a common gun the enemy troups use.
Then you decide to choose a path for yourself, but wait. Suddenly 5 enemies literally spawn in front of you, just popping into existence in your field of view and instantly start showering you with bullets. Another time the game is like "Ok this guy is in our way. Take him out." You got it. One shot one. Mission failed? What? Oh.. I was not allowed to shoot yet. I had to wait another 3 seconds for god knows what. Thanks, game.
Towards the end, this game gives you a suppressed sniper rifle. And besides the fact that none of the NPCs are actually sneaking anywhere, the scripts are really desynced. It's as if the game is expeciting you to be like "Oh. But I don't want to shoot this guy." Well why did you buy a shooter game then?
Tl;dr: This game is saying: Follow me, I'll take you by the hand. This is the experience I want you to have. And don't you dare betray my expectations and try to be creative or explorative. I'm going to punish you for that. It literally slows you down at every possible moment.
