Today, I was attempting to enjoy the fun times of playing this wonderful game, Battlerite, with a friend. I was enjoying climbing the ranked ladder and getting matched with people of equal skill and having fun-filled matches. However, every game I came across an Ashkah or a Sirius I noticed the quality of my gaming experience drastically declined. I came to the conclusion that perhaps these two characters in particular were not very well thought out. Before you stop reading and assume I am insulting you, let me explain. In a game where the arena is constantly shrinking, a character that has a knock-back on nearly every ability in their kit seems a bit extreme. I believe a simple solution to this problem would be to remove said knock-backs. Not all of them, but enough to where when the game goes on for more than 30 seconds, I don't find myself being pelted with fire to the point where I have no chance of returning to the field of battle. As for Sirius, I can tell this character was purposely mislabeled a support as an inside joke in the studio. A character that can heal, deal massive amounts of damage, debuff you, and has a 5 second stun that is not very hard to hit, hardly seems like a "support" to me. I bet everyone had a good laugh about this one, but let's be real. This guy is absolutely insane and has way too much in his kit. Every time I see one on the enemy team, I come closer to bringing myself to the sweet release of death. These two characters have little to no counter-play and are ruining what little of a game you have.
To sum it up, ♥♥♥♥ fire midget and the cancer monk. 7/10 game.

If I were to write a one-word-long review of "Homefront", I would call the whole game as one, big "Scriptfest". Seriously, it's been a while since a shooter gave me that kind of an experience. I like scripts if they are well placed in the game, in example like in "Call of Duty" franchise. What we see in "Homefront" is a bad joke - scripts that even don't allow a player to go in his own pace through the door. What's more, a player must wait untill all teammates pass (sic!) and they do it rather slowly. And it is only one of many situations in which scripts are poorly placed in the gameplay.
Scriptfest also causes massive amounts of enemies going out of scripted spots. Basically, if the game wants you to go onward, then you need to go onward, because waiting in one spot will end in shooting with legions of the enemies. Scriptfest is "supported" by many invisible walls - sometimes you can i.e. hop on one brick, sometimes not, because there is an invisible wall. Both of those elements lead to many deaths, unfortunatelly. Replaying on and on the same part of a level is very annoying, because firstly you fell because of bugs or glitches or whatever other invisible-walls-like things, but secondly you have to replay sometimes a fine amount of a stage because of badly placed checkpoints.
The worst from the things mentione above though is the randomness of enemies' spawn, or rather lack of this randomness. You know from which direction they are going to come out, you know that this or that enemy is gonna shoot in that direction. Maybe I'm wrong,  I haven't tested it more than 2-3 times (it happened mostly when this scriptfest led my character to be eliminated, lol), but I don't expect from the game I play to be something like a material ready for tests with me as a tester. I'm a customer and I want to play something that it is pleasant for me to play.
I haven't tried the multiplayer, because as I see it's dead, or at least noone played it when I wanted to enter a server and play with other players.
This game had a huge potential and have many good and interesting features, such as the general idea or weapon design. But those shiny elements start to fade if confronted to the disadvantages I wrote about earlier.

How would modern war look and feel like for normal people? That is the question this game is trying to answer for the players. And it does it in a quite immersive and unique fashion.
The War of Mine wants you to "write" the story for a group of citizens, which found shelter in a city at war. You are controlling their actions and are responsible for their survival. They need food, safety and warmth and how you get that is all up to you. You can give the characters their own personality by the way you play - friendly, passive, aggressive or something in between. Based on your actions, the characters will struggle with different type of issues - hunger, depression or sickness. The atmosphere you receive from all that is fantasticly emotional and feels like you are a witness of war.
Not only are there tons of ways you can play out the story for the characters, but there are also many different scenarios for each scene, which add a lot to the replay value of the game. Even if you get through the game entirely, there is nothing that stops you from starting all over and writing another story.
While the gameplay, the atmosphere and the variety are great, sometimes this game can become frustrating because of it. Since you are expecting a realistic behavior at all times, you can get caught off guard by it because it is not the case for everything. For example in reality it should be easy to kill somebody with a knife after sneaking up to him from behind. But that is not the case in this game: They just lose a bit of health, turn around and shoot you. And then you lost a character, just because you expected the game to act realistic on that action. And there is no direct save-load-system to try out such mechanics.
I still highly recommend this game for pretty much anybody. It is surely worth the couple of bucks for the unique experience (even educational-wise) it offers.

Jalopy.  It’s a game where you take a complete lemon of a car and take it for several road trips across Europe after the fall of the Soviet Union (correct me if I’m wrong) and all the while you take care of the vehicle and become a… road… pirate.  Kind of.
[GRAPHICS]
Graphically Jalopy isn’t some AAA title.  It’s not 2015/2016’s Need for Speed.  It’s not supposed to look like real life.  In fact, the graphics are simple, yet easy on the eyes.  It’s more of an art style than anything and the entire world of Jalopy has a painted, blocky style reminiscent of N64 games, only better.  From the look of your car, to the cities, landscapes, and people, it feels very uniform and pulls it off really rather well.  Engine parts look pretty and each and every little thing in the game has a discernible look to it.  The colors are nice and landscapes are never really bland or grey.  Think of it like driving through North Dakota – if ND were a digital landscape and if ND had hills… and trees.
[AUDIO]
Your car will constantly sound like it has a piston slap in it because some dumbass forgot to put oil in the engine and it’s going to die any second you start the car.  It will sound like a potato, but don’t worry.  Your potato will run fine if you take care of it.  Outside of the car, the world of Jalopy sounds nice.  Cars will honk and be ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s because people are dumb, but it’s the little things that make the game real.  Swapping engine parts make nice clunking sounds, and each little mechanical cling, clang, clunk, and thunk from changing tires or closing doors, slamming your hood shut after realizing you ran out of fuel halfway to Dresden brings it to life.  Doors will open with a delightful ring of a bell and it’s all very nice to hear.
[GAMEPLAY]
Jalopy at its heart is definitely an arcade driver with some car “simulation” added to it.  Your car parts will break down over time, and you need to keep a constant check on their deterioration and upkeep.  Despite the arcade driving, the realism of replacing and maintaining your car’s parts will be enough.  It’s not really in-depth but it’s just enough to keep you on the lookout for that next upgrade to your engine, battery, ignition coils, carburetor, air filter, and fuel tank.  You can also hunt down crates of goodies to sell at gas stations.  You can find wine (arguably the best thing you can find on the road), cigarettes (the next best thing), rope (?) (worthless), medicine (okay to sell but a lot of them will come in handy to sell), and other such odds and ends to make cash.
Jalopy also offers the chance to paint your car to your heart’s desire, bring illegal goods over the border, and generally drive how you want to – including driving 100+ MPH through a city just so you can find the damn Motel.  Or for ♥♥♥♥♥ ‘n giggles.  Your pick.
[OVERALL]

After careful consideration, I can't recommend this game as it stands. It has a lot of potential, but due to various bugs and imbalances it fails to live up to that potential. The system it uses to classify mission difficulties is spotty (some very high risk missions are easy, while some low risk missions are very difficult). Escort missions are extremely buggy: escorts path back and forth regularly, they have almost no armor and NPCs don't have aggro tables AFAIK, if you engage personal warp for even a moment you immediately fail the escort. Some missions have you kill another faction's ships with no warning, so it's tricky to farm faction rep when a mercenary guild mission for 15 rep might have you killing merchant guild ships and losing 30 rep with them. On top this, it's extremely grindy. Get to a system, buy modules that are ~50% stronger than the ones you entered the system with, move to the next system since all the content in that system is obsolete now. Aside from the story, it's the same missions grinded over and over. "Go here and kill these two groups of enemies" "Escort this trade prince to that station" "Take this cargo from point A to point B". Honestly, this feels like a game that someone worked long and hard on, but then 80% of the way in they decided they needed to wrap it up ASAP and filled the last 20% with hollow, paper mache content. For the first 10 hours or so it was fun, but once you realize that it's just going to be the same recycled grind over and over it leaves you with a sinking feeling of "why am I still doing this?"

In the year 2000 I remember walking into a Game shop and browsing their PC games and seeing a title called Hitman: Codename 47. I was intrigued so went to pay and as soon as I got it to the counter the guy behind the desk told me he had been playing it for days and it was brilliant.
I had never played a game like it. The atmosphere, the music and the game mechanics were incredible. Killing someone, dumping their body and then wearing their clothes just never seemed to get old. I still smile when I hear someone say ‘He’s packing!’
I stopped playing the first game when Hitman 2 came out, which I also loved. I then bought Hitman Contracts which was just a re-hash of the missions in Hitman: Codename 47 with a few added, but enjoyable all the same. I couldn’t help but feel the formula was a little tired in Hitman: Blood Money. It was still fun though although I stopped playing at mission 10. I always meant to go back to finish it, but never did.
Right from the off this game did not feel like a Hitman game to me. Firstly there is no Jesper Kyd, so basically no Hitman music. I can’t express how much this changes the atmosphere of the game. His music really made the games for me, he won a BAFTA for Best Original Music for his work on Hitman Contracts, that’s how good he was. The music in this game is poor - at least for a Hitman game.
The save system is also rubbish. In the first game Hitman: Codename 47 the missions were tough, no save points. When a mission went wrong you shoot it out or start again. Some missions took an hour or two to complete. Things were hardcore back then, I can’t believe I had the patience for that kind of play (no mistakes in 2 hours of play - or you start again). It seems like they have gone back to something like that, perhaps to make it more of a challenge but it is just annoying now particularly as the gameplay and scoring system have changed.
In the original Hitman, and every one since, you try things, experiment and see what you can get away with. You see what works, who is where and who sees you when you take out other people then just restart the mission or save point. Part of the fun of these games, if not the most of the fun, was the varied ways of taking people out and learning the timings for the best methods.
Now you get penalised for this. If someone sees you, they see you permanently, no matter how many times you reloaded since. That spotted penalty (and all the others) are taken off your score at the end! It also doesn’t help that the trespass warning only comes up once you have taken several steps into a restricted area so you get spotted before you even knew you weren’t meant to be there - 1000 points lost. Even the original Hitman wasn’t that hardcore. That throws my favourite strategy for Hitman right out of the window. I always start a mission guns blazing to see who is where, which doors I can get through, where the objectives are etc. Then I reload and test stuff out. Eventually I play through perfectly and onto the next mission. With this game I found myself finding the quickest and easiest way through the mission each time. Not the best, quirkiest or the most stealthy, just the path of least resistance. Where is the fun in that? I don’t know what the point of this idea was, that you’d intuitively know the best way of doing a mission perfectly first time? You end up not wanting to take risks and just trudging through.
The game also deviates from classic Hitman by having lots, and by that I mean most, levels where there are no targets. Your aim is to simply evade, as if you’re playing Thief, Splinter Cell or Batman. This is made tougher by the ridiculous amount of henchmen on each level. It seems lazy to me, rather than have some decent puzzles and varied ways of finishing missions, just turn up the amount of stealth needed and have 47 hide for most of the game. It was barely an assassination game for me and it really made me lose interest. I struggled to get through this game as I felt like I was just grinding to actually get to a decent kill mission and there were several points where I just took every one out to try and get to a fun part as I was bored with hiding.
On the back of all this, I really can't recommend this as a Hitman game. As a game it is OK, but if you're a Hitman fan, this is not a good Hitman game. Get it cheap, give it a playthrough and you may like it. But it seems like the days of Hitman games having mindblowing gameplay and mechanics are long gone.
I am not sure whether things have improved with the more recent Hitman game, but as the reviews for that are mixed, I am going to assume not. It is sad, but I have to say that I am done with the Hitman franchise.

Amazing game. Rebel Galaxy eschews physics for fun, and does a great job doing it. Despite the game not having the more serious elements usually found in Space combat sims like full freedom of movement, the combat mechanics are a mix of Space & Sail tactics. RG utilitzes broadsize based attacks not seen since the real pirate age.  A large variety of ships to suit any playstyle, and a healthy mix of enemy ship designs means that combat doesn't get stale quickly.
cThe game does offer Trading/Mining as a means to garner income, but while a staple of the genre, it's not really a focus of this game. Lot of missing elements make those carreer paths less enticing. Moreover, the store is combat oriented and will require you at some point to shoot something other than a rock to move forward.
FYI, Tennhausen was my favorite ship, and I was able to stick with it through the game. While it doesn't take weeks of grinding to get a Dreadnaught, I found the Stargate SG1-esq Battle cruiser equipped with neutron beams (a.k.a. Asguard weapons) to be an endless source of fun combat. Fully upgraded and in skilled hands, there isn't anything I can't kill. It doesn't melt stuff quite like a BlackGate, but it keeps everything interesting and still has enough DPS/Tank to down one.
All in all its a really fun, almost arcade like game for Space sim fans with an incredible sound track and a Western flavor. Is easily worth its full asking price, especially considering that letdown NOMANSKY was 3 times the cost for less than half the game that is Rebel Galaxy.

After waiting many weeks after the release of this game i decided to break down an throw more money into the Codemaster's pool of racing games. As many do now a days, i searched the web of pre-access user videos and reviewers to see how the in-game play would be. So before even purchasing i could tell there would be a lot of things i wouldn't like about the game, and somethings i would.  Overall this game is not worth the price it is going for, there are so many things that are off about this game or just not worth the value. If you still need a reason why you shouldn't buy it, keep reading.
I own and play many codemaster games( F1 2010-13 , Grid, Dirt 2,3) so i have a good idea of how Codemasters work SHOULD be, but it seems they decided to cut every corner possible in this game. The AI, the physics, the track design/layout, have all been half arsed in comparison to the other games they have made, specifically F1 2013 which is by far the best version to date. It's strange to even think that this game is even made by the same people unless you look real close at some of the details in this game.
My biggest gripe with this game, is the horrible attempt of the interior design of the vehicles, it's unbelievable how little f*cKs were given when they put these vehicles together. Considering games like Shift 2, forza 3-4 , which were made years ago, have superb interior and exterior design and a lot more cars! So there really isn't any reason for the excuse the designers may have.
Some may still have an issue with the driving physics including myself, but i will say it can be pretty fun (like 20 minutes fun) when sliding about and buzzing of into the distance. Plus it's not like its uncontrollable, so i'm not going to knock on that door to much. Yes the problem is that tje they drifted towards....drifting physics, allowing the car to get extremely tail happy and overly dramatic body roll (tilt and lean) is apart of normal turning style, but in some cases it's a bit much considering that even the extreme formula cars suffer from snap oversteer and understeer if you don't get it just right.
One thing that is decent about the game, is the basic tuning parameters. Even if you're a noob when it comes to vehicle tuning( unlike Forza where you have to be just shy of a mechanical engineer), you can get a sense of (hot or cold) when it comes to picking the right settings, and even if you are cold when it comes to choosing the right balance, you aren't severly punished on track, yes your times will be off but you now know why and can easily change it accordingly.
But my last issue comes down to the detail in resolution. Its simply not there, there are still many areas through out the game that are simply too pixelated or not optimized. This may be a gripe with people who have spent a lot of money on their gaming rigs and want the best, of the best of the best, and for us this is not.
It seems to me this game was probably meant to work well for people who have basic or mid range computers, so I can see where over a wider audience why it has been optimized at this level. Even maxed out on all settings my computer doesn't even break a sweat, which means there is a lot of graphical computing that is still bottled away to keep from killing users computer's. Though i've yet come across glitching issues, which some people like, to me it means not to many areas have been pushed to its maximum potential. A good example of this is Ubisoft games, they crash like hell and glitch like no other, but for the 15 minutes it plays, the quality is superb!

This game, unfortunately, just does not offer enough to keep my interest. The gameplay is slow and uninteresting, the character types are too limited and the game just feels like less of what Dungeon Keeper is. The narration is the best part about this game, not surprising as its the same narrator as The Stanley Parable. He does a great job in this as well but its not enough to hold this game together. I had frame drops as well, and I couldn't load my save after trying to reload my last play session so I had to start the campaign mission over again even though I was almost done. Luckily the campaign progress does save properly.
The good things. First, the tone is exactly what you'd want from a dungeon keeper cloan. Its amusing and it has that generic charm of good vs evil, but its entirely intentional. Second, exploring the overworld while also keeping track of your dungeon adds an interesting dynamic, unfortunatly the gameplay isn't engaging or challenging enough to make it interesting. Just keep orcs in your dungeon and you'll be fine, thats basically the strategy. The game also looks quite good, the design of the dungeon is particularly nice.
Unfortunately for me this is about where the good ends. The sound design leaves a lot to be desired, from the contact hits to the footsteps, to slapping your minions, it all sounds like it was made by a rookie sound team. The rooms aren't varied enough, the enemy and minion design isn't close to varied enough, even in the sandbox mode. I think this game could have been a lot better with more unique minion types and room types.
Overall, I think Dungeons 2 was a nice attempt at a fun Dungeon Keeper cloan, but it falls flat. Even if your a fan of the genre I wouldn't bother picking this up unless it has a serious discount

I like the idea of a spiritual successor to the Dungeon Keeper series, but this falls flat. It's a lot better than the first game, but there are still loads of problems with this:
- There is no sandbox gameplay (Skirmish mode is not sandbox, the dungeon area and top world are not generated but presets, so once you've beaten a level, you'll always beat it)
- The voice acting and writing for campaign mode falls flat. If you want to have a "cutesy comedy evil" approach to the game, that's fine, but stay away from obvious and lame jokes that fall really flat. Either go for it or not, don't half♥♥♥♥♥it.
- Having an overworld that plays completely differently (RTS style) while still having a dungeon to maintain is simply not a good split of focus. Is it a dungeon builder or not? For my two cents, I would throw away the overworld and be happy building dungeons all the way instead of bothering about the overworld.
If you want a few hours  fun here and there and the game is on sale, then okay, consider getting it - otherwise, stay clear.

I was going to start another game of Terraria when I decided that I have played that game so much that maybe a similar but fresh experience was in order. That's what I was hoping to find with Crea. Here is what I found:
The leveling system seemed like a nice addition but quickly starts to feel formulaic when you realize that you are just fighting the same few monsters with the same strategies over and over as they level up along with you... until you learn how to abuse the quake spell to kill things from a distance. This may sound like a cheap solution but it is pretty hard to fight against enemies, some of which can do scummy things like hide and shoot at you from in the walls among other things that you have to avoid while combattng the most difficult enemy in the game: THE LAG. This game lags so much that I often find myself staring at the screen waiting to regain control of my character.
In addition to the lag, this game is full of bugs and issues that should have been caught with even a minimal amount of playtesting. Sometimes I log in and am spawned in complete darkness in the ground. I defeat a dungeon only to think I'm trapped until I realize that the crystal needed to exit is hidden in a lava lake. Items randomly get deleted from my inventory. The mod system is a mess and easily breaks your world.
If this game were in early development, I could understand all the issues and I might have even looked forward to seeing how it came along but as a game that had it's full release over half a year ago, I can't recommend buying it. I guess I'll start that Terraria world after all.
